title: Tommy Robinson: Where’s the Money Gone? review – endless shocking allegations  | Television | The Guardian
description: From his claim of being ‘de-banked’ to a disturbing detail about a rape survivor’s story being used to fundraise, this film puts big questions to the co-founder of the English Defence League. But it is frustratingly hard to get answers
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: From his claim of being ‘de-banked’ to a disturbing detail about a rape survivor’s story being used to fundraise, this film puts big questions to the co-founder of the English Defence League. But it is frustratingly hard to get answers
Content: Matt Shea presenting Tommy Robinson: Where’s the Money Gone for Dispatches.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenMatt Shea presenting Tommy Robinson: Where’s the Money Gone for Dispatches.Photograph: Channel 4TV reviewTelevisionReviewTommy Robinson: Where’s the Money Gone? review – endless shocking allegationsFrom his claim of being ‘de-banked’ to a disturbing detail about a rape survivor’s story being used to fundraise, this film puts big questions to the co-founder of the English Defence League. But it is frustratingly hard to get answersJack SealeWed 9 Sep 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can’t say it would be a huge surprise if a leading figure of the British far right turned out to be a fraudster: that whole strand of politics is, after all, a con job preying on angry citizens who are daft enough to believe that immigrants, and not the rapaciously greedy super-rich, are somehow the cause of the nation’s problems. If people will fall for that, fleecing them out of their money is not a big leap.Tommy Robinson, co-founder of the English Defence League and now an influencer, independent documentary-maker and international flag-shaggers’ guru, was convicted of mortgage fraud in 2014, but what about 2026? Is he a scam artist juicing idiots for cash? Robinson, real name Stephen Christopher Yaxley-Lennon, is undeniably a talented harvester of donations from his fans, whether it’s in person at his rallies or via the internet: in a video posted online, he admits to “continually ask[ing] you, the people, to support us”, and in another he boasts of having once convinced his admirers to hand over £350,000 in the space of two weeks. If you try to avoid seeing or hearing about Robinson, the amount of money he generates may shock you.As a piece of theatre, Matt Shea’s Dispatches film is suitably foreboding, with his findings presented inside a half-lit industrial space furnished with those transparent white boards TV detectives use because they look better on camera. Shea sticks up photos and draws arrows forcefully in marker pen. The dramatic highlight is a phone call with, and then a voice note from, Robinson himself, accusing Shea of “chatting shit”.In his slightly more cogent right-of-reply statements sent to the programme-makers, Robinson’s contention is that, although he is the public face of the fundraising, the money doesn’t go to him: he works for a Portuguese company that pays him “contract fees”, and which uses donations to pay for “overheads, events, campaigns, documentaries and related work”.Shea first looks into a claim Robinson has made that he has been “de-banked” in the UK – in other words, that no British bank will let him have an account. This was the justification Robinson gave after an incident in 2024 when, following a rally in Trafalgar Square the day before, where buckets had been passed around the crowd collecting cash, he was stopped by police on his way out of the country and found to have £13,000 in the car. Shea has details of an account in the name of Stephen Lennon with Metrobank in the UK; he tests it by sending it £1; it works. Robinson’s response is that this is merely a “personal basic account … I do not have a normal current account”, and that supporter funds don’t go into it.Next, Shea turns to appeals made on behalf of needy individuals, be they the families of deceased Robinson supporters or survivors of grooming gangs. Here, the reporting gets bogged down: it seems to be true that there are multiple instances of the advertised recipients ultimately not getting the money, but Robinson’s contention that, in each example, the person either broke contact or actively rejected the donation is one Shea can’t quite defeat. Shea’s interview with a rape survivor who was involved in one of Robinson’s grooming-gang documentaries, and who makes disturbing allegations about how her story was used, is compelling – but it’s inconclusive with regard to possible fraud.Shea makes more progress when he looks into a practice that always makes fraud-hunters’ antennae twitch: the use of multiple limited companies. Shea identifies five that have at some stage been behind fundraising drives fronted by Robinson, finding that four never filed accounts and three went into liquidation owing money to HMRC. Robinson points out that he was not a director of any of them.In 2018,Robinson lost a libel casehaving failed to back up allegations he made about young Syrian refugee Jamal Hijazi. The damages Hijazi was awarded were never paid, with Robinson claiming to have no money or assets – but in order to do that, he made statements under oath about his financial arrangements that Shea thinks raise further questions. Shea cites evidence suggesting that those claims, which Robinson stands by, might not be accurate and posits this as the mistake that could ultimately bring him down.After a final allegation that a cryptocurrency wallet used to accept donations was also used to transfer funds to a gambling platform – Robinson, who during the Hijazi case told the court he had lost £100,000 gambling, issues another flat denial that supporter funds have been misappropriated – Shea departs. Has he landed an unanswerable haymaker? Not quite. Would any evidence of impropriety cause the flow of money from the faithful to dry up? Probably not. But this programme asks a lot of the right awkward questions.Tommy Robinson: Where’s the Money Gone? is on Channel 4 now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewTommy RobinsonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Mr Congeniality’ Burnham advises Badenoch to ditch the point-scoring on defence  | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Leader of the opposition rehashes last week’s questions as she comes up short against a PM who preaches consensus politics
Author: John Crace
Headline: Leader of the opposition rehashes last week’s questions as she comes up short against a PM who preaches consensus politics
Content: Burnham during PMQs on Wednesday, when he invited Kemi Badenoch to work with him.Photograph: House of Commons/PAView image in fullscreenBurnham during PMQs on Wednesday, when he invited Kemi Badenoch to work with him.Photograph: House of Commons/PAThe politics sketchPolitics‘Mr Congeniality’ Burnham advises Badenoch to ditch the point-scoring on defenceJohn CraceLeader of the opposition rehashes last week’s questions as she comes up short against a PM who preaches consensus politicsWed 9 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareThe case of the dog that didn’t bark in the night. Sometimes prime minister’s questions are as notable for the topics that the leader of the opposition doesn’t ask about as for the ones she does. So you have to assume Kemi Badenoch now realises she was on the wrong side of public opinion on the weekend’s protests and the government’s decision toimpose sanctionson Israeli illegal settlements.I guess it’s hard to be too vocal when you fundamentally agree with the rioters. And maybe she has noticed that many of her own party are a little queasy about Palestinian land being seized and people being killed. And no reaction from the US about the sanctions.Instead, Kemi chose to rehashlast week’s questions on defence. It didn’t end well then, and it didn’t end well now. Rather, it exposed Kemi’s fundamental limitations. She appears to have been blindsided by Andy Burnham’s self-invention as Mr Reasonable. The man who listens to the questions and attempts to give an honest answer. Often at great length. The man who repeatedly asks her to step back from point-scoring and invites her to work with him.Andy Burnham faces an impossible job. At least he’s got a secret weapon – Kemi BadenochRead moreThis is a problem for the Conservative leader. Not only does she have an inability to work with anyone, her whole shtick is point-scoring. She lives for division. Against Keir Starmer this didn’t seem to matter so much, but Burnham’s more open affability exposes her as an opportunist.She has no real investment in the questions she asks. They are only a means to an end. A chance to expose some weakness in the government. Kemi isn’t really bothered if people go homeless or we don’t spend 3% of GDP on defence as she is going to be OK either way. In fact she would rather the country fell apart as she has more chance of getting into Downing Street that way. Bring it on. She hadn’t gone in to politics to problem solve. Her goal was her own career development.Burnham had started the session by mentioning that Friday would mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11. A turning point in global history. Though not apparently for Kemi. Let’s try to be generous. She was only 21 at the time and even more solipsistic than she is now. So perhaps she has never heard of it. Just a little difficulty local to NYC.Either way, Kemi didn’t feel the need to add any condolences of her own to the families affected. Many of whom were British. She also missed out on her chance to congratulate Donald Trump for his efforts. In recent days, the US president has taken toreimagining himself as one of the great heroes of the terrorist attack. A man who rose from the ashes of the twin towers. Even though he wasn’t there. I still find it amazing that Trump’s fantasies are so readily indulged. No one seems that bothered by his lies. Maybe it’s the true American dream. Anyone can be whatever they want to be.You had to assume Kemi was focused on defence mainly because she couldn’t come up with anything else. So what we got was the leader of the opposition on repeat. Living in her own echo chamber. Could the government get to 3% of GDP by 2030? Andy looked vaguely surprised to have time travelled back a week and he clearly didn’t have any of the answers in his folder. A couple of times he searched in vain for something new to say, before getting thoroughly pissed off and chucking the folder on the floor.So the old answers would have to do. Read my lips. It was a bit of a cheek for the Tories to complain about defence when they had repeatedly hollowed out the budget but he would give it a go. The chancellor had been picked precisely because he could be trusted todeliver 3.5% by 2035. But the government wouldn’t be doing a trade off between national security and social security. The Tories’ plan to cut housing benefits by £4bn to fund defence were brain dead as they would only be adding to the number of homeless people for whom councils would have to provide accommodation.Burnham would not compromise on either national security or essential welfare budgets. The money would come from elsewhere. But the Tories would have to be patient and wait for both the budget and the strategic defence review. That’s if we had that long. There had just been a report thatAI might wipe out humanity inside 10 years. Run for the hills everyone.AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?Read morePerhaps Kemi could try yoga or get a massage to help her chill out in the meantime. But she was too far gone for that. The more affable, the more consensual – “we can do this together, Kemi. Honest” – Mr Congeniality became, the more Kemi looked like she was on the point of losing it. She can bear anything but kindness.Come the final question and Kemi’s immense surprise that a billionaire had chosen to seek out a tax haven – who would have believed such a thing? – Burnham had the floor to himself. Kemi had teed things up by both accusing him of being a new government and a continuation of the old one –er … make your mind up – which gave him the space to emphasise the difference between himself and Starmer.This was the moment Andy had been waiting for all morning. What he had come prepared for. If you’re going to be picky, then it was also a bit self-righteous. There again, how often does a prime minister get to be on the right side of history. His chance to say that imposing sanctions on Israeli settlements had been the moral choice. It was only right to expect higher standards of your friends than your enemies. You don’t give your mates a free pass to kill people. To back him up, it wasn’t just most of the Tory party who were with him. It wasFrance, Canada and nine other countries.There was one more thing that didn’t get a mention. That was Reform’s local difficulties with theMet widening an investigation into its party funding. This was yet another break from Starmer. Keir always used to make a point of calling out Reform and Nige and co used to love the attention. Burnham’s approach has been to freeze Reform out. To ignore them completely. And it seems to be working so far. To be ignored is a fate worse than death.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsThe politics sketchAndy BurnhamKemi BadenochDefence policyPMQsSeptember 11 2001LabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m sick of her talking about it’: 11 readers share how GLP-1s have affected their relationships | Well actually | The Guardian
description: As weight loss drugs have risen all around the world, it has reshaped users’ relationships for better and for worse
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: As weight loss drugs have risen all around the world, it has reshaped users’ relationships for better and for worse
Content: Changes can elicit mixed reactions from partners, family and friends.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChanges can elicit mixed reactions from partners, family and friends.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesWell actually‘I’m sick of her talking about it’: 11 readers share how GLP-1s have affected their relationshipsAs weight loss drugs have risen all around the world, it has reshaped users’ relationships for better and for worseMadeleine AggelerWed 9 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsGLP-1 usecontinues to rise inthe USandthe UK, people’s bodies are being reshaped – as are their relationships.“Relationships tend to develop a sense of equilibrium and predictability over time,” says Dr Lindsey Berisha, a licensed clinical psychologist who has worked with clients using GLP-1s for over 10 years. “When one partner undergoes a significant change, it can shift that equilibrium, and even positive change can create uncertainty for both partners.”Berisha says that her clients who use GLP-1s often report feeling relieved that they are no longer consumed with thoughts of food. These users often develop moreself-compassion, she says, as they realize what they previously interpreted as a failure or lack of self-control was a legitimate biological drive and food preoccupation that made life harder for them. “This shift can often be more impactful than the weight loss itself,” she says.But these changes can elicit mixed reactions from partners, family and friends, says psychologist Dr Rachel Goldman, ranging “from being supportive to feeling insecure, left behind, or worried that the relationship itself is changing”.None of these reactions mean there is a problem with the medication or the relationship, Goldman emphasizes: “The goal is to recognize those shifts, communicate about them, and find new ways to connect rather than assuming the other person knows what you’re experiencing.”Below, 11 Guardian readers share how GLP-1 use has shaped their relationships.I can’t share my experience with my unsupportive husbandMy husband is unsupportive. He’s afraid of long-term, currently unknown side-effects and likens GLP-1s toFen-phen. As a result, I don’t discuss my experience with him. This has been a life-changing drug so far, and I can’t share it with the person I’m closest with. I can’t share the wins, the way I’m amazed and thrilled with how I feel, and I certainly can’t share any concerns or worries. It’s contributed to a distance between us.I’ve struggled with obesity for my entire adult life, and my family and personal health history put me at very high risk of dying young due to complications from the disease. But my husband scoffs at characterising obesity as a chronic and recurring disease. Instead, he thinks people should just make better lifestyle choices and stop making excuses – which tells me a lot about how he views me, too.–AnonymousThe biggest impact has been on my daughterI have been on Wegovy for six months and have lost over two stone (28lb; 13kg). The biggest impact has been on my 20-year-old daughter. I didn’t tell her I was on it and she found out when one of her friends went in the fridge and spotted it. I didn’t deliberately hide it in the fridge, but I also didn’t make it easy to find. We had discussed weight, identity and GLP-1s, but I was so ashamed of going on it that I didn’t want to tell anyone.People’s bodies are changing in the age of Ozempic. How are we meant to talk about it?Read moreMy daughter felt worried, angry and jealous. Food is a huge part of our family life – when everyone is home, we cook together and eat together. What kind of signal am I giving her and her brothers? So much of my insecurity about my weight and appearance is offloaded on to an injectable pen. My husband hasn’t really said much. He’s observing me. He also wants to lose weight, but maybe not enough to intervene in that way. I’m the family guinea pig.I feel conflicted but mostly positive. I am carrying less weight. My back doesn’t hurt like it did. I can put on socks and shoes without being sore. I am more flexible. Calmer. I feel better. I care more about what I wear. I feel confident. I eat more healthily and drink less alcohol. The conflict comes in feeling like I’m cheating, like I don’t have enough willpower or strength to lose weight independently. What I need to do is own it and say, “Fuck it, I feel so much better.” But it’s not that simple.–AnonymousIt makes me feel greedy and slightly enviousMy partner takes GLP-1s. I’m glad he is losing weight and is happy in himself, though it’s hard when we go out for a meal and have something to share. It makes me feel greedy. I feel slightly envious too, which is illogical. I would like to lose weight and am doing so without GLP-1s as I have ahistory of eating disordersand was recently pregnant but sadly miscarried. Maybe my partner being healthier will help us conceive.View image in fullscreen‘I feel conflicted but mostly positive.’Photograph: Niall Carson/PAI think GLP-1s are brilliant and can really help people. My partner has struggled [with weight loss] before and this seems to be working. I am concerned about people using it who don’t need it, though. It’s complicated.–AnonymousI’m sick of her talking about nothing elseMy best friend of 15 years has recently lost three stone (42lb; 19kg) after being on a GLP-1. I am pleased for her as she seems incredibly happy. Unfortunately, she regularly talks about food and weight now. She talks at length about how much weight she has lost, the old clothes she fits into, and how good everyone says she looks. I am pleased for her but sick of her talking about nothing else.I have struggled with weight and food. I don’t want to go on a GLP-1, but I am struggling even more being surrounded by people who are on it. I don’t like how [these drugs] seem to be shifting the narrative around weight so that fatness is suddenly massively unacceptable again.–AnonymousWhat’s it got to do with anything?The truth is that [using] GLP-1s hasn’t really affected my relationships at all. My partner knows about it but forgets all the time, because it’s not changed our lives together. My friends don’t know, but they don’t know about my iron supplements either – what’s that got to do with anything?For me, my main issue is binge eating, which is a very private and isolating habit. Nobody I love saw me tear through three takeaways a night – I’d hide that, which would create a distancing sense of shame. If anything, the medication means I can be more present and open with the people I care about.It’s funny that people talk about GLP-1s being the “easy” way to lose weight. Yes! Isn’t that the point? I got my first fillings at 23 and remember telling my dentist how amazing anaesthetic is. Yes, I could get a root canal without anaesthetic, or lose weight by white-knuckling hunger pangs and miserable restrictions. Or I could use the brilliant medical invention that makes reaching my health goal feel just fine.–Anonymousskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI have pretended I don’t care about being fat all my lifeI have been on a GLP-1 for nearly two years and have kept it largely secret. Weight stigma is real. At work, people respect me more – people I don’t know have more time for me, and I get more praise than before. It’s ridiculous and so fucking rude.Generally, my friends are really pleased for me. They have seen my weight fluctuate over the years. My concern is that I am still concealing my secret. I don’t want people to think I’ve cheated. I guess there is still fat shame somewhere. I have pretended I don’t care about being fat all my life. If I told people I was on this damn drug, they would know I was lying [about not caring]. I may tell them as time goes on. Some will have guessed. It’s the wild west out here, in social terms.My partner is really happy for me. She loves that I look fire so much these days, and that is partly because I can dress well. I think she has felt insecure at times because of my glow-up. But that is only one thing. It doesn’t change our combined life, our shared ambitions and understanding.–AnonymousI love myself for the first time in a long timeAs soon as I lost 5 stone (70lb; 32kg), my husband told me he’s no longer in love with me. It totally floored me. I knew that I had become the woman I wanted to be, but I was no longer the woman who needed his validation.Millions of people are losing weight using GLP-1s. How do the drugs affect their love lives?Read moreAfter a lot of heartache, I decided to stay and fix whatever broke between us. We have been together for 32 years, married for 25; we have three children and a beautiful home. We are trying to be the best for each other and have started dating again. There is still no intimacy, but the love and respect are there.I love myself for the first time in such a long, long time. I only want the best for me.–AnonymousI feel like I’m being dishonestI have been using a GLP-1 for two years and have lost nearly ⅓ of my former body weight. Almost nobody in my life knows. I have family members and close friends who have used them and have been open about it. I really admire their ability to be so honest with everyone. I feel like I am being dishonest with people even though I don’t ever deny using them – I just don’t offer the information.I’ve started a new relationship and my partner doesn’t know. I like to think he would be with me regardless of my weight. I think the main difference in myself that led to the relationship is my confidence and my willingness to put myself out there. Maybe one day I will tell him, but not yet.– AnonymousNow I’m divorcedMy ex-wife started using them to lose weight a few years ago. After about a year, she had lost 70lb (31.8kg). I was super proud and excited for her. But then she left me for another guy and now I’m divorced.–AnonymousShe was chubby but happyThe drug not only destroyed any appetite that my wife had, but it destroyed any desire she had for anything other than sitting around watching TV. My wife used to be a little chubby, but she was happy and we had a good life. Now she says she is “skinny, ugly and hates [herself]”.–AnonymousIf he hadn’t been supportive, it would have been much harderI’ve lost 35kg (77.2 lb) on Mounjaro, which I started in December 2024. I’ve maintained my weight loss on a micro-dose for almost a year. I feel calmer, more confident, and much more inclined to initiate sex. I’ve lost my appetite for greasy, heavy foods, and probably still eat under half of what I used to. This was hard on my foodie partner, but he knew how important it was for me to achieve a healthy weight.I started exercising daily, and now my husband has joined me. Now, instead of drinking wine and eating cheese together, we go to the pool or the hot springs, and on evenings and weekends we walk. If he hadn’t been supportive and willing to join me on my health journey, it would’ve been much harder.–Sara, 42, Brunswick, UKExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyWeight-loss drugsHealthRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Britain’s Forgotten Girls review – police saying they have ‘bigger fish to fry’ than groomers will horrify you | Television | The Guardian
description: The stories of teenagers abused by gangs of men around the UK are incredibly harrowing. But it is the countless failures of the authorities that will leave you completely incensed
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The stories of teenagers abused by gangs of men around the UK are incredibly harrowing. But it is the countless failures of the authorities that will leave you completely incensed
Content: Your mind can hardly take it in … survivor Christine in Britain's Forgotten Girls.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jamie TahsinView image in fullscreenYour mind can hardly take it in … survivor Christine in Britain's Forgotten Girls.Photograph: BBC Studios/Jamie TahsinTV reviewTelevisionReviewBritain’s Forgotten Girls review – police saying they have ‘bigger fish to fry’ than groomers will horrify youThe stories of teenagers abused by gangs of men around the UK are incredibly harrowing. But it is the countless failures of the authorities that will leave you completely incensedLucy ManganWed 9 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 17.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen 13-year-old Christine first saw the “boy” who had moved from the group chat she was in into her private messages, she was shocked. “Oh my gosh,” she remembers thinking. “That’s a grown man.” When she told him how old she was, he – 23 – said it didn’t change anything. He still wanted to be with her. Lonely at school, after a move precipitated by the end of her mother’s relationship with Christine’s father, she took the apparent affection offered.The rest of the women contributing to Britain’s Forgotten Girls – a harrowing hour-long documentary about the sexual and criminal exploitation of young girls over the last 20 years by drug gangs acting with virtual impunity – have similar stories to tell. The approach by the gangs happens at 12, 13, 14. Grooming follows. Then the game is switched. Rape or sexual assault occurs (“I was so scared, so scared,” says Annie, who was 14 when “all aspect of choice just got taken away from me” by the three older boys who had befriended her) and, through threatened and actual violence – perhaps supplemented by blackmail or by the lack of anywhere else for the child to turn – continues for years thereafter. The details are few and horrifying. A number of them mention having to go to school as if nothing had happened the night after an inaugural gang-rape. Your mind can hardly take it in.“When I would misbehave,” says Christine, which seems to mean something akin to objecting to her abuse, “he would give people no rules.” Which meant they could do whatever they wanted to her. Sometimes he stayed and watched. “It just depended,” she whispers.They all talk of reporting some of their assaults to the police and being met with indifference or silence. Violet was groomed by members of the local drugs gang when she was 13. She came home one morning “in a dissociative state, really” after being raped and her parents reported it immediately to the police. Swabs found multiple people’s DNA inside her. “Hideous thing to know, to be honest.” Social workers classified hers as a case of parental neglect (“So far from the truth,” she says) and she was put into care. When she called the police for an update they told her, she says, “they had bigger fish to fry”. An anonymous female police officer from another force talks of a culture in which the girls were endlessly blamed for “putting themselves in risky situations” and otherwise causing their own downfall.The BBC says it has been told that parental neglect is a common misclassification by social workers of sexual assault involving young girls. It’s not clear whether this is because it makes for a smaller workload or because they are untrained in seeing what’s really going on – but perhaps, given that either seems like a huge dereliction of duty, it doesn’t matter.View image in fullscreenSue Berelowitz.Child advocates and experts working in the field fill in the outlines of the broader institutional failures. They speak of conspiracies of silence, of barriers thrown up when they try to broach the specific subject of girls’ sexual as well as criminal exploitation by gangs, of a pervasive unwillingness among the police, local councils, social services and others in supposed authority to entertain the idea, never mind the scale, of the problem.What we might call the first officially missed opportunity to help what was estimated to be at least 16,500 children at risk was the reaction to the national inquiry led by the then deputy children’s commissioner Sue Berelowitz. Those 2013 findings were largely lost in a welter of recriminations and accusations that the report (which found drug gang abuse cut across all demographics) underplayed the role of ethnicity. It was as if the preceding scandal about grooming gangs had used up the media and public’s allowance of sympathy and at the same time set up a popular narrative from which they didn’t want to deviate.In 2015 there was an outcry over the recruitment of children to ferry drugs across county lines. But it focused mainly on boys, who did most of the transporting, and not on the girls who were being used partly for that and partly for yet more awful things.And in 2025 there was the national audit on group-based child sexual exploitation and abuse. “The issue of girls exploited by drug gangs did not form a significant part of the report,” says Carlene Firmin from the Global Centre for Contextual Safeguarding, with quiet frustration.So we have another film documenting another set of wilful, persistent and profound failures of the system to carry out the protective duties it supposedly exists precisely to perform, another film testifying to the perception of girls and women as second-class citizens, as sirens who bring it on themselves, and another frightening look into the moral, social and cultural abyss that shows no signs of closing.Britain’s Forgotten Girls aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s top six falsehoods about 9/11 as 25th anniversary nears | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: US president often brings up al-Qaida attack that struck his home town New York City almost 25 years ago
Author: Chris Stein
Headline: US president often brings up al-Qaida attack that struck his home town New York City almost 25 years ago
Content: Donald Trump on the Ellipse near the White House on Tuesday in Washington DC.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump on the Ellipse near the White House on Tuesday in Washington DC.Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty ImagesSeptember 11 2001Trump’s top six falsehoods about 9/11 as 25th anniversary nearsUS president often brings up al-Qaida attack that struck his home town New York City almost 25 years agoChris Steinin WashingtonWed 9 Sep 2026 12.44 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpoften brings up September 11, the devastating al-Qaida attack that struck his home town New York City almost 25 years ago.His recollections of that day have repeatedly included exaggerations and falsehoods – including this week, when he shared an anecdote at a White House event commemorating the attacks that appears to be untrue.Here are some of the ways Trump has stretched the truth about September 11, beginning shortly after the attacks and continuing into his second presidential term:1.Claiming the attacks made his building the tallest in downtown New YorkNot long after the attacks, Trump said in a telephone interview with a local news anchor that the destruction of the World Trade Center – previously New York City’s tallest building – meant his 40 Wall Street property was now the tallest in downtown Manhattan.“I mean, 40 Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan. And it was actually before the World Trade Center was the tallest,” Trump claimed. “And then when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest. And now it’s the tallest.”It was not: 70 Pine Street, about a block away, held that distinction.2.Claiming he helped clean upTrump has repeatedly claimed to have assisted with the recovery from the World Trade Center’s collapse. “Everyone who helped clear the rubble, and I was there, and I watched, and I helped a little bit,” he said at a campaign stop in 2016.That comment was a rehash of one he made shortly after the attack, where he told a German broadcaster that “we’ll have a couple hundred people down here” helping with the cleanup.In 2019,PolitiFactinterviewed a New York City fire department battalion chief who did not recall Trump sending any workers to the site.3.Lying about MuslimsWhen he first campaigned for the presidency in 2016, Trump repeated a story that “thousands and thousands” of Muslim Americans “were cheering” in Jersey City, New Jersey, on the day of the attacks in 2001.Despitemanyfactchecks, no evidence has been discovered to back up this claim.4.Lying about Ilhan OmarIn September 2019, Trump retweeted a video that purported to show the Democratic congresswomanIlhan Omar, a Muslim and the first Somali American to serve in the US Congress, dancing on the anniversary of the attacks, calling her: “The new face of the Democrat Party!”CBS Newsreportedthat Omar had been dancing at an event organized by the congressional Black caucus, which was not held on September 11.5.Claiming to have predicted the attacksIn his 2000 book, The America We Deserve, Trump mentioned the al-Qaida leader Osama bin Laden as among “a bewildering series of smaller crises” faced by the US.At the time, Bin Laden was known to Americans because al-Qaida had in 1998 orchestrated the bombings of US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania.That didn’t stop Trump from in 2018 writingon Xthat the US “should have captured Osama Bin Laden long before we did”, adding: “I pointed him out in my book just BEFORE the attack on the World Trade Center.”6.Fumbling the facts on firefightersDuring a ceremony at the White House ellipse on Tuesday to honor emergency workers who responded to the attacks, Trump said that when he and a group of workers went to visit lower Manhattan shortly after the attacks, he was carried out by firefighters worried that the lower Manhattan skyscraper One Liberty Plaza – formerly known as the US Steel Building – would collapse.“Two firemen, big strong guys – and I’m not the smallest guy in the world – they grabbed me under the arm, said: ‘Got to get out of here.’ And they literally lifted me up,” the president claimed. “This is not easy to do – I’m big. They lifted me up and they started running with me. I said: ‘Fellas, I can run myself,’ but they were amazing. But they thought it was coming down. It didn’t come down.”PolitiFactnotesthat Trump has told a version of this story before, including in an interview with Fox News that aired earlier this week. It appears to be a stretch.While concerns about One Liberty Plaza’s stability did prompt the evacuation of at least one nearby building the day after the attack, there’s no evidence Trump was present, while his claim of bringing workers to the site is unsupported.Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001Donald TrumpUS politicskey takeawaysShareReuse this content

title: Call My Agent! The Movie review – the gang get back together and c’est formidable | Movies | The Guardian
description: The screwball French comedy is back as a film that actually works, thanks to putting Andréa and Noémie at the heart of chaotic events and bringing all the old faces back
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: The screwball French comedy is back as a film that actually works, thanks to putting Andréa and Noémie at the heart of chaotic events and bringing all the old faces back
Content: Hitting her stride ... Camille Cottin as Andréa in Call My Agent! The Movie.Photograph: Christophe Brachet/NetflixView image in fullscreenHitting her stride ... Camille Cottin as Andréa in Call My Agent! The Movie.Photograph: Christophe Brachet/NetflixMoviesReviewCall My Agent! The Movie review – the gang get back together and c’est formidableThe screwball French comedy is back as a film that actually works, thanks to putting Andréa and Noémie at the heart of chaotic events and bringing all the old faces backLeslie FelperinWed 9 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt last: a beloved-TV-show-to-film-spinoff that doesn’t suck! The original French series is a screwball-speed office comedy about a boutique Parisian talent agency, and was a ratings and critical success in its homeland when it started back in 2015. Its acquisition by Netflix grew the audience internationally and spawned a stable full of remakes across Europe and Asia. In the meantime, several members of the original French cast have become proper stars in their own right, especially Camille Cottin and Laure Calamy, and this sequel, set five years on, is smart to put these two at the heart of the latest instalment. And of course, there are the obligatory turns from properly famous actors playing themselves, including Laetitia Casta, Vincent Macaigne, Laurent Lafitte and some guy namedGeorge Clooney, best known these days for appearances on vaporettos in the Venice lagoon.Like many great sitcoms, this one always understood that failure, rather than success, keeps the wider narrative arc more interesting and relatable. So the last episode of the series left the gang at talent agency ASK (which stood for Agence Samuel Kerr, after the founder, who died in the first episode), dispersed to new gigs and careers; the band, in effect, broke up. Five years on, the stars have aligned to bring them all back together to work on Andréa (Cottin) and Noémie’s (Calamy) new film project, so the title Call My Agent! The Movie works on more than one level.So now, silver fox smoothie Mathias (Thibault de Montalembert) is running a small agency with his daughter Camille (Fanny Sidney) while Mathias and his secretary-lover Noémie are finally officially together. Noémie, always a natural organiser, has become a producer with her own hit TV show that looks suspiciously just like Call My Agent! Thanks to complicated (and mostly backfiring) machinations on Mathias’s part, Noémie ends up producing their former colleague Andréa’s first feature as a writer-director.Enter Casta and Macaigne as the leads of the film within the film, the latter represented by ASK alumnus Gabriel (Grégory Montel), who went off to be the token nice guy for a hateful all-business rival agency. Andréa has in the interim split up with her girlfriend and co-parent Colette (Ophélia Kolb), although that means we get a custody battle to add a bit of drama. Thankfully, everyone’s favourite comic reliefs, old salt Arlette (Liliane Rovère) and assistant turned actor Hervé (Nicolas Maury) are still in the ensemble – even if Arlette is somewhat underused until the last act.Writers Fanny Herrero, Lison Daniel and Violaine Bellet, along with director Émilie Noblet, skilfully open the tap and let the stream of industry-insider jokes flow at an even pace but make sure that the final product never feels smug, sentimental or self-congratulatory. The energy flags a tad in the midsection, but by the time Andréa’s film starts shooting and a cascade of bad luck descends on the set to wreak havoc, the comedy hits its stride again. Formidable.Call My Agent! The Movie is on Netflix from 10 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsFranceComedyGeorge ClooneyFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Spiritual leaders stress diversity of views within Jewish community and warn against inaction on settler violence
Author: Aamna Mohdin
Headline: Spiritual leaders stress diversity of views within Jewish community and warn against inaction on settler violence
Content: Construction in the Jewish settlement of Alfei Menashe on the West BankPhotograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConstruction in the Jewish settlement of Alfei Menashe on the West BankPhotograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesForeign policySenior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlementsSpiritual leaders stress diversity of views within Jewish community and warn against inaction on settler violence‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctionsAamna MohdinCommunity affairs correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 13.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProminent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end.The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis,described UK sanctionsagainst illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”.The sanctions were also condemned by the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership council.Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at riskRead moreBut other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with somebacking Miliband’s sanctions, while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further.Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of MasortiJudaism, said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”.“What is taking place today in theWest Bankis a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said.Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake ofIsraeland Judaism. We cannot turn away.”While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.”Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”.‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctions on illegal settlementsRead moreShe said: “The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’.”Wright, who had recently visited the Palestinian village Umm al-Khair, which has faced relentless attacks by Israeli settlers, called on the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.Jeremy Gordon, the rabbi of New London Synagogue, who came out in favour of Miliband’s sanctions, said: “It is wrong to argue for silence, inaction or ‘the use of carrots’ – appeasement – before the settler movement and those who support it. The playbook of these settlers is predicated on the notion that they will be appeased or ignored, and that well-meaning Jews the world over overlook their illegal and criminal actions.”Lev Taylor, rabbi of Kingston Liberal Synagogue in London, described the sanctions as a sign “the government is moving in the right direction”. He added: “Some of my Israeli members have been campaigning for sanctions exactly like this … The Judaism in which I believe repudiates this brutal occupation.”He pointed to the statements from the Israeli member of the Knesset Gilad Kariv, who said: “The blame for the European countries’ announcement of sanctions falls squarely on the shoulders of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich,[Israel] Katz, and [Gideon] Sa’ar.”There is some consternation within the Orthodox community at the suggestion British Jews are uniformly opposed to the sanctions.Miliband, the foreign secretary, announced the sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state.Jonathan Boyd, the executive director for Institute for Jewish Policy Research, explained there are no robust survey data on whether British Jews support sanctions on Israeli settlements specifically. “However, the available evidence shows that views on Israeli government policy and the conflict are quite diverse, varying by age, denomination and political outlook.“At the same time, they also show that most British Jews feel a strong emotional attachment to Israel and have become increasingly concerned about antisemitism in Britain since October 7.”Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leaders of Progressive Judaism, which represents about one-third of Jews affiliated to synagogues and estimates the same proportion of non-affiliated Jews share its values, described sanctions as a “clumsy tool” that could have unintended consequences. But they said that “measures directed at Israeli settlements are not the same as an attack on Jews. We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them.”View image in fullscreenRabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThey called on those against sanctions to offer more than statements condemning violence, adding: “Inaction is not neutral. It too is a political and moral choice.”Wittenberg, Baginsky and Levy all asserted their opposition to theBoycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and welcomed Miliband’s stance against it.Tuesday’s sanctions announcement prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.The UK foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”.Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance of this”.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyWest BankJudaismReligionIsraelPalestineEd MilibandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Met police launch inquiry into alleged overseas donations to Reform UK  | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Scotland Yard confirms it is investigating allegations broadcast by Channel 4 News after undercover sting
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Scotland Yard confirms it is investigating allegations broadcast by Channel 4 News after undercover sting
Content: Nigel Farage addressing delegates at the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham last week.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNigel Farage addressing delegates at the Reform UK party conference in Birmingham last week.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianReform UKMet police launch inquiry into alleged overseas donations to Reform UKScotland Yard confirms it is investigating allegations broadcast by Channel 4 News after undercover stingRowena MasonWhitehall editorWed 9 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe financial scandal aroundReform UKhas deepened as police expanded their investigation into allegations of illegal foreign donations and the elections watchdog said it was considering regulatory steps.Police confirmed on Wednesday they would broaden their inquiries into Reform after Channel 4 News broadcast an undercover sting by a group called Verbatim, in which a reporter posed as a foreign donor seeking to fund Reform.The Electoral Commission also said on Wednesday that it was “considering all relevant information and regulatory steps” in parallel with the police inquiry.Two of Nigel Farage’s close advisers, Dan Jukes and James Orr,resigned last weekafter footage was broadcast showing them discussing ways to get around electoral law with a reporter posing as the son of a foreign businessman.The fake US-based donor also paid for more than £30,000 of polling intended to benefit Reform that was not publicly declared. In the footage, Jukes also appeared to suggest the impermissible US donor could contribute through his UK-based son as a way to get round election law banning foreign donations.The police investigation will form part of an existing inquiry into Reform’s political funding before July 2024, including allegations that it took impermissible donations.It means the party is facing intense scrutiny on multiple fronts, with a separate parliamentary standards investigation into Farage’s gift of £5m received from an overseas donor, first revealed by the Guardian, and calls for a wider investigation into his undeclared funding from his unpaid aide, the fraudster George Cottrell.It also raises the prospect that Farage and other senior figures linked to the party could end up being interviewed by detectives, although the force stressed that no arrests had been made so far, and no one had been interviewed under caution, in relation to the latest allegations.The initial police investigation into Reform, launched in February last year, relates to allegations about £500,000 donations to Reform UK before the 2024 election from Fiona Cottrell, the mother of George Cottrell. Both have been interviewed under caution.The financial scandals overshadowed Reform’s autumn conference last week, with the party beginning to slip in some polls into second place behind Labour and opinion surveys suggesting voters are have noticed stories about the party’s funding.‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meetingRead moreAMetropolitan policespokesperson said: “Following a broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday 3 September, the Met received a number of reports relating to donations and polling involving a political party.“Detectives have assessed the information provided and determined that there are potential offences requiring investigation.“The potential offences are similar in nature to matters already under investigation by the Met’s special enquiry team relating to donations made to the same political party. As a result, these matters will form part of that ongoing investigation.“Detectives are now seeking to obtain relevant footage relating to the broadcast and are liaising with the Electoral Commission and Crown Prosecution Service as inquiries progress.”A Reform UK spokesperson said the party “denies any wrongdoing and will fully cooperate with the investigation”. It added: “We won’t be commenting further while a live investigation is under way.” Jukes and Orr have both also denied wrongdoing.In the undercover investigation, the journalists posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers.If found to have been a donation in kind and made from abroad, it would have been impermissible as it was a foreign source and was not registered with the Electoral Commission.Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”. He said: “It worked. Boom.”In footage of another meeting, Jukes appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.” Farage has since said he was not listening.At another point, Orr appeared to suggest that the fake UK-based donor and his US father might secure a meeting with Farage if he could promise a five- or six-figure sum. The meeting later took place in Clacton with Jukes over oysters and champagne.In a different clip, Orr can be heard saying of the poll funding arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”.The Guardian reported last week that the police were highly likely to launch a full investigation into the allegations.Reform initially dismissed the investigation by Verbatim as a hoax and Farage responded by reading out a legal statement in which he described it as “a little local difficulty” and an “an exercise in entrapment”.Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true” – despite Jukes having been the Reform UK leader’s very close adviser for more than decade.A spokesperson for Verbatim, which was founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, said the group would cooperate with the police investigation.The initial police investigation into Reform was launched in February last year after a referral from the Electoral Commission. Lawyers acting for George Cottrell, who lives in Montenegro, have previously said he had no comment to make. In a prior letter to the Guardian, the lawyers stated that “his mother’s donations have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”.Both George and Fiona Cottrell were previously interviewed under criminal caution by Scotland Yard detectives. They attended voluntarily.Fiona Cottrell, who lives in Worcestershire and once dated King Charles, has not responded to questions from the media about any issues involving her support for the Reform party.Lisa Smart, the Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokesperson, said: “Thanks to Channel 4’s investigation we all saw with our own eyes Farage’s true colours … we welcome the Met police’s criminal inquiry into their finances, and if proven,Nigel Farageand his cronies should face the full force of the law.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKParty fundingNigel FarageMetropolitan policenewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew and Tristan Tate denied US bail as brothers fight extradition to UK | Andrew Tate | The Guardian
description: Brothers, arrested in Miami in July on UK rape and sex trafficking charges, to remain in custody in Florida
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Brothers, arrested in Miami in July on UK rape and sex trafficking charges, to remain in custody in Florida
Content: Tristan and Andrew Tate at UFC 327 in Miami in April.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/ReutersView image in fullscreenTristan and Andrew Tate at UFC 327 in Miami in April.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/ReutersAndrew TateAndrew and Tristan Tate denied US bail as brothers fight extradition to UKBrothers, arrested in Miami in July on UK rape and sex trafficking charges, to remain in custody in FloridaAnna BettsWed 9 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 16.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US judge denied the bail request of the controversial social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate on Wednesday, ordering the brothers to remain behind bars as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom.The Tate brothers, prominent figures in the so-called “manosphere”, werearrested in Miamion 18 July after British prosecutors filed new charges against them and sought their extradition to the UK. Those charges included criminal charges of rape and sex trafficking. British prosecutorspreviously chargedthe brothers with rape, human trafficking and sexual assault. The Tates, who are dual British-US citizens, have repeatedly denied the accusations against them.The brothers have been held at the federal detention center in Miami since their arrest while they contest their extradition.Andrew Tate rented supercars to appear ‘uberwealthy’, says his lawyerRead moreIn a 30-page order issued on Wednesday, the US magistrate judge Lauren Louis wrote that the brothers “failed to meet their burden to demonstrate that they do not present a risk of flight or danger to the community, or that special circumstances warrant their release”.“Respondents have failed to demonstrate that special circumstances here warrant relief, whether their proposed special circumstances are considered singly or together,” Louis said.Louis also said the brothers “possess an exceptional capacity to flee the jurisdiction”.A lawyer for the brothers, Joesph McBride,criticizedthe ruling. “Detention first. Evidence later, maybe,” he wrote in a statement on X. “Andrew and Tristan Tate have been in federal detention since July 18 on a foreign accusation the United Kingdom has not yet been required to support with a single piece of evidence.”“Every burden in that courtroom falls on Andrew and Tristan,” he continued. “None of it falls on the government that wants Andrew and Tristan handed over. Two American citizens, on American soil, ordered to prove a negative against a case that does not yet exist on paper.”“September 16 is coming,” he said. “God bless.”According to court documents, the UK government has until 16 September to provide information supporting its extradition request and the allegations against the brothers.Explore more on these topicsAndrew TateCrimeUS crimeFloridanewsShareReuse this content

title: UK chancellor urged to remove £100k childcare ‘cliff edge’ prompting parents to cut work hours | Children | The Guardian
description: Critics say threshold pushes higher-paid staff to cut back on work and often mothers to stop working to avoid losing entitlement
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Critics say threshold pushes higher-paid staff to cut back on work and often mothers to stop working to avoid losing entitlement
Content: Families in which both parents earn less than £100,000 a year can be entitled to 30 hours a week of care, but none at all if one of them cross that threshold.Photograph: Guido Mieth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFamilies in which both parents earn less than £100,000 a year can be entitled to 30 hours a week of care, but none at all if one of them cross that threshold.Photograph: Guido Mieth/Getty ImagesChildrenUK chancellor urged to remove £100k childcare ‘cliff edge’ prompting parents to cut work hoursCritics say threshold pushes higher-paid staff to cut back on work and often mothers to stop working to avoid losing entitlementHeather StewartEconomics editorWed 9 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has been urged to fix the £100,000 childcare “cliff edge”, that means some higher-paid employees cut back on work to avoid losing their entitlement.Since the latest expansion of taxpayer-funded childcare in 2024, families with young children in which both parents earn less than £100,000 a year can be entitled to 30 hours a week of care - or none at all, if one of them cross that threshold.In a report, researchers from the Centre for Tax Reform (CenTax) said that, by the end of this parliament in 2030, the average parent crossing this “cliff edge”, will have to earn £124,000, to be no worse off after losing their free childcare.Arun Advani, director of CenTax, said: “Our analysis shows the childcare cliff edge stands to grow dramatically by the end of this parliament, but there are solutions available to the government.”The researchers find that “bunching” of incomes just below the threshold suggests that even in 2022 – the latest year for which data is available – about 1,000 families were artificially suppressing their earnings to avoid falling foul of the threshold. That could rise to almost 12,000 by the end of this parliament.The thinktank, based at Warwick University, also suggested the policy may be incentivising some mothers to drop out of work. Below the £100,000 threshold, 6% of lower-paid partners – usually the mother – are out of work; but above the threshold that rises to 9%.“The jump in non-working mothers at the point where their partner exceeds £100,000 income suggests the loss of childcare entitlement as a cause, with possible long-term consequences for those mothers’ earnings,” the report said.CenTax also criticised the fact that the threshold is based on how much parents expect to earn in the year ahead – pointing out that some families appear to be claiming it, despite eventually earning more than £100,000.It proposes several potential solutions. Restricting free childcare to 15 hours to families above the £100,000 threshold, instead of withdrawing it altogether, would cost £210m by 2030, it said.Gradually tapering away the entitlement at 28p for each £1 earned above the threshold would be revenue neutral, but less problematic for parents, it adds.Healey is set to deliver his first budget on 28 October, against a backdrop of renewed fears about higher inflation andfebrile global bond markets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnalysts believe higher than expected interest rates on the Treasury’s debt are likely to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn headroom that Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves built up against the government’s fiscal rules.In hisfirst major speechin Coventry on Monday, Healey promised to put growth at the heart of his approach; but also warned that Labour must “be honest” about the constraints on public spending in the years ahead.Since taking over as Labour leader in July, Andy Burnham has announced a VAT cut on electricity bills and capped bus fares; but Healey has also suggested the government is keen to do more to give hard-pressed consumers a “breathing space”.Explore more on these topicsChildrenChildcareJohn HealeyBudgetBudget 2026Tax and spendingBenefitsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Teachers say holidays in term can be worth more than time in school | School attendance and absence | The Guardian
description: School staff tell focus groups they believe school system in England and Wales cannot deal with attendance crisis
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: School staff tell focus groups they believe school system in England and Wales cannot deal with attendance crisis
Content: One teacher said: ‘If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school.’Photograph: redsnapper/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne teacher said: ‘If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school.’Photograph: redsnapper/AlamySchool attendance and absenceTeachers say holidays in term can be worth more than time in schoolSchool staff tell focus groups they believe school system in England and Wales cannot deal with attendance crisisAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeachers have so little belief in the importance of pupils’ full school attendance that they would take their own children on term time holidays if they could, staff have told a three-year research programme.Frontline staff do not believe the school system is set up to deal with an ongoing attendance crisis in England and Wales, where nearly one in five children are now missing at least 10% of school, according to a report based on in-depth conversations with teachers.Despite a hardline approach from schools to tackle the crisis, evidence from focus groups containing teachers from schools in low-income areas suggests many share the same scepticism as parents and pupils about theefficiency of holiday fines, according to the report by youth charityImpetusand policy and polling research firmPublic First.“If I wasn’t a teacher, I would take my daughter out of school and take her on holiday because it would be cheaper,” said one teacher.Another noted: “If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school in January.”The report comes as the children’s commissioner warned of tens of thousands of hidden Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), with analysis suggesting that an estimated 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds enrolled in colleges in England are attending less than half the time.Rachel de Souza warned that the number of Neets is almost twice as large as official figures indicate, according to a new analysis of 262 of England’s 290 college groups, which are not included in Department for Education attendance figures.‘Cheap travel is not a defence’: the parents facing court for school absences in EnglandRead more“We have a blind spot: hidden Neets slipping through the cracks,” she said. “Young people with all the negative impacts of not being in employment, education or training, but with none of the targeted interventions.”Researchers compiling the report, A Crisis of Disengagement, spoke to 62 secondary school staff from schools where more than 25% of pupils were eligible for free school meals.They spoke of the work of chasing pupils’ attendance as “relentless” and expressed the view that an occasional holiday or minor absence was less worrying than sustained disengagement.While some staff saw fines as a necessary tool, many believed they damage trust and undermine the relational work needed to support pupils and families to re-engage with school.“We’ll send a penalty notice out and then we’ve really annoyed that parent,” said one senior leader. “We’ve just broken a relationship between a family that we want to get into school.”A record 492,825 penalty notices for unauthorised absences were issued to parents in England in 2024-25, a sharp rise from pre-Covid levels. Researchers have previouslywarned of a “seismic shift” in attitudesto attendance since the pandemic, with concern that some parents no longer believe children needed to be in school full-time. The absence rate for pupils in England in 2025-26 was 6.93%, significantly above the 2018-19 pre-Covid level of 4.7%Teachers and senior leaders in schools also argued that gaps in mental health support for struggling students, unmet special educational needs and a paucity of social workers was making their jobs more difficult with schools seen as “the one-stop shop for everything”.“We’ve got children who should have specialist provision, and they’re in our building every day,” said one senior leader. “We also need external agencies such as CAMHS [Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services] and social workers to have the right capacity and not turn us down.”Staff also told researchers the most effective interventions were also the hardest – including building relationships, mentoring and home visits.“I think it takes up a lot of adult hours,” she said. “If you looked proportionally at how time was broken down, attendance is very, very time consuming.”Susannah Hardyman, CEO of Impetus, said teachers could not solve the attendance crisis alone.“We now know that not only are pupils, families and teachers unconvinced that every day in school matters, but what we are facing is a wider crisis of disengagement driven by pressures often outside the control of school staff,” she said.Explore more on these topicsSchool attendance and absenceTeachingSchoolsPrimary schoolsSecondary schoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Uganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chief | Uganda | The Guardian
description: Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’
Content: Kainerugaba’s announcement follows an official letter sent to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of King Charles which reiterated the status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.Photograph: Abubaker Lubowa/ReutersView image in fullscreenKainerugaba’s announcement follows an official letter sent to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of King Charles which reiterated the status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.Photograph: Abubaker Lubowa/ReutersUgandaUganda to withdraw from Invictus Games ‘out of respect for King Charles’, says military chiefGen Muhoozi Kainerugaba announces decision to pull out in post on X, citing tensions over ‘Harry-Meghan nonsense’Caroline DaviesWed 9 Sep 2026 14.20 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUganda is withdrawing from the Duke of Sussex’sInvictus Games, the country’s military chief has said, out of respect for King Charles amid division over the “Harry-Meghan nonsense”.Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, son of the Ugandan president, made the surprise announcement in a post on X on Wednesday.Kainerugaba wrote: “In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games. We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty’s approval.”Harry and Meghan ‘surprised’ at king’s letter reiterating they are non-working royalsRead moreThe timing of the post suggests it may be in response to an official letter to UK senior government and military officials on behalf of Charles that reiterated the Duke and Duchess of Sussex were not working royals and would not use their HRH styles.When askedby the Timesabout what had motivated the move, Kainerugaba is reported to have said: “I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period.”The news, first reported by theUganda Pulse news website, will be a blow to Harry, who two months ago stood alongside Uganda’s defence minister, Kiryowa Kiwanuka, at an Invictus Games event in London to announce that the East African nation would be the 26th country to enter the multisport event for wounded service personnel.At the time, Kiwanuka praised the Ugandan president, Yoweri Museveni for his “visionary leadership” and Kainerugaba, a Sandhurst graduate, for “championing our team’s entry”, adding that their support “marks a new chapter for our servicemen and women”.The Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja confirmed to the BBC: “Gen Kainerugaba decides whether or not the UPDF [Uganda People’s Defence Force] participates in the Invictus Games. What you saw is his stated position. If it changes, he will let the world know.”The decision to withdraw may be an unintended consequence of the official letter, issued on Monday by the head of the royal household, the lord chamberlain, Richard Benyon, at Charles’s behest, clarifying the position of the Sussexes after their return to the UK two weeks ago.The letter directed that the couple were “no longer working members of the royal family”, that their charitable work “is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity” and “their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests”.Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in 2024 and is widely seen as his 81-year-old father’s successor to the presidency. He has made several provocative posts on X, including threats to invade neighbouring Kenya, demands that Jay-Z hand over his wife, Beyoncé, so he could marry her, and threatsagainst Bobi Wine, Museveni’s principal political rival.The Invictus Games and representatives for the Duke of Sussex have been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsUgandaInvictus GamesPrince HarryMeghan, the Duchess of SussexAfricaMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: Indonesian foragers may have sucked on mind-altering nuts 25,000 years ago, research finds | Science | The Guardian
description: Analysis of two skeletons reveals tooth wear and traces of psychoactive substance in what may be earliest known evidence for human drug taking
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Analysis of two skeletons reveals tooth wear and traces of psychoactive substance in what may be earliest known evidence for human drug taking
Content: The researchers examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers.Photograph: Pubu Alar_sulsel/View image in fullscreenThe researchers examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers.Photograph: Pubu Alar_sulsel/ScienceIndonesian foragers may have sucked on mind-altering nuts 25,000 years ago, research findsAnalysis of two skeletons reveals tooth wear and traces of psychoactive substance in what may be earliest known evidence for human drug takingIan SampleScience editorWed 9 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat may be the earliest known evidence for human drug taking has been traced to ancient Indonesian foragers who sucked on mind-altering nuts as long as 25,000 years ago.Analysis of two exceptionally rare skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi revealed dramatic tooth wear and traces of a psychoactive substance in the individuals’ remaining teeth, suggesting they routinely sucked on hard, abrasive betel nuts.Although little known in western societies, betel nuts are the world’s fourth most widely used psychoactive substance after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, with an estimated tenth of the global population chewing the seeds.View image in fullscreenBetel nuts.“We’ve found evidence for how this very common drug use habit, which is found throughout a lot of the Asia-Pacific region today, might have evolved,” said Prof Adam Brumm at Griffith University’s AustralianResearchCentre for Human Evolution in Brisbane.The work began when the team examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers unearthed at two different sites on the island. One was dated to about 7,000 years old, the other more ancient at 16,000 to 25,000 to years old.Writing inScience Advances, the researchers describe how both adults had deep, rounded grooves in their teeth. Some went so deep they would have exposed the dental pulp. “I was thinking, what the hell were these people doing? It’s like someone had a drill head shaped like a gobstopper and wore away the inner part of the tooth,” said Brumm.Betel nuts are actually the seeds of theAreca catechupalm, but are misnamed because they are often wrapped in betel vine leaves for chewing. Today, the nuts are typically chewed after being mixed with slaked lime made by grinding burnt shells to form a “quid”.View image in fullscreenInferred positions of the nuts based on the dental wear patterns.Photograph:Brumm suspected the bizarre tooth wear was caused by the foragers holding hard, round and abrasive objects in their mouth, but what sort of object? “Imagine you kept a stone in your mouth and you moved it from one part of your mouth to another, and if you did that day after day, hour after hour. Eventually it would wear down your extremely hard dental tissue to form these grooves,” he said.The team wondered whether the grooves were the result of foragers sucking on betel nuts before people realised that mixing the nuts with slaked lime helped release more of the psychoactive drug and intensify the “high”.To test the hunch, the scientists soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva and found that it soon contained enough of the psychoactive compound arecoline to induce a high, albeit a milder one than when the nut is chewed. Analysis of the foragers’ teeth found traces of arecoline in the tissues.“I’ve sucked on a nut as an experiment and it’s a really bitter, astringent taste. It makes your mouth go numb and I think that’s what they were interested in,” Brumm said.“This might have been a traditional remedy for toothache, but if they did it for too long, sucking on the nut wore down their teeth so badly that it actually created much worse dental pain in the long term.
