These individuals were seemingly caught in a self-perpetuating cycle where they were continually sucking on the nuts to treat the tooth pain caused by this nut-sucking habit.”While humans probably began using mind-altering plants as soon as they encountered them, the oldest traditions of psychoactive drug use are thought to have arisen about 13,000 years ago with fermented drinks such as barley beer.Dr Elisa Guerra-Doce, an associate professor in European prehistory at the University of Valladolid in Spain, said the study provided “direct evidence of the antiquity of human drug use”.“These findings not only represent the earliest known evidence to date of the use of psychoactive plants anywhere in the world, but also demonstrate that the consumption of Areca nuts is a millennia-old tradition dating back to prehistoric times,” she added.Explore more on these topicsSciencePalaeontologyDrugsIndonesiaAsia PacificResearchHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Courage and contradictions’: what Gloria Steinem meant to feminist writers from around the world  | Rebecca Solnit, Rokhaya Diallo, Mona Eltahawy, V (formerly Eve Ensler), Julia Gillard, Jennifer Robinson, Elif Shafak and Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: Our global panel of writers reflect on the great legacy of the American feminist and civil rights activist, who died last week aged 92
Author: Rebecca Solnit
Headline: Our global panel of writers reflect on the great legacy of the American feminist and civil rights activist, who died last week aged 92
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe panelGloria Steinem‘Courage and contradictions’: what Gloria Steinem meant to feminist writers from around the worldRebecca Solnit,Rokhaya Diallo,Mona Eltahawy,V (formerly Eve Ensler),Julia Gillard,Jennifer Robinson,Elif ShafakandRhiannon Lucy CosslettOur global panel of writers reflect on the great legacy of the American feminist and civil rights activist, who died last week aged 92Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTShareI’m grateful for the role Gloria Steinem played from the 70s to the 90sRebecca SolnitGuardian US columnist and authorAs far as I can tell, the US women’s movement was mostly clustered in coastal cities and university towns untilMs magazine, which Gloria Steinem cofounded and for many years co-managed, made it national. My mother in suburban California was an early subscriber and I was a tween who voraciously devoured every issue. I think it played a role in stiffening her resolve and her sense of her own rights, which led to her leaving my violent father.Some of the hot takes I’m seeing now on Steinem, and the women’s movement she was at the heart of, act as reminders that a lot of people have no idea of what women’s lives were like before second-wave feminism. Of how women were routinely described as weaker, less intelligent, less rational and less objective than men, and therefore less believable, less qualified to work, testify, participate. No understanding of how utterly disempowered and excluded women were in both law and society, how women were rendered radically unequal economically in so many ways, including exclusion from professions and education and without rights to equal pay, to be free from workplace sexual harassment and discrimination. No memory of how marriage was a relationship of radical inequality in which a woman surrendered many rights and her identity to her husband, not even reserving the right to say no to sex until pressure from feminists made marital rape a crime in a growing number of American states in the 1970s and 1980s.We now face a huge backlash, maybe even huger than the backlash we’ve always faced, but I believe feminism is just getting going in reversing not centuries but millennia of patriarchy, and I’m grateful for the role Gloria Steinem played in giving those decades of the 1970s to 1990s the transformative momentum that has made my life so much better, in so many ways, than my mother’s, let alone my grandmother’s.Her relationships with women of colour informed her feminist activismRokhaya DialloFrench journalist, writer, film-maker, activist and Guardian Europe columnistGloria Steinem understood early on that the feminist struggle would be fought through the media as well as campaigning, and inspired generations of journalists, myself included. As co-founder of Ms magazine, the first in the US run entirely by women, she strengthened the connection between journalism and activism.View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem and the late author and activist Dorothy Pitman Hughes in 2014.Photograph: Scott Roth/Invision/APSteinem’s feminism was more attentive to race than that of many of her white contemporaries in the “second wave”. Her first explicitly feminist essay, After Black Power, Women’s Liberation, displays a keen understanding of the need to connect feminist struggles with other movements for justice. She wrote about poor women and mothers, and imagined an alliance between radical feminists, middle-class women and “poor women of all colors”, although some of the dated terminology may now appear offensive. Her relationships with prominent women of colour – including Dorothy Pitman Hughes,Shirley ChisholmandWilma Mankiller– informed every aspect of her work. As sheacknowledged: “Personally, I learned feminism disproportionately from Black women.” In 1971, she served as treasurer of the fund for the legal defence of Angela Davis, the Black feminist philosopher unjustly prosecuted for murder who faced the death penalty.Steinem leveraged her privilege as an educated white woman with access to elite media circles, but could not escape the dynamics of public life that made hers “the face of feminism” within a diverse and collective movement: the names of the women of colour who stood alongside her have not left the same imprint on public memory.While I admired Steinem immensely, I regretted that her feminism remained so closely aligned with the Democratic party. This led her todefend Bill Clintonin 1998 and minimise Monica Lewinsky’s allegations, before acknowledging this failing two decades later. Her support forHillary Clintonalso exposed the limits of a feminism centred on representation.But at a time of rising femonationalism (the use of women’s rights to advance nationalist and racist agendas), Steinem’s legacy reminds us of the urgent need for a feminism rooted in international solidarity and committed to fighting every form of oppression.Gloria’s kindness and empathy were like steroids that strengthened usMona EltahawyEgyptian-American journalist and author of theFEMINIST GIANTnewsletterA couple of days after Egyptian riot policeassaulted meduring a protest near Tahrir Square in November 2011, Gloria Steinem emailed me with news of what she called my “girl gang”: feminists and activists from around the world who had been writing to each other to find the best ways to support me. “No matter where you are, please tell me if there is anything at all I can do to make your life easier – or our outrage more effective, with friendship and empathy from your Girl Gang!” she signed off.I had met Gloria just once, a month before, when the Hammer museum in Los Angeles hosted us for a feminist conversation in front of a live audience. She was a gracious interlocutor who treated me like a peer. We met several times since that conversation, each a reminder of the power of the feminist girl gang.I was among a girl gang of 25 that she invited to send her questions for anInterview magazine column. My question was about us both being childfree by choice. “I would put the emphasis on ‘free’. It has increased my freedom,” she replied.I am a feminist who will tell you to fuck off to your face. Kindness and empathy did not make it to my second book, The Seven Necessary Sins for Women and Girls. Gloria blurbed it thus: “Mona Eltahawy’s Necessary Sins is shocking, brave, gloriously unfeminine, and right on time … Reading it will free you, and acting on it will free us all.”My “sins” – anger, profanity, violence etc – are necessary in our fight against patriarchy. Gloria’s kindness and empathy were like steroids that strengthened us for that fight: batons she passed across feminist generations and borders – and especially vital when that fight against patriarchy leaves us bruised, with broken limbs, and broke. She lent me $1,000 during a particularly tight financial time and I was mortified at how long it took me to repay her. She was unfazed.Farewell, Gloria. To quote your 2011 email: “you should see the … loving outpouring from your girl gang from around the world!”She’d want us to remember that the backlash against women is a sign of our powerV (formerly Eve Ensler)American playwright and activistI will always be grateful to Gloria for her early support of my playThe Vagina Monologues. After she came to see me perform in a little theatre way downtown, she agreed to write the foreword to the book. She showed up decking her red boa at every event we held early on to birth theV-Day movementto end violence against women, gender-expansive people and girls – now 30 years old – into the world. The Vagina Monologues was very outside the mainstream at the time and her support of it helped other people be brave.View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem, Glenn Close and V at a V-Day benefit performance of The Vagina Monologues in New York, 2001.Photograph: Darla Khazei/Associated PressShe did that same thing for so many women, catalysing their dreams, their visions, their advocacy, their emerging non-profits by lending her support, her strategy, her kindness.It’s not lost on me that Gloria left this world in the midst of one of the greatest periods of attacks on women’s rights – the destruction of maternal health care; women being forced out of the labour market in the hundreds of thousands, especially Black women; the siege on reproductive rights; rape academies emerging online; the Epstein files still not being prosecuted; and having a convicted felon as president who has been found liable in a civil court for sexual abuse. But if Gloria had anything, she had stamina and infinite hope, and she would want us to remember that the backlash is an indication of our victories and our power.Now we need to go beyond where we’ve been, to new imaginings in order to fight off the racist, fascist, capitalist patriarchy that is actively working to kill our world.It is impossible to write the history of the women’s movement without herJulia GillardFormer Australian prime minister and former leader of the Australian Labor party. She was the first woman to hold either positionI am deeply saddened by the passing of feminist icon Gloria Steinem. Gloria was at the vanguard of the women’s rights movement as a political activist, journalist and editor, writer and thinker for more than 60 years. It is impossible to write the history of the women’s movement without her name being at the centre of the narrative. Indeed, her name is synonymous with feminism.I felt incredibly fortunate to interview Gloria in 2022 forA Podcast of One’s Own. Then 88, Gloria was as passionate as ever about achieving equality and advocating for others. I greatly admired her steadfast commitment to the cause, even when progress was not linear, and backwards steps were taken – especially for reproductive freedom in the United States.Gloria’s dedication to equality and empowerment for women everywhere, and from all walks of life, will continue to endure around the world. Her legacy is now ours to take forward. My heartfelt condolences go out to Gloria’s family and friends.She was the truth-teller who inspired my grandmother, my mother – and meJennifer RobinsonAustralian barrister working at at Doughty Street Chambers, and co-author ofHow Many More Women?When I heard the news Gloria Steinem had died, everything stopped.I had just walked out of the Sydney opening of our documentary,Silenced, which is about the legal backlash against #MeToo and how the law silences women from speaking out about abuse. Women were walking out of the cinema crying and angry about how far we still have to go – and activated about what we need to do to change it.And then we were hit with the news that we had lost Steinem. The news spread by hushed whispers through in the crowd in front of me. The grief was palpable.Steinem, the silence-breaker. The truth-teller who had inspired millions of women around the world to find our voices and use them. The woman who inspired my grandmother, my mother – and me. My grandmother is a survivor of domestic violence and later worked in the women’s refuge movement to make it easier for the women and children who came after her. She is in our film because her work inspired mine. I grew up hearing my grandmother quote Steinem and, whenever I speak – including the other night in Sydney – her words and her ideas can be found.It hit me hard. I had to take a moment. I wanted to cry. But then I looked around at the sea of women in front of me – victim-survivors, frontline services workers, lawyers from women’s legal services, and engaged and concerned community members, inspired to help create the change we need for women.It was beautiful. And it made me think of one of my favourite Steinem quotes: “People are always asking me, ‘Who will you pass the torch to?’ The question makes me angry. There is no one torch – there are many torches – and I’m using my torch to light other torches.”In her lifetime, she lit so many torches – all over the world – including in me and among the women gathered with me in Sydney the other night. What an incredible legacy.As she said, “The future depends entirely on what each of us does every day; a movement of people is only people moving.” The best way to celebrate and honour her legacy is to continue it – and keep moving.She passionately wanted to connect local, national and global feminismsElif ShafakBritish-Turkish novelist and political scientistIn my mid-20s I left Istanbul to become a fellow in women’s studies at Mount Holyoke College in Massachusetts. I arrived without knowing a single soul, entranced by the splendour of autumnal colours in Boston. The libraries there hold one of the best archives in the US on the history of feminist theory and practice, and, as winter descended, I burrowed myself into reading Audre Lorde, Maya Angelou, Doris Lessing, Toni Morrison … and that was when I properly discovered Gloria Steinem.Steinem had an unconventional, nomadic upbringing, and until she was 11 she had not spent a full year at school. In the absence of stable education, it was books – including Louisa May Alcott’s Little Women – that helped and guided her. “I was rescued by librarians,” she would explain later.View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem in her New York City flat, November 1990.Photograph: Barbara Alper/Getty ImagesI was struck by the courage she had shown in exposing the reality of the shiny world of Playboy bunny clubs, and the magazine she co-founded, Ms, never shied from covering difficult issues, such as sex trafficking and sexual harassment. But it was her books that stayed with me: Moving Beyond Words, Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, Marilyn: Norma Jean …Steinem believed that any meaningful change had to grow like a tree. From the bottom up. She not only founded women’s organisations and became a leading voice in second-wave feminism, she also saw the women’s movement as her chosen family. She said she had learned feminism from Black women. For her, race and gender were inextricably connected: “It is not possible to be a feminist without being anti-racist.” She was equally cognisant of class barriers. She passionately wanted to connect local, national and global feminisms.When people asked her how she managed to remain optimistic, she said it was because she did not stay in one place. Just like in her childhood, she kept travelling. “Perhaps the most revolutionary act for a women will be a self-willed journey – and to be welcomed when she comes home.”She was not perfect and not always right, and we also need to be able to talk about that – in a calm and nuanced way. Her contribution to generations of civil rights and women’s rights has been immense and genuine.Gloria Steinemwould have made a fascinating character in a novel – with her resilience, her courage, her determination, her trailblazing and her contradictions.She would not give up the fight for women’s liberation, and nor must weRhiannon Lucy CosslettBritish Guardian columnistI first encountered Gloria Steinem in much the same way as I met her feminist contemporaries – on my mother’s bookshelves, which I ransacked. Although as a teenage girl in the late 1990s I had very much swallowed the post-feminist narrative (much to my mother’s disappointment) that the women’s movement had accomplished all it needed to, I still read every book for adult women that I could get my hands on. I credit Steinem’sundercover Playboy Bunny piece– which was extracted in one of the books – with the fact that I started to question the raunch culture that was all around me (and never bought a Playboy T-shirt). That is the power of good journalism – it echoes through the decades.I found Steinem again at university, in the aftermath of a violent attack that galvanised me, as it can so many women, and have been a great admirer ever since. When I was in my 20s, setting up my own feminist magazine – the Vagenda – her work was a big influence. Her vocal and inclusive activism, her willingness to reflect on her missteps, her sense of humour and her refusal to give up the fight even when times were very dark indeed have all been an inspiration.Her book dedication to the British doctor who granted her an abortion at the age of 22 despite it not then being legal – in which she writes “I’ve done the best that I could with my life”, as she had promised him he would – struck a chord with so many for a reason: it’s a profoundly moving testament to the freedom that access to abortion grants a woman, even more so in the aftermath of the repeal of Roe v Wade. I find it so very sad that Steinem leaves a world where reproductive rights remain under severe threat. She devoted her life to this and other crucial questions of women’s liberation. She would not give up the fight, and nor must we. Onwards, in her honour.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsGloria SteinemThe panelFeminismJournalism booksRebecca SolnitV (formerly Eve Ensler)Julia GillardElif ShafakcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Baggage reclaim was pandemonium’: passengers hit by airport IT chaos in UK recount their ordeals | Airline industry | The Guardian
description: From hours stuck on planes awaiting takeoff, to sleeping the night on the floor at Heathrow. Here are some travellers’ experiences
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: From hours stuck on planes awaiting takeoff, to sleeping the night on the floor at Heathrow. Here are some travellers’ experiences
Content: Tens of thousands of passengers at airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick, faced travel chaos after planes could not take off safely.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenTens of thousands of passengers at airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick, faced travel chaos after planes could not take off safely.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAAirline industry‘Baggage reclaim was pandemonium’: passengers hit by airport IT chaos in UK recount their ordealsFrom hours stuck on planes awaiting takeoff, to sleeping the night on the floor at Heathrow. Here are some travellers’ experiencesAlfie PackhamandJane ClintonWed 9 Sep 2026 14.31 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 2,000 flights have been cancelled after an air traffic control system failure that has thrown airports across the UK into chaos. Nats, the air traffic control provider, fixed the problem within hours on Tuesday, but hundreds of thousands of passengers were hit byfurther delays and cancellations on Wednesday.Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, has been given a week to report back on the reasons for the technical failure.People affected by the disruption talked about their frustration during the two days of chaos – from hours spent stuck on planes waiting to take off, to spending the night sleeping on the floor ofHeathrow airport. Here are some of their experiences:‘People were sleeping on every spare inch of flooring’Daniel Garrick, 32, a software engineer, was scheduled to leave Heathrow on a flight to Austin, Texas, on Tuesday. After waiting for seven hours on the asphalt, “we were released from the plane only to find Heathrow in absolute chaos”, he says.View image in fullscreenLuggage in Heathrow’s Terminal 5 on Tuesday.“My baggage was lost, and British Airways employees were nowhere to be found. People were sleeping on every spare inch of flooring, in arrivals and at security.”Baggage reclaim was “pandemonium”, he says. “All the screens just said it was closed. You couldn’t tell where your baggage was supposed to be.“I found some other Texans going back to Austin on our flight. Someone had an air tag in their luggage and we figured out that the bags were still on the plane. Eventually, there was some announcement where we were told they were not going to finish getting all the bags off the planes tonight, so we’re just going to have to leave.” At the time of writing, Garrick still had not retrieved his case with a week’s worth of clothes.Garrick’s airline, British Airways, sent a mass email apology at about 9pm on Tuesday. “Then in the app, it automatically rebooked me for a flight tomorrow [Thursday] morning, 48 hours after my first flight. Luckily I’m staying with a friend of a friend in Surrey. It was over £100 just for the Uber here.”‘We were left to our own devices’View image in fullscreenMelanie Thompson on her train from Edinburgh.Melanie Thompson, 71, an interdisciplinary artist, was on a 14-hour flight returning from her performance at a mixed media festival with her son in Tokyo on Tuesday when she was told the flight would not land in London. “We were exhausted. About 40 minutes before we arrived, the pilot very politely said, ‘because of IT problems and disruptions at Heathrow, we are going to have to divert to Edinburgh’.“There was a big silence. About 20 minutes later, he said: ‘We were hoping we could refuel and then take you on to Heathrow. But we can’t do that, so we would like you to stay in Edinburgh tonight.’ Then we were left to our own devices to find travel and accommodation for the night.“We suddenly found ourselves in Edinburgh with nowhere to stay because all the hotels and Airbnbs had been filled up,.“We finally found a flat for £500, paid for the taxi to get there and stayed the night there last night.”Thompson spoke to the Guardian on her train journey from Edinburgh to London as there were no flights available on Wednesday.‘It’s Kafkaesque’Thomas Reilly, 55, was due to fly with BA from Marrakech to Gatwick on Tuesdayand then on to Marseille, where he lives and works as a freelance geopolitical adviser. It was only when he got to the airport that he was told his flight was cancelled.“I am currently stuck in Morocco,” says Reilly. “I did not receive any information from BA about the disruption before getting to the airport.”He says that, once at the airport, BA staff were helpful and courteous but he has been left with no option but to book a hotel to stay an extra two nights in Marrakech – at his own expense. (BA staff at the airport did tell him he could “pay and reclaim” for his hotel expenses.)He has been trying to rearrange his journey, attempting to cancel with BA and fly directly to Marrakech through a different airline.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe says: “BA’s customer services operator is not taking calls as ‘the lines are too busy’. There is no email address. And their chatbot cannot help. It is Kafkaesque.”Reilly says he has worked out “alternative travel arrangements, namely to fly direct from Marrakech to Marseille on Thursday 10 September” but he wanted to get his “refund agreed first before outlaying more money on the replacement flight.”When Reilly got through to someone at BA, he says the airline told him they “would not refund the Heathrow-Marseille ticket”. “It’s absurd,” Reilly adds.A spokesperson for British Airways said: “Since yesterday, we’ve rebooked more than 60,000 customers to travel on alternative flights, getting them to their destinations as quickly as we can. Today, we’ve been able to operate almost 80% of our schedule across our whole network.“We know this has been a very challenging and frustrating time for our customers, and we’re incredibly sorry for the experience they’ve endured because of an issue that has been entirely out of our control.”‘We have also lost two days of our trip’Keith Sessions, 74, a computer engineer from Cobham, Surrey, and his wife were due to fly from Heathrow to Tahiti via LA on Tuesday with a five-hour stopover at LAX airport.For the first leg of their journey, they were to fly Virgin, but once on the plane it was clear there were problems.He says the pilot informed them there were delays. Five and a half hours later, with the plane still on the asphalt, the pilot announced that the flight had been cancelled.View image in fullscreenKeith Sessions was due to fly Virgin on the first leg of the trip to Tahiti.Photograph: Anthony Upton/PASessions says they were not offered a meal in that time, “only water, soft drinks and courtesy snacks”.The couple decided to return home via taxi and their flights were auto-rebooked. They will now fly out on Thursday with an 11-hour stopover at LAX airport. They will arrive in Tahiti at 5.30am on Friday.“The 11-hour stopover is not ideal,” says Sessions. “We have also lost two days of our trip and had to spend an extra £340 when you factor in extra cabs to and from the airport and the cost to reserve seating on our flight. Communication from Virgin has been very poor, diabolical.”A Virgin Atlantic spokesperson said: “We’d like to sincerely apologise to our customers for the widespread disruption … We know how frustrating delays and changes to travel plans can be and appreciate our customers’ patience.”Explore more on these topicsAirline industryTravel & leisureHeathrow airportGatwick airportStansted airportAir transportBusiness travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why is Trump silent on UK sanctions against Israeli West Bank settlements? – The Latest | Ed Miliband | The Guardian
description: The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is facing a backlash over the UK government’s sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank. US president Donald Trump, however, has failed to comment on the UK government’s action. Lucy Hough speaks to diplomatic editor Patrick Wintour
Author: Zoe Hitch

title: AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligence
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligence
Content: A safety expert at Anthropic believes there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could spark an event that wipes out humanity.Illustration: Ales Utouka/AlamyView image in fullscreenA safety expert at Anthropic believes there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could spark an event that wipes out humanity.Illustration: Ales Utouka/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligenceRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 9 Sep 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoes artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”. Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade?These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine.Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist.Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.”The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI).On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm.Predictions for when ASImight be reached vary from several years to more than a decade.Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead atAnthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”.Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race.Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue.OpenAIpointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing.Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.”View image in fullscreenThe Labour MP Darren Jones has written to world leaders to call for a multinational treaty to ensure AI is developed safely.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThe Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”.Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.”On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action.The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe US senator Bernie Sanders wants Congress to regulate the ‘greedy’ AI industry.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out.Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity.He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.”Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI.The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.”Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”.OpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan LlerenaRead moreOther contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.”David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”.“AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable.“What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.”Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.“These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.”Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not.“It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicComputer science and ITOpenAIComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: The Fire Within You review – overheated family Christmas boils up too many stereotypes | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Edoardo De Angelis’s claustrophobic drama brings a raging mother up from Naples for the holidays, with a capon. What could possibly not go wrong?
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Edoardo De Angelis’s claustrophobic drama brings a raging mother up from Naples for the holidays, with a capon. What could possibly not go wrong?
Content: Cut … Vanessa Scalera and Lino Musella in The Fire Within You.Photograph: Anna CamerlingoView image in fullscreenCut … Vanessa Scalera and Lino Musella in The Fire Within You.Photograph: Anna CamerlingoVenice film festivalReviewThe Fire Within You review – overheated family Christmas boils up too many stereotypesVenice film festival:Edoardo De Angelis’s claustrophobic drama brings a raging mother up from Naples for the holidays, with a capon. What could possibly not go wrong?Xan BrooksWed 9 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf there were a Golden Lion award for the most Italian film in Venice competition it would go to Edoardo De Angelis’s squawking domestic spat of a picture which contains an imperious matriarch, a pained Catholic priest, an argumentative family, and food, so much food. Bowls are stirred and pans are brandished. Pots are seen rattling angrily on the stove. The festival organisers like to deploy a little judicious home cooking when it comes to the selection and De Angelis is already a favoured guest, having opened the 2023 event with his war dramaComandante. But I fear they may have miscalculated with this one. It’s overdone, on the turn and too liberally salted with tears. It’s liable to provoke the occasional stab of heartburn.At the head of the table sits the incorrigible Angela (Vanessa Scalera). She’s up from Naples (where she was presumably once a girl from the backstreets, begging in rags) to supervise Christmas Eve dinner at her son’s book-lined apartment in Milan. Angela’s a relic of the old world, breezily unreconstructed and openly disgusted by the woke state of her grandchildren. “One’s a gay dancer and the other’s a vegetarian,” she scoffs. They in turn are perturbed by the fact that she has brought in a live chicken to be cooked as the main course. Who’s going to catch it? Who’s going to kill it? What even is this creature, exactly? “It’s not a hen, it’s a capon,” sighs middle-aged Anto (Lino Musella), who dearly wishes his mother had never come at all. She’s a beautiful woman, he says, but she smells.If Angela blows in as the embodiment of humid, fetid old Naples, then Anto represents the Milanese middle class. He’s the moderately successful editor of literary fiction, braced for the imminent arrival of a famous author, which might mean the deal of a lifetime, assuming Angela doesn’t stick her spoon in. The pained Catholic priest has blessed every room of the flat but it’s not nearly enough, the family tensions keep rising. Now Anto’s bohemian sister is blithely lighting cigarettes as she helps prepare the salt cod, and that cursed, flapping capon keeps getting under everyone’s feet. “It can’t fly,” Anto says. “But at this time it would have thrown itself off the balcony.”Shot up close and personal with a small handheld camera, The Fire Within You seems intent on prompting a similar response in the viewer. That’s mostly intentional, a consequence of the drama, although it’s perhaps a given that a film about a claustrophobic family gathering eventually turns a little oppressive itself, and there’s only so long we can spend in these cramped quarters, amid the pistoning elbows and spitting frying pans, before we start to worry that we might lose an eye. The dinner is a disaster; the yellow wallpaper closes in. Anto loathes Angela but he is a mama’s boy at heart and much closer to her than he cares to admit. And so when the film belatedly changes gears, swinging from fraught farce to anxious mercy dash, you can be sure that he’s going along for the ride.Might this win the top prize? God forbid, let’s pray not, because it’s an indulgent bubbling stew of national stereotypes. Still, De Angelis’s film is at least acted with gusto and contains a core of human truth in its depiction of the clotted, knotted intimacy of the typical Christmas gathering. It shows us that families can be hazardous and exert an irresistible magnetic pull. Nobody gets out in one piece, except maybe the capon.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalFestivalsItalyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought a devil was about to appear from the smoke’: Jerry Hsu’s best photograph | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘The black cloud emerged from a grate in the street. I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic – just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city’
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: ‘The black cloud emerged from a grate in the street. I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic – just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city’
Content: ‘There is a noir that is pervasive here’ … an image from the photobook How About Never.Photograph: © Jerry Hsu. Courtesy of the artist and MACKView image in fullscreen‘There is a noir that is pervasive here’ … an image from the photobook How About Never.Photograph: © Jerry Hsu. Courtesy of the artist and MACKMy best shotPhotography‘I thought a devil was about to appear from the smoke’: Jerry Hsu’s best photograph‘The black cloud emerged from a grate in the street. I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic – just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city’Interview byCharlotte JansenWed 9 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis image was taken in 2011 or 2012, just after I had moved toLos Angeles. I was downtown, an area I don’t go to that much, walking around with my camera. Some black smoke started to emerge from a grate in the street – I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic, as if some sort of devil was going to appear. It was really just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city. There is a very powerful feeling of surrender when I am photographing. I have to submit to the authority of ignorance when I’m out there.I grew up in San Jose, which is a sprawling American suburb – there’s no city about it. I came to LA because I was depressed where I lived, and I had just met my future wife, who didn’t want to live in San Jose either. LA is not really a city, it’s hundreds of places. You can drive 15 minutes and be in a completely different environment – the beach, the mountains. There’s a weird sentience to the city, if you let it take you. I get an inexplicable desire to just get in the car and go.Despite the fact it’s sunny every day, there is a noir that is pervasive here. I really like the dark part of the city. There’s a transgressive pulse, and if you search hard enough, there’s a lot of intimacy too. In my book How About Never, there are photographs of big things – fires, hard-hitting events – but at the same time, the smaller things. Cities are cruel and I wanted to capture that, but I also found compassion.double quotation markAs a skateboarder, I’m hardwired to react quicklyAfter I had done the edit for the book, I looked at it and realised that it was also about my relationship with my wife. The photographs span from the time we met to when our marriage ended earlier this year. My wife is a prominent character in it, although you don’t see her face until the end. It’s a very vulnerable photograph of her in a hospital bed. I have a lot of beautiful photographs of her, but I didn’t choose those. I think that in all relationships, vulnerability is the key to how we truly connect, and that was difficult for us. The book is a fantasy of what I was searching for, a dream about what I wanted it to look like and what it couldn’t be – all of the opposing forces, all the fire, water, destruction – and at the same time, hope and beauty. These are the contradictions you find in a relationship.I started skateboarding at 12, and at 16 I turned pro. I was a professional for 25 years. I guess the most obvious connection between that and photography is that skateboarders are constantly seeing the environment in a way other people don’t. We see a park bench, a handrail or an embankment and we think about how we can manipulate it for our purposes. There’s a constant searching and endless curiosity, thinking about how to make an environment our own. As a skateboarder, you’re also hardwired to react quickly – you have to reach a flow state and not hesitate to do something that might be life-threatening. It takes a lot of focus to process information quickly – it’s a type of premonition about what’s about to happen.Skateboardingtaught me from an early age that I have permission to view reality how I want; to take from it what I want. It gave me the permission I needed to make my own choices, which helped a lot with photography, and in my life generally.I am interested in dreams, and in my book I treated the city as if it were my subconscious. I wander through it as if I am in a dream. A dream shows you images and is trying to tell you something about yourself. LA was doing that to me, it was showing me all these things I was attracted to, and I was capturing and collecting them without knowing what I was going to do with them.I have always been painfully shy and interacting with the world is not easy, but this connects me with it and it’s how I can speak about it.Photographyis a solitary practice and making work can be so isolating - I was scared to show my work, scared of being rejected or misunderstood, but I wanted to tell this story. People look at this book and think it’s bleak – and sure, it is, but there’s also a lot of hope in it. The last image of a cat, moving out of the frame to the right, is about moving forward and going on living, despite all of this.How About Neveris published by MACK.View image in fullscreenJerry Hsu’s CVBorn:San Jose, California 1981High point:My new book, How About Never.Top tip:Always research. Copy artists you are drawn to and your voice will eventually emerge.Explore more on these topicsPhotographyMy best shotLos AngelesSkateboardingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The death of the dining room: how mealtimes moved to the kitchen – or the sofa | Homes | The Guardian
description: The idea of a room that you use only occasionally for sit-down meals has gone out of fashion. Now people have found better ways to use the space
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The idea of a room that you use only occasionally for sit-down meals has gone out of fashion. Now people have found better ways to use the space
Content: Waste of space … a traditional dining room.Photograph: xavierarnau/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWaste of space … a traditional dining room.Photograph: xavierarnau/Getty ImagesPass notesHomesThe death of the dining room: how mealtimes moved to the kitchen – or the sofaThe idea of a room that you use only occasionally for sit-down meals has gone out of fashion. Now people have found better ways to use the spaceWed 9 Sep 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Dining rooms.Age:Ancient Romans took meals ina room called a triclinium.Appearance:A room with a big table in the middle, surrounded by chairs.You mean a kitchen?No, a kitchen has a fridge and an oven. This doesn’t.Like a conference room in an office?A little, but this room is in your house and it’s just for eating in.What am I, royalty?Hardly. The dining room was a standard feature of a typical middle-class home.When was all this?From Victorian times until quite recently.Why did they decide they needed special dining rooms?Once upon a time, homes tended to have a single, all-purpose entertainment space, but as furnishings in the living room became more elaborate and upholstered, it was thought desirable to designatea separate space for eating.I guess that makes sense.By the 20th century, dining rooms – once the preserve of the rich – were part of the architecture even in modest homes.In that case, where did they all go?Most of them have been turned into something else. According to research byinsurance provider Aviva, nearly a quarter of homeowners have repurposed their dining rooms.Into what, exactly?Sometimes, people knock down a wall to make a bigger living room or a bigger kitchen. Others turn dining rooms into gyms or home offices.Or panic rooms?Possibly. However personal the change, few people feel the need to maintain a separate room just to eat in occasionally.And theydon’t miss their dining rooms?The fashion for bigger kitchens has moved the social focus of mealtimes. These days, people tend to cook and eat their food in the same space.Really? I eat in front of my computer, on the sofa.In many ways we’ve come full circle: back to spilling food on upholstery.I don’t think I’ve ever seen a regular house with a dining room.That’s because the shift started some time ago. In 2008, it was predicted thatthe dining room would be extinct by 2020. According to a study from the time, more than half a million homeowners had plans to renovate by knocking through their dining room in the following 12 months.And all that knocking through just carried on.Indeed. The vogue for open-plan living has all but obliterated the very idea of rooms.Do say:“As our lives and ways of interacting change, so the interiors of our homes change with them.”Don’t say:“This used to be the dining room, but now it’s where three of my nine housemates sleep.”Explore more on these topicsHomesPass notesHome improvementsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Farage is clearly struggling – I saw that for myself. But his legacy will be a poison that runs deep | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: The mood at the Reform conference was volatile and brittle. But the forces massing further to the right of the party are testament to its impact, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The mood at the Reform conference was volatile and brittle. But the forces massing further to the right of the party are testament to its impact, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Nigel Farage delivers his keynote speech on the first day of the Reform party conference at the NEC in Birmingham, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNigel Farage delivers his keynote speech on the first day of the Reform party conference at the NEC in Birmingham, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionReform UKFarage is clearly struggling – I saw that for myself. But his legacy will be a poison that runs deepAndy BeckettThe mood at the Reform conference was volatile and brittle. But the forces massing further to the right of the party are testament to its impactWed 9 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareFor much of the time sinceNigel Farageresumed the Reform UK leadership two long years ago, his party has been an island of relative stability in the increasingly rough sea of British politics. While other parties plunged queasily in the polls, messily purged dissidents, argued publicly about their direction and changed leaders, Farage dominated Reform UK and gave impregnably self-assured interviews. The party’s popularity moved steadily upwards, comfortably above that of all the others.It is a paradox that a new party with wildly expectant members, not many experienced politicians and few properly worked-out policies became the pole around which the country’s political debate revolved, and yet this seemed to do no harm to Reform’s chances of winning the next general election. As with rising rightwing populist parties across the world, Reform’s tendency to make it up as it went along appeared to be not a weakness but, for many voters, much of its appeal.That seems less the case now. Amid multiple, worsening funding scandals, and with the party openly divided about how to respond to them, this year Reform has lost about a quarter of its support and its poll lead over Labour. There are internal mutterings about the attention-seeking and leadership ambitions of its home affairs spokesperson, the relentlessly abrasive Zia Yusuf, and its Treasury spokesperson, the slippery former Tory Robert Jenrick.Meanwhile, Farage himself, who at 62 is two decades older than them, and has been active in politics for more than 40 years, may be finally losing his composure. Interviewed by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberglast weekend, after months of largely and uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, he switched between anger at his enemies, claims to victimhood and unconvincing insouciance: eyes bulging with fury one moment, head bobbing with forced laughter the next. Even by the feverish standards of modern British politics, it was a strange, almost manic performance.What might happen to Reform and our wider politics if the party’s troubles continue and deepen? The answers may be less reassuring than Reform’s enemies like to think. While the diminishing likelihood of a Reform government is welcome, the party’s crisis could change Reform, and the forces massing further to the right of it – both in parliament and on the streets – in unpredictable and dangerous ways.At the party’s conference last week, the mood felt brittle and volatile. Whereas speakers insisted that Reform was still a “government in waiting”, and banners, lanyards and speeches relentlessly hyped its potential “first 100 days”, the delegates I spoke to were worried about the party’s slide in the polls and general election chances, Andy Burnham’s assured start as prime minister, and the growing pressure Farage was under. After his speech was repeatedly interrupted by hecklers from the green group Climate Resistance, I overheard two delegates, mild-looking, middle-aged men in suits, discussing the protest. “It’s got to stop,” said one. The other said: “Smash ’em in the face!”Another Reform reaction to the party’s difficulties has been to announce ever more extreme, dramatic policies, such asdeporting foreign prisoners,possibly to the infamously brutal jails of El Salvador, and deploying the Royal Navy and Royal Marines to intercept and take all small boat migrants back to France, in “the biggest military operation in the English Channel since the second world war”. In his conference speech, Yusuf described “Operation Fortress” with lingering detail, while huge images of a military helicopter and warship were projected on to the set behind him, and a storm of applause came from the packed hall. Perhaps the potential for such authoritarian political theatre and performatively aggressive policy was always there in Reform, but both feel much more central to its activities now.“All parliamentary recesses will be cancelled,” declared Farage in his speech. “Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, six days a week, until we pass the necessary legislation.” Nothing would be allowed to obstruct “the will of the people” – even though, with modern election turnouts low and half a dozen parties now competing seriously across the country, a Reform victory might represent the will of only a fifth of voters, or less.This year, with the party losing the electoral initiative, new movements have appeared on the anti-migrant right: the even more hardline Restore Britain, andPatriot Platform, the black-clad blockaders of Dover and Portsmouth. Though Farage has criticised both groups, the latter for wearing balaclavas at their protests, the boundaries between Reform and these rivals are not as firm as he would like more mainstream rightwing Britons – whose support Reform badly needs – to think. Restore and Reform’s rhetoric and policiescan be hard to distinguish, while on Monday, Yusuf visited Portsmouth and spoke amicably with Patriot Platform’s organiser, Daniel Thomas, a convicted attemptedkidnapper.Thomas told Yusuf he was upset by Farage’s criticism, and that the protests were not meant to intimidate, but that he still considered Farage a “hero” for his campaigning against the small boats. “You have done really well,” said Thomas. “A lot of people support you.” “Thank you,” said Yusuf, who listened to him at length, nodding respectfully. Then Yusuf replied: “I will take that message – you’ve got my word … take that back to him [Farage].”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe encounter suggested that Reform’s problems may create new alliances and opportunities for the hard right, reshaping but not weakening anti-migrant politics. While the Conservative shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, condemned the Portsmouth violence, he added: “People are genuinely angry at the government’s failure to stop the boats.” Even Labour dares not challenge the legitimacy of what the policing minister, Sarah Jones, called on Monday “the frustration we see in our communities today” about the boats. Just as Reform’s rise made both Labour and the Tories more nationalist and socially conservative, there is a danger that its decline, temporary or otherwise, could continue that process, as they compete for its former supporters.If you’re opposed to Reform’s policies, and especially if you might become one of their victims, then its setbacks this year may be a relief. But that relief will only be partial while its ideas and claims remain so thoroughly embedded across politics and the media, and in many people’s everyday conversations and thinking. One day, Farage will retire, but what he represents will be even harder to stop.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsReform UKOpinionNigel FarageMigrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: Jamaica’s plea to the king: use your authority to ensure colonial slavery is examined | Jamaica | The Guardian
description: The UK drew immense wealth from our country. But was the slavery that underpinned the empire ever lawful? We deserve a fair hearing
Author: Olivia Grange
Headline: The UK drew immense wealth from our country. But was the slavery that underpinned the empire ever lawful? We deserve a fair hearing
Content: Olivia Grange MP, Jamaica’s minister of culture, gender, entertainment and sport, leads the government of Jamaica delegation at Buckingham Palace.Photograph: Jess HurdView image in fullscreenOlivia Grange MP, Jamaica’s minister of culture, gender, entertainment and sport, leads the government of Jamaica delegation at Buckingham Palace.Photograph: Jess HurdCotton Capital: ongoing seriesJamaicaJamaica’s plea to the king: use your authority to ensure colonial slavery is examinedOlivia GrangeThe UK drew immense wealth from our country. But was the slavery that underpinned the empire ever lawful? We deserve a fair hearingJamaican delegates arrive in UK to hand slavery reparations petition to King CharlesWed 9 Sep 2026 11.44 EDTShareOn 6 September 1781, the Zong slave ship set out on the final leg of its voyage to Black River,Jamaica. Four hundred and forty two enslaved Africans were on board – twice the number of people the ship could safely accommodate.Twelve weeks later, 132 enslaved people were murdered by the ship’s crew by being pushed overboard to their deaths. The crew’s justification was the ship had insufficient water supplies to keep everyone alive for the rest of the voyage – a claim later proved false in the British courts.This event, and the legal case that followed, added significant weight to the abolitionist movement in the UK, as did uprisings throughout the Caribbean led by the enslaved.My ancestors achieved their emancipation in 1834, more than 50 years on from the horrors of the Zong. It took a further 128 years for Jamaicans to achieve our independence, on 6 August 1962.At that time, Jamaica ceased to be a British colony. But the legacies of our colonial past linger, not least because we remain a member of the Commonwealth, with King Charles as our head of state.The consequences of the slave trade reverberate deeply to this day. The UK drew immense wealth from Jamaica during the colonial era, but centuries of exploitation left us with an economic and social deficit we are still fighting to overcome.Our natural resources were ravaged during the colonial period, leaving us one of the most vulnerable regions in the world in relation to the climate crisis and extreme weather events.Our infrastructure is massively underdeveloped; our most talented young people often choose to immigrate to the US or come here to the UK. Poverty levels remain high; educational disadvantage persists; health outcomes are poor – all of this can be directly linked to our history of enslavement and colonialism.While the government of Jamaica works tirelessly to address the economic and social deficits, legacy issues persist.Here in the UK, meanwhile, hundreds of thousands of people have African-Caribbean heritage.It is against this backdrop that we have, this week,filed a petitionwith King Charles, asking him to refer three specific questions on transatlantic chattel enslavement to the judicial committee of the privy council. The questions focus on whether enslavement in Jamaica was ever lawful and whether there is an obligation on the UK to provide some form of reparatory remedy.It is important to stress we are not asking King Charles to answer these questions himself. Rather, the people of Jamaica are asking him, as our head of state, to allow our case to have a fair hearing in the British courts.Drawing on the Judicial Committee Act of 1833 – which confers a special power on King Charles to refer questions of legal and constitutional importance to the judicial committee – this is the first time any Commonwealth state has pursued this legal route for the cause of reparatory justice. It is, in fact, such a rarely used legal route that it took us some time – with both the palace and the privy council – to confirm the exact process for filing the petition correctly.In pursuing this route, we are placing our faith in the British legal system, one of the longest-established in the world.We are seeking a chance to put forward the legal argument for reparations – and our legal case coincides with growing political and public momentum on this issue.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn March, the UN passed a motion, recognising enslavement as“the gravest crime against humanity”. In May, Pope Leo XIV made a historic apology forthe Vatican’s role in legitimising enslavement.In June, heads of state, policymakers and activists from more than 80 countries (including some former European colonial powers) gathered in Ghana for the Accra Reparatory Justice Conference. A Global Advisory Council on Reparatory Justice was established after the event, of which our own prime minister, Dr Andrew Holness, is a member.Just last week, the UN committee on the elimination of racial discrimination (CERD)issued guidancestating countries were legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave trade and to take other ⁠measures to address the enduring ⁠legacy of racial ​discrimination.Now, through our petition, Jamaica is adding our own distinct effort to the global campaign for reparatory justice, aiming to test the legal principles of relevance to this issue.Our petition has been endorsed by the heads of government of all Caricom countries, while Ghana’s president, John Dramani Mahama, has also expressed his strong support.King Charles has previouslyexpressed deep personal sorrowabout the history of enslavement. He has the constitutional power and the personal moral authority to allow this question to now be legally examined. Two hundred and forty-five years on from the Zong massacre, we are asking him to grant this request.Olivia Grange is the Jamaican government’s minister for culture, gender, entertainment and sportExplore more on these topicsJamaicaCotton Capital: ongoing seriesKing Charles IIIColonialismCommonwealth of NationscommentShareReuse this content

title: Seven of my colleagues were killed in Gaza. There and in Ukraine, aid workers are no longer safe | José Andrés | The Guardian
description: It seems the attack on World Central Kitchen workers was a deliberate IDF military tactic. The protections of the Geneva conventions are now paper thin, says World Central Kitchen founder José Andrés
Author: José Andrés
Headline: It seems the attack on World Central Kitchen workers was a deliberate IDF military tactic. The protections of the Geneva conventions are now paper thin, says World Central Kitchen founder José Andrés
Content: Gaza residents inspect the remnants of the vehicle that had been carrying World Central Kitchen workers, April 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGaza residents inspect the remnants of the vehicle that had been carrying World Central Kitchen workers, April 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionHumanitarian responseSeven of my colleagues were killed in Gaza. There and in Ukraine, aid workers are no longer safeJosé AndrésIt now seems the 2024 attack on World Central Kitchen workers was a deliberate IDF tactic. The protections of the Geneva conventions have become paper thinJosé Andrés is the founder of the food aid charity World Central KitchenWed 9 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTShareIn times of war, the hard and vital work of supplying food, water and medicine has been protected by international agreements foralmost 80 years. Yet those protections have been systematically and repeatedly ignored in the two most bloody wars of recent years: Ukraine and Gaza.Russia has attacked healthcare targets in Ukraine more than 3,200 times since the full-scale invasion in February 2022,according to the World Health Organization: about twice a day on average. That includes many “double-tap” attacks on the same target in quick succession, which are especially lethal for first responders.In April, the UN security council heard that in the past three years, at least1,010 humanitarian workers had diedin 21 countries. More than half of those were in Gaza and the West Bank. That is three times more than the 377 killed in the previous three years.“This is not an accidental escalation,” said Tom Fletcher, the UN’s undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs. “It is the collapse of protection.” This collapse of protection has led directly to the airstrikes on aid workers in Gaza, including seven of my own World Central Kitchen (WCK) team, who werekilled by the IDF in April 2024despite full cooperation and coordination with the military.At the time, the IDF concluded that the attacks had been “a grave mistake” and a breach of its own standard operating procedures.It stated: “We consider the vital humanitarian activity of international aid organizations to be of utmost importance, and we will continue to work to coordinate and assist their activities, while ensuring their safety and safeguarding their lives.” The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, was dismissed for his actions.However, these fine words were undercut by the IDF itself, when its military prosecutor decided last monthnot to open a criminal investigationinto the airstrikes on our convoy. Now we understand, because of a Guardian investigation, that the targeting of the WCK convoy was the result of a military tactic ofguilt by association. It means that lethal force can be triggered by suspicions, shadows, or simply prejudice. This undefined, unjustified and unlawful tactic is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. What are the protections under these conditions?It is worth remembering why the fourth Geneva convention was created in 1949 and embraced by the world, with the express intention of protecting civilians in war and meeting basic humanitarian needs. In the immediate aftermath of the second world war, the scale of civilian suffering shocked the world’s conscience. Indeed, one of the key architects of the convention was Georges Cahen-Salvador, a French Jewish civil servant, whose family was imprisoned at the Drancy internment camp. They were being deported to Auschwitz in 1943 when they managed to escape to Switzerland. He was one of several survivors who drafted the fourth convention.The convention’s assertions of shared values in war are not lost today, but they are struggling to survive.David Ben-Gurion, Israel’s founding father, famously said: “The fate of Israel depends on two things: its strength and its righteousness.” It’s something that Israel’s military leaders like to quote, but their record falls far short. Humanitarian values are the foundation of righteousness; they are what separate responsible nation states from terrorist groups or rogue states who don’t care about civilian suffering. The protection of aid workers allows the world to ensure that civilians are cared for.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe might be numb to the sight of Russia disregarding our values. But we surely cannot tolerate the only democracy in the Middle East behaving the same way.José Andrés is the founder of the food aid charity World Central Kitchen, and a Michelin-starred chefDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
