title: The Gate theatre’s creative daring gave a tiny stage international scope | Theatre | The Guardian
description: For five decades, this enterprising venue – which is now shutting up shop – broadened the horizons of British theatre
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: For five decades, this enterprising venue – which is now shutting up shop – broadened the horizons of British theatre
Content: Shattering … Paterson Joseph in The Emperor Jones at the Gate theatre in 2005.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenShattering … Paterson Joseph in The Emperor Jones at the Gate theatre in 2005.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreThe Gate theatre’s creative daring gave a tiny stage international scopeMichael BillingtonFor five decades, this enterprising venue – which is now shutting up shop – broadened the horizons of British theatreWed 9 Sep 2026 08.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 08.41 EDTShareLondon’s Gate theatre, not to be confused with its Dublin namesake,is no more. A combination of factors, including rising costs, declining funding and its move in 2022 from its original home in Notting Hill Gate, means that it will cease trading next month. But it is worth celebrating its achievement over five decades. It has been an astonishing nursery of talent and has always stood for a defiant internationalism. “I sometimes think,” I once wrote, “that one learns more about world drama at the Gate than at any other London theatre.”That was the dream of its founder, Lou Stein, who in 1979 took a tiny room over the Prince Albert pub and turned it into a 56-seat theatre that kicked off with Flann O’Brien’s At Swim-Two-Birds. You climbed the pub’s well-worn stairs and found yourself in a space that embraced the world. Not only that. In 1982 Stein launched an offshoot above another pub, the Latchmere in Battersea, where I still recall Susannah York as the Amazonian protagonist of Kleist’s Penthesilea.Where Stein led others followed. His successor was Giles Croft, who ran the Gate from 1985 to 1989 and, taking a snapshot of his final year, I find the following list of shows: two Russian plays in Denis Fonvizin’s The Infant and Bulgakov’s Adam and Eve, a Marivaux double bill of The Colony and Island of Slaves, Heiner Müller’s The Task and a neglected English classic in Susannah Centlivre’s The Wonder. Nowhere else in the UK could you find a programme of such rich eclecticism.View image in fullscreenUnrivalled eclecticism … Pioneers in Ingolstadt by MarieLuise Fleisser at the Gate theatre in 1991.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStephen Daldry took over in 1989 and I remember this young man in specs and scuffed sneakers standing at the top of the stairs welcoming people to the theatre as if they were guests in his home. Daldry not only introduced thematic programming – one of his seasons was called Women in World Theatre – he also showed that anything is possible in a small space. One of his discoveries was of a Bavarian dramatist, Marieluise Fleisser whose Pioneers in Ingoldstadt from the 1920s involved, in Ian MacNeil’s breathtaking design, a cast of 30 crossing a bridge. I recall Daldry telling me that such ventures were only possible because the Gate was unsubsidised: plug into public funding and it would not only be artistically accountable but would also have to pay Equity rates.Daldry was clearly a brilliant director. He also encouraged others. It was at the Gate that I first became aware of Katie Mitchell through her productions of Euripides’ Women of Troy and Gorky’s Vassa Zheleznova in which Paola Dionisotti in the title role memorably demonstrated the private cost of capitalist success. Daldry stimulated another young director and his eventual successor, Laurence Boswell, to pursue his obsession with Spanish drama. It was thanks to Boswell that we got to know such classics as Tirso de Molina’s Don Gil of the Green Breeches, Lope de Vega’s The Gentleman from Olmedo and The Great Pretenders in which Louis Hilyer was an actor-manager who so identified with a Christian martyr he was playing that he ended up being spectacularly crucified.View image in fullscreenGenuine domestic tragedy … Paul Ready and Kelly Hunter  in Cuckoos at the Gate theatre in 2000.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianIf I dwell on those early years it was because the Gate, particularly during the mean and insular Thatcherite 80s, was proving that there was a world elsewhere and that it was possible to create infinite riches in a little room. But all the directors who followed put their own individual stamp on the Gate. During David Farr’s tenure we saw Sarah Kane’s incest-dominated Phaedra’s Love. Mick Gordon’s reign gave us Peter Hall’s staging in 2000 of Giuseppe Manfridi’sCuckoos, which showed two lovers permanently stuck in an act of anal intercourse: for all its sensational surface a genuine domestic tragedy.‘This is not sustainable’: London’s Gate theatre to close after nearly 50 yearsRead moreA succession of female directors went on to reconfigure the space while extending the repertory. Erica Whyman staged a season of adapted Greek myths. Thea Sharrock gave us a shattering production of O’Neill’sThe Emperor Jones, later seen at the Olivier, with Paterson Joseph as the fugitive hero. The joint tenure of Carrie Cracknell and Natalie Abrahami saw Lucy Kirkwood’s post-IbseniteHeddaand Christopher Haydon and Ellen McDougall each valiantly kept the show on the road while reinforcing the Gate’s capacity to take one by surprise. But when it left its Notting Hill Gate premises and moved to Camden Town it inevitably sacrificed some of its identity. Other London theatres, such as the Almeida, the Finborough and the Arcola, were increasingly venturing into the territory it had once owned. The public funding which Daldry had once eschewed also proved unreliable. But, while dwelling on the Gate’s demise, we should glory in its success in enhancing so many careers and in showing that the one sure way for a small theatre to make its mark is by taking gigantic risks.Explore more on these topicsTheatreSarah KaneStephen DaldryPaterson JosephCarrie CracknellLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Want to start lazymaxxing? Here are some low-effort ways to improve your life | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: CEOs may like to get up at the crack of dawn and go for a run, but I prefer optimising my life with lie-ins, trashy films, swearing and coffee, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: CEOs may like to get up at the crack of dawn and go for a run, but I prefer optimising my life with lie-ins, trashy films, swearing and coffee, writes Arwa Mahdawi
Content: ‘I have never once felt guilty for hitting the snooze button …’Photograph: Olga Rolenko/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I have never once felt guilty for hitting the snooze button …’Photograph: Olga Rolenko/Getty ImagesOpinionLife and styleWant to start lazymaxxing? Here are some low-effort ways to improve your lifeArwa MahdawiCEOs may like to get up at the crack of dawn and go for a run, but I prefer optimising my life with lie-ins, trashy films, swearing and coffeeWed 9 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.07 EDTShareThis evening I’m going to tuck my five-year-old into bed and read her a chapter from one of her princess books, followed by a summary of research recently presented at the annual congress of the European Society of Cardiology. Once upon a time, I’ll tell her, there was a scientist called Dr Nawon Lee who authored a study that found having a weekend lie-in may bevery good for youand can protect against high blood pressure. Our accomplished protagonist Dr Lee said: “People should not feel lazy or guilty for sleeping a little longer on the weekend.” And the moral of this story, dear child, is that you should try not to wake your mothers up at 6am every day.Unfortunately, I’m not sure that all the peer-reviewed science in the world will convince my early riser to have a weekend lie-in. Still, as a big fan of sleep and someone who has never once felt guilty for hitting the snooze button, I have to say I feel vindicated by this new study.CEOscan getup at 4amand run 10 miles before eating five foraged mushrooms if they want to, but I’m going to protect my heart health by sleeping in, any opportunity I can get, thank you very much.The rich world is currently in thrall to tech-enabled self-optimisation. Or as some people (people you do not want to end up seated next to at a dinner party) call it:humanmaxxing. We’re told we should track our biomarkers and optimise every second of our days, often in complicated and joyless ways. If that works for you, great. But, personally, I’m a big fan of lazymaxxing and finding low-effort ways to improve my life. Weekend lie-ins are obviously one, drinking coffee is another. A 2025study foundthat morning coffee drinkers were 16% less likely to die early of any cause. Swearing is alsosurprisingly good for you: uttering a profanity can decrease physical pain and increase focus. And while I can’t go so far as to say that bingeing Love is Blind has health-giving properties, I didunearth researchconcluding that enjoying trashy films is a sign you’re a well-educated cultural omnivore. I still haven’t found a study proving that lying on the couch, eating crisps, reading thrillers and ignoring your obligations is good for you, but I live in hope.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I’ve spent my whole life looking miserable. It’s time for a change | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: When you smile, the world smiles back. Not at me it doesn’t – because even when I’m smiling, I exude gloom, says Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: When you smile, the world smiles back. Not at me it doesn’t – because even when I’m smiling, I exude gloom, says Adrian Chiles
Content: ‘The gloomy 59-year-old.’Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘The gloomy 59-year-old.’Photograph: Ken McKay/ITV/ShutterstockOpinionSocial etiquetteI’ve spent my whole life looking miserable. It’s time for a changeAdrian ChilesWhen you smile, the world smiles back. Not at me it doesn’t – because even when I’m smiling, I exude gloomWed 9 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareIwant to change my face. I’m not talking cosmetic surgery, although if chubby cheeks could be surgically de-chubbed I’d have to consider it. Surgery can’t help me – if only it were that simple. What I seek to change is the expression on my face, my whole disposition, the face I present to the world. Mine’s all wrong, insomuch as I look as if there’s something wrong. Very often I’ll be asked what the matter is.“Nothing,” I say.“Sure?”“Yes, why do you ask?”“Well, you just look miserable.”Point taken. Very often, when I tell a friend that all is good with me, they ask if I’ve thought about telling that to my face.Well, now I am – I am telling my face to cheer up. I don’t know how or when it got stuck this way. It’s been at least 13 years. I know this because back then something was written in the Daily Mirror which second-mentioned me as “the gloomy 46-year-old”. Not angry, or sad, or scornful. Just gloomy. Tragic, really. And now I’m the gloomy 59-year-old.Last month I saw this bloke in a cafe in Trieste. So entranced was I at the sunniness of his disposition that I couldn’t take my eyes off him. It wasn’t just the faintest of smiles on his lips, it was the kindness in his eyes and the aura of quiet contentment. It wasn’t some smug satisfaction with his own circumstances so much as contentment with the world as a whole. He radiated the conviction that everything and everyone was just fine. It was infectious. That cafe, the square, the city, all felt afloat on a sea of gladness. It was that profound. A rising tide of serenity raises all boats.He didn’t betray any alarm even as he registered me, this gloomy stranger, staring at him in wonder. He merely widened his eyes a little and gave an almost imperceptible nod in acknowledgment of the happy fact that life could be worse.I want to be him instead of his opposite, exuding bleakness. It’s high time – I will be 60 next year. My seventh decade will be my cheery era. Who says you can’t teach an old dog new tricks? It just takes longer than you might hope. After a lifetime of defaulting to an upside-down smile, a resting happy face is not something you can paint on just because you like the cut of a stranger’s jib in a cafe in Trieste. I discovered this there and then when I tried a big grin on for size; it didn’t fit. Even Happy Man looked unsettled.What did I learn in the kitchen this week? The longer it takes to cook, the less you want to eat it | Adrian ChilesRead moreWhen you smile, the world smiles back. Not at me it doesn’t. Try as I might, I can’t smile right. Yes, I smile nicely if I bump into someone I like, or my team score a goal, or someone says something amusing – but getting a default, not-thinking-about-it, resting happy face is quite beyond me. I think it’s all the thinking about it. Out for a walk, if I was thinking non-stop about walking, I’d soon be tripping over my feet. So it is with smiling. My lips and cheeks are all over the shop, while my facial muscles are in constant motion in search of a natural smile they can live with.I can’t settle on anything suitable. Smiling the wrong smile, especially at women, feels a bit forward; smiling at blokes might even invite a fight. WTF are you grinning at, mate? I’m spooking people. And, clocking my reflection in a shop window, I spook myself. How do I find the face I want? A survey perhaps – “Excuse me, madam, may I ask what my facial expression is conveying?” In the meantime, I’ll practise into a mirror seeking a countenance suggesting mildness, tolerance, hope, openness. Anything but gloom.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsSocial etiquetteOpinionHappinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generation, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generation, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anaïs Mims/GettyOpinionThe far rightEuropean democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyssRafael BehrFar-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generationWed 9 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTShareNot all that long ago,Europewas a beacon of liberal idealism. One memoir recalls it as an era “comfortably saturated with confidence in the unfailing and binding power of tolerance and conciliation”. The economic system seemed obviously preferable to barbarous alternatives. “People honestly believed that the divergencies and the boundaries between nations and sects would gradually melt away into a common humanity,” the author added.Those words could describe the spirit of globalisation at the turn of the millennium. They werewritten in the 1930s by Stefan Zweig, reflecting on the optimism of late 19th-century Vienna from the perspective of a Jewishémigréwhose world had been destroyed by murderous nationalism. Zweig took his own life in 1942. He never saw fascism defeated. He couldn’t have imagined a renaissance of liberalism in the second half of the 20th century so complete as to attain a pitch of complacency rivalling the one he remembered from his childhood.Now momentum is with the nationalists again. Victory for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in the region of Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend is not the biggest electoral prize won by a far-right party in Europe in recent years, but it isone of the most shockingbecause it is Germany. No country had more to learn from history if it wanted to immunise its democracy against extremism. None pursued a more systematic programme of inoculation. The word for it isVergangenheitsbewältigung– hard to say and tricky to translate, meaning roughly coming to terms with a shameful past.There is no excuse of ignorance about the AfD’s rise. It is a knowing repudiation of atonement. The party flirts with Nazi imagery and embraces racist definitions of nationhood, seeking to deport Germans whose credentials it sees as biologically improper. It is extreme enough toinduce squeamishnessin Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally (RN). She has spent years carefully cultivating respectability and is leading the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election. She doesn’t want to jeopardise her mainstream credentials by association with the unambiguous extreme.That is less of an impediment across the Atlantic.Elon Musk is an AfD fan, deploying his control of X to boost the party’s campaign messages.Last year, the US vice-president, JD Vance, met Alice Weidel,AfD co-leader, during a visit to Munich. There was no space in his diary for Olaf Scholz, then the German chancellor. Clearly, the AfD meets the criteria for endorsement set out in Donald Trump’snational security strategy, which pledges support for “patriotic resistance” movements committed to halting the “civilisational erasure” of Europe by immigration.In Britain,Nigel Faragecould once have assumed entitlement to that status as an early and enthusiastic cheerleader for Trump. But in the competition for Maga accolades, Reform UK has lost ground to parties and people even further to the right – Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain; ultra-nationalist agitator Tommy Robinson; pretty much anyone who can muster a mob of blackshirts or a passing troll who catches Musk’s eye posting racist conspiracy theories online.27:02Rise of the far right: can Farage get a boost from AfD’s win in Germany? | Politics WeeklyIt would be absurd if it wasn’t so effective. “We never fall into the same abyss twice,” writes Éric Vuillard, the French novelist. “But we fall in the same way, in a mixture of ridicule and dread.”The reach and pungency of the US right, drenched in white supremacism, interferes with Farage’s old strategy of banking far-right support and feinting moderation to make gains in the mainstream. Chasing credibility with fanatical racists in an international digital arena makes it hard to reassure a domestic analogue audience that he should be allowed near Downing Street.The tension shows in Farage’s attitude to the AfD. He spoke at a rally for it in 2017. Now he describes it as a“mixed bag” of a party, whose cultural stances are “utterly respectable and decent” but whose enthusiasm for dictators is “very difficult”.Farage has called AfD support for Vladimir Putin “hard to understand”. It can’t be that far beyond comprehension for a man who, in 2014, described the Russian president as theworld leader he most admired, albeit “as an operator, not a human being”.If Farage needs further insight into what might motivate a Kremlin fellow traveller, he could reach out to Reform’s former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, who isserving a prison sentence for accepting bribes to make pro-Russian speechesin the European parliament when he was a Brexit party MEP.Proximity to the Moscow line is a fairly reliable measure of fanaticism and venality on the spectrum from far-right to even further-right politics in Europe and the US. The same applies on the left, where a credulous appetite for Russian propaganda endures decades after the demise of Soviet ideology.Thankfully, there is not much of a market in British politics for openly pandering to Putin. That is one reason why Trump is also unpopular, although opinion polls suggest he is viewed more favourably by Reform supporters than the wider public. Farage has stopped boasting of his White House connections, perhaps because they have dried up, or maybe because sycophantic flapping around a foreign tyrant, even an American one, doesn’t project strength in a wannabe prime minister.It is striking how little the Reform leader has to say about the rest of the world and Britain’s place in it. The topic was hardly mentioned at the party’s annual conference last week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was atheatrical appearance by Jordan Bardella, the young Le Pen protege and likely prime minister if she wins the presidency. He signed a legally meaningless “deal” with Farage on stopping small-boat traffic across the Channel and wasimmediately criticised back homefor selling out to the UK. The likelihood of a French far-right government taking in more migrants as a policy favour to the UK is close to zero. Having xenophobic nationalists setting the agenda in Paris and London wouldn’t make relations easier, no matter what ideological amity they now claim.As the architect of Brexit, Farage is one of the most consequential politicians of his generation, but he can’t plausibly claim it as an achievement, even when addressing an auditorium of loyal fans. They know it has failed as well as everyone else.A Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any more | Gaby HinsliffRead moreFarage probably misses the simplicity of his old crusade against Brussels. He might envy nationalist counterparts on the continent, who get to rail against liberal Europeanism while enjoying the economic and strategic privileges afforded by EU membership. They don’t have to explain why it’s so cold on the outside. They play the Eurosceptic game, mobilising the same resentments, targeting the same scapegoats, but modifying the demands in recognition that Farage’s victory was pyrrhic. It doesn’t pay to actually leave. The ambition is to capture the European project, not destroy it, although it amounts to the same thing if the transformation happens through connivance with Maga ideology and Kremlin money.This doesn’t have to be Europe’s destiny. Nationalists do not form a monolithic bloc. The essence of their creed militates against cross-border partnership. Their egos generate more rivalries than alliances. Their selfishness sabotages deals. Countervailing forces can be mustered. There is no law of history that says a height of liberal optimism must be followed by an equivalent fall into chaos. The “binding power of tolerance and conciliation” was not defeated in the 20th century and it won’t be suffocated in this one either. We see the abyss. We can pass without plunging to the bottom.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on UK-EU relations: voters would reward greater ambition | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The architects of Brexit know it has failed. That presents Andy Burnham with an opportunity to set a bolder new agenda
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The architects of Brexit know it has failed. That presents Andy Burnham with an opportunity to set a bolder new agenda
Content: ‘Nigel Farage will for ever be associated with the demand for emancipation from Brussels but is rarely heard celebrating its completion’: Reform UK party conference, Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Nigel Farage will for ever be associated with the demand for emancipation from Brussels but is rarely heard celebrating its completion’: Reform UK party conference, Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Temilade Adelaja/ReutersOpinionBrexitThe Guardian view on UK-EU relations: voters would reward greater ambitionEditorialThe architects of Brexit know it has failed. That presents Andy Burnham with an opportunity to set a bolder new agendaWed 9 Sep 2026 13.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareModesty is not a trait commonly associated with Nigel Farage. Something else must explain theReform UKleader’s reluctance to talk about what is undoubtedly his biggest achievement.Few individuals can boast of having influenced British politics as drastically as Mr Farage, with his record of campaigning for Brexit before that word was even coined. He will for ever be associated with the demand for emancipation from Brussels, but is rarely heard celebrating its completion. It barely earned a mention in speeches at his party’sannual conferencelast week. The simple reason is that none of the promises made about the benefits of life outside the EU have been fulfilled. Leaving made thecountry poorer, and voters know it.Opinion polls routinely show that a majority are dissatisfied with the way Brexit has turned out. In asurveypublished this week by the thinktank British Future, 57% of respondents judged it to be “more a failure than a success”. Only 21% took the opposite view. There were also clear majorities in favour of closer ties when it comes to trade, defence and even health policy; 57% support a youth-mobility scheme for 18- to 30-year-olds, restoring some of the opportunities to live and work abroad that were curtailed by departure from the EU.Those attitudes should not be confused with appetite for a complete reversal, still less a referendum to make it happen. Memories of a divisive campaign and exit process are a powerful deterrent against relitigating the question all over again.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesBut the balance of public opinion is skewed against the enterprise that defined Mr Farage’s political ascent and was enacted with fervour by the Conservative party. The ideological parents ofBrexitare understandably embarrassed by their progeny.That presents Andy Burnham with an opportunity. The prime minister has said he wants to be “bolder” in pursuing a closer EU relationship. He has permission from the electorate to do just that. He inherited a European “reset” from his predecessor, but it was advancing slowly. The scope of potential agreement was also limited by Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, ruling out single market and customs union membership.Mr Burnham inherits that mandate too, and has indicated his intention to adhere to it. A UK-EU summit to advance cooperation in a range of areas – trade in agricultural goods, energy, defence and security, youth mobility – was due in July. Sir Keir’s departure led to apostponement. It has not yet been rescheduled. Technical negotiations have continued under the new government, but there is not much sense of political urgency coming from either side. That must change.A new prime minister’s in-tray is always busy. The EU is a slow-moving apparatus. There are few incentives to grant favours to the UK when the terms of the existing Brexit deal are skewed in Brussels’ favour. Without infusions of political will from No 10, inertia will prevail.Meanwhile, the case for closer UK-EU cooperation gets ever more compelling with each act of vandalism perpetrated by Donald Trump against thetransatlantic allianceand internationaltrading system. This strategic imperative is something the public can understand and that ideological Brexiters refuse to see. If Mr Burnham has the imagination and courage to outline an ambitious new model of UK-EU relations, he will have the majority of British voters on his side.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanity | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel bills
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel bills
Content: Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, at the signing of an oil agreement with the US in Caracas, 2 September  2026.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVenezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, at the signing of an oil agreement with the US in Caracas, 2 September  2026.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionVenezuelaThe Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanityEditorialThe US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel billsWed 9 Sep 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.46 EDTShareImperialism does not require a flag to be planted or a governor dispatched. It can be a powerful nation deciding who governs a smaller, weaker country, and on what terms and for whose benefit its resources will be developed. Donald Trump’s kidnapping of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro, putting his deputy – Delcy Rodríguez – in his place as president, and then her signing a deal handing afifth of the country’s proven oil reserves to the US, amount to a modern version of 19th-century gunboat diplomacy. Regime change supplied America’s commercial concession.This won’t bother Mr Trump. But it should. The US president has oversold his neocolonial spoils. The additional production Venezuela is supposed to bringonlinemight bring down oil prices eventually, but notanytimesoon. Crucially, what Mr Trump calls “the biggest oil deal in history” won’t cause the price at the pump to fall before November’s midterms. When so many American votersare struggling to pay energy bills, it’s hard to see how unrealised Orinoco Belt riches are going to help Republican candidates.View image in fullscreenUS president Donald Trump.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APThe US president alsopromotesthe idea that he is transforming the US’s industrial landscape through fossil fuels. Although the Venezuela oil grab might be highly profitable for a fewselected companies, the windfall is dwarfed by the size of the US economy. Mr Trump is not getting cheap energy but a spectacle of American power. That may be enough for him.Before Mr Maduro was captured, Mr Trump haddecidedthat Venezuela’s oil belonged to the US. The Venezuelan strongman was offeredexileif he gave Washington want it wanted. When he dithered, a USarmadaassembled off Venezuela’s coast. Yet Mr Trump did not replace Mr Maduro with María Corina Machado from the democratic opposition. He instead backed the authoritarian regime that could secure the oilfields from ambitious army generals and spare the costs of occupation.The US doesn’t rule Venezuela directly, but it is exercising power through a lifelong socialist, Ms Rodríguez. She is remaking Chavismo, the revolutionary movement launched by Hugo Chávez, in her image – enraging someleftists. Ms Rodríguez has grantedNorth American Blue Energy Partners(Nabep) concessions to 17 oilfields in Venezuela for decades to come. Nabep’s boss, Alejandro Betancourt, acontroversialVenezuelan oil billionaire, popped up in Caracas for this week’s visit by the US energy secretary, Chris Wright. Nabep has in turn granted the Pentagon a35% equity stakeat no cost to the US taxpayer.The charge of “Yankee imperialism” was often dismissed as kneejerk anti-Americanism. Mr Trump has turned it into an American boast. Ms Rodríguez argues that she is no puppet. Cooperation with Mr Trump, she says, will bring Venezuela investment and couldgenerate$200bn in oil revenues. Unequal bargains have often benefited local rulers and intermediaries. The question is: what kind of economy and social order will that revenue produce? Oil cash is not the same as sovereign development.Mr Trump is a playground bully handed the world’s most powerful military. He mistakes coercion for greatness and sovereign nations for toys. He uses US power to feed his bottomless ego – recently claiming himself to be a biggerhistoricalfigure than Caesar, Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Stalin and Mao. When he departs the stage, others will have to rebuild what he has squandered: the US’s authority, its alliances and its reputation.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Bayeux tapestry: why more women should be stitched into the fabric of history | Bayeux tapestry | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the loan of the Bayeux tapestry
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the loan of the Bayeux tapestry
Content: One of the few women depicted in the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersView image in fullscreenOne of the few women depicted in the Bayeux tapestry.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersBayeux tapestryLettersThe Bayeux tapestry: why more women should be stitched into the fabric of historyReaders respond to the loan of the Bayeux tapestryWed 9 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareI enjoyed your photograph of Andy Burnham, Macron and King Charles admiring the Bayeux tapestry and the king’s comment about the“entente amicale”between France and the UK (Bayeux tapestry loan symbolises ‘entente amicale’ between France and UK, says King Charles, 2 September). I also enjoyedBurnham’s wry referenceto a tapestry that “shows a new leader emerging from a northern territory, travelling to the south of England in search of the crown. Something clearly that couldn’t happen today.”There is a certain irony, however, in there being, I gather, 93 penises portrayed in the tapestry, and six women – three known and three anonymous. Yet all the beautiful and exquisitely observed needlework was done by women. Observation, detail and creativity – significant and often unremarked.It would be good to hear more about the women involved and less about male leadership, power grabs and violence. Surely we are living too much with this legacy of an over-concentration on only one half of the world’s population?Jane KeareyBristolThis exchange of treasures is indeed a welcome symbol of friendship and cooperation – at least for now – between our respective elites. Yet the tapestry itself, and the history around it, portray the recurrent theme of history shaped by (pretty much exclusively) male ego, greed and lust for power; thence deceit, treachery, war, massacre, misogyny and psychopathic levels of inhumanity. Looking around the world today, one muses (perhaps in a Norman accent), “Plus ça change, plus c’est la même chose.” I wonder if we’ll ever find a solution.Richard O’BrienHighbridge, SomersetLet’s hope Jonathan Jones’s vivid review of the Bayeux tapestry will encourage people to engage with English and British history (The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth, 3 September). However, discussing the invasion by the Normans, he states that “William succeeded where those later would-be cross-Channel invaders – Philip II of Spain, Napoleon and Hitler – would all fail.”True (although the Germans did occupy the Channel Islands during the second world war), but he overlooks the successful invasion of 1688 when another William, the Dutch William of Orange, or William III, invaded with 500 ships and 20,000 soldiers and after some skirmishes forced James II to flee to exile in France, with profound consequences for the religion, constitution and monarchy of England and later Great Britain.Jones is not alone in forgetting, or misunderstanding, what happened in 1688. In an editorial (28 August), you quoted Nigel Farage as saying, in 2014, that the Bayeux tapestry depicted “the last time we were invaded and taken over”). Let’s hope such ignorance is not widespread and that the loan of the Bayeux tapestry leads to a revival of interest in the study and teaching of history.Richard RossLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: An education in the arts should be available to all | Education | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial calling for Andy Burnham to relieve pressure on arts funding in English schools
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to an editorial calling for Andy Burnham to relieve pressure on arts funding in English schools
Content: ‘With fees, instrumental lessons – and the musical careers that rely on them – become the preserve of those whose families can afford to pay.’Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘With fees, instrumental lessons – and the musical careers that rely on them – become the preserve of those whose families can afford to pay.’Photograph: Keith Morris/AlamyEducationLettersAn education in the arts should be available to allReaders respond to an editorial calling for Andy Burnham to relieve pressure on arts funding in English schoolsWed 9 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareYour editorial on the decline of music and drama in state schools (4 September) is right to highlight what has been lost. Education should enable young people to enjoy learning as well as achieve.Michael Gove’s reforms, rooted in a dewy-eyed vision of a mythical golden age of education that never existed, diminished arts subjects in which many students found success. The EBacc prioritised academic subjects and measurable outcomes; the arts were squeezed from timetables.Schools knew the cost. At the special school where I was the headteacher, we kept drama as a core subject because it developed social skills, an awareness of body language, confidence and empathy – essential skills for life. In mainstream schools, I often saw the pride and confidence gained through performance carry over into a student’s wider learning.I remember a father in tears of joy because he had never imagined his child with special needs performing in a school choir. I remember a mother telling me that a mainstream school production transformed her disaffected daughter’s confidence. No league table measures moments like these.With rising numbers outside education, employment or training, we should ask whether losing such opportunities contributes to disengagement.Music and drama are not luxuries. For many young people they provide something fundamental: a reason to believe they belong in education at all.Pete CrockettRoyal Wootton Bassett, WiltshireThe Guardian is right to highlight theperilous position music educationhas been placed in by successive governments, and the importance of every child having access to high-quality music education in school.The National Centre for Arts and Music Education is apparently opening this month. The centre, while a welcome addition to the music education ecosystem, will never be the answer to all problems, particularly when its new funding is just £13m over three years.We don’t know when the centre will open because the process has been beset by delays, there is no announcement on who received the tender to manage it, and the Department for Education hasn’t officially announced that its opening is delayed yet.One must question whether the DfE would treat any other core curriculum subject this way.Lucy Powellhas the goodwill of the music education centre, but, as your article eloquently sets out, she has inherited a serious problem that needs urgent attention.Deborah AnnettsChief executive, Independent Society of MusiciansI travel four hours a day by bus to the closest state sixth form offering drama and textiles A-levels. It’s 20 miles away: 65 stops and a change, with no direct route. I get up at 5.30am and get home tired and too late for evening clubs. The bus service is unreliable and my pass costs £700 a term. I’ve spoken to the local MP about how hard this is, but nothing has changed.There’s only one secondary school in my home town, which I was going to stay at until it dropped drama at the last minute because I was the only person in my year who’d signed up. I want a career designing costumes for theatre and film, and spend all my free time making costumes, so not doing drama wasn’t an option.The school I now attend, Northampton School for Girls, has been hugely encouraging. It also let me travel miles away for work experience at a costume supplier for film. My old school allowed only very local placements.Why has the country decided young people in small towns aren’t allowed to be creative? We’re pushed towards engineering or hairdressing, and told to stop wanting anything different.Molly StubbsBrackley, NorthamptonshireIt has been my privilege and honour to lead a state school that has chosen over decades to invest in the performing arts for its students. This is increasingly difficult; schools are so constrained by the curriculum and funding that it is now nigh on impossible to achieve.Students who leave my school and continue to conservatoires or music degrees are invariably the only ones in their cohorts from the state sector. This must change to ensure our vibrant arts heritage reflects the diversity of our society in the future; besides which, young people from all backgrounds deserve to benefit from the richness participation in the arts brings us.Matthew ParrisKinoulton, NottinghamshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Spyware can easily fall into the wrong hands – investors should take note | Surveillance | The Guardian
description: Letters: The reported targeting of student activists in Serbia is an example of increased misuse, with serious consequences for the commercial spyware industry
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: The reported targeting of student activists in Serbia is an example of increased misuse, with serious consequences for the commercial spyware industry
Content: A protester against Aleksandar Vučić’s government in Belgrade, May 2026.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersView image in fullscreenA protester against Aleksandar Vučić’s government in Belgrade, May 2026.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersSurveillanceLettersSpyware can easily fall into the wrong hands – investors should take noteThe reported targeting of student activists in Serbia is an example of increased misuse, with serious consequences for the commercial spyware industryWed 9 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.03 EDTShareThe targeting of Serbian activists with advanced spyware (Report, 4 September) is the latest warning in a mounting record of abuse that makes thesystemic and foreseeable risksof the commercial spyware industry increasingly impossible to ignore. Investors who aren’t paying attention are leaving their portfolios exposed to growing financial, reputational and human rights risks.Despite industry assurances that its technology is intended only for investigating terrorists and criminals, spyware hasrepeatedly been linkedto the targeting of journalists, activists, elected officials, opposition leaders, lawyers, judges, academics and civil society. The fallout for the companies involved has been serious:costly litigation,criminal complaints, cripplingsanctions,judicial investigations, tighteningexport restrictions,executivesbeingconvicted, severereputational damageand, in some cases,financial collapse.That’s before accounting for the damage spyware can inflict elsewhere in an investor’s portfolio. Companies more profitable than spyware firms are forced to defend against attacks, respond to breaches and protect their users and commercially sensitive information. Funding spyware often means funding an attack on their far more valuable portfolio companies.Investors shouldn’t wait for the next scandal to discover their exposure. They should screen commercial spyware companies from their investment universe, require fund managers to identify and prevent exposure across investment chains, and urge portfolio companies to take action to prevent spyware proliferation.This is particularly important for development finance institutions, pension funds and other responsible investors whose mandates and reputations rest on creating long-term social value. Financing companies whose products can be used to silence journalists, intimidate civil society and undermine democratic institutions creates risks that extend far beyond any single investment.The Serbian case should prompt investors to question whether their firm is exposed to commercial spyware. And citizens should be asking, are my tax dollars or pension savings funding this?Meredith VeitTechnology and human rights researcher, Business and Human Rights CentreHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: Double talk | Tilting the scale | Far-right protests | Names in lights
Content: The Coach & Horses pub in Soho, central London, 7 August 2026.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenThe Coach & Horses pub in Soho, central London, 7 August 2026.Photograph: Yui Mok/PABrief lettersPubsLettersPub nomenclature doesn’t stand upDouble talk | Tilting the scale | Far-right protests | Names in lightsWed 9 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareI was interested to read your article regarding “vertical drinking” (Curbs on vertical drinking in Soho pubs to go ahead as Khan criticises council’s ‘breathtaking arrogance’, 8 September). When I was a lad we used to call this “drinking”. It’s a bit like “wild swimming”. Again, in my day, we used to call this “swimming”. Whatever next? Eyeball reading? Horizontal sleeping? Mobile walking? Audible talking?Joe HydeBilsborrow, LancashireRe your report (UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale, 4 September), it’s good to see the UN catching up with the Guardian, which uses an equal-area world map in the “The week that was” feature in Saturday’s paper. title: Alexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat Atlético | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Alexis Mac Allister scored Liverpool’s winner as they began their Champions League campaign with a 2-1 victory over Atlético Madrid
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Alexis Mac Allister scored Liverpool’s winner as they began their Champions League campaign with a 2-1 victory over Atlético Madrid
Content: Alexis Mac Allister celebrates alongside teammates Rio Ngumoha and Milos Kerkez after scoring Liverpool’s winner.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlexis Mac Allister celebrates alongside teammates Rio Ngumoha and Milos Kerkez after scoring Liverpool’s winner.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueAlexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat AtléticoAndy Hunterat AnfieldWed 9 Sep 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was the time and place for Alexis Mac Allister to do his talking on the pitch and the disgruntled Liverpool midfielder delivered on cue. “Very sad” over Liverpool’s refusal to offer him a new contract, while Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch were getting theirs, Mac Allister made Anfield very happy with a match-winning display againstAtlético Madrid.The Argentina international, one of five World Cup finalists involved in an absorbing, delicately-poised contest, vented his frustrations in the best possible and most professional way – from behind an immaculate 20-yard strike into Jan Oblak’s goal rather than a microphone. Mac Allister believes he is playing for a new deal this season and promised to give “100% to my last day” at the pre-match press conference. He was true to his word to extend Atlético’s winless sequence against English opposition in theChampions Leagueleague phase to 11 matches.Liverpool 2-1 Atlético Madrid, PSG 6-1 Slovan Bratislava; Chelsea v Leeds – liveRead moreFor Andoni Iraola, it was the perfect start to life as a Champions League coach after an imperfect start to the game. Diego Simeone’s switch to a 3-5-2 formation caughtLiverpoolcold and it was only when they regrouped in the aftermath of Marcos Llorente’s latest Anfield goal, and again during the half-time interval, that their performance level improved. Mac Allister’s timely moment, Alexander Isak’s relentless industry, Florian Wirtz’s creativity and another performance of drive and intelligence from Szoboszlai ensured the Liverpool head coach had plenty to savour.“I have to blame myself a bit for the start of the game,” Iraola said. “Atlético surprised us with the way they approached the game. They haven’t used that system too much this season and it’s difficult if you are not ready for it, but we adjusted and played better. In the second half we were the best team. We came back for the third time [this season] and that showed the players are pushing and they have character.”It was a night of firsts. Iraola coached a Champions League game for the first time in his career – he did take charge of 12 Europa League matches with AEK Larnaca in 2018-19 – Bradley Barcola made his first Liverpool start following a £123m move from Paris Saint-Germain and Julián Álvarez was in Atlético’s starting lineup for the first time this season since his failed attempt to join Barcelona. All appeared to have been forgiven – for now at least – as his name was cheered by the small pocket of Atlético fans when the teams were announced before kick-off and he repaid them by creating the opening goal.View image in fullscreenDominik Szoboszlai scores Liverpool’s equaliser late in the first half.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APLlorente was the scourge of Anfield yet again when Álvarez threaded a pass behind the home defence and the right wing-back raced clear on goal. The man who named his dog Anfield after scoring twice to eliminate Jürgen Klopp’s team from the competition in 2020, in the game played while Madrid was in lockdown from the Covid pandemic, lofted a confident finish beyond Alisson. It was Llorente’s fifth goal at Anfield, half of his entire total of Champions League goals. He had been kept onside by Milos Kerkez, who endured a poor night with his positioning and distribution before atoning with a key role in Liverpool’s equaliser.Álvarez almost doubled the visitors’ lead when granted far too much time and space to take aim from almost 30 yards. Alisson, at full stretch, intervened with a superb finger-tip save. Anfield was growing restless at Liverpool’s carelessness on the ball and Atlético’s comfort on it. But the threat and control from the hosts increased.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWirtz drew a fine save from Oblak at the end of a flowing move involving Barcola and Isak. Liverpool then drew level thanks to tenacity from Kerkez, a lovely touch from Ronald Araújo and Szoboszlai’s instinctive finish. The left-back won possession with a clean, crunching challenge on Lee Kang-in before finding Barcola. The France international was denied a goal on his full debut by Oblak’s low save but Wirtz kept the pressure on and Szoboszlai, having been halted on the edge of the area, got a second bite from Araújo’s clever flick. The midfielder’s first time shot sailed into the far corner.Barcola should have put Liverpool ahead when played through on goal by Wirtz early in the second half. The winger had time to measure the finish but pulled it wide of Oblak’s right-hand post. He would later depart with cramp. Liverpool were ahead one minute later when the lively Rio Ngumoha beat Llorente and his cross fell to Mac Allister via a deflection off Isak. Mac Allister told Szoboszlai to leave the ball and drilled home an unstoppable left-footed drive from 20 yards. Atlético remained dangerous and the introduction of Ademola Lookman added an extra dimension to the visitors’ attack but Liverpool defended impressively to secure a deserved victory.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueLiverpoolAtlético MadridEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Rybakina sinks Zheng to grab No 1 spot and set up US Open semi-final with Gauff | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Elena Rybakina will be the new world No 1 after ending Zheng Qinwen’s US Open run, with Coco Gauff up next in the semi-finals
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Elena Rybakina will be the new world No 1 after ending Zheng Qinwen’s US Open run, with Coco Gauff up next in the semi-finals
Content: ‘It’s just a number right now’: Elena Rybakina was typically understated after becoming world No 1.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘It’s just a number right now’: Elena Rybakina was typically understated after becoming world No 1.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026Rybakina sinks Zheng to grab No 1 spot and set up US Open semi-final with GauffRybakina into semis after 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 victoryCoco Gauff battles back to beat Mirra AndreevaTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsWed 9 Sep 2026 17.57 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElena Rybakina will become the No 1 woman in the world for the first time after orchestrating a supreme recovery to reach the semi-finals of the US Open with a 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 win over the Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen.By becoming just the 30th player in the history of the WTA to reach the No 1 ranking, Rybakina ends Aryna Sabalenka’s extended spell at the top. The Belarusian has held the position for 99 successive weeks, the sixth-longest consecutive reign in history, and 107 weeks in total.US Open 2026 quarter-finals: Andreeva v Gauff, Rybakina beats Zheng to become world No 1 – liveRead moreDuring last year’s North American hardcourt swing, Rybakina fell out of the top 10 and she was struggling badly with her health and game. She has responded with by far the best year of her career, following up her WTA Finals triumph in November with her second grand slam titleat the Australian Open, four years after her first triumph at Wimbledon. She has also won titles in Ningbo and Stuttgart in addition to finishing runner-up in Indian Wells and Toronto.Between Sabalenka’s difficult past five months and Rybakina’s resurgence, the Kazakhstani arrived in New York fully conscious of the opportunity before her. The No 1 ranking was always in her hands, with a run to the semi-final guaranteeing it from the beginning.However, so many things seemed to be conspiring against Rybakina. She was forced to retire from her quarter-final against Iga Swiatek at the Cincinnati Open, 12 days before her first round in New York, due to an achilles injury. Rybakina said she did not train for seven days and she was unsure of how her body would react. “I couldn’t do much in the gym movement-wise, so we had to really go day by day,” she said. “It’s an amazing progress. I’m really glad how everything worked out. We didn’t even know if I’m going to be able to play or not. I have a great team. Also, a good doctor on the phone all the time.”View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina shakes hands with Zheng Qinwen after their three-set tussle.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAWhile a semi-final has always been attainable, the US Open has long stood as her most challenging major, the one grand slam Rybakina has struggled to perform at. Her fourth-round loss last year was previously her best result in New York. This time, she has maintained her focus and navigated each challenge.Rybakina started slowly against a Zheng radiating confidence after her previouscomeback victoriesover Madison Keys and Swiatek and in a contest between two of the biggest servers in the world, one sloppy service game from Rybakina marked the difference between them in set one.But the 27-year-old responded brilliantly, finding rhythm behind her destructive serve and dominating the baseline with her easy power to quickly force a third set. Although Rybakina eased through her service games early in set three, it was Zheng who generated the first opportunity, earning a break point at 4-3 in the third set. A tentative forehand approach shot and volley from Rybakina provided Zheng with a straightforward pass, but the Chinese fired her backhand long. Rybakina immediately slammed the door shut with some excellent serves, and she completed a sequence worthy of the best player in the world by rolling through the final three games.As Zheng’s final feeble forehand landed in the bottom of the net, Rybakina celebrated this career-defining milestone in a typically understated manner, her expression barely changing as she meekly closed her hand into a fist. This is a huge achievement that has surely secured her status as a future hall of famer, but the end goal of this week, winning her first US Open title, has still not been attained. After handling the pressure of grabbing the No 1 ranking so impressively, she will be even tougher to beat.“It’s just a number right now,” said Rybakina. “Of course, I’m in the semis so my goal is to win the tournaments which I play, I go just one match at a time. It’s an amazing achievement but you know how quickly everything can change in tennis. I just need to focus on my game, try to recover and enjoy tomorrow.”View image in fullscreenCoco Gauff celebrates after fighting back from a nightmare first set to beat Mirra Andreeva.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPARybakina, the second seed, will next face the fourth seedCoco Gauffafter the American produced a remarkable comeback win against the fifth seedMirra Andreeva, eventually triumphing 2-6, 7-6 (7), 6-2. After struggling with her serve throughout the first half of the match, Gauff saved two match points in the second-set tie-break before marching to victory.With the top-seeded Sabalenka facing Jessica Pegula, the third seed, in the other semi-final, this is the first time in 51 years that each of the top four seeds have reached the US Open women’s semi-finals. It also means that four American players have reached the men’s and women’s singles semi-finals, with two home favourites in each draw.In the men’s draw, the unseededKaren Khachanovadvanced to the semi-finals after his opponent, Alexander Blockx, retired while trailing 6-2, 7-5, 3-2.Blockx was carrying a rib injury into the quarter-final and was visibly hampered by further physical issues, with a brace on his right ankle and strapping on his thigh. Shortly after calling for the trainer at two sets down, the Belgian withdrew after Khachanov broke his serve in the fifth game of the third set.“I was preparing really well for that match-up, it’s not easy because I feel I was dominating then ‌I felt he was struggling more and more,” Khachanov said on court. “He was suffering, but I wanted to ​keep the energy there. I wish him a speedy recovery but I’m super happy I’m in the semis.”Khachanov, who is currently No 50 in the world – his lowest ranking at a major since 2017 – will take on either the No 1 seed, Alexander Zverev, or Botic van de Zandschulp in the semi-finals.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisCoco GauffnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ødegaard ‘edge’ delights Arteta as Arsenal secure narrow win at Napoli | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Martin Ødegaard’s second-half strike gave Arsenal a 1-0 Champions League win in Naples, with Mikel Arteta praising the playmaker’s recent impact
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Martin Ødegaard’s second-half strike gave Arsenal a 1-0 Champions League win in Naples, with Mikel Arteta praising the playmaker’s recent impact
Content: Martin Ødegaard (right) wheels away alongside Bruno Guimarães after scoring the winner.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersView image in fullscreenMartin Ødegaard (right) wheels away alongside Bruno Guimarães after scoring the winner.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersChampions LeagueØdegaard ‘edge’ delights Arteta as Arsenal secure narrow win at NapoliEd Aaronsat the Stadio Diego Armando MaradonaWed 9 Sep 2026 17.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter their record-breaking feats last year in theChampions League, Arsenal are at it again. But having been delayed along with hundreds of travelling supporters by travel chaos on Tuesday, Mikel Arteta’s side had to bide their time against Napoli until Martin Ødegaard continued his rich vein of goalscoring with the crucial strike 15 minutes from full time.Perhaps it was the fact that, at Uefa’s insistence, they were forced to wear red shorts for the first time since a Premier League game against Watford in 2022 thatArsenalwere not quite at their flowing best here and missed a hatful of chances.Alexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat AtléticoRead moreYet they were deserved winners in the end and the substitute Noni Madueke should have made the ­victory more comprehensive late on.Having come so close to breaking their duck in this competition last year after becoming the first team to win all eight of their league stage matches, Arsenal look capable of going one better this time if Ødegaard can keep up this sparkling form.He now has four goals in his last five games after scoring once in all competitions last year and it was the Norway captain whose name was being chanted by the fans who were kept behind more than an hour after the final whistle.“That’s what we need – players with that mindset to decide the game and to play with that personality,” said Arteta. “He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games and I feel he has this emotional state that he knows that the ball can go in. He’s got that edge and he’s now got different relationships around him [in the team] as well. That helps.”Arteta has bad memories of this stadium after being sent off in a 2-0 defeat during the Champions League group stage in 2013. But Arsenal’s most recent match here ended in victory as they qualified for the Europa League semi-finals under Unai Emery in 2019. Both clubs have been crowned domestic champions since then, withNapoliending their 33-year wait in 2023 then doing it again two years later. Yet Champions League success has continued to elude them after finishing 30th in the league phase last season.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta talks with Kevin De Bruyne, the former Manchester City midfielder, after the match.Photograph: Ciro De Luca/ReutersThat was in stark contrast to Arsenal, who were unbeaten over 14 matches before falling at the final hurdle. It was telling that Arteta kept faith with four of his back five that started against Chelsea on Sunday, with Piero Hincapié replacing Riccardo Calafiori at left-back but failing to match the Italian’s finishing ability with one glaring miss. Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyökeres also made their first starts of the season but largely disappointed, with the Sweden striker making way for Kai Havertz just before Ødegaard’s winner.Those Arsenal supporters that did make it to southern Italy had no problem making themselves heard throughout, with plenty of empty seats in the home sections despite Max Allegri’s attempts to rally Napoli’s fans beforehand. The game quickly settled into a pattern as the visitors set up camp in Napoli’s half and the hosts attempted to hit them on the break. Kevin De Bruyne – no stranger to facing Arsenal after a decade in the sky blue of Manchester City – forced David Raya into a rare mistake after a typically driving run through the midfield but the ball was scrambled away to safety.That came just after a spectacular overhead kick from Bukayo Saka at the other end had been saved by Alex Meret. Merino should have scored when he was set up by Eze’s clever header across the face of goal before Ben White drilled a shot straight into Meret’s grateful gloves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMatteo Politano managed to test Raya again as Napoli continued to find gaps in Arsenal’s normally watertight defence. Saka blazed over after a brilliant through ball from Ødegaard on the stroke of half-time, with replays confirming the assistant had been wrong to raise his flag.View image in fullscreenMartin Ødegaard scores the only goal of the match at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesMeret did not return for the second half and was replaced by Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, once on Manchester United’s books. The Serbia goalkeeper was a mere spectator for a flowing Arsenal move featuring a sumptuous scooped pass into the area that ended with Hincapié missing the target after being picked out at the far post by Ben White’s header. Suddenly Napoli found themselves suffocated by a blanket of red. Allegri, who knows what it feels like to have lost in a Champions League final after suffering that fate twice in three years at Juventus, responded by switching to a back five and trying to hang on.Arsenal’s pressure eventually told when another substitute, Christos Tzolis, exchanged passes with White and teed up Ødegaard, whose shot flew in off the post despite Milinkovic-Savic just getting his fingertips to the ball. Havertz had a goal disallowed for offside in injury time, but the mission was already complete.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueNapoliArsenalEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Cole Palmer powers Chelsea to comeback win over Leeds in nine-goal epic | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Chelsea scored six second-half goals after making four half-time substitutions in a thrilling 6-3 win against Leeds in the Carabao Cup third round
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Chelsea scored six second-half goals after making four half-time substitutions in a thrilling 6-3 win against Leeds in the Carabao Cup third round
Content: Cole Palmer plays to the crowd after starting Chelsea’s fightback against Leeds.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCole Palmer plays to the crowd after starting Chelsea’s fightback against Leeds.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesCarabao CupCole Palmer powers Chelsea to comeback win over Leeds in nine-goal epicJacob Steinbergat Stamford BridgeWed 9 Sep 2026 17.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhere’s the fun in doing it the easy way? Chelsea remain chaotic at the back but can drag their opponents into horrible places. It helps, mind you, to have some assistance from the referee. Jarred Gillett and Cole Palmer? They made for a killer ­combination as Chelsea swerved embarrassment and treated Stamford Bridge to one of life’s rarities: a classic in the third round of theCarabao Cup.Gillett, a referee who always seems to be guessing when he makes key calls, was the villain as far as Leeds were concerned. They had just gone 2-0 up when Gillett altered the flow of the tie by pointing to the spot after Pep Chavarría made the most of slight contact from Daniel James. The subsequent conversion from Palmer was inevitable and from there so was the comeback fromChelsea, who rattled through four goals in 12 minutes before eventually reaching the last 16 by winning 6-3.Ødegaard stuns Napoli as Arsenal make winning start in Champions LeagueRead moreIt made little sense. It could have gone down as Xabi Alonso’s first ­misjudgment as Chelsea’s manager. The Carabao Cup is important given the Spaniard’s side are not in Europe, but his rotation almost backfired. Chelsea were shambolic after making nine changes – the 16-year-old debutant Reggie Watson was overrun in midfield while Estêvão Willian and Jamie Gittens struggled in attack – and Alonso was in emergency mode when he made a quadruple change at half-time.“I take responsibility,” Alonso said. “No player is to blame. It’s the ­decisions we took. When you don’t have this time to work with them, it’s difficult to compete at this level. I need to take my own blame for the things that happen. I need to be able to help them better. They are not responsible. After you need to react and think what’s better for the team.”Quick GuideChampionship: Ten-man West Brom win at Derby to go topShowWest Bromwich Albion held on for a memorable 1-0 victory over Derby at Pride Park, after playing for more than an hour with 10 men. Aune Heggebø's early goal proved enough to take the Baggies top of the table, despite Brayann Pereira being dismissed on his debut after collecting two first-half yellow cards.Derby had started the stronger, but West Brom swept downfield to score in the 16th minute, Jimmy-Jay Morgan whipping in a low cross from the left which Heggebø [pictured] finished at the near post. The visitors were rocked by the dismissal of Pereira in the 34th minute, as he was shown a second yellow card for a clumsy challenge on Charlie Taylor.The hosts went close just before half-time when David Ozoh flashed a low ball across the six-yard box with no white shirt able to turn it in. Derby should have levelled in the 68th minute but Lars-Jørgen Salvesen headed over from Joe Ward’s cross. Late on, Nat Phillips made a great clearance after a late goalmouth scramble, summing up a performance full of grit and resolve.James Morrison's side move above West Ham to top the Championship table with 13 points from six games. EitherCharltonorQPRcould have joined them on 13 points, but the sides played out a stalemate at the Valley. Derby, meanwhile, slipped into the bottom three with their fourth defeat in six games.Norwichmoved up to ninth in the table as they edged past visitorsBirmingham2-1 to make it three wins in four league games. Oscar Schwartau's screamer opened the scoring, the young Dane lashing an unstoppable right-footed drive past James Beadle from 25 yards out.Papa Diallo's first goal for the Canaries doubled their advantage before the break, as the Senegal winger sidefooted home from Andre Brooks' cross. Carlos Vicente pulled a goal back for the visitors, but wasted a glorious chance to equalise near the end as Chris Davies’ men suffered their first league defeat this season.Press AssociationPhotograph: Morgan Harlow/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Equally Alonso can take credit for responding. His moves were decisive. Reece James offered security after replacing Watson and Pedro Neto scored after coming on for Malo Gusto, who could barely complete a pass during a wretched first half. Leeds, beaten at this stage for the 14th time in 18 years, were overwhelmed once their lead was halved. Morgan Rogers and Palmer were devastating after replacing Estêvão and Gittens. Rogers had a hand in four goals and Palmer, who scored twice, seemed affronted by the notion of Leeds going through.It finished as another thrilling attacking display from Chelsea, who have scored 16 goals in Alonso’s first five games. There are flaws to fix at the other end, though. Leeds also experimented, Daniel Farke making eight changes, but controlled the first half. They led when the Bosnia and Herzegovina centre-back Tarik Muharemovic, signed from Sassuolo last summer, headed Harry Wilson’s corner past Mike Penders in the 23rd minute.Chelsea have already conceded 10 goals in all competitions. Leeds could have doubled their lead through Sean Longstaff. Valentín Barco and ­Watson, son of the former Wigan ­midfielder Ben Watson, were second best in midfield.Leeds were on their way when Barco lost possession three minutes into the second half. Ethan Ampadu charged past Rogers and found Lukas Nmecha, who teed up Brenden ­Aaronson to make it 2-0.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPedro Neto fires home Chelsea’s third goal at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAChelsea needed a lift. Chavarría crossed from the left and went to ground. Gillett whistled and Palmer scored with 53 minutes played. “He gave out of nothing a penalty where it wasn’t even a chance for them,” Farke said. “A quality player scores and the body language of the Chelsea players was different.”Palmer was in his element, equalising in the 55th minute after Rogers laid the ball off for his pal to stroke a casual finish past Michael Zetterer from 20 yards. Chelsea were rampant and led on the hour, Palmer and Rogers combining for Neto to finish well. Leeds looked dizzy. They readied the changes but Danny Welbeck made it 4-2 with a sharp turn and finish in the 65th minute.Leeds kept fighting. Dominic Calvert-Lewin came on and pulled one back to remind Alonso of Chelsea’s defensive weaknesses. Chelsea responded, Rogers crossing for Barco to score his first goal for the club. The sixth followed, Barco’s mis-hit shot diverted in by Welbeck. “A crazy nuts game,” Farke said. That’s been the way for Chelsea under Alonso.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupChelseaLeeds Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Grim predictability blights Pakistan’s brief moments of light amid Test gloom | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Razaullah offered the tourists a glimpse of audacity but it was Babar Azam who embodied the wider loss of hope
Author: Andy Bull
Headline: Razaullah offered the tourists a glimpse of audacity but it was Babar Azam who embodied the wider loss of hope
Content: Babar Azam’s continued struggles summed up where Pakistan’s Test team finds itself.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBabar Azam’s continued struggles summed up where Pakistan’s Test team finds itself.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesEngland v Pakistan 2026AnalysisGrim predictability blights Pakistan’s brief moments of light amid Test gloomAndy Bullat EdgbastonRazaullah offered the tourists a glimpse of audacity but it was Babar Azam who embodied the wider loss of hopeWed 9 Sep 2026 14.37 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareIt was still morning when Babar Azam came in to bat at Edgbaston. The Test was only 45 minutes old but you could already see which direction it was heading. Pakistan were three wickets down. The floodlights were on, a thick smear of black cloud was moving slowly over the ground, there were odd spots of rain in the air. Ollie Robinson was bowling from one end, with the keeper standing up and five slips spread in a line just behind, and Jofra Archer was on at the other, four overs into his spell and only just warming up. It was a hell of a time to be batting.But then it always seems to be, lately.Once upon a time, and not so very long ago, Babar was one of the very best batters in the game. In the space of eight Tests in 2022 he scored 196 against Australia in Karachi, 119 against Sri Lanka in Galle,136 against England in Rawalpindi, and 161 against New Zealand back in Karachi. He finished that year with a Test batting average of 49, third in the world rankings, and as the ICC’s Men’s Cricketer of the Year. But he hasn’t scored a Test hundred since. In his past 20 Tests, his top score is 88 and his batting average is 29.Gay and Brook put England in complete control after Pakistan crumble once moreRead moreStill, if you shut your eyes a moment and played out the day in your head you could just about imagine that he would be able to steer his team through this, the way he often used to be able to do when he was at his best. And then you opened them again.Babar set himself for Robinson’s first ball. He seemed uncertain of whether or not to play it, and pulled his bat inside the line at the very last moment. The next delivery beat his outside edge, then he clipped the third through square leg to score his first couple of runs. Second over, Babar slashed at a short ball from Archer, but missed it. Third over, he was up against Gus Atkinson, and was beaten twice before squirting an edge away for four. In the fourth he was clean bowled by Josh Tongue for seven off 18 balls.There was a grim predictability to all this. Pakistan have scored 171, 135, 110, 194 and now 133 in this series. If they’re bowled out cheaply again in their second innings here they will be the first team since the 19th century to be dismissed for under 200 in every innings of a three-Test series in this country. They are a broken side,and leading them is an impossible job. Babar, who is notionally one of their selectors, said he didn’t even know that the management were goingto send him seven new players for this match.“It was news to me,” Babar said when he was asked about it. “I found out after.”It was one of those seven late replacements who came striding into the Test later in the day, when he came on first change from the City End. Bowler’s name? Who is this again? You needed to be a keen follower of Pakistani domestic cricket to have any real idea. Razaullah is 21, and only played his first game of big-time cricket last November when he made his debut for Peshawar in the Quaid-e-Azam Trophy, Pakistan’s main first-class tournament. Since then he’s played seven first-class matches, nine one-dayers, and seven T20s, and now, after being flown over for this one Test, here he was.The first thing we found out about Razaullah was that he is a lashing bat, the second was that he is lightning quick, and the third was that he is richly gifted. His first three deliveries hurried Joe Root. Then his fourth came whistling in and beat the inside of Root’s bat as he dropped it in a late attempt to block the ball. It hit him on the front pad flush in front of middle stump. Root, bamboozled, called for a review which only confirmed what everyone else already knew.He was out LBW (again).Razaullah had his first international wicket, and with it he gave every cricket fan in the ground a little glimpse of some of what they love about Pakistani cricket:the speed, the audacity, the vivacity, the immaculate hair. Later on he got another of them, Emilio Gay this time, with a 90mph delivery that flew off the inside edge of Gay’s bat as he tried to drive and clattered into his stumps.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenRazaullah’s promising debut included dismissing Joe Root after tea with his fourth delivery in Test cricket.Photograph: Philip Brown/Getty ImagesPakistan has never, will never, lack for natural talent. Even when everything else is falling apart, another fine fast bowler turns up. Only, if you’ve a long memory, you might remember the way Naseem Shah and Shaheen Shah Afridi bowled here on their first tour of England back in 2020 and ask exactlywhy neither of them made it back here this year. You might ask what the Pakistani set-up has done for all the fast-bowling talent they have had come through in the past decade. You might look at what’s become of Babar’s batting over the same period.And you might wonder what, exactly, lies along the road for Razaullah in the years ahead.And the problem is, you probably know the answer.Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketanalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m not a robot’: Josh Kerr primed to peak against arch rival Ingebrigtsen  | Athletics | The Guardian
description: A $150,000 prize in Budapest has the record-breaking Scot buzzing but the middle-distance star insists he’s no longer chasing paydays
