Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: A $150,000 prize in Budapest has the record-breaking Scot buzzing but the middle-distance star insists he’s no longer chasing paydays
Content: Josh Kerr has had to rely on a wild card to compete at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJosh Kerr has had to rely on a wild card to compete at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianAthleticsInterview‘I’m not a robot’: Josh Kerr primed to peak against arch rival IngebrigtsenSean IngleA $150,000 prize in Budapest has the record-breaking Scot buzzing but the middle-distance star insists he’s no longer chasing paydaysWed 9 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe richest event in track and field history launches in Budapest this weekend, and the prospect of walking away with $150,000 at the WorldAthleticsUltimate Championship has got Josh Kerr ready to rumble again, on and off the track.Some critics have noted that the Scot has run only five times in 2026 – compared with Amy Hunt’s 43 races – and has had to rely on a wild card from World Athletics to even compete in Budapest.Others, including the double Olympic championJakob Ingebrigtsen, have questioned why Kerr swerved the chance to race in front of his home fans at the European championships in Birmingham last month.Josh Kerr: ‘What has running taught me about life? If you are determined enough, you can 100% do it’Read moreKerr’s response? To insist that “I’m not a robot”, before pointing out that in four of his five races this year he hasbroken the world mile record, set a personal best over 800m, and won gold at the world indoor championships over 3,000m and the Commonwealth Games over 1500m.“I’m tired of just saying it,” he says. “I’m a human being at the end of the day. And to run a world indoor championships and come out with a gold medal there, go after a PB over 800m, which I was able to do for the first time in seven years, get a Commonwealth Games gold medal, and and also go get a a world record, and then go after an outdoor major championships, that’s enough for me. I’m not a robot.“The first question I was asked after running the mile world record is: ‘When are you going to go after the 1500m world record?’ And it’s just not that simple to peak like we did for London, and then to reset for the Commonwealth Games, and then reset again for a world record attempt, and then reset again for Europeans, and then reset again for Ultimates.”Kerr has not been seen on a track since competing in Glasgow in early August, which has meant missing out on paydays and a chance to further promote his sport. But the 28-year-old athlete insists he deliberately targets “two to four big dates a year” and wants to race only when he is in prime shape.“I’m not trying to avoid racing. I love racing. I just don’t love racing when I’m not ready to go. And the reason I can race so well is because I pick my races. These next three years are going to be some of the biggest in my career. So I’m not going to get greedy.“If you race a bunch, you’re going to have long-term injury problems, if you want to have a career that’s 10 or 12 years long, then you can’t do that. I’ve been caught chasing paydays early on in my career, and it doesn’t end up with long-term success.”However, Kerr is excited by the Ultimate Championship, a new three-day competition which effectively serves as a mini world championships. The event, which has a $10m prize fund, is also being used as a testing ground for innovations in the sport, including a black infield, athletes being allowed to make content, and a more party-style atmosphere, all designed to attract a younger audience.View image in fullscreenJosh Kerr surges past Jakob Ingebrigtsen on the final bend on his way to world 1500m glory in 2023 in Budapest, where they will renew their rivalry on Sunday.Photograph: Tim Clayton/Corbis/Getty Images“I think it would be a lot more of an off-year, or a dud year, without a championship that we can all attend in September,” Kerr says. “Packing out stadiums, putting on a championship that people enjoy, and pushing the marketing on it. There’s only really one step left of how the sport gets bigger, and I think it’s sports betting.”Kerr is in no doubt who his money will be on if he ends up racing his nemesis Ingebrigtsen, who is scheduled to compete in the 5,000m on Friday and then against the Scot in the 1500m final on Sunday.“I’m very happy that he’s back running and racing,” Kerr says. “I think it’s great. He’s one of the best 1500m and 5k runners of all time, and I’m excited to go out and race him. I’m not going to lose, but I’m excited to go out there and race.”Kerr is also excited about athletics being able to capitalise on the global running boom, and says the improved prize money is another sign that the sport is heading in the right direction. “We’re seeing progress, I’m not going to complain about progress,” he says.double quotation markI’m here to prove that I’m going to be the best 1500m runner of all timeJosh Kerr“Obviously, $150,000 is is a lot of money. It’s not as much as other big sports, but they’ve earned that through years and years of continuing to push into marketing, and we’re moving in the right direction with these championships, and so I can’t complain.”As Kerr points out, it’s also harder for lots of athletes to make money because there are so many events. “In tennis, there’s one winner,” he says. “In track and field, there’s 25 winners. But races and contracts are doing a lot better than they’ve ever been. Running is going through a boom, and we’re seeing that in shoe sales, on the athlete side, as well as social media.”Meanwhile, returning to Budapest brings back happy memories for Kerr, given it was where he won his first world title in 2023. “It was an incredibly pivotal day for me. Your first world title is the most special. I just hadn’t really won a lot. And it was starting to really piss me off.”While Kerr faces a strong field that includes the Olympic championCole Hockerand theDiamond League final winner Cameron Myers, it is clear he expects to win again. “I’m here to prove that I’m going to be the best 1500m runner of all time or of our generation at least,” he says.“There are different ways to win a championship. One is to be so dominant that no one else has an option to win. That is what we are going for this year. If you want to make it fast, if you want to make it slow, you are going to be in trouble either way. That’s what Budapest should be for me.”Explore more on these topicsAthleticsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Infantino installs loyalist to oversee Caribbean as he splits Fifa management  | Football politics | The Guardian
description: Fifa president’s move is widely regarded by his opponents as an attempt to split the Concacaf nations working with Uefa to remove him from office
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa president’s move is widely regarded by his opponents as an attempt to split the Concacaf nations working with Uefa to remove him from office
Content: Gianni Infantino last weekend reaffirmed his intention to seek re-election as Fifa’s president.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino last weekend reaffirmed his intention to seek re-election as Fifa’s president.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersFootball politicsInfantino installs loyalist to oversee Caribbean as he splits Fifa managementCritics view Fernandes job as move to shore up positionFifa says change is designed to make sport ‘truly global’Exclusive byMatt HughesandNick AmesWed 9 Sep 2026 13.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino has separated Fifa’s management of the Caribbean countries from the rest of Concacaf in a move widely regarded by his opponents as an attempt to split the alliance to remove him from office.Concacaf covers North and Central America as well as the Caribbean and was previously managed as one bloc. Butthe Guardian has learned that the former Switzerland midfielder Gelson Fernandes, an Infantino loyalist, has been appointed as the director of member associations for the Caribbean, in addition to his position looking after Fifa’s African members.More than 100,000 people add names to complaint against Gianni InfantinoRead moreFernandes, who played for Manchester City, Leicester and eight other clubs, joined Fifa in 2022 as director of member associations for Africa and was promoted two years later to become deputy chief members associations officer globally.The 40-year-old works closely with Fifa’s chief members associations officer, Elkhan Mammadov, a close ally of Infantino described by many national associations as the president’s key enforcer.Fernandes has replaced Jair Bertoni as Fifa’s liaison with the 21 Caribbean-based members, with the national associations and Concacaf informed of the change last week without consultation.In a statement Fifa confirmed the appointment, which it said was designed to support Infantino’s vision of making the sport truly global.“Fifa can confirm that Gelson Fernandes has taken on responsibility for the Caribbean region, in addition to his current role as regional director Africa,” it said. “With his extensive experience at Fifa and strong knowledge of football development programmes, Gelson will lead the regional team and will work closely with the member associations across the Caribbean to further support the development of football in their respective countries, following the Fifa president’s vision: making football truly global.”Concacaf is attempting with Uefa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC)to oust Infantino. Sources at several member associations in Europe and North America regard the change as an attempt to split the Concacaf vote before March’s presidential election, with one characterising it as “an administrative war” against its president,Victor Montagliani.The Canadian is viewed by many in Uefa as the most credible candidate to beat Infantino, although Montagliani has yet to decide whether to stand and is committed to seeking re-election as Concacaf’s president.Infantino has stepped up his re-election campaign in the aftermath of the World Cup sell-off scandal, ignoring a written request from Montagliani to stay away from a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) in the Dominican Republic last month.Asrevealed by the Guardian, Infantino used the CFU meeting to announce approval for numerous Fifa-funded development projects for the region worth millions of dollars in what some observers described as an attempt to lobby for votes.Mexico has split from Concacaf by announcing its support for Infantino, and losing the backing of the Caribbean would be a significant setback for those pushing to remove Infantino.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere have been some early signs that Infantino’s tactics are paying off, with the president of the Jamaican federation, Michael Ricketts, this week backing the status quo and comparing Uefa to spoiled children.“Infantino might have made a mistake, but the intentions were to help Caribbean countries or help smaller countries,” Rickets told the Jamaica Observer. “Can you imagine Jamaica getting $40m to invest in football? Can you imagine the difference that would make in four or five years?“I am not supporting Uefa because I think that they always want to be in opposition and always want to oppose. It doesn’t matter who is president, they are going to have issues. It doesn’t matter how well the president does, they are going to have issues and I think that Uefa is behaving like a set of spoilt kids.”Uefa’s 55 members are believed to be united but the strength of the AFC alliance is unclear, with Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates having defied the confederation by endorsing Infantino.Infantino last weekend reaffirmed hisintention to seek re-electionfor a fourth term. The deadline for other candidates seeking to stand is 18 November.Explore more on these topicsFootball politicsGianni InfantinoFifanewsShareReuse this content

title: NFL 2026 season predictions: which teams can bring down the Rams juggernaut? | NFL | The Guardian
description: The new season kicks off on Wednesday night. Our writers have their say on the MVP, rookies to watch and the disasters waiting to happen
Author: Doug Farrar
Headline: The new season kicks off on Wednesday night. Our writers have their say on the MVP, rookies to watch and the disasters waiting to happen
Content: Fernando Mendoza, Josh Allen, Myles Garrett, Patrick Mahomes and Ja'Marr Chase will play prominent roles this season.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty)View image in fullscreenFernando Mendoza, Josh Allen, Myles Garrett, Patrick Mahomes and Ja'Marr Chase will play prominent roles this season.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty)NFLNFL 2026 season predictions: which teams can bring down the Rams juggernaut?The new season kicks off on Wednesday night. Our writers have their say on the MVP, rookies to watch and the disasters waiting to happenDoug Farrar,Bryan Armen Graham,Andrew LawrenceandGraham SearlesWed 9 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis will be the year of ...Quarterbacks living under center.The NFL has developed into a shotgun league, where most quarterbacks take the majority of their snaps three to seven yards away from the center.But the increase in efficiencywhen it comes to snaps taken right behind the center should have coaches directing their quarterbacks to do more of it. Matthew Stafford, Caleb Williams, and Sam Darnold led the way in 2025, and others will follow.DFSuperteams.The Rams have pushed their chips to the middle of the table by loading up on high-end veterans and deferring much of the cost to future years. Myles Garrett and the unretired Aaron Donald join Stafford, Puka Nacua and a secondary reinforced by Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. Superteamsare never a sure thingin the NFL, but the Rams’ terrifyingly stacked roster looks awfully close.BAGSuper Bowl sequel hype, the year the scriptwriters lay a path for a Rams-Bengals rematch in Los Angeles. Both teams have gone to considerable lengths to shore up the defensive side of the ball, with the Rams swinging a mega trade for Garrett on the heels of the Bengals’ draft-week swap for Pro Bowl tackle Dexter Lawrence.ALFinally saying goodbye to Aaron Rodgers. Let’s forget allthe weirdnessaround the latter years of his career and remember Rodgers as simply one of the best to ever do it. Maybe with Mike McCarthy calling plays again, he can keep Pittsburgh in contention for a wildcard. Even if he fails, you can guarantee seeing some of the old magic in his final season in the NFL.GSBest team that won’t make the playoffs ...This is the second straight seasonI’ve pushed theVikingshere, and for the same reasons – the NFC North is the league’s most competitive division, and there is no outstanding candidate at quarterback. Brian Flores’s defense will be marvelous as it always is,and were it not for his ongoing lawsuit against the league, he’d probably be a head coach right now. A three-man quarterback competition is not the best way to maximize one’s competitive window, though.DFDak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb are back for an offense that can put up points with almost anybody. But the NFC is deep and unforgiving and theCowboys’ front seven looks alarmingly short of difference-makers beyond star defensive tackle Quinnen Williams and Rashan Gary. Nine wins, constant frustration and a third straight January on the couch sounds about right.BAGTheVikings’ defense always gives them a chance, and their offensive skill players are elite. It just comes down to what Murray can give them and, historically, that’s been a lot of inconsistency.ALIt will be a battle for Ben Johnson to keep the lightning in the bottle with aBearsdefense that thrived on takeaways rather than fundamentals last season. They haven’t made many significant moves – outside first-round safety Dillon Thieneman – to tune things up, then the impressive offense could be let down with a near miss in the wildcard race.GSMost underrated team ...It’s easy to forget that in the 2021 season, theBengalslost the Super Bowl by three points, and in 2022, they lost the AFC Championship game by the same margin. Those close calls were followed by matching 9-8 seasons in 2023 and 2024, and last season’s 6-11 faceplant. But if Joe Burrow can stay healthy, these Bengals have a ton of talent on both sides of the ball (led by new defensive line monster Lawrence).DFJustin Herbert is class and Mike McDaniel’s arrival as offensive coordinator will add some imagination and flair to the offense. But winning 11 games still leaves you overshadowed when Denver’s complete roster and Patrick Mahomes’ Kansas City headline your division. TheChargersare quiet contenders hiding in plain sight.BAGLast I checked, theChiefsnot only return Patrick Mahomes – the QB standard before the ACL injury (hardly the career killers they used to be) – but also Eric Bieniemy, the offensive coordinator who held players accountable and infused the team’s gameplay with so much confidence and whimsy.ALBaker Mayfield was quietly brilliant last season and theBuccaneershave a strong roster across the board that finished 8-9 after a 6-2 start because of a number of key players missing time through injury. A bit of luck with the injury bug and the Bucs could spring a surprise.GSView image in fullscreenDeshaun Watson: the worst quarterback $230m can buy.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APJohnny Manziel disaster waiting to happen department ...The Browns’ quarterback situation.What else could it be? At this point, the Browns may as well bring Manziel back to add even more of a tragic comic cast to the whole thing. Head coach Todd Monkennaming Deshaun Watson the Week 1 starterafter Watson played horriblyandalienated the fanbase in the preseason – never mind the horrid off-field history for which Watson has never taken an ounce of accountability – is merely the first level of Dante’s Inferno.DFCleveland naming Watson their Week 1 starter. A $230m albatross coming off multiple achilles tears would have been a risky first choice even if he’d been playing well before getting hurt. The Browns’ decision to roster three other quarterbacks, including Dillon Gabriel on injured reserve, feels prescient here.BAGAnthony Richardsonsurvived trade rumors and played well enough in camp to win the Colts’ backup QB job. But I say the detente only holds up as long as Daniel Jones’s health, which has never been the greatest, and Richardson’s uneven play in relief makes him a lame duck QB all over again – and his controversial behavior gives the organization cover for the bad fit once more.ALThe Brownsmissing Garrett’s tremendous pass rush and leadership is a recipe for a very tricky season if they make a slow start. And with Watson starting at quarterback they most likely will.GSMVP …Drake Maye, QB, New England Patriots.While I don’t have the Patriots winning the AFC East this season, I think that with the additions of receivers AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs, and coming off a full season in Josh McDaniels’ offense, Maye has everything he needs to take the next step to become an unquestioned Top 10 quarterback. He was exactly that until the Patriots faced a murderers’ row of defenses in the playoffs and his protection fell apart, but the growth he showed in everything from reading the field to taking disguised coverages apart presaged that next level.DFLamar Jackson, QB, Baltimore Ravens.The Ravens enter a new era under first-year coach Jesse Minter, but their fortunes still revolve around the NFL’s most disruptive player. The 29-year-old Jackson can unhinge defenses with his arm, legs or simply the threat of either. If Baltimore can get to 12 or 13 wins, he becomes the best bet to enter the exclusive club of three-time MVPs.BAGJoe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals.Now that he has a defense behind him again, Joe Cool can get back to lighting up the scoreboard and his cigar after the dubs.ALJoe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals.The quarterback finished last year showing some of his best work, so this could be Burrow’s time with incredible weapons Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins at his disposal.GSThe best rookie will be ...Caleb Downs, DB, Dallas Cowboys.The Cowboys’ 2025 defense was one of the worst in recent memory, which is why they replaced Matt Eberflus with Christian Parker as defensive coordinator. Parker’s background with the Philadelphia Eagles and defensive wizard Vic Fangio should pay immediate dividends, and Downs, the Ohio State alum selected with the 11th overall pick, should thrive in Parker’s concepts.DFJadarian Price, RB, Seattle Seahawks.With Kenneth Walker III gone and Zach Charbonnet starting the season on the Physically Unable to Perform list, the Seahawks will plug-and-play their first-round draft pick from Notre Dame into a backfield fresh off a Super Bowl title.BAGJeremiyah Love, RB, Arizona Cardinals.The Notre Dame prospect shouldn’t lack for opportunities to get the ball off tackle, in space or however else coach Mike LaFleur seeks to make use of the Saquon Barkley clone he simply couldn’t pass up in this year’s draft.ALCarnell Tate, WR, Tennessee Titans. The No 4 pick has the total package of speed, route running and size. Tate caught the eye in training camp working with second-year quarterback Cam Ward. He will continue to do so throughout 2026.GSAFC East championI’m picking theBillsfor one reason, and it’s not Josh Allen – it’s Jim Leonhard. Buffalo’s new defensive coordinator is one of the finest minds in football, and he’ll have that defense asserting itself in ways it never did under Sean McDermott. New England will still be up there after 2025’s Cinderella season, but a tougher schedule andpossible regression when it comes to their unusual injury luckshould have them taking a step back.DFNew England won it last year and added star wideout Brown, but a regression from 14 wins is almost inevitable even if the Super Bowl loser’s cursehas mostly been debunked. TheBillshave Allen, DJ Moore and enough defensive talent for first-year coach Joe Brady to take back a division the Bills owned for five straight years before last season.BAGNot because theBillsare necessarily better than the team that beat them to the top last year. But because New England’s schedule is so much tougher this year, and one loss makes all the difference in this chilly rivalry.ALA straight shootout between New England and Buffalo. With fresh ideas from Brady, theBillscould have an important edge but there’s not much wriggle room in their opening five games against the Texans, Lions, Chargers, Patriots and Rams. Escaping with a winning record from that run would provide a solid platform to regain dominance.GSView image in fullscreenJoe Burrow is an MVP candidate. But will he stay healthy?Photograph: Chris Szagola/APAFC North championTrading for Lawrence was the splashy story of theBengals’ offseason, but there’s a lot more to like here – especially if Burrow can stay healthy. If he can, I like the Bengals to outpace the Ravens and Steelers based on star power with receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, and a defense that has a lot of ascending players.DFMinter has been dealt an enviable hand with Jackson, Derrick Henry and a roster built to win now. Cincinnati should push them, but theRavens’ combination of quarterback play, running game and defensive stability remains the division’s safest bet.BAGTheBengals. Here’s a sentence no one’s ever written until now: Mike Brown, the NFL’s resident cheapskate, is all in.ALIf Burrow just has a full season working behind an improved offensive line, then theBengalshave a great shot at unseating the Ravens. Their schedule is soft enough that they should be aiming for well over 10 wins.GSAFC South championI’m taking theTexansover the Jaguars because of a defense that needs no schematic tricks to upend enemy offenses – they’re good enough to just line up and go right at you. All the Texans need from quarterback CJ Stroud is a level of play a bit above league-average.DFTheTexansdefense is one of the NFL’s best with Will Anderson Jr, Derek Stingley Jr and Kamari Lassiter leading the way. Whether Stroud and the offense can hold up their end of the bargain remains the rub, but it should be enough in this middling division.BAGTheJaguarsrepeatedly found ways to win tight games in 2025, giving a young team meaningful late-game experience – and a plausible foundation to turn last year’s surge into a deep postseason run.ALThe defense returns almost unchanged after a brilliant 2025 with some good additions in safety Reed Blankenship and rookie run-stopper Kayden McDonald. TheTexanshave quality and consistency a level above the messy Jaguars and Colts.GSAFC West championI really like what new Chargers offensive coordinator McDaniel will do for Herbert, and I expect the Chiefs to rebound to a point from last season’s disaster. But the 2025Broncosgot all the way to the AFC Championship game, and they may have progressed further had quarterback Bo Nix not suffered a broken ankle in the divisional round. Now, Nix has a new best buddy to help him – former Miami Dolphins receiver Jaylen Waddle,who gives that offense a level of vertical juiceit hasn’t had before.DFThey’d probably be defending NFL champions if not forNix’s untimely injuryin the playoffs. TheBroncosdefense remains elite, the offensive line is right there with it and the addition of Waddle gives them another weapon on offense alongside Courtland Sutton. Nix’s mission with the AFC’s deepest roster boils down to three words: do no harm.BAGTheChargersmade many of the right moves this offseason: keeping most of their receiving corps intact, adding David Njoku and big-play tailback Keaton Mitchell, and rebuilding the interior offensive line. Losing new center Tyler Biadasz to injury is a major blow, but if the line holds together well enough, Herbert and a deep, balanced roster give the Bolts a real chance to edge Kansas City and Denver.ALThe Chiefs and Chargers should be well in the mix but theBroncosstill have the edge after last year’s dominance before Nix went down in the playoffs.GSNFC East championTheCowboysbag the crown based on an offense that’s already fully loaded, and a defense that should be worlds better than in 2025. They are the Inverse Houston Texans in that all that defense has to do is play at a pretty good level to blow a lot of opponents away.DFBrown is gone and Jalen Hurts will be working with his seventh different play-caller in as many NFL seasons, but theEagles’ institutional strength has been the envy of the NFC East for decades now. A potentially top-five defense and a rejuvenated ground game featuring Saquon Barkley will provide enough margin for error to outlast a division filled with flawed rivals.BAGWith Brown and coordinator Kevin Patullo gone, theEaglesoffense should fly again behind Barkley and Hurts – in make or break year mode not that long after leading the team to Super Bowl glory.ALTheCowboysare hardly a sleeping giant, but if the defense is as reborn as defensive tackle Williams claims it is then maybe Dallas can finally balance the books with their dynamic offense and reclaim the division.GSView image in fullscreenCaleb Williams faces one of the toughest divisions in football.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APNFC North championClose your eyes and throw a dart at the NFL’s toughest division, and you have a 25% chance of being right. The Lions, Packers, and Vikings all have reason for hope, but ifBearshead coach Ben Johnson can refine quarterback Caleb Williams, and Dennis Allen’s defense can improve over last season’s boom-or-bust results –they led the NFL in turnover differential, butranked 23rd in points allowed– it’s Chicago’s time to shine.DFChicago may be the trendy pick and Green Bay dangerous floaters, but theLionsstill have enough offensive firepower and strength along the line of scrimmage to hold them off in the NFL’s deepest division.BAGTheLionswere burned by injuries last year and still stayed in the playoff hunt almost to the end. They are positioned for a rebound, with more of their core available and one of the league’s easiest schedules – a chance to bank early wins while key pieces work their way back from early-season absences.ALThePackersremain without Micah Parsons until at least Week 5 but a look at their first four opponents – the Vikings, Jets, Falcons and Buccaneers – points to a hot start.GSNFC South championMayfield was outstanding in the first half of the 2025 seasonbefore his own injuries, and the injuries of those around him, took their toll. TheBuccaneersstarted the season 6-2 before falling off to 8-9. With better luck things should look quite a bit better in 2026.DFTheBuccaneershave the most settled quarterback situation, enough skill-position talent and a defense that’s just good enough. Carolina are the likeliest threat while neither Atlanta nor rebuilding New Orleans have enough to mount a serious challenge.BAGThere’s little incentive to go against theBuccaneers, the gold standard in the league’s most volatile division.ALOff the back of late-season success in 2025, theSaintswill be feeling good about their chances. If second-year quarterback Tyler Shough maintains his upward trajectory they should be confident.GSNFC West championWhile there arereasons to questionthe ultimate validity of theRams’ “all-in” approach that culminated with the return of Donald, there’s enough in the hypothetical to give Sean McVay’s team a slight edge over the Seahawks – if only because Seattle didn’t follow their Super Bowl win by radically stocking their defense as the Rams did.DFThere are legitimate durability questions around the aging Stafford and the returning Donald for theRams. But it’s hard to imagine anyone challenging a roster tricked out with as much high-end talent as any NFL team in years. Anything short of a division title would qualify as a serious underachievement.BAGTheRams. With apologies to the reigning Super Bowl champs, the moves GM Les Snead and Co made in the offseason to shore up their defense are eerily similar to the big swings they took in the 2021 season. And we all know how that turned out.ALDonald and Garrett have five defensive player of the year awards between them and link up with former Super Bowl winners from the Chiefs in Watson and McDuffie. TheRamsare stacked and then some.GSAFC wildcard teamsPatriots, Jaguars, Chargers.DFPatriots, Bengals, Chargers.BAGPatriots, Ravens, Chiefs.ALChargers, Ravens, Jaguars.GSNFC wildcard teamsSeahawks, Lions, Eagles.DFSeahawks, Packers, Bears.BAGSeahawks, 49ers, Cowboys.ALBuccaneers, Lions, Seahawks.GSAFC championship gameBills over Broncos.DFBroncos over Bills.BAGBengals over Jaguars.ALBroncos over Bengals.GSNFC championship gameRams over Seahawks.DFRams over Eagles.BAGRams over Seahawks.ALRams over Cowboys.GSView image in fullscreenMatthew Stafford is looking to win a second Super Bowl in LA.Photograph: Ariana Ruiz/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockYour Super Bowl LXI winner will be …Rams over Bills.The Rams’ “F Them Picks” philosophy served them well when they gave up a ton of draft capital for Stafford, Jalen Ramsey, and Von Miller, and they won the Super Bowl as a result. If the 2026 Rams find that their go-for-broke philosophy works once again with a radical reshuffling of their defense, it’s hard to bet against them, because the offense was already so on point.DFRams over Broncos.The Rams have spent the offseason putting together a star-studded roster unlike anything we’ve seen in years, adding Garrett, McDuffie and Watson before Donald decided he wasn’t finished after all. Denver’s elite defense is capable of making it ugly, but Sean McVay’s embarrassment of riches on both sides of the ball will ultimately prove too much.BAGBengals over Rams.Burrow avenges the biggest loss in his career, and it’s in no small part thanks to Brown and player personnel director Duke Tobin pulling the trigger one last time on a piece that helps neutralize the effects of the Garrett-Donald pocket collapse (an extra guard, a fullback – don’t hold me to specifics). The confusion over what to make of Zac Taylor as a Super Bowl-winning coach quickly gives way to the confusion over what to make of a championship parade festooned with tributes to the world’sweirdest chili. In other words, the renovations on ancient Paycor Stadiumpay for themselves.ALBroncos over Rams.Denver can argue they were a broken ankle away from the Super Bowl last season. Handily for the Broncos they come back with almost an identical roster this year. They kept starting running back JK Dobbins and brought in Waddle to help out Sutton. The Broncos already have the AFC’s best defense to go with a sublime offensive line and exciting weapons that can take down the Rams.GSExplore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Man in Swindon charged with assisting Russian intelligence agency | Swindon | The Guardian
description: Joshua Cammidge, 31, arrested after investigation led by counter-terrorism policing London
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Joshua Cammidge, 31, arrested after investigation led by counter-terrorism policing London
Content: Counter-terrorism policing London were supported by officers from Wiltshire police when making an arrest in Swindon on Friday 4 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCounter-terrorism policing London were supported by officers from Wiltshire police when making an arrest in Swindon on Friday 4 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianSwindonMan in Swindon charged with assisting Russian intelligence agencyJoshua Cammidge, 31, arrested after investigation led by counter-terrorism policing LondonRaphael BoydWed 9 Sep 2026 15.10 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been charged with offences related to national security as part of an ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing (CTP) London, according to the Metropolitan police.Joshua Cammidge, 31, was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday 4 September by CTP London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire police. Searches were also carried out at a different address in Swindon. He was further arrested and detained the following day, being charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and intending to commit or engage in conduct to prepare an act of sabotage.The Met have claimed that Cammidge’s arrests relate to alleged contact with a representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency that have been accused of previously engaging in acts of sabotage against Britain and its allies.The National Security Act, which Cammidge was arrested and charged under, was introduced in 2023 to help increase the measures that law enforcement can take in order to protect the UK from security threats such as espionage, foreign interference or influence, and sabotage.Frank Ferguson, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Joshua Cammidge with National Security Act offences following a counter-terrorism policing investigation.“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.“It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.”Cammidge will appear at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday 10 September.Explore more on these topicsSwindonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Protesters outside Portsmouth hotel mistake Pakistan U19 cricket team for asylum seekers | Cricket | The Guardian
description: A group of masked agitators gathered outside a four-star hotel in Portsmouth after reports a group of asylum seekers had been taken there, when it was in fact Pakistan’s under-19 cricket team on a tour
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: A group of masked agitators gathered outside a four-star hotel in Portsmouth after reports a group of asylum seekers had been taken there, when it was in fact Pakistan’s under-19 cricket team on a tour
Content: Police officers at Eastney beach, Portsmouth, where hundreds of protesters gathered on Sunday, leaving tensions high in the Hampshire city.Photograph: PAView image in fullscreenPolice officers at Eastney beach, Portsmouth, where hundreds of protesters gathered on Sunday, leaving tensions high in the Hampshire city.Photograph: PACricketProtesters outside Portsmouth hotel mistake Pakistan U19 cricket team for asylum seekersReform councillor said he urged activists to stand downECB checks on young players’ welfarePeter WalkerandSimon BurntonWed 9 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA group of masked agitators gathered outside a four-star hotel inPortsmouthafter reports a group of asylum seekers had been taken there, when it was in fact Pakistan’s under-19 cricket team on a tour.George Madgwick, a Reform councillor called to the hotel to mediate between staff and the assembled crowd, said it was a “massively unfortunate incident”.Madgwick, who leads the Reform group on Hampshire council and whose ward includes the four-star Marriott hotel, said he nonetheless believed the incident was understandable given recent coverage of asylum seekers arriving in the city via small boats.‘Army of Christian patriots’: how a black-clad vigilante group swarmed PortsmouthRead moreHundreds of people, many wearing balaclavas, clashed withpolice in Portsmouth on Sunday eveningafter a dinghy carrying asylum seekers reached its coastline from France. Police are investigating potential assaults and criminal damage.It came a day after crowds of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road around the port of Dover for several hours. Daniel Thomas, a far-right activist closely linked toTommy Robinson, claimed to have arranged both demonstrations.Madgwick said he was at home on Tuesday evening when he was called and told that about 40 people had gathered outside the Marriott hotel, many wearing balaclavas or other face coverings, after reports that asylum seekers were staying there.He went there and spoke to the hotel manager, who “explained the situation” – the hotel was hosting members of an under-21 cricket team from Pakistan, who are touring the south coast and using the Marriott as their base.Madgwick said the group massed outside after reports that about 40 men who did not seem to be English had arrived at the hotel, and that the coach which took them was from the same company who moved the asylum seekers who came by boat.“I also spoke to the coach of the team, who was very understanding,” Madgwick said. “I went out to the protesters and told them, ‘You’ve got it wrong guys, it’s a cricket club.’ They left within a couple of minutes. It was a massively unfortunate incident.“From the perspective of the people ofPortsmouthwho are already on high alert, this was a coach from the same company which was turning up with about 40 foreign men.”Madgwick said he accepted it was far from ideal for a masked group to assemble outside a hotel purely because a group of apparently foreign men had arrived.He said: “It doesn’t make our city look like the welcoming city it is. But it’s reflective of the climate we live in, and where people are deeply concerned about the issues.”The news first emerged after Madgwick put out a Facebook post urging people to stay away from the area. He wrote: “There were reports that possible migrants were staying in the Marriott hotel. I can confirm that is NOT the case. Please don’t attend the hotel.“A number of concerned local residents spotted what they believed to be migrants going into the Marriott hotel. A number of you messaged me and asked me to come down. I spoke to the hotel and they agreed to meet me.”At the hotel, as well as speaking to the hotel staff and team coach, Madgwick was shown “proof” that the men were indeed cricketers, he added. Madgwick said he had subsequently made the post private as it was attracting abusive comments.Since the incident, the England and WalesCricketBoard has contacted the Pakistan Cricket Board to check on the wellbeing of those involved, and is reviewing security arrangements for the remainder of the squad’s tour.The team played England Under-19s in a four-day Test last week, losing by 10 runs, and are playing a one-day game against the same opponents on Wednesday at Arundel, around 25 miles from Portsmouth. A final game, also an ODI, is scheduled to be played in Guildford on Saturday. Pakistan’s senior men’s team is also in the country, playing the third and final Test against England at Edgbaston.Explore more on these topicsCricketPortsmouthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald V | Norway | The Guardian
description: Europe’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a close
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Europe’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a close
Content: King Harald is taken to the royal mausoleum in the crypt at Akershus Castle after the funeral ceremony in Oslo.Photograph: Terje Pedersen/EPAView image in fullscreenKing Harald is taken to the royal mausoleum in the crypt at Akershus Castle after the funeral ceremony in Oslo.Photograph: Terje Pedersen/EPANorwayTens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald VEurope’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a closeJon HenleyEurope correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of ​national mourning that followedthe popular monarch’s deathlast month at the age of 89.Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades.With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress.View image in fullscreenNorway’s Prince Sverre Magnus, King Haakon VIII, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Princess Martha Louise.Photograph: Ole Berg-Rusten/EPAKing Haakon VIII, whosucceeded hisfather on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked in the cortege, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car.View image in fullscreenDespite its recent scandals, the monarchy remains broadly popular.Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix/APThe procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; ‌Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino.Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”.View image in fullscreenThe Prince of Wales and Princess Anne leaving the funeral service.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersThe prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.”After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony.View image in fullscreenA portrait of Norway’s King Harald V, painted by Valeria Duca, is displayed among flowers and Norwegian flags at a makeshift memorial outside the royal palace in Oslo.Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty ImagesNorwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss ⁠classes for the occasion.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHarald’s death came at a time of numerous crises for the Norwegian royal family, with Mette-Marit, 53, in particularcoming under heavy criticism– including from the prime minister – for her association with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.View image in fullscreenMarius Borg Høiby leaves the funeral service.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersThe new queen’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle monitor pending his appeal against a conviction for rape and domestic violence, was given permission to attend the funeral and was a pallbearer during the transfer to the royal chapel.Despite its recent scandals, however, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a poll for the public broadcaster NRK.View image in fullscreenThe casket of King Harald V leaves the royal palace for Oslo Cathedral.Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsNorwayEuropeMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: Notorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by US | Drugs trade | The Guardian
description: Trump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics trafficking
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Trump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics trafficking
Content: People walk past a house in Guayaquil, Ecuador, with graffiti reading ‘Tiger Zone’, referring to the Los Tiguerones gang.Photograph: Marcos Pin/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople walk past a house in Guayaquil, Ecuador, with graffiti reading ‘Tiger Zone’, referring to the Los Tiguerones gang.Photograph: Marcos Pin/AFP/Getty ImagesDrugs tradeNotorious Ecuadorian crime gang designated a terrorist group by USTrump administration to seek extra funding from Congress to ‘dismantle’ Los Tiguerones over narcotics traffickingAndrew Rothand agenciesWed 9 Sep 2026 18.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 18.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has designated Ecuador’s Los Tiguerones gang, whichstormed a television stationduring a live broadcast in 2024, as a terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour throughLatin Americathat began on Tuesday.Rubio said theLos Tiguerones gangwas linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended onEcuadorto take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country.1:02Footage shows armed gang storming studio live on Ecuadorian TV station – video reportForced disappearances, killings and torture: why is Ecuador’s brutal drug war being backed by the west?Read moreIn its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, theTrump administrationhas also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region.During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America.On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that havekilled at least 227 peoplewhom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence.Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”.View image in fullscreenMarco Rubio (left) is welcomed to Ecuador on Wednesday by its president, Daniel NoboaPhotograph: Dolores Ochoa/AFP/Getty ImagesRubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inauguratedpresident Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations.During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of theAmericasinitiative only after its change in government.During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy.Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.Explore more on these topicsDrugs tradeTrump administrationEcuadorDrugsAmericasUS politicsMarco RubionewsShareReuse this content

title: Victoria’s koalas in chronically poor health and population is half what was previously estimated | Victoria | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: State government delayed releasing major report into the health of the koala population for more than 12 months
Author: Lisa Cox
Headline: Exclusive: State government delayed releasing major report into the health of the koala population for more than 12 months
Content: An overabundance in some local koala populations had created a perception that Victoria’s overall population was thriving, researchers say.Photograph: Penny Stephens/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn overabundance in some local koala populations had created a perception that Victoria’s overall population was thriving, researchers say.Photograph: Penny Stephens/The GuardianVictoriaVictoria’s koalas in chronically poor health and population is half what was previously estimatedExclusive:State government delayed releasing major report into the health of the koala population for more than 12 monthsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLisa CoxEnvironment and climate correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 16.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 18.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Victorian government sat on a report for more than 12 months that found the state’s koala population was in chronically poor health.Thereviewof the state’s koala populations, led by state science agency the Arthur Rylah Institute in conjunction with scientists from major universities, was completed for the Victorian government in June 2025.It estimated there were 217,000 koalas in the state in 2023 and 224,800 in 2024 – a dramatic drop frompast estimatesof 460,000, which the report attributed to different survey and modelling methodology, rather than an actual population decline.As part of the research, scientists conducted health and disease assessments on 68 koalas, with 29 of the koalas (43%) found to be in such poor health they “were euthanised on welfare grounds”.The report warned the surveys found “a higher-than-expected proportion of koalas from seven geographically distinct regions in a state of chronically poor health and welfare”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe government published the report on Wednesday morning as the new environment minister, Jaclyn Symes, announced $2.6m for koala conservation, including for habitat restoration and research into koala health and genetics.Leanne Wicker, a wildlife veterinarian who was one of the authors on the report, said researchers had been shocked by the poor health of some of the koalas they found in the field.“While we were doing this research we knew we were seeing something that urgently needed attention and understanding,” she said. “And it’s been very difficult to get the support and resources needed because the report hadn’t been made public.”She said the overabundance of certain local Victorian koala populations – such as those at French Island and in western Victoria – had created a perception that the state’s overall koala population was thriving. “What we’ve missed is we have a crisis in our koala populations in Victoria because we have a very concerning level of poor health and welfare.”Deakin University’s Desley Whisson, another author on the report, said while the 2024 population estimate of about 225,000 koalas “seems like a lot, most of those koalas are in areas where there are high densities of animals”.“There’s large parts of the state where koalas occur at low densities and are probably in poor health,” she said.She said the government needed to turn its attention to areas with low numbers “because we could be losing koalas in some parts of the state without even knowing”.The report used systematic visual and acoustic surveys in 2023 and 2024 to monitor koalas at 182 sites. That data was then used to estimate the overall abundance and distribution of Victoria’s koala population.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPossums in the roof, koalas in bed: study shows how animals resort to Australian homes after habitat lossRead moreThe report states the drop in the estimated population from previous estimates of 460,000 was due to changes in the methodology used. It said the new data also represented the first time koala populations had been surveyed statewide.Of the 68 koalas sampled for health and welfare checks, 39 healthy individuals were rereleased, with healthy animals present at all of the locations sampled, according to the report. But 29 koalas were euthanised due to ill health.Koalas that were euthanised were more likely to have poor coat condition, dental disease and “wet bottom” (an advanced urinary tract infection, most commonly caused by chlamydia), and were more likely to occur in areas with high koala densities. Dental disease was recorded in 37% of koalas across all life stages and regions, except Mallacoota, according to the report.The report states that these findings raised concerns “for the health of Victorian koalas”.“Clinical signs consistent with chronic ill-health were observed across all life stages, suggesting that multiple individual, environmental and demographic stressors may be contributing to prolonged physiological stress within these populations,” the scientists wrote.Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said the research painted a grim picture of the health and wellbeing of Victoria’s koalas.“It is clear that we need to use every lever possible to ensure they’re given the best chance at survival, or we will soon be just like the many states across Australia where koalas are listed as endangered,” she said.The report also found that 23% of Victoria’s koala population now lived in the state’s blue gum plantation estate “where they occur at much higher density than koalas in neighbouring native forest”.“Given the high estimated density of koalas within blue gum plantations, changes to the plantation estate size and/or stand ages may result in significant changes to population size,” it states.Jessica Robertson, from advocacy group the Koala Alliance, called Wednesday’s funding announcement “a calculated political rescue mission for Labor, not for koalas”.“Sitting on critical ecological data for over a year while koalas continued to suffer and disappear is a shocking failure of transparency and responsibility,” she said.A Victorian environment department spokesperson said since receiving the report it had been working with other agencies, and consulting external groups, “to prioritise actions and design projects that address its findings and recommendations”.A spokesperson said Wednesday’s funding announcement was the result of this work.The environment department’s spokesperson said the timing of the report’s public release had not affected “important work” the government was already doing to manage the health of the state’s koalas.Explore more on these topicsVictoriaWildlifeAnimalsConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Can an entire Arctic ecosystem evolve to adapt to the climate crisis? | Alaska | The Guardian
description: In the first project of its kind, scientists are trying to answer if the future of Alaska’s streams and tundra may depend not on survival of the fittest but on how species adapt together
Author: Gloria Dickie
Headline: In the first project of its kind, scientists are trying to answer if the future of Alaska’s streams and tundra may depend not on survival of the fittest but on how species adapt together
Content: A white-crowned sparrow, a common bird found in Alaska’s riparian stream ecosystems. Photograph: EvomeIn the first project of its kind, scientists are trying to answer if the future of Alaska’s streams and tundra may depend not on survival of the fittest but on how species adapttogetherByGloria DickieThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentWed 9 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Alaska’s North Slope, scientists tread carefully across clumps of tussock grasses toward a fast-flowing stream draining the imposing Brooks Range of ice and snow. Near Galbraith Creek, they string out a mist net for white-crowned sparrows. The birds have recently arrived from southerly latitudes, intent on feasting on the insects that will soon descend on the tundra like storm clouds.TheArcticsummer is short-lived, and sparrows have only a few weeks to establish territories, find mates, lay eggs and raise their chicks on a steady diet of bugs. From every ensnared bird, the scientists collect blood, feather and faecal samples to see what they are eating and how that changes over the summer.One thing they want to know is whether the sparrows are consuming a lot of stream insects, such as stoneflies and mayflies, says Ian Shuman, a doctoral student in quantitative ecology at Columbia University. As willow shrubs claim new territory along the Arctic’s rivers and streams – aprocess scientists call “shrubification”– this could disrupt the life cycles of stoneflies and mayflies. If the songbirds also depend on aquatic insects to thrive, that might affect the sparrows’ prospects.The tundra can feel immutable in its vastness. A sea of grass and moss extends as far as the eye can see. But above the Arctic Circle, change is happening faster than anywhere else on Earth. Snow is melting earlier in the spring, sending torrents of water downstream. By late summer, such early season deluges have given way to parched creek beds. The Arctic grayling – cold water fish in the salmon family – that swim between deep lake winter refuges and shallow summer spawning streams may become stranded in isolated pools. Their survival, too, rests on the mayflies and stoneflies.View image in fullscreenGalbraith Creek on Alaska’s North SlopeView image in fullscreenIan Shuman, a PhD student at Columbia University, downloads the data from an autonomous recording unit set up on the tundra of Alaska’s North Slope to listen for bird callsView image in fullscreenAn Arctic grayling, a freshwater fish in the salmon family, caught in Toolik Lake, AlaskaAcross the planet, global heating is reshuffling the order of life. Some species will prosper, while those that can’t adapt quickly enough will nosedive toward extinction. Evolution and adaptation have long been thought of as solitary endeavours – a survival of the fittest. But what if species could instead draw on their longstanding relationships not to succeed or fail alone, but to swiftly evolve and adapttogetherto climate breakdown, keeping whole ecosystems intact?That’s the question evolutionary ecologists, biologists, physiologists and geneticists are trying to answer from Alaska’s stream and tundra ecosystems in a first-of-its-kind $15m (£11m) project, supported by the US National Science Foundation. Over six years, scientists will closely assess five species and their connections to one another: the white-crowned sparrow, the feltleaf willow, the Arctic grayling, an aquatic mayfly and a ground beetle (the exact species are yet to be determined). If species adapt in response to temperature, they may also adapt in response to each other – and each other’s adaptations.“There is how organisms respond individually, but then all those organisms also live in a matrix that is an ecosystem,” says Linda Deegan, a senior scientist at Woodwell climate research center in Massachusetts who is leading the project, known as the Evolving Meta-Ecosystems Institute (Evome). “We think those connections will help them prosper in climate change. Things won’t completely fall apart.”Scientists chose Alaska’s tundra and stream ecosystems to study, not only because the Arctic is the fastest-warming region on Earth, but because it is also home to relatively simple ecosystems where a handful of species shape the environment. Still, what they find in the far north will help inform how ecosystems around the world, from the tropics to the alpine regions, might be able to withstand the climate crisis.The land on either side of the Dalton Highway, the road that connects Fairbanks to the oilfields of Prudhoe Bay, serves as a sprawling laboratory for the 50 scientists from US research institutions working on the project. Almost every day throughout the spring and summer, scientists trawl the 15 field sites scattered along a nearly 190-mile stretch of road that runs from just south of the Brooks Range up toward Sagwon Creek, 60 miles south of the Arctic Ocean.View image in fullscreenThe Brooks Range peeks out from behind the sprawling tundra of northern AlaskaIt is impossible to walk very far on the tundra without stumbling across a research project tucked into the willows or sedges. Dozens of sticky traps poke out of the permafrost to collect bugs. Recording boxes listen for bird calls. Temperature sensors lie submerged in frigid streams. Mesh bags flap around on the tundra to gather willow leaves. In the distance, the silver Alyeska pipeline cuts through the rugged terrain, transporting crude oil to Valdez – a reminder of why scientists are here in the warming landscape.“We follow the road and the pipeline all summer,” says Andie Norton, a Woodwell research assistant who is studying the impact of encroaching willows on nutrient flows in Alaska’s streams.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAndie Norton, an ecologist with Woodwell Climate Research Center, examines a water sample taken from Alaska’s Hershey Creek for aquatic mayflies and stoneflies, and a feltleaf willow, one of Evome’s main study species, in the early stages of leafing outA shadier stream means less algae is produced through photosynthesis to feed the mayflies and caddisflies, she says. But if more willows are dropping their foliage, shredding insects that enjoy munching on leaves – such as stoneflies – might become more abundant. The question is whether fish and birds will be able to take sufficient advantage. Unlike mayflies, stoneflies generally don’t form large swarms and they emerge earlier, during the spring melt.Still, there is good reason to think that Alaska’s stream and tundra ecosystems will continue to function, Deegan says, though she notes such an optimistic outcome is only a best guess. Few studies have looked at how adaptive evolution can affect entire ecosystem dynamics – including nutrient and energy flows – and none have assessed how evolution could affect connections between two adjacent ecosystems.Individual species can adapt to a warmer world in one of three ways. They can adjust their behaviour, such asbirds shifting their migration routes. They can acclimatise at the physiological level, for instance treestemporarily altering photosynthesis during a drought. Or they can draw upon evolution – passing on genetic changes to their offspring, sometimes within just a few generations.View image in fullscreenScientists measure the beak length of a newly arrived, migratory white-crowned sparrow on the tundra of Alaska’s North SlopeStudies reveal that many plants and animals have been able to persist through evolutionary rescue – the process by which a population on the brink of extinction survives and rebounds through rapid genetic adaptation.Scarlet monkeyflowersin Oregon and California, for example, rapidly evolved during the 2010s to survive a four-year drought.“Across hundreds of experiments, we have seen this happening,” says Mark Urban, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Connecticut working on the project. “There is this incredible buffer ability of adaptive evolution.”View image in fullscreenAlpine azalea, a common dwarf shrub found on the Alaska tundraHow the evolution of one species can help the holistic ecosystems depends on how an adaptive trait ultimately translates into ecological properties. For example, if a fish species can quickly evolve, it means that not only is the population maintained, but so is the stream’s productivity. “Any ecological properties that depend on those populations are maintained as well,” Urban says.To get a better idea of whether the Arctic’s stream and tundra habitats will continue to prosper, scientists are mapping the genetic diversity of each of the five study species to see if there is enough to allow for adaptation – influencing the ecosystems’ resilience potential.“We can get so far with ecology, but at some point we want to get down to the basics of why organisms do the things they do, and can they change the things they do,” says Urban. “That’s something only genetics can explain.”Certain genes control the traits associated with succeeding in different environments. “The holy grail in genomics is to find that one gene that affects everything. The gene that rules them all,” he says. “I think that’s optimistic. Most of the traits are going to be determined by hundreds of thousands of genes.”The Arctic grayling is, in many ways, the crown jewel of the scientists’ investigation. The migrating fish – distinguished by its iridescent body and flamboyant dorsal fin – connect Alaska’s watersheds, moving nutrients between streams and lakes. They are also exceptionally vulnerable to changes in the climate. Grayling require cold water to develop into adults. They feed on the stoneflies and mayflies likely to be affected by increased shrubbiness. And unpredictable summer stream flows can block their movement back to winter lakes.“The snow is melting earlier most years, but summers are also getting drier and grayling have to move,” says environmental ecologist Chris Neill, also at Woodwell, who is looking at stream flows, water chemistry and plant communities for the project. Certain cues tell grayling when they should begin migrating. “Those cues may be programmed into their genome – or they may not.”View image in fullscreenHarrison Dubois and Chris Neill, members of the Evome project, measure the late spring stream flow of Galbraith Creek on Alaska’s North SlopeIn May, University of Alaska Fairbanks students Matthew Zimmerman and Roberto Ponce Velez travelled to a lake just south of the Brooks Range hoping to collect fertilised eggs from the spawning grayling for a pilot experiment. Just finding a spawning event is “like throwing a hammer at a nail”, Zimmerman says.Things only got harder from there. The students had hoped to transport their bounty back to a laboratory on the university campus along the notoriously bumpy Dalton Highway. More than half of their eggs perished en route.The survivors that made it to Fairbanks were placed into four tanks with five different water temperatures ranging between 4C and 20C. At the same time, the students collected fertilised eggs from a channel of the Chena River a few miles outside Fairbanks, where grayling were spawning at just 4C – six degrees cooler than the grayling up north – and transferred them to the tanks.The idea is that by collecting species from different geographies and growing them together under shared conditions, scientists will be able to see how genetic variations and adaptations differ across the Arctic. “Temperature is really controlling how quickly things develop,” says Ponce Velez. “There are a lot of trade-offs. At higher temperatures, we have much quicker development of fish. But we have really high mortality.” Next year, they’ll gather more fertilised eggs from other lakes and streams spread across the North Slope to see how each population fares in the lab.View image in fullscreenMatthew Zimmerman, a PhD student at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, holds up an Arctic grayling caught in Toolik LakeEvome scientists are close to completing the first reference genome for the Arctic grayling, which will allow them to compare differences in temperature responses between populations and search for the specific genes that may be tied to local adaptations.They lived through the ice age. Can the mighty musk ox survive the heat?Read moreMist-netting for birds, scrubbing rocks for algae, assembling genomes, and trucking grayling eggs down the Dalton Highway, scientists hope, will eventually allow them to forecast how this fragile place at the top of the world might manage to persist under the weight of immense change.Will Alaska’s streams and tundra bounce back, bend, or snap entirely? “I think there are going to be a lot of springs,” says Urban. “But we’ll also witness a few breaks or bends in the system.”Find moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsThe age of extinctionAlaskaArcticClimate crisisBirdsEndangered habitatsConservationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Birdwatch: the avian equivalent of a catwalk model, blue cranes are under threat | Birds | The Guardian
description: Numbers of the exquisitely graceful species are falling amid loss of food supply and habitat
Author: Stephen Moss
Headline: Numbers of the exquisitely graceful species are falling amid loss of food supply and habitat
Content: A worker interacts with a blue crane in an enclosure at World of Birds in Cape Town, South Africa. Today only 25,000 to 46,000 individuals remain in the wild.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersView image in fullscreenA worker interacts with a blue crane in an enclosure at World of Birds in Cape Town, South Africa. Today only 25,000 to 46,000 individuals remain in the wild.Photograph: Esa Alexander/ReutersBirdwatchBirdsBirdwatch: the avian equivalent of a catwalk model, blue cranes are under threatNumbers of the exquisitely graceful species are falling amid loss of food supply and habitatStephen MossWed 9 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFew birds are quite as elegant as the blue crane. As I watched a pair feeding alongside a busy road inSouth Africa, against the rather incongruous backdrop of a herd of cows, I was struck by their sheer beauty. With a slender body, curved neck, long legs, elongated tail plumes and a subtle, dove-grey plumage, this bird really is the avian equivalent of a catwalk model.But not all is well for the blue crane. It has the smallest global range of any of the world’s 15 crane species: apart from an isolated population in Namibia, almost all are found in SouthAfrica, where it is celebrated as the national bird.Once common and widespread, blue crane numbers have fallen steadily over the past 50 years, and today between only 25,000 and 46,000 individuals remain in the wild. If the downward trend continues, this species faces a genuine risk of extinction.The reasons for the decline are tediously predictable. As a grassland specialist, when intensive farming takes over, the food supply is inevitably reduced. A lethal cocktail of threats, including illegal poisoning, disturbance, habitat loss and the climate crisis – which this year brought unseasonably early rains followed by drought – mean that its future is far from rosy.But as I watched these beautiful birds, I could forget about their plight for a few moments and quietly rejoice in their exquisite grace.Explore more on these topicsBirdsBirdwatchWildlifeSouth AfricaEndangered speciesAfricaAnimalsConservationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Noel Clarke charged with six sexual offences including assault and voyeurism | UK news | The Guardian
description: CPS says charges relate to alleged sexual misconduct by the actor towards five women between 2007 and 2016
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: CPS says charges relate to alleged sexual misconduct by the actor towards five women between 2007 and 2016
Content: Noel Clarke is known ​for his ​role ​in Doctor ​Who and for writing and starring in Kidulthood.Photograph: Karl Black/AlamyView image in fullscreenNoel Clarke is known ​for his ​role ​in Doctor ​Who and for writing and starring in Kidulthood.Photograph: Karl Black/AlamyUK newsNoel Clarke charged with six sexual offences including assault and voyeurismCPS says charges relate to alleged sexual misconduct by the actor towards five women between 2007 and 2016Matthew WeaverWed 9 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe actor and film-maker Noel Clarke has been ⁠charged ​with six sexual offences, including two counts of sexual assault, after allegations made by five women.The charges against the former Doctor Who actor also include three counts of voyeurism and one count of exposure.Announcing the charges, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said the alleged offences took place between 2007 and 2016, and involved allegations made by five women.Clarke is due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on 21 October. The charges were brought after an investigation that began in September 2025.Det Supt Mike Cagney said: “The women connected to these charges continue to receive support from specially trained officers. We urge anyone who has been a victim of sexual assault to contact police. The information you provide will be dealt with in the utmost sensitivity and we have trained investigators on hand to support you.”Bethan David, the deputy chief crown prosecutor for London, said: “The CPS has decided to prosecute Noel Clarke with two counts of sexual assault, three counts of voyeurism and one count of exposure. This follows allegations made by five women in connection to sexual misconduct that took place between 2007 and 2016.“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court and that it is in the public interest to do so. We have worked closely with the Metropolitan police as they have carried out their investigation into the allegations.”David reminded the public that legal proceedings were active and Clarke had the right to a fair trial. She said: “It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in any way prejudice these proceedings.”Clarke, 50, is known ​for his ​role ​in Doctor ​Who and for writing and starring in Kidulthood, which explored bullying, drug abuse and extreme violence among young ⁠people in London.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ministers to put white working-class people in UK at heart of new equalities unit | Class issues | The Guardian
description: Bridget Phillipson to announce creation of unit which will make class a key part of its equalities agenda
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Bridget Phillipson to announce creation of unit which will make class a key part of its equalities agenda
