Content: As a former education secretary, Bridget Phillipson said ‘for the first time in a long time white working-class children have a government that will fight for them’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAs a former education secretary, Bridget Phillipson said ‘for the first time in a long time white working-class children have a government that will fight for them’.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesClass issuesMinisters to put white working-class people in UK at heart of new equalities unitBridget Phillipson to announce creation of unit which will make class a key part of its equalities agendaUK politics live – latest updatesAletha AduPolitical correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 06.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 16.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government is putting class at the heart of its equalities agenda by creating a new unit that will make tackling white working-class inequality a priority.The unit, which the minister for women and equalities,Bridget Phillipson, will announce on Wednesday, will sit within the Office for Equality and Opportunity and examine disparities linked to class and socioeconomic background across all ethnic groups.Improving outcomes for white working-class people will be a focus of its work, even though government sources insisted it would not be a dedicated white working-class unit.It comes as part of a government shake-up of its equalities work that will result in the Social Mobility Commission (SMC) being abolished. Social class will not, however, be given a new legal status as a protected characteristic under the Equality Act.The unit will act as a centre for government analysis of class and socioeconomic inequalities in public services and outcomes.One of its first priorities will be the introduction of the socioeconomic duty, which will force public bodies to consider how their decisions could reduce inequalities felt by lower income families, caused by socioeconomic disadvantages such as transport and services.Alun Francis, the chair of the SMC, accused ministers of making a false claim to justify its closure, saying it was “not true” that there were no examples of the watchdog directly informing government policy.Francis said the commission’s data had helped shape the government’sclean energy jobs plan, that it was working with the work and pensions department on barriers to social and economic progress, and that ministers had previously asked mayors to engage with it as part of new devolution arrangements.He also criticised Phillipson for an alleged lack of engagement before the decision was taken. Francis said he had met the minister only once in two years before being told on Monday that the commission would close, despite writing to her several times.Francis also questioned whether the new unit would be more effective, arguing that class was a “messy concept” to organise policy around and warned that equating being working class with disadvantage risked being “deeply patronising”.Phillipson is expected to announce plans to change the way deprivation is measured across the country, with an assessment on how funding is distributed across services such as childcare and health.The new unit is being established as the Social Mobility Commission (SMC) is abolished. The SMC was established in 2010 to monitor progress on social mobility and advise ministers.Government insiders are thought to believe the commission has not been effective enough in guiding policy, given it can only advise ministers when requested.Some of the 20 civil servants who work in the Cabinet Office and supported the SCM’s work are expected to move to the new unit.The SCM’s latest report, titled State of the Nation, says “entrenched disadvantages” lie in former industrial communities across Britain, which face “extreme regional differences”, fewer job opportunities and poorer childhoods.Anindependent inquiry into white working-class educational outcomesfound Britain’s education system was not “serving the interests of white working-class children”.It also said high-performing primary and secondary schools in England should be encouraged to admit more disadvantaged pupils from white working-class backgrounds to help reverse a continuing crisis in underachievement.At the time of its conclusion in June, Phillipson, the then education secretary, said “for the first time in a long time white working-class children have a government that will fight for them”.She added that generations had been “robbed of opportunity” and “the communities in this report are my communities. I know what they’ve given this country and what this country has failed to give back.”The inquiry was commissioned by Star Academies and supported by the Department for Education to understand why white working-class children were the lowest performing demographic in England’s school system.The Sutton Trust educational charity warned at the time against setting one disadvantaged group against another, noting that disadvantaged young people from Black Caribbean backgrounds were just as unlikely to become top earners.Explore more on these topicsClass issuesInequalityRaceBridget PhillipsonPovertyEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Streeting praises new series The Wargame for highlighting Britain’s defence needs | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Show depicting attack on UK and featuring Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon will ‘make people think’, minister says
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Show depicting attack on UK and featuring Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon will ‘make people think’, minister says
Content: The Wargame, due to air this month, features a host of former politicians who have to deal with a ‘war-gamed’ attack on Britain.Photograph: Dave Benett/Alan Chapman/Getty Images for SkyView image in fullscreenThe Wargame, due to air this month, features a host of former politicians who have to deal with a ‘war-gamed’ attack on Britain.Photograph: Dave Benett/Alan Chapman/Getty Images for SkyDefence policyStreeting praises new series The Wargame for highlighting Britain’s defence needsShow depicting attack on UK and featuring Michael Gove and Nicola Sturgeon will ‘make people think’, minister saysDan SabbaghDefence and security editorWed 9 Sep 2026 08.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 16.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA docudrama depicting a Russian attack on a Britain led by an unlikely pairing of Michael Gove andNicola Sturgeonhas been praised by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, for writing “my spending review submission”.The Wargame, due to be broadcast on Sky this month, features a string of former politicians advised by ex-securocrats, grappling with an unusually powerful Moscow, while highlighting limitations in the British military.It features Gove, who was a Conservative minister for more than a decade, as prime minister – a job he unsuccessfully ran for in 2016 – and Sturgeon, the former first minister and leader of the Scottish National party, as his deputy, in a mock Downing Street Cobra emergency situation room.Russian warship carries out rare live-fire exercise 45 miles off UK coastRead moreLabour figures involved in the production include the former Scotland secretary Jim Murphy as foreign secretary, as well as Harriet Harman and the peer Ayesha Hazarika, who plays the role of director of communications in the embattled team.After a preview screening at the National Gallery in central London, with many of the former politicians present, Streeting quipped: “On behalf of the association of UK defence secretaries, thank you for my spending review submission.”Though the war depicted was of “a low likelihood, albeit high impact”, Streeting said he anticipated the show would stimulate publicdebate on defence spending, currently planned to rise by about £30bn by 2035.Streeting said The Wargame would “play a role in making people think about where they would put defence in the order of priorities as voters”, though he added that wildfires, floods and other natural disasters should also prompt the public to think how they would be able to cope in a crisis.The scale of the cash increase, pushed for by the US president Donald Trump but signed up to by the UK and other Nato allies, is such that it would require taxes or borrowing to be raised, or substantial cuts from other government spending after the next election.The five-part programme is a spin-off from a Sky News podcast presented by the journalist Deborah Haynes, who has helped to develop the television show. “We want our country to understand better what the threat is, what credible defence is”, she said.Producers said a series of incidents involving Russian sabotage in the UK and Europe had made the programme more relevant. During filming in mid-June, a Russian frigate south of the Isle of Wightunexpectedly fired warning shots near an approaching pleasure yacht in the Channel, terrifying a British couple onboard.Gove – who was a minister between 2010 and 2024 – said it had come as a surprise to him how limited Britain’s missile defence capability was during filming, an issue highlighted in the show. “For anyone watching, they will think: ‘WTF. How did we get into that situation?’” It was, he said, “quite sobering” for somebody who had been in government for as long as he had, though he had not been a defence minister.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA succession of cuts to defence spending made by Conservative and Labour governments from the end of the cold war until the early part of the decade have reduced defence investment and left the navy struggling to deploy warships and submarines.Since then, there has been a growing consensus across the centre of British politics for increased defence spending. Though Russia remains fully engaged in its war in Ukraine, Moscow retains the ability to conduct cyber, sabotage and disinformation operations in the UK.Sturgeon said the programme could help dispel “the optimism bias that this won’t happen”. Gove said: “I never thought I would say this, but I agree 100% with Nicola”.The Wargame airs onSky Onefrom 21 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsDefence policyDocumentaryWes StreetingMichael GoveNicola SturgeonLabourConservativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Liz Truss relaunches podcast on channel of broadcaster famous for ‘grow concrete’ exchange | Liz Truss | The Guardian
description: Podcast is now on YouTube site of Mike Graham, fired from TalkTV after racist post appeared on his Facebook page
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Podcast is now on YouTube site of Mike Graham, fired from TalkTV after racist post appeared on his Facebook page
Content: Truss has so far failed to find a wide audience in her media career.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenTruss has so far failed to find a wide audience in her media career.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersLiz TrussLiz Truss relaunches podcast on channel of broadcaster famous for ‘grow concrete’ exchangePodcast is now on YouTube site of Mike Graham, fired from TalkTV after racist post appeared on his Facebook pageUK politics live – latest updatesHelena HortonandMichael SavageWed 9 Sep 2026 08.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Liz Trusslaunched her podcastlast year, she declared it would bring a “counter-revolution” to take on the “deep state”, which, she said, “tried to destroy” her.The revolution, however, has not yet arrived. Truss, whose stint as UK prime minister abruptly ended after her disastrous mini-budget crashed the economy, has so far failed to find a wide audience in her media career.Her podcast episodes hosted onYouTubeoften receive fewer than 4,000 views each, which is understood to be below the amount generally needed to monetise a video.The Liz Truss Show review – hapless ravings from a cupboardRead moreNow, Truss is relaunching her podcast and joining the former TalkTV host Mike Graham’s YouTube channel, UKLive, where she will be livestreaming twice a week.Grahamwas dismissed fromRupert Murdoch’s digital channel after the company said he had failed to cooperate with an investigation into a racist post that appeared on his Facebook account. The post inquired: “Why are we surrounded by non-white people?” Graham claimed he did not post it and that he was hacked.The presenter, whose new channel calls itself “the home of common sense”, came to public prominence after claiming on air that it waspossible to grow concrete. Graham was questioning the eco-activist and carpenter Cameron Ford on whether timber was a sustainable building material. Cameron said timber was “regenerative”, adding: “You can grow trees. You can’t grow concrete.” Graham replied: “Yeah, you can.”View image in fullscreenThe former TalkTV presenter Mike Graham.Photograph: Andrew Stehrenberger/AlamyGraham’s channel does generate income, securing enough views to qualify for YouTube’s scheme that shares ad revenue with creators. While UKLive only averages about 24,000 views a video, its prolific output of 1,700 posts in the last year means it has secured 41m views in that time, according to the Socialpruf analytics site. That is enough to generate thousands of pounds a month in ad revenue.The rise of YouTube has created a home for those shunned by mainstream outlets, but its growth has also in effect created a whole world of broadcasting outside of the regulated world of mainstream TV.“Since Ofcom took over broadcast regulation in 2003, the way we watch television has changed beyond recognition,” said Chris Banatvala, who was Ofcom’s founding director of standards. “We now have a huge range of content that looks and feels like television – and is often available on the same television set – but isn’t subject to the same standards.“Viewers may have no idea whether what they are watching is regulated by Ofcom or not – and these regulatory grey areas are only likely to grow.“It is a good thing that the public has access to such a wide range of views and content. But the law has not kept pace, parliament has yet to confront the implications of this increasingly blurred distinction, and the platforms themselves have not always proved able to prevent serious harm.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTruss will be joining a host of other presenters including the former actor Laurence Fox, who wassuspended from GB Newsafter making sexualised comments on air about a female journalist. Also on the roster is Mark Littlewood, a former director of the Institute of Economic Affairs thinktank, which praised many of Truss’s economic policies, and the pro-Reform commentator Ellie Hodges.Truss may hope to benefit from Graham’s larger following; his channel has 179,000 subscribers compared with her 32,300. Recent podcasts from Truss include one in which the commentator June Slater claimed “Labour is panicking as Reform surges in Makerfield byelection”. Andy Burnham won for Labour in Makerfield by a wide margin.Another is an interview with Lucy Connolly in which she complains she was “jailed for a tweet”. Connolly was sent to prison in 2024 for stirring up racial hatred against asylum seekers in a post in which she called for asylum hotels to be burned down.The former prime minister said her new show would have “exciting new guests”. Truss has been attempting to relaunch her career in recent months, including setting up a new private members’ club in Mayfair with the property tycoon Robert Tchenguiz.The club, named the Leconfield, states on its website that it is a “beacon of sophistication and refined elegance” that has “curated an exclusive sanctuary where tradition meets contemporary luxury”.Explore more on these topicsLiz TrussYouTubeDigital mediaPodcastsConservativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russian director refuses to denounce lead actor despite criticism from Ukraine | Venice film festival | The Guardian
description: Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU, about physicist Lev Landau, stars Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis who has refused to speak out against Putin’s war
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU, about physicist Lev Landau, stars Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis who has refused to speak out against Putin’s war
Content: Russian film-maker Ilya Khrzhanovsky at the premiere of DAU in Venice.Photograph: Ettore Ferrari/EPAView image in fullscreenRussian film-maker Ilya Khrzhanovsky at the premiere of DAU in Venice.Photograph: Ettore Ferrari/EPAVenice film festivalRussian director refuses to denounce lead actor despite criticism from UkraineIlya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU, about physicist Lev Landau, stars Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, who has refused to speak out against Putin’s warPhilip Oltermannin VeniceWed 9 Sep 2026 12.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe director of a controversial new Russian film has said “everyone pays for his own choice” when asked about his lead’s refusal to condemn Russia’s war in Ukraine.In film-maker Ilya Khrzhanovsky’s DAU, which premiered at theVenice film festivalon Wednesday, Greek-Russian star conductor Teodor Currentzis plays the eponymously nicknamed protagonist, Nobel prize-winning quantum physicist Lev Landau.DAU review – Ilya Krzhanovsky’s crazed Soviet inferno reaches its central characterRead moreIn the run-up to the festival, the film’s inclusion in the lineup was heavily criticised by the Ukrainian ministry of foreign affairs, in part over the fact that Athens-born Currentzis continues to live and work in Russia, and has never publicly denounced Putin’s war.“It’s his choice,” Khrzhanovsky said at a press conference on the Lido. “But I think everyone is paying for his own choice, his own life, his own destiny,” added the film-maker, who has renounced his Russian citizenship over the full-scale invasion and lives in exile in Germany.He referred to his film, in which Currentzis’s character Landau is put under pressure to work on the development of the nuclear bomb and eventually reluctantly agrees. “As you can see in the movie, the main character is also making different choices, and he’s paying for his choices.”Currentzis did not attend the Venice premiere due to a “last-minute emergency”, but Khzhanovsky said he was still in touch with his lead actor and that he was “one of the greatest conductors of our time”.Asked about his own position on the state of the war in Ukraine, Khrzhanovsky said: “The only thing I can wish for is peace and success for the Ukrainian government to succeed in the best possible way, to save the country and to win this war.”Dau director Ilya Khrzhanovsky: my ‘pornographic propaganda’ recreating the USSR is more important than everRead moreDAU was a highly controversial project long before Russian tanks started rolling on to Ukrainian soil. Originally pitched to producers in 2006 as a conventional biopic, and shot between 2008 and 2011 in Kharkiv, Ukraine, the film grew into a gargantuan piece of experimental performance art, with 400 principal roles and approximately 10,000 extras. Some critics have likened it to a “Stalinist Truman Show”.Inside Dau, the 'Stalinist Truman Show': 'I had absolute freedom – until the KGB grabbed me'Read moreAllegations of behind-the-scenes misconduct have dogged the project for more than a decade, with reports that on-set “KGB officers” – played by real-life ex-KGB officers – were allowed to control and punish the rest of the cast. Author Michael Idov, who was one of the few journalists allowed to spend time on set, described Khrzhanovsky as “unhinged” in a2011 GQ article.In Venice, Khrzhanovsky said he left the 700 hours of footage shot in Kharkiv untouched between the end of filming and 2023, in order to concentrate on art-project DAU off-shoots.Experimental films DAU. Natasha and DAU. Degeneratsiya were screened at the Berlin film festival in 2020, but Khrzhanovsky has described the three-hour feature presented in Venice as the “mother film”.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalClassical musicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikes | Iran | The Guardian
description: Oil price rises above $100 a barrel as Tehran responds to US attacks that sunk five Iranian tankers
Author: William Christou
Headline: Oil price rises above $100 a barrel as Tehran responds to US attacks that sunk five Iranian tankers
Content: Iranians drive past a billboard hanging on a pedestrian bridge in Tehran featuring a US underwater drone captured by the Iranian military and a sentence reading: ‘Hunting the Hunter.'Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAView image in fullscreenIranians drive past a billboard hanging on a pedestrian bridge in Tehran featuring a US underwater drone captured by the Iranian military and a sentence reading: ‘Hunting the Hunter.'Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPAIranIran claims to have attacked 10 ships near strait of Hormuz after US strikesOil price rises above $100 a barrel as Tehran responds to US attacks that sunk five Iranian tankersWilliam ChristouWed 9 Sep 2026 12.18 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTehran has said it attacked 10 ships around the strait of Hormuz after the US sunk five Iranian tankers, as escalating strikes between the two countries sent the oil price above $100 a barrel for the first time since July.The attacks were the sharpest flare-up of strikes in weeks, as the two sides struggled to break a deadlock in the six-month-long war. Fighting in recent weeks has largely revolved around who controls the strait of Hormuz, as Iran attempts to close off the waterway and Washington enforces a blockade of Iranian ports.The strait is a critical route for global energy supplies, with up to 20% of the world’s oil and gas transiting it before the US-Iran war. The rising price of oil, above the psychologically significant $100 mark, is likely to raise inflation and the price of goods.Stocks fell on Wall Street while rising fuel and food prices in the US will further frustrate the Trump administration, which faces a midterm election with an unpopular war and a cost-of-living crisis.Among the vessels struck by Iran were two US vessels and eight oil tankers, the Iranian’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said on Wednesday.The IRGC said the 10 vessels were “noncompliant” – a likely reference to ships that tried to traverse the waterway without its permission. At least one sailor was killed and another was missing.The US denied that its vessels were hit, with US Central Command saying on social media that all “attempted attacks failed”.A tanker in Iraqi waters carrying 2mi barrels of fuel oil was also struck by a drone, according to Iraqi officials. There were no reports of casualties among the crew and the Iraqi government said there were no reported oil leaks.Iran said it also fired missiles at US bases in Jordan – 18 of which authorities said were intercepted while two fell in unpopulated areas.View image in fullscreenCommercial vessels remain anchored off Bandar Abbas.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe US had said it destroyed five Iranian oil tankers overnight, publishing videos of ships on fire. The US military said the attacks were a response to Iran targeting a US navy warship twice in the previous two days.Iranian state TV said the US strikes had followed a “complex intelligence and operational action at dawn” to seize a US underwater drone in the strait. The US said the seized craft was a “defective” older model that did not carry any sensitive data.The back-and-forth strikes signalled an intensifying escalation between the two sides as Washington announced a new policy of attacking Iranian tankers if Iran targets its warships.“Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” the US secretary of state,Marco Rubio, told reporters.Iran said it would also escalate its attacks, and that for every two or three tankers struck it would respond by hitting 20. The IRGC said it would also release maps of a new, much-larger area near the strait that it considers forbidden for ships to traverse, extending as far as the Gulf off Chabahar for the first time.The conflict has also taken on an increasingly regional dimension as the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen traded strikes with Saudi Arabia.The Houthis launched a wave of attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, causing large fires at oil installations and wounding 73 people. The Houthis said dozens of people have been killed in Saudi airstrikes, something unconfirmed by Riyadh.Fighting re-ignited between the two sides after the Houthis launched an offensive against the Saudi-backed government of Yemen in south Yemen last week, aimed at reaching the Red Sea.The group is trying to enforce a Red Sea blockade against Saudi Arabia, announced in July. If enforced, it would cut off another route for the kingdom to export its oil.Explore more on these topicsIranStrait of HormuzOilUS foreign policyMarco RubionewsShareReuse this content

title: Merz accuses AfD of ‘ethnic cleansing’ policy and cancels call with Trump | Germany | The Guardian
description: German chancellor attacks Alternative für Deutschland after far-right party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt election
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: German chancellor attacks Alternative für Deutschland after far-right party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt election
Content: 0:41German chancellor accuses far-right AfD of calling for 'ethnic cleansing' – videoGermanyMerz accuses AfD of ‘ethnic cleansing’ policy and cancels call with TrumpGerman chancellor attacks Alternative für Deutschland after far-right party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt electionEurope live – latest updatesDeborah Colein BerlinWed 9 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany’s chancellor,Friedrich Merz, has accused the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with its “remigration” drive, after the nativist party’s seismic weekend victory in a state election.In his first public confrontation with the AfD since Sunday’sshock outcome in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz said at a raucous parliamentary debate that the far-right party would take an axe to one of the pillars of the German economy with a racist campaign of mass deportations.‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capitalRead more“The term ‘remigration’ is nothing but a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” he said on Wednesday to applause from the other parties in the Bundestag lower house.In a fiery speech addressed to the AfD parliamentary group, which repeatedly interrupted him with loud taunts and heckling, Merz said millions of working immigrants were crucial to German society.“If those working inGermanyhave to leave the country again because you are championing ‘remigration’,” Merz said, “then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function: not a single care home will remain open, not a single hospital in Germany will remain operational, and not a single restaurant in Germany will be able to stay in business.”He said the AfD’s rhetoric, which propelled it to the strongest showing for a far-right party in a German state since the Nazi period, “is precisely what is dividing our society so deeply”.The AfD has repeatedly called for large-scale expulsions of irregular migrants, a policy that would face stiff challenges under German law.View image in fullscreen(L-R) The AfD’s Tino Chrupalla, Ulrich Siegmund and Alice Weidel after the Saxony-Anhalt election win.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAIn the election, the party rode an international wave of populism, nationalism and discontent with mainstream parties, underscored overnight by congratulations fromDonald Trump.In a post on his Truth Social platform, the US president hailed the AfD’s “really big night” in Saxony-Anhalt. “They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly,” Trump wrote.Merz responded by cancelling a planned phone call with Trump on Wednesday. A spokesperson for the chancellor declined to explain but noted that Merz had always objected “in general terms” to “interfering in or commenting on the domestic political situation, particularly regarding elections”.Support for Merz, a conservative Christian Democrat, has plummeted in the 16 months since he took office at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, amid disappointment over slow progress oneconomic growthand the cost of living.He has adopted ahard line on border policyin a faltering effort to win back AfD supporters, and acknowledged Germany still had “problems in the area of migration”.“We still have many people in Germany who should not have permanent residency. This is consensus in the [ruling] coalition, that we need to deport more people,” he said on Wednesday.“But we make a careful distinction between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, and who are welcome here, and those who do not have permanent residency in Germany and who must leave our country. Unlike you [the AfD], we take great care to make this distinction.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe AfD won nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is seeking potential supporters among the other parties to elect him as state premier.Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more statesRead moreMerz, who has acknowledged his unpopularity played a role in the halving of support for his party in the state, tried to put a brave face on the rout. “Fifty-six percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt didn’t vote for you,” he told the AfD.He accused Siegmund, whose party is classed as rightwing extremist by domestic intelligence, of “electoral fraud” by already breaking a campaign promise not to seek to govern the state if he failed to win an absolute majority.“And you won’t manage that in Germany either [at the federal level],” Merz told the AfD co-leader Alice Weidel. “Nowhere in Germany will you get a majority. You are and remain a destructive force.”Merz also attacked the AfD for its opposition to military assistance for Ukraine, and accused it of making common cause with Russia, which Berlin has alleged is mounting a sabotage and disinformation campaign on its soil.He said that despite “clear evidence”a failed drone bomb attack at Leipzig airportlast month “had been planned in Russia for months and was specifically directed against Germany”, the AfD had remained silent on it.Earlier, Weidel had savoured her party’s resounding election victory from the podium, saying the CDU had been “pulverised” and calling it a referendum on Merz’s leadership.Attacking the government’s migration policy and blaming it for crime and other security problems, Weidel said: “Your time is up. The public want a change in policy, and they will get it,” reiterating her party’s aim to form a federal government in the foreseeable future.Polls show Merz’s fractious coalitionwould not have a majorityin a general election, though the next national vote is not due until 2029. The AfD is polling in first place at 28% to 29%, with the wind at its back before another two state polls this month,in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)EuropeThe far rightRaceDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: EU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter China | European Union | The Guardian
description: Authorities and public bodies to be urged to buy goods and services from Europe, but without binding quotas
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Authorities and public bodies to be urged to buy goods and services from Europe, but without binding quotas
Content: A Chinese-made electric bus in Copenhagen. Brussels is concerned about inroads Beijing is making into EU markets for transport and infrastructure.Photograph: Francis Joseph Dean/Dean Pictures/AlamyView image in fullscreenA Chinese-made electric bus in Copenhagen. Brussels is concerned about inroads Beijing is making into EU markets for transport and infrastructure.Photograph: Francis Joseph Dean/Dean Pictures/AlamyEuropean UnionEU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter ChinaAuthorities and public bodies to be urged to buy goods and services from Europe, but without binding quotasJennifer Rankinin BrusselsWed 9 Sep 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean authorities will be encouraged to buy more domestic goods and services when they spend public money under the EU latest effort to counter China’s economic might.In a further “Buy European” plan, theEuropean Commissionpublished proposals on Wednesday for a sweeping overhaul of EU public procurement rules.National authorities and public bodies, such as schools and hospitals, will be encouraged to buy goods and services made in Europe but, unlike earlier plans topromote domestically manufactured clean tech, there will be no binding “made in Europe” quotas.Brussels officials are concerned that many public agencies think existing EU rules oblige them to choose the cheapest bid when spending public money, which can lead to the contract going to a non-European firm.The European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, Stéphane Séjourné, told reporters the regulation would give public sector buyers greater legal certainty and clarity about purchasing goods and services made in Europe.“Purchasers can have a more preferential approach to European bids [and] restrict or reject bids from countries which do not have a public procurement agreement or do not play by binding rules in terms of public procurement internationally,” he said.Public procurement is estimated by EU officials to amount to 15% of the bloc’s gross domestic product, about €2.6tn (£2.2tn) a year, and is seen in Brussels as an underused lever already deployed by Washington and Beijing to support their respective domestic companies.The new rules will oblige public buyers in the EU to put more emphasis on quality and metrics such as environmental sustainability and local supply chains, rather than opting for the cheapest bid.Under the proposals public agencies will be obliged to give a minimum 30% weighting to quality when they draw up conditions to award a contract, or explain why they chose to disregard this indicator.Labour-intensive contracts will have a minimum 50% weighting for quality, so purchasers must ensure decent jobs when awarding the contract, not simply the cheapest price.Séjourné hopes the proposals will encourage more democratic scrutiny over the spending of public money by local authorities. “It won’t be the European Commission’s fault if purchasers were to prefer Chinese buses to European buses because … in the [draft regulation] there is every possibility to give preference to European buses.”View image in fullscreenStéphane Séjourné, who it the European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, is a close ally of Emmanuel Macron.Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPABrussels is concerned about inroads Beijing is making into European markets for transport and infrastructure, especially Chinese firms benefitting from state subsidies that make them cheaper than European alternatives.In April, the commission blocked a Chinese rolling-stock company from joining a consortium to build a new line on the Lisbon metro after an investigation found the firm had benefited from state subsidies that gave itan “unfair competitive edge”.Last year, Brussels opened an investigation into Chinese security company Nuctech, which has supplied European airports and ports with security scanners. EU officialssuspect the company was helped by subsidies and tax breaksthat gave it an unfair advantage in the European market, although the investigation has not reached final conclusions.Séjourné – a close ally of France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, who has long championed European preference – said spending public money on goods made in Europe should become “part of public discourse and accountability”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “It should be very clear that it’s not because ofEuropean Unionrules that a foreign product was preferred over a European one, but because it was a political choice that was made.”The draft regulation, which also aims to radically simplify rules by merging three laws into one, must be agreed by the European parliament and the EU ministers before it enters into force. It is likely to be altered during the legislative process.Séjourné is also spearheading a push for made-in-Europe rules toapply to the public purchase of renewable energy products and electric carsunder the the Industrial Accelerator Act. The IAA, which also is likely to be changed by MEPs and ministers, marks a departure for Brussels, long a bastion of open markets.The plans have alarmed the British government, but EU officials said the latest draft rules on procurement would not disadvantage UK firms because existing agreements ensured both sides played by the same rules.Séjourne said the EU had agreements with the UK whereby reciprocal market access was respected. “There should not be any difficulties for the UK,” he added.Non-EU countries that have agreements with the bloc on public procurement are not expected to face barriers.An online tool will allow public purchasers to see which countries are covered by the EU’s web of free-trade agreements and other international deals that cover procurement.Membership of the World Trade Organization’s agreement on government procurement (GPA), which promotes fair competition in markets to supply state bodies, will be an important indicator. The GPA has 22 members including the EU (counted as one), the UK, the US, Canada and Japan. MainlandChinais not party to the agreement.Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionEuropean CommissionChinaEuropeManufacturing sectorGlobal economyChinese economynewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo as new CEO takes center stage | Technology | The Guardian
description: The passport-size iPhone Duo serves as the first big test for John Ternus, who took over for Tim Cook last week
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: The passport-size iPhone Duo serves as the first big test for John Ternus, who took over for Tim Cook last week
Content: The iPhone Duo is displayed on Wednesday, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, California.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APView image in fullscreenThe iPhone Duo is displayed on Wednesday, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, California.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APTechnologyApple unveils folding iPhone Duo as new CEO takes center stageThe passport-size iPhone Duo serves as the first big test for John Ternus, who took over for Tim Cook last weekJohana BhuiyanWed 9 Sep 2026 14.45 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApplehas unveiled theiPhoneDuo,the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007.The nearly $2,000 device takes inspiration from iPads’ wide screens and combines them with the portability and camera features of iPhones. When opened, it is the company’s largest phone display and thinnest phone. The Duo opens and closes like a passport to double its screen size.“iPhone Duo brings an entirely new design while preserving everything you love from an iPhone,” saidJohn Ternus, the company’s new chief executive. “It feels effortless to use and it makes new experiences possible.”The phone will start at $1,999 and be available on 23 October.Apple’s new CEO introduces himself at annual showcase: ‘I continue to be inspired every single day’Read moreThe product release event, titled “Surprise and Shine”, began at 10am Pacific Standard Time on Apple’s campus in Cupertino,California, south of San Francisco.“I started the day with an intelligent personal hub and why there’s no product in the world that is better to be that hub than iPhone,” Ternus said. “We think the best way to achieve that is with a foldable design. Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones stuck together … scrolling through vertical content feels compromised.”Apple releases its first foldable phoneWhile competitors have released foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model is a first for the iPhone maker, and its rollout serves as the first big test for Ternus, who assumed the role on 1 September. He claimed the Duo “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”.Apple reportedly began testing prototypes of its folding iPhone display in early 2021 – though at the time there were no plans for its launch, according to a Bloombergreport.The company started the event with its more routine announcements, including the new iPhone 18 Pro, which starts at $1,199, and 18 Pro Max models, which start at $1,299.Appleemphasized the AI-enabled features that will be integrated throughout the phone. Called Siri AI, the company said it will be able to tap into third-party apps and already works with over 300,000 apps.View image in fullscreenJohn Ternus, Apple’s new CEO, holds the new foldable iPhone Duo during Apple’s event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Cupertino, California, on 9 September.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersAmong the many AI-related features available on the new iPhones will be a novel mechanism that fingerprints an image and identifies as captured by an iPhone’s camera – not generated by AI. The feature, called Apple Reference Image, will act as a “digital negative”, as one Apple executive described it, and serve as proof that the the original image was not AI-generated.Both new iPhones also represent a “massive leap” in battery life, executives said – the iPhone 18 Pro Max will have 45 hours of battery life and the iPhone 18 pro will have 36 hours of battery life.Though the foldable iPhone took center stage on Wednesday in California, overall demand for foldable phones makes up only a small sliver of overall mobile device sales. Customers’ interest in standard iPhones, by contrast, remains high, as evidenced in Apple’smost recent robust earnings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe company also unveilednew iterations of some of its other product offerings at its events and over the next few months, including updates to itsApple Watchand AirPods lines.The company announced the fifth generation of its AirPods headphones, describing them as 50% more noise cancelling than AirPods 4 and sporting five hours of battery life. The latest iteration starts at $129.The company also introduced its latest watches, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, pitching them as some of the most advanced and accurate wearable devices to support health and fitness goals.Tim Cook handed $47m package for new role as executive chair of AppleRead moreThe updated watch will include several new AI features, including “Health Age”, which analyzes heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition and measures how users stack up to their chronological age.The watch will also include “audio intelligence”, meant to enable your watch to record ambient conversations throughout the day and take notes, producing a transcript of what someone said 15 seconds earlier in case you missed it. At the end of the day, a watch user can review a summary of their day, called a “Siri Recap”.The company said these recordings are stored on the device and anything that is collected is end-to-end encrypted.Ternustookthe stageas CEO for the first time, marking the beginning of his tenure as the head of Apple, replacing theoutgoing CEO,Tim Cook. In anoteto employees on his first day, Ternus said that he was excited about “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined”.“I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store,” Ternus wrote in his letter. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyiPhoneAppleSmartphonesCaliforniaComputingMobile phonesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Supercar maker McLaren to create 1,000 UK jobs in £450m tech investment | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: New roles at Woking-based centre a welcome boost to ailing automotive industry
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: New roles at Woking-based centre a welcome boost to ailing automotive industry
Content: A McLaren sports car: the company currently employs 2,500 staff.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA McLaren sports car: the company currently employs 2,500 staff.Photograph: UCG/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesAutomotive industrySupercar maker McLaren to create 1,000 UK jobs in £450m tech investmentNew roles at Woking-based centre a welcome boost to ailing automotive industryMark SweneyWed 9 Sep 2026 04.34 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British supercar manufacturer McLaren is to create 1,000 jobs in a welcome boost to the UK’s struggling automotive industry.The carmaker is creating the jobs as part of a £450m investment in its technology centre in Woking,Surrey, near to the plant where it manufactures all of its vehicles.McLaren, which last year merged with the premium UK electric vehicle startup Forseven Holdings, employs 2,500 staff. The new jobs will include indirect and agency workers, according to the Financial Times, which first reported the investment.The news comes days after Jaguar Land Rover confirmed plans tocut 4,000 jobs over the next two years. JLR, which is restructuring to address falling sales and financial challenges, including Donald Trump’s tariff wars and thefallout from a cyber-attack last year, employs 44,000 people globally and 34,000 in the UK.The cuts will mainly affect the 26,000 UK employees who are salaried, and management workers.Last year, CYVN Holdings, an Abu Dhabi government-owned investment company, acquired McLaren’s automotive business from Bahraini sovereign wealth fund Mumtalakat.CYVN has said that it plans to invest $2bn (£1.4bn) over the next five years in the loss-making group.McLaren Automotive, one of the UK’s best-known sports carmakers, is thought to be planning a product overhaul after years of manufacturing only performance cars such as the F1 model, first launched in 1992.It was last year reported to be planning a new SUV as part of the turnaround plan under its boss Nick Collins, a former JLR executive, though no new information has emerged since then. It appointed a new chief creative officer, David Woodhouse, formerly of Nissan and Ford, over the summer.CYVN also holds a minority stake in McLaren Racing, the parent company of the Formula One team which has won the last two constructors championships in the sport and is also based in Woking. Mumtalakat still has majority control of McLaren Racing.European carmakers have faced tough trading conditions as Chinese rivals, such as BYD and Chery, have enjoyed soaring sales across the UK and mainland Europe.In July, Chery, which also owns the Omoda and Jaecoo brands, accounted for nearly 8% of UK market share, up from 3% last year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT).Last week, Volkswagen announced it wouldcut 100,000of its more than 650,000 global workforce by 2030, and halve the number of models it produces. VW group also includes the Bentley, Audi, Skoda, Seat, Porsche, Cupra and Lamborghini brands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom early next year, UK carmakers face a 10% tariff for electric vehicles shipped to the EU. UK-made vehicles do not qualify for “made in Europe” subsidies, under current proposals.The UK government is alsoconsulting on loosening its battery EV sales targetsfor manufacturers, after extensive lobbying by the industry.The chief executive of the SMMT, Mike Hawes, said earlier this summer that companies with existing UK operationswere considering building new models, but were holding back until ministers relaxed EV sales rules.Lachlan Buirds, managing director of manufacturer Edale, said: “McLaren’s investment is a welcome reminder that UK manufacturing is a sector with a future.“Recent redundancy announcements understandably attract attention, but they risk giving young people the impression that UK manufacturing is an industry in decline. In reality, modern manufacturing increasingly depends on engineering, automation, software and digital technology, creating a much broader range of career opportunities.”Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryManufacturing sectorSurreyJaguar Land RoverTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: UK datacentres will create just 25% of jobs predicted by tech sector, analysis finds | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Facilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank says
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Facilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank says
Content: An Equinix datacentre under construction in Slough, near London. Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres amid growing public scepticism.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Equinix datacentre under construction in Slough, near London. Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres amid growing public scepticism.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesDatacentres - UKUK datacentres will create just 25% of jobs predicted by tech sector, analysis findsFacilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank saysHeather StewartEconomics editorWed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDatacentres in the UK will create just a quarter of the jobs predicted by the tech sector, while consuming vast amounts of energy, according to new research.Environmental thinktank Verdant predicts that all the datacentres currently planned are likely to directly employ 10,400 workers – compared with the more than 40,000 cited in projections by the industry lobby group TechUK.Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres in the face of growing public scepticism, amid concerns about their demand for water and energy. The government has also echoed TechUK’s claims about job creation.Verdant’s analysis is based on 20 projects for which data on staffing levels are publicly available, including via planning applications, company accounts and press releases – as well as international comparisons.It says the datacentres that have already been built have directly created fewer than 4,400 jobs – about 8.6 jobs for each megawatt of energy they consume, against the 43.7 jobs claimed in TechUK’s projections.Verdant also argues that the many future projects currently at the planning stage are on a far larger scale, and so likely to be much less job-intensive – perhaps creating as few as 1.6 permanent positions per megawatt.Its analysis focuses on the permanent workers needed to maintain and operate datacentres, setting aside the much larger number of temporary construction jobs needed to build them.James Meadway, the thinktank’s co-director, said: “We’re being rushed into supporting a frantic pace of datacentre buildout on very flimsy economic grounds.“Clearly artificial intelligence and related technologies have great potential. But vast new datacentres arrive at significant real costs to local communities and even our climate ambitions, and their use case has to be made by the government and industry – rather than assuming we can build first and then work out why we did later.”View image in fullscreenDemonstrators protest against redevelopment plans for the 10-acre Truman Brewery site in Brick Lane, which include a datacentre.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesTo underline the resource intensity of the vast data warehouses, Verdant compared the 8.6 jobs they currently create per megawatt of power used with about 400 in a car plant and more than 3,600 in a hospital or health facility.The government rejected this comparison, and questioned Verdant’s methodology. A spokesperson said: “This report relies on a deeply misleading jobs-per-megawatt metric, makes false comparisons with hospitals and schools, and appears to confuse electricity capacity with actual consumption. More seriously, it discounts the wider economic value of compute [computing capacity] and the national security and sovereignty case for building critical digital infrastructure in Britain.”Verdant said it had based its calculations on the electricity capacity that tech firms claim they need – which could still crowd out alternative plans, even if the completed datacentres don’t end up using all the capacity.Labour has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure in an attempt to speed up the planning process, and Andy Burnham has underlined his backing for the sector by appointing AI minister Kanishka Narayan to his cabinet.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNarayan has advocated a rapid increase in datacentres, partly on grounds of national sovereignty. He told the Times last month: “The British public is very clear that it wants strong defence. It wants strong, sovereign capability, it doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity in this country.”By contrast, the Green party in Englandhas called for a moratorium on buildingdatacentres, whilethere have been protests in Scotland, amid claims that massive projects are being rushed through.Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England, said: “The government is planning to steamroller local opposition so private companies can build datacentres – but it can’t explain what the benefits are.‘“England and Wales are still facing drought after our hottest summer ever, but these datacentres are set to be given priority access to water. Meanwhile, this latest research suggests far fewer jobs may actually be created in constructing and staffing them than the government claims.”In response to the Green party’s call for a “pause”, a government spokesperson insisted that it would “simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data”.A spokesperson for TechUK said: “Our estimates that the UK datacentre industry supports 43,500 jobs, and could support 40,000 more by 2035, are built on a published methodology using industry data and standard economic impact assessment techniques. The figures were built transparently from the best available industry data at the time, and we are confident they remain a reasonable estimate of the sector’s employment contribution.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKAI (artificial intelligence)Technology policyEnergyComputingEnergy industryTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Forget vinyl v digital debates, this kind of musical ‘authenticity’ brings real rewards | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Period instruments are miles away from retro affectation, and as two Proms this week will show, can actually bring historical music up to the moment
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Period instruments are miles away from retro affectation, and as two Proms this week will show, can actually bring historical music up to the moment
Content: Timely … Mary Bevin (Euridice) reaches up for Gyula Orendt (Orfeo), in the final act of Orfeo, a collaboration between the Roundhouse and the Royal Opera featuring the Early Opera Company’s period instrument orchestra.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTimely … Mary Bevin (Euridice) reaches up for Gyula Orendt (Orfeo), in the final act of Orfeo, a collaboration between the Roundhouse and the Royal Opera featuring the Early Opera Company’s period instrument orchestra.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTom Service on musicClassical musicForget vinyl v digital debates, this kind of musical ‘authenticity’ brings real rewardsTom ServicePeriod instruments are miles away from retro affectation, and as two Proms this week will show, can actually bring historical music up to the momentWed 9 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.26 EDTShareNostalgia. What a kick. And what a commercial boon for the music industry. Love the sound of 60s pop and 70s disco? You need the original synths if you’re a composer or producer. You listen to music on digital streams? Loser! Join the retro-future of vinyl enthusiasm, and feel the grooves under your fingers like your parents or grandparents used to. Or you can even make music physical again through the horrible medium of cassettes: all that plastic, all those tiny liner notes, all that high-speed dubbing.Retro-futurists cherish what they claim is the extra warmth and sonic richness of vinyl, but there is no acoustic reason why vinyl is better. It is in fact objectively worse as a carrier of sonic information than any high-resolution stream of the same track, song or symphony. For cassette nostalgists, if it’s got that old-fashioned tape hiss, it sounds more “real”. We’re now looking for things to sound less clean. Because we distrust today’s technological utopia, we want signs that our music is less polished, less perfect, and thus more human.But what the recording industry is doing now with its return to vinyl, classical music has been doing for decades. Musicians and musicologists have long been obsessed with learning about the origins of the music they study and play, to experience what the technology of instruments and performing cultures of earlier centuries actually sounded like, whether the 12th-century Germany of Hildegard of Bingen or the 19th-century Vienna of Beethoven and Schubert.View image in fullscreenJan Steen’s A Young Woman playing a Harpsichord to a Young Man (probably 1659) in the National Gallery, LondonPhotograph: The National Gallery Photographic Department./The National Gallery, LondonDavid Munrowbrought medieval and Renaissance music to the mainstream across TV, radio and recordings in the 1970s and showing what instruments such as shawms and crumhorns could do;Roger Norringtonand John Eliot Gardiner set up choirs and ensembles to do the same for 17th and 18th-century music, and Nikolaus Harnoncourt led the charge through the music of later centuries, putting the ethos of early music research into the lifeblood of chamber groups and large-scale symphony orchestras in music from Schubert to Bruckner.But where the claims for vinyl or cassettes’ “authenticity” are bogus when it comes to actual sonic fidelity, it’s different when comparing older instruments in classical cultures and their modern counterparts. Earlier instruments have different qualities of sound and expression. The sound and feel of a harpsichord that Bach was writing for in the 18th century is vastly different to a grand piano made today: the plucked strings of the harpsichord mean that the sound of each note disappears quickly, where a Steinway can create halos and continuities of sound. French horns that can play in any key are taken for granted today, where previous generations had to literally pull their brass instruments apart to play one set of notes or another. It’s a similar story for strings and woodwinds, as earlier generations of musicians had to play with the temperamental realities of gut strings that don’t stay in tune, and reeds that couldn’t be relied on.But the sounds that earlier orchestral instruments make aren’t “worse” in the way that cassettes or vinyl are. Instead, their differences invite other ways of playing for the musicians, and they open up new dimensions of feeling for us. The difference between Bach’s music when it’s played on modern instruments in what is now – ironically – an old-school approach, using vibrato in the strings, lush lyricism in the rest of the orchestra, and full-scale choral forces, compared with the leaner sounds that smaller period instrument ensembles make, isn’t only a difference of soundworld, it’s a gulf of meaning and feeling.Listen to these two performances of the opening chorus of Bach’s Matthew Passion:Karl Richter conducting his massed Munich forces in 1979, andPaul McCreesh leading the Gabrieli Consort in 2003.They’re playing the same piece, but these are radically different experiences. Richter’s reading of the work is about making a vast immovable musical monument, while McCreesh’s – played nearly twice as fast, using just one voice to each part – is an invitation to us as individuals to empathise, to bear witness, to be part of the drama.View image in fullscreenJean Rondeau plays Bach’s Goldberg Variations at Milton Court on the harpsichord for a 2018 Barbican concert (read our review)Photograph: Alecsandra Raluca Drăgoi/The GuardianThat’s the key: these are new, contemporary feelings that period instrument performances open up. As the pianistVikingur Ólafsson said, the idea that if you play on old instruments you’re making the exact sounds that Bach, or Beethoven or Mahler would have heard is neither truly possible, and nor is it the point. Our ears, our bodies, and our whole listening culture is different. (Which reminds me ofJaneane Garofalo’s immortal cameo as the “serving wench” Melindain the medieval-themed restaurant in The Cable Guy: “There were no utensils in medieval times, hence there are no utensils at Medieval Times. Would you like a refill on that Pepsi?”)In the final few Proms concerts of the season you can hear the latest developments of classical’s retro-future explorers, all playing “period instruments”. On Thursday, the musicians of Arcangelo performBach’s B Minor Masson original instruments, and the next night, there’sMahler’s Ninth symphonyfrom the Mahler Academy Orchestra playing instruments that fit the specifications of the ones that Mahler himself ordered for the Vienna opera in the early 1900s. Period instruments have more grain, more colour, more guttural directness and more lyrical intensity than their modern counterparts and so to my mind are better equipped to reveal the emotional imperfections, ambiguities, and expressive complexities of the music they’re playing.That makes me sound like a cassette-fetishising nerd. Oh dear ... In fact, I’ll go further and say that performances such as the Mass in B Minor and Mahler’s 9th at the Proms will have an authenticity that no recording format, analogue or digital, can reproduce. These are one-off performances that will be made and witnessed by those human beings, true to themselves in every moment. All these historical instruments aren’t really about getting closer to past times but to the power of the present tense.This week Tom has been listening to:On repeat, the Berlin Philharmonic’s Proms with Kirill Petrenko. I know, I’m a broken record on this, but theirElgar and Tchaikovskywas inspired and inspiring: they found new depths of feeling and resonance in every moment. Magic.View image in fullscreenInspired and inspiring: Kiril Petrenko conducts the Berlin Philharmonic at 2026’s BBC PromsPhotograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouExplore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicProms 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Evanescence review – devastating power and range from one of rock’s great vocal talents | Music | The Guardian
description: The titanic choruses and stormy metal riffs of latest album Sanctuary are the perfect foundation for Amy Lee’s astonishing, skyscraping vocal range
Author: Christopher Lord
Headline: The titanic choruses and stormy metal riffs of latest album Sanctuary are the perfect foundation for Amy Lee’s astonishing, skyscraping vocal range
Content: Moving through the registers … Amy Lee of Evanescence on stage at the First Direct Arena.Photograph: Seanen MiddletonView image in fullscreenMoving through the registers … Amy Lee of Evanescence on stage at the First Direct Arena.Photograph: Seanen MiddletonMusicReviewEvanescence review – devastating power and range from one of rock’s great vocal talentsFirst Direct Arena, LeedsThe titanic choruses and stormy metal riffs of latest album Sanctuary are the perfect foundation for Amy Lee’s astonishing, skyscraping vocal rangeChristopher LordWed 9 Sep 2026 08.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 08.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo watch Evanescence in concert is to be spellbound by founder Amy Lee’s astonishing voice. The Arkansas band’s gifted mezzo-soprano lends their music vocals that range from skyscraping and spectacular to haunting and devastating. She soon moves through the registers on the opener Sanctuary, setting the stage for a show during which her vocals seem to scale ever greater peaks, even when you are convinced that there are no octaves left to conquer. And she makes it look effortless, striding around the stage, headbanging and fist-pumping the air.It’s standard promotional protocol for a band to lean on their new album on tour, but it still shows impressive faith in their audience that tonight Evanescence perform all but one song from Sanctuary, which is also the title of their sixth LP. Jordan Fish, formerly of Bring Me the Horizon, produced most of it and his metallic influence is clear: pummelling drums, titanic choruses and walls of stormy riffs make the band’s new material noticeably heavier than the gothic hard rock of their earlier years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAmy Lee of Evanescence: ‘I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers’Read moreGoing Under is one of those brooding, decades-old staples. Caustic chugging guitar clears the way for towering choruses to explode into life, sparking enormous singalongs with Lee at the helm. Afterlife is anthemic, anguished pop metal while Calm Down is a groovy, synth-heavy number that creeps towards the most colossal breakdown of the night. It’s also the point when the band first utilise every inch of the stage, activating rising platforms and synchronised tongues of flame – drummer Will Hunt bolts upright from his stool to give the floor toms an almighty whack.Perched at the keyboard for the penultimate song, My Immortal, Lee thanks the band’s crew, her fellow musicians, and the fans who have brought them “across the ocean over and over again, growing up together” for more than 20 years. Lee, 44,recently told this paperthat she can see herself performing into her 60s, which is good news. In music generally – not just rock – a singular talent like hers is not so easily replaced.Explore more on these topicsMusicMetalPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Uprising review – the peasants are revolting in muddled historical epic | Movies | The Guardian
description: Andrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period piece
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Andrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period piece
Content: The film The Uprising is about the historical 1381 Peasants’ Revolt in plague-ravaged England.Photograph: Betina La Plante/Focus Features/APView image in fullscreenThe film The Uprising is about the historical 1381 Peasants’ Revolt in plague-ravaged England.Photograph: Betina La Plante/Focus Features/APMoviesReviewThe Uprising review – the peasants are revolting in muddled historical epicAndrew Garfield’s charisma can’t save Paul Greengrass’s grim and depressingly generic period pieceOwen MyersWed 9 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 09.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHollywood loves giving young actors their own historical epic as much as audiences seem to dislike watching them. Timothée Chalamet and Chris Pine’s least remembered roles are in the medieval set filmsThe KingandOutlaw King(no relation), Ridley Scott’sThe Last Duelmade back only a third of its $100m budget and earlier this year, the Saudi-backed seventh-century dramaDesert Warriorstarring Anthony Mackie and Ben Kingsley quietly became one of the biggest flops of all time. Last week, it was reported that Scott blamed the failure of Gladiator II on Paul Mescal not being“masculine enough”in a logical leap which only makes sense if your barometer for masculinity is a man whothrows hotel phonesand yells at producers in storage closets.Practical Magic 2 review – Bullock and KIdman return for odd sequel that still casts a spellRead moreOn paper, The Uprising should be different: it’s a historical epic from a blue-chip director (the Bourne trilogy’sPaul Greengrass), a nuanced, introspective leading man (Andrew Garfield) and a milieu that uncomfortably chimes with the western world’s backslide into repressive authoritarianism (The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381). In reality, it is a disjointed slog through the mud with the emotional depth of a History Channel rerun.Through Greengrass’s lens, late 14th-century England seems like an utterly wretched place, not only because of the sludge-grey sky, scratchy brown sacks that everyone wears and the fact that no one seems to have had a wash in weeks, but because a despotic king treats the country’s people like scum, gouging them out of what little they have with hefty taxes to advance his own vainglorious agenda. Garfield’s character, who identifies only as Ploughman (“I am what I do,” he grunts), is mourning the loss of his wife and two children after they died from the plague, and will not stand for it any more. When asked for proof of his family’s death, one day he swipes clean the table of the taxman. “We’ve given you enough,” he cries, as the townspeople’s collective rage boils over into a riot.He’s an unconvincing hero, this gruff Ploughman. The character seems to have been constructed as an everyman figure who unites the common people of England, but without any particular magnetism or spice, he often feels like he could beanyman. His troupe soon meets two people who actually were in the Peasants’ Revolt: the priest John Ball and rebel leader Wat Tyler (Jamie BellandCosmo Jarvis: both great and, unlike Garfield, both look like they actually could be from the late middle ages). “Join us, Ploughman,” beckons Tyler, as Garfield’s character, his band of brothers and a tomboy named Alyce,Thomasin McKenzie, unite to march on London with an aim to confront the king and restore England to the egalitarian principles of the Domesday Book.Runner review – Alan Ritchson and Owen Wilson thriller is serviceable B-movie campRead moreThus follows a rather hectic-feeling race from one greige setting to the next as the rebels have their run of modern-day Kent, assembling in Maidstone before storming Canterbury cathedral, and then traveling to meet the king and his men in Blackheath. Greengrass’s camerawork can occasionally swoon, with stunning aerial shots of a flotilla on the Thames, but his signature handheld style is a trick that has gone stale: the only uprising I felt during the seasick fight scenes was my breakfast threatening to return on me.View image in fullscreenTom Hollander, Woody Norman and Katherine Waterston in The Uprising.Photograph: Courtesy of Focus FeaturesHigh points briefly come from Katherine Waterston’s satisfyingly icy turn as the king’s mother as well asTom HollanderandStephen Dillaneas members of the slimy royal counsel, and there is one wickedly gruesome moment in the third act that feels genuinely envelope-pushing. But there are far too many scenes revolving around the Ploughman ominously polishing his scythe or extended debates at Windsor Castle.Marketing meltdown: why has Andrew Garfield’s new film suddenly added Robin Hood?Read moreGarfield does the best he can with the material, but by the time Ploughman has a righteous and rageful awakening, it is far too late. And the failure of the film to nail the uneasy parallels to today’s political life feels like looking a gift horse in the mouth. There’s certainly a lot of points of identification for a modern audience with downtrodden people who don’t feel heard by the powers that be, but Greengrass barely lets the audience pause for breath, let alone trust them to join those dots.A couple of weeks before release, the US distributor Focus Featuresbriefly changedthe film’s title to The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood, suggesting that it would show events “that helped inspire the legend of Robin Hood”, even though the Peasants’ Revolt took place nearly 200 years after the time of the folkloric outlaw and his merry men. Meanwhile, The Uprising makes no mention of Robin Hood: almost as if it was all a last-ditch attempt to drum up buzz for a movie that is about as fun as trench foot.The Uprising is out in the US on 11 September, the UK on 9 October and Australia on 22 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmAction and adventure filmsAndrew GarfieldPaul GreengrassJamie BellStephen DillaneCosmo JarvisreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Inglourious baristas: why is Brad Pitt making coffee for 16 abusive dogs? | Brad Pitt | The Guardian
description: In new film The Heart of the Beast, the A-lister’s bond with his loyal mutt proves crucial. In Spike Jonze’s new advert, Pitt is rather more subservient
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: In new film The Heart of the Beast, the A-lister’s bond with his loyal mutt proves crucial. In Spike Jonze’s new advert, Pitt is rather more subservient
Content: Well groomed … Brad Pitt in the advert.Photograph: De'LonghiView image in fullscreenWell groomed … Brad Pitt in the advert.Photograph: De'LonghiBrad PittInglourious baristas: why is Brad Pitt making coffee for 16 abusive dogs?In new film The Heart of the Beast, the A-lister’s bond with his loyal mutt proves crucial. In Spike Jonze’s new advert, Pitt is rather more subservientStuart HeritageWed 9 Sep 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrad Pitt has a new movie out this month, The Heart of the Beast, about an emotionally damaged man who forms a life-saving bond with a dog. If that sounds familiar, maybe it is because you have seen The Call of the Wild. Or maybe it is because you have seen A Dog’s Way Home. Or maybe it is because you have seen Dog. Or, look, you get the idea.But perhaps Brad Pitt knows that getting people to see something as unimaginative as The Heart of the Beast is an uphill struggle, because that would explain why he has just made an advert that looks and feels much more like the Brad Pitt dog movie that deserves to be made. In short, it is an advert where Brad Pitt gets loudly disparaged by a number of dogs for an extended period of time.As reported by Variety, the commercial is for the De’Longhi Magnifica Duo, an all-singing, all-dancing coffee machine that retails in the UK for about £700. But really the product is beside the point. The main point is that the advert, running to almost two minutes, sees Brad Pitt stumble around cluelessly while a small army of real dogs – all of whom have names, some of whom are dressed in human clothes – shout insults at him.As he wanders into his living room, some of the dogs (in subtitle) tell him that he woke up too late. They tell him to make a hot coffee and, even though he has started to make a cold one, he drops his head and sullenly obliges. Then another dog says that he can’t have any coffee at all until his attitude improves. “OK,” he mumbles in return, like a put-upon sitcom dad. The dogs berate him for his slovenliness and his stupidity and, when he finally snaps and tells them to go and fetch a stick, they make him fetch a stick for them instead.It’s a weird advert. It is slightly reminiscent of that bizarre Chinese commercial for Chinese vitamins from a few years back, whenTom Hiddleston cooks you breakfastbefore looking straight into your eyes and promising that he’s going to have sex with you. The difference is that, while you could tell that Hiddleston desperately hoped that nobody would see his ad, Pitt’s has been made for an American market. He wants you to see this.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: De’LonghiOf course, it helps that the weirdness is deliberate. The commercial was directed by Spike Jonze, the visionary director of no films at all for the last 13 years. The world has been crying out for a new film by Jonze, and if the closest we’re going to get is a film where Brad Pitt gets insulted by a dog named Kyle, then that will have to do.In fact, the more you consider it, the better a move this advert seems for Pitt. Compared with the derivative grit-jawed Americana of The Heart of the Beast, it demonstrates that he’s much better when he’s allowed to be funny. And if it underlines a connection between Pitt and dogs along the way, creating an implied synergy with his movie, then that’s OK too.It’s also a big step up from Pitt’s previous De’Longhi commercials, the majority of which just required him tostand still and smoulder for a while. Those commercials could have starred anyone. You could have put a carrot on human growth hormones and it would have adequately done the job. At least this one has a bit of personality.Only the De’Longhi sales team will know if this has been a successful gambit or not, but speaking personally I think it works perfectly. With any luck it will bring Spike Jonze out of retirement, and Brad Pitt Gets Shit-Talked by SomeDogswill be a motion picture by next Christmas.Explore more on these topicsBrad PittAdvertisingDogsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Union Town review – passionate exposé of US delivery workers’ employment conditions | Venice film festival | The Guardian
