description: Barbara Kopple returns with her third film investigating US workers’ rights – this time, undocumented ‘deliveristas’ and the attempts to unionise Amazon staff
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Barbara Kopple returns with her third film investigating US workers’ rights – this time, undocumented ‘deliveristas’ and the attempts to unionise Amazon staff
Content: ‘A battle-hardened affair’ … Union Town.Photograph: Hannes Hosp/Cabin Creek FilmsView image in fullscreen‘A battle-hardened affair’ … Union Town.Photograph: Hannes Hosp/Cabin Creek FilmsVenice film festivalReviewUnion Town review – passionate exposé of US delivery workers’ employment conditionsVenice film festival:Barbara Kopple returns with her third film investigating US workers’ rights – this time, undocumented ‘deliveristas’ and the attempts to unionise Amazon staffXan Brooksin VeniceWed 9 Sep 2026 11.49 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarbara Kopple’s documentary about app-based delivery workers is a stirring, defiant, battle-hardened affair, swinging between the fraught picket line and the still more hazardousNew YorkCity streets. It’s a new film that feels old in the best sense of the word; a hoarse battle cry that summons the ghosts of The Grapes of Wrath and the New Deal, Eugene Debs and Woody Guthrie. That America is long dead and buried, a casualty of changing times, but Kopple sees no reason why it should not rise again.Union Town, tellingly, is the third part of a loose trilogy which serves as an ongoing audit of US workers’ rights. This began with 1976’s Harlan County, USA, which tackled a Kentucky miners’ strike, and continued through 1990’s American Dream, which covered a meatpacking plant in Austin, Minnesota. Since then, however, the culture has shifted, atomised, with the big corporations increasingly reliant on a shadow economy of undocumented workers. Kopple’s “deliveristas” ferry packages for the likes of Amazon and DoorDash but they are technically third-party contractors. That means if, say, they happen to be injured in the line of duty, they cover the hospital bills and repairs to the bike. It also means that they are likely to be fired while they’re laid up in bed.View image in fullscreenAn Amazon worker in Union Town.Photograph: Hannes Hosp/Cabin Creek FilmsKopple spotlights a push by the Teamsters union to unionise Amazon’s disparate workforce, which culminates in a paralysing six-day strike over the 2024 Christmas period (“You’re killing Santa,” a disapproving news anchor tells Teamster president Sean O’Brien). Along the way, the film collates a lengthy and damning rap sheet. We hear from the warehouse employees who pack boxes in 105-degree (40.5C) heat, the delivery drivers who sleep in their cars and earn $7 an hour, and the exhausted migrant workers who live under threat of being apprehended by ICE. Kopple’s fly-on-the-wall approach ensures that these invisible workers have names, faces and voices – and it’s only the bosses who refuse to break cover. The sole one we hear from is Carol Tomé, the grandmotherly CEO of UPS. She materialises on a TV business show to enthuse about the benefits of putting robots in the warehouse. Robots would be better, she giggles. More efficient; “No attitude.”Union Town is keen to emphasise the positives. Solidarity pays dividends. David slew Goliath. “Jeff Bezos is Darth Vader,” says one Teamster. “And we’re the rebel army.” And yet the unavoidable takeaway of this bleakly potent picture is that this struggle is Sissyphian, with the membership split and confused and actively voting against their own interests. The Amazon drivers envy the UPS drivers; 60% of Teamster members support Trump. Outside the Amazon headquarters at night, the union’s Chris Williamson maintains what is effectively a one-man picket line after everyone else has gone home. He’s freezing his feet off in the New York slush and angrily, desperately calling for reinforcements.Explore more on these topicsVenice film festivalDocumentary filmsFestivalsNew YorkUS unionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: DAU review – Ilya Krzhanovsky’s crazed Soviet inferno reaches its central character | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director’s bleak epic project about the scientist Lev Landau finally focuses on the genius maudit who inspired the series
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The director’s bleak epic project about the scientist Lev Landau finally focuses on the genius maudit who inspired the series
Content: Spectacularly pessimistic … DAU.Photograph: Phenomen BerlinView image in fullscreenSpectacularly pessimistic … DAU.Photograph: Phenomen BerlinMoviesReviewDAU review – Ilya Krzhanovsky’s crazed Soviet inferno reaches its central characterVenice film festival:The director’s bleak epic project about the scientist Lev Landau finally focuses on the genius maudit who inspired the seriesPeter BradshawWed 9 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow would it be if Christopher Nolan got sidetracked while making Oppenheimer, and decided to spend 20 years and millions of dollars of other people’s money reconstructing the Los Alamos HQ in all its minute detail, which would be the site of a gigantic immersive multimedia project, releasing epic and sexually explicit sidebar movies about … someone who worked in the commissary … or a scary incidental guy from the CIA … before finally getting round to the fundamental main-event movie with Cillian Murphy as the A-bomb’s father?Perhaps it would be something like Ilya Krzhanovsky’s authentically mad, obsessively sexual, and spectacularly pessimistic epic project about the Soviet scientist and Nobel laureate Lev Landau, or “Dau”, whose work spanned the 1920s to the postwar and cold war eras, and whose notional endorsement of free love the DAU movies escalate into a dissolute sex addiction. Khrzhanovsky gives this a kind of classical Hellenic distinction by fictionalising a Greek background for our mysterious horny hero, whose indulgences coexist with his self-questioning obsession with his own genius and loneliness. It would be vulgar and irrelevant to wonder if Khrzhanovsky, like any artist, is in fact working on a self-portrait. But you surely can’t work on a (still unfinished) project like this without a strong personal connection.Here, at all events, is the latest Dau iteration, a more conventionally conceived biopic about Lev Landau (although we don’t see him getting the Nobel – perhaps that’s a separate film). Apparently this is the feature that Khrzhanovsky originally envisioned before the creative Big Bang that created the Dau multimedia universe. His first offshoot pictureDAU. Natasha(2020) was about two women who work in the canteen of Dau’s research institute, a place drenched in sexual tension and political paranoia and violence. The next film to come was the grisly epicDAU. Degeneration(2020), set in the late 60s with Dau himself – still here a peripheral character – on his deathbed.Now we have a more straightforward story, albeit one streaked with Boschian visions, and stroboscopic visual breakdowns. Dau, played by Greek-Russian musician and actor Teodor Currentzis, is a garrulous, brilliant, melancholy theoretical physicist touched with genius which the audience has to take on trust (none of the various setpiece speeches about quantum mechanics are assigned to him). He cheats on his wife Nora (Radmila Shchogolieva), humiliating her with his flagrant extramarital indulgences; he is interested in human nature, human behaviour and human ethics and the way in which these correlate with the coming revolution in physics.Dau is also part of a consensus among scientists that their work should not be used for warlike purposes. This lands him in big trouble with the military authorities, particularly the terrifying bullet-headed KGB man Vladimir (Vladimir Azhippo), a chilling character from DAU.Degeneration. He is saved from prison by his friend Kruptisa (Anatoly Vasilyev), a fictional variant of the real Soviet scientist Pyotr Kapitsa – on condition that he swallows his pride and his principles and agrees to work on the bomb. Dau rewards Krupitsa by letting him down, vacillating and betraying him.It is a mad, daunting, haunting film which somehow persuades you that Landau is at the sulphurous centre of Soviet tyranny. How is it that this figure has spawned, is spawning, this massive, proliferating, multiplatform, multimedia phenomenon, so bizarre, so detached from what we think of as the accepted commercial rules for any artwork, that it is still difficult to believe it exists at all? What an enigma it is – and what an adventure.DAU screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsVenice film festivalRussiaEuropeFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Even better than the Real Thing? The overlooked Black music scene of 1970s Liverpool | Music | The Guardian
description: Despite the city’s backdrop of deprivation and racism, vibrant nightclubs and daring artists thrived – but after No 1 success for the Real Thing, why was the scene ignored?
Author: Claudia Efemini
Headline: Despite the city’s backdrop of deprivation and racism, vibrant nightclubs and daring artists thrived – but after No 1 success for the Real Thing, why was the scene ignored?
Content: The Real Thing, at the time of their No 1 hit You to Me Are Everything.Photograph: Screenbound International Pictures LtdView image in fullscreenThe Real Thing, at the time of their No 1 hit You to Me Are Everything.Photograph: Screenbound International Pictures LtdMusicEven better than the Real Thing? The overlooked Black music scene of 1970s LiverpoolDespite the city’s backdrop of deprivation and racism, vibrant nightclubs and daring artists thrived – but after No 1 success for the Real Thing, why was the scene ignored?Claudia EfeminiWed 9 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMonths before the Real Thing’s You to Me Are Everything became a UK No 1 hit in 1976, lead singer Chris Amoo took the unreleased song to the Timepiece, a nightclub devoted to Black music tucked in between bars on Liverpool’s Fleet Street. His DJ friend Les Spaine stuck it on, and the empty dancefloor “just filled up, and nobody, not one person in that place, had heard the song before”, Amoo says with pride on a call from his home on the outskirts ofLiverpool. “That’s when me and Les looked at each other and thought: you’ve got something there, brother.”The track’s symphonic majesty and romantic vocals captured the hearts of millions, and it peaked in the charts during 1976’s summer heatwave. Fifty years later, Amoo is on tour with his fellow bandmate Dave Smith in celebration of its anniversary. But the Real Thing were just the most high-profile group from an underground funk and R&B scene which emerged in 1970s Liverpool, upheld by a generation, predominately from the Toxteth area south of the city centre, that embraced Black American culture.They were not inspired by the city’s household names like the Beatles, Amoo says; instead, it was from seeing groups like the Jackson 5 and the Temptations on television that he thought: “They look like us – we can do that!” Likewise Spaine, now considered a godfather of the UK’s funk scene, grew up in a household with a deep love for Black American music: “Nat King Cole, the Drifters, the Ink Spots, Five Blind Boys of Alabama, all them sorts of things that my old man used to play.”Black US soldiers residing in Burtonwood, a nearby airbase, brought the latest records to Toxteth on weekends, leaving them with friends or at clubs, as well as “clothes, those really fantastic baseball boots and the apple hats that they used to wear. We’d learn all the new dances and songs,” Amoo says.View image in fullscreenLes Spaine, photographed at home in Hampshire in 2022.Photograph: David Levene/the GuardianSpaine started DJing with the imported records he amassed, Amoo formed the Real Thing, and as each made a name for themselves in the music business, they became mostly immune to the colour ban that Black people faced. “I could get into many clubs, Chris could, but the majority of people from Toxteth couldn’t,” Spaine says. “We weren’t morbid about it; there was a saying back then, ‘that’s the way it is’. You could have signs saying no this, no that. This was before laws came in prohibiting that.”Located in town among nightclubs that enforced a colour ban, the Timepiece became the club for Toxteth’s Black community to let loose. “We had big screens and I’d go and visit all the record companies to get these 16mm films,” Spaine remembers. “Then we’d have a back projector and all of a sudden these people could see Michael Jackson, Rufus and Chaka Khan.” As for the dress code, “we were soul boys, so you had to be immaculate; we had mohair suits and Ben Sherman shirts”.People of all races would travel from across the country for their all-nighters. “Everybody who loved Black music went,” says Barbara Phillips, former member of Distinction, a vocal harmony band formed in Liverpool in 1976. “It was the only place where you kind of felt safe.”View image in fullscreenThe Real Thing pictured in Toxteth in 1977.Photograph: Goddard Archive/AlamyLiverpool had been home to Black communities since the 18th century. During the transatlantic slave trade, enslaved Africans were brought to work as servants or sold at auctions in the dock area. Following the abolition of slavery, sailors from across the world, many from West Africa, worked on trade ships and contributed to the war effort during the world wars. Many settled in Toxteth. “The Windrush is a wonderful thing that we should all be proud of, but Black people have been contributing and in this country, especially in Liverpool, for hundreds of years and there’s a narrative to make it sound as if we all came in 1948,” says Spaine, whose Sierra Leonean father was a merchant seaman in Liverpool.Both Spaine and Amoo speak fondly of their experiences growing up in Toxteth in the 1950s and 60s, “this melting pot of poor white people, Chinese people and Black people and we all just got on really well,” Spaine says.“If you were getting up to a little bit of mischief, you’d have older women shouting ‘I can see you Christopher, I’m going to tell your mother and father’,” Amoo laughs. “They shouldn’t be shouting at us because we were 16 at that point, but there you go.”The warmth in the community was offset by deprivation. “There was no money coming into Toxteth, no businesses that could thrive,” Amoo says. Those hardships, along with racial profiling by police, were a driving force for 1981’s Toxteth riots, which lasted nine days and resulted in widespread damage, hundreds of injured officers and the death of a man who was rammed by a police vehicle.View image in fullscreenDistinction. Left to right: Donna Alleyne, Mandy Smith, Barbara Phillips and Sue PhillipsBut when the Real Thing topped the charts in 1976, their entire community was jubilant. A Black band from Liverpool had got to No 1 – the first Black British band to do so. “The whole city was behind them,” says Phillips, and her group Distinction soon had a first of their own: never before had a Black British female group been signed to a major record label.Distinction formed in the basement of their local community centre where they had vocal lessons from Vic Christian, whose brother Garry had success with the multi-racial Liverpool band the Christians; Phillips’s father was calypso musician Lord Woodbine, who mentored the Beatles. “We liked to think that we were funky, also harmonies were our big thing,” Phillips says. “We used to copy the Three Degrees because that was the nearest to what we saw ourselves as. But I think we were too young to be like anybody, because everybody we looked up to they were proper women, and we were just girls.”The band members – Phillips and her sister Sue, plus Donna Alleyne and Mandy Smith – were still just teenagers when they got a deal with EMI, but, Phillips says, the label “would sign an artist but just sit on them for a year. You wouldn’t get to release anything, and that kind of happened with us.” They got picked up in Germany by the Hansa label who released their single That’s the Way I Like It in 1982, “the nearest we got to making it”. They spent a month in Germany touring cities and US air force bases, but their career soon fizzled out.Spaine describes Distinction as “wonderful: they could harmonise, they could move”, and highlights other Black Liverpudlian acts such as the Chants and Colin Areety, “but most of them just kept local. I think in them days we always had this idea that everything American was best; the Real Thing were holding their own but there were lots of acts here which weren’t given the push given to American acts. You just did not have that interest from London.”The UK recording industry and music fans “absolutely weren’t ready,” says Phillips. “They didn’t mind blue-eyed soul – white singers who covered Black music – but they didn’t really want to buy into Black UK artists. I can remember a poster of us and it had on it ‘four coloured girl singers’. That sounds like 200 years ago!” Instead, Phillips found success elsewhere, writing for stage, TV and radio and setting up a talent development agency.Making an album in the 1970s was incredibly costly compared to now, Amoo says, which stripped some artists of opportunities. “First, record companies would have to find you a writer if you didn’t write yourself. Then they’d have to bring you down to London because there was nowhere up here to do it. Then you’re paying God knows how much an hour for studio time. For a vocal group like Distinction, you’d have to bring in a musician to make the track. For acts like them it was difficult, and they were good: a nice female vocal group, basically like our younger sisters.”‘We had no future. So we made a future for ourselves’: the untold history of Welsh reggae sound systemsRead moreEven the Real Thing, Les argues, do not get the credit they deserve as a band. Their song Children of the Ghetto released in 1977 has been remade by several artists from Earth, Wind & Fire’s Philip Bailey to Mary J Blige. “Chris and Eddie wrote Children of the Ghetto, and Americans pay it more credit than the UK lot do.” But the Real Thing eventually had their story told in Everything, an acclaimed 2019 documentary, and Amoo remains grateful for his career. “We have been airbrushed out quite a lot,” he says, “but there’s a hell of a lot of experiences that the Real Thing have had that most other bands in the country can only dream of.”And for all the difficulties the scene faced, Spaine’s memories of Liverpool’s Black music scene in the 70s still remain equally strong and rosy. “You didn’t make a great amount of money but you worked for the weekend – you literally lived for the weekend. Those nights, you forgot all your troubles.”The Real Thing play We Love the 70s at Butlins, Bognor Regis, 12 September;then touringinto 2027Explore more on these topicsMusicR&BPop and rockLiverpoolRaceBlack British cultureSoulfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It detonated right outside our house’: the explosion that started an incredible podcast series | Podcasts | The Guardian
description: Josh Baker is the journalist behind the BBC’s smash hit I’m Not a Monster. He’s back with his most extraordinary investigation yet – to solve the mystery of Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria 14 years ago
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Josh Baker is the journalist behind the BBC’s smash hit I’m Not a Monster. He’s back with his most extraordinary investigation yet – to solve the mystery of Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria 14 years ago
Content: ‘A car bomb broke my back’ … Josh Baker in Raqqa, Syria.Photograph: Mauricio GrisView image in fullscreen‘A car bomb broke my back’ … Josh Baker in Raqqa, Syria.Photograph: Mauricio GrisPodcasts‘It detonated right outside our house’: the explosion that started an incredible podcast seriesJosh Baker is the journalist behind the BBC’s smash hit I’m Not a Monster. He’s back with his most extraordinary investigation yet – to solve the mystery of Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria 14 years agoZoe WilliamsWed 9 Sep 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2012, the US marine turned freelance foreign correspondent Austin Tice disappeared inSyria. If he’s still alive, he’ll be the second-longest detained journalist in the world. That, says Josh Baker (speaking to me from Wales), was the podcast he thought he was making: “We thought we were looking for a missing person, and what we fell into was almost like a Bourne novel, utterly extraordinary. A world of espionage, spies, dictatorship.”It’s also a story of American exceptionalism – the way the US saw itself in relation to the rest of the world. Moreover, “I don’t mean this in a crass way,” Baker says, “but through Austin’s story, we also learn a lot about the last 14 years of the civil war in Syria. We really go inside the regime’s industrial complex of disappearance and torture. As episode two begins, Assad is gone, and we enter into these facilities.”Ultimately, the hunt for the people who know the truth about Tice, and the hunt for those responsible for these atrocities, are one and the same. “A lot of my work for the last decade has involved intelligence and espionage and dealing with intelligence agencies, and I have never received so many leaks from so many different places as I have with Austin Tice – from every direction imaginable. It is absolutely extraordinary.”This is Baker’s third series of I’m Not a Monster for the BBC. The first two – one about an American woman, Sam, who disappears into theIslamic Statecaliphate with her young children when her husband becomes a sniper, and the other one about Shamima Begum – are extraordinary pieces of journalism. But just as extraordinary is the backstory of how they came about.View image in fullscreen‘We fell into a world of espionage, spies, dictatorship’ … I’m Not a Monster host Josh Baker.Photograph: Jamie Simonds/BBCNow 37, Baker started as a night editor on the foreign desk of the Times, and did “a little bit of reporting on the Serbian refugee crisis, and from the Middle East”. By the mid-10s, he was directing Battle for Iraq (a Guardian/PBS co-production), embedded with Iraqi special forces. “The story of the day was that the coalition forces were defeating Isis, were kicking their ass basically. And the reality was quite different.” He got caught in the centre of Mosul and by nightfall had been offered a place to stay by a family, explosions and fighting happening all around. A radio operator woke the team with a warning, “and I could hear shooting”, he remembers, “but without wanting to sound like a war bro, it was all going one way and it was all American weaponry. The sound is different when it’s Isis.”What he didn’t hear until too late was a massive articulated lorry, trying to manoeuvre its way down the street to deliver a car bomb. “I know this bit because Isis, the bastards, were filming from a drone. It detonated right outside our house and I was buried in the collapsing building, and broke my back.”As he was recovering in England after his evacuation, a source of his heard he’d been injured and got in touch. “He’s now almost like a friend, but a source like that always has an agenda,” Baker says. “He showed me a home video from inside Raqqa, which was then the Isis capital, of a young American boy called Matthew being forced to assemble a suicide bomb. This wasn’t a propaganda video, it was a home video.”Matthew was Sam’s oldest son. “I was obviously in a mental state, having just walked out of something by the skin of my teeth. But I thought: ‘I’m gonna find this kid,’ which sounds incredibly idealistic, but seven months later, I did.”View image in fullscreenAn undated photo of Shamima Begum.Photograph: PA/PA WireThe Begum season also came out of that suicide bombing – a Dutch IS bride had been in Mosul at the same time, and some years later privately messaged Baker on Twitter, saying she was in the same refugee camp as Shamima Begum and her children (all three of whom have now died). Baker was more than familiar with Begum’s story – he’d been working as assistant producer onWelcome to the Mosqueand had been inside her east London mosque the day she and her school friends disappeared in 2015. But his new source was the start of an incredibly rich picture of what life was like for these girls and young women when they reached Syria – the deprivation, the violence, the forced marriage, the jeopardy.Baker was also, after a long research trip to Turkey, able to piece together the role of Canadian intelligence in getting Begum across the border, an act which in itself (in my view) was cynical enough that it should solidify Begum’s case that she is more victim than terrorist. He plays down the credit for that exclusive – had it been an action of British intelligence, he says, he’d never have been able to prove it, “because of the tradecraft. Whereas if you look at some of the American or Canadian, or even some European agencies, the tradecraft doesn’t seem to be there in the same way.”The Dutch woman was repatriated to the Netherlands, where she served some of her prison sentence, before it was overturned on the basis that she had been groomed and abused by her husband. “Tens of thousands of people from potentially as many as 100 nations were convinced to go to Isis,” Baker says. “They had a highly effective campaign. Which isn’t to say that someone who’s been with Isis isn’t a threat, but you will struggle to find a security expert who’ll say that our current strategy” – stripping people like Begum of statehood – “is making us safer.”Baker and his colleagues received a large number of death threats after that documentary. It touched on everything: terrorism and foreign policy, who gets to be British and whose Britishness will always be conditional, how much transparency one can ever expect from one’s government. “By the end of that programme, it wasn’t really about Shamima any more.”“In Britain, when people say they have an intelligence source, they often mean they’ve spoken to a press officer,” Baker says. “In America, and particularly in Washington, that world is much more accessible. You can meet intelligence officers or senior law enforcement at dinner parties or even in bars. And still, a great deal of what I’m told I either can’t stand up or I’m told I can’t use. I will say, though, that under the Trump administration, people have become much less inclined to speak.”View image in fullscreenThe second-longest detained journalist in the world? … Marc and Debra Tice, the parents of Austin (seen in the portrait to the left), speak at a press conference in Beirut, 2020.Photograph: Joseph Eid/AFP/Getty ImagesThat access really shows in the Austin Tice podcast, which feels extremely close to the source, and urgent in a way that you wouldn’t think possible for a case that, 14 years on, one would expect to be cold. “Genuinely, our first mission was to try to get answers to Austin’s mum. But also, I really want people to care about what happened in Syria, because it’s obscene. Conservatively, 100,000 people have been disappeared. One of the reasons I left news is I got very tired of having to explain complex things in a matter-of-fact way. The privilege of doing this kind of narrative investigative journalism is that I can slow down and make you care about the people.”I wonder whether Baker chose Tice’s story because he identified with him: a young guy in a war zone, playing stark odds and never knowing which, among myriad dangers, might be decisive. “No, what I identified with was his mother. I remember seeing her do a press conference, nine or 10 years into his disappearance, and thinking about my own mum. I’m from a single-parent household – we’re very close. I just thought, ‘Jesus Christ, what an awful existence to have.’”He thinks he has emerged from this investigation with “a pretty decent idea about what may have happened to Austin. Whether or not we could ever be definitive about it is a different thing.”In the UK, the first episode of season three of I Am Not a Monster is availableon BBC Sounds nowExplore more on these topicsPodcastsSyriaShamima BegumIslamic StatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling review – a joyous love letter to Diana Rigg  | Biography books | The Guardian
description: Beautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated women
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: Beautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated women
Content: Diana Rigg in 1967.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library/AllstarView image in fullscreenDiana Rigg in 1967.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library/AllstarBiography booksReviewAll About My Mother by Rachael Stirling review – a joyous love letter to Diana RiggBeautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated womenFiona SturgesWed 9 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe late actorDiana Riggdeclined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage was “all rather pagan, don’t you think? … A lot of women see it as security. Well, I’m not a woman who yearns for security.”Taking over from Honor Blackman as the high-kicking Emma Peel in the 1960s spy series The Avengers, Rigg refused to play subordinate sidekick to Patrick Macnee’s Steed, turning her character into a beacon of female empowerment. When Rigg learned that not only was Macnee paid significantly more than she was, but the camera operator was too, she demanded a raise. She got it, but that didn’t stop the press from labelling her as a grasping diva. Fifty years later, she told Newsnight: “Equal pay. That’s what feminism means to me, only that.”On the stage and screen, Rigg specialised in fierce, complicated women: Medea, Phèdre, Mother Courage, the wimple-clad Olenna Tyrell in Game of Thrones. Yet in life she refused to take herself or her job seriously. Her fear of appearing earnest led her to decline offers of a biography. Now, six years after her death from cancer, her daughter, the actor Rachael Stirling, has taken on the task of documenting Rigg’s life. All About My Mother is a funny, intimate, often joyous and beautifully written eulogy to a woman who didn’t suffer fools yet remained blithely self-mocking and down to earth. Asked what it meant to be made a dame, she replied: “I think it means I’m not supposed to say ‘fuck’ anymore.”Blending memoir and biography, Stirling builds a portrait based on her own recollections, plus research into Rigg’s performances, writings, recorded interviews and press cuttings collected and stashed in a trunk by her late grandmother Beryl. The book, Stirling says, “is not a detached narrative … This is what I know, what she said, what I’ve learned, what I want to write, what she wrote and what I think she wouldn’t mind my telling you.”Wild anecdotes of stars behaving badly include the time Rigg was lured to Benny Hill’s house with the promise of a party, only to find she was the sole guest. When he appeared in the garden proffering a drink and a semi-erect penis, Rigg turned away, shouted “LOOK! PARSLEY!” and scarpered. George Lazenby’s claim – false apparently – that Rigg deliberately ate garlic before their love scene in On Her Majesty’s Secret Service led to a scathing war of words between the two actors via a series of open letters.As a youngster cutting her teeth on the stage, Rigg was a livewire: funny, rebellious, ambitious, given to corpsing from her own onstage pranks. Landing the role of Peel at 27, she found herself with a throng of male fans who wrote in their droves. Rigg put her mother in charge of letters, some of which took Beryl by surprise. She went to the police about a man who regularly sent clippings of his pubic hair in the post. “It turned out he had been bombarding loads of other women with the fruits of his bush,” notes Stirling. “How he managed to maintain his steady, seemingly luxuriant supply we will never know.”As a mother, Rigg was doting and intense. She would weep dropping Stirling off at boarding school and in the holidays they were inseparable. “I suppose we became what you could call co-dependent, though I didn’t know the word for it then,” Stirling reflects. In a hilariously stomach-churning chapter called “Squeezums”, Stirling describes their ritual of zapping each other’s pimples using tweezers, a piece of loo paper and perfume as antiseptic.Stirling followed her mother into acting, and Rigg could be fiercely critical of her daughter. On the rare occasions they performed together, Rigg would treat her less like a co-star than a personal assistant, though Stirling nearly always saw the funny side. Her book doesn’t shrink from her mother’s flaws and contradictions, but it remains, above all, a feel-good tale and a love letter. Now, before the first night of a new play, Stirling eats a grain of her mother’s ashes in order that “I am cloaked in her, shielded and shrouded by her. I am her. My mother is my superpower. She always was.”All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling is published by John Murray (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroom  | Technology books | The Guardian
description: A refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from them
Author: Simon Usborne
Headline: A refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from them
Content: A teacher guiding a group of kids in a coding class.Photograph: Hispanolistic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA teacher guiding a group of kids in a coding class.Photograph: Hispanolistic/Getty ImagesBook of the dayTechnology booksReviewWhat Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroomA refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from themSimon UsborneWed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation that was suddenly becoming available to the average consumer: the calculator.Many parents and teachers feared that the gadget would undermine a basic skill and a pillar of education – one of the sacred three Rs – producing generations of dumbed-down drones who could reach for a device in their pockets to avoid the hard graft of arithmetic.But Cockcroft didn’t see it that way. Instead, he proposed embracing rather than fearing the calculator. Students should be taught with and without one – and tested accordingly.“Cockcroft is unwilling to pretend that the oncoming wave of technological progress can be dodged,” economist Daniel Susskind writes in his urgent new book.A former Downing Street policy wonk who is now also a researcher at the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford University, Susskind casts himself as the Cockroft of the 2020s. In an era of confusion and hand-wringing (if not outright panic) about the implications of AI, he makes the technologist’s case for breathing, learning and grasping the opportunities it presents.double quotation markHe warns against the folly of ‘future proofing’ when the horizon is so foggyThe maths comparison only goes so far, of course; even accounting for the hubris of the AI industry, its achievements have already wrought changes that now make the calculator seem about as consequential as the corkscrew. But while the scale of the disruption is new, the historical context is, to some extent, reassuring.The book’s title neatly taps into the techno-angst of the modern parent about a future of extreme uncertainty. If traditionally we passed down wisdom with an open-minded but fairly clear sense of how it might apply to a new generation, “today, it feels like that sense of continuity has broken. In truth, we cannot be sure the advice we gave our children last year still works for the next.”Susskind, a father of young children himself, tries to anticipate a future of artificial general intelligence (AGI) – when AI will outperform us at every economically useful task. (We now have access, via ChatGPT, Claude and the like, to what’s known as artificial narrow intelligence: systems that are good at performing specific tasks.)In an AGI world – one that it’s easy to imagine is round the corner after reading Susskind’s book –whole careers but also the very meaning of work will change. Susskind urges politicians, parents and teachers to start paddling into that wave now.He warns against the folly of “future proofing” when the horizon is so foggy. He recalls the David Cameron government’s rush to teach kids how to code, just a few years before it emerged as one of the things that AI does best. Instead, schools should teach children to learn with and without AI, while also doubling down on the basic skills that we should never lose sight of.He envisages a future of personalised learning, in which AI-trained teachers will deploy the technology as assistant tutors rather than attempting to cater to 30 children as a blob. Graduates entering white-collar industries that stand to be most disrupted should harness AI to free them from the drudgery of, say, reviewing legal documents in a basement and instead hone their craft earlier in AI-simulated trials. Middle-aged careerists should not “retreat to inherited practices” or kid themselves that they occupy “safe” professions; we must remember the underlying problem our professions seek to solve and reimagine how to do so in an AI-assisted age.Susskind neatly weaves the conceptual and the practical. And while there was apparently no time in this slim work to consider the more immediate ethical implications of AI (its reliance on stolen creative work, its environmental toll) and the questionable personal qualities of so many AI bosses), as a call to action in the face of an unstoppable tide, his book is at once challenging, compelling and refreshingly optimistic.What Should My Children Do? How to Flourish in the Age of AI by Daniel Susskind is published by Allen Lane (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
