title: Streaming from the cloud was meant to change games forever – what happened? | Games | The Guardian
description: Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable
Content: Fans playing the cloud-based game Doom at the 2019  Gamescom in Cologne, Germany.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFans playing the cloud-based game Doom at the 2019  Gamescom in Cologne, Germany.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesStreaming from the cloud was meant to change games forever – what happened?Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordableDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 9 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is anancient videoof that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future.Since then, plenty of companies havetried to be the firstto truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later.Despite the fact that people simply don’t seem to want game streaming services – or at least not enough to pay a stand-alone monthly subscription for them – Sony and Microsoft have remained steadfastly committed to the idea, bundling game streaming into their PlayStation Plus and Xbox Game Pass services. I use both quite regularly when I want to check out a game quickly, mostly because modern download sizes are ridiculous (Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, say, takes up nearly 150GB of my PS5 space, almost a quarter of its usable storage). Who wants to do 30 minutes of hard drive management every time they want to play something new?Last week, however, Microsoft announced that it wasintroducing time limitsfor game streaming: you’re now allowed 5-15 hours a month, depending on your subscription tier. And yes, you’re right:that is not enough time to play through even one single average-sized game. This brings Microsoft’s previously unwavering commitment to cloud gaming into question – and when even Microsoft with its infinite resources can’t seem to make it work, is the writing on the wall for game streaming as a whole?View image in fullscreenData-hungry ... streaming games such as Mario Kart World requires a whole load of data.Photograph: NintendoIn the early days, the biggest problem with streaming was input lag: the time it took for the game to respond to your button-pressing. Normally, when you’re playing a game this lag is imperceptible. Via streaming, it would often be horribly obvious, your character taking maybe a full second to jump after you’d pressed the A button. Not all games rely heavily on timing and finesse, but a lot of them do, and playing games on a minor time-delay felt nauseating.This is much less of an issue now, but another problem has only gotten worse: game streaming requires the instantaneous transmission of alotof data, making it taxing on your internet connection and expensive for the service provider. Here’s a comparison: watching an hour of Netflix uses about 1GB of data. An hour of game streaming via Xbox requires about 4GB. Microsoft’s servers have to stream you the video of your live gameplay, and continually receive and interpret your controller inputs. No wonder Microsoft suddenly wants to limit your hours.The cloud gaming model has always been based on the idea that data infrastructure would become faster and cheaper in the future. Its selling point is outsourcing computing power so that you can play whatever you want without upgrading your console or PC, or even without having one at all. Unfortunately, thanks to AI companies and their chatbots’ bottomless demand for computing power and energy, the opposite has happened. Data and computing power are nowmoreexpensive. Ironically, this change has been driven by Microsoft itself as much as anything else: a huge chunk of the company’s spendingwent on data centres and AI infrastructurein the last fiscal year. This suggests that Microsoft is choosing to prioritise data provision for users of Azure and Copilot over its gaming customers.Will this affect you? Probably not. Only 4% of all Game Pass subscribers use it for more than 15 hours a month, Microsoft said in ablog postannouncing the changes. Which brings us right back to the question: if cloud gaming really is the future, why is nobody using it? It’s been a long time since that 2009 demo, and this technology has still yet to meaningfully break through. Is it time to give up on it?Alongside Sony and Microsoft, there is one other player left in this death match: the US-based tech firm Nvidia, whose GeForce Now game-streaming service (launched in 2013 and revamped many times since) might just be the world’s most successful. Nvidia has beenriding highon the AI boom, becoming the most valuable company in the world. Its computing hardware powers all the datacentres that the rest of the tech industry has been building, to satisfy imagined future AI demand. Perhaps, when all of this shakes out, it will be the only company left that can afford to provide game streaming services at all.What to playView image in fullscreenUnashamedly laborious … Kingdom Come Deliverance II.Photograph: Warhorse StudiosI have been variably unwell for most of the summer, and in need of something absorbing, so I dived intoKingdom Come Deliverance II– think Skyrim, but 15th-century historical fiction.I was impressed immediately by the outstanding script, story and performances, all of which are much more humorous and entertaining than I was expecting from a hardcore medieval RPG. And I also love how unashamedly laborious this game is: you must control each swipe of a drawn-out sword fight; you have to manually grind and mix herbs for health-restoring concoctions; and if you want anyone to speak to you, you must regularly wash your face (and grubby tunic) so you don’t stink. Last night, I spent 20 minutes hammering out horseshoes in the forge. The opening hours have you hauling sacks of flour around while a tavern landlady swears at you.I can’t help but respect this naturalist commitment to grime and busywork; knight-life isn’t all horseplay, you know. I have spent many, many hours with this game and I am still basically a stinking peasant. I may well never finish it, but I am resolved to atleastget to the point where I have my own steed and a pair of decent boots.Available on:Xbox, PlayStation 5, PCEstimated playtime:55+ hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenLooking beautiful … The remastered Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.Photograph: NintendoA Nintendo broadcast on Tuesday spilled a bunch of new details about the upcomingZelda: Ocarina of Timeremake, which I’m relieved to say is looking beautiful. Link looks doll-like in the updated style, and Hyrule Castle Town looks a bit like a living Playmobil village overlaid with a watercolour-ish filter that makes the whole game look like something half remembered. (I am somewhat less enthused by the addition of voice acting to the cutscenes; Navi was already annoying enough.) Check out thedemo here.For the Ringer, frequent Guardian games contributor Lewis Gordon has writtenthis excellent long-readon Japanese publisherCapcom’s current streak of brilliance, talking to a host of executives and developers about exactly how the company has bucked the trend while the rest of the games industry is on fire.Patrick Miller– better known as pattheflip – has published athought-provoking reflectionon how and why some players become overinvested – even dependent – on video games. “I say this as someone who has loved video games his whole life; if games serve a load-bearing function in someone’s life, it’s the life that needs fixing, not the games.”At the end of last week, theWhite Housereleased this horrible littlepropaganda arcade, featuring nasty riffs on popular games, such as a version of Tetris where you have to build a wall on the Mexican border to stave off “the coming horde”. That particular gamewas later removedafter The Tetris Company expressed its opposition.What to clickGrand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged worldQuestion BlockView image in fullscreenNo combat required … Eastshade, where you take on the role of a painter rather than a fighter.Photograph: Eastshade StudiosReaderPierosent in this question (along with some super-nice feedback on the newsletter – thank you, Piero!):“I enjoy the occasional foray into story-driven RPGs, such asKingdom Come Deliverance,Skyrimandthe Baldur’s Gateseries, but as I get older I’m finding the continual combat sections overwhelming and dull. Could you recommend me some good RPGs that don’t rely on combat as the main game mechanic?”You’re not alone, Piero – for a surprising proportion of players, combat is just something you have to do in order to get to the bits of a game that you find more interesting. Most RPGs these days have a “story mode” option that at least makes all the fighting trivially easy, if you’re not interested in engaging with it. There is of courseDisco Elysium, a complex role-playing game with no combat at all; likeCitizen Sleeper,it is mostly text-based. I have heard good things aboutEastshade, an open-world game where you’re a painter rather than a fighter. I’d also suggestPentiment, though it’s a very different style from Skyrim. AndYonder: The Cloud Catcher Chroniclesis worth a look if you don’t mind cutesy.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner? | Grand Theft Auto VI | The Guardian
description: Historically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romance
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Historically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romance
Content: Couple who slay together … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenCouple who slay together … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesGrand Theft Auto VIGrand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?Emma FlintHistorically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romanceWed 9 Sep 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.33 EDTShareThere was never any doubt that Grand Theft Auto VI’s extended look would elicit a viral reaction from the internet. Having won the Game Awards’ Most Anticipated award twice consecutively, Rockstar’s forthcoming crime opus is one of the most frothed-over games in recent memory, or indeed ever. It’s nothing short ofa cultural phenomenon.One aspect of the game has provoked an unexpectedly vehement response on social media: not violence, but romance. Protagonists Lucia and Jason are in love, you see, and as a player, part of your job is keeping their spark alive and their relationship strong, so that their criminal escapades are underpinned by a strong connection to one another. Holding hands, enjoying a date at the beach, spontaneously texting one another when apart – all of these interactions will strengthen their bond. You’ll be putting in a lot of work to ensure this couple thrives, which is why some people have come to believe that playing GTA VI counts as micro-cheating.View image in fullscreenCheating at games … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesTakes on this are all over social media. Multiple users have shared posts claiming that if you romance characters in video games such as GTA VI you’ve been unfaithful to your partner;TikTok account El Michelle remarkedthat simply playing the game is cheating. “In absolutely no human way is my fiance playing GTA VI,”posted Shelby Haas, another TikTok user. “You literally have to maintain a relationship with a girl […] you have to take her on dates, and you can have sex with her. […] Don’t let your boyfriend or fiance or husband play GTA 6.”Over on TikTok,a post by Landrystates that GTA VI “is basically the same as cheating”, continuing: “I guarantee you, if your man is playing GTA VI and keeping his little girlfriend alive on that video game, he’s most definitely the type that’s following models.”GTA VI is by no means the inventor of in-game dating – hello,Baldur’s Gate 3, in which you can romance and have sex with any (or several) of your eight companions, including a druid who transforms into a bear. And surely we all remember trying to persuade our Sims to get off with each other. For at least 20 years dating and romance have been a significant element of all sorts of different titles; there is an entire (immensely popular) genre of dating games devoted to playfully living out virtual relationships.Even so, due to its unrivalled online presence, GTA VI will be many people’s first exposure to the idea. Video game newcomers on TikTok seem especially exercised about the lengths their partners will go to to maintain a happy in-game relationship with Lucia, though it’s worth pointing out that it goes both ways: playing as Lucia, you’ll have to put just as much effort into maintaining a strong relationship with Jason. (The notion of maxing out the romance with Jason hasn’t provoked nearly as intense a response.)It’s easy for people to revert to off-the-shelf misogynistic accusations about “jealous” and “overreactive” spouses in a situation like this, and indeed, many counter-commentators have done just that. “‘GTA VI is literally cheating’ is something I would say if I was a jealous, insecure hag […]”declares one TikToker.In the comments on one Instagramvideo, someone opined that GTA VI “promotes lust”, resulting in a massive pile-on.But what if this isn’t knee-jerk jealousy? Behind these rather laughable concerns about virtual girlfriends, there are valid insecurities here over the idea of one’s real-life partner being more invested in a fictional character than a real-life relationship. Especially for young people, we’re in an age of loneliness and disconnection, fuelled by being chronically online. It’s one of the greatest paradoxes of modern society: despite being able to instantly engage with anyone or anything, these interactions are superficial and fleeting.View image in fullscreenLovers’ arms … Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesThe dating scene right now is bleak. Dating columnist-cum-novelistAnnie Lord believesthe way we treat each other is part of the problem: “People treat each other as disposable because they’ve got the mindset of an app.” Factor in the growing influence of the manosphere, which many say has“ruined dating”, and it’s not hard to comprehend why experts say we’re experiencing a global dating crisis. Since 2014, the number of young people without close friendships/relationshipshas “risen fivefold”. Joke all you want about oversensitive gen Zs, but they are experiencing life in a social vacuum.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf you’re dealing in real life with men who don’t even text you back, let alone take you on a date, it’s easy to see why it would sting to watch them engage enthusiastically in a video-game relationship with a virtual woman whom they shower with expensive gifts, bouquets, and thoughtful messages. AsTikToker RawTJR’s postjoked: this is “how mfs gonna be treating Lucia in GTA 6 while treating their irl gf like shi”.“I will NOT stand for people calling these partners ‘jealous’ or ‘overreacting’ when they clearly are trying to voice real concerns about their relationships,” wrote trans activist and sex educator Dee Whitnell in anInstagram post. “If someone feels underappreciated in their relationship but sees their partner fulfilling these needs for someone else (even if it is a game character), it’s totally understandable why they would feel a bit frustrated.”As someone who exploreseveryromance option in all games that allow it, I personally think it’s absurd to class in-game romances as a form of cheating – though I appreciate that individual boundaries can differ. People might more reasonably channel their concerns into conversations around AI companionship sites, such as Candy AI and DreamGF, that offer virtual sexbots. As far back as 2023 we were asking if anAI chatbot could be classed as cheating– and the technology has vastly improved since then.More than anything else, this unexpected controversy around GTA VI highlights how dissatisfied and lonely many people are within their relationships. And a video game isn’t going to change that one way or another.Explore more on these topicsGrand Theft Auto VIGamesGrand Theft AutocommentShareReuse this content

title: Jane Eyre: A Musical review – more Disney romance than Victorian gothic | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This production has a talented cast and looks the part, but the characterisation is thin and the songs are often cloying
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: This production has a talented cast and looks the part, but the characterisation is thin and the songs are often cloying
Content: Fairytale echoes … Charlie Burn and Ashley Gilmour in Jane Eyre: A Musical.Photograph: Victoria DaviesView image in fullscreenFairytale echoes … Charlie Burn and Ashley Gilmour in Jane Eyre: A Musical.Photograph: Victoria DaviesTheatreReviewJane Eyre: A Musical review – more Disney romance than Victorian gothicSouthwark Playhouse Elephant, LondonThis production has a talented cast and looks the part, but the characterisation is thin and the songs are often cloyingHolly O'MahonyWed 9 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMuch like Emerald Fennell’s film ofWuthering Heights, this musical version of another Brontë sister’s literary masterpiece is lovely to look at. Designer Morgan Large’s monochrome palette fashions the women in black corseted dresses with attractive ruffles and delicate mesh detailing. Behind them on a screen, a mist appears to roll over sketches of moorland, graves and barren trees. It’s winningly atmospheric. But also like Fennell’s film, there’s too little beneath the frills in an adaptation (music and lyrics by Paul Gordon, book and additional lyrics by John Caird) that struggles to tap into the substance of Charlotte Brontë’s 1847 novel.Though smart-mouthed and bolshie as a child (played commendably on press night by Emily-Rose Samuel), there’s scant sense of a strong-willed, independent thinker in Charlie Burn’s adult Jane, who under Caird and Megan McGinnis’s direction is as pure and polite as a fairytale princess. Nor is there anything dark or dangerous about Ashley Gilmour’s courteous, too-charming Rochester.View image in fullscreen‘Flimsy material’ … the cast of Jane Eyre: A Musical.Photograph: Victoria DaviesThere are echoes of Cinderella and Beauty and the Beast in Jane’s journey here, the Gateshead Hall and Lowood school chapters of which are rushed through in order to bring her into Rochester’s orbit at Thornfield Hall.The songs dilute the story’s grit and hardship with syrupy sentiment. The overuse of twinkly wind chimes and pop-style scoop notes become musical tics, shifting the dial closer to Disney romance than Victorian gothic. Early numbers The Governess and Forgiveness are particularly cloying. But the better songs – including Jane’s Sweet Liberty and Rochester’s As Good As You – contain hints of Schönberg and Boublil’s Les Misérables (the original UK production of which Caird co-directed). And if the material itself is broadly one-note, this is still a fine-tuned production that runs like clockwork.The cast of 11 – about half the size of the musical’s original Broadway run in 2000 – is packed with West End talent for this long-awaited London premiere. It’s just a shame they’re working with such flimsy material.AtSouthwark Playhouse Elephant, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsSouthwark PlayhouseCharlotte BrontëreviewsShareReuse this content

title: East Is East review – the classic cross-cultural comedy is as sharp as ever | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Thirty years on, Ayub Khan Din’s play about dual-heritage life in the 70s is revived for a tour with an exceptional cast
Author: Nick Ahad
Headline: Thirty years on, Ayub Khan Din’s play about dual-heritage life in the 70s is revived for a tour with an exceptional cast
Content: Tyrannical patriarch … Bhasker Patel  as George (front) in East Is East at the Bolton Octagon, with Zaki Ali as Tariq, Matthew Khan as Saleem and Maya Dhokia as Meenah.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenTyrannical patriarch … Bhasker Patel  as George (front) in East Is East at the Bolton Octagon, with Zaki Ali as Tariq, Matthew Khan as Saleem and Maya Dhokia as Meenah.Photograph: Pamela RaithTheatreReviewEast Is East review – the classic cross-cultural comedy is as sharp as everBolton OctagonThirty years on, Ayub Khan Din’s play about dual-heritage life in the 70s is revived for a tour with an exceptional castNick AhadWed 9 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThirty years ago a play opened at Birmingham Rep that might have been expected to have limited appeal. East Is East, the story of a mixed-race family from the north of England surviving 1970s Britain as the father tries to marry off two of his sons, was then turned into a film. It crossed cultures and became a Bafta-winning box-office hit, following the success of Ayub Khan Din’s play.View image in fullscreenBetween cultures … Samantha Power as Ella, Maya Dhokia as Meenah and Victoria Brazier as Auntie Annie.Photograph: Pamela RaithBolton Octagon, 10 miles down the road from the story’s setting of Salford, celebrates the anniversary with a new production directed by Kash Arshad. In Arshad’s hands the script’s comedy is mined and brought to life by an exceptional cast, with Samantha Power as Ella, the matriarch of the Khan family, giving an award-worthy performance.East Is East is an important piece of work for people such as myself, Arshad and much of the cast playing Khan’s children. The language of the play describes us as “half-caste”; I tend to use mixed-race and some of the cast prefer dual heritage. Whatever the preferred term, the play captures the nuance of growing up between cultures.Eating bacon while throwing around curry powder to cover the smell, laughing at racist jokes where people who look like your family are the punchline – these are moments recognisable to mixed-race families. Khan Din’s cleverness was to capture the subtleties of having a white mum and a brown dad and, in that specificity, find universal appeal.The tyrannical patriarch of the family, George, is played by Bhasker Patel. He lacks the gravitas and intimidating physique of Om Puri, who took the role in the film, and the production is better for it. Here is someone who feels ignored and, with his smaller frame, when he explodes it is the lashing out of a man who cannot bend the world to his will. He has a softness with his children, who all create distinct personalities, Maya Dhokia particularly good as the family’s sole daughter.When the children discuss whether or not they are English, the echoes of balaclava-wearing men in Dover might be heard by some in the auditorium. A surprisingly funny and relevant piece of work, three decades on.AtBolton Octagonuntil 3 October. Then atCitizens theatre, Glasgow, 7-17 October;Derby theatre, 20-24 October;Salisbury Playhouse, 3-14 November.Explore more on these topicsTheatreBoltonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: You’re So Special review – painfully funny tragedy of a stardom seeker | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A dance teacher for toddlers dreams of bigger things in Julia Grogan’s frantic one-woman show
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: A dance teacher for toddlers dreams of bigger things in Julia Grogan’s frantic one-woman show
Content: You daren’t look away … Julia Grogan in You're So Special at Soho theatre.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenYou daren’t look away … Julia Grogan in You're So Special at Soho theatre.Photograph: Alex BrennerTheatreReviewYou’re So Special review – painfully funny tragedy of a stardom seekerSoho theatre, LondonA dance teacher for toddlers dreams of bigger things in Julia Grogan’s frantic one-woman showAnya RyanWed 9 Sep 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe mind of a performer, hungry for her big break, is cracked open in Julia Grogan’s one-woman follow-up to her dramaPlayfight.At first, her dream is in motion: Miss June (played by Grogan) is on a chat show, giving breezy answers about her Oscar nominations and being recognised by monks in Holland & Barrett. And then, with one question from the audience – “Any advice for people who want to be something?” – the stage warps back to reality. Actually, Miss June is a baby ballet teacher, with a class of toddlers ready to be taught turnouts and pliés.But all her lusting after Daisy Edgar-Jones’s life may have paid off. Miss June has been offered a spot on a TV show, and you can bet she’s told everyone in the town she grew up in – where she still lives – about her good fortune.Directed by Rachel Lemon, this is a story of success and stardom in reverse which is played out like a horror show. Soon it turns out the producers don’t actually need her, so it’s back to the village hall, jointly used by Twinkly Stars ballet school and an All Addictions group, to beg for her job back and prepare for the end-of-term sharing.View image in fullscreenOnly a second away from a screaming outburst … Grogan.Photograph: Alex BrennerFramed as an epic tragedy and told in acts, You’re So Special shows fame as a manic obsession. Miss June has bulging, twitching eyes and is always one second away from a screaming outburst. She speaks to the three-year-olds with a desperate, Dance Mom-esque quality: “You might feel pressure to lose weight – do it,” she commands. When she learns that one child’s parents are TV producers, she sets her sights on grabbing herself some time in the spotlight. And the whole time she is spurred on by the memory of her own dance teacher telling her she was “special” as a child.Despite being alone on stage, Grogan conjures a vivid whole world. The personalities of the mind-drifting kids are unmistakable through her expert miming, and never once do we doubt her frantic, deep need to reach for higher things. Grogan is a wonderfully watchable actor – you don’t dare look away for fear of missing another flash of a breakdown. She is also painfully funny. Miss June’s career may have stagnated but Grogan is doing brilliant things.AtSoho theatre, London, until 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreComedy (Stage)Soho theatreComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Why we’re giving £100,000 apiece to a horse box gallery, high-street drop-in and Midlands museum | Art | The Guardian
description: Culture is part of how we rebuild communities – these awards by the Freelands foundation recognise organisations promoting creativity and opportunity at grassroots level
Author: Henry Ward
Headline: Culture is part of how we rebuild communities – these awards by the Freelands foundation recognise organisations promoting creativity and opportunity at grassroots level
Content: Art movement … the Burton at Bideford’s Art Box.Photograph: Olga VynnykView image in fullscreenArt movement … the Burton at Bideford’s Art Box.Photograph: Olga VynnykArtWhy we’re giving £100,000 apiece to a horse box gallery, high-street drop-in and Midlands museumHenry WardCulture is part of how we rebuild communities – these awards by the Freelands foundation recognise organisations promoting creativity and opportunity at grassroots levelWed 9 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTShareIf politicians are serious about rebuilding our communities, they need to recognise that art and creativity are not the finishing touches. They are part of the foundations.Andy Burnham recently said that culture is too often dismissed as a distraction, a “nice to have”. Yet, as he put it, “it’s about making sense of your own reality”.Culture is not something we add once the work of rebuilding communities has been done. Culture is part of how we rebuild them. It creates places where people meet, gives them agency, opens doors into careers they might otherwise never have imagined, brings life back to empty buildings and struggling high streets, and gives communities the opportunity to tell their stories.But we have been steadily stripping away the infrastructure of arts education that makes this possible.View image in fullscreenNew horizons … an Artist Lab walk and talk organised by Signal.Photograph: Courtesy of SignalIn schools, provision for arts subjects has declined. TheCultural Learning Alliancereports a 42% fall in arts GCSE entries since 2010. At universities, art education has faced an increasing battle to justify its existence in relation to future economic validity. And in museums, learning teams are often the first to face cuts when funding is stretched.The government’s curriculum review and renewed commitments to museum funding suggest an appetite to think differently. But if we are serious about changing the direction of travel, we should look beyond policies to the organisations already doing the work.The newFreelands awardsare one way of doing that, committing £1.5m over five years to recognising progressive visual art education across museums, galleries and arts organisations. It’s central to Freelands Foundation’s mission to champion art education.Our first three winners, each of whom receive £100,000, demonstrate what is possible.In Barrow-in-Furness,Signalhas become an essential part of a community dominated by the shipyard and now building nuclear submarines, that is remote and culturally underserved. Their artist development programme gives local people the agency to respond to their surroundings and create opportunities for others. After years of occupying temporary spaces, Signal has transformed a vacant building in the town centre into a place with real community purpose.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMore than one route into cultural life … Wolverhampton Art Gallery.Photograph: Tyler Whiting. Courtesy of Wolverhampton Art Gallery.Burnham has ambitions to revitalise high streets and give communities back the spaces they value. Signal shows what that looks like. An empty building becomes a cultural space, which becomes a community asset, and this becomes part of the renewal of a town.The programmes for young people atWolverhampton Art Gallerydemonstrate another essential principle: that there is more than one route into cultural life and creative employment. They’re giving opportunities to develop projects, build confidence and explore careers outside conventional academic pathways. If we are serious about widening access to the creative industries, we need programmes like these.In rural North Devon,the Burton at Bidefordhas responded to a very practical problem. Teachers told the gallery that their schools could no longer afford trips. Their answer was theBurton Art Box: a converted horse box that takes art directly into primary schools. It is wonderfully simple. And it tells us something important: access to culture is not just about whether an institution exists. It is about whether people can get to it.These organisations are working in places where opportunities to engage with art, develop creative skills or enter the cultural sector can be severely limited. They are not waiting for perfect conditions. They are finding imaginative ways around the barriers in front of them. We should be paying attention.We need to rebuild the infrastructure of art education. That means schools, colleges, universities, museums, galleries, libraries, studios and community organisations. It means ensuring that the people of Barrow,Wolverhampton, North Devon and every other location across the UK have the opportunity to encounter and make art. We need an education that equips us not only to know things, but to imagine, question, collaborate, make and contribute. And we should put the organisations already embedded in our communities at the centre of that ambition.Because if art really is about making sense of our own reality, then access to it cannot be a luxury reserved for those who happen to live in the right place, attend the right school or can afford to pay.Culture is not what we can afford once everything else is fixed. It’s one of the things that will help us fix it.Henry Ward is artistic director of the Freelands FoundationExplore more on these topicsArtArts and humanitiesArts policyWolverhamptonDevoncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Would they fight or hug?’ The Oasis comeback film’s makers on shooting fans, vicars, police – and the Gallaghers | Music documentary | The Guardian
description: The crowds wept and prayed, police used their song lyrics for briefings and a vicar gave a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. The directors of Don’t Look Back in Anger relive their wildest ride ever
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: The crowds wept and prayed, police used their song lyrics for briefings and a vicar gave a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. The directors of Don’t Look Back in Anger relive their wildest ride ever
Content: ‘You could see them getting closer every night’ … Liam and Noel on stage in Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Harriet TK BolsView image in fullscreen‘You could see them getting closer every night’ … Liam and Noel on stage in Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Harriet TK BolsMusic documentary‘Would they fight or hug?’ The Oasis comeback film’s makers on shooting fans, vicars, police – and the GallaghersThe crowds wept and prayed, police used their song lyrics for briefings and a vicar gave a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. The directors of Don’t Look Back in Anger relive their wildest ride everDave SimpsonWed 9 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger review – mammoth tour movie brings the joy and poignancy of reunionRead moreOn 4 July last year,Oasiswere all set to start the first gig of their hugely anticipated comeback, 16 years since the band imploded after Liam Gallagher swung a guitar in the direction of brother Noel’s head backstage in Paris. However, just 20 minutes before showtime, there was no sign of the singer. Some 74,500 fans in Cardiff’s Principality Stadium were going crazy, while Noel was left impatiently pacing around the venue’s loading bay, presumably wondering if everything was about to fall apart again.“Then the monitor I was watching all this on suddenly cut out,” says Will Lovelace, the director who was filming the comeback. “When it came back to life, suddenly Liam and Noel were there chatting. Then they walked out to this eruption.” Later, Noel is filmed expressing incredulity that his long-estranged younger sibling could “skip the final rehearsal, then just rock up, grab my hand, and I’m like, ‘What the fuck?’ And off he goes, sounding like he’s 30 years younger. And I’m like, ‘You absolute mad cunt.’”double quotation markThey hadn’t been in a room together for 16 years. Then Liam walks in, drops his bag and goes: ‘Are we ready then?’The Cardiff entrance is one of the more dramatic scenes in Lovelace and co-director Dylan Southern’s film Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger, which briefly dwells on how the fractious working-class Manchester tearaways became the biggest rock band in the world in the 1990s before concentrating on how, 30 years later, they did it all again.The Oasis Live 25 tour consisted of 41 concerts across 14 countries and five continents, playing to more than two million people. Don’t Look Back In Anger captures the supersized raw power of those gigs but also packs an unexpectedly emotional wallop, showing how a bitter, long-fractured relationship between two feuding brothers was healed by the power of their own music – not just over themselves but over those millions of fans.View image in fullscreen‘It seemed bigger than Oasis, something a lot of people needed’ … rapturous fans at one gig.Photograph: Courtesy of Oasis: Don’t Look Back in AngerThe cameras capture Noel’s stunned admission that he “wasn’t prepared for the intense outpouring, a sense of what it meant to people”. Lovelace insists it was the same for the directors. “We arrived in Cardiff unprepared for this tidal wave of emotion. It seemed bigger than Oasis, something a lot of people needed. I don’t think we understood the magnitude of it. I was overwhelmed.”Southern and Lovelace’s previous music films include the New York indie scene rockumentaryMeet Me in the Bathroom(2022) and LCD Soundsystem’s live farewell,Shut Up and Play the Hits(2012). Southern says it “never came up” that the pair also madeNo Distance Left to Run, the 2010 documentary about Oasis’s avowed rivals, Blur.The directors have their own history with the Manchester band – as fans. Lovelace remembers, as a teenager growing up in the Fens, East Anglia, listening to Definitely Maybe on a Walkman and thinking: “This is the first music that feels like my own.” Southern saw them in 1994 at the 200-capacity Hull Adelphi, when the working-class northerners “felt like our band”. When tickets went on sale for Oasis Live 25, Lovelace was “in a car on my phone failing to get a ticket” while Southern “eventually gave up”.double quotation markA guy sits cross-legged on the floor and prays while singing along to Slide AwayThey were later approached about “a big project”, but weren’t told what it was and were sworn to secrecy. Then they were put together with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, as scriptwriter, and the project got under way. “Filming rehearsals in London took a lot of negotiating because they’ve never allowed that,” says Lovelace. “It was never going to work if we just went in there with our cameras,” adds Southern. “We had to come up with a way to be invisible.”So they hid cameras in all the sound kit. “We had a grotty Portakabin outside in a heatwave so we could monitor everything,” says Southern. “It was completely unglamorous,” grins Lovelace. “But for six weeks, Oasis didn’t see us or our crew.”The band reacquainted themselves with songs they hadn’t played for years, at this point with Noel singing, while the directors trained a camera on the door to catch Liam’s grand arrival. They waited and waited.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to be in there among the crowd’ … Dylan Southern, right, with Will Lovelace and at the UK premiere.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for The Walt Disney Company Limited“Nobody knew exactly when he was coming,” says Southern. “There was a palpable tension. We knew we had these historically volatile characters, so you ask yourself, ‘Are they going to fight – or hug each other? And of course they do neither. They have a job to do. Apart from a very brief photoshoot, they hadn’t been in a room together for 16 years. Then Liam walks in, drops his bag and goes, ‘Are we ready then?’ Two hours later, while they’re playing the outro to Champagne Supernova, he picks up his bag and leaves. He did that every single day. And then suddenly they were playing the gigs – and the tension started melting. You could see Noel and Liam getting closer every night.”Thirteen gigs were filmed, but the directors wanted more than a concert film so they recruited people with what Southern calls “a unique eye. We employed cinematographers to hold every camera, rather than someone who filmed Stereophonics last week.”This meant the likes of Haris Zambarloukos (Belfast, Beetlejuice, Beetlejuice), Lol Crawley (who won an Oscar for The Brutalist) and Moonlight Oscar-nominee James Laxton. Southern had observed that classic rockumentary films such as Monterey Pop and Gimme Shelter were made by “the greats of the period”. He even held a camera himself. “I wanted to be in there among the crowd,” he explains.View image in fullscreen‘I’d forgotten how funny Liam was’ … the brothers backstage in Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Simon EmmettThe film includes unusually personal footage of fans of all ages. A South Korean free diver explains how the band’s lyrics helped her through depression; a teenager in floods of tears is comforted by a stranger; a guy sitting cross-legged on the floor prays while singing along to Slide Away; a young woman who survived the 2017 Manchester Arena bomb but was left with “survivor’s guilt” realises the meaning of it all is “to not look back in anger”. Southern sums it up: “The effect the music has on people is like magic. In the film, Liam says, ‘It’s like it comes from somewhere else.’”The narrative was further helped by a series of “unexpected gifts”, as Southern calls them. “Before we filmed, we went to Burnage [where the Gallaghers grew up] and took everything in. We went in St Bernard’s Church, opposite their old primary school, and asked Father Luke if we could film. We had no idea that, on the only day we could shoot, he would read the passage from the Bible where St Peter asks Jesus, ‘How many times must I forgive my brother who sinned against me?’ And he is told, ‘Not seven times but 77 times.’ Then he built his whole sermon that morning around Noel and Liam.”Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger: what we learned from the year’s biggest rockumentaryRead moreAnother gift was unearthing archive footage of Noel revealing he has a “character flaw that means I can never forgive … anyone, ever”. This is then gradually demolished over the film. There’s also a comical police sergeant at one gig whose team briefing is formed from Oasis song titles. “We’re just going to have to Roll With It,” he says. “It’s The Masterplan.”A sadder moment arrives in Sao Paulo, as the band hear that Stone Roses bassistGary “Mani” Mounfieldhas died aged 63. We see the musicians in shock, Liam dedicating Live Forever to “our dear friend, our hero”, and a visibly shaken Noel playing the guitar solo while staring up at Mounfield’s face on a screen above the stage. “There are probably versions of Live Forever that were technically better,” says Southern, “but that had to be in.”With as many as 20 cameras on the go at once, the directors ended up with “hundreds and hundreds of hours” of footage. Among the more painful editing decisions was having to omit a three-minute close-up of a teenage girl in tears to Talk Tonight, because it just didn’t fit anywhere. And, while the film is low on gossip and revelations, there is power in what remains unsaid.View image in fullscreen‘Caught beneath the landslide’ …Noel on stage.Photograph: Courtesy of Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger“The reconciliation didn’t happen in rehearsals,” says Southern. “It started happening on stage and continued happening.” Lovelace adds: “They’re healing this enormous chasm not in private, but in public. And things were forgiven without saying a word. Maybe that’s part of what people are responding to.” Mostly, the Gallaghers are interviewed separately, but by the end they’re giving their first joint interview for two decades – as reflective older men, praising each other’s contributions, laughing at each other’s humour and the “madhouse” of Oasis.“We are in contact way more than we ever were before,” says Noel. “I’d forgotten how funny Liam was. All the little things that used to annoy us about each other have gone away.”Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger is in Imax and cinemas on 9 September in the UK, 10 September in Australia and 11 September in the USExplore more on these topicsMusic documentaryOasisPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Reclaiming the streets: the architects clawing back Europe’s car-centric spaces | Architecture | The Guardian
description: The European Prize for Urban Public Space’s shortlist highlights projects helping people cope with climate crisis
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The European Prize for Urban Public Space’s shortlist highlights projects helping people cope with climate crisis
Content: Housed in an obsolete roundabout, Round About Baths transformed the site into a place of refuge from extreme heat.Photograph: Josema CutillasView image in fullscreenHoused in an obsolete roundabout, Round About Baths transformed the site into a place of refuge from extreme heat.Photograph: Josema CutillasArchitectureReclaiming the streets: the architects clawing back Europe’s car-centric spacesThe European Prize for Urban Public Space’s shortlist highlights projects helping people cope with climate crisisPhilip OltermannEuropean culture editorWed 9 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the words of Joni Mitchell, the planners of many urban centres around the world “paved paradise and put up a parking lot”. The European Prize for Urban Public Space tries to show that cities don’t have to be locked in the automotive age for ever.The prize’s latest shortlist, announced on Wednesday, highlights architectural projects that convert infrastructure for cars into spaces that help urban dwellers cope with the soaring temperatures of theclimate crisis: roundabouts that have become splash pools, thoroughfares turned into green havens, and car parks into gardens.Among the most eye-catching of the five finalists is Leopold Banchini’s Round About Baths in Logroño, northernSpain. The Swiss architect’s project sought to revive what he called a “lost space” on one of the main thoroughfares in the city, a concrete island with a broken fountain.View image in fullscreenRound About Baths attempted to reclaim a space that would normally be out-of-bounds for those without a motor vehicle.Photograph: Josema CutillasInspired by 19th-century public baths, Banchini’s studio used uncut timber panels to build and place a simple structure directly on to the fountain. The existing water basin became a shallow pool, while cast-iron flower pots were repurposed as fire bowls that heat a steam room.“We have given up so much public space to cars, and if you live in a city with kids you live in constant fear that they will be hit by a passing vehicle”, Banchini said. “It restricts our movement so much that we almost can’t see it anymore.”Those trying to catch a glimpse of the roundabout baths in situ will be disappointed, however: Banchini’s structure was only erected for a week as part of the city’s Concéntrico architecture festival in June 2025 – inadvertently showing how difficult it is to permanently alter car-centric infrastructure.View image in fullscreenLeopold’s Banchini’s project in Logroño only stood for a week.Photograph: Josema Cutillas“If we had built something more permanent, we would have had to engage with safety concerns”, said Banchini, noting that bathers were only able to access the roundabout via a zebra crossing on one side.“The rules around car traffic are hard to modify, and any requests usually go all the way up to municipal authorities”, he added. “And politicians are really scared to touch anything with cars, because they fear it will cost them in votes.”The creators of another Spanish finalist, Barcelona’s Plaça de les Glòries Catalanes, were more successful: the three thoroughfares that used to bring traffic into the Glòries cloverleaf interchange were partly laid underground to make room for open green space.View image in fullscreenBarcelona’s Plaça de les Glóries Catalanes has proved to be a success with the city’s residents.Photograph: Fernando LuaView image in fullscreenPeople enjoy games of table tennis in the Spanish sun.Photograph: Aitor Estévez OlaizolaAntwerp’s Zuidpark is the result of a similar attempt to banish cars from cityscapes. Located in the southern Zuid district of the Belgian city, the 800-metre green space covers an area that used to be taken up by a large free car park.In 2015, municipal authorities launched a competition for a public space to fill the site. “I have done projects like this for 25 years, but this park had to be completely different to anything we’ve done before, and that’s because of the climate issue”, said Bart Van Gassen of Tractebel, the urban architecture company that won the commission.The firm decided to excavate 70% of the new park’s area and put in place a 1.5-metre top layer of soil that would allow trees and bushes to grow more rapidly. Two years after its opening in 2024, Zuidpark is lined by double rows of 500 new trees that provide shade during heatwaves.View image in fullscreenZuidpark was built on the site of a former car park in Antwerp.Photograph: Isabelle PateerView image in fullscreenAdding a deep top layer of soil has helped plants in Zuidpark thrive.Photograph: Isabelle Pateer“The planting is really booming”, said Van Gassen. “We have projects we constructed 10 years ago and the trees are still smaller than here.” He said recent research by the University of Antwerp showed there were significantly lower temperatures inside the park than elsewhere in the city.Climate breakdown is bringing not just waves of intense heat but also extreme precipitation, which Zuidpark seeks to anticipate with lowered spaces, called “rain gardens”, designed to collect rainwater. Filled with old bluestone blocks unearthed during construction and vegetation that can grow in a wet environment, these wilder spaces have become popular play areas for children.Still, the cars haven’t vanished altogether: a new car park, no longer free, is now positioned across four storeys underneath Zuidpark’s northern and southern wings, and can be accessed from entry points outside the park.“You could be critical because it’s still a car park with 2,000 spaces that is very close to the city,” said Van Gassen. “If you’re thinking sustainably, maybe it should have been built more outside of the city. But then, maybe if there was no parking we wouldn’t have been able to build a park at all.”Also on the shortlist for the prize, which is held every two years, are the Leça Green Corridor in northwest Portugal and Peace Park in Vicenza, Italy.The winner of the award, organised by Spain’s Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona with six other European architecture institutions, will be announced on 15 October.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureEuropeClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Péter Nádas obituary | Fiction in translation | The Guardian
description: Hungarian author who explored memory and history in his fiction and was nominated for a Nobel prize
Author: Boyd Tonkin
Headline: Hungarian author who explored memory and history in his fiction and was nominated for a Nobel prize
Content: Péter Nádas said: ‘True insights tend to come from the periphery, from the provinces.’ He lived in a village in western Hungary from the 1980s until his death.Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy Live NewsView image in fullscreenPéter Nádas said: ‘True insights tend to come from the periphery, from the provinces.’ He lived in a village in western Hungary from the 1980s until his death.Photograph: TT News Agency/Alamy Live NewsFiction in translationObituaryPéter Nádas obituaryHungarian author who explored memory and history in his fiction and was nominated for a Nobel prizeBoyd TonkinWed 9 Sep 2026 14.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe writer Péter Nádas, who has died aged 83, transformed the modern history of his nativeHungaryinto epic fiction that rooted its upheavals and calamities in the minds, and bodies, of his all-too-human characters. “I’m not a historian,” he said. “I’m not an anthropologist, nor am I a sociologist. I work with the fates of individuals.”Those individuals filled a series of books that, in their scope, depth and stylistic ambition, made Nádas a perennial contender for the Nobel prize in literature. Yet it would be his younger compatriot László Krasznahorkai, drawing on the senior writer’s example,who took that honour in 2025.Nádas had lived, as he reflected, under a succession of Hungarian regimes – fascist, communist, oligarchical and populist – “that strove against knowledge”. As these grand designs succeeded one another, always undermined by human weakness and delusion, he embarked instead on an inner history of his times rooted in the entangled desires and dreams of people who seek, but never find, escape from their besetting isolation.He owed his international reputation to a pair of massive novels that convey the experience of Hungary’s 20th-century tragedies as a circuitous progress of the body, and soul, rather than a procession of events:A Book of Memories(1986, published in English in 1997), and the even more gargantuan Parallel Stories (2005; English translation 2011). “His method,” wrote the American novelist William T Vollmann “is to spiral outward from erotic activity into memory and history.”View image in fullscreenLabyrinthine, recursive, discontinuous, his way of telling stories of the intersection of private and public lives drew criticism as well as praise. In the Guardian, Tibor Fischer slammed Parallel Stories as a monumental pile-up of“disjointed vignettes”. Admirers saw these delays and ellipses as valid artistic responses to the lingering traumas of Nádas’s age. For Vollmann, “Remembering atrocity is painful, and so we circle around our nightmares.” ToSusan Sontag, A Book of Memories was, in its combination of grand historical sweep and modernist technique, “the greatest novel written in our time”.The atrocities in Nádas’s own life began soon after his wartime birth in Budapest. His Jewish, but secular and communist, family hid within and outside Budapest from the fascist Arrow Cross regime, as Soviet forces subjected the city to a brutal siege through the winter of 1944-45. Almost half a million Hungarian Jews had been deported to death camps. His earliest memory was of a bombing raid. He and his brother Pál were baptised into the Calvinist church.His mother, Klára Tauber, died of cancer when he was 12. His father, László Nádas (originally Neumayer), became a senior Communist party functionary after the war. Falsely accused of embezzlement, and eventually exonerated, he killed himself in 1958.As a teenager, Nádas witnessed the Soviet suppression of the Hungarian revolution of 1956. He later studied photography and, in the 1960s, worked as a photojournalist, a discipline that fed his gift for atmosphere and observation. He began writing fiction and, in 1967, published largely autobiographical short stories in his debut, The Bible.At the same time he sickened of compromise with a regime he detested. Disgusted by Hungarian complicity in the Soviet occupation of Prague in 1968, he determined to devote himself to literature and quit the city for the village of Kisoroszi, beside the Danube. He was accompanied by his life-partner, Magda Salamon: they married in 1990.At Kisoroszi, embedded in a peasant community as a near-penniless “village fool”, he became the countryman that he remained (although he did later keep a flat in Pest, and for a few years worked on a children’s magazine in the capital). “Poor as a church mouse”, he wrote with fierce application, at first in a tumbledown house without electricity, foraged for their food and practised the wisdom he attributed to Magda: “What you don’t have, you won’t miss.”Periods of study in East Berlin nourished him with links to a wider cultural world. Tangles with the Hungarian censors meant that his novelThe End of a Family Storyhad to wait until 1977 for publication. The secret police offered him an easier ride, and foreign-travel privileges, if he informed for them. He did not.In the 80s, the increasingly relaxed policies ofJános Kádár’s “goulash communism” lifted the threat of persecution, but Nádas still preserved his rural independence. He and Salomon moved to Gombosszeg, a village in western Hungary, where they remained until his death. From the early 90s, translations of A Book of Memories established him as an author of European stature who braided vividly rendered erotic and domestic lives into fragmentary panoramas of epochal events: war, revolution, genocide.View image in fullscreenForeign awards accumulated, especially in German-speaking territories: the Leipzig book fair prize, the Austrian state prize for European literature, the Franz Kafka prize. Central Europe had found the latest wide-screen chronicler of its traumatic outer and inner life, in the tradition ofRobert Musilor Hermann Broch.“I live modestly, and have no desire to do otherwise,” he maintained. In Gombosszeg, as in Kisoroszi, he relished the stubborn persistence of a peasant culture immune to ideology, where “value is determined by local custom, by familial relation, and need”.His surroundings gave him the stable foundation for the massive fresco of Parallel Stories, almost two decades in the making. Its entwined families – one German, one Hungarian – witness and suffer the tumults of their century on every interconnected level from the sexual (always a Nádas speciality) to the political and spiritual.He endured personal blows as well. Own Death (2002) recounts his near fatal heart attack (he was deemed clinically dead), along with his photos of a pear tree through its annual cycle of departing and returning life. Translated by Imre Goldstein, the stories and essays collected as Fire and Knowledge (2007) can serve as an beginner’s guide to the sometimes opaque Nádas universe.He observed Hungary’s slide into the authoritarian populism under the (recently ousted) Viktor Orbán with typical detachment and acerbity. For the ever-sceptical Nádas, “True insights tend to come from the periphery, from the provinces,” not from centres of power. He cultivated his garden on the sidelines.In his later years, he deplored what he saw as another era of descent into “opportunism, group-think, tribalism”. The rebel against all overarching systems continued to ask “whether capitalism can be reconciled with human reason”. He published an acclaimed two-volume memoir, Shimmering Details, in 2017 (with the English translation appearing in 2023), its episodes and characters captured with the same immersive intensity as in his fiction.His long, fascinated encounter with Hungarian country life bore fruit in a 2022 novel, Horror Stories. In 2025, his final work appeared, My Dead Friends: a fictionalised memoir of literary colleagues such as the writers Péter Esterházy and Miklós Mészöly. He called it “an old man’s joke”, an “autumn crocus”, but it revealed an enduring faith in literature as a strongbox for meaning and value amid uncontrollable change.“Literature is a personal matter,” he said last year, “not a public one, not a national one, but if no one cultivates it, the world will grow stupid.”He is survived by Magda and his brother, Pál.Péter Nádas, novelist, born 14 October 1942; died 26 August 2026Explore more on these topicsFiction in translationFictionAwards and prizesHungaryCommunismobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this sweltering summer, I finally stopped giving a tuck | Women | The Guardian
description: I’ve always cinched my outfits at the waist, but shifting to a looser silhouette has helped me keep my cool in more ways than one
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: I’ve always cinched my outfits at the waist, but shifting to a looser silhouette has helped me keep my cool in more ways than one
Content: Video: David Newby. Styling: Melanie WilkinsonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Jess Cartner-Morley on fashionWomenJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this sweltering summer, I finally stopped giving a tuckI’ve always cinched my outfits at the waist, but shifting to a looser silhouette has helped me keep my cool in more ways than oneJess Cartner-MorleyWed 9 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis was the summer of the Great Untuck. The long hot summer of 2026 finally taught me to do what fashion has been nagging me about for years, which is to quit tucking in my shirts and T-shirts. To stop assuming that the top half of an outfit must be neatly cinched by the waistband of the skirt or trousers.It wasn’t a style epiphany, to be fair. It was just too hot to do anything else. An extended run of hot weather at home changes how you dress. In the old-school type of British heatwave, which lasted about half a week, I was too giddy with excitement at not having to wear a cardigan to think more strategically. But this summer was different. And eventually I discovered what hot-climate cultures have always known, which is that loose, generously sized clothing that maximises sun protection while minimising skin contact is way more pleasant to wear in the heat than anything short and tight.double quotation markTucking my shirt in was making me hot, and – this is the really bad part – making me look out of touchAnd it wasn’t just me. I was at haute couture shows in Paris and Rome back in July, and it was crazy hot. The super-wealthy women who get invited because they actually buy the stuff, were wearing shoulder-padded cocktail suits or sequin-embellished dresses, or whatever they had ordered from the latest collection. Fair play: if I had bought £100,000-worth of embroidery I might also feel compelled to wear it, even at risk of heatstroke. But pretty much everyone else was wearing a loose shirt – could be Carven, could be Uniqlo – over some sort of filmy skirt, or hanging over loose trousers. Sometimes unbuttoned over a bra top, sometimes buttoned through, but never tucked in.This summer has been a learning curve for me. My instinct is always to tuck a shirt in, or at the very least French tuck the front. I would love to say this is just because it feels smarter but, if I’m honest, it is also because my instinctive response to seeing myself in a mirror is to try to make myself look smaller. Yes, this is idiot-level behaviour, I know that. But the impulse – to hold your tummy in, or to belt your jacket to give it a waist – is so ingrained in many women that I’m not sure we recognise it for what it is a lot of the time.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: David Newby/The GuardianAnyway, this summer snapped me out of it. Because I realised that tucking my shirt into my trousers was making me hot and flustered, and – this is the really bad part – also making me look old-fashioned and out of touch. The cool kids are letting their clothes hang loose. Tucking your shirt in is becoming a bit like matching your shoes to your handbag: you think it makes you look polished, but in fact it just makes you look a bit passe.Alexa Chung was way ahead of me here. Obviously. So if you won’t listen to me, take it from Alexa. Speaking on a podcast in February, she told Harper’s Bazaar she had been “trying something on the other day, and tucking it in felt weird. I immediately, instinctively, went for the tuck. And then I thought: ‘Oh no, wait, that feels weird.’”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJess Cartner-Morley on fashion: the secret to summer layering? Sheer braveryRead moreProportions change. These tides come and go, and it is my job to keep an eye on them so that you and I don’t get beached. This hot summer has accelerated a shift to a looser silhouette. Volume has been around in fashion for a while, but mostly the exaggerated shapes – bell sleeves, A-line skirts – have been offset by a narrow torso. This is about a more fluid line.If you really can’t deal with letting it all hang out, there is a workaround. I saw it on TikTok, so it must be OK, right? I’m calling it the Reverse French. Instead of tucking a shirt or long top into the front of your waistband, you gather some of the fabric at the back – you can use a ponytail band – and hide this inside the back of your waistband. At the front, the fabric hangs out. You still get the looseness, but with less extra fabric.A record-breaking heatwave has given us a chance to catch up with loosey-goosey fashion, but old habits die hard: I will be keeping a ponytail band in my handbag just in case.Styling: Melanie Wilkinson. Styling assistant: Charlotte Gornall. Model: Moli at Milk. Hair and makeup: Sophie Higginson using Davines and Reome.Shirt, £220, Navygrey.Bralette, £35, Stripe & Stare.Trousers, £69.99, Mango. Author: Alix Fox
Headline: Sexual culture and wellbeing expert Alix Fox answered your questions about how to have a healthier, happier, hornier love life
Content: 10h ago11.10 EDTThat's all, folks!Alix FoxThis has been appropriately pleasurable. Thank you for being such good spurts…I mean,sports, and for your generosity in sharing such sensitive, thoughtful and vulnerable questions. There are still a huge number of queries I’d love to respond to, so hopefully the Guardian will have me back for a second date and this won’t be a one-night stand.Sexisn’t a one-size-fits-all affair. The advice and ideas I’ve given today can’t possibly be comprehensive, and there is so much more to say on almost every topic we’ve touched upon.
