title: Don’t bin those spent corn cobs! Turn them into a delicious chowder instead – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A simple, stripped-back soup that lets the freshest, sweetest corn and fluffy, floury potatoes do all the work
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: A simple, stripped-back soup that lets the freshest, sweetest corn and fluffy, floury potatoes do all the work
Content: Tom Hunt’s corn cob chowder.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s corn cob chowder.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian.Waste notFoodDon’t bin those spent corn cobs! Turn them into a delicious chowder instead – recipeA simple, stripped-back soup that lets the freshest, sweetest corn and fluffy, floury potatoes do all the workTom HuntWed 9 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleToday’s super-simple corn chowder is inspired byone I came across on NewEngland.comthat relies on an old zero-waste trick; namely, scraping the spent cobs to release the pulp and sweetcorn “milk” still left on the cob. Like asparagus, corn is best eaten as fresh as can be, so look for whole ears with bright green husks. Keep in the fridge and, for the most flavourful soup, aim to cook them the same day.Corn cob chowder“Keep it simple” is my new motto. My favourite way to cook at home is as simple as possible: steamed vegetables, ferments and one-pot dishes such as pilafs, risottos, soups and stews. This means an easier life, with less time grafting in the kitchen, so I can cook from scratch for the whole family almost every day without burning out.Sticking to that motto, I wanted to create a very simple, stripped-back chowder that can be made with just fresh corn and a few pantry staples. There’s no cream, stock, garlic, flour or chives, not least so I can honour this incredible ingredient during its short season when it is at its absolute best. Fluffy, floury potatoes and fresh, sweet corn cobs do the heavy lifting, delivering intense flavour and a creamy texture without the need for stock or cream.Serves22corn cobs40g butter1 onion, peeled and finely diced200g floury potato(about 1-2; maris piper, king edward, estima, say), finely dicedFinely grated zest and juice of¼ unwaxed organic lemon, or lime500ml whole milk1 bay leaf(optional)Chopped parsley, to finish (optional)Remove the husks and silk from two ears of corn. Stand each cob on its end in a wide bowl, hold on firmly and use a sharp knife to cut off the kernels in strips. Hold each cob over a second bowl and use the back of the knife or tablespoon to scrape off all the mushy pulp and milk from the cob.Melt 40g butter in a heavy-based saucepan on a medium heat. Add the diced onion and saute gently for five minutes, until soft and translucent but without browning. Add the corn kernels, diced potato and lemon zest, then cook, stirring, for a few minutes.Add the milk and optional bay leaf, then simmer gently for 15 minutes, until the potato is tender.Ladle a third of the chowder into a bowl, leave it to cool a little, then blend with an immersion blender (or mash with a masher). Stir this back into the pot and bring back to a gentle simmer. To finish, stir in the reserved corn milk and the lemon or lime juice, season generously and serve with extra pepper and optional chopped parsley.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteVegetablesSoupAmerican food and drinkSummer food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In praise of the bitter: Alexina Anatole’s recipes for tahini panzanella and curried corn farinata | Food | The Guardian
description: In Ayurvedic cooking, bitter ingredients are celebrated for their ability to refresh and rebalance. Here, the elegance of tahini and the cleanliness of grapefruit do the heavy lifting
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In Ayurvedic cooking, bitter ingredients are celebrated for their ability to refresh and rebalance. Here, the elegance of tahini and the cleanliness of grapefruit do the heavy lifting
Content: Alexina Anatole’s tahini panzanella.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenAlexina Anatole’s tahini panzanella.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodIn praise of the bitter: Alexina Anatole’s recipes for tahini panzanella and curried corn farinataIn Ayurvedic cooking, bitter ingredients are celebrated for their ability to refresh and rebalance. Here, the elegance of tahini and the cleanliness of grapefruit do the heavy liftingAlexina AnatoleWed 9 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 01.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBitterness has long had an image problem: is it delicious or disgusting? Here’s another contradiction: though bitterness seems as if it should sit alongside hot, pungent flavours such as mustard and horseradish, in reality it cools more than it builds. In Ayurvedic cooking, for instance, bitter ingredients are valued for their ability to refresh and rebalance, and those are qualities that run through both of today’s dishes, from the elegant bitterness of tahini in the panzanella to the clean bite of grapefruit in the dipping sauce for the farinata.Tahini panzanella (pictured top)Prep10 minCook25 min, plus restingServes2-4500g largetomatoes, eg, beef, oxheart or monterosa1 tsp flaky sea salt½ small garlic clove1 tbsp sherry vinegar, or red-wine vinegar1 tbsp pomegranate molasses1 small red onion, peeled and very thinly sliced½ tbsp capers, finely chopped, or nonpareilles, which are already petite enough½ tbsp sesame seeds, lightly toastedBasil leaves, to garnishFor the croutons125g sourdough, crusts on,torn into rough pieces2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil½ tsp flaky sea saltFor the tahini dressing2 tbsp tahini1 tbsplemon juice1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil¼ tsp fine sea saltHeat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Chop the tomatoes into haphazard, chunky pieces and put them in a colander set over a bowl. Toss with the flaky salt and leave to drain for 10–15 minutes.Meanwhile, spread the bread pieces on a baking tray, toss with the olive oil and salt, then bake for 10 minutes, until golden. In a bowl, grate the garlic into the tablespoon of sherry vinegar, to help take the edge off.Make the tahini dressing by whisking the tahini, lemon juice, olive oil and salt, then gradually add about two tablespoons of ice-cold water until the mix is the consistency of double cream (the amount of water will depend on the thickness of the tahini).Transfer the drained tomatoes to a serving bowl and stir in the pomegranate molasses, sliced red onion and capers. Add the sherry vinegar and garlic mix, and the croutons, and toss thoroughly. Stir through the tahini dressing, then leave for five to 10 minutes, so the croutons soften a little. Serve garnished with the toasted sesame seeds and basil leaves.Curried corn farinata with grapefruit dipping sauceView image in fullscreenAlexina Anatole’s curried corn farinata with grapefruit dipping sauce.Prep10 minRest15 minCook40 minServes3-4 as a light lunchFor the farinata100g chickpea flour½ tsp ground turmeric½ tsp garlic powder/granules½ tsp fine sea salt1 tsp cumin seeds, toasted1 tsp coriander seeds,toasted4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil75g tinned sweetcorn, drained, or frozen and defrosted3 spring onions, finely slicedMint leaves, to serveFor the grapefruit dipping sauce4 tbsp fresh red grapefruit juice(from about 1 grapefruit)1 tbsp rice vinegar1 tsp caster sugar1 red chilli,finely chopped (seeds and all, if you like things spicy)In a large jug, combine the chickpea flour, turmeric, garlic powder or granules and salt. Gradually whisk in 230ml cold water, ensuring there are no lumps, then leave to rest for 15 minutes.Heat the oven to 230C (210C fan)/450F/gas 8. Roughly crush the cumin and coriander seeds, until broken up but not fully ground.Make the dipping sauce by mixing all the ingredients in a small bowl.Place a 20cm nonstick, ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat. Once hot, add three tablespoons of olive oil and leave to heat for a minute. Meanwhile, whisk the last tablespoon of oil into the batter.Add the crushed spices to the pan, let them sizzle lightly in the oil for 30 seconds, then pour the batter into the centre – it should sizzle. Sprinkle over the corn and spring onions, then bake for 25 minutes, until golden and crisp around the edges. Remove, leave to sit for a minute, then turn out on to a board. Cut into wedges and serve at once with the dipping sauce and mint leaves.Alexina Anatole is the author of theSmall Wins Substackand Sweet: the Secret to the Best Desserts, published by Square Peg at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, go toguardianbookshop.com.Explore more on these topicsFoodSaladTomatoesFruitVegetablesBreadHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Drinking very hot drinks could triple risk of oesophageal cancer, study finds | Cancer | The Guardian
description: Research finds temperature and amount of hot drinks consumed heightens possibility of developing disease
Author: Denis Campbell
Headline: Research finds temperature and amount of hot drinks consumed heightens possibility of developing disease
Content: Experts say people should let very hot cups of tea and coffee cool down until they are comfortable to drink in order to reduce risk of the disease.Photograph: Alextype/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenExperts say people should let very hot cups of tea and coffee cool down until they are comfortable to drink in order to reduce risk of the disease.Photograph: Alextype/Getty Images/iStockphotoCancerDrinking very hot drinks could triple risk of oesophageal cancer, study findsResearch finds temperature and amount of hot drinks consumed heightens possibility of developing diseaseDenis CampbellHealth policy editorWed 9 Sep 2026 02.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDrinking very hot tea and coffee triples the risk of developing cancer of the gullet, the world’s largest study of the link between them has found.The findings show that people should let very hot cups of tea and coffee cool down until they are comfortable to drink, in order to reduce their risk of the disease, cancer experts said.The temperature of the drink and the number of very hot drinks someone consumes increase the chances of getting oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the research found. However, hot drinks do not heighten the risk of getting adenocarcinoma (AC), the other form of oesophageal cancer.“Consumption of drinks at a ‘very hot’ versus ‘warm’ temperature was associated with a threefold greater SCC risk but not with AC risk, after adjustment for consumption frequency”, according to the study, which was published on Wednesday in the International Journal ofCancer.“After controlling for drink temperature, daily consumption of six or more versus fewer than six hot drinks was associated with a 71% increase in SCC risk, with little association with AC risk”, said researchers. The study was led by Dr Keren Papier, a senior nutritional epidemiologist at the University of Oxford’s population health department.The findings are based on analysis of the consumption of hot drinks by almost 980,000 people in the UK – the largest number of people globally in any related studies to date. It followed participants over 14 years to give a long-term picture of their habits and health.They were asked how they preferred to consume hot drinks. Available answers included “very hot”, “hot”, “warm” and “do not drink hot drinks”. The conclusions were based on people’s estimation of how hot the drinks were that they had consumed rather than their exact temperatures.The study produced conclusions for a western European population that mirrored similar findings already seen in studies conducted in Asia, Africa, South America and the Middle East, which found that drinking tea or mate – a caffeinated herbal drink popular in South America – at or above 70C increased the risk of oesophageal cancer.The International Agency for Research on Cancer, part of the World Health Organization, said in 2016 thathot drinks were “probably carcinogenic to humans” and “one probable cause of oesophageal cancer”. They are thought to heighten the risk of the disease by causing heat damage to the cells which line the oesophagus, which is also known as the body’s foodpipe. Alcohol and smoking are other major risk factors for that type of cancer.Health authorities could use these latest findings to encourage the public to consume cooler drinks and fewer very hot drinks to help ensure that fewer people are diagnosed with that form of oesophageal cancer, the study team said.For example, one in seven cases of SCC in the UK “could be avoided if individuals who reported consuming their drinks at a ‘very hot’ temperature instead consumed them at a temperature more representative of the temperature range described as ‘hot’.The researchers said: “The fact that we observed a clear trend in risk across self-reported temperature categories suggests that further limiting the temperature at which individuals consume their drinks to something well below average for this population may well avoid an even greater proportion of SCC cases.“This large UK study of middle-aged adults, amongst whom hot drinks are widely consumed, provides clear evidence that temperature and frequency of hot drink consumption represent useful targets for SCC prevention.”Fiona Osgun, the head of health information at Cancer Research UK, which funded the study, said: “It’s difficult to put an exact time on how long a hot drink should be left to cool. But if you’re worried, we’d suggest just waiting until it’s comfortable to drink rather than drinking it while it’s still very hot.”However, the charity does not believe that cafes, coffee shops and restaurants should start serving tea and coffee at a lower temperature in order to reduce the risk of SCC.Muy-Teck Teh, a professor of molecular oral oncology at Queen Mary University of London, said the research’s reliance on self-reported temperatures may have affected the findings.“A key limitation, however, is that perceived drink temperature is inherently subjective, and it remains unclear whether individuals who tolerate or prefer very hot drinks have altered thermosensation or mucosal sensitivity that might itself reflect underlying biological predisposition to squamous cell carcinoma and lead them to prefer hotter drinks.“This possibility cannot be excluded and complicates interpretation of causality”, he added.Explore more on these topicsCancerHealthCoffeeTeaCancer researchFood & drink industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Babies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study finds | Global development | The Guardian
description: Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems
Author: Kat Lay
Headline: Key regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problems
Content: A study looking at anaemia in pregnancy and the brain development of babies.Photograph: The Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience, King’s College LondonView image in fullscreenA study looking at anaemia in pregnancy and the brain development of babies.Photograph: The Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience, King’s College LondonGlobal developmentBabies born to anaemic mothers have smaller brains, study findsKey regions of the brain linked to movement, learning and emotions were affected and may lead to cognitive problemsSupported byAbout this contentKat Lay, Global health correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBabies born to mothers with anaemia have smaller brains, particularly in key regions linked to movement, learning and the regulation of emotion, according to a study.Researchers said the differences, first detected at the age of one, could lead to cognitive problems when children started school.More than a third of pregnant women worldwide have anaemia – a condition typically caused by iron deficiency in which the number of red blood cells in the body is lower than normal. Symptoms include fatigue, shortness of breath and dizziness. Rates are highest in sub-SaharanAfricaand south Asia.Researchers from King’s College London in the UK, and the University of Cape Town inSouth Africa, followed more than 300 mothers and their babies in Cape Town, scanning the brains of the infants several times between the ages of three months and two years.On average, the total brain volume of babies born to anaemic mothers was 4% lower than that of babies born to non-anaemic mothers – despite all the anaemic mothers being diagnosed only with a mild version of the condition.Differences were recorded in three specific regions of the brain: the putamen, caudate nucleus and corpus callosum.“All three of these brain regions are implicated in key neuropsychological functions,” said Jessica Ringshaw, first author and researcher at King’s Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology &Neuroscience(IoPPN) and the University of Cape Town, citing processing speed, emotion regulation and executive function as examples.The gap between the groups of babies widened over the first two years of life – the corpus callosum, for instance, was about 4% smaller at 12 months in the group whose mothers had been anaemic but 6% by 24 months.Earlier research in South Africa looking at toddlers and school-age children found comparable differences in brain volume.“These aren’t children who are catching up, where the brain differences are disappearing over time,” said Ringshaw. “They are still there when the children are six years old and going to school, and when these things might then start translating into more noticeable cognitive difficulties.”The findings offer a potential explanation for earlier studies showing that children born to mothers with anaemia scored less well on tests of development, she added.The mothers with and without anaemia were otherwise very similar in terms of factors such as household income and food security, Ringshaw said, making her confident that maternal anaemia caused the differences the team observed.The results reinforced the importance of tackling anaemia in women of reproductive age, Ringshaw said. “We should be screening for anaemia and iron deficiency, particularly during pregnancy,” she said, recommending the use of oral or even intravenous iron supplementation where appropriate.The causes of anaemia were complex and could include infectious diseases, she said, with the study finding higher rates of anaemia in women living with HIV, “so having our iron interventions, but also appropriate infection management in conjunction with that [is important]”.While the World Health Organization lists reducing rates of anaemia as a priority, progress hasstagnated over the past two decades.“Now more than ever, anaemia needs to be placed at the forefront of public health efforts if we are to ensure that children are not only surviving but thriving,” said Ringshaw.The research, published in the journal Brain Communications, used special new MRI scanners that are cheaper and more portable than the conventional machines used in hospitals.It compared images taken using the traditional “high-field” MRI machines with those taken by the portable “low-field” options, and found the latter were sensitive enough to detect the same differences in the brains of babies born to anaemic mothers.Steve Williams, professor of neuroimaging at King’s, said: “This study has proved that our novel technology can measure the impact of malnutrition on the developing brain, at scale, in some of the most challenging environments. This will provide an early, sensitive assessment of planned interventions.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentGlobal healthChildren's healthEarly years educationChildrenPregnancyParents and parentingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sali Hughes on beauty: the hero products that kept me cool in the long hot summer of 2026 | Skincare | The Guardian
description: From face tints and self-tan to summer scents, these lightweight buys saw me through multiple heatwaves
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: From face tints and self-tan to summer scents, these lightweight buys saw me through multiple heatwaves
Content: Bag: Tory Burch.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBag: Tory Burch.Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Sali Hughes on beautySkincareSali Hughes on beauty: the hero products that kept me cool in the long hot summer of 2026From face tints and self-tan to summer scents, these lightweight buys saw me through multiple heatwavesSali HughesWed 9 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ll normally find me looking back on my favourite products of the past 12 months at year’s end. But this summer has been so freakishly hot and sweaty it has required its own toolkit and, by extension, its own list of exceptionally well-performing products that deserve rapturous commendation.The first is Refy’sSkin Base(£30), a sheer face tint so thin and so lightweight it has been all I could bear to wear since July. It’s suitable for all skin types, but not at all appropriate for those who hate any hint of shine. While the texture is totally ungreasy, breathable and so comfortable as to be imperceptible, it doeslookunmistakably dewy, so avoid if you’re devoted to matte. Personally, I take the view that, in this heat, one might as well steer into the skid, but I am, admittedly, at an age when a juicier look works in my skin’s favour. Anyway, this is makeup that trulyfeelslike absolutely nothing, and what it lacks in coverage can be made up with concealer where needed. Maximum points from me (I wear shade 140N).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIt’s the skincare equivalent of sleeping underneath a silk sheet instead of a 9-tog duvetSali Hughes on beauty: a shortcut to glass skin? Try these one-step moisturisersRead moreMoisturiser is another step that humidity has forced me to downsize. The heat has made wearing heavy face cream as appealing as a 5km parkrun, so I’ve switched to lighter liquids to quench my skin’s thirst. The Prequel skincare line, which recently launched in the UK, is consistently good, but itsHalf & Half Fluid Moisturizer(£28) has been a godsend. This very lightweight emulsion pours like semi-skimmed milk, satisfies like double cream and barely adds any weight to sweaty skin. The glycerin and ceramides keep everything supple until bedtime, and give a smooth, plump base for SPF and makeup. It’s the skincare equivalent of sleeping underneath a silk sheet instead of a 9-tog duvet.St Tropez’s newInstant Glow Mousse(£25) has never been far from my reach. It’s a fast, mess-free and streakless way to make exposed legs golden until your next soapy shower. Stroke on with a mitt, wash off only when you’re ready. Absolutely no fussy prep required.I’ve relied heavily on zingy, fresh, enlivening scents to keep me in good spirits. The summer 2026 perfume playlist I’ve had on repeat is Dedcool’sXtra Milk(from £24) – a dreadful name, but a very gentle, happy and wearable fragrance – and Penhaligon’sLuna(from £32), all wet roses, zesty citrus and airy green forests. Like a cold compress for the senses.Explore more on these topicsSkincareSali Hughes on beautyBeautyWomenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route: a trek through the mountains of north-west Sweden | Sweden holidays | The Guardian
description: A remote 18th-century chapel deep in Sami lands is the goal of the Präststigen, a 37-mile trail that traverses some of the country’s most spectacular scenery
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A remote 18th-century chapel deep in Sami lands is the goal of the Präststigen, a 37-mile trail that traverses some of the country’s most spectacular scenery
Content: The Präststigen or Priests’ trail in northern Sweden.Photograph: Arctic SwedenView image in fullscreenThe Präststigen or Priests’ trail in northern Sweden.Photograph: Arctic SwedenSweden holidaysEurope’s wildest pilgrimage route: a trek through the mountains of north-west SwedenA remote 18th-century chapel deep in Sami lands is the goal of the Präststigen, a 37-mile trail that traverses some of the country’s most spectacular sceneryHugh CollinsWed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwasn’t exactly in “Sunday best”, but I had madesomeeffort. Well, I’d changed my underwear for the first time in a couple of days and given myself a baby-wipe bath. Still, as we filed into the chapel at Alkavare, I felt more a member of an expedition than a congregation. We sat on the low wooden benches, waterproof jackets rustling and leather walking boots stamping on the flagstone floor to keep warm. Fortunately, the priest, Mogens Amstrup Jacobsen, appeared to be a “man of the Gore-Tex”, as well as a man of the cloth, as he unzipped his own black rain jacket to reveal his dog collar. As the service began, the Arctic wind whipped through cracks in the dry stone walls, insulated only with reindeer hair, and candles flickered in their brass sconces.My slow Swedish summer on the tranquil islands of ÖstergötlandRead moreI had hiked to Alkavare following thePräststigen, or “Priests’ trail”, a 37-mile (60km) route from Kvikkjokk that could stake a claim as Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route, and certainly one of its most beautiful. The Präststigen follows the path that priests would once have taken to the chapel, built in 1788, to perform a service each summer, and today, on the last weekend in July, intrepid hikers and perseverant pilgrims can attend that same service.Alkavare sits on the western border of Sweden’s Sarek national park, home to many of the country’s highest mountains and steepest valleys, yet with no campsites or tourist huts and only scant sections of the more famous Kungsleden trail. There are no other marked paths and to hike here means wild camping, a heavy backpack and a sense of adventure. It was described by famed Swedish diplomat Dag Hammarskjöld in 1926 asvår sista stora vildmark– “our last great wilderness”.View image in fullscreenWild camping en route.Photograph: Arctic Sweden“I hate it when people use the term ‘wilderness’,” Christian Heimrot from Laponia Adventures, a local guiding operator, told me, as I joined him on the research exhibition for a new Präststigen group trip launching next year. “This is a living landscape, people have lived, worked and shaped this land for thousands of years.” Indeed,Sarek national park, (as part of the wider Laponia region), was recognised as a Unsesco World Heritage Site in 1996 for both its cultural and natural value.double quotation markThere are no other marked paths, and to hike here means wild camping, a heavy backpack and a sense of adventureThe Sami, Europe’s last Indigenous population, have braided themselves into these landscapes as tightly and beautifully as the thread of pewter in their traditionalhandicrafts. The Sami word for the Laponia area isSápmi, the same word they use to refer to themselves, highlighting the indelible link between people and their environment. Sarek sits on the Sami’s traditional reindeer herding grounds. While they might now use motorcycles and snowmobiles to follow and herd the reindeer, their knowledge of and kinship with this landscape remains undimmed.So, not wilderness, then, but certainly wild. To even reach the start of the Präststigen, I had crossed the Arctic Circle on the road north from Luleå, met with Christian at his warehouse in Jokkmokk (home to the famous Sami winter markets each February) to load up our rucksacks for the six-night trip, and journeyed an hour farther west to the town of Kvikkjokk. From there the trailhead was a short boat ride across Sakkat lake.The first section of the trail climbed steeply, switchbacks tightly coiled in birch woodland; wild blueberries and cloudberries littered the path. Eventually we left the woodland and reached the ridge for our first proper view of Sarek. Away to the north was the cloud-covered summit of Bårddetjåhkkå, where in 1911 Swedish geologist Axel Hamberg built an observatory to conduct meteorological and glacial studies.View image in fullscreenThe trail involves walking through icy rivers, as there are no bridges.Photograph: Arctic SwedenWe slept soundly, as we eased into the rhythms of wild camping – water collected from a gin-clear lake, a hearty supper of reindeer stew, and an eye mask to keep out the midnight sun. The next day we hiked deeper into Sarek via the Vállevágge, the skies the blue of the Swedish flag, the silence only disrupted by the occasional breath of wind.We were following the guidebook Priest’s Path by Hans Fowelin (currently only published in Swedish), and while there was no marked trail, Fowelin had plotted a path of cairns we were supposedly to follow. While some were solidly built square towers, most were little more than one rock propped up against another, mere whispers of waymarkers in a landscape of scree and moraine.Alongside the familiar buttercups and heather there were bright blue blossoms of mountain gentian, red ptarmigan berries and otherworldly looking wild angelica, a source of vitamin C for the Sami. Sarek was visited by botanist Carl Linnaeus during his epic expedition through northern Sweden in 1732, and the first part of the Priest’s trail is sometimes referred to as Linnaeus’s trail.On our fourth day of hiking Alkavare chapel appeared on a bluff above the glacial blue waters of Alggajavvrelake, surrounded by high peaks and valleys. It was utterly beautiful. I had a grin on my wind-burnt face for most of the day, one that even wading across rivers (a common feature of hiking in Sarek), shin-high in glacial meltwater, failed to dim.After rowing across the Miellätno river, using one of the rowing boats left on each bank by the park rangers, we climbed up to the chapel late on Saturday evening where Jacobsen greeted us with a beaming smile.View image in fullscreenPriest Mogens Amstrup Jacobsen was flown in by helicopter to lead the service.Over tea, he told us he had been dropped off by helicopter at Alkavare with his family on Friday morning and this was his first time leading the service here. Others in the diocese no longer volunteered. “It is physical, hard work and the days are long,” he said, before heading off to re-tar the chapel’s roof and fix one of the rowing boats that had come loose and floated away down the river – returned, later, swinging beneath a helicopter.double quotation markThe chapel had been originally built not as an act of benevolence, but as part of the forced Christianisation of the SamiSunday mass began promptly at 11am the following morning for our small band of pilgrims (we numbered 11 in total, including the priest). The altar had a simple wooden cross and cloths on loan from the church in Jokkmokk. They were in the poster paint palate of traditional Sami clothing and a reminder that it was for the Sami that the chapel had been originally built – not an act of benevolence, but as part of the forced Christianisation and eradication of their shamanistic beliefs in the 18th century.View image in fullscreenAlkavare chapel.Photograph: Hugh CollinsAfter the service we sat outside for coffee and pastries, before beginning our hike home. Christian was keen that we hiked via Sweden’s point of inaccessibility orotillgänglighetspunkten, just over the border from Sarek in the Padjelanta national park. This is the country’s point furthest from any road or town, about 31 miles (50km) in fact, and is often cited as western Europe’s remotest too. Marked with no cairn or monument, just a circle of quartz stones and a trio of reindeer antlers, it felt no more or less remote than most of the previous week’s hiking. And I was struck that what made Sarek and the Präststigen special wasn’t just the scenery, as beautiful as it was, it was the people – the Sami, Hamberg and Linneaus, and the motley congregation we’d briefly joined, and it was a route firmly deserving of more visitors. “I told you,” Christian said, grinning, “It isn’t a wilderness.”The trip was provided byLaponia Adventures, which willlead a guided, small-group trip along the Priest’s Path to Alkavare in July 2027, and offers equipment rental and advice for independent hikers. For more information on Sarek national park and northern Sweden, visitarcticsweden.comExplore more on these topicsSweden holidaysScandinavia holidaysWalking holidaysEurope holidaysWalkingAdventure travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I climbed into the car with three friends. I woke in hospital to find I’d lost them all – and my legs | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Rob Pike was 17 when he and three of his closest friends were in a car that smashed into a tree and split in half. He explains how he coped with the devastation
Author: Rachel Dixon
Headline: Rob Pike was 17 when he and three of his closest friends were in a car that smashed into a tree and split in half. He explains how he coped with the devastation
Content: Pike in Glasgow in July for the Commonwealth Games. He is head coach for the Australian women’s 3x3 wheelchair basketball team, who took the bronze medal.Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPike in Glasgow in July for the Commonwealth Games. He is head coach for the Australian women’s 3x3 wheelchair basketball team, who took the bronze medal.Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/The GuardianHow we surviveLife and styleI climbed into the car with three friends. I woke in hospital to find I’d lost them all – and my legsRob Pike was 17 when he and three of his closest friends were in a car that smashed into a tree and split in half. He explains how he coped with the devastationRachel DixonWed 9 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter the car stopped rolling and came to rest on its side, Rob Pike remembers being “hyperfixated” on the rainwater pouring down his face. When he tried to wipe it away with his arm, he realised it wasn’t water. “I look at my arm and it is covered in blood. The next moment, it hit me: oh my gosh, we crashed.”He was in the back seat next to his best friend, Daniel McCoy. “I look up to my left to see if Daniel’s OK. He’s probably about a foot away from my face and … he’s not OK. I’m looking at my dead best friend and I wish that wasn’t my last memory of him, seeing how broken he was.” They were 17.“I lost control,” he says. “I am screaming at the top of my lungs. I’m yelling, I’m crying.” Even though he knew that Daniel was dead, he hoped for a miracle. “You spend your life watching Home and Away and Neighbours and you see people getting pulled out of cars and having CPR. If I can scream loud enough, then maybe somebody might come along and save his life.”A woman had rushed out of her house when she heard the crash and run towards Pike’s screams. She found the car in the bushes. Pike remembers begging her: “‘Please help Daniel. You gotta do something.’ And then she gets down on her hands and knees, in the mud, in the rain, and she looks inside. And I remember her saying: ‘There’s nothing we can do for him. He’s already gone.’“All of a sudden, I am very aware that I’m trapped in this car. I start freaking out. I’m trying with all my might to pull myself out of this little back window. I’m cutting my hands and I can’t get out.”The woman stayed with Pike for about 15 minutes, trying to calm him down, until the fire engine and ambulance arrived. “I remember thinking, as soon as they arrived: ‘Everything’s going to be OK.’” The next two weeks are a blank.View image in fullscreenTributes at the scene of the accident.Photograph: Courtesy of Rob PikePike grew up in a mining town in the far north-west of Western Australia, with five older half-brothers and half-sisters. He was particularly close to one of his brothers, who taught him to play cricket and football in the back yard. When he was 12, the family moved to Baldivis, a small town about 50km south of Perth.Life was good. “I was in my final year of high school, I had good friends and I knew what I wanted to do in my life. I had two options: I wanted to go into the Defence Force or I wanted to go and play AFL football for the best AFL football team in Australia, the Fremantle Dockers.” He grins – Fremantle is one of only three AFL teams never to have won a premiership.On the day of the crash in Baldivis, on 17 August 1999, he was in lessons until lunchtime. His friends Christian Iezzi-Carrello and Adam Stribling, who were a year older and already at university, picked him up from school to go to play golf. “We weren’t any good,” he says. “We just loved getting out there, mucking around, getting in the golf carts – you know, being a little bit silly and having a good time.” McCoy was off sick that day, but Pike was pretty sure he’d want to join them. So he said the words that would later torture him: “Hey, let’s go get Daniel.”It started to rain, so they went bowling instead. “As much as that day was a horrendous day, I’ll always remember that afternoon and those two games of 10-pin bowling as a fun time with my friends,” he says. “And I’m very grateful for that memory.”View image in fullscreenChris Bond of the Fremantle Dockers visits Pike in hospital after the crash.Photograph: Courtesy of Rob PikeIezzi-Carrello, the driver, suddenly realised the time. It was nearly 4pm and he had to get to his part-time job at McDonald’s. “So we rushed out of there. We ran out of the building, across the car park, jumped into his car and took off.” It was now pouring with rain. “We were zipping in and out of traffic. We were probably going between 10 and 20 kilometres over the speed limit.” It didn’t cross his mind to object. “At 4.16, everything’s fine. At 4.17, I am the most scared I’ve ever been in my life.”They were laughing and joking and listening to the radio. Then the car hit a big puddle of water and Iezzi-Carrello lost control. “I can go back to that moment right now,” says Pike. “I can remember closing my eyes and almost in slow motion thinking to myself: this is gonna be bad.” The car aquaplaned, went into a spin, smashed into a tree and split in half.Pike woke up in Fremantle hospital after a fortnight on life support. At that point, he had no memory of the accident. “I had tubes and cords that were connected to me, keeping me alive. I had one going down my throat and I couldn’t speak. I’m in a back brace, almost like I’m strapped to the bed. I can’t move.”His father was sitting by his bed. “He must have seen the fear on my face because he grabbed me by the hand. And I remember him saying: ‘Hey, Bob, I’m here.’ I remember that calming me.” His father was silent for a while. “Then he goes to me: ‘Bob, I got to tell you something. Christian, Adam and Daniel have died.’” Iezzi-Carrello and Stribling had been flung out of the car and died on impact.Pike thought he was dreaming. He started pinching his arm and his chest, hard enough to leave bruises, trying to wake himself. “And I never woke up out of the nightmare. This is real; my friends have gone.”View image in fullscreen‘I can remember closing my eyes and almost in slow motion thinking to myself: this is gonna be bad.’Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/The GuardianNo one told him the extent of his injuries. He was told he’d had more than 300 stitches and that he’d broken his back. He knew he needed to wear the back brace or risk severing his spinal cord. But he felt cramps and itches in his feet, and he could feel himself wiggling his toes, so he was confident he would eventually walk again.About four weeks after the accident, he felt an unbearable itch in his foot that he simply had to scratch. “So I’m trying to contort my body to reach down under the blankets. All I feel are bandages. That’s the moment where I’m like: oh my God, what’s this? I rip the blankets off and then, even in this back brace, I sit up, because I need to see. I look down. Now, what I’m expecting to see is two feet and 10 toes. But all I see is bandages where both my legs finish just after my knees. I reckon that was one of the worst moments.” More than half of people who lose a limb experience phantom pains, including itches.The doctors hadn’t amputated his legs; they had been severed in the crash. When the car hit the tree, the back panel sliced through his legs. “It actually took both my feet. So my feet, still in the shoes, ended up going in the front half of the car, jammed under the front seat, and my body was in the back half of the car.” This panel trapped him inside and saved his life. “It was so tight on my legs that it acted as a tourniquet. Ask any emergency services person: if there is an amputation in a car crash, nine times out of 10, that person dies at the scene because they can’t stop the blood flow.”His dream of playing for the Dockers was over. “I’m lying in this bed and I’m like: well, that’s not my future any more. You can’t play football because you don’t have feet.”Over seven weeks in hospital, he had to go through the embarrassment of nurses seeing him naked, bathing him and cleaning him up after he went to the bathroom. “I feel like I’ve lost everything. I’ve lost my friends. I’ve lost my legs. The last thing I had was my dignity and there it goes.”View image in fullscreen‘I remember saying to myself: “I can’t give up.”’Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/The GuardianHe cried himself to sleep every night. He had “massive survivor’s guilt” and wished he could exchange his life for one of his friends’. “You almost create this rationale within your own mind: they were a little bit more popular, so less people would be sad if I’d died.” He couldn’t bear the fact that it was his words that had put McCoy in the car. He started making a plan to end his life.One night, there was a knock at the door of his hospital room. It was McCoy’s parents. He tried to compose himself for their sake, but he couldn’t. “Daniel’s dad puts his arms around me and I bawl my eyes out. He’s saying: ‘It’s gonna be OK, Bob. We’re gonna get through this.’ And I’m thinking to myself: it’s not gonna be OK. I’m not gonna get through this because I’ve checked out. I don’t want to be here any more.“He grasps me by the shoulders and looks me in the eyes and he goes: ‘Bob, we are so happy that you are alive.’ And those words hit me in my heart.” He knew he couldn’t do anything to add to their pain. He had no choice but to live.“I remember saying to myself: ‘I can’t give up.’ And I would say it every day, multiple times a day for the first three to four months, over and over.” One day, he realised he’d only had to say it five times instead of 100. Eventually, he didn’t have to say it at all. “I’m not living for them any more,” he realised. “I’m living for me.”Pike learned to use his prosthetic legs before his stumps had even fully healed; he was determined to walk into his end-of-year school celebration. He started playing cricket again. He got a girlfriend.View image in fullscreenPike on his wedding day.Photograph: Courtesy of Rob PikeTo friends, he was the lucky one, the brave one. But he was still full of guilt and very self-conscious about his disability. There were false reports in local newspapers that the boys had been drinking before the crash and that the car was stolen. People would accost him in the street to ask: “What were you guys thinking?” He started self-medicating with alcohol, binge-drinking every weekend to mask “this brokenness within me”. After six months, he finally accepted that he needed therapy.The other thing that saved him was wheelchair basketball. His dad persuaded him to try it. “I was very ignorant. I’m like: a bunch of disabled people playing basketball?” He went to a game and was “blown away. What I’m watching is athletes flying around this court, hitting each other, smacking each other. And I’m like: yes, this is awesome!”It helped fill the gap left by football and he loved the physicality of it. “No one was like: I can’t hit you because you’ve got no legs.” He threw himself into the sport and ended up playing for Perth Wheelcats and Australia, then moved to Spain for a couple of years to play professionally. Today, he is the head coach of the Wombats, the Australian women’s 3x3 wheelchair basketball team. We meet in Glasgow on the opening day of the Commonwealth Games; they will go on to take the bronze medal.Pike, 44, is married with two children. He is proud to be on the board of the Paraplegic Benefit Fund of Australia, which supports people with spinal cord injuries, and to do road safety advocacy. Reliving the worst day of his life is tough, but it helps give his friends’ deaths meaning. “I can share it with 16-, 17-year-old students and hopefully inspire them to be better drivers, but also better people.” He says that he is a “nicer, more empathetic” person since the accident.View image in fullscreen‘It’s very easy to look at what you don’t have.’Photograph: Jeremy Sutton-Hibbert/The GuardianHe still has setbacks. During Covid, more than 20 years after the crash, he woke up with “extreme panic attacks”. All he could think was: “I’ve gotta get out.” He slept outside on garden furniture for two weeks, then took off the window in the front room and slept on a recliner for a month. He had another panic attack when he was driving. “I remember feeling: oh my gosh, I’m trapped to my legs and I’m trapped in this car. And then – it’s strange how the mind works – I actually feel like I’m trapped in this world.” He saw a tree and, for a split second, it seemed like a way out. That was when he knew he needed to see a psychiatrist again.“You think you’re done,” he says, referring to his initial therapy after the crash. “But what the psych said to me is that your body protects itself. And then when it feels like it’s in a safer space, things start to come to the surface, which was my trauma of being stuck in the car.” Now, he says, “I’ve come through the other side. And I feel like I’m a pretty complete, whole person, and I’m in a really positive place.”Life still throws curveballs. Towards the end of our conversation, he casually mentions that he had a heart attack three months ago. He thought he’d pulled a muscle; he ended up “going into complete heart failure” and being hospitalised for 12 days. It turned out he has hereditary high cholesterol – his dad had a heart attack in his early 50s. “I thought I could just be healthier and eat well and go to the gym. I learned the hard way that it doesn’t matter how fit you are. If your cholesterol is an issue, it’s an issue.”These days, he believes in counting his blessings. “It’s very easy to look at what you don’t have. We should be looking at what we do have. I don’t think we’re called to just sit there and exist and wait till the end. I think we’re called to go out there and live life and be kind and be the best person we can.”In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsLife and styleHow we surviveDisability and sportYoung peopleCommonwealth Games 2026Commonwealth GamesAustralia sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: I spent a day with some naturists – and it cured my shy bladder | Life and style | The Guardian
description: For decades, I had been haunted by paruresis, an inability to urinate in public toilets. But that day of nakedness suddenly, surprisingly, led me to shed my inhibitions
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For decades, I had been haunted by paruresis, an inability to urinate in public toilets. But that day of nakedness suddenly, surprisingly, led me to shed my inhibitions
Content: ‘People really do come in all shapes and sizes’… Ashton.Photograph: Callum Hoffman/Hoff MediaView image in fullscreen‘People really do come in all shapes and sizes’… Ashton.Photograph: Callum Hoffman/Hoff MediaA moment that changed meLife and styleA moment that changed me: I spent a day with some naturists – and it cured my shy bladderFor decades, I had been haunted by paruresis, an inability to urinate in public toilets. But that day of nakedness suddenly, surprisingly, led me to shed my inhibitionsRobert AshtonWed 9 Sep 2026 01.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor as long as I can remember, I’ve suffered from a condition called paruresis – also known as shy bladder syndrome. This means that, unless I’m alone in public toilets, I cannot pee, however badly I need to go. I developed tactics to deal with this, such as loitering outside the gents if I see someone going in, so that I can walk in as they walk out. But if someone follows me in, I find I’m just standing there, which I worry looks odd.I’m a writer, so am often out and about meeting people in cafes, hotels and at events. My agricultural background means I also meet a lot of my interviewees on farms – but at least there I could pop behind a hedge if I needed to go, and be assured of privacy.It was while I was doing research for a book on the spiritual connections humans once had with the land that I stumbled across the Christian Naturist Fellowship: a network of people who believe that Christianity and naturism are entirely compatible. Here, I thought, were a community who clearly get closer to nature than most – I was keen to meet them.One of their committee members, Nigel, suggested I visit his naturist club near Colchester. So one Saturday morning in 2025, I set off to discover what Christian naturists really think and do. He had said that I’d not have to strip off – many don’t on their first visit – but when the time came, that is exactly what I did.View image in fullscreenAshton (left) and Nigel from Christian Naturist Fellowship.Photograph: Courtesy of Robert AshtonI’d been naked in public once before, but then I’d been one of more than 3,000 people who, in 2016, had stripped off in a Hull city centre park at dawn, daubed themselves with blue body paint, and beenphotographed by Spencer Tunickas a visual celebration of the city’s relationship with the sea. Then, I’d enjoyed the anonymity of being one in a crowd and, strangely, it still felt as if I was wearing something, albeit just blue paint. Visiting a small naturists’ collective would be different.After arriving at Springwood Sun Club, Nigel greeted me wearing a warm smile – and a pair of shorts. As it happened, he was not in a rush to shed his clothes either, and we both walked to the clubhouse fully dressed. It could have been any social club, except that the foursome playing miniten outside were in the buff.Nigel then took me to a clearing in the woods, where he told me he believed it important to touch the ground with your bare feet – so we slipped off our shoes and socks and gave it a go. He introduced me to several of the other naturists and, after a while, I began to feel a little overdressed. I suggested that the time had come for me to go with the flow; I returned to my car and stripped off, while Nigel popped into his cabin to do the same. When I nipped to the loos later on, I thankfully found them to be empty – although walking in with no clothes on, and not having to zip up before washing my hands, did feel strange.Before I left for home, our conversation returned to Christianity and, knowing that I was a Quaker, Nigel invited me to come back as a visiting speaker at an interfaith event Springwood was hosting later that summer. On my second visit, I felt no hesitation and stripped off on arrival.View image in fullscreen‘I’d enjoyed the anonymity of being one in a crowd’ … Ashton took part in Spencer Tunick’s 2016 photographic installation Sea of Hull.Photograph: Danny Lawson/PAMy inhibitions about being seen without clothes left me after that first visit – but, to my surprise, so too did my paruresis. Looking back, I realise that it had always been connected to a fear of nakedness, of people being able to see me urinate. I remember how, at primary school, I would refuse to use the school toilets, despite clearly needing a wee.I stopped at a garden centre for a coffee on my way home and, when visiting the loos, was horrified to discover that only the centre urinal of three was not being used. But rather than feel so embarrassed that I was forced to walk out, I stepped forward and, astonishingly, had no problem at all. A few days later, visiting Norwich, I discovered once more that I could pee in company. Since then, I’ve not experienced any difficulty, no matter how busy the toilets. Spending a day with the naturists seemed to have cured a problem that had haunted me for decades.My time with the Christian Naturist Fellowship also helped me realise that people really do come in all shapes and sizes, and that very few of us have the kind of physique we are encouraged to aspire to, especially by social media. Dipping my toe into this world made me realise how, when clothes are shed, so too can we let go of inhibitions and pretences – and even lifelong anxieties.Down to Earth by Robert Ashton ispublished by Wilton Square Books (£16.99).
