terrorist organisation as the Trump administration expands its campaign against narcotics traffickers it says are destabilising Latin America.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, made the announcement in Quito, where he met Ecuadorian president Daniel Noboa, one of several rightwing allies of Donald Trump whom Rubio is courting as a security partner during a three-nation tour throughLatin Americathat began on Tuesday.Rubio said theLos Tiguerones gangwas linked to narcotics trafficking, as well as attacks on civilians, law enforcement officers and journalists.“We are not talking about an ordinary mafia, nor are we talking about common criminals, we are talking about terrorists who, in many cases, possess weapons and equipment resembling the national armies of certain countries,” he said.The heavily armed gang’s attack on the TC Televisión network in 2024 prompted Noboa to declare a state of “internal armed conflict”, amid claims foreign drug gangs had descended onEcuadorto take control of important routes for coca grown in neighbouring Colombia and Peru and then shipped to the US.Live footage from the El Noticiero news programme showed men toting pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and sticks of dynamite. The viral images quickly became a symbol of the drug violence destabilising the country.1:02Footage shows armed gang storming studio live on Ecuadorian TV station – video reportForced disappearances, killings and torture: why is Ecuador’s brutal drug war being backed by the west?Read moreIn its efforts to fight against narcotics trafficking and illegal migration from Latin America, theTrump administrationhas also empowered a number of hardline leaders through its “Shield of the Americas” coalition that aims to tighten security cooperation with rightwing allies in the region.During his trip, Rubio plans to visit several newly elected conservative leaders amid a significant political shift to the right in Latin America.On Wednesday, Rubio hailed Ecuador as being the Trump administration’s most “aggressive” partner in its military campaign against alleged drug traffickers, including in the controversial strikes against boats that havekilled at least 227 peoplewhom the Trump administration has called drug traffickers without providing evidence.Rubio said that he would seek $45m (£33m) in additional funding from Congress towards efforts aimed at “dismantling these terrorist groups”, although he did not go into details. He also told reporters that elite forces from both countries were “working jointly on a day-to-day basis in a way that has no precedent in order to try to dismantle these terrorist organisations”.View image in fullscreenMarco Rubio (left) is welcomed to Ecuador on Wednesday by its president, Daniel NoboaPhotograph: Dolores Ochoa/AFP/Getty ImagesRubio visited Colombia on Tuesday, where he met its newly inauguratedpresident Abelardo De La Espriella, who narrowly won a June election against leftist leader Gustavo Petro with whom the Trump White House had cold relations.During his remarks, Rubio took something of a victory lap, saying that the two sides would seek to “[confront] the mistakes of the past four years” and called Petro’s leadership of the country “unnatural”. Colombia joined the Shield of theAmericasinitiative only after its change in government.During the meeting, the two men discussed security and counternarcotics policy, and signed memorandums of understanding on critical minerals and nuclear energy.Rubio is expected to next travel to Peru, where he will meet Keiko Fujimori, who defeated a leftwing candidate by a margin of just 50,000 votes during a close election in July. She has promised to fight crime with an “iron fist” and adopt some controversial policies from neighbouring El Salvador, which has been a close ally of the US on security policies.Explore more on these topicsDrugs tradeTrump administrationEcuadorDrugsAmericasUS politicsMarco RubionewsShareReuse this content

title: Family of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigators | Grenada | The Guardian
description: Andrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in January
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Andrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in January
Content: A Grenada police officer on the beach.Photograph: Robert Nickelsberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Grenada police officer on the beach.Photograph: Robert Nickelsberg/Getty ImagesGrenadaFamily of British man found dead in Grenada ask local police to work with UK investigatorsAndrew Frederick’s body was found in property he was staying at in Grenada in JanuaryNatricia Duncanand agenciesWed 9 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe family of a British father who was found dead in theCaribbeanin January is urging authorities in Grenada to work with UK police to uncover the truth about his death.Andrew Frederick’s body was found in the property he was staying at inGrenadaon 4 January. An autopsy, performed in the same week by a privately hired pathologist, concluded that the 47-year-old’s death was a homicide.In June, Grenada’s director of public prosecution, Howard Pinnock, said at a press conference that Frederick’s and another pending case would be sent to the coroner to determine the cause of death “because there is no basis in terms of both investigations that any homicide has occurred”.After a sustained campaign by the family, British authorities became involved and Frederick’s body was repatriated to the UK last month, where a second autopsy was carried out.The UK coroner has noted that Frederick’s organs are missing and the death is currently “unascertained”.At the start of an inquest at West London coroner’s court last week, senior coroner Lydia Brown said the Metropolitan police are now investigating Frederick’s death.The family, who attended the court hearing by video link, said the coroner’s “decision to suspend Andrew’s inquest to allow the Metropolitan police to conduct a criminal investigation marks a significant turning point”.In statement to the Guardian, they urged Grenada and the UK to work together to find out what happened to Frederick.“We are encouraged and grateful that the Metropolitan police investigation is now under way. Justice for Andrew depends on everyone with the power to act, on both sides of the Atlantic, doing what is right,” the statement said.Family accuse UK government of lack of support over death of Briton in GrenadaRead moreIt added: “Andrew was a deeply loved member of a close-knit family; a son, brother, father and grandson. He leaves behind his cherished daughter, who should be growing up with him beside her, not learning to live without him.“Our family remain determined to uncover the truth about what happened to Andrew and to see justice follow. We hope this ruling is the step that finally enables a complete, properly coordinated investigation and that everyone who can assist will now do so.”This year,the family had called for an urgent reviewof the policies governing UK assistance to the loved ones of Britons killed abroad, after they were forced to launch their own public appeals for information, and commission an independent forensic pathologist and a private investigation.“Eight months have passed since Andrew was taken from us. In that time, we have learned what no family should ever have to learn, and fought battles no family should ever face alone,” their statement said.It added: “We have relentlessly sought answers and support while carrying the weight of Andrew’s loss and the horror of what was done to him. We still do not have a complete account of what happened, and important questions remain unanswered.“We hope the Grenadian authorities with knowledge of the case will now share that information and work collaboratively with the Metropolitan police, allowing the investigation to proceed without further delay. We are also seeking urgent answers as to why Andrew’s organs were absent when his body was returned to the UK for further examination.”In Grenada, the Office of the Commissioner told the Guardian that “the matter will be progressing to the coroner’s court for the parish of Saint George”.A Met spokesperson said: “The Met is investigating the death of 47-year-old Andrew Donald Frederick, who died in Grenada on 4 January.“Mr Frederick’s family are being supported by specialist officers.“No arrests have been made at this stage and inquiries are ongoing.”Officers have contacted the Royal Grenada Police Force to offer assistance and discuss how the investigation can be progressed.Inquest proceedings have been suspended pending the outcome of police investigations.Explore more on these topicsGrenadaAmericasCaribbeannewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s hell’: father of slain Australian surfers tells Mexico homicide trial about identifying sons’ bodies | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Three men are on trial over the death of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend, US citizen Jack Carter Rhoad, in Ensenada
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Three men are on trial over the death of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend, US citizen Jack Carter Rhoad, in Ensenada
Content: Jake and Callum Robinson’s father Martin gave evidence on Tuesday in the homicide trial, telling the court he doubts he will ever ‘regain my balance’ after the loss.Photograph: Enrique Botello/ReutersView image in fullscreenJake and Callum Robinson’s father Martin gave evidence on Tuesday in the homicide trial, telling the court he doubts he will ever ‘regain my balance’ after the loss.Photograph: Enrique Botello/ReutersMexico‘It’s hell’: father of slain Australian surfers tells Mexico homicide trial about identifying sons’ bodiesThree men are on trial over the death of brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their friend, US citizen Jack Carter Rhoad, in EnsenadaAgence France-PresseWed 9 Sep 2026 00.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 00.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe father of two Australian surfers killed inMexicotwo years ago testified in court on Tuesday that his life had been turned into hell, as the high-profile trial continued into its second day.Three men are charged in the killing of Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad, who were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast in April 2024.Authorities say the three were killed in an attempted robbery, and their bodies were found dumped in a cliff-top shaft with gunshot wounds to their heads.‘I heard a lot of noise’: trial begins in Mexico for alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friendRead more“It’s hell,” the victims’ father Martin Robinson told the court. “It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons.”“It’s not just the loss, but also the potential they had the dreams that lay ahead of them, the places they travelled, and the love they had for others,” he said.Robinson described the ordeal of having to identify his sons’ bodies: Callum by a tattoo on his forearm, while identifying Jake was more difficult and required photographs.Rhoad’s mother Page compared the crime to an execution.“I miss my son every day, and I don’t know if I will ever be able to regain my balance,” she testified. “Carter loved Mexico. He spoke fluent Spanish and loved dancing, Mexican food and its people.”Authorities say the men were killed during an attempt to steal their pickup truck, which was later found burned near their bodies.A protected witness testified Monday that they accompanied one of the defendants to the crime scene and fled after hearing gunshots, and were later threatened into silence.The surfers’ disappearances and deaths sparked widespread outrage and grief in Australia and the United States, prompting a major social media search for their bodies.“We hold no resentment toward the people who did this, but we cannot understand how they could have taken the lives of two beautiful people,” Martin Robinson told the court.The trial is expected to run until the end of September.Rhoad’s widow, Natalie, is scheduled to testify on Wednesday.Explore more on these topicsMexicoCrime - AustraliaWestern AustraliaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Indonesian foragers may have sucked on mind-altering nuts 25,000 years ago, research finds | Science | The Guardian
description: Analysis of two skeletons reveals tooth wear and traces of psychoactive substance in what may be earliest known evidence for human drug taking
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: Analysis of two skeletons reveals tooth wear and traces of psychoactive substance in what may be earliest known evidence for human drug taking
Content: The researchers examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers.Photograph: Pubu Alar_sulsel/View image in fullscreenThe researchers examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers.Photograph: Pubu Alar_sulsel/ScienceIndonesian foragers may have sucked on mind-altering nuts 25,000 years ago, research findsAnalysis of two skeletons reveals tooth wear and traces of psychoactive substance in what may be earliest known evidence for human drug takingIan SampleScience editorWed 9 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat may be the earliest known evidence for human drug taking has been traced to ancient Indonesian foragers who sucked on mind-altering nuts as long as 25,000 years ago.Analysis of two exceptionally rare skeletons from the Indonesian island of Sulawesi revealed dramatic tooth wear and traces of a psychoactive substance in the individuals’ remaining teeth, suggesting they routinely sucked on hard, abrasive betel nuts.Although little known in western societies, betel nuts are the world’s fourth most widely used psychoactive substance after alcohol, caffeine and nicotine, with an estimated tenth of the global population chewing the seeds.View image in fullscreenBetel nuts.“We’ve found evidence for how this very common drug use habit, which is found throughout a lot of the Asia-Pacific region today, might have evolved,” said Prof Adam Brumm at Griffith University’s AustralianResearchCentre for Human Evolution in Brisbane.The work began when the team examined skeletal remains of two pre-agricultural foragers unearthed at two different sites on the island. One was dated to about 7,000 years old, the other more ancient at 16,000 to 25,000 to years old.Writing inScience Advances, the researchers describe how both adults had deep, rounded grooves in their teeth. Some went so deep they would have exposed the dental pulp. “I was thinking, what the hell were these people doing? It’s like someone had a drill head shaped like a gobstopper and wore away the inner part of the tooth,” said Brumm.Betel nuts are actually the seeds of theAreca catechupalm, but are misnamed because they are often wrapped in betel vine leaves for chewing. Today, the nuts are typically chewed after being mixed with slaked lime made by grinding burnt shells to form a “quid”.View image in fullscreenInferred positions of the nuts based on the dental wear patterns.Photograph:Brumm suspected the bizarre tooth wear was caused by the foragers holding hard, round and abrasive objects in their mouth, but what sort of object? “Imagine you kept a stone in your mouth and you moved it from one part of your mouth to another, and if you did that day after day, hour after hour. Eventually it would wear down your extremely hard dental tissue to form these grooves,” he said.The team wondered whether the grooves were the result of foragers sucking on betel nuts before people realised that mixing the nuts with slaked lime helped release more of the psychoactive drug and intensify the “high”.To test the hunch, the scientists soaked betel nuts in artificial saliva and found that it soon contained enough of the psychoactive compound arecoline to induce a high, albeit a milder one than when the nut is chewed. Analysis of the foragers’ teeth found traces of arecoline in the tissues.“I’ve sucked on a nut as an experiment and it’s a really bitter, astringent taste. It makes your mouth go numb and I think that’s what they were interested in,” Brumm said.“This might have been a traditional remedy for toothache, but if they did it for too long, sucking on the nut wore down their teeth so badly that it actually created much worse dental pain in the long term. These individuals were seemingly caught in a self-perpetuating cycle where they were continually sucking on the nuts to treat the tooth pain caused by this nut-sucking habit.”While humans probably began using mind-altering plants as soon as they encountered them, the oldest traditions of psychoactive drug use are thought to have arisen about 13,000 years ago with fermented drinks such as barley beer.Dr Elisa Guerra-Doce, an associate professor in European prehistory at the University of Valladolid in Spain, said the study provided “direct evidence of the antiquity of human drug use”.“These findings not only represent the earliest known evidence to date of the use of psychoactive plants anywhere in the world, but also demonstrate that the consumption of Areca nuts is a millennia-old tradition dating back to prehistoric times,” she added.Explore more on these topicsSciencePalaeontologyDrugsIndonesiaAsia PacificResearchHigher educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Singapore boosts PM’s salary by $1m amid major pay rise for ministers | Singapore | The Guardian
description: The affluent city-state has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The affluent city-state has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance
Content: Singapore has announced a significant pay rise for government ministers including the prime minister, Lawrence Wong, whose annual salary will increase to Sg$3.6m ($2.8m).Photograph: Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSingapore has announced a significant pay rise for government ministers including the prime minister, Lawrence Wong, whose annual salary will increase to Sg$3.6m ($2.8m).Photograph: Roslan Rahman/AFP/Getty ImagesSingaporeSingapore boosts PM’s salary by $1m amid major pay rise for ministersThe affluent city-state has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governanceAgence France-PresseTue 8 Sep 2026 20.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSingapore’s prime minister has been given a $1m pay rise as the affluent city-state announced a dramatic one-off salary boost for government ministers.The pay increases add more than 60% to what are already the world’s highest ministerial salaries.Singapore has justified high-end salaries for its political leaders, arguing they attract talent and ensure good governance. The issue is nevertheless politically sensitive, with cabinet members’ income far exceeding that of most ordinary citizens.Prime minister Lawrence Wong’s benchmark annual salary will rise from S$2.2m ($1.7m) to S$3.6m ($2.8m).Singapore asks the $70,000 question: who wants to start a family?Read moreThe deputy prime minister’s benchmark will lift from S$1.8m to S$3m. Cabinet ministers will get between S$1.8m and S$2.8m, depending on the seniority and weight of their portfolio.Wong said he would donate the entire increase of his salary to “suitable good causes” during his term.Even before the raise, the Singaporean prime minister’s paycheck vastly outstripped the wages of many other leaders, including in the US and other G7 nations. The US president earns $400,000 a year, while the UK prime minister is paid about $230,000 annually.“Political salaries are a difficult and emotive issue,” said Wong, whose long-ruling People’s Action Party dominates Singapore’s parliament and its 21-member cabinet. “The sums involved are more than what most citizens earn, so I understand why Singaporeans scrutinise them closely, and why many feel strongly about the matter.”However, the issue is “ultimately about whether Singapore will continue to have the quality of political leadership we need to take our country forward” in the decades ahead, he said.“Our starting point is this: good government depends on good leadership.”The South-east Asian nation, which last adjusted ministerial salaries 15 years ago, is regularly ranked among the world’s least corrupt countries.Wong said the pay raises were recommended by an independent committee, adding that existing office holders would not be moved immediately to the new benchmarks.They will receive a one-off adjustment of up to 9% from 15 October, depending on individual circumstances, including performance.Explore more on these topicsSingaporeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Victoria’s koalas in chronically poor health and population is half what was previously estimated | Victoria | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: State government delayed releasing major report into the health of the koala population for more than 12 months
Author: Lisa Cox
Headline: Exclusive: State government delayed releasing major report into the health of the koala population for more than 12 months
Content: An overabundance in some local koala populations had created a perception that Victoria’s overall population was thriving, researchers say.Photograph: Penny Stephens/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn overabundance in some local koala populations had created a perception that Victoria’s overall population was thriving, researchers say.Photograph: Penny Stephens/The GuardianVictoriaVictoria’s koalas in chronically poor health and population is half what was previously estimatedExclusive:State government delayed releasing major report into the health of the koala population for more than 12 monthsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLisa CoxEnvironment and climate correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 16.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 18.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Victorian government sat on a report for more than 12 months that found the state’s koala population was in chronically poor health.Thereviewof the state’s koala populations, led by state science agency the Arthur Rylah Institute in conjunction with scientists from major universities, was completed for the Victorian government in June 2025.It estimated there were 217,000 koalas in the state in 2023 and 224,800 in 2024 – a dramatic drop frompast estimatesof 460,000, which the report attributed to different survey and modelling methodology, rather than an actual population decline.As part of the research, scientists conducted health and disease assessments on 68 koalas, with 29 of the koalas (43%) found to be in such poor health they “were euthanised on welfare grounds”.The report warned the surveys found “a higher-than-expected proportion of koalas from seven geographically distinct regions in a state of chronically poor health and welfare”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe government published the report on Wednesday morning as the new environment minister, Jaclyn Symes, announced $2.6m for koala conservation, including for habitat restoration and research into koala health and genetics.Leanne Wicker, a wildlife veterinarian who was one of the authors on the report, said researchers had been shocked by the poor health of some of the koalas they found in the field.“While we were doing this research we knew we were seeing something that urgently needed attention and understanding,” she said. “And it’s been very difficult to get the support and resources needed because the report hadn’t been made public.”She said the overabundance of certain local Victorian koala populations – such as those at French Island and in western Victoria – had created a perception that the state’s overall koala population was thriving. “What we’ve missed is we have a crisis in our koala populations in Victoria because we have a very concerning level of poor health and welfare.”Deakin University’s Desley Whisson, another author on the report, said while the 2024 population estimate of about 225,000 koalas “seems like a lot, most of those koalas are in areas where there are high densities of animals”.“There’s large parts of the state where koalas occur at low densities and are probably in poor health,” she said.She said the government needed to turn its attention to areas with low numbers “because we could be losing koalas in some parts of the state without even knowing”.The report used systematic visual and acoustic surveys in 2023 and 2024 to monitor koalas at 182 sites. That data was then used to estimate the overall abundance and distribution of Victoria’s koala population.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPossums in the roof, koalas in bed: study shows how animals resort to Australian homes after habitat lossRead moreThe report states the drop in the estimated population from previous estimates of 460,000 was due to changes in the methodology used. It said the new data also represented the first time koala populations had been surveyed statewide.Of the 68 koalas sampled for health and welfare checks, 39 healthy individuals were rereleased, with healthy animals present at all of the locations sampled, according to the report. But 29 koalas were euthanised due to ill health.Koalas that were euthanised were more likely to have poor coat condition, dental disease and “wet bottom” (an advanced urinary tract infection, most commonly caused by chlamydia), and were more likely to occur in areas with high koala densities. Dental disease was recorded in 37% of koalas across all life stages and regions, except Mallacoota, according to the report.The report states that these findings raised concerns “for the health of Victorian koalas”.“Clinical signs consistent with chronic ill-health were observed across all life stages, suggesting that multiple individual, environmental and demographic stressors may be contributing to prolonged physiological stress within these populations,” the scientists wrote.Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said the research painted a grim picture of the health and wellbeing of Victoria’s koalas.“It is clear that we need to use every lever possible to ensure they’re given the best chance at survival, or we will soon be just like the many states across Australia where koalas are listed as endangered,” she said.The report also found that 23% of Victoria’s koala population now lived in the state’s blue gum plantation estate “where they occur at much higher density than koalas in neighbouring native forest”.“Given the high estimated density of koalas within blue gum plantations, changes to the plantation estate size and/or stand ages may result in significant changes to population size,” it states.Jessica Robertson, from advocacy group the Koala Alliance, called Wednesday’s funding announcement “a calculated political rescue mission for Labor, not for koalas”.“Sitting on critical ecological data for over a year while koalas continued to suffer and disappear is a shocking failure of transparency and responsibility,” she said.A Victorian environment department spokesperson said since receiving the report it had been working with other agencies, and consulting external groups, “to prioritise actions and design projects that address its findings and recommendations”.A spokesperson said Wednesday’s funding announcement was the result of this work.The environment department’s spokesperson said the timing of the report’s public release had not affected “important work” the government was already doing to manage the health of the state’s koalas.Explore more on these topicsVictoriaWildlifeAnimalsConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: The RBA hoped this year’s three interest rate rises would tame inflation – but nothing is going their way | Australian economy | The Guardian
description: The breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, rising oil prices and the explosion in datacentre investment are making the central bank’s task harder
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: The breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, rising oil prices and the explosion in datacentre investment are making the central bank’s task harder
Content: Fuel prices are rising again in Australia, with petrol nearing $2.10 a litre and diesel passing $2.50.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenFuel prices are rising again in Australia, with petrol nearing $2.10 a litre and diesel passing $2.50.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPAustralian economyAnalysisThe RBA hoped this year’s three interest rate rises would tame inflation – but nothing is going their wayPatrick ComminsEconomics editorThe breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, rising oil prices and the explosion in datacentre investment are making the central bank’s task harderFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 9 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 18.27 EDTShareFor five years the Reserve Bank has been trying to wrangle inflation back to its 2.5% target, and for years it has essentially failed.The result isa cost-of-living crisisthat has generated intense community grievance.The RBA’s deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, acknowledged as much on the ABC’s 7:30 report on Tuesday.“People are furious about inflation,” Hauser said.“Inflation has been above target for a long period of time and, at some point, we will have to say, ‘That is long enough’.”Inflation graphAre we at that point? Not yet, said Hauser, even as he hinted we are getting closer every day.The RBA’s nine-member board had hoped this year’s three interest rate hikes would be enough to bend the arc of inflation slowly back to reach 2.5% by the end of next year.But nothing is going their way.The latest blow is the complete breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, with escalating tit-for-tat strikes on oil tankers and infrastructure in and around the strait of Hormuz.The global oil benchmarkhas risen above $US100 a barrelfor the first time since July. Fuel prices are tracking higher once again, with unleaded approaching $2.10 a litre and diesel passing $2.50.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThen there is this year’s suddenexplosion in datacentre investment. That has heaped pressure on a construction sector already struggling to get the materials and labour it needs to build the massive pipeline of work to build homes, roads and rails.Households are complaining a lot and feeling depressed, but there’s still a surprising lot of spending happening, which is keeping consumption growth ticking along.Meanwhile, Australia’s productivity performance – the thing that could make it easier for the economy to grow without pushing inflation up – remains flat.Investors and an increasing number of economists believe we are approaching that point when the RBA has to say “enough is enough” and act more aggressively to get price rises back under control.Financial markets are pricing in more than a 70% chance of another rate hike on 29 September, and even the chance of a second by the end of the year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Of course we could raise interest rates sharply,” Hauser said.“We could do it tomorrow. We could no longer take seriously the full employment part of our objective [and say] we’re gonna bring inflation down come hell or high water.”Here Hauser is pointing out that the RBA has not been asleep at the wheel, but has been making a conscious calculation.Since mid-2021, annual inflation has only been below 3% for one year.On the other hand, unemployment has been below 5% for almost all of that time – a labour market record unmatched in modern Australia history.“The reason as a board we have decided to take it slowly is to preserve as many jobs in this country as we could,” Hauser said, and not for the first time.But the balance is starting to shift.“We have one big problem, and that’s inflation,” he said.“Inflation is too high, that’s why we raised interest rates three times at the beginning of this year. The question now, frankly, for us, is have we done enough, or is more needed?”Explore more on these topicsAustralian economyReserve Bank of AustraliaInflationInterest ratesanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Peter’s farm is on ‘flood country’. As Australia’s sea levels rise, safe land is vanishing and costs are huge | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Climate Council forecasts more than 267,000 coastal properties will be damaged by flooding by 2100, costing hundreds of billions of dollars
Author: Donna Lu
Headline: Climate Council forecasts more than 267,000 coastal properties will be damaged by flooding by 2100, costing hundreds of billions of dollars
Content: Peter Lake's NSW northern rivers property after a flood in 2022 flood. The cattle farm has flooded five times since 2009.Photograph: Peter LakeView image in fullscreenPeter Lake's NSW northern rivers property after a flood in 2022 flood. The cattle farm has flooded five times since 2009.Photograph: Peter LakeClimate crisisPeter’s farm is on ‘flood country’. As Australia’s sea levels rise, safe land is vanishing and costs are hugeClimate Council forecasts more than 267,000 coastal properties will be damaged by flooding by 2100, costing hundreds of billions of dollarsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastDonna LuWed 9 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 20.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen grazier Peter Lake moved to the Clarence Valley in theNew South Walesnorthern rivers region in 2007, he knew was “buying in flood country with … eyes open”.His cattle farm, about halfway between Yamba and Grafton, borders the Coldstream River and has flooded five times since 2009.“Out of 130 acres … in a major flood we would have maybe 15 acres that were flood-free,” he said. Lake has systems in place to prepare for such events, including moving cattle to the dry paddocks, where they would also store fodder to feed the animals.But the amount of safe ground is shrinking: in the historically big flood in 2022, “we only had just a few acres of flood-free land”. Because of both drought and frequent floods, “we just haven’t been able to successfully grow a fodder crop for some years”.“If we’re going to have more frequent and more severe major events … we need to change the way we think about how we manage,” Lake said. “If rising sea levels impact on us, it’ll just make property less and less viable.”View image in fullscreenGrazier Peter Lake on his Clarence Valley cattle farmAgricultural damages are among $855.1bn in economic losses projected Australia-wide by the end of the century due to coastal flooding, according to a Climate Council report released on Thursday.The report forecasts that more than 267,000 coastal properties and 2m hectares (4.9m acres) of Australian land will be damaged by flooding by 2100 as sea levels rise.Queensland (93,157 properties), NSW (71,210) and Western Australia (51,366) are the three states with the greatest number of homes at risk.The Gold Coast, Brisbane and Melbourne are the metropolitan areas expected to be worst affected.View image in fullscreenCoastal areas around Brisbane and the Gold Coast are at significant risk, the Climate Council says.Illustration: Climate CouncilThe Gold Coast, the country’s most exposed urban area, faces $84.4bn in projected economic losses, while in Melbourne losses are concentrated in low-lying areas around Port Phillip Bay and the Yarra River.The Climate Council report is based on mapping coastal flooding by 2100, taking into account both sea level rise and storm surges under the climate scenario known as RCP4.5 – which projects a 2.7C increase in global temperature by the end of the century, similar to expected heating based on current policies worldwide.View image in fullscreenCoastal areas around Port Phillip Bay are vulnerable to rising seas.Illustration: Climate CouncilIt was co-authored by Prof Tom Kompas at the University of Melbourne, whose modelling of the economic impacts was also published in the peer-reviewed journalScientific Reportsand drew upon localised projections at 239 hotspots around Australia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKompas said the costs – an estimated $274.3bn in property losses and $580.7bn in land use damages – were a conservative estimate and did not take into account the additional impacts of coastal erosion or significantice sheet melt.He said due to the scale of agricultural losses there was a food security issue potentially coming as well: damage is projected to affect 619,713 hectares (1.5m acres) of farming land.View image in fullscreenA map showing coastal areas at risk in NSW and the projected economic damage.Illustration: Climate CouncilSea levels have risen, on average by more than22cm globallysince 1900, with human-caused global heating the dominant cause of the rise since 1970. An additional 14cm rise is expected in Australia by 2050, increasing the frequency of permanent inundation and tidal flooding.Kompas said that while reducing greenhouse gas emissions to limit global heating was of paramount importance, “we have to start planning and responding and adapting now”.“The nice thing about the work is it shows where the hotspots are and what … assets will be impacted. So we can start to plan for how to deal with that.“The first thing, of course, is not to build on flood plains, which is common still.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisNew South WalesRural and regional AustraliaVictoriaQueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Air traffic control boss given a week to report after UK flight chaos causes 2,000 cancellations | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Government remains confident in under-pressure Martin Rolfe but transport secretary believes glitch was avoidable
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Government remains confident in under-pressure Martin Rolfe but transport secretary believes glitch was avoidable
Content: Passengers at Heathrow airport on Wednesday morning.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenPassengers at Heathrow airport on Wednesday morning.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAAir transportAir traffic control boss given a week to report after UK flight chaos causes 2,000 cancellationsGovernment remains confident in under-pressure Martin Rolfe but transport secretary believes glitch was avoidableHow have you been affected by UK air traffic disruption?Gwyn TophamandMark SweneyWed 9 Sep 2026 12.09 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 03.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of the air traffic control provider Nats has been given a week to report back on the reasons for a technical failure that grounded thousands of flights, as the transport secretary said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”.Heidi Alexander said on Tuesday she had also commissioned an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the latest Nats meltdown, which severely disrupted travel for hundreds of thousands of passengers.The comments will pile pressure on the Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, despite Downing Street saying the government still had confidence in him after a morning meeting with Alexander, and as the number of flight cancellations passed 2,000.The minister told the Commons: “Safety must remain air traffic controllers’ overriding priority, and this morning I have spoken to Nats chief executive, Martin Rolfe, who informed me this outage was due to a technical issue at their Swanwick site.“So, while my understanding from Nats is that we can rule out a cyber-attack on this occasion, I do not believe this issue was unavoidable.”The CAA said passengers were “unlikely to be entitled to compensation for delays and cancellations” as the problem was likely to be considered the result of “extraordinary circumstances”.View image in fullscreenHeidi Alexander, who said she would ‘leave absolutely no stone unturned in understanding what has happened here’.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersAirlines have urged action, with Rolfe facing increasing pressure to quit, after thethird large-scale stoppage to flightsin just over three years.Latest industry estimates say about 330,000 passengers had their travel disrupted and delayed, with many stuck on grounded planes for hours during the incident . Other passengers were stranded overnight at airports in the UK and abroad. More than 155,000 passengers had flights cancelled, while flights were delayed for more than 180,000 passengers.A Downing Street spokesperson earlier said Alexander had asked Rolfe to “carry out a full investigation into what happened to make sure that lessons are learned, so that this doesn’t happen again”.Tell us: how have you been affected by UK air traffic disruption?Read moreAlexander said she would “leave absolutely no stone unturned in understanding what has happened here, and what can be done to drastically reduce the likelihood of something like this ever happening again.“I do think we need to ask tough questions about the resilience of Nat systems … We also need to think about consumer redress issues as well.”The prime minister’s spokesperson added: “We have confidence in him and he’s been tasked with the investigation, which will report in a week’s time.”Airlines includingRyanairand Wizz called for Rolfe to resign or be sacked by Alexander. He had earlier defended the resilience of the systems run by Nats, which provides services to 15 UK airports.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUK airport disruption: what are your rights if you have been affected?Read more“We will be doing a very thorough and full investigation,” he told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. “We have at this point ruled out a cyber-attack … This will be something we haven’t seen in more than 50 years of operation.”Nats said the problem occurred in its flight processing system but was not the same fault as the issues that caused outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.Ryanair queried the explanation and said lessons had not been learned. The carrier, which on Tuesday said more than 65,000 of its passengers had been disrupted when 50 flights were cancelled, said it had now cancelled more than 250 flights and that its costs would run into millions.The airline’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, said: “Martin Rolfe’s position as Nats CEO is untenable. We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports, and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience, and will promise an effective backup system.”He said the UK’s air traffic control services were one of the most expensive inEurope“and yet it keeps repeatedly failing”. O’Leary said Alexander should “today demand that failing Martin Rolfe must quit, or be dismissed”.Yvonne Moynihan, the managing director of Wizz Air UK, called on Rolfe to consider resigning. “In any industry when you’ve had three failures, you need to consider three strikes and you’re out,” she told Today. “A third time and a third excuse is not enough any more. What we need to see from leadership is accountability.”Luke Petherbridge, the director of public affairs at the travel association Abta, said: “While the immediate priority is supporting customers … the industry and the public will want answers as to what has gone wrong.”Nats said the fix it eventually implemented on Tuesday, almost four hours after the incident first occurred, had been a “very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover”.More than 300 flights were cancelled on Wednesday in the continuing fallout from the outage. According to data from the analysts Cirium, nearly 2,100 flights in and out of UK airports have been cancelled because of the failure, including 1,750 on Tuesday out of 5,800 scheduled flights. Of these, 541 were at Heathrow.A spokesperson for British Airways said: “Tuesday’s air traffic control issue has forced us into cancelling almost 550 of our flights, affecting more than 85,000 of our customers. We’re incredibly sorry for the experience they’ve endured because of an issue that has been entirely out of our control.” The airline operated nearly 80% of its typical flight schedule.Rail passengers affected by flight disruption could use booked tickets on a different date or to a different airport if needed, or apply for a refund, the Rail Delivery Group said.The airport breakdown started at about 1pm on Tuesday and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Stansted.London airports as well as Manchester were among the most directly affected, with operations in effect suspended for hours in the afternoon. While Heathrow said the fault initially only stopped takeoffs, the airport was soon too full to accommodate more planes, with arriving flights diverted to other European airports.Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Birmingham, Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted.The air traffic control problems follow an“isolated event” a year agothat caused widespread disruption, and appeared less severe than the fullgrounding of flights in August 2023, which prompted a parliamentary inquiry.Explore more on these topicsAir transportAirline industryHeathrow airportGatwick airportTransportFlightsHeidi AlexandernewsShareReuse this content

title: Germany’s Merz cancels phone call with Trump after social media post celebrating AfD win – as it happened  | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Spokesperson for Merz declines to give a reason for cancellation, but notes that it was not due to scheduling
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Spokesperson for Merz declines to give a reason for cancellation, but notes that it was not due to scheduling
Content: 08.02 EDTGermany's Merz cancels phone call with Trump after social media post celebrating AfD win to 'make Germany great again'German chancellorFriedrich Merzcancelled a planned phone call with US President Donald Trump on Wednesday, hours after Trump publicly celebrated a regional election win by Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland party.US president Donald Trump holds up a jersey with the number 47 as German chancellor Friedrich Merz look on during a working session at the G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France in June.Photograph: Thibault Camus/ReutersA spokesperson for Merzdeclined to give a reason for the cancellation, but noted in response to questions from journalists that it was not due to scheduling conflicts, AFP said.Trump, in a post on his Truth Social platform,hailed the “really big night” for the AfD,and used an abbreviation MGGA, apparent reference to an adapted version of Trump’s trademark slogan,“makeGermanygreat again.”“Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night. They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly.THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore!MGGA!!! President DJT”AFP saidMerz’s spokesman did not directly respond to Trump’s commentsand declined to comment if there is a link between the two developments,but noted that the chancellor had frequently objected “in general terms” to “interfering in or commenting on the domestic political situation, particularly regarding elections”.ShareUpdated at08.09 EDT

title: Tens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald V | Norway | The Guardian
description: Europe’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a close
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Europe’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a close
Content: King Harald is taken to the royal mausoleum in the crypt at Akershus Castle after the funeral ceremony in Oslo.Photograph: Terje Pedersen/EPAView image in fullscreenKing Harald is taken to the royal mausoleum in the crypt at Akershus Castle after the funeral ceremony in Oslo.Photograph: Terje Pedersen/EPANorwayTens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald VEurope’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a closeJon HenleyEurope correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of ​national mourning that followedthe popular monarch’s deathlast month at the age of 89.Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades.With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress.View image in fullscreenNorway’s Prince Sverre Magnus, King Haakon VIII, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Princess Martha Louise.Photograph: Ole Berg-Rusten/EPAKing Haakon VIII, whosucceeded hisfather on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked in the cortege, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car.View image in fullscreenDespite its recent scandals, the monarchy remains broadly popular.Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix/APThe procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; ‌Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino.Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”.View image in fullscreenThe Prince of Wales and Princess Anne leaving the funeral service.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersThe prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.”After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony.View image in fullscreenA portrait of Norway’s King Harald V, painted by Valeria Duca, is displayed among flowers and Norwegian flags at a makeshift memorial outside the royal palace in Oslo.Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty ImagesNorwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss ⁠classes for the occasion.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHarald’s death came at a time of numerous crises for the Norwegian royal family, with Mette-Marit, 53, in particularcoming under heavy criticism– including from the prime minister – for her association with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.View image in fullscreenMarius Borg Høiby leaves the funeral service.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersThe new queen’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle monitor pending his appeal against a conviction for rape and domestic violence, was given permission to attend the funeral and was a pallbearer during the transfer to the royal chapel.Despite its recent scandals, however, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a poll for the public broadcaster NRK.View image in fullscreenThe casket of King Harald V leaves the royal palace for Oslo Cathedral.Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty ImagesExplore more on these topicsNorwayEuropeMonarchynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German city where the far right surged | World news | The Guardian
description: After the AfD’s landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt, people in the state capital share what they make of the result – and what comes next
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: After the AfD’s landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt, people in the state capital share what they make of the result – and what comes next
Content: Top AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund in front of a sign reading ‘It starts here’ at an election party after the Saxony-Anhalt state elections in Magdeburg.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APView image in fullscreenTop AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund in front of a sign reading ‘It starts here’ at an election party after the Saxony-Anhalt state elections in Magdeburg.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APThis Is EuropeWorld news‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German city where the far right surgedAfter the AfD’s landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt, people in the state capital share what they make of the result – and what comes nextDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKate Connollyin MagdeburgWed 9 Sep 2026 10.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAsking residents in a city where a seismic political event has just taken place ‘How do you feel?’ demands chutzpah – this struck me as I walked around Magdeburg, Germany on Monday. The night before, the far-right populist, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin party Alternative für Deustchland (AfD) had landslide 44% win in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, sending shock waves to Berlin, across Germany and way beyond. Regardless of how people in the capital voted, it felt like a bit of an affront to probe. Given the radical plans of the victors, a party classified by domestic intelligence as“rightwing extremist”, that is what I wanted to know. But from the 21-year-old Guinean-German paramedic I met at the central bus station, collecting donations for a local hospice, to the elderly couple returning to their apartment after a stroll down the Elbe river, almost everyone I met opened up to me warmly.Judith, 88, was initially reluctant to talk, but shared some of her life story. Her experience as an eight-year-old refugee, forced to leave Poland in 1946 and eventually ending up move with her family in Magdeburg, had shaped her outlook on life, her successful career as a project engineer – as well as her politics. The news that AfD had not only won the election, but by such a wide margin, was “heartbreaking”, she said.Huy, from Vietnam, who runs a newsagents in the city centre, was also reticent, but laughed and rolled his eyes as he sold the last copy of that day’s local paper, Die Volksstimme, and pointed to the headline that read: “Landslide in Saxony-Anhalt”. Shaking his head, he said: “44%!” “I don’t want to think what it might mean … but maybe it will all be OK?” His question hung in the air.A glance at the AfD’s manifesto, in particular its pledge for the first 100 days, focuses the mind. Top of the list: challenging Germany’s post-war memory culture (which it says stands in the way of national pride) – so, “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as they put it. “From the first minute”, they say, the party will start the deportation of what it refers to as “irregular migrants”.I met Franz-Josef, a 71-year-old retired mechanic and Green voter, on holiday from a small west German town. He called the election a “catastrophe”, particularly in the light of the country’s Nazi past.Luisa, a 34-year-old bank teller told me she hopes “those who voted for the AfD thought about what they were doing”. It was one thing, she said, to “deliver a kick in the shins” to Berlin, over its failure to pull the German economy out of the doldrums. And maybe the AfD would fail to push through its promises in government. “But we cannot know, and I fear the price could be high.”Fragrance of powerView image in fullscreenA damaged banner depicting the top candidate of the far-right AfD party, Ulrich Siegmund, the day after the elections in Magdeburg.Photograph: Annegret Hilse/ReutersIt remains unclear how precisely the AfD, led by charismatic former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, might take the reins of power in Saxony-Anhalt, if at all. He lacks an absolute majority by a whisker.There have been rumblings for days – even prior to the election – of an AfD charm offensive to try to lure members of chancellorFriedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats,to make up the necessary numbers. The CDU denies any defections are expected.Some AfD members have brazenly appropriated Ronald Reagan’s appeal to the Soviets to “tear down this wall”, from his 1987 speech in West Berlin. They are calling on mainstream parties to “tear down the firewall”, a reference to theBrandmauer, or refusal to ever coalesce with the AfD in an effort to prevent the far-right populists from coming to power. Yet an increasing number doubt that the firewall will hold much longer. Especially now that almost one in two of those who cast their votes on Sunday have opted for the party. Turnout at 78% was a record for the state.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhatever the outcome, we can expect weeks, even months of wrangling. Expect stasis in the meantime on the federal government front, as we’re close to elections on 20 September in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, where the AfD is also expected to do well. Merz will be wary of doing anything that might drive more voters away. At the same time politicos in Berlin are debating how long he has in the job. In the Bundestag today, Merzaccused the AfDof seeking “ethnic cleansing”.No wonder Maryam, 16, whom I met as she returned from work experience at a retirement home, said she and her family were on edge. The Syrian teenager, whose father arrived in Germany in 2015, followed by her and her mother, told me she couldn’t stop thinking about what this vote might mean for her family. She wished, she said, for a return to the days of Angela Merkel, the German chancellor who welcomed in a million migrants including Maryam’s father, resentment over which turbo-charged support for the then-fledgling AfD.Across the road, Doreen, a cleaner, who reluctantly admitted voting for the AfD, said: “What on Earth is there to thank Merkel for? It’s owing to her that we are in the state we’re in.” She recalled an attack near the Christmas market in the city centre in 2024, where six people were killed when a Saudi doctor drove a car into the crowd, an incident that helped fuel support for the AfD. “That attack is symbolic for a whole lot of misery, the decision to open our doors to strangers has brought us,” Doreen told me. “I say, good on the AfD for promising to clean up the mess.”For such a small state, home to 2.1 million people, Saxony-Anhalt has managed to create a political maelstrom, the ramifications of which will be felt acrossEurope.To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsThis Is EuropeEuropeGermanyAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)The far rightFriedrich MerznewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Merz accuses AfD of ‘ethnic cleansing’ policy and cancels call with Trump | Germany | The Guardian
description: German chancellor attacks Alternative für Deutschland after far-right party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt election
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: German chancellor attacks Alternative für Deutschland after far-right party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt election
Content: 0:41German chancellor accuses far-right AfD of calling for 'ethnic cleansing' – videoGermanyMerz accuses AfD of ‘ethnic cleansing’ policy and cancels call with TrumpGerman chancellor attacks Alternative für Deutschland after far-right party’s win in Saxony-Anhalt electionEurope live – latest updatesDeborah Colein BerlinWed 9 Sep 2026 09.43 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGermany’s chancellor,Friedrich Merz, has accused the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with its “remigration” drive, after the nativist party’s seismic weekend victory in a state election.In his first public confrontation with the AfD since Sunday’sshock outcome in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz said at a raucous parliamentary debate that the far-right party would take an axe to one of the pillars of the German economy with a racist campaign of mass deportations.‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capitalRead more“The term ‘remigration’ is nothing but a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” he said on Wednesday to applause from the other parties in the Bundestag lower house.In a fiery speech addressed to the AfD parliamentary group, which repeatedly interrupted him with loud taunts and heckling, Merz said millions of working immigrants were crucial to German society.“If those working inGermanyhave to leave the country again because you are championing ‘remigration’,” Merz said, “then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function: not a single care home will remain open, not a single hospital in Germany will remain operational, and not a single restaurant in Germany will be able to stay in business.”He said the AfD’s rhetoric, which propelled it to the strongest showing for a far-right party in a German state since the Nazi period, “is precisely what is dividing our society so deeply”.The AfD has repeatedly called for large-scale expulsions of irregular migrants, a policy that would face stiff challenges under German law.View image in fullscreen(L-R) The AfD’s Tino Chrupalla, Ulrich Siegmund and Alice Weidel after the Saxony-Anhalt election win.Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPAIn the election, the party rode an international wave of populism, nationalism and discontent with mainstream parties, underscored overnight by congratulations fromDonald Trump.In a post on his Truth Social platform, the US president hailed the AfD’s “really big night” in Saxony-Anhalt. “They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly,” Trump wrote.Merz responded by cancelling a planned phone call with Trump on Wednesday. A spokesperson for the chancellor declined to explain but noted that Merz had always objected “in general terms” to “interfering in or commenting on the domestic political situation, particularly regarding elections”.Support for Merz, a conservative Christian Democrat, has plummeted in the 16 months since he took office at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, amid disappointment over slow progress oneconomic growthand the cost of living.He has adopted ahard line on border policyin a faltering effort to win back AfD supporters, and acknowledged Germany still had “problems in the area of migration”.“We still have many people in Germany who should not have permanent residency. This is consensus in the [ruling] coalition, that we need to deport more people,” he said on Wednesday.“But we make a careful distinction between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, and who are welcome here, and those who do not have permanent residency in Germany and who must leave our country. Unlike you [the AfD], we take great care to make this distinction.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe AfD won nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is seeking potential supporters among the other parties to elect him as state premier.Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more statesRead moreMerz, who has acknowledged his unpopularity played a role in the halving of support for his party in the state, tried to put a brave face on the rout. “Fifty-six percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt didn’t vote for you,” he told the AfD.He accused Siegmund, whose party is classed as rightwing extremist by domestic intelligence, of “electoral fraud” by already breaking a campaign promise not to seek to govern the state if he failed to win an absolute majority.“And you won’t manage that in Germany either [at the federal level],” Merz told the AfD co-leader Alice Weidel. “Nowhere in Germany will you get a majority. You are and remain a destructive force.”Merz also attacked the AfD for its opposition to military assistance for Ukraine, and accused it of making common cause with Russia, which Berlin has alleged is mounting a sabotage and disinformation campaign on its soil.He said that despite “clear evidence”a failed drone bomb attack at Leipzig airportlast month “had been planned in Russia for months and was specifically directed against Germany”, the AfD had remained silent on it.Earlier, Weidel had savoured her party’s resounding election victory from the podium, saying the CDU had been “pulverised” and calling it a referendum on Merz’s leadership.Attacking the government’s migration policy and blaming it for crime and other security problems, Weidel said: “Your time is up. The public want a change in policy, and they will get it,” reiterating her party’s aim to form a federal government in the foreseeable future.Polls show Merz’s fractious coalitionwould not have a majorityin a general election, though the next national vote is not due until 2029. The AfD is polling in first place at 28% to 29%, with the wind at its back before another two state polls this month,in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.Explore more on these topicsGermanyFriedrich MerzAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)EuropeThe far rightRaceDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Spiritual leaders stress diversity of views within Jewish community and warn against inaction on settler violence
Author: Aamna Mohdin
Headline: Spiritual leaders stress diversity of views within Jewish community and warn against inaction on settler violence
Content: Construction in the Jewish settlement of Alfei Menashe on the West BankPhotograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConstruction in the Jewish settlement of Alfei Menashe on the West BankPhotograph: Amir Levy/Getty ImagesForeign policySenior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlementsSpiritual leaders stress diversity of views within Jewish community and warn against inaction on settler violence‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctionsAamna MohdinCommunity affairs correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 13.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProminent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end.The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis,described UK sanctionsagainst illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”.The sanctions were also condemned by the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership council.Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at riskRead moreBut other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with somebacking Miliband’s sanctions, while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further.Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of MasortiJudaism, said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”.“What is taking place today in theWest Bankis a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said.Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake ofIsraeland Judaism. We cannot turn away.”While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.”Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”.‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctions on illegal settlementsRead moreShe said: “The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’.”Wright, who had recently visited the Palestinian village Umm al-Khair, which has faced relentless attacks by Israeli settlers, called on the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”.Jeremy Gordon, the rabbi of New London Synagogue, who came out in favour of Miliband’s sanctions, said: “It is wrong to argue for silence, inaction or ‘the use of carrots’ – appeasement – before the settler movement and those who support it. The playbook of these settlers is predicated on the notion that they will be appeased or ignored, and that well-meaning Jews the world over overlook their illegal and criminal actions.”Lev Taylor, rabbi of Kingston Liberal Synagogue in London, described the sanctions as a sign “the government is moving in the right direction”. He added: “Some of my Israeli members have been campaigning for sanctions exactly like this … The Judaism in which I believe repudiates this brutal occupation.”He pointed to the statements from the Israeli member of the Knesset Gilad Kariv, who said: “The blame for the European countries’ announcement of sanctions falls squarely on the shoulders of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich,[Israel] Katz, and [Gideon] Sa’ar.”There is some consternation within the Orthodox community at the suggestion British Jews are uniformly opposed to the sanctions.Miliband, the foreign secretary, announced the sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state.Jonathan Boyd, the executive director for Institute for Jewish Policy Research, explained there are no robust survey data on whether British Jews support sanctions on Israeli settlements specifically. “However, the available evidence shows that views on Israeli government policy and the conflict are quite diverse, varying by age, denomination and political outlook.“At the same time, they also show that most British Jews feel a strong emotional attachment to Israel and have become increasingly concerned about antisemitism in Britain since October 7.”Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leaders of Progressive Judaism, which represents about one-third of Jews affiliated to synagogues and estimates the same proportion of non-affiliated Jews share its values, described sanctions as a “clumsy tool” that could have unintended consequences. But they said that “measures directed at Israeli settlements are not the same as an attack on Jews. We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them.”View image in fullscreenRabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThey called on those against sanctions to offer more than statements condemning violence, adding: “Inaction is not neutral. It too is a political and moral choice.”Wittenberg, Baginsky and Levy all asserted their opposition to theBoycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, and welcomed Miliband’s stance against it.Tuesday’s sanctions announcement prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel.Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised.The UK foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”.Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance of this”.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyWest BankJudaismReligionIsraelPalestineEd MilibandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctions on illegal settlements  | Israel | The Guardian
description: Ed Miliband’s intervention was ‘inevitable’ after Israeli government and security failures, say former ministers and diplomats
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Ed Miliband’s intervention was ‘inevitable’ after Israeli government and security failures, say former ministers and diplomats
Content: Soldiers halt an Israeli peace activist trying to reach Palestinians facing a blockade in their dispute with settlers near Qusra in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSoldiers halt an Israeli peace activist trying to reach Palestinians facing a blockade in their dispute with settlers near Qusra in the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesIsrael‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctions on illegal settlementsEd Miliband’s intervention was ‘inevitable’ after Israeli government and security failures, say former ministers and diplomatsEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemWed 9 Sep 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProminent Israelis have welcomednew UK sanctionsas a necessary response to settlement expansion and spiralling violence in the occupied West Bank.The intervention was described – by the president of theIsraelAcademy of Sciences and Humanities, a former prime minister, an ex-head of the army and former ministers and diplomats – as an “inevitable consequence” of Israeli government and security failures.“Sanctions [are being imposed] against Jewish terrorists, and not against the legitimacy of the state of Israel,” they wrote in a joint statement. “There is no basis to the [Israeli] government’s response that the decision to impose sanctions against Jewish terrorists is an expression of antisemitism.”Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, had indicated Britain was planning new sanctions but the strength of his language and the scale of the controls he announced on Tuesday were a surprise.It was the most significant attempt in many years, from a close Israeli ally, to leverage economic power to force change in the occupiedWest Bank.“Israel’s government has caused a rupture in the longest-standing diplomatic convention of all: using obfuscation and plenty of ‘very concerned’ statements instead of actually doing anything,” Esther Solomon wrote in the Haaretz newspaper.The impact was multiplied when France and Canada announced plans for trade bans on settlement goods and 10 other European countries backed similar measures. Nor did any senior figure in the Trump administration, which was briefed in advance on the UK plans, criticise the measures.View image in fullscreenThe Jewish settlement of Karnei Shomron, north-east of Tel Aviv. A poll suggests almost three-quarters of Jewish Israelis want to annex the occupied West Bank.Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty Images“Jerusalem had prepared for rain, but what arrived yesterday was a full-blown storm,” Itamar Eichner wrote in Yedioth Ahronoth. “Yesterday Israel was caught off guard, to the point that senior Israeli officials used the term ‘an intelligence-diplomatic failure’.”Nearly three-quarters of Jewish Israelis favour partial or total annexation of the occupied West Bank, apollfor the Jewish People Policy Institute found. All leading candidates in the upcoming election reject a Palestinian state.However, there is increasingly vocal opposition to settler violence and expansion from some members of the country’s security, political and cultural elites.
