They threatened legal action against their government this summer over its support for Jewish terrorism and an “ideology of ethnic cleansing” in the occupied West Bank.Prof David Harel, British-born president of the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities, is among those who signed a statement backing the UK measures.He said the sanctions offered urgently needed support for Israelis like him, who are trying to stop attacks on Palestinians and end the occupation.“I personally would fight until my last breath against antisemitism and against anti-Israelism. For that reason, I’m against general wall-to-wall boycott, divest, sanction-style sanctions on the state of Israel,” the leading scientist told the Guardian.“But what is justified, and I do support, is being anti things that Israel is doing, and these days in particular what it is doing in the West Bank.”He said that Israelis calling for a delay until after the elections were ignoring both the escalating violence that Palestinians faced every day and the risks the occupation posed to Israel’s future.“Getting out of there [occupied Palestine], or, at least for the present, stopping these things from happening and starting to really talk about a two-state solution is not only good for the Palestinians. It’s not that we’re doing these poor people a favour. We’re doing a favour to ourselves, no less, maybe even more.”The joint statement backing the UK sanctions was also signed by former prime minister Ehud Olmert, former commander of the Israeli military Dan Halutz, former ministers Yuli Tamir and Roni Bar-On and former ambassador to Germany Yoram Ben Zeev.“This decision is precisely what the state of Israel should have received in order to remove the disgrace of Jewish terrorism from the face of the country,” they wrote.Map showing countries with sanctions on Israeli settlementsNadav Tamir, a former diplomat, also described the measures as good for Israel.“Any move to prevent annexation and ethnic cleansing of the Palestinians in the West Bank [and Gaza] is serving the long-term interests of the Zionist vision of Israel as the democratic homeland of the Jewish people,” he said. “It will help us to be more secure and moral.”The value of goods exported from occupied territories to Britain last year was only $45m (£33m) out of total $4.4bn trade in goods and services, according to Roey Fisher, head of Israel’s Foreign Trade Administration.However, plans to place sanctions on any company that finances or facilitates settlement expansion could force Israel’s main banks and insurance companies to choose between their business interests in the UK and those in occupied Palestine.Miliband has not provided details of the new measures but the move has the potential to slow or stop construction.Avraham Burg, a former speaker of the Knesset, thanked Miliband for setting a global example. “Like many Israelis and Palestinians I am grateful for the courageous moral leadership of Miliband. It’s a good beginning. Do not stop,” he said.But Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, attacked Miliband for “blatant interference” in his country’s domestic affairs before a late October election. Opposition politicians suggested instead that Benjamin Netanyahu might weaponise the UK sanctions to bolster his campaign to remain prime minister.View image in fullscreenGideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister (left), strikes a deal with his Slovenian counterpart, Tone Kajzer, in Ljubljana on Wednesday. He said the UK sanctions were ‘blatant interference’ in Israeli affairs.Photograph: Darko Bandić/APDahlia Scheindlin, one of Israel’s leading political analysts, said the UK move was very unlikely to affect the October election, because Israeli voters were more focused on domestic issues.“Since 7 October [2023], Israel has become much more inward-looking and provincial, and generally the attitude to the rest of the world is just that ‘they all hate us’,” Scheindlin said.“If you are a Netanyahu supporter you might take this as evidence that they are against us because of antisemitism, and if you are in the opposition camp you might take this as further evidence that the world is turning against us because of Netanyahu’s policies. But it’s hard to see how these policies change the breakdown of the electoral map.”Miliband made his speech on a day when political parties finalised their candidate lists and Haaretz had a bombshell story aboutsecurity warnings delivered to Netanyahu– and apparently ignored – before the 7 October attacks.Fourteen Israeli human rights organisations welcomed the sanctions. “This is an important and necessary first step to meet states’ legal obligation,” said the statement from groups including B’Tselem, Physicians for Human Rights Israel and Breaking the Silence.“We urge the international community to take further concrete measures to ensure that its relations with Israel no longer enable Israel’s settlement enterprise, forced displacement and ethnic cleansing in the occupied West Bank, or its broader assault on Palestinian human rights across all territories under its control.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineWest BankMiddle East and north AfricaEd MilibandForeign policyIsrael-Gaza warnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says Miliband | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: UK foreign secretary says international community including US shares ‘frustration’ at Israel’s failure to constrain illegal settlers
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: UK foreign secretary says international community including US shares ‘frustration’ at Israel’s failure to constrain illegal settlers
Content: A man watches Israeli bulldozers demolish a Palestinian home in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. Miliband says intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA man watches Israeli bulldozers demolish a Palestinian home in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. Miliband says intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and the West Bank.Photograph: Hazem Bader/AFP via Getty ImagesForeign policyIsrael sanctions will not hurt intelligence sharing between spy agencies, says MilibandUK foreign secretary says international community including US shares ‘frustration’ at Israel’s failure to constrain illegal settlersPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorWed 9 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBritish intelligence has been given assurances by its Israeli counterpart that information sharing with the UK will continue as before,Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has said.The disclosure counters predictions that hisdecision to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlementswould lead to a collapse in cooperation between the agencies.The exchanges of information are seen as mutually beneficial and it is understood that Israeli intelligence was never willing to become mired in any political dispute between the two governments.Miliband insists the intelligence sharing from the UK has not aided the Israeli occupation or its actions in Gaza and theWest Bank.Miliband also expressed confidence that the US shared some of his exasperation with Israel’s reluctance to constrain the settlers in the West Bank, or to engage fully with the 20-point plan for Gaza set out by Donald Trump’s Board of Peace.As yet there has been no explicit criticism of the UK’s actions by the White House.Trump avoided taking a hard stance when pressed about the coalition of countries, including the UK, France, and Canada, that have imposed new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.“I’ll be speaking to Israel, I’ll be speaking to them, and I’ll find out what’s their thinking,” he said on Wednesday.Trump, now locked in fighting midterm elections, appears reluctant to leap to the aid of Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, who persuaded him to go to war against Iran. That decision has pushed oil prices beyond $100 a barrel, helping to swell a threatened “blue wave” that could leave the Democrats in charge of both the House and the Senate.There is also cross-party concern in the US at theviolent tactics adopted by some Israeli settlers.Ed Miliband gives statement on UK plans to sanction Israel – watch liveMiliband said on Sky News on Wednesday: “We obviously talked to the Americans in advance of our announcement. I think the whole international community, let me say this, has been quite frustrated, to put it mildly, with some of the actions of the Israeli government.“I think there is real concern about what is happening … underlying so much of the conflicts in the Middle East is this failure to really grasp the situation between Israel andPalestine.“It’s in our interest to act not just because it’s standing up for our values, but because it’s in our interests to have this two-state solution as a rock of stability in the Middle East.”The US decision not to oppose the UK over its sanctions and ban on trade with the Israeli settlements follows conversations between Trump and the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, on Monday, as well as previous diplomatic exchanges at lower levels.Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, was careful not to endorse the UK sanctions, but affirmed he shared the objective of securing greater stability.Miliband can also claim credit for persuadingCanada and France to join the trade ban, the surprise element in the package announced on Tuesday.The agreement came together late in the process. Eight other European countries have announced their intention to introduce such measures or to support the measures within the EU, a statement of solidarity that represents probably less of a shift than headlines might suggest.Some of the signatory countries had already taken steps independent of the EU, or had long been advocating for measures such as suspension of the Israel-EU trade agreement.MapFor France, the decision to join the British initiative was formalised relatively late during Emmanuel Macron’s trip to London, when he met Burnham on 3 September and celebrated the display of the Bayeux tapestry at the British Museum.France acted after a Franco-Swedish proposal made to the EU27 in April appeared to be making little progress.The French plan aimed to establish an embargo or tariff on products from the occupied territories, but resistance from a constellation of countries including Germany, Italy and Bulgaria blocked progress. The commission also appeared to raise objections.Paris last year had led the push to recognise the state of Palestine as critical to the two-state solution, but much of the French diplomatic energy had subsequently drifted. The UK, along with Jordan, will hold a meeting concerning improving humanitarian supplies into Gaza at the UN general assembly later this month.In advance of Miliband’s statement, Trump had been hinting that he might support the Argentinian claim to sovereignty over the Falklands, a proposal mooted by Netanyahu’s son.But in a little-noticed move likely to please Washington, Miliband this week supplemented the action against Israel by announcing fresh nuclear-related sanctions against Iran, including targeting Iranian ships involved in “malign behaviour”.The UK also said it was backing a motion to be put to the UN stating Iran was in breach of its obligations on nuclear proliferation.The new sanctions are extended to cover energy, software, metals, gold and related activities such as shipping, insurance and banking. Most Iranian aircraft will be prohibited from landing in the UK.In response to the UK ban on goods, not due to come into force for at least six months, Israel has said it will:close the British consulate in in occupied East Jerusalem; remove British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel; terminate the UK’s role in training Palestinian Authority forces in the West Bank; and deny 12 mainly leftwing MPs entry to Israel.Explore more on these topicsForeign policyEd MilibandIsraelWest BankMI5MI6UK security and counter-terrorismnewsShareReuse this content

title: John Malkovich cancels Israel trip over fabricated solidarity quote | Movies | The Guardian
description: The Wild Horse Nine actor had been due to appear on stage in The Music Critic in Tel Aviv – but pulled out over PR firm’s ‘unacceptable and untenable’ attribution of statement
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: The Wild Horse Nine actor had been due to appear on stage in The Music Critic in Tel Aviv – but pulled out over PR firm’s ‘unacceptable and untenable’ attribution of statement
Content: John Malkovich on the red carpet of the Venice film festival for the film Wild Horse Nine.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APView image in fullscreenJohn Malkovich on the red carpet of the Venice film festival for the film Wild Horse Nine.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/APMoviesJohn Malkovich cancels Israel trip over fabricated solidarity quoteThe Wild Horse Nine actor had been due to appear on stage in The Music Critic in Tel Aviv – but pulled out over PR firm’s ‘unacceptable and untenable’ attribution of statementCatherine ShoardWed 9 Sep 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Malkovich has cancelled a planned trip to Israel next year to appear on stage after a PR firm hired by the show attributed quotes to the actor that the company had written.Malkovich, who is a leading Oscar contender for his role inMartin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, was due to appear in The Music Critic, a theatrical-musical satire composed by the Jewish violinist Aleksey Igudesman, in Tel Aviv’s Charles Bronfman Auditorium on 13 April.A press release circulated on 5 September quoted Malkovich as saying he was “thrilled to return to Israel” and looked “forward to meeting the warm Israeli audience once again, to whom I feel a strong closeness and solidarity”.The actor, 72, was alerted to the quotes after reading them in the Hollywood Reporter, who picked them up from the Jerusalem Post. In a statement to the Hollywood Reporter on 8 September, Malkovich said that a “PR company hired by the Israeli promoter drafted a quote for the article that was attributed to me, though I never made the statements that were quoted, nor was I consulted before they were printed.”He added: “I did not utter these phrases, and they most certainly are not approved by me, nor do they reflect my feelings. The fact that they were printed as direct quotes from me is unacceptable and untenable. For this reason, I have decided I cannot participate in the Tel Aviv performance.”The PR firm admitted the error, releasing a statement apologising for “incorrectly” attributing the quotes to Malkovich. “Mr Malkovich did not make, provide, authorise or approve this statement, nor was it approved by his representatives,” said the firm. “We sincerely apologise to Mr Malkovich and his representatives for the incorrect attribution and regret that this occurred.”In his lengthy statement to the Hollywood Reporter, Malkovich went on to distance himself from any implied endorsement of any country’s political actions.“Throughout my long career, I’ve been lucky to perform across a quite wide swath of the world – in countries with governments whose values or culture I do not share and in front of audiences of many differing faiths and ideologies,” he wrote. “Travelling to places whose view of the world may not align with mine has given me a chance to observe and to listen and learn and to share my idea of what makes good storytelling and what makes beautiful music and how they can complement each other and illuminate the human condition.“My appearance in any country, even my own, does not constitute approval of said country’s policies, nor actions, nor its elected or unelected leaders. My appearances would also not condone nor mean that I am in supposed ‘solidarity’ with any particular political cause, nor with the killing of innocents, nor with any acts of terrorism, nor any other kind of barbarity.”Malkovich last visited Israel in 2013 when he appeared on stage in The Infernal Comedy: Confessions of a Serial Killer; five years previously he was guest of honour at the Jerusalem film festival.Wild Horse Nine review – Malkovich and Rockwell head to Easter Island for McDonagh’s acid bromanceRead moreIn 2011, he told an interviewer he was not a “political person”, lacked “an ideology”, and hadn’t voted since 1972. In 2002, speaking at the Cambridge Union, Malkovich said the two people he’d most like to kill were journalist Robert Fisk and politician George Galloway.The actor did not elaborate on his comments, but some speculated they concerned the then-MP’s call the previous month for people in Scotland to boycott goods from Israel.The actor’s statement to the Hollywood Reporter closed with a caution, saying: “I look forward to continuing to exercise my artistic freedom, come what may. However, only playwrights, novelists and screenwriters can put words in my mouth, and even then, only in the service of storytelling, and no one else should think they can do that without my consent and without the resultant consequences.”In Wild Horse Nine, Malkovich plays a terminally ill CIA agent who travels to Easter Island with colleague Sam Rockwell in the mid 1970s. The film, which premiered at Venice earlier this month, is widely expected to land the actor his third Academy Award nomination.Explore more on these topicsFilmJohn MalkovichIsraelMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham sees sanctions against Israeli settlements as an electoral asset | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: While a survey found Labour, Lib Dem and Green voters to be the strongest backers of such a ban on trade, even Tory and Reform voters were in favour overall
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: While a survey found Labour, Lib Dem and Green voters to be the strongest backers of such a ban on trade, even Tory and Reform voters were in favour overall
Content: Andy Burnham told the Commons that ‘Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice’.Photograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham told the Commons that ‘Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice’.Photograph: House of Commons/AFP/Getty ImagesAndy BurnhamAnalysisBurnham sees sanctions against Israeli settlements as an electoral assetKiran StaceyPolicy editorWhile a survey found Labour, Lib Dem and Green voters to be the strongest backers of such a ban on trade, even Tory and Reform voters were in favour overallUK politics live – latest updatesWed 9 Sep 2026 10.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareThere was a time when placing Israel under strict trade sanctions would have been a politically risky thing for a British prime minister to do.Andy Burnham, however, considers it an electoral asset.As Kemi Badenoch attacked him over defence spending at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham deliberately turned the topic to the trade ban on illegal settlements which he had announced on Tuesday.With the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, sitting to his left, the prime minister said: “In this difficult and dangerous world Britain has to stand for something, Britain has to show leadership, Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice.“Where people are being bullied out of their homes and intimidated, we will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them. That, Mr Speaker, is leadership on the world stage: Britain being true to what it’s always been about.“That is what the British people expect of us and that is what this government will do.”Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at riskRead moreUnder the new sanctionsannounced on Tuesday, goods produced in illegal settlements in occupied Palestine will be banned from being imported into the UK and those who help build or finance settlements will face sanctions.The measures drew a sharp response from the Israeli government, which announced the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.Domestically, the opposition has been led by Badenoch, who has long been a staunch ally of Israel.Ina piece in the Jewish Chronicle, the Conservative leader warned that the prime minister risked “fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home”.“For allLabourclaim to have rooted out antisemitism internally, the degree of anti-Israel hatred means that Labour’s approach to many of these issues is Corbyn in all but name,” she added.Others in her party, however, have struck a less aggressive tone.On Tuesday, the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said: “None of us here rejects the government’s stated aim that we must do everything we can to end the circle of violence and support theAbraham accordsand the two-state solution.“What we reject is performative politics, acting alone, that leaves our envoys irrelevant and our voice weaker.”Some senior Conservatives even backed the government.Edward Leigh, who as father of the house has held his seat longer than any other MP, told the Commons on Tuesday: “I am proud to say that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today, because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and for justice for all people in this world.”I believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive | Andy BurnhamRead moreThe government has reason to believe it is on strong electoral ground with this decision.11:05Why is Trump silent on UK sanctions against Israeli West Bank settlements? - The LatestApoll by YouGovearlier in the summer found 50% of British voters supported a ban on trade with West Bank settlements, while only 16% were opposed.While Labour, Liberal Democrat and Green voters were the strongest backers of such a move, even Conservative and Reform voters were in favour overall.Labour officials hope the announcement may help them make up ground with progressive and Muslim voters who have moved away from the party since the 2024 election.Many say they remain angry about aninterview given by Keir Starmersoon after the Gaza war began in which the then prime minister said he thought Israel had the right to withhold water and electricity from Palestinians.The disillusionment among Muslim voters was particularly important in theGreen party’s victory in Gorton and Denton.Meanwhile Labour lost a large part of its broader progressive base during the local elections, in which the Greens took a number of councils and mayoralties in central London.Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales,tweeted on Tuesday: “Ed Miliband’s statement on Israel is only a first step. We need to go further: a full ban on goods, services & investment.”Labour and the Greens are now again locked in battle, over the Holborn and St Pancras seat,which Starmer has vacated.Though the policy was in train long before that byelection was called, it could prove an important campaign tool for Labour canvassers looking to reassure their core voters.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamIsraelPalestineLabourMiddle East and north AfricaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: UK chancellor urged to remove £100k childcare ‘cliff edge’ prompting parents to cut work hours | Children | The Guardian
description: Critics say threshold pushes higher-paid staff to cut back on work and often mothers to stop working to avoid losing entitlement
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Critics say threshold pushes higher-paid staff to cut back on work and often mothers to stop working to avoid losing entitlement
Content: Families in which both parents earn less than £100,000 a year can be entitled to 30 hours a week of care, but none at all if one of them cross that threshold.Photograph: Guido Mieth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFamilies in which both parents earn less than £100,000 a year can be entitled to 30 hours a week of care, but none at all if one of them cross that threshold.Photograph: Guido Mieth/Getty ImagesChildrenUK chancellor urged to remove £100k childcare ‘cliff edge’ prompting parents to cut work hoursCritics say threshold pushes higher-paid staff to cut back on work and often mothers to stop working to avoid losing entitlementHeather StewartEconomics editorWed 9 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has been urged to fix the £100,000 childcare “cliff edge”, that means some higher-paid employees cut back on work to avoid losing their entitlement.Since the latest expansion of taxpayer-funded childcare in 2024, families with young children in which both parents earn less than £100,000 a year can be entitled to 30 hours a week of care - or none at all, if one of them cross that threshold.In a report, researchers from the Centre for Tax Reform (CenTax) said that, by the end of this parliament in 2030, the average parent crossing this “cliff edge”, will have to earn £124,000, to be no worse off after losing their free childcare.Arun Advani, director of CenTax, said: “Our analysis shows the childcare cliff edge stands to grow dramatically by the end of this parliament, but there are solutions available to the government.”The researchers find that “bunching” of incomes just below the threshold suggests that even in 2022 – the latest year for which data is available – about 1,000 families were artificially suppressing their earnings to avoid falling foul of the threshold. That could rise to almost 12,000 by the end of this parliament.The thinktank, based at Warwick University, also suggested the policy may be incentivising some mothers to drop out of work. Below the £100,000 threshold, 6% of lower-paid partners – usually the mother – are out of work; but above the threshold that rises to 9%.“The jump in non-working mothers at the point where their partner exceeds £100,000 income suggests the loss of childcare entitlement as a cause, with possible long-term consequences for those mothers’ earnings,” the report said.CenTax also criticised the fact that the threshold is based on how much parents expect to earn in the year ahead – pointing out that some families appear to be claiming it, despite eventually earning more than £100,000.It proposes several potential solutions. Restricting free childcare to 15 hours to families above the £100,000 threshold, instead of withdrawing it altogether, would cost £210m by 2030, it said.Gradually tapering away the entitlement at 28p for each £1 earned above the threshold would be revenue neutral, but less problematic for parents, it adds.Healey is set to deliver his first budget on 28 October, against a backdrop of renewed fears about higher inflation andfebrile global bond markets.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnalysts believe higher than expected interest rates on the Treasury’s debt are likely to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn headroom that Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves built up against the government’s fiscal rules.In hisfirst major speechin Coventry on Monday, Healey promised to put growth at the heart of his approach; but also warned that Labour must “be honest” about the constraints on public spending in the years ahead.Since taking over as Labour leader in July, Andy Burnham has announced a VAT cut on electricity bills and capped bus fares; but Healey has also suggested the government is keen to do more to give hard-pressed consumers a “breathing space”.Explore more on these topicsChildrenChildcareJohn HealeyBudgetBudget 2026Tax and spendingBenefitsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Teachers say holidays in term can be worth more than time in school | School attendance and absence | The Guardian
description: School staff tell focus groups they believe school system in England and Wales cannot deal with attendance crisis
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: School staff tell focus groups they believe school system in England and Wales cannot deal with attendance crisis
Content: One teacher said: ‘If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school.’Photograph: redsnapper/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne teacher said: ‘If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school.’Photograph: redsnapper/AlamySchool attendance and absenceTeachers say holidays in term can be worth more than time in schoolSchool staff tell focus groups they believe school system in England and Wales cannot deal with attendance crisisAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTeachers have so little belief in the importance of pupils’ full school attendance that they would take their own children on term time holidays if they could, staff have told a three-year research programme.Frontline staff do not believe the school system is set up to deal with an ongoing attendance crisis in England and Wales, where nearly one in five children are now missing at least 10% of school, according to a report based on in-depth conversations with teachers.Despite a hardline approach from schools to tackle the crisis, evidence from focus groups containing teachers from schools in low-income areas suggests many share the same scepticism as parents and pupils about theefficiency of holiday fines, according to the report by youth charityImpetusand policy and polling research firmPublic First.“If I wasn’t a teacher, I would take my daughter out of school and take her on holiday because it would be cheaper,” said one teacher.Another noted: “If it’s the only holiday you get to experience in a five-year period, I think that’s probably worth more than a week in school in January.”The report comes as the children’s commissioner warned of tens of thousands of hidden Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), with analysis suggesting that an estimated 42,000 16- and 17-year-olds enrolled in colleges in England are attending less than half the time.Rachel de Souza warned that the number of Neets is almost twice as large as official figures indicate, according to a new analysis of 262 of England’s 290 college groups, which are not included in Department for Education attendance figures.‘Cheap travel is not a defence’: the parents facing court for school absences in EnglandRead more“We have a blind spot: hidden Neets slipping through the cracks,” she said. “Young people with all the negative impacts of not being in employment, education or training, but with none of the targeted interventions.”Researchers compiling the report, A Crisis of Disengagement, spoke to 62 secondary school staff from schools where more than 25% of pupils were eligible for free school meals.They spoke of the work of chasing pupils’ attendance as “relentless” and expressed the view that an occasional holiday or minor absence was less worrying than sustained disengagement.While some staff saw fines as a necessary tool, many believed they damage trust and undermine the relational work needed to support pupils and families to re-engage with school.“We’ll send a penalty notice out and then we’ve really annoyed that parent,” said one senior leader. “We’ve just broken a relationship between a family that we want to get into school.”A record 492,825 penalty notices for unauthorised absences were issued to parents in England in 2024-25, a sharp rise from pre-Covid levels. Researchers have previouslywarned of a “seismic shift” in attitudesto attendance since the pandemic, with concern that some parents no longer believe children needed to be in school full-time. The absence rate for pupils in England in 2025-26 was 6.93%, significantly above the 2018-19 pre-Covid level of 4.7%Teachers and senior leaders in schools also argued that gaps in mental health support for struggling students, unmet special educational needs and a paucity of social workers was making their jobs more difficult with schools seen as “the one-stop shop for everything”.“We’ve got children who should have specialist provision, and they’re in our building every day,” said one senior leader. “We also need external agencies such as CAMHS [Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services] and social workers to have the right capacity and not turn us down.”Staff also told researchers the most effective interventions were also the hardest – including building relationships, mentoring and home visits.“I think it takes up a lot of adult hours,” she said. “If you looked proportionally at how time was broken down, attendance is very, very time consuming.”Susannah Hardyman, CEO of Impetus, said teachers could not solve the attendance crisis alone.“We now know that not only are pupils, families and teachers unconvinced that every day in school matters, but what we are facing is a wider crisis of disengagement driven by pressures often outside the control of school staff,” she said.Explore more on these topicsSchool attendance and absenceTeachingSchoolsPrimary schoolsSecondary schoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labour picks former child refugee to stand in byelection for Starmer’s seat | Byelections | The Guardian
description: Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came from Somalia in the 1990s, likely to face Zack Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras contest
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came from Somalia in the 1990s, likely to face Zack Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras contest
Content: Councillor Sagal Abdi-Wali is currently the leader of Camden council.Photograph: Justin Thomas/Camden councilView image in fullscreenCouncillor Sagal Abdi-Wali is currently the leader of Camden council.Photograph: Justin Thomas/Camden councilByelectionsLabour picks former child refugee to stand in byelection for Starmer’s seatSagal Abdi-Wali, who came from Somalia in the 1990s, likely to face Zack Polanski in Holborn and St Pancras contestAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 17.56 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 16.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA former child refugee who became the leader of Camden council has been selected to be theLabourcandidate for the byelection in Holborn and St Pancras.Sagal Abdi-Wali, who came to the UK from Somalia as a child in the 1990s and was elected leader of Camden council in May, was chosen by Labour members to contest the northLondonseat vacated by Keir Starmer.She was previously the chair of the local constituency Labour party, after first being elected as a Labour councillor in 2022.Abdi-Wali, 42, said she was “delighted” and promised to put the community at the heart of her campaign. “This place welcomed my family as refugees and gave us hope when we needed it most,” she said.“I am so grateful to have had the opportunity to build a life here, serving our community as a councillor, school governor and community activist. Now I am standing to say thank you and to give back the hope you gave me.“Throughout this campaign, I promise to put our communities at the heart of everything I do, now and for the future. Together, we can make hope win.”Abdi-Wali has worked for more than a decade as a volunteer and trustee for local charities and is a governor of two schools in the borough, according to Labour. The party’s members queued outside St Pancras church in Euston for the selection meeting on Wednesday night, with voters including MP Georgia Gould and her mother, Lady Gail Rebuck.‘I am seen as a Marmite figure’: Margaret Hodge on political battles, victories, errors – and regretsRead moreThe local figure will probably go head to head with Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, who announced his intention to fight for the Commons seat.Local Greens in Holborn and St Pancras still have to formally select their candidate under a process that will not be completed until next Friday. But itseems likelythey will endorse Polanski, under whose leadership the party has soared in the polls, with membership more than tripling.The high-stakes byelection on 8 October will pit the star power of Polanski against a resurgent Labour under Andy Burnham. Starmer announced he was stepping down from the seat he has represented since 2015 last week, in after his departure as prime minister.Starmer saw his majority more than halve at the last election from nearly 28,000 to 11,500 amid a challenge from the left. The Greens came third, with Starmer’s main competitor being Andrew Feinstein, a leftwing independent.In a boost to Polanski, Feinstein has sinceconfirmedhe would not stand, indicating that the Camden People’s Alliance, the group which emerged from his campaign, would most likely back the Greens.Labour have further lost support to the Greens in the area since the general election. The Greens made gains on Camden council in the local elections in May, although they failed to take control of it.But recent missteps by Polanski have dented his popularity, while Burnham’s arrival in Downing Street has boosted Labour’s standing in the polls.Abdi-Wali became the focus of unwanted attention last week when Reform’s Zia Yusuf suggested she was not British in a social media post that was described as “straightforward racism” by Labour.Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson, posted on X: “The frontrunner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former prime minister Keir Starmer in our parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?”The Greens are planning to flood the constituency with volunteers, while Labour said all members of the cabinet were likely to campaign in the seat, with campaigners calling the first official weekend of the campaign the “Make Hope Win Weekend”.Labour’s byelection campaign lead, Liam Conlon MP, said Abdi-Wali was a “fantastic local champion” with a strong delivery record on “revamping council homes, reducing homelessness, and tackling nuisance antisocial behaviour”.He added: “She will be a powerful progressive voice for Holborn and St Pancras to work alongside our Labour government to improve the lives for local people.“Labour will run a positive campaign that brings people together and restores hope. I look forward to joining hundreds of members to campaign with Sagal over the coming weeks.”Explore more on these topicsByelectionsLabourLocal politicsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealed  | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures
Author: Sandra Laville
Headline: OS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperatures
Content: The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenThe City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAExtreme heatCities in Great Britain most vulnerable to extreme heat revealedOS index examines which ‘urban heat islands’ suffer the most – and which cope the best with rising temperaturesSandra LavilleEnvironment correspondentWed 9 Sep 2026 15.16 EDTFirst published on Mon 7 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePortsmouth, Leicester, Exeter, Bristol andNottinghamwill be among the cities that warm the most by the end of this century as global heating turns British cities into urban heat islands, according to research.Analysis from Ordnance Survey (OS) has created a heat vulnerability index for all cities in Great Britain.Portsmouth, which sits on the south coast of England and is home to 208,000 people, is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research from the OS, the Met Office and the data analysis company 4 Earth Intelligence.Concrete, asphalt, buildings and hard surfaces in cities absorb solar radiation during the day and act like giant radiators, holding on to the heat rather than cooling down at night as in more rural areas. Cities can be up to 10C hotter than surrounding areas.Areas most at risk of extreme warming are those with the leasttree cover,green spaceand waterways.View image in fullscreenPortsmouth is the most vulnerable to extreme heat today and into the future, according to the research.Photograph: Peter Titmuss/AlamyThis summer was provisionallythe UK’s hottest on record, and the research reveals which cities are suffering now from intense urban heat and which will be among the warmest in future.The research analyses 71 cities granted by royal charter across England, Scotland and Wales but excluding Northern Ireland. The OS heat vulnerability index suggests that by 2040 all 71 cities will reach high heat vulnerability. By the turn of the century, almost two-thirds could reach the most severe level. Those facing the most severe impact by the end of the century are predicted to be Portsmouth, the City of Westminster, Plymouth,Leicesterand Exeter, according to the analysis.Nick Bolton, the chief executive of Ordnance Survey, said: “Cities are where millions of people live, work and spend their everyday lives.“Extreme and sustained heat can affect people’s health and wellbeing, how comfortable our homes and workplaces are, and put additional pressure on transport, energy and emergency services. Understanding how and where this vulnerability is changing depends on an accurate view of how the country is built, based on trusted authoritative data, which is critical for planners, developers and local authorities preparing for a warmer future.”UK ‘built for climate that no longer exists’ and needs urgent changes to survive global heating, report warnsRead morePortsmouth is today the most heat-vulnerable city and will remain at the highest level for warming until the end of the century, according to the research. The city of Leicester is projected to show the biggest rise in Britain’s heat vulnerability rankings, climbing from 10th now to fourth by the end of the century, while Exeter and Nottingham also rise into the 10 most vulnerable cities, alongside Bristol andBrightonand Hove by the end of this century.Leaders in Portsmouth have identified areas including Somerstown, Portsea, Southsea and Fratton as those particularly exposed to urban heat because of their limited green areas and hard surfaces, and noted that areas with less green space overlap with those of deprivation.Chart showing that August was the world's warmest month on recordThe City ofLondonand the City of Westminster areas rank among the most heat-retentive urban environments in the UK.The City of London records the highest built-environment score and the least effective natural cooling of any city, given the concentration of buildings, roads and hard surfaces as well as limited green space, trees and water. Westminster ranks third for overall heat vulnerability today and second in both future periods behind Portsmouth.Astudycommissioned by the mayor of London has put the total economic cost of the 2022 London heatwaves at £1.5bn, including productivity losses, health impacts, education disruption, energy demand, transport and emergency services.The OS heat vulnerability index combined current observed temperatures with the structural characteristics of Britain’s built environment and climate projections into the future to produce a score for every city on a scale of 1 to 5, where 3 to 4 is high and 4 to 5 is severe.View image in fullscreenTree cover, green space and waterways can help mitigate the effects of global heating.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAmong cities coping the best with the changing climate is Milton Keynes, which ranks 69th out of 71 cities for heat vulnerability today. Milton Keynes has the lowest built-environment vulnerability in England and the most effective natural cooling of any city in the analysis, with 46 sq km of natural surfaces, against almost 40 sq km of hard made surfaces.Jonathan Hendry, the chief executive of 4 Earth Intelligence, said exposure varied street by street within a single city. “The areas consistently subjected to higher temperatures than their surroundings are the ones that overheat first during a heatwave,” he said.“We’re mapping how to turn thermal threats into actionable blueprints for urban resilience, supporting decisions on where heat refuges are sited and how emergency responses are planned in advance rather than in the middle of climate events.”Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatClimate crisisPortsmouthConstruction industryThe sunLondonPlymouthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man in Swindon charged with assisting Russian intelligence agency | Swindon | The Guardian
description: Joshua Cammidge, 31, arrested after investigation led by counter-terrorism policing London
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Joshua Cammidge, 31, arrested after investigation led by counter-terrorism policing London
Content: Counter-terrorism policing London were supported by officers from Wiltshire police when making an arrest in Swindon on Friday 4 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenCounter-terrorism policing London were supported by officers from Wiltshire police when making an arrest in Swindon on Friday 4 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianSwindonMan in Swindon charged with assisting Russian intelligence agencyJoshua Cammidge, 31, arrested after investigation led by counter-terrorism policing LondonRaphael BoydWed 9 Sep 2026 15.10 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been charged with offences related to national security as part of an ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing (CTP) London, according to the Metropolitan police.Joshua Cammidge, 31, was arrested at an address in Swindon on Friday 4 September by CTP London officers, supported by officers from Wiltshire police. Searches were also carried out at a different address in Swindon. He was further arrested and detained the following day, being charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and intending to commit or engage in conduct to prepare an act of sabotage.The Met have claimed that Cammidge’s arrests relate to alleged contact with a representative of the GRU Volunteer Corps, a group controlled by Russia’s military intelligence agency that have been accused of previously engaging in acts of sabotage against Britain and its allies.The National Security Act, which Cammidge was arrested and charged under, was introduced in 2023 to help increase the measures that law enforcement can take in order to protect the UK from security threats such as espionage, foreign interference or influence, and sabotage.Frank Ferguson, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS special crime and counter-terrorism division, said: “The Crown Prosecution Service has decided to prosecute Joshua Cammidge with National Security Act offences following a counter-terrorism policing investigation.“Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring the case to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue criminal proceedings.“We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial.“It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information online which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.”Cammidge will appear at Westminster magistrates court on Thursday 10 September.Explore more on these topicsSwindonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bond market rebuffs US treasury’s plan to buy back $6bn in government debt | US economy | The Guardian
description: Scott Bessent made announcement on Wednesday as bond yields rose to highest point since 2008 financial crisis
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: Scott Bessent made announcement on Wednesday as bond yields rose to highest point since 2008 financial crisis
Content: Even after Scott Bessent announced the operation would target $6bn worth of government bonds, yields on Wednesday continued to rise.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEven after Scott Bessent announced the operation would target $6bn worth of government bonds, yields on Wednesday continued to rise.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesUS economyBond market rebuffs US treasury’s plan to buy back $6bn in government debtScott Bessent made announcement on Wednesday as bond yields rose to highest point since 2008 financial crisisUS politics live – latest updatesLauren ArataniWed 9 Sep 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 12.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US treasury moved to cut the cost of borrowing on Wednesday only to be swiftly rebuffed by the bond market.Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, announced the US would buy back $6bn worth of government debt – treasuries – in an effort to alleviate a selloff in the USbond marketthat has put pressure on interest rates.But the size of the deal failed to appease bond buyers and the yield on 10-year treasuries rose to a three-year high.Rising inflation and uncertainty from thewar in Iranhave spooked investors from US bonds, what has historically been known to be one of the safest investment vehicles. Treasury yields have been rising, with the yield for the 30-year treasury bond hitting about 5.2% – the highest yield since the 2008 financial crisis.In an attempt to alleviate the bond market, Bessent on 19 Augustannouncedthe treasury would at least double its typical buyback operation. The move is meant to stabilize the market: fewer bonds on the market should mean that yields go down.But in the weeks since the announcement, treasury yields have continued to rise. Even after Bessent announced the operation would target $6bn worth of government bonds, yields on Wednesday continued to rise.Electronic shelf labels likely to cost jobs and drive up grocery prices, US report warnsRead moreIn August, US government debt for the first time in the country’s historyreached $40tn– double the amount of debt from just 10 years ago.Higher yields could ultimately mean higher interest rates on loans, including mortgages, student debt and car loans, as these loans are often tied to the bond market.The move puts more pressure on the US Federal Reserve to deal with inflation, which has been pushed up by the war in Iran. The annualized inflation rate hit a three-year high in May before going down to 3.4% in July – 0.7% higher than the same time last year – largely because of higher energy prices.Donald Trump on Wednesday warned that oil prices were unlikely to come down before the midterm. Though Iran “can’t hold out any longer”, its leaders are “desperate to try and affect the election”, he said.“Right after the election, oil prices are going to be tumbling downward,” Trump predicted.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices,rosepast $100 for the first time since July on Wednesday as conflict in the Middle East continued to escalate.The Fed could raise interest rates to mitigate higher prices, at the risk of upsetting the White House. Last week, Trump said the Fed “must get smart” and lower interest rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE,” he wrote on social media.The pressure puts the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, who stepped into the role in May, in a bind: manage inflation or face the president’s wrath.In a closely watchedspeechat the Fed’s Jackson Hole symposium in August, Warsh affirmed that it was “the Fed’s job to deliver stable prices”, but held off on whether the the central bank would raise rates any time soon.Explore more on these topicsUS economyBondsInflationUS interest ratesTrump administrationEconomicsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oil prices rise above $100 a barrel for first time since July as Iran war escalates | Oil | The Guardian
description: Brent crude up by more than 3% after latest fire between US and Iran in Gulf and Houthi attacks on Saudi cities
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Brent crude up by more than 3% after latest fire between US and Iran in Gulf and Houthi attacks on Saudi cities
Content: Oil and gas prices have jumped since the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenOil and gas prices have jumped since the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAOilOil prices rise above $100 a barrel for first time since July as Iran war escalatesBrent crude up by more than 3% after latest fire between US and Iran in Gulf and Houthi attacks on Saudi citiesLauren AlmeidaandMark SweneyWed 9 Sep 2026 15.09 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 03.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe price of oil has risen above $100 a barrel for the first time since July as the escalating conflict in the Middle East threatens further disruption to global supplies.Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by more than 3% to top $101 after tensions increased in the Gulf amid the latest tit-for-tat exchange of fire between the US and Iran.The US militarysaid it had “destroyed” multiple Iranian tankers, after Tehran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles. The previous nightm Iran-backed Houthisattacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze.UK and mainland Europe gas prices also soared on Wednesday. The benchmark Dutch gas contract rose by almost 4% to €78.73 a megawatt hour, the highest since January 2023. Meanwhile, the British contract rose by 7.77p to 196.57p a therm, the highest since December 2022.Chart showing how natural gas prices have risen in the UKOn Tuesday, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, said the latest rise in oil prices was putting pressure on inflation and interest rates. “The risks, I’m afraid, are on the upside,”he told MPs. “And that’s really the risks coming from energy prices.”The oil price has jumped by a quarter since early August as hopes for a permanent resolution to the six-month-old war faded.The climb in costs has hit UK motorists, with petrol at the pump reaching an average of 166.2p a litre on Tuesday, the highest level in four years, according to the motoring body the AA.The AA said diesel hit an average of 187.7p, a price it last reached in May. Prices for a litre of petrol have risen 4.4p since the August bank holiday, with diesel up 4.1p.Chart showing how natural gas prices have risen in the EUHouseholds will face further pressure on their bills whenOfgem’s energy price cap rises by 4% in October. Andrew Goodwin, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Oxford Economics, has predicted that the cap could now rise by a further 13% in January.“Wholesale prices are currently well above the level of the previous observation window, and our commodities team expect them to remain high in the near term,” he said.The energy companies BP, Shell and the BritishGasowner, Centrica, were among the top performers across the FTSE 100 on Wednesday morning, with their shares rising by at least 1% on the back of the higher oil price. The index was down by 0.5% overall.Brent is up more than 60% this year, and has risen above the $100 mark for three periods so far in 2026.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChina, the world’s largest importer of crude, has increased purchases in recent days, after a hiatus that had been a factor keeping oil prices somewhat in check in the early part of the conflict.Giovanni Staunovo, a commodity analyst at UBS Global Wealth Management, said: “For the direction of crude prices, we are also monitoring Chinese crude imports as a key indicator.“Chinese crude imports recovered to nearly 9m barrels per day in August, up from the June low of 7.15m, but still lower compared to the [pre-conflict] February imports of 12.6m. It looks like the recovery trend could continue.”Oil prices have fluctuated in the six months since the start of Tehran’s block on the strait of Hormuz prompted what many feared would be the greatest energy supply disruption in history.In the first weeks after the first US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, oil prices soared past $100 a barrel. The oil pricepeaked at $126in April but later fell back amid hopes of a ceasefire. The price then began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and hostilities restarted.The rise in energy prices has stoked fears about inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates this year. In the US, economists are expecting at least one interest rate rise from the Federal Reserve by the end of the year.Explore more on these topicsOilCommoditiesUS-Israel war on IranGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Electronic shelf labels likely to cost jobs and drive up grocery prices, US report warns | US unions | The Guardian
description: AFL-CIO calls for ban on such labels to protect consumers and workers from surveillance pricing and job cuts
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: AFL-CIO calls for ban on such labels to protect consumers and workers from surveillance pricing and job cuts
Content: An employee arranges a digital price tag for vegetables at Whole Foods in Silver Lake, Los Angeles.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn employee arranges a digital price tag for vegetables at Whole Foods in Silver Lake, Los Angeles.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesUS unionsElectronic shelf labels likely to cost jobs and drive up grocery prices, US report warnsAFL-CIO calls for ban on such labels to protect consumers and workers from surveillance pricing and job cutsMichael SainatoWed 9 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe universal adoption of electronic shelf labels in grocery stores across the US could cost tens of thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in lost wages while further driving up grocery costs, according to a report released on Tuesday.An analysis by the AFL-CIO Tech Institute of the label manufacturers’ own marketing materials found the universal adoption of electronic shelf labels, which are marketed to retailers as a cost-cutting measure, could cost workers between $1.6bn and $6.9bn in lost wages annually and affect between 44,223 and 191,633 jobs.The policy brief – Priced Out, Pushed Out: Electronic Shelf Labels Raise Prices and Shrink Paychecks – calls for a ban on electronic labels to protect consumers and workers.Manufacturers have hailed the labelsasa way to collect huge amounts of personal data from customers, increase profits and cut labor costs.The report argues that electronic shelf labels use the same pricing systems that allow dynamic pricing – price changes such as increasing allergy medication prices when pollen counts are high – to surveillance pricing, changing prices based on personal data.These technologies are being implemented across the US retail industry at a time when food prices havesurpassedinflation and wage gains,increasing 33%over the past seven years.“Through our analysis, we found that the implementation of electronic shelf labels are likely going to drive prices even higher. The reason being that these labels are connected to the same algorithmic pricing software that online retailers are already using,” said Sunny Glottmann, policy and programs managers at the AFL-CIO Tech Institute and co-author of the report.“Electronic shelf labels create the infrastructure that would make rapid algorithmic price changes easier to implement at scale, and this raises concerns for consumers that are already struggling with grocery costs.”The report comes as several states have begunintroducing legislationto ban surveillance pricing and electronic shelf labels. In April, Marylandbecame the first statein the US to ban surveillance pricing. Connecticutsigneda ban into law in June and New Jerseysigned a baninto law in July.Electronic shelf labels “enable instantaneous price changes”, said Lauren McFerran, executive director of the AFL-CIO Tech Institute and former chairman of the National Labor Relations Board.“This is a technology that both is enabling this kind of ‘how do we extract the absolute most money out of grocery shoppers that is humanly possible’ and ‘how do we squeeze our workers as much as is humanly possible’,” said McFerran.AMay pollreleased by the United Food and Commercial Workers union found 68% of Americans believe surveillance pricing will increase grocery costs and 65% say digital price tags will do the same. About 67% support banning digital price tags and surveillance pricing, with only 26% opposing a ban.Ademola Oyefeso, vice-president of UFCW International, said that as retailers are implementing electronic shelf labels, the labor cuts occur gradually, with workers who typically change prices on shelves losing work hours.“Slowly, if someone has a full-time job or a part-time job, they go from full-time to part-time, from part-time to no time, and that’s what’s going to start happening across the entire industry,” said Oyefeso. “We have gone with paper labels for over 100 years. It’s worked. It’s the trust stores have built with people. I know [that] you and I are paying the same price.“If we come there on Monday, you and I are going to pay the same price on Monday, on Tuesday, on Wednesday.”Oyefeso said workers were also consumers, and that electronic shelf labels allow price changes to occur multiple times a day.In December, Instacartended a pilot program practicethat allowed retailers to charge online shoppers different prices for the same products after an investigation by Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found grocery prices could differ by as much as 23% between customers.“ESLs are the embodiment of surge pricing and surveillance pricing,” Oyefeso said. “Shelf labels allow grocery shopping to become airline ticket shopping.”Explore more on these topicsUS unionsRetail industryUS economyEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat Atlético | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Alexis Mac Allister scored Liverpool’s winner as they began their Champions League campaign with a 2-1 victory over Atlético Madrid
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Alexis Mac Allister scored Liverpool’s winner as they began their Champions League campaign with a 2-1 victory over Atlético Madrid
Content: Alexis Mac Allister celebrates alongside teammates Rio Ngumoha and Milos Kerkez after scoring Liverpool’s winner.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlexis Mac Allister celebrates alongside teammates Rio Ngumoha and Milos Kerkez after scoring Liverpool’s winner.Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueAlexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat AtléticoAndy Hunterat AnfieldWed 9 Sep 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was the time and place for Alexis Mac Allister to do his talking on the pitch and the disgruntled Liverpool midfielder delivered on cue. “Very sad” over Liverpool’s refusal to offer him a new contract, while Dominik Szoboszlai and Ryan Gravenberch were getting theirs, Mac Allister made Anfield very happy with a match-winning display againstAtlético Madrid.The Argentina international, one of five World Cup finalists involved in an absorbing, delicately-poised contest, vented his frustrations in the best possible and most professional way – from behind an immaculate 20-yard strike into Jan Oblak’s goal rather than a microphone. Mac Allister believes he is playing for a new deal this season and promised to give “100% to my last day” at the pre-match press conference. He was true to his word to extend Atlético’s winless sequence against English opposition in theChampions Leagueleague phase to 11 matches.Liverpool 2-1 Atlético Madrid, PSG 6-1 Slovan Bratislava; Chelsea v Leeds – liveRead moreFor Andoni Iraola, it was the perfect start to life as a Champions League coach after an imperfect start to the game. Diego Simeone’s switch to a 3-5-2 formation caughtLiverpoolcold and it was only when they regrouped in the aftermath of Marcos Llorente’s latest Anfield goal, and again during the half-time interval, that their performance level improved. Mac Allister’s timely moment, Alexander Isak’s relentless industry, Florian Wirtz’s creativity and another performance of drive and intelligence from Szoboszlai ensured the Liverpool head coach had plenty to savour.“I have to blame myself a bit for the start of the game,” Iraola said. “Atlético surprised us with the way they approached the game. They haven’t used that system too much this season and it’s difficult if you are not ready for it, but we adjusted and played better. In the second half we were the best team. We came back for the third time [this season] and that showed the players are pushing and they have character.”It was a night of firsts. Iraola coached a Champions League game for the first time in his career – he did take charge of 12 Europa League matches with AEK Larnaca in 2018-19 – Bradley Barcola made his first Liverpool start following a £123m move from Paris Saint-Germain and Julián Álvarez was in Atlético’s starting lineup for the first time this season since his failed attempt to join Barcelona. All appeared to have been forgiven – for now at least – as his name was cheered by the small pocket of Atlético fans when the teams were announced before kick-off and he repaid them by creating the opening goal.View image in fullscreenDominik Szoboszlai scores Liverpool’s equaliser late in the first half.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APLlorente was the scourge of Anfield yet again when Álvarez threaded a pass behind the home defence and the right wing-back raced clear on goal. The man who named his dog Anfield after scoring twice to eliminate Jürgen Klopp’s team from the competition in 2020, in the game played while Madrid was in lockdown from the Covid pandemic, lofted a confident finish beyond Alisson. It was Llorente’s fifth goal at Anfield, half of his entire total of Champions League goals. He had been kept onside by Milos Kerkez, who endured a poor night with his positioning and distribution before atoning with a key role in Liverpool’s equaliser.Álvarez almost doubled the visitors’ lead when granted far too much time and space to take aim from almost 30 yards. Alisson, at full stretch, intervened with a superb finger-tip save. Anfield was growing restless at Liverpool’s carelessness on the ball and Atlético’s comfort on it. But the threat and control from the hosts increased.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWirtz drew a fine save from Oblak at the end of a flowing move involving Barcola and Isak. Liverpool then drew level thanks to tenacity from Kerkez, a lovely touch from Ronald Araújo and Szoboszlai’s instinctive finish. The left-back won possession with a clean, crunching challenge on Lee Kang-in before finding Barcola. The France international was denied a goal on his full debut by Oblak’s low save but Wirtz kept the pressure on and Szoboszlai, having been halted on the edge of the area, got a second bite from Araújo’s clever flick. The midfielder’s first time shot sailed into the far corner.Barcola should have put Liverpool ahead when played through on goal by Wirtz early in the second half. The winger had time to measure the finish but pulled it wide of Oblak’s right-hand post. He would later depart with cramp. Liverpool were ahead one minute later when the lively Rio Ngumoha beat Llorente and his cross fell to Mac Allister via a deflection off Isak. Mac Allister told Szoboszlai to leave the ball and drilled home an unstoppable left-footed drive from 20 yards. Atlético remained dangerous and the introduction of Ademola Lookman added an extra dimension to the visitors’ attack but Liverpool defended impressively to secure a deserved victory.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueLiverpoolAtlético MadridEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: NFL 2026 season predictions: which teams can bring down the Rams juggernaut? | NFL | The Guardian
description: The new season kicks off on Wednesday night. Our writers have their say on the MVP, rookies to watch and the disasters waiting to happen
Author: Doug Farrar
Headline: The new season kicks off on Wednesday night. Our writers have their say on the MVP, rookies to watch and the disasters waiting to happen
Content: Fernando Mendoza, Josh Allen, Myles Garrett, Patrick Mahomes and Ja'Marr Chase will play prominent roles this season.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty)View image in fullscreenFernando Mendoza, Josh Allen, Myles Garrett, Patrick Mahomes and Ja'Marr Chase will play prominent roles this season.Composite: Guardian Pictures (via Getty)NFLNFL 2026 season predictions: which teams can bring down the Rams juggernaut?The new season kicks off on Wednesday night. Our writers have their say on the MVP, rookies to watch and the disasters waiting to happenDoug Farrar,Bryan Armen Graham,Andrew LawrenceandGraham SearlesWed 9 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis will be the year of ...Quarterbacks living under center.The NFL has developed into a shotgun league, where most quarterbacks take the majority of their snaps three to seven yards away from the center.But the increase in efficiencywhen it comes to snaps taken right behind the center should have coaches directing their quarterbacks to do more of it. Matthew Stafford, Caleb Williams, and Sam Darnold led the way in 2025, and others will follow.DFSuperteams.The Rams have pushed their chips to the middle of the table by loading up on high-end veterans and deferring much of the cost to future years. Myles Garrett and the unretired Aaron Donald join Stafford, Puka Nacua and a secondary reinforced by Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson. Superteamsare never a sure thingin the NFL, but the Rams’ terrifyingly stacked roster looks awfully close.BAGSuper Bowl sequel hype, the year the scriptwriters lay a path for a Rams-Bengals rematch in Los Angeles. Both teams have gone to considerable lengths to shore up the defensive side of the ball, with the Rams swinging a mega trade for Garrett on the heels of the Bengals’ draft-week swap for Pro Bowl tackle Dexter Lawrence.ALFinally saying goodbye to Aaron Rodgers. Let’s forget allthe weirdnessaround the latter years of his career and remember Rodgers as simply one of the best to ever do it. Maybe with Mike McCarthy calling plays again, he can keep Pittsburgh in contention for a wildcard. Even if he fails, you can guarantee seeing some of the old magic in his final season in the NFL.GSBest team that won’t make the playoffs ...This is the second straight seasonI’ve pushed theVikingshere, and for the same reasons – the NFC North is the league’s most competitive division, and there is no outstanding candidate at quarterback. Brian Flores’s defense will be marvelous as it always is,and were it not for his ongoing lawsuit against the league, he’d probably be a head coach right now. A three-man quarterback competition is not the best way to maximize one’s competitive window, though.DFDak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb are back for an offense that can put up points with almost anybody. But the NFC is deep and unforgiving and theCowboys’ front seven looks alarmingly short of difference-makers beyond star defensive tackle Quinnen Williams and Rashan Gary. Nine wins, constant frustration and a third straight January on the couch sounds about right.BAGTheVikings’ defense always gives them a chance, and their offensive skill players are elite. It just comes down to what Murray can give them and, historically, that’s been a lot of inconsistency.ALIt will be a battle for Ben Johnson to keep the lightning in the bottle with aBearsdefense that thrived on takeaways rather than fundamentals last season. They haven’t made many significant moves – outside first-round safety Dillon Thieneman – to tune things up, then the impressive offense could be let down with a near miss in the wildcard race.GSMost underrated team ...It’s easy to forget that in the 2021 season, theBengalslost the Super Bowl by three points, and in 2022, they lost the AFC Championship game by the same margin. Those close calls were followed by matching 9-8 seasons in 2023 and 2024, and last season’s 6-11 faceplant. But if Joe Burrow can stay healthy, these Bengals have a ton of talent on both sides of the ball (led by new defensive line monster Lawrence).DFJustin Herbert is class and Mike McDaniel’s arrival as offensive coordinator will add some imagination and flair to the offense. But winning 11 games still leaves you overshadowed when Denver’s complete roster and Patrick Mahomes’ Kansas City headline your division. TheChargersare quiet contenders hiding in plain sight.BAGLast I checked, theChiefsnot only return Patrick Mahomes – the QB standard before the ACL injury (hardly the career killers they used to be) – but also Eric Bieniemy, the offensive coordinator who held players accountable and infused the team’s gameplay with so much confidence and whimsy.ALBaker Mayfield was quietly brilliant last season and theBuccaneershave a strong roster across the board that finished 8-9 after a 6-2 start because of a number of key players missing time through injury. A bit of luck with the injury bug and the Bucs could spring a surprise.GSView image in fullscreenDeshaun Watson: the worst quarterback $230m can buy.Photograph: Carolyn Kaster/APJohnny Manziel disaster waiting to happen department ...The Browns’ quarterback situation.What else could it be? At this point, the Browns may as well bring Manziel back to add even more of a tragic comic cast to the whole thing. Head coach Todd Monkennaming Deshaun Watson the Week 1 starterafter Watson played horriblyandalienated the fanbase in the preseason – never mind the horrid off-field history for which Watson has never taken an ounce of accountability – is merely the first level of Dante’s Inferno.DFCleveland naming Watson their Week 1 starter. A $230m albatross coming off multiple achilles tears would have been a risky first choice even if he’d been playing well before getting hurt. The Browns’ decision to roster three other quarterbacks, including Dillon Gabriel on injured reserve, feels prescient here.BAGAnthony Richardsonsurvived trade rumors and played well enough in camp to win the Colts’ backup QB job. But I say the detente only holds up as long as Daniel Jones’s health, which has never been the greatest, and Richardson’s uneven play in relief makes him a lame duck QB all over again – and his controversial behavior gives the organization cover for the bad fit once more.ALThe Brownsmissing Garrett’s tremendous pass rush and leadership is a recipe for a very tricky season if they make a slow start. And with Watson starting at quarterback they most likely will.GSMVP …Drake Maye, QB, New England Patriots.While I don’t have the Patriots winning the AFC East this season, I think that with the additions of receivers AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs, and coming off a full season in Josh McDaniels’ offense, Maye has everything he needs to take the next step to become an unquestioned Top 10 quarterback. He was exactly that until the Patriots faced a murderers’ row of defenses in the playoffs and his protection fell apart, but the growth he showed in everything from reading the field to taking disguised coverages apart presaged that next level.DFLamar Jackson, QB, Baltimore Ravens.The Ravens enter a new era under first-year coach Jesse Minter, but their fortunes still revolve around the NFL’s most disruptive player. The 29-year-old Jackson can unhinge defenses with his arm, legs or simply the threat of either. If Baltimore can get to 12 or 13 wins, he becomes the best bet to enter the exclusive club of three-time MVPs.BAGJoe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals.Now that he has a defense behind him again, Joe Cool can get back to lighting up the scoreboard and his cigar after the dubs.ALJoe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals.The quarterback finished last year showing some of his best work, so this could be Burrow’s time with incredible weapons Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins at his disposal.GSThe best rookie will be ...Caleb Downs, DB, Dallas Cowboys.The Cowboys’ 2025 defense was one of the worst in recent memory, which is why they replaced Matt Eberflus with Christian Parker as defensive coordinator. Parker’s background with the Philadelphia Eagles and defensive wizard Vic Fangio should pay immediate dividends, and Downs, the Ohio State alum selected with the 11th overall pick, should thrive in Parker’s concepts.DFJadarian Price, RB, Seattle Seahawks.With Kenneth Walker III gone and Zach Charbonnet starting the season on the Physically Unable to Perform list, the Seahawks will plug-and-play their first-round draft pick from Notre Dame into a backfield fresh off a Super Bowl title.BAGJeremiyah Love, RB, Arizona Cardinals.The Notre Dame prospect shouldn’t lack for opportunities to get the ball off tackle, in space or however else coach Mike LaFleur seeks to make use of the Saquon Barkley clone he simply couldn’t pass up in this year’s draft.ALCarnell Tate, WR, Tennessee Titans. The No 4 pick has the total package of speed, route running and size. Tate caught the eye in training camp working with second-year quarterback Cam Ward. He will continue to do so throughout 2026.GSAFC East championI’m picking theBillsfor one reason, and it’s not Josh Allen – it’s Jim Leonhard. Buffalo’s new defensive coordinator is one of the finest minds in football, and he’ll have that defense asserting itself in ways it never did under Sean McDermott. New England will still be up there after 2025’s Cinderella season, but a tougher schedule andpossible regression when it comes to their unusual injury luckshould have them taking a step back.DFNew England won it last year and added star wideout Brown, but a regression from 14 wins is almost inevitable even if the Super Bowl loser’s cursehas mostly been debunked. TheBillshave Allen, DJ Moore and enough defensive talent for first-year coach Joe Brady to take back a division the Bills owned for five straight years before last season.BAGNot because theBillsare necessarily better than the team that beat them to the top last year. But because New England’s schedule is so much tougher this year, and one loss makes all the difference in this chilly rivalry.ALA straight shootout between New England and Buffalo. With fresh ideas from Brady, theBillscould have an important edge but there’s not much wriggle room in their opening five games against the Texans, Lions, Chargers, Patriots and Rams.
