Escaping with a winning record from that run would provide a solid platform to regain dominance.GSView image in fullscreenJoe Burrow is an MVP candidate. But will he stay healthy?Photograph: Chris Szagola/APAFC North championTrading for Lawrence was the splashy story of theBengals’ offseason, but there’s a lot more to like here – especially if Burrow can stay healthy. If he can, I like the Bengals to outpace the Ravens and Steelers based on star power with receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, and a defense that has a lot of ascending players.DFMinter has been dealt an enviable hand with Jackson, Derrick Henry and a roster built to win now. Cincinnati should push them, but theRavens’ combination of quarterback play, running game and defensive stability remains the division’s safest bet.BAGTheBengals. Here’s a sentence no one’s ever written until now: Mike Brown, the NFL’s resident cheapskate, is all in.ALIf Burrow just has a full season working behind an improved offensive line, then theBengalshave a great shot at unseating the Ravens. Their schedule is soft enough that they should be aiming for well over 10 wins.GSAFC South championI’m taking theTexansover the Jaguars because of a defense that needs no schematic tricks to upend enemy offenses – they’re good enough to just line up and go right at you. All the Texans need from quarterback CJ Stroud is a level of play a bit above league-average.DFTheTexansdefense is one of the NFL’s best with Will Anderson Jr, Derek Stingley Jr and Kamari Lassiter leading the way. Whether Stroud and the offense can hold up their end of the bargain remains the rub, but it should be enough in this middling division.BAGTheJaguarsrepeatedly found ways to win tight games in 2025, giving a young team meaningful late-game experience – and a plausible foundation to turn last year’s surge into a deep postseason run.ALThe defense returns almost unchanged after a brilliant 2025 with some good additions in safety Reed Blankenship and rookie run-stopper Kayden McDonald. TheTexanshave quality and consistency a level above the messy Jaguars and Colts.GSAFC West championI really like what new Chargers offensive coordinator McDaniel will do for Herbert, and I expect the Chiefs to rebound to a point from last season’s disaster. But the 2025Broncosgot all the way to the AFC Championship game, and they may have progressed further had quarterback Bo Nix not suffered a broken ankle in the divisional round. Now, Nix has a new best buddy to help him – former Miami Dolphins receiver Jaylen Waddle,who gives that offense a level of vertical juiceit hasn’t had before.DFThey’d probably be defending NFL champions if not forNix’s untimely injuryin the playoffs. TheBroncosdefense remains elite, the offensive line is right there with it and the addition of Waddle gives them another weapon on offense alongside Courtland Sutton. Nix’s mission with the AFC’s deepest roster boils down to three words: do no harm.BAGTheChargersmade many of the right moves this offseason: keeping most of their receiving corps intact, adding David Njoku and big-play tailback Keaton Mitchell, and rebuilding the interior offensive line. Losing new center Tyler Biadasz to injury is a major blow, but if the line holds together well enough, Herbert and a deep, balanced roster give the Bolts a real chance to edge Kansas City and Denver.ALThe Chiefs and Chargers should be well in the mix but theBroncosstill have the edge after last year’s dominance before Nix went down in the playoffs.GSNFC East championTheCowboysbag the crown based on an offense that’s already fully loaded, and a defense that should be worlds better than in 2025. They are the Inverse Houston Texans in that all that defense has to do is play at a pretty good level to blow a lot of opponents away.DFBrown is gone and Jalen Hurts will be working with his seventh different play-caller in as many NFL seasons, but theEagles’ institutional strength has been the envy of the NFC East for decades now. A potentially top-five defense and a rejuvenated ground game featuring Saquon Barkley will provide enough margin for error to outlast a division filled with flawed rivals.BAGWith Brown and coordinator Kevin Patullo gone, theEaglesoffense should fly again behind Barkley and Hurts – in make or break year mode not that long after leading the team to Super Bowl glory.ALTheCowboysare hardly a sleeping giant, but if the defense is as reborn as defensive tackle Williams claims it is then maybe Dallas can finally balance the books with their dynamic offense and reclaim the division.GSView image in fullscreenCaleb Williams faces one of the toughest divisions in football.Photograph: Nam Y Huh/APNFC North championClose your eyes and throw a dart at the NFL’s toughest division, and you have a 25% chance of being right. The Lions, Packers, and Vikings all have reason for hope, but ifBearshead coach Ben Johnson can refine quarterback Caleb Williams, and Dennis Allen’s defense can improve over last season’s boom-or-bust results –they led the NFL in turnover differential, butranked 23rd in points allowed– it’s Chicago’s time to shine.DFChicago may be the trendy pick and Green Bay dangerous floaters, but theLionsstill have enough offensive firepower and strength along the line of scrimmage to hold them off in the NFL’s deepest division.BAGTheLionswere burned by injuries last year and still stayed in the playoff hunt almost to the end. They are positioned for a rebound, with more of their core available and one of the league’s easiest schedules – a chance to bank early wins while key pieces work their way back from early-season absences.ALThePackersremain without Micah Parsons until at least Week 5 but a look at their first four opponents – the Vikings, Jets, Falcons and Buccaneers – points to a hot start.GSNFC South championMayfield was outstanding in the first half of the 2025 seasonbefore his own injuries, and the injuries of those around him, took their toll. TheBuccaneersstarted the season 6-2 before falling off to 8-9. With better luck things should look quite a bit better in 2026.DFTheBuccaneershave the most settled quarterback situation, enough skill-position talent and a defense that’s just good enough. Carolina are the likeliest threat while neither Atlanta nor rebuilding New Orleans have enough to mount a serious challenge.BAGThere’s little incentive to go against theBuccaneers, the gold standard in the league’s most volatile division.ALOff the back of late-season success in 2025, theSaintswill be feeling good about their chances. If second-year quarterback Tyler Shough maintains his upward trajectory they should be confident.GSNFC West championWhile there arereasons to questionthe ultimate validity of theRams’ “all-in” approach that culminated with the return of Donald, there’s enough in the hypothetical to give Sean McVay’s team a slight edge over the Seahawks – if only because Seattle didn’t follow their Super Bowl win by radically stocking their defense as the Rams did.DFThere are legitimate durability questions around the aging Stafford and the returning Donald for theRams. But it’s hard to imagine anyone challenging a roster tricked out with as much high-end talent as any NFL team in years. Anything short of a division title would qualify as a serious underachievement.BAGTheRams. With apologies to the reigning Super Bowl champs, the moves GM Les Snead and Co made in the offseason to shore up their defense are eerily similar to the big swings they took in the 2021 season. And we all know how that turned out.ALDonald and Garrett have five defensive player of the year awards between them and link up with former Super Bowl winners from the Chiefs in Watson and McDuffie. TheRamsare stacked and then some.GSAFC wildcard teamsPatriots, Jaguars, Chargers.DFPatriots, Bengals, Chargers.BAGPatriots, Ravens, Chiefs.ALChargers, Ravens, Jaguars.GSNFC wildcard teamsSeahawks, Lions, Eagles.DFSeahawks, Packers, Bears.BAGSeahawks, 49ers, Cowboys.ALBuccaneers, Lions, Seahawks.GSAFC championship gameBills over Broncos.DFBroncos over Bills.BAGBengals over Jaguars.ALBroncos over Bengals.GSNFC championship gameRams over Seahawks.DFRams over Eagles.BAGRams over Seahawks.ALRams over Cowboys.GSView image in fullscreenMatthew Stafford is looking to win a second Super Bowl in LA.Photograph: Ariana Ruiz/PI/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockYour Super Bowl LXI winner will be …Rams over Bills.The Rams’ “F Them Picks” philosophy served them well when they gave up a ton of draft capital for Stafford, Jalen Ramsey, and Von Miller, and they won the Super Bowl as a result. If the 2026 Rams find that their go-for-broke philosophy works once again with a radical reshuffling of their defense, it’s hard to bet against them, because the offense was already so on point.DFRams over Broncos.The Rams have spent the offseason putting together a star-studded roster unlike anything we’ve seen in years, adding Garrett, McDuffie and Watson before Donald decided he wasn’t finished after all. Denver’s elite defense is capable of making it ugly, but Sean McVay’s embarrassment of riches on both sides of the ball will ultimately prove too much.BAGBengals over Rams.Burrow avenges the biggest loss in his career, and it’s in no small part thanks to Brown and player personnel director Duke Tobin pulling the trigger one last time on a piece that helps neutralize the effects of the Garrett-Donald pocket collapse (an extra guard, a fullback – don’t hold me to specifics). The confusion over what to make of Zac Taylor as a Super Bowl-winning coach quickly gives way to the confusion over what to make of a championship parade festooned with tributes to the world’sweirdest chili. In other words, the renovations on ancient Paycor Stadiumpay for themselves.ALBroncos over Rams.Denver can argue they were a broken ankle away from the Super Bowl last season. Handily for the Broncos they come back with almost an identical roster this year. They kept starting running back JK Dobbins and brought in Waddle to help out Sutton. The Broncos already have the AFC’s best defense to go with a sublime offensive line and exciting weapons that can take down the Rams.GSExplore more on these topicsNFLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ultrarunner Megan Eckert shatters US men’s and women’s records with 636 miles in six days | Sport | The Guardian
description: The American shattered the women’s world record, which she had already set herself, and broke the US men’s mark by more than 30 miles
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The American shattered the women’s world record, which she had already set herself, and broke the US men’s mark by more than 30 miles
Content: Megan Eckert, pictured at a six-day race in France last year, made more ultrarunning history this week.Photograph: Sam Lhermillier/Mount to CoastView image in fullscreenMegan Eckert, pictured at a six-day race in France last year, made more ultrarunning history this week.Photograph: Sam Lhermillier/Mount to CoastSportUltrarunner Megan Eckert shatters US men’s and women’s records with 636 miles in six daysDistance tops US men’s mark by more than 30 milesEckert also beat women’s world record she set last yearGuardian sportWed 9 Sep 2026 16.32 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 16.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile some teachers spent the second week of September easing into their school routines,Megan Eckertwas making more ultrarunning history.The New Mexico middle school math teacher shattered the six-day women’s world record and the American men’s record by running 636.482 miles, completing her feat on Wednesday morning in Balatonfüred, Hungary.606 miles in six days: teacher Megan Eckert chases ultrarunning history – and a men’s recordRead moreThe 40-year-oldenteredthe Global Organization of Multi-Day Ultramarathoners Six-Day World Championship aiming to break both records. She finished as the event’s overall winner, beating Norwegian Simen Holvik, who logged 584.631 miles.“It’s the longest and the shortest thing,” she toldRunner’s Worldafter the race. “It’s unbelievable. There’s so much that goes on, so many ups and downs. But we had a good time. It’s going to take a long time to process.”This was the second time she has broken the women’s world record: she set it for the first time last year by running 603.155 miles at the world championships in France. The men’s American record (606.243 miles) had stood since Joe Fejes set it in 2015.Eckert surpassed both marks by more than 30 miles. The results are pending ratification by the International Association ofUltrarunning.The feat involved 1,140 loops around a 0.5581-mile flat and paved track. Eckert maintained an average pace of 4.420 miles per hour over the 144-hour stretch, which included pauses for rest, food and logistics.“I didn’t even know six-day runs existed until a few years ago, but I fell in love with them the minute I found them,” she told the Guardian recently. “When I’m training for a big goal like the American men’s record, I don’t dwell on fear because I get so excited about how the goal is pushing me to train harder – and how I get to go and run with a community who’s turning the same 144-hour race into our own little world.”According toI Run Far, Eckert was ahead of Fejes’s overall pace about 30 hours in and increased her lead as time went on. She reached the 550-mile mark after 123 hours and was reportedly still moving strongly and smoothly after taking two-hour sleeps and 15-minute naps throughout.Eckert became the first woman to pass the 1,000km (621-mile) mark, which she did in 139 hours 55 minutes 46 seconds. She finished only about 14 miles short of the overall six-day world record (650.919 miles) set by Russia’s Iván Zaborski in France last year.“I like to choose goals where I have a 50% chance of success and a 50% chance of failure,” she said. “It’s amazing what can happen when you go after goals that scare you – and that just might not be possible.”Explore more on these topicsSportUltrarunningUS sportsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ben Shelton wins on a night of vomit, sweat and home hopes at US Open | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 23-year-old’s epic win over Carlos Alcaraz means there is a real chance of an American man winning the US Open for the first time since 2003
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: The 23-year-old’s epic win over Carlos Alcaraz means there is a real chance of an American man winning the US Open for the first time since 2003
Content: Ben Shelton is through to an all-American US Open semi-final.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APView image in fullscreenBen Shelton is through to an all-American US Open semi-final.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APUS Open Tennis 2026Ben Shelton wins on a night of vomit, sweat and home hopes at US OpenThe 23-year-old’s epic win over Carlos Alcaraz means there is a real chance of an American man winning the US Open for the first time since 2003Andrew Lawrenceat Flushing MeadowsWed 9 Sep 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn yet another graveyard shift at the US Open, Ben Shelton showed he can hang around late, ousting defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in five sets in a quarter-final that started on Tuesday nightand finished on Wednesday morning. When Shelton fired the final ball out wide for his seventh ace of the night, the clock on the Arthur Ashe Stadium court read 3.33am. It was the latest-ever finish at the Open and the fifth-latest finish in grand slam history.After embracing Alcaraz at the net, he pumped his fists and greeted his coach’s box with a primal scream. Parents have a name for this: the zoomies. Then Shelton looked to the stands and gestured at his mother and his girlfriend, soccer star Trinity Rodman. In his on-court interview, he asked that his sister, Emma, be given the day off. She had spent the entire night and much of the early morning watching her little brother play.Ben Shelton dethrones Carlos Alcaraz in five-set thriller after latest US Open finishRead more“I’m tired,” he told a gaggle of bleary-eyed reporters. “That was a war, an epic match.”Shelton had not only equaled his deepest run in a grand slam; he made sure that the US will have at least one representative in Sunday’s final – he will play compatriot Frances Tiafoe in the semi-finals. The victor could become the first American man to win the US Open since Andy Roddick in 2003. One of them will become the first Black American man to reach a US Open final since Ashe in 1972.Shelton, seeded eighth, enters the semi-final with a 3-1 head-to-head edge, including a win over Tiafoe in the 2023 US Open quarter-final that announced him as a force to be reckoned with. And as much as Shelton believed in his potential to contend for major titles (“I wanna be that dude in the draw that there’s not one player who wants to see me”, he saidthree years ago), he still had yet to prove he could meet the big moments.That’s not to knock Shelton. A 6ft 4in southpaw with a thunderous serve, he’s the best American men’s prospect to come along in a generation. He’s also exactly what US commentators had been wishing for with their pleas for some basketball forward or football wide receiver to pick up a racket and focus on tennis instead. In short order, Shelton went from winning a college national championship at the University of Florida to cracking the top 50 in the world to pushing Novak Djokovic in the 2023 US Open semi-finals. During that tournament, Shelton celebrated his victories by holding an imaginary phone to his ear, a gesture meant to show he had “answered the call”. But when Djokovic beat him en route to winning the title, the Serb infamously stole the celebration for himself.This season has seen Shelton overtake Tiafoe, Tommy Paul and Taylor Fritz as the American men’s standard bearer while racking up titles on Munich clay and Stuttgart grass and defending his Masters 1000 crown in Canada. But despite that progress, there remained a gap between what Shelton looked capable of doing and what he actually did on the biggest stages: he held a 9-24 record against top-10 players and an 0-17 mark against the top three coming into the match against Alcaraz. The fact that the last three of his top-10 victories had all come against Fritz didn’t exactly portend a star turn against Alcaraz – who entered Tuesday’s match with a 3-0 record against Shelton.View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz and Ben Shelton greet each other after their quarter-final.Photograph: Brian Hirschfeld/EPAEarly on, it seemed the seven-time grand slam champion would find his way to the finish line even as he was still shaking off the rust from an extended layoff to heal an injured wrist. Alcaraz struck the ball firmly enough to stay in the long rallies with Shelton and nose ahead in a first-set tiebreak. (“I was pissed,” Shelton said afterward.) But no sooner had Alcaraz taken the match lead, his feel deserted him and the errors began piling up on his forehand and serve.Seeing his opening, Shelton pounced, reeling off nine straight games on the way to a two-sets-to-one advantage. Shelton outmuscled Alcaraz from the service line, lashing 145mph fastballs with ease. He also outfoxed him at net, retrieving Alcaraz’s surprise drop shots and countering with some impressive volley work of his own. He extended what are ordinarily short rallies for Alcaraz by forcing him to hit extra balls for winners, pressing to end exchanges that went on too long, and goading him into more mistakes.“I made him play a lot,” Shelton said. “I didn’t worry or stress too much when he hit his spot, hit unreturnable or an ace. I think for me to be able to hang in there in the rallies, have a gameplan from the ground and be able to execute that gameplan and not be losing all the baseline points also helps with the return.”Altogether, Alcaraz finished with 134 errors – 53 of them unforced. Making matters worse, he didn’t have his own reliable serve or even his steady return game to fall back on. “Obviously when he’s serving, he puts a lot of pressure on you,” the Spaniard said afterward, smiling despite the tough loss. “You’re trying to put the return in. It’s an unknown if you’re going to play the point or [if] he’s going to get a free point with his serve. In these moments, he takes a lot of [the] advantage. It’s not an excuse, but I would say [his serve] is an important weapon in those moments.”Alcaraz would storm back, of course, compensating for his miscalibrated game by chipping away at Shelton’s lethal first strike to give himself 11 break-point chances, converting three. (Until this match, Shelton hadn’t been broken in his prior eight sets.) As the pressure mounted, the defending champion showed signs of wear, hunching over his racket for support and angrily shooing away a cameraman from his chair before vomiting into a towel monogrammed to commemorate his US Open victory last year. Meanwhile Shelton held his nerve through to the tiebreak, scoring a late mini-break to go up 7-6 and consolidating with a pair of aces, the last torching the radar at 146mph to become the first American to defeat Alcaraz at a major. (The 14th try was the charm.)Long before that blistering final shot touched down, the tennis center custodians were mopping up the aisles inside the stadium in preparation for Wednesday’s matches. When the diminished crowd that hung on till the bitter end wasn’t tearing their hair out over which player to support, the beeping of the grounds crew utility trucks trundling outside the stadium would pierce through the din like a bedside alarm clock. Shelton now has a golden opportunity to contend for a major, without Alcaraz and the injured Jannik Sinner standing in his way. It’s a big moment – one that, after Tuesday night and some of Wednesday morning, is so hazy it almost feels like a dream.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026TennisUS Open tennisUS sportsCarlos AlcarazfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Infantino installs loyalist to oversee Caribbean as he splits Fifa management  | Football politics | The Guardian
description: Fifa president’s move is widely regarded by his opponents as an attempt to split the Concacaf nations working with Uefa to remove him from office
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa president’s move is widely regarded by his opponents as an attempt to split the Concacaf nations working with Uefa to remove him from office
Content: Gianni Infantino last weekend reaffirmed his intention to seek re-election as Fifa’s president.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino last weekend reaffirmed his intention to seek re-election as Fifa’s president.Photograph: Kacper Pempel/ReutersFootball politicsInfantino installs loyalist to oversee Caribbean as he splits Fifa managementCritics view Fernandes job as move to shore up positionFifa says change is designed to make sport ‘truly global’Exclusive byMatt HughesandNick AmesWed 9 Sep 2026 13.17 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino has separated Fifa’s management of the Caribbean countries from the rest of Concacaf in a move widely regarded by his opponents as an attempt to split the alliance to remove him from office.Concacaf covers North and Central America as well as the Caribbean and was previously managed as one bloc. Butthe Guardian has learned that the former Switzerland midfielder Gelson Fernandes, an Infantino loyalist, has been appointed as the director of member associations for the Caribbean, in addition to his position looking after Fifa’s African members.More than 100,000 people add names to complaint against Gianni InfantinoRead moreFernandes, who played for Manchester City, Leicester and eight other clubs, joined Fifa in 2022 as director of member associations for Africa and was promoted two years later to become deputy chief members associations officer globally.The 40-year-old works closely with Fifa’s chief members associations officer, Elkhan Mammadov, a close ally of Infantino described by many national associations as the president’s key enforcer.Fernandes has replaced Jair Bertoni as Fifa’s liaison with the 21 Caribbean-based members, with the national associations and Concacaf informed of the change last week without consultation.In a statement Fifa confirmed the appointment, which it said was designed to support Infantino’s vision of making the sport truly global.“Fifa can confirm that Gelson Fernandes has taken on responsibility for the Caribbean region, in addition to his current role as regional director Africa,” it said. “With his extensive experience at Fifa and strong knowledge of football development programmes, Gelson will lead the regional team and will work closely with the member associations across the Caribbean to further support the development of football in their respective countries, following the Fifa president’s vision: making football truly global.”Concacaf is attempting with Uefa and the Asian Football Confederation (AFC)to oust Infantino. Sources at several member associations in Europe and North America regard the change as an attempt to split the Concacaf vote before March’s presidential election, with one characterising it as “an administrative war” against its president,Victor Montagliani.The Canadian is viewed by many in Uefa as the most credible candidate to beat Infantino, although Montagliani has yet to decide whether to stand and is committed to seeking re-election as Concacaf’s president.Infantino has stepped up his re-election campaign in the aftermath of the World Cup sell-off scandal, ignoring a written request from Montagliani to stay away from a meeting of the Caribbean Football Union (CFU) in the Dominican Republic last month.Asrevealed by the Guardian, Infantino used the CFU meeting to announce approval for numerous Fifa-funded development projects for the region worth millions of dollars in what some observers described as an attempt to lobby for votes.Mexico has split from Concacaf by announcing its support for Infantino, and losing the backing of the Caribbean would be a significant setback for those pushing to remove Infantino.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere have been some early signs that Infantino’s tactics are paying off, with the president of the Jamaican federation, Michael Ricketts, this week backing the status quo and comparing Uefa to spoiled children.“Infantino might have made a mistake, but the intentions were to help Caribbean countries or help smaller countries,” Rickets told the Jamaica Observer. “Can you imagine Jamaica getting $40m to invest in football? Can you imagine the difference that would make in four or five years?“I am not supporting Uefa because I think that they always want to be in opposition and always want to oppose. It doesn’t matter who is president, they are going to have issues. It doesn’t matter how well the president does, they are going to have issues and I think that Uefa is behaving like a set of spoilt kids.”Uefa’s 55 members are believed to be united but the strength of the AFC alliance is unclear, with Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates having defied the confederation by endorsing Infantino.Infantino last weekend reaffirmed hisintention to seek re-electionfor a fourth term. The deadline for other candidates seeking to stand is 18 November.Explore more on these topicsFootball politicsGianni InfantinoFifanewsShareReuse this content

title: Men’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will there be an English winner for the first time in 25 years? | Ballon d'Or | The Guardian
description: We assess the standing of the players on the shortlist for the award before the winner is announced in October
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: We assess the standing of the players on the shortlist for the award before the winner is announced in October
Content: Kylian Mbappé, Harry Kane, Lamine Yamal and Ousmane Dembélé are among the front runners for the Ballon d’Or.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKylian Mbappé, Harry Kane, Lamine Yamal and Ousmane Dembélé are among the front runners for the Ballon d’Or.Composite: Getty ImagesBallon d'OrMen’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will there be an English winner for the first time in 25 years?We assess the standing of the players on the shortlist for the award before the winner is announced in OctoberJeff RueterWed 9 Sep 2026 09.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1) Harry Kane (England/Bayern Munich)Even adjusting for the goal-drunken Bundesliga, his 61 goals in 51 matches for Bayern last season undersells his all-around impact, considering his playmaking and hold-up skills. Kane was gameplanned out of England’s later games at the World Cup, but he was unstoppable through the last 16 to close out the finest year of his career to date. If not now, when?2) Rodri (Spain/Manchester City – now at Barcelona)He boasts a comparable case to when he won this prize in 2024 – Rodri remains the epicenter of an incredibly effective Spanish collective. This time around, there’s no Premier League glory to bolster his hopes, as City’s late challenge fizzled out with the club “only” winning domestic cups in his final season at the Etihad. Back to his best en route to Spain’s second World Cup title, though only one of the four previous World Cup champions had the corresponding Ballon d’Or winner (Lionel Messi, 2023).3) Kylian Mbappé (France/Real Madrid)Mbappé and José Mourinho have launched an aggressive campaign for the Frenchman to win his first Ballon d’Or. He was even more difficult to slow in his second Spanish season, with 40 goals in 42 matches across La Liga and the Champions League; the less said about his pressing, the better. Few players captivated and dominated like Mbappé at the World Cup, as he won the Golden Boot. But a lack of team accomplishments could set back his candidacy, made even more glaring given Madrid’s chronic success.4) Lamine Yamal (Spain/Barcelona)Another member of the World Cup champions, although injuries limited his impact in North America – the master of suspense was not as involved as he’d have liked. Then again, he managed greater consistency in his third season as a regular for Barcelona, with 41 goal contributions in all competitions across 45 appearances. He only just turned 19 in July.Dani Olmo: ‘Winning the World Cup changes you, it changes your life’Read more5) Lionel Messi (Argentina/Inter Miami)Messi could well have ranked higher had Argentina won the World Cup this summer, as the 39-year-old was the heart and soul of their campaign. Alas, a putrid final showing (by his teammates, more than Messi) dulls the sheen on his hopes for a ninth Ballon d’Or, and he is also hit by the fact that he doesn’t play for one of Europe’s elite clubs, even though Inter Miami won the MLS title. His remarkable 17th appearance on a Ballon d’Or shortlist is well deserved.6) Michael Olise (France/Bayern Munich)Who knew Bayern’s most thrilling attack in recent memory would be spearheaded by signings from Tottenham and Crystal Palace? An elite secondary attacker, and one who has come to relish operating as the string-puller in transition and at the edge of the final third. Spain masterfully closed his passing lines and took him out of the semi-final, but a pair of assists in the third-place match put him top in that category at the World Cup. A career year, or evidence he’s set a new standard for himself?7) Erling Haaland (Norway/Manchester City)Even as City stumbled down the stretch, this was another season to pad his growing legacy as one of the game’s great strikers of any era. He made the most of Norway’s return to the World Cup, finishing as the tournament’s joint-third top goalscorer (seven) despite exiting in the quarter-final.8) Jude Bellingham (England/Real Madrid)Birmingham City’s decision to retire his number when his career had barely started has aged well. A man for the big moments, he forged a rare tandem with Kane at the World Cup, alternating headline hero shifts en route to another semi-final heartbreaker. His goals and assists plummeted in his third season with Madrid, though most of his teammates saw diminishing returns in a forgettable campaign.9) Ousmane Dembélé (France/Paris Saint-Germain)Lacking some of the bombast that typifies his rivals, Dembélé remains a silky threat for club and country. His stats for PSG dipped from last year’s award-winning campaign, from 35 goals in 53 games to 20 in 40. His partnership with Mbappé and Olise for France was as dangerous as the international game has seen. If nothing else, Dembélé has made certain that he is no one-year wonder.10) Khvicha Kvaratskhelia (Georgia/Paris Saint-Germain)On a per-minute basis, few players are more effective in the biggest games. Unfortunately, his club’s domestic dominance means he can take more shifts off than most of his gilded peers, logging a measly 1,479 Ligue 1 minutes in 28 appearances. Georgia’s absence from this summer’s World Cup also limits the evidence available to bolster his case. Nonetheless, his barnstorming exploits in the Champions League knockouts saw the 25-year-old hit rare form.11) Declan Rice (England/Arsenal)The most vital cog in Mikel Arteta’s meticulous machine, and a key all-around impact in England’s run to the World Cup semi-final, even if he at times understandably looked tired after a long domestic campaign.12) Bruno Fernandes (Portugal/Manchester United)One of a few Portuguese players whose cases for this prize were scuppered by this summer’s underwhelming showing under the stubborn Roberto Martínez. Truly sensational to restore the Red Devils to prouder days.13) Pau Cubarsí (Spain/Barcelona)Looked every part the lead center-back that his club and country need to play in a possession-dominant way. Then again, these prizes seldom skew towards defenders.14) Fabián Ruiz (Spain/Paris Saint-Germain)Success in the Champions League and World Cup has seen this fine facilitator get his due at age 30.15) Vitinha (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)Involved in PSG’s best stuff no matter the competition, with six of his seven club goals coming in the Champions League last season. Unable to shed the stench of Portugal’s World Cup, but he is the world’s finest deep-lying playmaker all the same.16) Luis Díaz (Colombia/Bayern Munich)Took to Germany with glee, bagging 26 goals and 19 assists in 51 appearances to dwarf his output at Liverpool. Struggled for most of the World Cup, however, as Colombia crashed out sooner than expected.17) Gabriel (Brazil/Arsenal)Always close to any fracas, Gabriel was steady as ever as Arsenal enjoyed a long-awaited Premier League title. Some great summer showings at the World Cup, especially against Japan, but struggled – like the rest of his team – against Norway.18) Nuno Mendes (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)Few opponents have found how to best neutralize Mendes, save for hoping that PSG give him another domestic day off between Champions League games.19) Lautaro Martínez (Argentina/Inter)Another dependable goalscoring campaign in Italy, and excelled in a super-sub role during Argentina’s knockout run. One of this era’s great strikers, and already off to a hot start this season.20) William Saliba (France/Arsenal)Especially steady in the Premier League and Champions League, helping Arsenal to their most successful year in decades. His injury hurt France’s chances against Spain in the World Cup semi-final, perhaps bolstering his reputation in absentia.And the rest of the field …21) Achraf Hakimi (Morocco/Paris Saint-Germain)22) Vinícius Júnior (Brazil/Real Madrid)23) Dayot Upamecano (France/Bayern Munich)24) Marc Cucurella (Spain/Chelsea – now at Real Madrid)25) João Neves (Portugal/Paris Saint-Germain)26) Willian Pacho (Ecuador/Paris Saint-Germain)27) Ferran Torres (Spain/Barcelona – now at Paris Saint-Germain)28) Marquinhos (Brazil/Paris Saint-Germain)29) Julián Quiñones (Mexico/Al Qadsiah)30) Sadio Mané (Senegal/Al Nassr)Explore more on these topicsBallon d'OrEuropean club footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: McIlroy warns tours have ‘decisions to make’ as LIV Golf exodus edges closer | LIV Golf Series | The Guardian
description: Rory McIlroy believes traditional tours will soon have ‘decisions to make’ as a player exodus from LIV Golf edges closer
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Rory McIlroy believes traditional tours will soon have ‘decisions to make’ as a player exodus from LIV Golf edges closer
Content: Rory McIlroy, here with Paul McGinley, will be playing against LIV golfers such as Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton in the Irish Open.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAView image in fullscreenRory McIlroy, here with Paul McGinley, will be playing against LIV golfers such as Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton in the Irish Open.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PALIV Golf SeriesMcIlroy warns tours have ‘decisions to make’ as LIV Golf exodus edges closer‘I would predict that you’ll see some guys leave’LIV bankruptcy will invalidate deals with playersEwan MurrayWed 9 Sep 2026 10.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRory McIlroy believes traditional tours will soon have “decisions to make” as a player exodus from LIV Golf edges closer. LIV filing for bankruptcy in the United States on Tuesday means its deals with several high-profile golfers will soon be invalid, leaving them free to negotiate a route back to the PGA and DP World Tours.When asked whether remaining with LIV in its planned, far-less lucrative form would hold appeal, McIlroy was characteristically candid. “I’m not in their shoes but LIV at the start looked a lot more attractive than what LIV 2.0 might be from a financial standpoint,” said the Masters champion.The Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing – stating around $45m (£33.2m) is owed to players – represented LIV’s latest step in rebooting the business due to the removal of funding from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF). Sources familiar with the situation insist contracts have not yet been breached. Terms in place with star names are now unaffordable for LIV. Contracts will inevitably either be renegotiated or cancelled.LIV Golf files for bankruptcy protection as it looks to ‘begin the next chapter’Read moreThe prevailing sense has been for some time that players such as Jon Rahm, Tyrrell Hatton and Cameron Smith will seek torelaunch their careers on the PGA Tour– in return for some form of sanction – when it becomes legally feasible for them to do so. Others, who are less attractive to the PGA Tour, are facing career limbo.“I’m not trying to predict the future but I would predict that you’ll see some guys leave,” said McIlroy. “I think that means other tours have decisions to make. Obviously there’s a lot of players on LIV that can strengthen golf tournaments and make them more competitive. So I would see that as a good thing for the DP World Tour.“I think the health of the DP World Tour is in a really good spot. They have a wonderful alliance with the PGA Tour. I think that alliance is only going to get stronger, especially with the PGA Tour committing to working with the DP World Tour for some of these international events at this time of the year.“So you have PGA Tour players really with nothing to do for five months in this period. If they are incorporated or whoever else is incorporated into these tournaments, that makes them more competitive. Overall, you know, I think with the way things are working out, it’s a very good thing for the golf ecosystem. I think it only makes these tournaments stronger with more competitive players in them.”LIV’s stated aim is to play 10 events, worth $10m each, with 75-man fields in 2027 with the monetary backing of BC Partners. However, huge questions exist over the calibre of player willing to feature. Bryson DeChambeau has been widely tipped to remain with LIV. Lee Westwood has suggested he could do likewise, albeit he has potential to play for high purses on the PGA Tour Champions for over-50s in the United States. “I think some will stay and some won’t,” Westwood told TalkSport. “We’re obviously all independent contractors and everybody’s got different options at different times in their careers, stuff like that. But my plan is to have a good look at LIV 2.0 and make a decision after that.View image in fullscreenBryson DeChambeau has been one of LIV Golf’s highest-profile recruits.Photograph: Justin Casterline/Getty Images“The new partner is coming in to make it a sustainable tour and a sustainable operation so that’s very good but, obviously, whenever bankruptcy is mentioned, that’s never a good idea. It’s bad for a lot of people.”Intriguingly, the PIF plans to loan LIV close to $50m to assist with the bankruptcy process. The role of Saudi Arabia in any future version of LIV is not at all clear. The LIV project has cost the PIF an estimated $5bn. Also unknown is the pace with which the courts will determine LIV’s next steps. Bankruptcy paperwork states LIV has secured $300m in sponsorship contracts from 2027 until 2029 with “blue chip partners.” A large number of staff have already left the business.McIlroy was speaking from the Irish Open at Donald Trump’s Doonbeg resort. The expectation there is that the US president will attend the event over the weekend. “They obviously have to lock down a specific area and make sure that it’s safe for him to travel into, and the entire delegation, whoever that is,” McIlroy said. “Logistically, it provides a bit of a challenge but we are at one of his properties that he has kindly provided for us to play a golf tournament.“The president of the United States wants to come watch a little bit of golf. I think we are all happy to be here, grateful to be here. His presence at the Irish Open makes it a truly international event. That brings more attention and eyeballs to the Irish Open and it can only be a good thing.”Explore more on these topicsLIV Golf SeriesRory McIlroyGolfSaudi Arabia and sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: An embattled Donald Trump is increasingly using sports as prop | Sport | The Guardian
description: Sports is the rare topic in which the president has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: Sports is the rare topic in which the president has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms
Content: Donald Trump attends the Super Bowl in February 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump attends the Super Bowl in February 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersSportAn embattled Donald Trump is increasingly using sports as propLeander SchaerlaeckensSports is the rare topic in which the president has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred termsWed 9 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTShareLately, it seems Donald Trump’s scope of interests has narrowed to a few things: remaking downtown Washington DC in his gaudy image; wars he thinks he can win quickly and easily, even though he can’t.Also, golf. Always golf.Ever golf.We hear less and less about Trump’s plans to overhaul healthcare, reshore manufacturing jobs or address the budget deficit. Yet one other subject, aligned with his lifelong interests, continues to preoccupy him: sports.And in this area, his ideological project has methodically and loudly – since nothing of consequence can ever be done quietly by this administration – made more gains than just about anywhere else.Which is to say that Trump, or more likelythose seeking to swiminthe slipstream of Trumpism, are hard at work trying to put sports back to how it looked in the 1980s. After all, that’s when the president’s view of the world, and how it should function, ossified.This manifests in ways big and small, in consequences intended and accidental.Here’s a relatively small and surely accidental one.When Los Angeles FC soldVenezuela international David Martínez to Denmark’s FC Midtjylland for $8.4m recently, the club did not do so for sporting reasons – or not entirely. The winger, named tothe Guardian’s 2023 Next Generationclass, had difficulty adapting to life in Los Angeles after arriving as an 18-year-old because his family couldn’t get visas to visit him,according to the club.If Trump and his goons had even heard of the now-20-year-old, which they almost certainly hadn’t, he would have hardly been a top target of their policies. But that they have driven him to leave the country will would satisfy them all the same. This is exactly what the administration’s travel bans and curbs on visas were intended to achieve: to put people off coming to the US, or staying here.Then there’s the big stuff.The rolling campaign to “save” women’s sports from transgender athletes, who exist in vanishingly small numbers and are far from the threat those on the right would have you believe. This panic is propagated by a rabble who very proudly didn’t care about women’s sports at all until they spotted an opening to make a political profit from it.Trump’slooming presenceover the summer’s World Cup, and hisactive interferencein it. His attendance at the NBA finals, the Daytona 500 and the Ryder Cup, appearances thatseemed to cursehis favored participants.There’s theexecutive orderattempting to unwind the decades-overdue gains made by college athletes in winning the right to be treated like every other American worker. They can finally be paid for their valuable labor and move (almost) freely between programs in search of the best opportunities – same as their coaches and administrators have always been able to do.Foreign students and college athletes, meanwhile, find it harder and less attractive to come to and stay in the US on account of the same difficulties in bagging visas that chased off Martínez. That makes college sports more homogeneous and therefore, in Trump’s thinking, better.In trying to rearrange things to how they once were – the exact moment in the past when things were great; a time that nobody can seem to pinpoint, but which you’ll no doubt remember with searing clarity – Trump has even gone so far as to issue an executive order to try to protect the Army-Navy football game’s exclusive TV time slot. The College Football Playoff’s lurching expansion threatened to creep into the second Saturday of December, traditionally and legally set aside for the Commander-in-Chief’s Trophy.“Such scheduling conflicts weaken the national focus on our Military Service Academies and detract from a morale-building event of vital interest to the Department of War,”the orderreads.Also apparently intended as a morale-building event wasthe much-panned UFC eventon the White House lawn to celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary, and, more pressingly, Trump’s 80th birthday. The first professional sporting event on the White House grounds managed tolose $30m, even though the fighters were apparently paidat least partly in cryptocurrencyissued by a Trump company.When he sensed he would be met by a friendly crowd, Trump became the first sitting president toattend the Super Bowl. In the same spirit, he traveled to a World Series game in 2021, when he was out of power,just to do the racist tomahawk chopwith Atlanta Braves fans.He more or less ordered an IndyCar race to be held in DC, the Freedom 250, which was well attended but severely disrupted car and plane traffic in the capital. The awkward layout of the course, meanwhile, meant that nearly half the cars didn’t finish all the laps. No matter, Trump took a lap around the track in his presidential limousine. With no other cars on the road, he finished first.Then there are the unprovoked and untethered broadsides. Such as the time Trump suggested the National Football League change its name to accommodate soccer. Orsuggested LeBron James was a racistbecause he doesn’t play golf with the president. Or when he plunged a cleaver into the culture war prime cuts ofrestoring the Washington Commanders and Cleveland Guardiansto their old, racist names.Several of Trump’s golf courses have hosted events staged by LIV Golf, the Saudi-backed breakaway golf circuit thatappears to be on life support. If it should croak, it would share this distinction with the last sporting venture that Trump was intimately entangled with: the New Jersey Generals of the old United States Football League. Trump, who owned the franchise,bungled it into bankruptcyand took the entire league down with him.Yet the lesson that has stuck with himsince childhoodis that sports holds a privileged place in our national conscience, and that it serves as a powerful messaging conduit. Now, as president, his efforts have hardly been concerted or coordinated, but sports is the rare topic where Trump has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.Explore more on these topicsSportDonald TrumpUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: Ødegaard ‘edge’ delights Arteta as Arsenal secure narrow win at Napoli | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Martin Ødegaard’s second-half strike gave Arsenal a 1-0 Champions League win in Naples, with Mikel Arteta praising the playmaker’s recent impact
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Martin Ødegaard’s second-half strike gave Arsenal a 1-0 Champions League win in Naples, with Mikel Arteta praising the playmaker’s recent impact
Content: Martin Ødegaard (right) wheels away alongside Bruno Guimarães after scoring the winner.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersView image in fullscreenMartin Ødegaard (right) wheels away alongside Bruno Guimarães after scoring the winner.Photograph: Guglielmo Mangiapane/ReutersChampions LeagueØdegaard ‘edge’ delights Arteta as Arsenal secure narrow win at NapoliEd Aaronsat the Stadio Diego Armando MaradonaWed 9 Sep 2026 17.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter their record-breaking feats last year in theChampions League, Arsenal are at it again. But having been delayed along with hundreds of travelling supporters by travel chaos on Tuesday, Mikel Arteta’s side had to bide their time against Napoli until Martin Ødegaard continued his rich vein of goalscoring with the crucial strike 15 minutes from full time.Perhaps it was the fact that, at Uefa’s insistence, they were forced to wear red shorts for the first time since a Premier League game against Watford in 2022 thatArsenalwere not quite at their flowing best here and missed a hatful of chances.Alexis Mac Allister makes his point as Liverpool fight back to defeat AtléticoRead moreYet they were deserved winners in the end and the substitute Noni Madueke should have made the ­victory more comprehensive late on.Having come so close to breaking their duck in this competition last year after becoming the first team to win all eight of their league stage matches, Arsenal look capable of going one better this time if Ødegaard can keep up this sparkling form.He now has four goals in his last five games after scoring once in all competitions last year and it was the Norway captain whose name was being chanted by the fans who were kept behind more than an hour after the final whistle.“That’s what we need – players with that mindset to decide the game and to play with that personality,” said Arteta. “He’s getting into those positions much more in recent games and I feel he has this emotional state that he knows that the ball can go in. He’s got that edge and he’s now got different relationships around him [in the team] as well. That helps.”Arteta has bad memories of this stadium after being sent off in a 2-0 defeat during the Champions League group stage in 2013. But Arsenal’s most recent match here ended in victory as they qualified for the Europa League semi-finals under Unai Emery in 2019. Both clubs have been crowned domestic champions since then, withNapoliending their 33-year wait in 2023 then doing it again two years later. Yet Champions League success has continued to elude them after finishing 30th in the league phase last season.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta talks with Kevin De Bruyne, the former Manchester City midfielder, after the match.Photograph: Ciro De Luca/ReutersThat was in stark contrast to Arsenal, who were unbeaten over 14 matches before falling at the final hurdle. It was telling that Arteta kept faith with four of his back five that started against Chelsea on Sunday, with Piero Hincapié replacing Riccardo Calafiori at left-back but failing to match the Italian’s finishing ability with one glaring miss. Mikel Merino, Eberechi Eze and Viktor Gyökeres also made their first starts of the season but largely disappointed, with the Sweden striker making way for Kai Havertz just before Ødegaard’s winner.Those Arsenal supporters that did make it to southern Italy had no problem making themselves heard throughout, with plenty of empty seats in the home sections despite Max Allegri’s attempts to rally Napoli’s fans beforehand. The game quickly settled into a pattern as the visitors set up camp in Napoli’s half and the hosts attempted to hit them on the break. Kevin De Bruyne – no stranger to facing Arsenal after a decade in the sky blue of Manchester City – forced David Raya into a rare mistake after a typically driving run through the midfield but the ball was scrambled away to safety.That came just after a spectacular overhead kick from Bukayo Saka at the other end had been saved by Alex Meret. Merino should have scored when he was set up by Eze’s clever header across the face of goal before Ben White drilled a shot straight into Meret’s grateful gloves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMatteo Politano managed to test Raya again as Napoli continued to find gaps in Arsenal’s normally watertight defence. Saka blazed over after a brilliant through ball from Ødegaard on the stroke of half-time, with replays confirming the assistant had been wrong to raise his flag.View image in fullscreenMartin Ødegaard scores the only goal of the match at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesMeret did not return for the second half and was replaced by Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, once on Manchester United’s books. The Serbia goalkeeper was a mere spectator for a flowing Arsenal move featuring a sumptuous scooped pass into the area that ended with Hincapié missing the target after being picked out at the far post by Ben White’s header. Suddenly Napoli found themselves suffocated by a blanket of red. Allegri, who knows what it feels like to have lost in a Champions League final after suffering that fate twice in three years at Juventus, responded by switching to a back five and trying to hang on.Arsenal’s pressure eventually told when another substitute, Christos Tzolis, exchanged passes with White and teed up Ødegaard, whose shot flew in off the post despite Milinkovic-Savic just getting his fingertips to the ball. Havertz had a goal disallowed for offside in injury time, but the mission was already complete.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueNapoliArsenalEuropean club footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Cole Palmer powers Chelsea to comeback win over Leeds in nine-goal epic | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: Chelsea scored six second-half goals after making four half-time substitutions in a thrilling 6-3 win against Leeds in the Carabao Cup third round
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Chelsea scored six second-half goals after making four half-time substitutions in a thrilling 6-3 win against Leeds in the Carabao Cup third round
Content: Cole Palmer plays to the crowd after starting Chelsea’s fightback against Leeds.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCole Palmer plays to the crowd after starting Chelsea’s fightback against Leeds.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesCarabao CupCole Palmer powers Chelsea to comeback win over Leeds in nine-goal epicJacob Steinbergat Stamford BridgeWed 9 Sep 2026 17.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhere’s the fun in doing it the easy way? Chelsea remain chaotic at the back but can drag their opponents into horrible places. It helps, mind you, to have some assistance from the referee. Jarred Gillett and Cole Palmer? They made for a killer ­combination as Chelsea swerved embarrassment and treated Stamford Bridge to one of life’s rarities: a classic in the third round of theCarabao Cup.Gillett, a referee who always seems to be guessing when he makes key calls, was the villain as far as Leeds were concerned. They had just gone 2-0 up when Gillett altered the flow of the tie by pointing to the spot after Pep Chavarría made the most of slight contact from Daniel James. The subsequent conversion from Palmer was inevitable and from there so was the comeback fromChelsea, who rattled through four goals in 12 minutes before eventually reaching the last 16 by winning 6-3.Ødegaard stuns Napoli as Arsenal make winning start in Champions LeagueRead moreIt made little sense. It could have gone down as Xabi Alonso’s first ­misjudgment as Chelsea’s manager. The Carabao Cup is important given the Spaniard’s side are not in Europe, but his rotation almost backfired. Chelsea were shambolic after making nine changes – the 16-year-old debutant Reggie Watson was overrun in midfield while Estêvão Willian and Jamie Gittens struggled in attack – and Alonso was in emergency mode when he made a quadruple change at half-time.“I take responsibility,” Alonso said. “No player is to blame. It’s the ­decisions we took. When you don’t have this time to work with them, it’s difficult to compete at this level. I need to take my own blame for the things that happen. I need to be able to help them better. They are not responsible. After you need to react and think what’s better for the team.”Quick GuideChampionship: Ten-man West Brom win at Derby to go topShowWest Bromwich Albion held on for a memorable 1-0 victory over Derby at Pride Park, after playing for more than an hour with 10 men. Aune Heggebø's early goal proved enough to take the Baggies top of the table, despite Brayann Pereira being dismissed on his debut after collecting two first-half yellow cards.Derby had started the stronger, but West Brom swept downfield to score in the 16th minute, Jimmy-Jay Morgan whipping in a low cross from the left which Heggebø [pictured] finished at the near post. The visitors were rocked by the dismissal of Pereira in the 34th minute, as he was shown a second yellow card for a clumsy challenge on Charlie Taylor.The hosts went close just before half-time when David Ozoh flashed a low ball across the six-yard box with no white shirt able to turn it in. Derby should have levelled in the 68th minute but Lars-Jørgen Salvesen headed over from Joe Ward’s cross. Late on, Nat Phillips made a great clearance after a late goalmouth scramble, summing up a performance full of grit and resolve.James Morrison's side move above West Ham to top the Championship table with 13 points from six games. EitherCharltonorQPRcould have joined them on 13 points, but the sides played out a stalemate at the Valley. Derby, meanwhile, slipped into the bottom three with their fourth defeat in six games.Norwichmoved up to ninth in the table as they edged past visitorsBirmingham2-1 to make it three wins in four league games. Oscar Schwartau's screamer opened the scoring, the young Dane lashing an unstoppable right-footed drive past James Beadle from 25 yards out.Papa Diallo's first goal for the Canaries doubled their advantage before the break, as the Senegal winger sidefooted home from Andre Brooks' cross. Carlos Vicente pulled a goal back for the visitors, but wasted a glorious chance to equalise near the end as Chris Davies’ men suffered their first league defeat this season.Press AssociationPhotograph: Morgan Harlow/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Equally Alonso can take credit for responding. His moves were decisive. Reece James offered security after replacing Watson and Pedro Neto scored after coming on for Malo Gusto, who could barely complete a pass during a wretched first half. Leeds, beaten at this stage for the 14th time in 18 years, were overwhelmed once their lead was halved. Morgan Rogers and Palmer were devastating after replacing Estêvão and Gittens. Rogers had a hand in four goals and Palmer, who scored twice, seemed affronted by the notion of Leeds going through.It finished as another thrilling attacking display from Chelsea, who have scored 16 goals in Alonso’s first five games. There are flaws to fix at the other end, though. Leeds also experimented, Daniel Farke making eight changes, but controlled the first half. They led when the Bosnia and Herzegovina centre-back Tarik Muharemovic, signed from Sassuolo last summer, headed Harry Wilson’s corner past Mike Penders in the 23rd minute.Chelsea have already conceded 10 goals in all competitions. Leeds could have doubled their lead through Sean Longstaff. Valentín Barco and ­Watson, son of the former Wigan ­midfielder Ben Watson, were second best in midfield.Leeds were on their way when Barco lost possession three minutes into the second half. Ethan Ampadu charged past Rogers and found Lukas Nmecha, who teed up Brenden ­Aaronson to make it 2-0.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPedro Neto fires home Chelsea’s third goal at Stamford Bridge.Photograph: Adam Davy/PAChelsea needed a lift. Chavarría crossed from the left and went to ground. Gillett whistled and Palmer scored with 53 minutes played. “He gave out of nothing a penalty where it wasn’t even a chance for them,” Farke said. “A quality player scores and the body language of the Chelsea players was different.”Palmer was in his element, equalising in the 55th minute after Rogers laid the ball off for his pal to stroke a casual finish past Michael Zetterer from 20 yards. Chelsea were rampant and led on the hour, Palmer and Rogers combining for Neto to finish well. Leeds looked dizzy. They readied the changes but Danny Welbeck made it 4-2 with a sharp turn and finish in the 65th minute.Leeds kept fighting. Dominic Calvert-Lewin came on and pulled one back to remind Alonso of Chelsea’s defensive weaknesses. Chelsea responded, Rogers crossing for Barco to score his first goal for the club. The sixth followed, Barco’s mis-hit shot diverted in by Welbeck. “A crazy nuts game,” Farke said. That’s been the way for Chelsea under Alonso.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupChelseaLeeds Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish roundup: Miovski hits last-gasp Rangers winner and Celtic keep 100% record | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: A dramatic last-gasp strike from substitute Bojan Miovski gave Rangers a 1-0 Premiership win over St Mirren, while Celtic were 1-0 winners over St Johnstone
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A dramatic last-gasp strike from substitute Bojan Miovski gave Rangers a 1-0 Premiership win over St Mirren, while Celtic were 1-0 winners over St Johnstone
Content: Rangers' Bojan Miovski celebrates his side's late winner at Ibrox.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAView image in fullscreenRangers' Bojan Miovski celebrates his side's late winner at Ibrox.Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PAScottish PremiershipScottish roundup: Miovski hits last-gasp Rangers winner and Celtic keep 100% recordRangers beat St Mirren 1-0 at IbroxCeltic also narrow winners at St JohnstonePress AssociationWed 9 Sep 2026 17.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA dramatic last-gasp strike from substitute Bojan Miovski
