title: Rosario ‘grabbed my bottom’ during Manchester City’s win at Porto, claims Haaland | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Erling Haaland has described the incident as ‘a little interesting’, while also revealing that heading practice with his dad, Alf Inge, helped him to score Manchester City’s opener
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Erling Haaland has described the incident as ‘a little interesting’, while also revealing that heading practice with his dad, Alf Inge, helped him to score Manchester City’s opener
Content: Erling Haaland grapples with Pablo Rosario during Manchester City’s 2-0 victory at Porto.Photograph: Sports Press Photo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenErling Haaland grapples with Pablo Rosario during Manchester City’s 2-0 victory at Porto.Photograph: Sports Press Photo/Getty ImagesManchester CityRosario ‘grabbed my bottom’ during Manchester City’s win at Porto, claims HaalandForward says incident was ‘a little interesting’Heading practice with Alf Inge helped with openerJamie JacksonWed 9 Sep 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleErling Haaland has claimed Pablo Rosario “grabbed my bottom” duringManchester City’s 2-0 win at Portoon Tuesday. The incident occurred in the 92nd minute, with Haaland having scored City’s goals. The forward and midfielder grappled, went to ground and were booked after being separated.“I was really keen on a hat-trick and it seemed like he was very eager to stop me from getting it,” Haaland told Norway’s TV 2. “It was a little interesting, that – you’ll be seeing a picture where he’s grabbing my bottom. It’ll be interesting to see that picture.”Haaland double gives Manchester City ideal Champions League start in PortoRead moreThe flashpoint followed one as half-time neared in a niggly encounter. After Marc Guéhi and Gabriel Veiga had a coming together that left the latter with a head injury, tempers frayed. When the teams walked off for the interval a bust-up occurred involving players and staff near the tunnel.Images showed Rúben Dias placing a hand on what appeared to be Francesco Farioli, thePortohead coach. Uefa will wait for the match report of the referee, Szymon Marciniak, and its delegate, Stéphanie Ford, before deciding whether to bring any action against the defender or City.Haaland’s 47th-minute opener was a header and the No 9 revealed he had been working on the skill recently with his dad, Alf Inge, a former City player.“Two days ago I was practising headers with my dad in the garden,” he said. “Over the years, I’ve worked a lot on my heading. I’ve improved it massively and it’s become a strength of my game. I think a lot of it comes down to experience.”Haalandconcurred with his manager, Enzo Maresca, that he may need a break soon. “It’s not easy to get any rest in this business,” the 26-year-old said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Like during the international break, we play four games in 10 or 11 days, so it’s not easy. But you have to try to squeeze in a few days here and there and give your mind a bit of a break.”Explore more on these topicsManchester CityErling HaalandPortoChampions LeagueEuropean club footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: Champions League roundup: Raphinha shines as Barcelona thrash Feyenoord | Champions League | The Guardian
description: Raphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice as Barcelona eased to a 5-1 win over Feyenoord in the Champions League
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Raphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice as Barcelona eased to a 5-1 win over Feyenoord in the Champions League
Content: Raphinha celebrates after scoring Barcelona’s third goal against Feyenoord.Photograph: Álex Caparrós/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRaphinha celebrates after scoring Barcelona’s third goal against Feyenoord.Photograph: Álex Caparrós/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueChampions League roundup: Raphinha shines as Barcelona thrash FeyenoordBrazilian scores twice in 5-1 victory at Camp NouTorres scores hat-trick as PSG thump Slovan BratislavaAgenciesWed 9 Sep 2026 18.08 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRaphinha let his goals do the talking after being omitted from the Ballon d’Or shortlist, striking twice asBarcelonaeased to a 5-1 win overFeyenoordin theChampions League.The Brazilian was a surprise omission fromthis week’s 30-strong list of candidatesfor the prestigious award but brushed any disappointment aside to continue his early season hot streak at a rain-soaked Camp Nou. The forward finished brilliantly in the third minute and added a second just before the hour mark to down the Eredivisie side and take his tally to eight goals in six outings at the start of the campaign.Ødegaard stuns Napoli as Arsenal make winning start in Champions LeagueRead moreThe summer signing Karim Adeyemi produced a stunning finish, Lamine Yamal stroked a free-kick through a gap in the Dutch wall and recent arrival Gabriel Jesus opened his account for the club just two minutes after stepping off the bench.There was little to celebrate for Giovanni van Bronckhorst on his Barça return but Sem Steijn gave the visiting fans something to enjoy when he poked in at far post late on.“The most important thing is we are playing like a team, like one unit,” theBarcelonahead coach, Hansi Flick, said. “We controlled the game, we are dominant and this is fantastic to see. This is our style and how we want to play.”Ferran Torres scored a hat-trick and Ousmane Dembélé also starred asParis Saint-Germainbegan their quest to win a third successive Champions League title by thrashingSlovan Bratislava6-1 at the Parc des Princes.View image in fullscreenParis Saint-Germain’s Ferran Torres celebrates scoring their fifth goal with Ousmane Dembélé.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersLast year’s Ballon d’Or winner Dembélé had scored twice by the midway point of the first half in the French capital, and then set up Spain’s World Cup final hero Torres to make it 3-0 by the interval.Torres, a close-season signing from Barcelona, added two more just after the restart to complete his hat-trick before the hour mark, with Suleiman Camara pulling one back for the Slovakian champions and Fabián Ruiz then sealing PSG’s win.Elsewhere,Stuttgart’sErmedin Demirovic struck a 12-minute first-half hat-trick to ⁠earn ⁠a ​3-1 victory overViking Stavanger.He opened the ​scoring after 20 minutes with a touch at the near post, but Viking, making their first appearance in the league phase of the Champions League, were level two minutes later when Zlatko Tripic finished a ⁠swift counter-attack with his left foot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDemirovic quickly re-established the lead ​in the ​26th minute and then completed ​the hat-trick with a hooked volley six minutes later. “For me personally it was the perfect start and also for the team as a whole,” Demirovic told Dazn.Quick GuideChampionship: Ten-man West Brom win at Derby to go topShowWest Bromwich Albion held on for a memorable 1-0 victory over Derby at Pride Park, after playing for more than an hour with 10 men. Aune Heggebø's early goal proved enough to take the Baggies top of the table, despite Brayann Pereira being dismissed on his debut after collecting two first-half yellow cards.Derby had started the stronger, but West Brom swept downfield to score in the 16th minute, Jimmy-Jay Morgan whipping in a low cross from the left which Heggebø [pictured] finished at the near post. The visitors were rocked by the dismissal of Pereira in the 34th minute, as he was shown a second yellow card for a clumsy challenge on Charlie Taylor.The hosts went close just before half-time when David Ozoh flashed a low ball across the six-yard box with no white shirt able to turn it in. Derby should have levelled in the 68th minute but Lars-Jørgen Salvesen headed over from Joe Ward’s cross. Late on, Nat Phillips made a great clearance after a late goalmouth scramble, summing up a performance full of grit and resolve.James Morrison's side move above West Ham to top the Championship table with 13 points from six games. EitherCharltonorQPRcould have joined them on 13 points, but the sides played out a stalemate at the Valley. Derby, meanwhile, slipped into the bottom three with their fourth defeat in six games.Norwichmoved up to ninth in the table as they edged past visitorsBirmingham2-1 to make it three wins in four league games. Oscar Schwartau's screamer opened the scoring, the young Dane lashing an unstoppable right-footed drive past James Beadle from 25 yards out.Papa Diallo's first goal for the Canaries doubled their advantage before the break, as the Senegal winger sidefooted home from Andre Brooks' cross. Carlos Vicente pulled a goal back for the visitors, but wasted a glorious chance to equalise near the end as Chris Davies’ men suffered their first league defeat this season.Press AssociationPhotograph: Morgan Harlow/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Sporting, quarter-finalists last season for the first time since 1983, fought back to see offGalatasaray3-1 in Lisbon.Galatasaray took an early lead through Gonçalo Inacio’s own goal but Geny ​Catamo punished poor defending to equalise in the 27th minute. Luis Suárez converted a 57th-minute penalty to putSportingahead and a blistering free kick from Rodrigo Zalazar six minutes later sealed the win.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueBarcelonaFeyenoordStuttgartViking FKLiverpoolAtlético MadridnewsShareReuse this content

title: Carrick up for ‘magical’ Champions League but derby timing ‘not ideal’ | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick admitted playing in the Champions League on Thursday night was ‘not ideal’ with the Manchester derby on Sunday
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Michael Carrick admitted playing in the Champions League on Thursday night was ‘not ideal’ with the Manchester derby on Sunday
Content: Marcus Rashford played in the Champions League last season with Barcelona, reaching the quarter-finals.Photograph: Alex Livesey/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarcus Rashford played in the Champions League last season with Barcelona, reaching the quarter-finals.Photograph: Alex Livesey/Getty ImagesManchester UnitedCarrick up for ‘magical’ Champions League but derby timing ‘not ideal’United play Sabah, then Manchester City on Sunday‘To win the Champions League was the ultimate’Will UnwinWed 9 Sep 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick is excited to leadManchester Unitedon their return to the “magical” Champions League but admitted playing on Thursday night was “not ideal” with the derby on Sunday.United welcome Sabah to Old Trafford after a two-yearChampions Leagueabsence. The Azerbaijani club are making their debut among Europe’s elite, having been in existence for less than a decade.Maitland-Niles stunner rescues late point for Everton against Manchester UnitedRead more“It’s a magical competition,” Carrick, who won the competition in 2008 with United, said. “It’s where we all want to be. When you’re out of it, you realise how special it is, and when you’re in it, you want to make the most of it. I think we’ve all seen some special, special nights and felt some special things in this competition over the years.“It’s where we want to be, it’s what we want to get back to, and it’s the best competition to challenge yourself and to push against the best. We’re delighted to be here, but we’re not here to just enjoy the occasion. We’re here to do business and go as far as we possibly can.“To win the Champions League for me was the ultimate and was the best feeling I’ve had. Be nice some day to feel that again.”United have made a mixed start to their Premier League campaign, picking up four points from three games, and this will be a testing period for a club that played just 40 games last season. If United reach the quarter-finals of the Carabao Cup, they will not have a free midweek until mid-January.View image in fullscreenMichael Carrick won the Champions League in 2008 against Chelsea in Moscow.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesManchester City visit Old Trafford on Sunday and will have an extra two days to recover from their gameat Porto on Tuesday. “I’m not concerned,” Carrick said of the turnaround.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I wouldn’t say it’s ideal in some ways, but it’s not something that we’ve given too much thought about. We’re not in control of that. We’ve got to deal with the cards that we’re dealt and that’s what it is, so we’ll make the most of it.”United’s only senior left-back, Luke Shaw, did not train on Wednesday after being given a further day of rest. “We’ll see by tomorrow how he is, but it’s not an ongoing thing or a plan,” Carrick said.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickChampions LeagueEuropean club footballnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A dream come true’: behind the scenes with Wolves Women as they enter new era | Women's Super League 2 | The Guardian
description: The Guardian joined Wolves at the start of their first season as a fully professional side, determined to show they’re no pushovers
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The Guardian joined Wolves at the start of their first season as a fully professional side, determined to show they’re no pushovers
Content: The Wolves Women squad visit the Guru Nanak Satsang Sikh Gurdwara during an afternoon city tour in Wolverhampton.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Wolves Women squad visit the Guru Nanak Satsang Sikh Gurdwara during an afternoon city tour in Wolverhampton.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianWomen's Super League 2‘A dream come true’: behind the scenes with Wolves Women as they enter new eraThe Guardian joined Wolves at the start of their first season as a fully professional side, determined to show they’re no pushoversTom GarryWed 9 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSuddenly the bustling classroom at the back of the Guru Nanak Satsang Sikh Gurdwara falls almost silent and all eyes are on Dan McNamara. The Wolves head coach, experiencing a wrestling lesson, is engaged in a tense tussle. He twists, panting and heaving, eventually ends up on top of his opponent, and the room erupts. Compared with some of the challenges McNamara and Wolves have grappled with during his eight and a half years coaching the team, this exercise was child’s play.Wolves, promoted to Women’s Super League Two in May, are visiting the gurdwara – which became Wolverhampton’s first in 1966 – as part of an afternoon city tour which has also included a trip to the historic The Halls music venue and a walk in the centre, as some of their new signings acquaint themselves with the area before the club’s first season as a fully professional women’s team, and their first WSL2 home match, against Sheffield United, on Sunday.View image in fullscreenThe Wolves head coach, Dan McNamara, in his new office at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianVictory against Plymouth in the third-tier promotion playoff was the culmination of years of hard graft in the amateur game, and McNamara pauses for reflection as he chats from his office overlooking the Sir Jack Hayward training ground in Compton.“Initially, I think my ‘office’ was me sitting in the driver’s seat of an old Ford Focus,” he says. “I first walked on to an Astroturf with about seven bibs, three footballs and 58 players and probably thought: ‘What the hell have I done?’ Now I’m in my own office. We’ve got a fantastic setup here, we’ve got our own spaces for the women, changing facilities, which have been added over the summer. It’s night and day.View image in fullscreenThe Wolves captain, Anna Morphet, leads players during a session at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian“Everybody grows up and dreams of being a professional footballer. I was no different. My claim to fame was I was in the same youth team as Wayne Rooney for a few years at Everton – our tactics were: ‘Pass the ball to Wayne and he will score.’ And [when I left Everton] I probably fell out of love with the game for a little bit. To be here now working professionally in football is a dream come true.“People always talk about what success looks like. And I think: ‘Leave the place in a better place than what you got it.’ I don’t think anyone could argue that we’re going to leave this place in a better place than when we first picked it up. It’s not been me; the girls have gone on the pitch and they’ve achieved it. But to have inputted a small bit into making dreams come true gets me quite emotional.”View image in fullscreenThe Wolves squad are put through their paces at the Sir Jack Haywood training ground.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianPromotion was a long time coming for Wolves, who won tier three’s northern division in 2022 but – with only one team promoted then – lost the playoff decider against the southern champions, Southampton. McNamara missed that because he was overseas with the Royal Air Force, and watched from the Falkland Islands. Since 2024, he has coached Wolves full-time as part of the RAF’s elite athlete scheme – “they have extended me for an additional year to continue at WSL2; hopefully I can do them proud and represent the air force in a good way over the next 12 months,” he says – and his team lost two league games across the next two seasons.In 2025, they finished second but were heartbroken to find the club hadnot applied for a licence for promotion. A year later, with a new executive chair in Nathan Shi, the club’s approach to the women’s team has changed, and McNamara’s team have cabins at the training ground as private changing areas, a meeting/analysis room and places to relax together. Some of the squad engage in a tense round of the card game Dobble after having breakfast together, before heading out for training. Further new training pitches will follow soon.View image in fullscreenThe England youth international goalkeeper Emily Orman has arrived on loan from London City Lionesses.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianThis summer the club also hired a new head of women’s and girls football, Russ Fraser, who worked in the WSL at Reading, West Ham, Leicester and Liverpool over the past decade, before a spell with Al-Qadsiah in Saudi Arabia. Many of last season’s squad left their day jobs and turned professional but there has also been a big recruitment drive. Signings include former WSL players such as Mel Lawley, Jasmine Matthews, Yana Daniëls and Mel Filis.“We don’t want to just be a team that goes up and then straight back down, so the work was almost immediately after the playoff,” McNamara says. “It’s been non-stop since. We were quite careful at what we went after. We wanted to bring in the right technical players, but also players that represent this great club and the city. And that’s hard work, ethics, having the right morals on the pitch, being quite energetic.”Another new signing the England youth goalkeeper Emily Orman, on loan from London City Lionesses, enjoyed taking part in the wrestling demonstration. “I’ve never wrestled before,” she says. “That was really tough. I got a real bead on doing that!” It is not the squad’s only team-building experience. They also went bouldering in the Lake District, and the midfielder Tammi George – who first joined Wolves aged 13, before a spell at Sunday’s opponents – says: “That brought the group together so much because people were put through difficult situations and needed an arm around them at times. Everybody really saw the benefit.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe Wolves squad take a walking tour through the city.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianOn the city walk the players learn about everything from the AD910 battle of Tettenhall to the origins of the Prince Albert statue, and are informed of the iconic sets played by bands such as Queen and Nirvana at The Halls. There is also an important stop at Molineux, first so the players can help out at a session run by the club’s foundation during the school holidays for youngsters, through Premier League Kicks, in partnership with West Midlands police. The squad play pool and help with arts and crafts before touring the club’s museum, where the women’s football writer and Wolves fan Tony Leighton has written the latest part of an exhibition charting the women’s team’s rise.View image in fullscreenThe Wolves players Mel Lawley (left) and Chloe Williams play table football with attendees during a summer youth club organised by the Wolves Foundation at Molineux.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianThe former BBC WM presenter Jenny Wilkes has been the chair of Wolves Women since 1999 and is full of pride. She knows how much the efforts of volunteers have helped the club. “I remember Rachael Heyhoe Flint, who had been such an amazing support for us in the days when it literally was one woman and a dog watching the game and she was one woman who brought her dog and walked her dog around the pitch,” she says. “We’re come a long way since then.“It’s incredible, being fully professional, which we never thought we’d manage to do. In the long history of the club, we have played in the top flight before but it was when the top flight wasn’t professional. Now to see professional footballers at Wolves Women for the first time really is incredible.”View image in fullscreenThe squad take part in wrestling at Wolverhampton Wrestling Club.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianThe captain, Anna Morphet, who handed in her notice for her day job as a physio a week after Wolves’ promotion, says: “We used to collect the kit out the back of Macca’s car boot. Those 90 minutes [against Plymouth] were the opportunity to change our lives. The work that’s gone on over the summer and in pre-season has been immense and I think now it’s about believing that we are ready for this level.”Wolves opened with a defeat, albeit a respectable one, 2-0 at one of the favourites for promotion, Newcastle. Fraser says: “Wherever we finish in the league, I want other teams to go: ‘Wow, Wolves were so much better than I thought they were,’ because I think a lot of teams will probably think: ‘Oh, Wolves have just come up, they’ll go straight back down.’ I think we’re better than that. I think we’ve got a good group here.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super League 2Women's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rybakina sinks Zheng to grab No 1 spot and set up US Open semi-final with Gauff | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Elena Rybakina will be the new world No 1 after ending Zheng Qinwen’s US Open run, with Coco Gauff up next in the semi-finals
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Elena Rybakina will be the new world No 1 after ending Zheng Qinwen’s US Open run, with Coco Gauff up next in the semi-finals
Content: ‘It’s just a number right now’: Elena Rybakina was typically understated after becoming world No 1.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘It’s just a number right now’: Elena Rybakina was typically understated after becoming world No 1.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026Rybakina sinks Zheng to grab No 1 spot and set up US Open semi-final with GauffRybakina into semis after 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 victoryCoco Gauff battles back to beat Mirra AndreevaTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsWed 9 Sep 2026 17.57 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElena Rybakina will become the No 1 woman in the world for the first time after orchestrating a supreme recovery to reach the semi-finals of the US Open with a 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 win over the Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen.By becoming just the 30th player in the history of the WTA to reach the No 1 ranking, Rybakina ends Aryna Sabalenka’s extended spell at the top. The Belarusian has held the position for 99 successive weeks, the sixth-longest consecutive reign in history, and 107 weeks in total.US Open 2026 quarter-finals: Andreeva v Gauff, Rybakina beats Zheng to become world No 1 – liveRead moreDuring last year’s North American hardcourt swing, Rybakina fell out of the top 10 and she was struggling badly with her health and game. She has responded with by far the best year of her career, following up her WTA Finals triumph in November with her second grand slam titleat the Australian Open, four years after her first triumph at Wimbledon. She has also won titles in Ningbo and Stuttgart in addition to finishing runner-up in Indian Wells and Toronto.Between Sabalenka’s difficult past five months and Rybakina’s resurgence, the Kazakhstani arrived in New York fully conscious of the opportunity before her. The No 1 ranking was always in her hands, with a run to the semi-final guaranteeing it from the beginning.However, so many things seemed to be conspiring against Rybakina. She was forced to retire from her quarter-final against Iga Swiatek at the Cincinnati Open, 12 days before her first round in New York, due to an achilles injury. Rybakina said she did not train for seven days and she was unsure of how her body would react. “I couldn’t do much in the gym movement-wise, so we had to really go day by day,” she said. “It’s an amazing progress. I’m really glad how everything worked out. We didn’t even know if I’m going to be able to play or not. I have a great team. Also, a good doctor on the phone all the time.”View image in fullscreenElena Rybakina shakes hands with Zheng Qinwen after their three-set tussle.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAWhile a semi-final has always been attainable, the US Open has long stood as her most challenging major, the one grand slam Rybakina has struggled to perform at. Her fourth-round loss last year was previously her best result in New York. This time, she has maintained her focus and navigated each challenge.Rybakina started slowly against a Zheng radiating confidence after her previouscomeback victoriesover Madison Keys and Swiatek and in a contest between two of the biggest servers in the world, one sloppy service game from Rybakina marked the difference between them in set one.But the 27-year-old responded brilliantly, finding rhythm behind her destructive serve and dominating the baseline with her easy power to quickly force a third set. Although Rybakina eased through her service games early in set three, it was Zheng who generated the first opportunity, earning a break point at 4-3 in the third set. A tentative forehand approach shot and volley from Rybakina provided Zheng with a straightforward pass, but the Chinese fired her backhand long. Rybakina immediately slammed the door shut with some excellent serves, and she completed a sequence worthy of the best player in the world by rolling through the final three games.As Zheng’s final feeble forehand landed in the bottom of the net, Rybakina celebrated this career-defining milestone in a typically understated manner, her expression barely changing as she meekly closed her hand into a fist. This is a huge achievement that has surely secured her status as a future hall of famer, but the end goal of this week, winning her first US Open title, has still not been attained. After handling the pressure of grabbing the No 1 ranking so impressively, she will be even tougher to beat.“It’s just a number right now,” said Rybakina. “Of course, I’m in the semis so my goal is to win the tournaments which I play, I go just one match at a time. It’s an amazing achievement but you know how quickly everything can change in tennis. I just need to focus on my game, try to recover and enjoy tomorrow.”View image in fullscreenCoco Gauff celebrates after fighting back from a nightmare first set to beat Mirra Andreeva.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPARybakina, the second seed, will next face the fourth seedCoco Gauffafter the American produced a remarkable comeback win against the fifth seedMirra Andreeva, eventually triumphing 2-6, 7-6 (7), 6-2. After struggling with her serve throughout the first half of the match, Gauff saved two match points in the second-set tie-break before marching to victory.With the top-seeded Sabalenka facing Jessica Pegula, the third seed, in the other semi-final, this is the first time in 51 years that each of the top four seeds have reached the US Open women’s semi-finals. It also means that four American players have reached the men’s and women’s singles semi-finals, with two home favourites in each draw.In the men’s draw, the unseededKaren Khachanovadvanced to the semi-finals after his opponent, Alexander Blockx, retired while trailing 6-2, 7-5, 3-2.Blockx was carrying a rib injury into the quarter-final and was visibly hampered by further physical issues, with a brace on his right ankle and strapping on his thigh. Shortly after calling for the trainer at two sets down, the Belgian withdrew after Khachanov broke his serve in the fifth game of the third set.“I was preparing really well for that match-up, it’s not easy because I feel I was dominating then ‌I felt he was struggling more and more,” Khachanov said on court. “He was suffering, but I wanted to ​keep the energy there. I wish him a speedy recovery but I’m super happy I’m in the semis.”Khachanov, who is currently No 50 in the world – his lowest ranking at a major since 2017 – will take on either the No 1 seed, Alexander Zverev, or Botic van de Zandschulp in the semi-finals.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisTennisCoco GauffnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ll be using it again’: Tongue unveils new trick as ‘raw talent’ Razaullah shines | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: The England fast bowler, who took four wickets, revealed he’s learnt wobble seam from his teammate Ollie Robinson
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: The England fast bowler, who took four wickets, revealed he’s learnt wobble seam from his teammate Ollie Robinson
Content: Josh Tongue bowled a wobble seam for the first time in a match, after picking up tips in training from his teammate Ollie Robinson.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenJosh Tongue bowled a wobble seam for the first time in a match, after picking up tips in training from his teammate Ollie Robinson.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersEngland v Pakistan 2026‘I’ll be using it again’: Tongue unveils new trick as ‘raw talent’ Razaullah shinesFast bowler learned wobble seam from Ollie RobinsonPakistan’s Saud Shakeel knew little about debutantSimon Burntonat EdgbastonWed 9 Sep 2026 15.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s four-man seam attack once again demonstrated its collective threat in bundling Pakistan out for 133 at Edgbaston. Josh Tongue highlighted the work the quartet have done together beyond ­matchdays by experimenting with a wobble seam delivery that he has honed with assistance from Ollie Robinson – work that brought immediate reward.“I’ve spoken to Robbo quite a bit about it,” said Tongue, who took four wickets, with the other six equally shared between Robinson and Jofra Archer. “Obviously he’s unbelievable at that and he’s showed that throughout the series. So I’ve been speaking to him quite a bit during the last couple of Tests and I tried a couple of things in training the other day. That was the first time I’d bowled it in the game and it got me a wicket, so I’ll be using it again. I want to get more skills under my belt.”Gay and Brook put England in complete control after Pakistan crumble once moreRead moreEngland ended the day 23 runs ahead, with six first-innings wickets in hand, but both sides still insisted the game is in the balance. “That first hour tomorrow morning is going to be very crucial,” Tongue said. “We’ve just got to get through that first bit.”Meanwhile Saud Shakeel, who top-scored for Pakistan with 43, said: “Early on, when we lost the toss, the pitch had some moisture in it and the overcast conditions helped their bowlers as well. We got some soft dismissals and we couldn’t come back from that. But we started well with our bowling and if we can get them out quickly there’s a good chance we can get back in the game.”It was the fifth time Pakistan have batted in this series and the fifth time they have been dismissed for a total below 200; England have not yet been bowled out for less than that figure and are 156 for four here.“We’re working hard, it’s not like we aren’t trying,” Shakeel said. “There’s a lot of lateral movement and we’re not used to facing that, but we are trying our best. I’m not saying our batting group has not struggled, we have accepted that. But the conditions have been difficult. Bowlers have been on top.”One ray of light for the tourists wasthe impact of the 21-year-old fast bowler Razaullah, playing just his ninth first-class game, who bowled with real menace and claimed the wickets of Emilio Gay, one of two English half-centurions alongside the unbeaten Harry Brook, and Joe Root.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I’ve just faced him one time in a domestic first-class game, so I haven’t seen him that much,” Shakeel said. “But he has some raw pace and a difficult action and we’re hoping he will continue bowling like this. With express fast bowlers, even if they haven’t played a lot of first-class cricket, it doesn’t matter. Their raw talent and pace is useful, which we saw from him today.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

Content: 6h ago15.29 EDTWarwickshire batter Glamorgan inside two daysWarwickshirethrew a bear-shaped gauntlet on the Championship turf by demolishingGlamorganin less than two days and taking temporary possession of top spot.After claiming a first-innings lead of 322 through half centuries from Sam Hain and Ed Barnard, Warwickshire’s bowlers spatchcockedGlamorganfor 65, including five noughts. Ed Barnard’s five for 13 topped the leaderboard. Glamorgan, who made just 130 runs in the match, fell to their biggest loss since 1936. Warwickshire waved 22 points.Jake Lehmann’s unbeaten 115 kept relegation-flirtersHampshirein it at Trent Bridge. A seventh-wicket stand of 97 with Scott Currie frustratedNottswho had one eye on events at Sophia Gardens.A second century partnership of the match between Tom Lammonby and Josh Thomas shimmied fellow pennant-chasersSomersetto a dominant position. They had earlier whipped outLeicestershirefor 157. Leicestershire’s top scorer was Nick Kelly, whose 39 was interrupted when a wasp flew inside his shirt.At the other end of Division One,Yorkshire’sDom Bess and Kuldeep Yadav bewilderedEssex, with three wickets each. They had earlier frustrated in an eighth-wicket stand of 83, Bess undefeated on 80. Essex were further hit when Jamie Porter limped off, though Sam Cook later returned from the Test.Durham’sserene passage back to Division One continued as their big beasts turned on the charm. Brydon Carse whistled through theMiddlesextail to finish with five wickets. Ben McKinney then delighted with his third free-flowing century of the summer.There were 22 wickets in the frantic basement battle at Old Trafford. After bowling outGloucestershirefor 212,Lancashirewere dismissed for 134, something of a triumph from 43 for six, with Will Williams pocketing a career best six for 24 at his former home. George Balderson top scored and then high-kneed through 13 overs on the trot to take four for 23 asGloucestershirewilted to 118 for eight – but with a crucial lead of 189.Ben Aitchison passed 50 wickets for the season asDerbyshiredominated againstKent, whose promotion rivalsNorthamptonshirehad a good day againstWorcestershirethanks to 110 from Saif Zaib and three evening wickets from Harry Conway.ShareUpdated at15.29 EDT

title: Vuelta a España: Matthew ⁠Brennan rounds off famous five with sprint success | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Matthew Brennan claimed a fifth Vuelta a España stage victory on Wednesday as the young British rider edged a bunch sprint in Seville to win the 17th stage
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Matthew Brennan claimed a fifth Vuelta a España stage victory on Wednesday as the young British rider edged a bunch sprint in Seville to win the 17th stage
Content: Matthew Brennan celebrates winning the 17th stage of the Vuelta.Photograph: Jorge Guerrero/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMatthew Brennan celebrates winning the 17th stage of the Vuelta.Photograph: Jorge Guerrero/AFP/Getty ImagesVuelta a EspañaVuelta a España: Matthew ⁠Brennan rounds off famous five with sprint successYoung British rider squeezes out Meeus and Cort NielsenMas moves step closer to landing first Grand Tour victoryAgenciesWed 9 Sep 2026 11.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMatthew Brennan claimed a fifthVuelta a Españastage victory on Wednesday as the young British rider edged a bunch sprint in Seville to win the 17th stage. The 21-year-old Grand Tour debutant crossed the finish line ahead of Jordi Meeus and Magnus Cort Nielsen.The general classification leader, Enric Mas, moved one step closer to claiming a first Grand Tour victory as he maintained his 2min 6sec lead on Felix Gall, with four-time Vuelta winner Primoz Roglic a further four seconds behind.The stage was set up for the bunch sprint finale, without a single climb on the long, flat, 185km ride from Dos Hermanas to the Andalusian capital.Sinuhe Fernandez and Enzo Paleni formed a two-man break early on, whipping up a gap of more than four minutes on the peloton, who were moving at a leisurely pace on another hot day with temperatures over 30C.The gap extended to more than five minutes around the halfway point, with Visma then working hard to reduce it. The Groupama FDJ-United rider Paleni dropped Fernandez but was absorbed by the peloton with just three kilometres remaining after a monumental effort.Brennan came around the Danish rider Cort to claim the sprint victory, holding off Belgium’s Meeus, who crossed the line in second. As with his other stage victories, the Briton raised his hand to the air, this time with all of his fingers up to represent his five victories.Brennan’s victory puts him in a small bracket of riders, including Tadej Pogacar – who was overwhelming favourite to win this year’s Vuelta before he suffered a season-ending injury in a crash in stage eight – to claim five or more stages at a single Grand Tour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Thursday, riders take on a 32.1km individual time-trial from El Puerto de Santa Maria to Jerez de la Frontera in stage 18, which is one of the last chances for Mas’s general classification contenders to cut down the gap on the Spaniard.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The heartbeat of game day’: how NWSL fans in Boston built culture from the ground up | NWSL | The Guardian
description: Through the loss of one franchise, name controversies and stadium changes, Legacy supporters have created an environment of advocacy and belonging
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Through the loss of one franchise, name controversies and stadium changes, Legacy supporters have created an environment of advocacy and belonging
Content: Women’s soccer fans in Boston have thrown their support behind the Legacy, one of the NWSL’s two expansion teams this season.Photograph: Maddie Schroeder/NWSL/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWomen’s soccer fans in Boston have thrown their support behind the Legacy, one of the NWSL’s two expansion teams this season.Photograph: Maddie Schroeder/NWSL/Getty ImagesNWSL‘The heartbeat of game day’: how NWSL fans in Boston built culture from the ground upThrough the loss of one franchise, name controversies and stadium changes, Legacy supporters have created an environment of advocacy and belongingFrankie de la CretazWed 9 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 09.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than two years of work had led to this moment for theBoston Independent Supporters’ Association(ISA). Even before Boston’s new NWSL team had a name, a mascot or a roster, there were fans organizing, ready and waiting to embrace the franchise.On 14 March 2026, it finally paid off. The Boston ISA members marched into Gillette Stadium for the Legacy’s opening match, following behind the marching band from Boston Public Schools and holding their “Up the Swans” scarves over their heads. The group arrived at their seats in the supporters’ section behind the north goal and unfurled the tifo they had spent many hours diligently painting.“Our Legacy Takes Flight” could be read from everywhere in the nearly 65,000-seat stadium, the image of a flying swan wearing a black and green scarf capturing the spirit of this new team lifting off in front of a crowd of more than 30,000 fans. From there, the members of the Boston ISA carried the enthusiasm for the next 90-plus minutes, chanting, dancing, waving flags and beating drums.Janine Sonis: ‘63,000 fans in Denver proves a women’s team was way overdue’Read more“We’d all been building up to this point, and then the players are coming on to the field, and the tifo is up, and it all just starts,” Paige Wetzel, a Boston ISA member, says of that first Legacy game. “After all of the years of planning and not having a team that we had even laid eyes on yet, we actually watched them play. They were on the field, and we were cheering for them, and it just kind of all melted into this like moment of super excitement.”That cheering, that energy and that support is something the Boston ISA has brought to every Legacy home game this season – rain or shine, win or lose, small crowd or large, Massachusetts or Rhode Island.“I see supporter groups as the heartbeat of game day,” says Jammy Torres Millet, the former community marketing manager for the Legacy who served as the ISA’s team liaison from September 2024 until they left the club this past June. “They’re the ones that are bringing the energy and bringing fandom to life through their chants and their drums.”View image in fullscreenBoston Legacy fans unveil the tifo for the club’s first NWSL game in March.Photograph: Winslow Townson/NWSL/Getty ImagesSupporters’ groups are a robust element of soccer culture. Creating one for a team without an identity, though, is a difficult task. While chants and traditions will develop over time, the Boston ISA members wanted players on the Legacy,one of two expansion teams to join theNWSLthis year, to feel supported from their first kickoff.They faced the challenge of the Legacy not yet having a home stadium to play in: the team are spending their first season bouncing between Gillette in Foxborough, Massachusetts and Centreville Bank Stadium in Pawtucket, Rhode Island while their eventual home in Boston, White Stadium, is under construction until 2028.Boston also hadn’t had a professional women’s soccer team in nearly a decade. The Boston Breakers, a club that played in the original eight-team NWSL and its three precursor leagues, folded suddenly after the 2017 season, and many Boston women’s soccer fans still mourn the loss. The NWSL announced Boston as an expansion city for the 2026 season back in September 2023, and the ISA came together shortly after.“For us, especially given the history of Boston losing and now regaining a professional women’s team, the folks who are building this organization and the folks who are joining are really super enthusiastic about making sure that support for this team is really strong in Boston and beyond,” says Anna Esten, the membership chair for the Boston ISA.Torres Millet says that when they joined the club back in September 2024, the ISA had already been in communication with one of the club’s founders. Before there was a club identity, the ISA members focused on networking with team leadership, going to events in the community hosted by the Boston ownership group and getting word to fans that visible and tangible support would be a crucial part of the team’s success.“Supporter groups are key partners in our sport,” says Meghann Burke, the executive director of the NWSL Players Association. “They do more than show up on match day; they do even more than create the environment that sets soccer fandom apart, with chants, drums, tifos and smoke. They give the game its sense of belonging and turn it into something people feel and carry with them.”The ISA has a board of directors with committee roles. As membership chair, Esten is involved in strategic conversations about how members can get the most out of being a part of the organization, brainstorming everything from hosting fun events to advocating with the team on things that members want or need to see at games. But the role also includes the nitty-gritty things, such as keeping spreadsheets and updating the membership base when needed.“We are independent from the team, and so we’re not relying on them financially,” Esten says. “And so we are in a position to be able to advocate and push for what we think is really important for fans and supporters.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA Boston Legacy supporter leads a chant during a match last month against Angel City.Photograph: Maddie Schroeder/NWSL/Getty ImagesThis role was tested almost immediately in October 2024, when the Boston ownership group rolled out its original branding with the name BOS Nation FC and adisastrous marketing campaignwhose tagline was “Too Many Balls”. (Yes, really.) After publicbacklash, team leadership went back to the drawing board, eventually landing on Boston Legacy FC as the team’s name and a swan as its logo. The ISA wasinvolvedin that process, providing feedback during multiple focus groups and stressing why the fandom was so disappointed in the initial branding.“I think [the focus group] was definitely a way to rebuild that trust and to nourish that relationship that was impacted by the original rollout,” Torres Millet says. “But then also, there’s something really special about the fan voice and giving fans input on building this club. That is something that is not always done when professional sports teams are built from scratch – offering the fans and the community a voice in the process so they can feel bought in from day zero.”The ISA hosts tailgates in the parking lot before home games and watch parties at local breweries for away games. Their drumming echoes throughout the stands, ensuring the energy players feel while on the pitch never wavers, even when the team are losing. Like most expansion teams in their debut seasons, the Legacy got off to a slow start. Many of their players were new to the NWSL and hadn’t had much time to practice together before the season began. The team started the season 0-5, drawing their sixth game, and finally getting their first win in their seventh. The Legacy are third-to-last in the league standings at 6-12-5.Esther González, Saudi Arabia and the questions around an unexpected transfer sagaRead moreBut they can always count on their supporters’ section for a pick-me-up. The group flies the flags of players’ home countries behind the goal. The fans blend player names with local references in their chants – for goalkeeper Casey Murphy, it’s “Dropkick Murphy” when she fires the ball out of her zone, a nod to the local band that sings the famous hype song “I’m Shipping Up to Boston”.And then there is the honking. Chant leaders hold megaphones and yell, “If you’re not honking, you’re not Boston”, and then the supporters yell “honk” in an increasingly fast tempo. It is, of course, meant to mimic the sound a swan makes, but it is also incredibly annoying – in the way swans (and sports fans) can be. That identity carries to the pitch; swans are an aggressive bird and the Legacy are an aggressive team, leading the NWSL in yellow cards this season.“We want people to come to Boston and hate it,” Murphy said in a postgame presser in March. “Regardless if we win or lose, we want them to hate playing us.” Defender Bianca St-Georges echoed that sentiment after a game in May. “Fouling is not an issue for us. It’s just us,” she said. “We’re not scared.”View image in fullscreenGoalkeeper Casey Murphy plays in front of supporters’ flags that display the home countries of the full Legacy roster.Photograph: Joe Buglewicz/NWSL/Getty ImagesThough the team and their fans may embrace the very Boston mindset of knowing everyone else probably hates them, that doesn’t mean that the stands are an unwelcoming place. A Pride flag and a trans flag always visibly wave in the ISA’s section. Even before the Legacy took the field, the ISA joined the “Trans People Belong” coalition created by NWSL supporters’ groups, ensuring Boston’s team had representation in advocacy for trans fans and athletes across the sport.“When it matters most, [supporters’ groups] show up for players, standing at the intersection of player rights and labor rights and pushing the game to be fairer and more accountable,” Burke says.The Boston ISA members are committed to continuing to show up, for the players, for the league and for each other. They look forward to 2028, when the Legacy will finally have a stadium to call their own and will no longer be the new kids on the block. For now, their drums will continue to carry the games in Centreville Bank Stadium and beyond.“It’s been a winding road and things have changed on us, between team branding and stadium locations,” Esten says. “But one thing that has been a key tenet for us is that we want to be a supporters’ group where everyone can join and everyone can belong. Whether you’re a Breakers diehard or someone who watched their first game on 14 March, we want you to be part of our group.”Esten cites the culture of women’s sports as one that lends itself to inclusivity. “The most rabid men’s sports fans can make you feel like not every fan has a place there, and we want to make it clear that no matter who you are, if you want to cheer for the Legacy then we want you here.”Explore more on these topicsNWSLWomen's footballUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content
