title: Ben Shelton dethrones Carlos Alcaraz in five-set thriller after latest US Open finish | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Carlos Alcaraz’s title defence was ended by Ben Shelton in the latest finish to a match in US Open history on Wednesday morning
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Carlos Alcaraz’s title defence was ended by Ben Shelton in the latest finish to a match in US Open history on Wednesday morning
Content: Ben Shelton celebrates after his five-set US Open victory against the defending champion Carlos Alcaraz.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APView image in fullscreenBen Shelton celebrates after his five-set US Open victory against the defending champion Carlos Alcaraz.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APUS Open Tennis 2026Ben Shelton dethrones Carlos Alcaraz in five-set thriller after latest US Open finishWinner claims 6-7 (5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (7) victoryEpic quarter-final ends after 3.30am in New YorkTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsWed 9 Sep 2026 04.04 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the 10th day of play in New York moved deeper into the remote hours of the new morning, every passing game imbuedCarlos Alcarazwith greater despair. From his focused start, the Spaniard’s intensity had flatlined and he could barely put a ball in court. He lost nine consecutive games against Ben Shelton and seemed to have nothing left.Instead,the defending championimprobably dragged himself back into a contest that soon developed into one of the most remarkable matches of the year. The latest attempt by the second seed at orchestrating a monumental comeback was denied by a brave, defiant Shelton, the eighth seed, who refused to be shaken by his legendary rival or the looming prospect of securing the greatest win of career.US Open 2026 quarter-final: Ben Shelton stuns Carlos Alcaraz in thriller after latest ever finish – liveRead moreAfter 4hr 28min and at 3.33am, with the sun not long from rising over Flushing Meadows but with a half-full Arthur Ashe Stadium still hollering in unison until the end, Shelton ended Alcaraz’s reign with a 6-7 (5), 6-1, 6-3, 1-6, 7-6 (7) victory to clinch his biggest win yet and reach the semi-finals of the US Open.In the aftermath of his dominant fourth-round victory against Tommy Paul, the expectations surrounding Alcaraz had risen exponentially as the seven-time grand slam winner attempted to defend his crown. His level in the first three sets of the match, however, more faithfully reflected the fact that this was his first tournament back from a four-and-a-half-month layoff.This was a massive opportunity for Shelton and, under such unique circumstances, he showed that he has the inner belief and resilience to rise to these occasions. He managed this match spectacularly, pairing his typically devastating serving, variation and athleticism with solid returning and steadfast consistency across five sets.View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz waves to the crowd after being defeated by Ben Shelton in the US Open.Photograph: Cristóbal Herrera/EPAMost important, he held his nerve until the end, even after squandering opportunities deep in the final set. “Carlos is one of the greatest champions in our sport already at 23 years old,” he said. “It’s always fun being on the court against him. It’s ridiculous some of the stuff he comes up with sometimes. The most enjoyable match that I’ve had in my career, for sure.”Alcaraz left everything on the court, his lack of physical preparation also reflected in periods of fatigue and even vomiting into his towel on the court towards the end of the fourth set. Afterwards, he refused to leave the tournament downbeat after being part of such an immense battle against one of the best players in the world so early in his comeback from a serious injury. “As I said before the tournament began, my expectation was to go there, compete, play in these kind of matches for me being healthy,” he said.“It was close. It was close. So I’m just not going to be disappointed about not getting the win at the end. You know, I’m just happy. I’m just proud about myself, about how I fought. After the third set, physically I was really tired, but you know I found a way to push myself up and physically giving extra.”As a result of Alcaraz’s defeat, a new US Open champion will be crowned: 23 years after Andy Roddick’s triumph here, the last time an American man tasted victory at any grand slam tournament, Shelton will face his compatriot and friend Frances Tiafoe. “I was playing against one of the best – he is a beast,” Alcaraz said. “Shelton is an unbelievable player, powerful. He just managed to play really, really well in every situation, so credit to him. I leave the court happy. I leave the court with a smile, healthy, and this is what I needed.”View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz vomited into a towel after the fourth set against Ben Shelton at the US Open.Photograph: Heather Khalifa/APThere are times when the tennis authorities make self-sabotaging decisions regarding scheduling, but sometimes it is just impossible to contain or plan for the greatness of this sport. This is, without doubt, one of the most incredible days of tennis in years. All four quarter-finals on Tuesday extended to deciding sets withAryna Sabalenka, Tiafoe and Jessica Pegula each dragging themselves through spectacular comeback victories against Linda Noskova, Alex Michelsen and Emma Navarro respectively.Alcaraz and Shelton did not start until 11.04pm, but over their subsequent four and a half hours on the court that was soundtracked by a delirious, raucous crowd until the very end, their battle provided the perfect climax to 16 hours of greatness, a night and morning that the thousands of roaring fans still present until the very end will never forget.“It was just enjoyable to be a part of that match,” Shelton said. “Obviously the level of tennis, how long the match was going, the fight that it was, how even of a match it was back and forth throughout, I think that’s something we can appreciate. Win or lose, we would have a smile on our face.”Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Carlos AlcarazUS Open tennisTennisUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them? | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligence
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligence
Content: A safety expert at Anthropic believes there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could spark an event that wipes out humanity.Illustration: Ales Utouka/AlamyView image in fullscreenA safety expert at Anthropic believes there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could spark an event that wipes out humanity.Illustration: Ales Utouka/AlamyAI (artificial intelligence)AI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?Alarming warnings from industry insiders increase pressure for curbs on artificial superintelligenceRobert BoothUK technology editorWed 9 Sep 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDoes artificial superintelligence really pose a risk greater than nuclear weapons? Is there a significant chance of “a Chornobyl-sized catastrophe”. Might there even be a greater than 10% chance that AI could “kill all humans” in the next decade?These warnings were issued over the past 48 hours on both sides of the Atlantic about the potential impact of a technology that most people still think of as a more talkative search engine.Some of the threats were raised in the UK as MPs and peers began to wrestle with the danger of AI outperforming human capabilities. The nuclear warnings came from Des Browne, a former defence secretary, and Prof Stuart Russell, an eminent Berkeley computer scientist.Beatrice Fihn, who won the 2017 Nobel peace prize for leading the International Campaign to Abolish Nuclear Weapons, told parliamentarians: “It is not the first time we’re confronted with abilities that could end up killing us all.”The session on Monday was convened by Control AI, a lobbying group pushing for international regulation of the technology. It is backing a bill tabled in parliament this week by the Labour MP Alex Sobel and aimed at banning the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI).On Tuesday night, a senior employee at Anthropic admitted he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could “kill all humans” in the next decade and warned that his AI company did not have a plan to ensure ASI was aligned, meaning it did no harm.Predictions for when ASImight be reached vary from several years to more than a decade.Evan Hubinger, alignment science lead atAnthropic, posted the comment after Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at the San Francisco company and previously at OpenAI, resigned, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”. He said they were “gambling with our lives”.Coxon said the risks at Anthropic were well understood but they were “locked in a race to get there first”. In a glimmer of hope, he added that he was optimistic about the potential for coordination between US labs on pacing their progress in the race.Anthropic has been approached for comment on the issue.OpenAIpointed to a statement from its chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, who said last week: “International coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.”The push for wider coordination to control ASI was at the heart of events at Westminster this week. According to the Financial Times, government officials voiced concern that Anthropic had declined to submit its latest model – Mythos 5.1 – to the UK’s AI Security Institute for pre-release testing.Only a few US organisations have had access to Mythos 5.1, the Cabinet Office confirmed. A spokesperson added: “The AI Security Institute continues to collaborate closely with industry partners, including Anthropic.”View image in fullscreenThe Labour MP Darren Jones has written to world leaders to call for a multinational treaty to ensure AI is developed safely.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianThe Labour MP Darren Jones has written to the prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the heads of the UN and the OECD calling for a “multinational treaty for the regulated and safe development of superintelligence – not a ban on innovation or scientific endeavour but a safety-first approach to the rapid development of this technology”.Citing Coxon’s resignation, Jones added: “The debate ranges from the end of humanity to claims of ‘marketing hype’. Either way, governments must now step in.”On the other side of the Atlantic, Bernie Sanders ratcheted up his AI safety campaign this week by again calling on Congress to regulate the technology. He pointed to polling suggesting that 81% of Americans believed their politicians should take action.The independent senator for Vermont said: “We can’t allow a handful of greedy people to play God and determine the future of humanity – our economy, environment, democracy, privacy and more – without public input.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe US senator Bernie Sanders wants Congress to regulate the ‘greedy’ AI industry.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianControlAI is funded by Jaan Tallinn, the multi-billionaire founder of Skype who calls himself an “anti-extinctionist”. He has dedicated part of his fortune to campaigning for AI safety and says some senior AI executives would be happy for humanity to be wiped out.Despite being an early investor in Anthropic and Google DeepMind, two of the leading AI labs, Tallinn estimates that 10-15% of AI employees believe the technology will be a worthy successor to humanity.He said in an interview earlier this summer: “A fairly known AI researcher said to me ‘Jaan, don’t worry about this. Humans are a disposable species’. From what I understand he was fine with becoming extinct.”Tallinn’s lobby group ran the session for MPs and peers at Westminster on Monday and urged them to back measures to curb the most powerful AI models. On every chair was a copy of the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: The Case Against Superintelligent AI.The politicians heard from Russell, who made the Chornobyl warning and said: “The other possibility is a much larger catastrophe, in which humanity loses control irreversibly. But we have no say over whether we continue to exist.”Browne said that when he was defence secretary he thought nuclear war was the most likely threat facing humanity. Now he believed “a superintelligent AI poses a threat on the same, possibly, a greater scale”.OpenAI models went rogue. We urgently need a better ‘hugging face’ investigation | Mackenzie Arnold and Stephan LlerenaRead moreOther contributors were more cautious. Dr Andrew Rogoyski, of the Surrey Institute for People-Centred AI, said: “In reality, these systems are nowhere near as versatile as humans, let alone humans acting collectively. I suspect we’re heading towards ‘the great disappointment’ where advanced AI turns out to be too expensive and not useful enough to continue in its current form.”David Barber, director of Sofair, a state-backed AI research lab combining academics from Oxford, Cambridge, Edinburgh and UCL, said he was worried about people “throwing the baby out with the bathwater”.“AI is not going to go away,” he said. “It’s incredibly useful, whether or not you allow it in a fully unconstrained way to access the internet and various systems that’s potentially problematic. We may need to learn how to better control these things. There are vulnerabilities in the software frameworks that need to be patched. But that’s doable.“What we need as a country is to get to grips with the duality that is both an incredibly important and useful technology, and at the same time, it’s something that needs to be carefully thought about and carefully controlled.”Sandra Wachter, a professor at the Oxford Internet Institute, said she did not believe in “Terminator scenarios” but that AI posed real threats including its environmental impact, spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.“These problems are real and urgent and need addressing now,” she said. “Terminator scenarios are a big distraction from real issues.”Gary Marcus, an AI industry commentator and academic, said: “There is a difference between superintelligence that is aligned (if such a thing is possible) and superintelligence that is not.“It is at least conceivable that the former might be net positive. So far we have neither, but a superabundance of hype combined with a striking lack of prudence on OpenAI’s part has gotten us where we are, with intense mistrust all around.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)AnthropicComputer science and ITOpenAIComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK datacentres will create just 25% of jobs predicted by tech sector, analysis finds | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Facilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank says
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Facilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank says
Content: An Equinix datacentre under construction in Slough, near London. Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres amid growing public scepticism.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn Equinix datacentre under construction in Slough, near London. Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres amid growing public scepticism.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesDatacentres - UKUK datacentres will create just 25% of jobs predicted by tech sector, analysis findsFacilities likely to employ 10,400 workers, compared with 40,000 in industry estimates, thinktank saysHeather StewartEconomics editorWed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDatacentres in the UK will create just a quarter of the jobs predicted by the tech sector, while consuming vast amounts of energy, according to new research.Environmental thinktank Verdant predicts that all the datacentres currently planned are likely to directly employ 10,400 workers – compared with the more than 40,000 cited in projections by the industry lobby group TechUK.Labour has defended the rapid rollout of AI datacentres in the face of growing public scepticism, amid concerns about their demand for water and energy. The government has also echoed TechUK’s claims about job creation.Verdant’s analysis is based on 20 projects for which data on staffing levels are publicly available, including via planning applications, company accounts and press releases – as well as international comparisons.It says the datacentres that have already been built have directly created fewer than 4,400 jobs – about 8.6 jobs for each megawatt of energy they consume, against the 43.7 jobs claimed in TechUK’s projections.Verdant also argues that the many future projects currently at the planning stage are on a far larger scale, and so likely to be much less job-intensive – perhaps creating as few as 1.6 permanent positions per megawatt.Its analysis focuses on the permanent workers needed to maintain and operate datacentres, setting aside the much larger number of temporary construction jobs needed to build them.James Meadway, the thinktank’s co-director, said: “We’re being rushed into supporting a frantic pace of datacentre buildout on very flimsy economic grounds.“Clearly artificial intelligence and related technologies have great potential. But vast new datacentres arrive at significant real costs to local communities and even our climate ambitions, and their use case has to be made by the government and industry – rather than assuming we can build first and then work out why we did later.”View image in fullscreenDemonstrators protest against redevelopment plans for the 10-acre Truman Brewery site in Brick Lane, which include a datacentre.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesTo underline the resource intensity of the vast data warehouses, Verdant compared the 8.6 jobs they currently create per megawatt of power used with about 400 in a car plant and more than 3,600 in a hospital or health facility.The government rejected this comparison, and questioned Verdant’s methodology. A spokesperson said: “This report relies on a deeply misleading jobs-per-megawatt metric, makes false comparisons with hospitals and schools, and appears to confuse electricity capacity with actual consumption. More seriously, it discounts the wider economic value of compute [computing capacity] and the national security and sovereignty case for building critical digital infrastructure in Britain.”Verdant said it had based its calculations on the electricity capacity that tech firms claim they need – which could still crowd out alternative plans, even if the completed datacentres don’t end up using all the capacity.Labour has classified AI datacentres as critical national infrastructure in an attempt to speed up the planning process, and Andy Burnham has underlined his backing for the sector by appointing AI minister Kanishka Narayan to his cabinet.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNarayan has advocated a rapid increase in datacentres, partly on grounds of national sovereignty. He told the Times last month: “The British public is very clear that it wants strong defence. It wants strong, sovereign capability, it doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity in this country.”By contrast, the Green party in Englandhas called for a moratorium on buildingdatacentres, whilethere have been protests in Scotland, amid claims that massive projects are being rushed through.Zack Polanski, the party’s leader in England, said: “The government is planning to steamroller local opposition so private companies can build datacentres – but it can’t explain what the benefits are.‘“England and Wales are still facing drought after our hottest summer ever, but these datacentres are set to be given priority access to water. Meanwhile, this latest research suggests far fewer jobs may actually be created in constructing and staffing them than the government claims.”In response to the Green party’s call for a “pause”, a government spokesperson insisted that it would “simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data”.A spokesperson for TechUK said: “Our estimates that the UK datacentre industry supports 43,500 jobs, and could support 40,000 more by 2035, are built on a published methodology using industry data and standard economic impact assessment techniques. The figures were built transparently from the best available industry data at the time, and we are confident they remain a reasonable estimate of the sector’s employment contribution.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKAI (artificial intelligence)Technology policyEnergyComputingEnergy industryTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: US allies lack resources to keep pace on AI, top Pentagon official says | US military | The Guardian
description: Cameron Stanley talks up ‘revolutionary’ AI capabilities and says Washington working with Nato and Five Eyes partners
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Cameron Stanley talks up ‘revolutionary’ AI capabilities and says Washington working with Nato and Five Eyes partners
Content: The Pentagon’s AI office has introduced several new artificial intelligence tools.Photograph: Alexander Drago/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Pentagon’s AI office has introduced several new artificial intelligence tools.Photograph: Alexander Drago/ReutersUS militaryUS allies lack resources to keep pace on AI, top Pentagon official saysCameron Stanley talks up ‘revolutionary’ AI capabilities and says Washington working with Nato and Five Eyes partnersJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonWed 9 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 08.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Pentagon’s top artificial intelligence official said on Tuesday that America’s closest allies lack the resources to keep pace with the US military’s adoption of AI, and that Washington is working to steer them away from mistakes it made along the way.“They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do, they don’t have the scale that we do,” Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer at the Department of Defense, said at an event at the Billington Cybersecurity summit. Of Nato and the Five Eyes, an intelligence-sharing partnership of the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Stanley said Washington was “actively working with a number of our partners” so “they don’t make the same mistakes that we make”.The comments come less than a year into Stanley’s tenure, during which the Pentagon’s AI office has rolled out several new tools while losing a number of senior staff. Since January, Stanleyhas overseen the launchof GenAI.mil, an internal chatbot platform he says has reached 1.7 million users, and Agent Network, a system designed to shorten the time between intelligence-gathering and a commander’s decision. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has directed Stanley’s office toreport AI deployment speedas a monthly metric, part of a wider push to expand military computing power.Much of Stanley’s appearance focused on speed. He described watching a commander halt a scheduled briefing to take a 30-second phone call and issue an order on the spot, without a formal decision brief or a review of the room’s security clearance level. He called the moment “revolutionary”.“I know it sounds simplistic,” Stanley explained. “It’s only simplistic because we’re good at it now.”It’s a term he has used before. Project Maven, the Pentagon’s original AI targeting program launched in 2017, became the Palantir-built Maven Smart System, which the US leaned on heavily during its 2026 air campaign against Iran, helping strike more than13,000 targets over the first 38 days, according to Stanley at conference in May. Speaking at Palantir’sAIPCon 9 conference in March, Stanley called Maven “revolutionary” too, saying it let commanders go from identifying a target to launching a strike within a single platform.But the campaignhas drawn scrutiny. More than 120 members of the US Congress signed a letter demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding civilian casualties and the use of artificial intelligence, following a 28 February strike on an elementary school in Minab, which Iranian officials say killed at least 168 people, many of them children.Stanley ended by telling the audience that the department’s old habits were now its biggest liability.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst ThingOur US morning briefing breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The way we’ve always done it is the most risky course of action,” he said, adding that the department needed to “think differently” if it wants AI tools in the hands of warfighters faster.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Apple unveils folding iPhone Duo as new CEO takes center stage | Technology | The Guardian
description: The passport-size iPhone Duo serves as the first big test for John Ternus, who took over for Tim Cook last week
Author: Johana Bhuiyan
Headline: The passport-size iPhone Duo serves as the first big test for John Ternus, who took over for Tim Cook last week
Content: The iPhone Duo is displayed on Wednesday, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, California.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APView image in fullscreenThe iPhone Duo is displayed on Wednesday, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, California.Photograph: Jeff Chiu/APTechnologyApple unveils folding iPhone Duo as new CEO takes center stageThe passport-size iPhone Duo serves as the first big test for John Ternus, who took over for Tim Cook last weekJohana BhuiyanWed 9 Sep 2026 14.45 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApplehas unveiled theiPhoneDuo,the company’s first foldable phone and the most significant change to the iPhone since the smartphone’s introduction in 2007.The nearly $2,000 device takes inspiration from iPads’ wide screens and combines them with the portability and camera features of iPhones. When opened, it is the company’s largest phone display and thinnest phone. The Duo opens and closes like a passport to double its screen size.“iPhone Duo brings an entirely new design while preserving everything you love from an iPhone,” saidJohn Ternus, the company’s new chief executive. “It feels effortless to use and it makes new experiences possible.”The phone will start at $1,999 and be available on 23 October.Apple’s new CEO introduces himself at annual showcase: ‘I continue to be inspired every single day’Read moreThe product release event, titled “Surprise and Shine”, began at 10am Pacific Standard Time on Apple’s campus in Cupertino,California, south of San Francisco.“I started the day with an intelligent personal hub and why there’s no product in the world that is better to be that hub than iPhone,” Ternus said. “We think the best way to achieve that is with a foldable design. Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones stuck together … scrolling through vertical content feels compromised.”Apple releases its first foldable phoneWhile competitors have released foldable smartphones since the late 2010s, the new model is a first for the iPhone maker, and its rollout serves as the first big test for Ternus, who assumed the role on 1 September. He claimed the Duo “will redefine the experience of using a foldable phone”.Apple reportedly began testing prototypes of its folding iPhone display in early 2021 – though at the time there were no plans for its launch, according to a Bloombergreport.The company started the event with its more routine announcements, including the new iPhone 18 Pro, which starts at $1,199, and 18 Pro Max models, which start at $1,299.Appleemphasized the AI-enabled features that will be integrated throughout the phone. Called Siri AI, the company said it will be able to tap into third-party apps and already works with over 300,000 apps.View image in fullscreenJohn Ternus, Apple’s new CEO, holds the new foldable iPhone Duo during Apple’s event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Cupertino, California, on 9 September.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersAmong the many AI-related features available on the new iPhones will be a novel mechanism that fingerprints an image and identifies as captured by an iPhone’s camera – not generated by AI. The feature, called Apple Reference Image, will act as a “digital negative”, as one Apple executive described it, and serve as proof that the the original image was not AI-generated.Both new iPhones also represent a “massive leap” in battery life, executives said – the iPhone 18 Pro Max will have 45 hours of battery life and the iPhone 18 pro will have 36 hours of battery life.Though the foldable iPhone took center stage on Wednesday in California, overall demand for foldable phones makes up only a small sliver of overall mobile device sales. Customers’ interest in standard iPhones, by contrast, remains high, as evidenced in Apple’smost recent robust earnings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe company also unveilednew iterations of some of its other product offerings at its events and over the next few months, including updates to itsApple Watchand AirPods lines.The company announced the fifth generation of its AirPods headphones, describing them as 50% more noise cancelling than AirPods 4 and sporting five hours of battery life. The latest iteration starts at $129.The company also introduced its latest watches, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, pitching them as some of the most advanced and accurate wearable devices to support health and fitness goals.Tim Cook handed $47m package for new role as executive chair of AppleRead moreThe updated watch will include several new AI features, including “Health Age”, which analyzes heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition and measures how users stack up to their chronological age.The watch will also include “audio intelligence”, meant to enable your watch to record ambient conversations throughout the day and take notes, producing a transcript of what someone said 15 seconds earlier in case you missed it. At the end of the day, a watch user can review a summary of their day, called a “Siri Recap”.The company said these recordings are stored on the device and anything that is collected is end-to-end encrypted.Ternustookthe stageas CEO for the first time, marking the beginning of his tenure as the head of Apple, replacing theoutgoing CEO,Tim Cook. In anoteto employees on his first day, Ternus said that he was excited about “the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined”.“I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store,” Ternus wrote in his letter. “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.”Explore more on these topicsTechnologyiPhoneAppleSmartphonesCaliforniaComputingMobile phonesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump administration to confront Australia over Labor’s social media algorithm plan | Social media | The Guardian
description: White House warns trading partners against ‘imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion’ on US tech sector
Author: Luca Ittimani
Headline: White House warns trading partners against ‘imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion’ on US tech sector
Content: Donald Trump in Washington DC. The US administration will raise concerns about Australia’s big tech company fines over online algorithms.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPAView image in fullscreenDonald Trump in Washington DC. The US administration will raise concerns about Australia’s big tech company fines over online algorithms.Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPASocial mediaTrump administration to confront Australia over Labor’s social media algorithm planWhite House warns trading partners against ‘imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion’ on US tech sectorFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastLuca IttimaniWed 9 Sep 2026 02.51 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 03.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Trump administration will confront Australia over its plan to force digital platforms to take down harmful content and let users opt out of algorithm-generated “for you” feeds.Big tech companies would be fined more than $100m for breaching the proposed laws and the Australian government is under pressure to raise those fines even further.A White House spokesperson, Kush Desai, said the US administration would raise its concerns with “trading partners”, in a statement released less than 24 hours after Australia’s announcement on Tuesday.Labor wants Australians to be able to opt out of online algorithms. How will it change your feed?Read more“President Trump has unequivocally warned trading partners against imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America’s leading technology sector,” Desai said.The communications minister, Anika Wells, downplayed the statement as “broad” and told News24 she had not directly received any such warning from a US representative.“We’re a sovereign nation,” Wells said. “We have the right to defend Australian parents and kids and we’ll do that.”Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereIf passed, the digital duty of care laws would require platforms to protect children from harmful content around eating disorders, misogyny, pornography, glorifying crime, abuse and cyberbullying. Adults and children would need to be protected from illegal material.They would also require platforms to send users a notification or “pop-up”, giving them a choice between a main feed that shows personalised content from across the platform or one that shows only content shared by their online connections.The Greens party has demanded the government make the latter option the default setting and force platforms to let users opt in to having personalised feeds.The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young repeated calls for higher fines to be pegged to companies’ global revenue, speaking to ABC radio on Wednesday.“Big tech is going to spend a lot of money fighting these laws in the first place and finding every which way to get around them,” Hanson-Young said.“You need to hit them really where it hurts, and that’s their revenue.”Big tech companies Meta, Google and TikTok have not publicly commented, though their representative lobby group, Digi, has said the law’s definitions of harmful content and impact on user experience would be crucial.OpenAI, owner of ChatGPT, said it planned to engage with the government on its laws to ensure they were “protecting Australians while enabling them to benefit from AI”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralian businesses have warned the rules could hurt their own revenue, as Australians who opt out of algorithms may stop seeing advertisements and buying from companies that sell via online platforms.The Council of Small Business Organisations Australia has asked the government to model the costs to small businesses and their visibility in feeds.The Labor government is also facing backlash from local conservatives, with the Coalition accusing Labor of using the bill to censor free speech.The proposal would give the communications minister the power to set new definitions for harmful content that would have to be taken down.The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said this could extend to political speech that opposed the government.“I don’t trust big tech, but I trust the Labor party a lot less,” Canavan said.The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said Canavan’s comments were “disingenuous” as the Senate would be able to reject the minister’s definitions.Wells has repeatedly committed to leaving political content and misinformation outside the scope of the laws.“Your right to be wrong on the internet remains preserved in the digital duty of care,” Wells said. “If you want to believe that the moon landing was fake, it is in no way impacted by the digital duty of care.”Explore more on these title: Streaming from the cloud was meant to change games forever – what happened? | Games | The Guardian
description: Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable
Content: Fans playing the cloud-based game Doom at the 2019  Gamescom in Cologne, Germany.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFans playing the cloud-based game Doom at the 2019  Gamescom in Cologne, Germany.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesStreaming from the cloud was meant to change games forever – what happened?Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordableDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 9 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is anancient videoof that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future.Since then, plenty of companies havetried to be the firstto truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later.Despite the fact that people simply don’t seem to want game streaming services – or at least not enough to pay a stand-alone monthly subscription for them – Sony and Microsoft have remained steadfastly committed to the idea, bundling game streaming into their PlayStation Plus and Xbox Game Pass services. I use both quite regularly when I want to check out a game quickly, mostly because modern download sizes are ridiculous (Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, say, takes up nearly 150GB of my PS5 space, almost a quarter of its usable storage). Who wants to do 30 minutes of hard drive management every time they want to play something new?Last week, however, Microsoft announced that it wasintroducing time limitsfor game streaming: you’re now allowed 5-15 hours a month, depending on your subscription tier. And yes, you’re right:that is not enough time to play through even one single average-sized game. This brings Microsoft’s previously unwavering commitment to cloud gaming into question – and when even Microsoft with its infinite resources can’t seem to make it work, is the writing on the wall for game streaming as a whole?View image in fullscreenData-hungry ... streaming games such as Mario Kart World requires a whole load of data.Photograph: NintendoIn the early days, the biggest problem with streaming was input lag: the time it took for the game to respond to your button-pressing. Normally, when you’re playing a game this lag is imperceptible. Via streaming, it would often be horribly obvious, your character taking maybe a full second to jump after you’d pressed the A button. Not all games rely heavily on timing and finesse, but a lot of them do, and playing games on a minor time-delay felt nauseating.This is much less of an issue now, but another problem has only gotten worse: game streaming requires the instantaneous transmission of alotof data, making it taxing on your internet connection and expensive for the service provider. Here’s a comparison: watching an hour of Netflix uses about 1GB of data. An hour of game streaming via Xbox requires about 4GB. Microsoft’s servers have to stream you the video of your live gameplay, and continually receive and interpret your controller inputs. No wonder Microsoft suddenly wants to limit your hours.The cloud gaming model has always been based on the idea that data infrastructure would become faster and cheaper in the future. Its selling point is outsourcing computing power so that you can play whatever you want without upgrading your console or PC, or even without having one at all. Unfortunately, thanks to AI companies and their chatbots’ bottomless demand for computing power and energy, the opposite has happened. Data and computing power are nowmoreexpensive. Ironically, this change has been driven by Microsoft itself as much as anything else: a huge chunk of the company’s spendingwent on data centres and AI infrastructurein the last fiscal year. This suggests that Microsoft is choosing to prioritise data provision for users of Azure and Copilot over its gaming customers.Will this affect you? Probably not. Only 4% of all Game Pass subscribers use it for more than 15 hours a month, Microsoft said in ablog postannouncing the changes. Which brings us right back to the question: if cloud gaming really is the future, why is nobody using it? It’s been a long time since that 2009 demo, and this technology has still yet to meaningfully break through. Is it time to give up on it?Alongside Sony and Microsoft, there is one other player left in this death match: the US-based tech firm Nvidia, whose GeForce Now game-streaming service (launched in 2013 and revamped many times since) might just be the world’s most successful. Nvidia has beenriding highon the AI boom, becoming the most valuable company in the world. Its computing hardware powers all the datacentres that the rest of the tech industry has been building, to satisfy imagined future AI demand. Perhaps, when all of this shakes out, it will be the only company left that can afford to provide game streaming services at all.What to playView image in fullscreenUnashamedly laborious … Kingdom Come Deliverance II.Photograph: Warhorse StudiosI have been variably unwell for most of the summer, and in need of something absorbing, so I dived intoKingdom Come Deliverance II– think Skyrim, but 15th-century historical fiction.I was impressed immediately by the outstanding script, story and performances, all of which are much more humorous and entertaining than I was expecting from a hardcore medieval RPG. And I also love how unashamedly laborious this game is: you must control each swipe of a drawn-out sword fight; you have to manually grind and mix herbs for health-restoring concoctions; and if you want anyone to speak to you, you must regularly wash your face (and grubby tunic) so you don’t stink. Last night, I spent 20 minutes hammering out horseshoes in the forge. The opening hours have you hauling sacks of flour around while a tavern landlady swears at you.I can’t help but respect this naturalist commitment to grime and busywork; knight-life isn’t all horseplay, you know. I have spent many, many hours with this game and I am still basically a stinking peasant. I may well never finish it, but I am resolved to atleastget to the point where I have my own steed and a pair of decent boots.Available on:Xbox, PlayStation 5, PCEstimated playtime:55+ hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenLooking beautiful … The remastered Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.Photograph: NintendoA Nintendo broadcast on Tuesday spilled a bunch of new details about the upcomingZelda: Ocarina of Timeremake, which I’m relieved to say is looking beautiful. Link looks doll-like in the updated style, and Hyrule Castle Town looks a bit like a living Playmobil village overlaid with a watercolour-ish filter that makes the whole game look like something half remembered. (I am somewhat less enthused by the addition of voice acting to the cutscenes; Navi was already annoying enough.) Check out thedemo here.For the Ringer, frequent Guardian games contributor Lewis Gordon has writtenthis excellent long-readon Japanese publisherCapcom’s current streak of brilliance, talking to a host of executives and developers about exactly how the company has bucked the trend while the rest of the games industry is on fire.Patrick Miller– better known as pattheflip – has published athought-provoking reflectionon how and why some players become overinvested – even dependent – on video games. “I say this as someone who has loved video games his whole life; if games serve a load-bearing function in someone’s life, it’s the life that needs fixing, not the games.”At the end of last week, theWhite Housereleased this horrible littlepropaganda arcade, featuring nasty riffs on popular games, such as a version of Tetris where you have to build a wall on the Mexican border to stave off “the coming horde”. That particular gamewas later removedafter The Tetris Company expressed its opposition.What to clickGrand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged worldQuestion BlockView image in fullscreenNo combat required … Eastshade, where you take on the role of a painter rather than a fighter.Photograph: Eastshade StudiosReaderPierosent in this question (along with some super-nice feedback on the newsletter – thank you, Piero!):“I enjoy the occasional foray into story-driven RPGs, such asKingdom Come Deliverance,Skyrimandthe Baldur’s Gateseries, but as I get older I’m finding the continual combat sections overwhelming and dull. Could you recommend me some good RPGs that don’t rely on combat as the main game mechanic?”You’re not alone, Piero – for a surprising proportion of players, combat is just something you have to do in order to get to the bits of a game that you find more interesting. Most RPGs these days have a “story mode” option that at least makes all the fighting trivially easy, if you’re not interested in engaging with it. There is of courseDisco Elysium, a complex role-playing game with no combat at all; likeCitizen Sleeper,it is mostly text-based. I have heard good things aboutEastshade, an open-world game where you’re a painter rather than a fighter. I’d also suggestPentiment, though it’s a very different style from Skyrim. AndYonder: The Cloud Catcher Chroniclesis worth a look if you don’t mind cutesy.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner? | Grand Theft Auto VI | The Guardian
description: Historically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romance
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Historically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romance
Content: Couple who slay together … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenCouple who slay together … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesGrand Theft Auto VIGrand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?Emma FlintHistorically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romanceWed 9 Sep 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.33 EDTShareThere was never any doubt that Grand Theft Auto VI’s extended look would elicit a viral reaction from the internet. Having won the Game Awards’ Most Anticipated award twice consecutively, Rockstar’s forthcoming crime opus is one of the most frothed-over games in recent memory, or indeed ever. It’s nothing short ofa cultural phenomenon.One aspect of the game has provoked an unexpectedly vehement response on social media: not violence, but romance. Protagonists Lucia and Jason are in love, you see, and as a player, part of your job is keeping their spark alive and their relationship strong, so that their criminal escapades are underpinned by a strong connection to one another. Holding hands, enjoying a date at the beach, spontaneously texting one another when apart – all of these interactions will strengthen their bond. You’ll be putting in a lot of work to ensure this couple thrives, which is why some people have come to believe that playing GTA VI counts as micro-cheating.View image in fullscreenCheating at games … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesTakes on this are all over social media. Multiple users have shared posts claiming that if you romance characters in video games such as GTA VI you’ve been unfaithful to your partner;TikTok account El Michelle remarkedthat simply playing the game is cheating. “In absolutely no human way is my fiance playing GTA VI,”posted Shelby Haas, another TikTok user. “You literally have to maintain a relationship with a girl […] you have to take her on dates, and you can have sex with her. […] Don’t let your boyfriend or fiance or husband play GTA 6.”Over on TikTok,a post by Landrystates that GTA VI “is basically the same as cheating”, continuing: “I guarantee you, if your man is playing GTA VI and keeping his little girlfriend alive on that video game, he’s most definitely the type that’s following models.”GTA VI is by no means the inventor of in-game dating – hello,Baldur’s Gate 3, in which you can romance and have sex with any (or several) of your eight companions, including a druid who transforms into a bear. And surely we all remember trying to persuade our Sims to get off with each other. For at least 20 years dating and romance have been a significant element of all sorts of different titles; there is an entire (immensely popular) genre of dating games devoted to playfully living out virtual relationships.Even so, due to its unrivalled online presence, GTA VI will be many people’s first exposure to the idea. Video game newcomers on TikTok seem especially exercised about the lengths their partners will go to to maintain a happy in-game relationship with Lucia, though it’s worth pointing out that it goes both ways: playing as Lucia, you’ll have to put just as much effort into maintaining a strong relationship with Jason. (The notion of maxing out the romance with Jason hasn’t provoked nearly as intense a response.)It’s easy for people to revert to off-the-shelf misogynistic accusations about “jealous” and “overreactive” spouses in a situation like this, and indeed, many counter-commentators have done just that. “‘GTA VI is literally cheating’ is something I would say if I was a jealous, insecure hag […]”declares one TikToker.In the comments on one Instagramvideo, someone opined that GTA VI “promotes lust”, resulting in a massive pile-on.But what if this isn’t knee-jerk jealousy? Behind these rather laughable concerns about virtual girlfriends, there are valid insecurities here over the idea of one’s real-life partner being more invested in a fictional character than a real-life relationship. Especially for young people, we’re in an age of loneliness and disconnection, fuelled by being chronically online. It’s one of the greatest paradoxes of modern society: despite being able to instantly engage with anyone or anything, these interactions are superficial and fleeting.View image in fullscreenLovers’ arms … Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesThe dating scene right now is bleak. Dating columnist-cum-novelistAnnie Lord believesthe way we treat each other is part of the problem: “People treat each other as disposable because they’ve got the mindset of an app.” Factor in the growing influence of the manosphere, which many say has“ruined dating”, and it’s not hard to comprehend why experts say we’re experiencing a global dating crisis. Since 2014, the number of young people without close friendships/relationshipshas “risen fivefold”. Joke all you want about oversensitive gen Zs, but they are experiencing life in a social vacuum.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf you’re dealing in real life with men who don’t even text you back, let alone take you on a date, it’s easy to see why it would sting to watch them engage enthusiastically in a video-game relationship with a virtual woman whom they shower with expensive gifts, bouquets, and thoughtful messages. AsTikToker RawTJR’s postjoked: this is “how mfs gonna be treating Lucia in GTA 6 while treating their irl gf like shi”.“I will NOT stand for people calling these partners ‘jealous’ or ‘overreacting’ when they clearly are trying to voice real concerns about their relationships,” wrote trans activist and sex educator Dee Whitnell in anInstagram post. “If someone feels underappreciated in their relationship but sees their partner fulfilling these needs for someone else (even if it is a game character), it’s totally understandable why they would feel a bit frustrated.”As someone who exploreseveryromance option in all games that allow it, I personally think it’s absurd to class in-game romances as a form of cheating – though I appreciate that individual boundaries can differ. People might more reasonably channel their concerns into conversations around AI companionship sites, such as Candy AI and DreamGF, that offer virtual sexbots. As far back as 2023 we were asking if anAI chatbot could be classed as cheating– and the technology has vastly improved since then.More than anything else, this unexpected controversy around GTA VI highlights how dissatisfied and lonely many people are within their relationships. And a video game isn’t going to change that one way or another.Explore more on these topicsGrand Theft Auto VIGamesGrand Theft AutocommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanity | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel bills
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel bills
Content: Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, at the signing of an oil agreement with the US in Caracas, 2 September  2026.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVenezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, at the signing of an oil agreement with the US in Caracas, 2 September  2026.Photograph: Juan Barreto/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionVenezuelaThe Guardian view on Donald Trump’s oil deal: Venezuela pays for his vanityEditorialThe US president seized a nation’s natural wealth in a modern-day version of gunboat diplomacy to feed his ego – not to lower Americans’ fuel billsWed 9 Sep 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.46 EDTShareImperialism does not require a flag to be planted or a governor dispatched. It can be a powerful nation deciding who governs a smaller, weaker country, and on what terms and for whose benefit its resources will be developed. Donald Trump’s kidnapping of Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro, putting his deputy – Delcy Rodríguez – in his place as president, and then her signing a deal handing afifth of the country’s proven oil reserves to the US, amount to a modern version of 19th-century gunboat diplomacy. Regime change supplied America’s commercial concession.This won’t bother Mr Trump. But it should. The US president has oversold his neocolonial spoils. The additional production Venezuela is supposed to bringonlinemight bring down oil prices eventually, but notanytimesoon. Crucially, what Mr Trump calls “the biggest oil deal in history” won’t cause the price at the pump to fall before November’s midterms. When so many American votersare struggling to pay energy bills, it’s hard to see how unrealised Orinoco Belt riches are going to help Republican candidates.View image in fullscreenUS president Donald Trump.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APThe US president alsopromotesthe idea that he is transforming the US’s industrial landscape through fossil fuels. Although the Venezuela oil grab might be highly profitable for a fewselected companies, the windfall is dwarfed by the size of the US economy. Mr Trump is not getting cheap energy but a spectacle of American power. That may be enough for him.Before Mr Maduro was captured, Mr Trump haddecidedthat Venezuela’s oil belonged to the US. The Venezuelan strongman was offeredexileif he gave Washington want it wanted. When he dithered, a USarmadaassembled off Venezuela’s coast. Yet Mr Trump did not replace Mr Maduro with María Corina Machado from the democratic opposition. He instead backed the authoritarian regime that could secure the oilfields from ambitious army generals and spare the costs of occupation.The US doesn’t rule Venezuela directly, but it is exercising power through a lifelong socialist, Ms Rodríguez. She is remaking Chavismo, the revolutionary movement launched by Hugo Chávez, in her image – enraging someleftists. Ms Rodríguez has grantedNorth American Blue Energy Partners(Nabep) concessions to 17 oilfields in Venezuela for decades to come. Nabep’s boss, Alejandro Betancourt, acontroversialVenezuelan oil billionaire, popped up in Caracas for this week’s visit by the US energy secretary, Chris Wright. Nabep has in turn granted the Pentagon a35% equity stakeat no cost to the US taxpayer.The charge of “Yankee imperialism” was often dismissed as kneejerk anti-Americanism. Mr Trump has turned it into an American boast. Ms Rodríguez argues that she is no puppet. Cooperation with Mr Trump, she says, will bring Venezuela investment and couldgenerate$200bn in oil revenues. Unequal bargains have often benefited local rulers and intermediaries. The question is: what kind of economy and social order will that revenue produce? Oil cash is not the same as sovereign development.Mr Trump is a playground bully handed the world’s most powerful military. He mistakes coercion for greatness and sovereign nations for toys. He uses US power to feed his bottomless ego – recently claiming himself to be a biggerhistoricalfigure than Caesar, Genghis Khan, Napoleon, Stalin and Mao. When he departs the stage, others will have to rebuild what he has squandered: the US’s authority, its alliances and its reputation.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: An embattled Donald Trump is increasingly using sports as prop | Sport | The Guardian
description: Sports is the rare topic in which the president has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms
Author: Leander Schaerlaeckens
Headline: Sports is the rare topic in which the president has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms
Content: Donald Trump attends the Super Bowl in February 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump attends the Super Bowl in February 2025.Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/ReutersSportAn embattled Donald Trump is increasingly using sports as propLeander SchaerlaeckensSports is the rare topic in which the president has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred termsWed 9 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTShareLately, it seems Donald Trump’s scope of interests has narrowed to a few things: remaking downtown Washington DC in his gaudy image; wars he thinks he can win quickly and easily, even though he can’t.Also, golf. Always golf.Ever golf.We hear less and less about Trump’s plans to overhaul healthcare, reshore manufacturing jobs or address the budget deficit. Yet one other subject, aligned with his lifelong interests, continues to preoccupy him: sports.And in this area, his ideological project has methodically and loudly – since nothing of consequence can ever be done quietly by this administration – made more gains than just about anywhere else.Which is to say that Trump, or more likelythose seeking to swiminthe slipstream of Trumpism, are hard at work trying to put sports back to how it looked in the 1980s. After all, that’s when the president’s view of the world, and how it should function, ossified.This manifests in ways big and small, in consequences intended and accidental.Here’s a relatively small and surely accidental one.When Los Angeles FC soldVenezuela international David Martínez to Denmark’s FC Midtjylland for $8.4m recently, the club did not do so for sporting reasons – or not entirely. The winger, named tothe Guardian’s 2023 Next Generationclass, had difficulty adapting to life in Los Angeles after arriving as an 18-year-old because his family couldn’t get visas to visit him,according to the club.If Trump and his goons had even heard of the now-20-year-old, which they almost certainly hadn’t, he would have hardly been a top target of their policies. But that they have driven him to leave the country will would satisfy them all the same. This is exactly what the administration’s travel bans and curbs on visas were intended to achieve: to put people off coming to the US, or staying here.Then there’s the big stuff.The rolling campaign to “save” women’s sports from transgender athletes, who exist in vanishingly small numbers and are far from the threat those on the right would have you believe. This panic is propagated by a rabble who very proudly didn’t care about women’s sports at all until they spotted an opening to make a political profit from it.Trump’slooming presenceover the summer’s World Cup, and hisactive interferencein it. His attendance at the NBA finals, the Daytona 500 and the Ryder Cup, appearances thatseemed to cursehis favored participants.There’s theexecutive orderattempting to unwind the decades-overdue gains made by college athletes in winning the right to be treated like every other American worker. They can finally be paid for their valuable labor and move (almost) freely between programs in search of the best opportunities – same as their coaches and administrators have always been able to do.Foreign students and college athletes, meanwhile, find it harder and less attractive to come to and stay in the US on account of the same difficulties in bagging visas that chased off Martínez. That makes college sports more homogeneous and therefore, in Trump’s thinking, better.In trying to rearrange things to how they once were – the exact moment in the past when things were great; a time that nobody can seem to pinpoint, but which you’ll no doubt remember with searing clarity – Trump has even gone so far as to issue an executive order to try to protect the Army-Navy football game’s exclusive TV time slot. The College Football Playoff’s lurching expansion threatened to creep into the second Saturday of December, traditionally and legally set aside for the Commander-in-Chief’s Trophy.“Such scheduling conflicts weaken the national focus on our Military Service Academies and detract from a morale-building event of vital interest to the Department of War,”the orderreads.Also apparently intended as a morale-building event wasthe much-panned UFC eventon the White House lawn to celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary, and, more pressingly, Trump’s 80th birthday. The first professional sporting event on the White House grounds managed tolose $30m, even though the fighters were apparently paidat least partly in cryptocurrencyissued by a Trump company.When he sensed he would be met by a friendly crowd, Trump became the first sitting president toattend the Super Bowl. In the same spirit, he traveled to a World Series game in 2021, when he was out of power,just to do the racist tomahawk chopwith Atlanta Braves fans.He more or less ordered an IndyCar race to be held in DC, the Freedom 250, which was well attended but severely disrupted car and plane traffic in the capital. The awkward layout of the course, meanwhile, meant that nearly half the cars didn’t finish all the laps. No matter, Trump took a lap around the track in his presidential limousine. With no other cars on the road, he finished first.Then there are the unprovoked and untethered broadsides. Such as the time Trump suggested the National Football League change its name to accommodate soccer. Orsuggested LeBron James was a racistbecause he doesn’t play golf with the president. Or when he plunged a cleaver into the culture war prime cuts ofrestoring the Washington Commanders and Cleveland Guardiansto their old, racist names.Several of Trump’s golf courses have hosted events staged by LIV Golf, the Saudi-backed breakaway golf circuit thatappears to be on life support. If it should croak, it would share this distinction with the last sporting venture that Trump was intimately entangled with: the New Jersey Generals of the old United States Football League. Trump, who owned the franchise,bungled it into bankruptcyand took the entire league down with him.Yet the lesson that has stuck with himsince childhoodis that sports holds a privileged place in our national conscience, and that it serves as a powerful messaging conduit. Now, as president, his efforts have hardly been concerted or coordinated, but sports is the rare topic where Trump has succeeded in shifting the conversation to his preferred terms.Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts,which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.Explore more on these topicsSportDonald TrumpUS sportscommentShareReuse this content

title: European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: Far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generation, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: Far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generation, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anaïs Mims/GettyOpinionThe far rightEuropean democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyssRafael BehrFar-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin money are conniving to suffocate liberal idealism for another generationWed 9 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 08.22 EDTShareNot all that long ago,Europewas a beacon of liberal idealism. One memoir recalls it as an era “comfortably saturated with confidence in the unfailing and binding power of tolerance and conciliation”. The economic system seemed obviously preferable to barbarous alternatives. “People honestly believed that the divergencies and the boundaries between nations and sects would gradually melt away into a common humanity,” the author added.Those words could describe the spirit of globalisation at the turn of the millennium. They werewritten in the 1930s by Stefan Zweig, reflecting on the optimism of late 19th-century Vienna from the perspective of a Jewishémigréwhose world had been destroyed by murderous nationalism. Zweig took his own life in 1942. He never saw fascism defeated. He couldn’t have imagined a renaissance of liberalism in the second half of the 20th century so complete as to attain a pitch of complacency rivalling the one he remembered from his childhood.Now momentum is with the nationalists again. Victory for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in the region of Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend is not the biggest electoral prize won by a far-right party in Europe in recent years, but it isone of the most shockingbecause it is Germany. No country had more to learn from history if it wanted to immunise its democracy against extremism. None pursued a more systematic programme of inoculation. The word for it isVergangenheitsbewältigung– hard to say and tricky to translate, meaning roughly coming to terms with a shameful past.There is no excuse of ignorance about the AfD’s rise. It is a knowing repudiation of atonement. The party flirts with Nazi imagery and embraces racist definitions of nationhood, seeking to deport Germans whose credentials it sees as biologically improper. It is extreme enough toinduce squeamishnessin Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right National Rally (RN). She has spent years carefully cultivating respectability and is leading the polls ahead of next year’s presidential election. She doesn’t want to jeopardise her mainstream credentials by association with the unambiguous extreme.That is less of an impediment across the Atlantic.Elon Musk is an AfD fan, deploying his control of X to boost the party’s campaign messages.Last year, the US vice-president, JD Vance, met Alice Weidel,AfD co-leader, during a visit to Munich. There was no space in his diary for Olaf Scholz, then the German chancellor. Clearly, the AfD meets the criteria for endorsement set out in Donald Trump’snational security strategy, which pledges support for “patriotic resistance” movements committed to halting the “civilisational erasure” of Europe by immigration.In Britain,Nigel Faragecould once have assumed entitlement to that status as an early and enthusiastic cheerleader for Trump. But in the competition for Maga accolades, Reform UK has lost ground to parties and people even further to the right – Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain; ultra-nationalist agitator Tommy Robinson; pretty much anyone who can muster a mob of blackshirts or a passing troll who catches Musk’s eye posting racist conspiracy theories online.27:02Rise of the far right: can Farage get a boost from AfD’s win in Germany? | Politics WeeklyIt would be absurd if it wasn’t so effective. “We never fall into the same abyss twice,” writes Éric Vuillard, the French novelist. “But we fall in the same way, in a mixture of ridicule and dread.”The reach and pungency of the US right, drenched in white supremacism, interferes with Farage’s old strategy of banking far-right support and feinting moderation to make gains in the mainstream. Chasing credibility with fanatical racists in an international digital arena makes it hard to reassure a domestic analogue audience that he should be allowed near Downing Street.The tension shows in Farage’s attitude to the AfD. He spoke at a rally for it in 2017. Now he describes it as a“mixed bag” of a party, whose cultural stances are “utterly respectable and decent” but whose enthusiasm for dictators is “very difficult”.Farage has called AfD support for Vladimir Putin “hard to understand”. It can’t be that far beyond comprehension for a man who, in 2014, described the Russian president as theworld leader he most admired, albeit “as an operator, not a human being”.If Farage needs further insight into what might motivate a Kremlin fellow traveller, he could reach out to Reform’s former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, who isserving a prison sentence for accepting bribes to make pro-Russian speechesin the European parliament when he was a Brexit party MEP.Proximity to the Moscow line is a fairly reliable measure of fanaticism and venality on the spectrum from far-right to even further-right politics in Europe and the US. The same applies on the left, where a credulous appetite for Russian propaganda endures decades after the demise of Soviet ideology.Thankfully, there is not much of a market in British politics for openly pandering to Putin. That is one reason why Trump is also unpopular, although opinion polls suggest he is viewed more favourably by Reform supporters than the wider public. Farage has stopped boasting of his White House connections, perhaps because they have dried up, or maybe because sycophantic flapping around a foreign tyrant, even an American one, doesn’t project strength in a wannabe prime minister.It is striking how little the Reform leader has to say about the rest of the world and Britain’s place in it. The topic was hardly mentioned at the party’s annual conference last week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was atheatrical appearance by Jordan Bardella, the young Le Pen protege and likely prime minister if she wins the presidency. He signed a legally meaningless “deal” with Farage on stopping small-boat traffic across the Channel and wasimmediately criticised back homefor selling out to the UK. The likelihood of a French far-right government taking in more migrants as a policy favour to the UK is close to zero. Having xenophobic nationalists setting the agenda in Paris and London wouldn’t make relations easier, no matter what ideological amity they now claim.As the architect of Brexit, Farage is one of the most consequential politicians of his generation, but he can’t plausibly claim it as an achievement, even when addressing an auditorium of loyal fans. They know it has failed as well as everyone else.A Reform UK without Nigel Farage used to be unthinkable. Not any more | Gaby HinsliffRead moreFarage probably misses the simplicity of his old crusade against Brussels. He might envy nationalist counterparts on the continent, who get to rail against liberal Europeanism while enjoying the economic and strategic privileges afforded by EU membership. They don’t have to explain why it’s so cold on the outside. They play the Eurosceptic game, mobilising the same resentments, targeting the same scapegoats, but modifying the demands in recognition that Farage’s victory was pyrrhic. It doesn’t pay to actually leave. The ambition is to capture the European project, not destroy it, although it amounts to the same thing if the transformation happens through connivance with Maga ideology and Kremlin money.This doesn’t have to be Europe’s destiny. Nationalists do not form a monolithic bloc. The essence of their creed militates against cross-border partnership. Their egos generate more rivalries than alliances. Their selfishness sabotages deals. Countervailing forces can be mustered. There is no law of history that says a height of liberal optimism must be followed by an equivalent fall into chaos. The “binding power of tolerance and conciliation” was not defeated in the 20th century and it won’t be suffocated in this one either. We see the abyss. We can pass without plunging to the bottom.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
