title: Horror warnings about Australia’s ‘collapsing’ housing market are absurd – and very much in bad faith | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: If prices were to take a 10% fall from the March 2026 peak, as CBA has suggested, that would still only mean prices were back where they were at the end of 2024
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: If prices were to take a 10% fall from the March 2026 peak, as CBA has suggested, that would still only mean prices were back where they were at the end of 2024
Content: Anthony Albanese in Adelaide last year. The median price of houses in the city has more than doubled in six years.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese in Adelaide last year. The median price of houses in the city has more than doubled in six years.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPGrogonomicsAustralian economyHorror warnings about Australia’s ‘collapsing’ housing market are absurd – and very much in bad faithGreg JerichoIf prices were to take a 10% fall from the March 2026 peak, as CBA has suggested, that would still only mean prices were back where they were at the end of 2024Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 9 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.22 EDTShareHouse prices in the June quarter fell slightly off the back of three interest rate rises and the changes to the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing. But prices remain extremely high.In the June quarter the total value of Australia’s housing fell $34bn. Sounds like a lot? In percentage terms it was just 0.3%. That’s because in the June quarter the total value of Australian housing was $12.18tn. And here’s the kicker: that is $948bn more than it was a year ago.The horror warnings about Australia’s “collapsing” housing market really are quite stupid – and very much in bad faith.Labor is in damage control over falling house prices. Why not take credit instead? | Tom McIlroyRead moreThat bad faith began before the budget when vested interest groups and the opposition suggested the capital gains tax (CGT) discount and negative gearing had no impact on housing affordability and cutting them would not do anything to house prices. Now they are to blame for prices falling!Those vested interests have beenloudly cryingabout the fall of house pricesand the “brutal” tax changes.On Tuesday the latesttotal value of dwellings(houses and apartments) figures provided some much-needed data on the idiocy of the debate.These latest figures only go to the end of June, so we have yet to see an entire quarter under the new rules, but they do give some insight.There was a fall in the average dwelling prices in the June quarter – 0.7% across Australia. Although that is very much affected by the 2.4% fall in New South Wales prices and 2.1% drop in Victoria. Prices still rose in all other states except the ACT:If the graph does not display click hereThe size of the housing problem is clear when you ponder that even with that 2.4% fall in NSW, which took average dwelling prices from $1.337m to $1.305m, they are still 2% higher than the $1.28m price they were a year ago.In every single state the average dwelling price was higher in June this year than a year ago:If the graph does not display click hereAnd even worse is that over the past six years (since the pandemic), only Victoria has seen house prices grow less than household income:If the graph does not display click hereBecause these figures include prices from April as well as after the budget in May and June, clearly they don’t register the impact of the tax changes. This may mean that the median house price in Adelaide does not hit the $1m barrier that Perth, Brisbane, Canberra and Sydney have all reached.If the graph does not display click hereBut here’s a juicy statistic to chew: in Adelaide, Perth and Brisbane, the median price of houses has more than doubled in six years.Just think on that. Yep, nice, steady Adelaide, historically the cheapest capital city on the mainland to buy a home. Back in June 2020, half of the houses sold in the city of churches went for less than $487,500. In the June quarter of this year, you needed a bid of at least $975,000 to have a chance of buying a median-priced house.If the graph does not display click hereAnd sure, the percentage growth of house price in Sydney over the past six years was not as large (a mere 56% jump compared with Adelaide’s 100%, Brisbane’s 111% or Perth’s 112% increase), but the median price of a Sydney house in the June quarter this year was $532,600 more than it was six years ago.Yes, the median price fell from $1.55m in March to $1.49m in June, but is anyone sauntering around Pitt Street chatting about how cheap the harbour city has become?Whenever we hear anyone, whether they be an economist seeking an AFR column or a wannabe comedy-influencer seeking a spot on Sky After Dark, talking about the fall in house prices and the end of time, we really do need to calm the hell down.As Inoted last month, the “scary” projections about how far house prices would fall would take prices in Sydney merely back to 2023 levels. In Brisbane the projected fall wouldn’t even get you back to the price they were at the end of last year!Currently the average dwelling price across Australia is $1.1m – if prices were to take a 10% fall from the March 2026 peak, as the Commonwealth Bank has suggested, that would mean prices would go back to where they were at the end of 2024.If the graph does not display click hereThe good news is because household incomes have been growing since 2024, that 10% price drop would take the value of an average dwelling in Australia from being equivalent to 16.9 years of average household disposable income to 15.4 years.That is marginally higher than it was in the middle of 2021.If the graph does not display click hereAnd what were people saying about housing back in 2021? Well, I wrotea columntalking about the howl of despair of those whose housing dreams were being dashed.The changes in the budget are working as expected and desired. And if anyone thinks they are about to destroy the wealth of Australians, they should think back to 2021 and remember that no one thought housing was cheap then.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyGrogonomicsHousingTaxAustralian politicsLabor partyBusinesscommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia is on a collision course with US big tech. Could it cause Trump to turn on his ‘mate’? | Mark Kenny | The Guardian
description: Anthony Albanese wants social media algorithms to be optional – and it’s not the first Musk-Zuckerberg irritant emanating from Australia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Anthony Albanese wants social media algorithms to be optional – and it’s not the first Musk-Zuckerberg irritant emanating from Australia
Content: The Australia-US relationship could be tested when Anthony Albanese and Donald Trump rub shoulders at the UN general assembly in New York later this month.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenThe Australia-US relationship could be tested when Anthony Albanese and Donald Trump rub shoulders at the UN general assembly in New York later this month.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPOpinionSocial mediaAustralia is on a collision course with US big tech. Could it cause Trump to turn on his ‘mate’?Mark KennyAnthony Albanese wants social media algorithms to be optional – and it’s not the first Musk-Zuckerberg irritant emanating from AustraliaFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 9 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 19.22 EDTShareNew risks to a deftly managed personal relationship with Donald Trump have not slowed the Australian prime minister’s plans for a showdown with America’s all-conquering social media companies.Anthony Albanese, who will rub shoulders with the US president and other world leaders in New York later this month at the UN general assembly, is pushing ahead with changes that would impose fines on big tech firms under a newly created “digital duty of care”.“Just as we have basic safety standards for cars, toys or food, the duty of care applies basic standards for the online products we use every day,” said the minister for communications, Anika Wells, while releasing the draft legislation.Labor wants Australians to be able to opt out of online algorithms. How will it change your feed?Read moreThe change would also require social media platforms toprovide users a guaranteed “opt-out” facilityfrom the opaque algorithms that funnel polarising and harmful content to subscribers and expose them to carefully targeted advertising.The government is calling it “empowering” for users, while critics are reaching for comparisons with communist China andusing words like “Orwellian”.Australia’s digital foray is being watched in Washington and Silicon Valley amid expectations it will stiffen the resolve of other countries to insulate their own polities from the wilds of disinformation, fakery and toxic political extremism.Australia’s relationship with the US is routinely described as an enduring “mateship” based on strategically aligned interests as well as more basic cultural commonalities.However, that amity will be tested if the famously tetchy Trump fixes on a new acronym for his Aussie “mate” – Make Albanese The Example.Even so, it would not the be the first Trump-Musk-Zuckerberg irritant emanating from Australia.These changes build on Australia’s world-firstsocial media banfor under-16s, legislated in November 2024.While only partially effective, the ban drew the ire of the Trump administration and the social media titans, all of whom favour the unregulated populist character of social media over the “elitist” variety.And there’s the news bargaining incentive, which forces social media companies to strike deals with Australian media outlets or pay a 2.5% tax on their Australian advertising revenues.Australia’s changes to the calculation of tax liabilities of these companies have also caused consternation inside the Trump administration, which remains hyper-alert to mechanisms it believes operate like tariffs in another form.Albanese’s apparent resolve to clip the powerful US corporations marks an interesting contrast with the more supine posture he adopted recently when addressing the flagrantsocial harms of gambling.There, he resisted majority public support for a phased advertising ban on online gambling, out of concern for the business models of mainstream broadcasters, and the major sporting codes.Australia instead adopted partial restrictions on advertising during children’s viewing hours and limits on in-game gambling promotions.The comparison suggests the Australian PM is more attuned to the special-interest arguments of domestic capital than to those of the foreign variety.So far, reactions out of the US on the digital duty of care have been at officer-level, with the president yet to take to social media with his thoughts – although that is rarely far away.On Wednesday, White House spokespersonKush Desai saidthe Trump administration would raise its concerns with “trading partners”.“President Trump has unequivocally warned trading partners against imposing digital services taxes, fines, and other forms of extortion on America’s leading technology sector”, Desai said.But even within Australia, the social media changes have provoked furious free-speech hyperbole, with the opposition branding the duty of care as the manifestation of its “worst fears”.The opposition’s communications spokesperson, Sarah Henderson, warned that the relevant minister would be armed “with unfettered powers to make any regulation into what she would describe as serious harm in the case of adults or harm concerning children”.“Now, this means almost anything,” Henderson told the conservative-aligned News24 broadcaster.An algorithm off switch isn’t enough. Big tech needs a duty of care over addictive designs | Zoe DanielRead more“The government could shut down any content or material that they deem to be harmful.“This is a very egregious breach of our freedom of expression, and we must fight this extremely hard.”Pauline Hanson, the leader of the hardline One Nation party, depicted the proposed curbs on social media firms in even more extreme terms.“Labor is copying the Chinese Communist Party’s censorship playbook,” Hanson fumed on Facebook.Australia’s regulatory creativity, some elements of which are novel while others have been finessed from Europe, will ensure Albanese has plenty to talk about during the looming “summit season”.Conversations with the US president, however, might be more problematic.Mark Kenny is a longtime press gallery journalist and is director of the Australian Studies Institute at the Australian National UniversityExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionSocial media banUS politicsDigital mediaAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Seven of my colleagues were killed in Gaza. There and in Ukraine, aid workers are no longer safe | José Andrés | The Guardian
description: It seems the attack on World Central Kitchen workers was a deliberate IDF military tactic. The protections of the Geneva conventions are now paper thin, says World Central Kitchen founder José Andrés
Author: José Andrés
Headline: It seems the attack on World Central Kitchen workers was a deliberate IDF military tactic. The protections of the Geneva conventions are now paper thin, says World Central Kitchen founder José Andrés
Content: Gaza residents inspect the remnants of the vehicle that had been carrying World Central Kitchen workers, April 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGaza residents inspect the remnants of the vehicle that had been carrying World Central Kitchen workers, April 2024.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionHumanitarian responseSeven of my colleagues were killed in Gaza. There and in Ukraine, aid workers are no longer safeJosé AndrésIt now seems the 2024 attack on World Central Kitchen workers was a deliberate IDF tactic. The protections of the Geneva conventions have become paper thinJosé Andrés is the founder of the food aid charity World Central KitchenWed 9 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.30 EDTShareIn times of war, the hard and vital work of supplying food, water and medicine has been protected by international agreements foralmost 80 years. Yet those protections have been systematically and repeatedly ignored in the two most bloody wars of recent years: Ukraine and Gaza.Russia has attacked healthcare targets in Ukraine more than 3,200 times since the full-scale invasion in February 2022,according to the World Health Organization: about twice a day on average. That includes many “double-tap” attacks on the same target in quick succession, which are especially lethal for first responders.In April, the UN security council heard that in the past three years, at least1,010 humanitarian workers had diedin 21 countries. More than half of those were in Gaza and the West Bank. That is three times more than the 377 killed in the previous three years.“This is not an accidental escalation,” said Tom Fletcher, the UN’s undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs. “It is the collapse of protection.” This collapse of protection has led directly to the airstrikes on aid workers in Gaza, including seven of my own World Central Kitchen (WCK) team, who werekilled by the IDF in April 2024despite full cooperation and coordination with the military.At the time, the IDF concluded that the attacks had been “a grave mistake” and a breach of its own standard operating procedures.It stated: “We consider the vital humanitarian activity of international aid organizations to be of utmost importance, and we will continue to work to coordinate and assist their activities, while ensuring their safety and safeguarding their lives.” The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, was dismissed for his actions.However, these fine words were undercut by the IDF itself, when its military prosecutor decided last monthnot to open a criminal investigationinto the airstrikes on our convoy. Now we understand, because of a Guardian investigation, that the targeting of the WCK convoy was the result of a military tactic ofguilt by association. It means that lethal force can be triggered by suspicions, shadows, or simply prejudice. This undefined, unjustified and unlawful tactic is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. What are the protections under these conditions?It is worth remembering why the fourth Geneva convention was created in 1949 and embraced by the world, with the express intention of protecting civilians in war and meeting basic humanitarian needs. In the immediate aftermath of the second world war, the scale of civilian suffering shocked the world’s conscience. Indeed, one of the key architects of the convention was Georges Cahen-Salvador, a French Jewish civil servant, whose family was imprisoned at the Drancy internment camp. They were being deported to Auschwitz in 1943 when they managed to escape to Switzerland. He was one of several survivors who drafted the fourth convention.The convention’s assertions of shared values in war are not lost today, but they are struggling to survive.David Ben-Gurion, Israel’s founding father, famously said: “The fate of Israel depends on two things: its strength and its righteousness.” It’s something that Israel’s military leaders like to quote, but their record falls far short. Humanitarian values are the foundation of righteousness; they are what separate responsible nation states from terrorist groups or rogue states who don’t care about civilian suffering. The protection of aid workers allows the world to ensure that civilians are cared for.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe might be numb to the sight of Russia disregarding our values. But we surely cannot tolerate the only democracy in the Middle East behaving the same way.José Andrés is the founder of the food aid charity World Central Kitchen, and a Michelin-starred chefDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsHumanitarian responseOpinionWar crimesUkraineIsrael-Gaza warAidcommentShareReuse this content

title: Farage is clearly struggling – I saw that for myself. But his legacy will be a poison that runs deep | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: The mood at the Reform conference was volatile and brittle. But the forces massing further to the right of the party are testament to its impact, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The mood at the Reform conference was volatile and brittle. But the forces massing further to the right of the party are testament to its impact, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Nigel Farage delivers his keynote speech on the first day of the Reform party conference at the NEC in Birmingham, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNigel Farage delivers his keynote speech on the first day of the Reform party conference at the NEC in Birmingham, 4 September 2026.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesOpinionReform UKFarage is clearly struggling – I saw that for myself. But his legacy will be a poison that runs deepAndy BeckettThe mood at the Reform conference was volatile and brittle. But the forces massing further to the right of the party are testament to its impactWed 9 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareFor much of the time sinceNigel Farageresumed the Reform UK leadership two long years ago, his party has been an island of relative stability in the increasingly rough sea of British politics. While other parties plunged queasily in the polls, messily purged dissidents, argued publicly about their direction and changed leaders, Farage dominated Reform UK and gave impregnably self-assured interviews. The party’s popularity moved steadily upwards, comfortably above that of all the others.It is a paradox that a new party with wildly expectant members, not many experienced politicians and few properly worked-out policies became the pole around which the country’s political debate revolved, and yet this seemed to do no harm to Reform’s chances of winning the next general election. As with rising rightwing populist parties across the world, Reform’s tendency to make it up as it went along appeared to be not a weakness but, for many voters, much of its appeal.That seems less the case now. Amid multiple, worsening funding scandals, and with the party openly divided about how to respond to them, this year Reform has lost about a quarter of its support and its poll lead over Labour. There are internal mutterings about the attention-seeking and leadership ambitions of its home affairs spokesperson, the relentlessly abrasive Zia Yusuf, and its Treasury spokesperson, the slippery former Tory Robert Jenrick.Meanwhile, Farage himself, who at 62 is two decades older than them, and has been active in politics for more than 40 years, may be finally losing his composure. Interviewed by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberglast weekend, after months of largely and uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, he switched between anger at his enemies, claims to victimhood and unconvincing insouciance: eyes bulging with fury one moment, head bobbing with forced laughter the next. Even by the feverish standards of modern British politics, it was a strange, almost manic performance.What might happen to Reform and our wider politics if the party’s troubles continue and deepen? The answers may be less reassuring than Reform’s enemies like to think. While the diminishing likelihood of a Reform government is welcome, the party’s crisis could change Reform, and the forces massing further to the right of it – both in parliament and on the streets – in unpredictable and dangerous ways.At the party’s conference last week, the mood felt brittle and volatile. Whereas speakers insisted that Reform was still a “government in waiting”, and banners, lanyards and speeches relentlessly hyped its potential “first 100 days”, the delegates I spoke to were worried about the party’s slide in the polls and general election chances, Andy Burnham’s assured start as prime minister, and the growing pressure Farage was under. After his speech was repeatedly interrupted by hecklers from the green group Climate Resistance, I overheard two delegates, mild-looking, middle-aged men in suits, discussing the protest. “It’s got to stop,” said one. The other said: “Smash ’em in the face!”Another Reform reaction to the party’s difficulties has been to announce ever more extreme, dramatic policies, such asdeporting foreign prisoners,possibly to the infamously brutal jails of El Salvador, and deploying the Royal Navy and Royal Marines to intercept and take all small boat migrants back to France, in “the biggest military operation in the English Channel since the second world war”. In his conference speech, Yusuf described “Operation Fortress” with lingering detail, while huge images of a military helicopter and warship were projected on to the set behind him, and a storm of applause came from the packed hall. Perhaps the potential for such authoritarian political theatre and performatively aggressive policy was always there in Reform, but both feel much more central to its activities now.“All parliamentary recesses will be cancelled,” declared Farage in his speech. “Parliament will sit, if necessary, for 24 hours a day, six days a week, until we pass the necessary legislation.” Nothing would be allowed to obstruct “the will of the people” – even though, with modern election turnouts low and half a dozen parties now competing seriously across the country, a Reform victory might represent the will of only a fifth of voters, or less.This year, with the party losing the electoral initiative, new movements have appeared on the anti-migrant right: the even more hardline Restore Britain, andPatriot Platform, the black-clad blockaders of Dover and Portsmouth. Though Farage has criticised both groups, the latter for wearing balaclavas at their protests, the boundaries between Reform and these rivals are not as firm as he would like more mainstream rightwing Britons – whose support Reform badly needs – to think. Restore and Reform’s rhetoric and policiescan be hard to distinguish, while on Monday, Yusuf visited Portsmouth and spoke amicably with Patriot Platform’s organiser, Daniel Thomas, a convicted attemptedkidnapper.Thomas told Yusuf he was upset by Farage’s criticism, and that the protests were not meant to intimidate, but that he still considered Farage a “hero” for his campaigning against the small boats. “You have done really well,” said Thomas. “A lot of people support you.” “Thank you,” said Yusuf, who listened to him at length, nodding respectfully. Then Yusuf replied: “I will take that message – you’ve got my word … take that back to him [Farage].”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe encounter suggested that Reform’s problems may create new alliances and opportunities for the hard right, reshaping but not weakening anti-migrant politics. While the Conservative shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, condemned the Portsmouth violence, he added: “People are genuinely angry at the government’s failure to stop the boats.” Even Labour dares not challenge the legitimacy of what the policing minister, Sarah Jones, called on Monday “the frustration we see in our communities today” about the boats. Just as Reform’s rise made both Labour and the Tories more nationalist and socially conservative, there is a danger that its decline, temporary or otherwise, could continue that process, as they compete for its former supporters.If you’re opposed to Reform’s policies, and especially if you might become one of their victims, then its setbacks this year may be a relief. But that relief will only be partial while its ideas and claims remain so thoroughly embedded across politics and the media, and in many people’s everyday conversations and thinking. One day, Farage will retire, but what he represents will be even harder to stop.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsReform UKOpinionNigel FarageMigrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Courage and contradictions’: what Gloria Steinem meant to feminist writers from around the world  | Rebecca Solnit, Rokhaya Diallo, Mona Eltahawy, V (formerly Eve Ensler), Julia Gillard, Jennifer Robinson, Elif Shafak and Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: Our global panel of writers reflect on the great legacy of the American feminist and civil rights activist, who died last week aged 92
Author: Rebecca Solnit
Headline: Our global panel of writers reflect on the great legacy of the American feminist and civil rights activist, who died last week aged 92
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe panelGloria Steinem‘Courage and contradictions’: what Gloria Steinem meant to feminist writers from around the worldRebecca Solnit,Rokhaya Diallo,Mona Eltahawy,V (formerly Eve Ensler),Julia Gillard,Jennifer Robinson,Elif ShafakandRhiannon Lucy CosslettOur global panel of writers reflect on the great legacy of the American feminist and civil rights activist, who died last week aged 92Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 12.42 EDTShareI’m grateful for the role Gloria Steinem played from the 70s to the 90sRebecca SolnitGuardian US columnist and authorAs far as I can tell, the US women’s movement was mostly clustered in coastal cities and university towns untilMs magazine, which Gloria Steinem cofounded and for many years co-managed, made it national. My mother in suburban California was an early subscriber and I was a tween who voraciously devoured every issue. I think it played a role in stiffening her resolve and her sense of her own rights, which led to her leaving my violent father.Some of the hot takes I’m seeing now on Steinem, and the women’s movement she was at the heart of, act as reminders that a lot of people have no idea of what women’s lives were like before second-wave feminism. Of how women were routinely described as weaker, less intelligent, less rational and less objective than men, and therefore less believable, less qualified to work, testify, participate. No understanding of how utterly disempowered and excluded women were in both law and society, how women were rendered radically unequal economically in so many ways, including exclusion from professions and education and without rights to equal pay, to be free from workplace sexual harassment and discrimination. No memory of how marriage was a relationship of radical inequality in which a woman surrendered many rights and her identity to her husband, not even reserving the right to say no to sex until pressure from feminists made marital rape a crime in a growing number of American states in the 1970s and 1980s.We now face a huge backlash, maybe even huger than the backlash we’ve always faced, but I believe feminism is just getting going in reversing not centuries but millennia of patriarchy, and I’m grateful for the role Gloria Steinem played in giving those decades of the 1970s to 1990s the transformative momentum that has made my life so much better, in so many ways, than my mother’s, let alone my grandmother’s.Her relationships with women of colour informed her feminist activismRokhaya DialloFrench journalist, writer, film-maker, activist and Guardian Europe columnistGloria Steinem understood early on that the feminist struggle would be fought through the media as well as campaigning, and inspired generations of journalists, myself included. As co-founder of Ms magazine, the first in the US run entirely by women, she strengthened the connection between journalism and activism.View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem and the late author and activist Dorothy Pitman Hughes in 2014.Photograph: Scott Roth/Invision/APSteinem’s feminism was more attentive to race than that of many of her white contemporaries in the “second wave”. Her first explicitly feminist essay, After Black Power, Women’s Liberation, displays a keen understanding of the need to connect feminist struggles with other movements for justice. She wrote about poor women and mothers, and imagined an alliance between radical feminists, middle-class women and “poor women of all colors”, although some of the dated terminology may now appear offensive. Her relationships with prominent women of colour – including Dorothy Pitman Hughes,Shirley ChisholmandWilma Mankiller– informed every aspect of her work. As sheacknowledged: “Personally, I learned feminism disproportionately from Black women.” In 1971, she served as treasurer of the fund for the legal defence of Angela Davis, the Black feminist philosopher unjustly prosecuted for murder who faced the death penalty.Steinem leveraged her privilege as an educated white woman with access to elite media circles, but could not escape the dynamics of public life that made hers “the face of feminism” within a diverse and collective movement: the names of the women of colour who stood alongside her have not left the same imprint on public memory.While I admired Steinem immensely, I regretted that her feminism remained so closely aligned with the Democratic party. This led her todefend Bill Clintonin 1998 and minimise Monica Lewinsky’s allegations, before acknowledging this failing two decades later. Her support forHillary Clintonalso exposed the limits of a feminism centred on representation.But at a time of rising femonationalism (the use of women’s rights to advance nationalist and racist agendas), Steinem’s legacy reminds us of the urgent need for a feminism rooted in international solidarity and committed to fighting every form of oppression.Gloria’s kindness and empathy were like steroids that strengthened usMona EltahawyEgyptian-American journalist and author of theFEMINIST GIANTnewsletterA couple of days after Egyptian riot policeassaulted meduring a protest near Tahrir Square in November 2011, Gloria Steinem emailed me with news of what she called my “girl gang”: feminists and activists from around the world who had been writing to each other to find the best ways to support me. “No matter where you are, please tell me if there is anything at all I can do to make your life easier – or our outrage more effective, with friendship and empathy from your Girl Gang!” she signed off.I had met Gloria just once, a month before, when the Hammer museum in Los Angeles hosted us for a feminist conversation in front of a live audience. She was a gracious interlocutor who treated me like a peer. We met several times since that conversation, each a reminder of the power of the feminist girl gang.I was among a girl gang of 25 that she invited to send her questions for anInterview magazine column. My question was about us both being childfree by choice. “I would put the emphasis on ‘free’. It has increased my freedom,” she replied.I am a feminist who will tell you to fuck off to your face. Kindness and empathy did not make it to my second book, The Seven Necessary Sins for Women and Girls. Gloria blurbed it thus: “Mona Eltahawy’s Necessary Sins is shocking, brave, gloriously unfeminine, and right on time … Reading it will free you, and acting on it will free us all.”My “sins” – anger, profanity, violence etc – are necessary in our fight against patriarchy. Gloria’s kindness and empathy were like steroids that strengthened us for that fight: batons she passed across feminist generations and borders – and especially vital when that fight against patriarchy leaves us bruised, with broken limbs, and broke. She lent me $1,000 during a particularly tight financial time and I was mortified at how long it took me to repay her. She was unfazed.Farewell, Gloria. To quote your 2011 email: “you should see the … loving outpouring from your girl gang from around the world!”She’d want us to remember that the backlash against women is a sign of our powerV (formerly Eve Ensler)American playwright and activistI will always be grateful to Gloria for her early support of my playThe Vagina Monologues. After she came to see me perform in a little theatre way downtown, she agreed to write the foreword to the book. She showed up decking her red boa at every event we held early on to birth theV-Day movementto end violence against women, gender-expansive people and girls – now 30 years old – into the world. The Vagina Monologues was very outside the mainstream at the time and her support of it helped other people be brave.View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem, Glenn Close and V at a V-Day benefit performance of The Vagina Monologues in New York, 2001.Photograph: Darla Khazei/Associated PressShe did that same thing for so many women, catalysing their dreams, their visions, their advocacy, their emerging non-profits by lending her support, her strategy, her kindness.It’s not lost on me that Gloria left this world in the midst of one of the greatest periods of attacks on women’s rights – the destruction of maternal health care; women being forced out of the labour market in the hundreds of thousands, especially Black women; the siege on reproductive rights; rape academies emerging online; the Epstein files still not being prosecuted; and having a convicted felon as president who has been found liable in a civil court for sexual abuse. But if Gloria had anything, she had stamina and infinite hope, and she would want us to remember that the backlash is an indication of our victories and our power.Now we need to go beyond where we’ve been, to new imaginings in order to fight off the racist, fascist, capitalist patriarchy that is actively working to kill our world.It is impossible to write the history of the women’s movement without herJulia GillardFormer Australian prime minister and former leader of the Australian Labor party. She was the first woman to hold either positionI am deeply saddened by the passing of feminist icon Gloria Steinem. Gloria was at the vanguard of the women’s rights movement as a political activist, journalist and editor, writer and thinker for more than 60 years. It is impossible to write the history of the women’s movement without her name being at the centre of the narrative. Indeed, her name is synonymous with feminism.I felt incredibly fortunate to interview Gloria in 2022 forA Podcast of One’s Own. Then 88, Gloria was as passionate as ever about achieving equality and advocating for others. I greatly admired her steadfast commitment to the cause, even when progress was not linear, and backwards steps were taken – especially for reproductive freedom in the United States.Gloria’s dedication to equality and empowerment for women everywhere, and from all walks of life, will continue to endure around the world. Her legacy is now ours to take forward. My heartfelt condolences go out to Gloria’s family and friends.She was the truth-teller who inspired my grandmother, my mother – and meJennifer RobinsonAustralian barrister working at at Doughty Street Chambers, and co-author ofHow Many More Women?When I heard the news Gloria Steinem had died, everything stopped.I had just walked out of the Sydney opening of our documentary,Silenced, which is about the legal backlash against #MeToo and how the law silences women from speaking out about abuse. Women were walking out of the cinema crying and angry about how far we still have to go – and activated about what we need to do to change it.And then we were hit with the news that we had lost Steinem. The news spread by hushed whispers through in the crowd in front of me. The grief was palpable.Steinem, the silence-breaker. The truth-teller who had inspired millions of women around the world to find our voices and use them. The woman who inspired my grandmother, my mother – and me. My grandmother is a survivor of domestic violence and later worked in the women’s refuge movement to make it easier for the women and children who came after her. She is in our film because her work inspired mine. I grew up hearing my grandmother quote Steinem and, whenever I speak – including the other night in Sydney – her words and her ideas can be found.It hit me hard. I had to take a moment. I wanted to cry. But then I looked around at the sea of women in front of me – victim-survivors, frontline services workers, lawyers from women’s legal services, and engaged and concerned community members, inspired to help create the change we need for women.It was beautiful. And it made me think of one of my favourite Steinem quotes: “People are always asking me, ‘Who will you pass the torch to?’ The question makes me angry. There is no one torch – there are many torches – and I’m using my torch to light other torches.”In her lifetime, she lit so many torches – all over the world – including in me and among the women gathered with me in Sydney the other night. What an incredible legacy.As she said, “The future depends entirely on what each of us does every day; a movement of people is only people moving.” The best way to celebrate and honour her legacy is to continue it – and keep moving.She passionately wanted to connect local, national and global feminismsElif ShafakBritish-Turkish novelist and political scientistIn my mid-20s I left Istanbul to become a fellow in women’s studies at Mount Holyoke College in Massachusetts. I arrived without knowing a single soul, entranced by the splendour of autumnal colours in Boston. The libraries there hold one of the best archives in the US on the history of feminist theory and practice, and, as winter descended, I burrowed myself into reading Audre Lorde, Maya Angelou, Doris Lessing, Toni Morrison … and that was when I properly discovered Gloria Steinem.Steinem had an unconventional, nomadic upbringing, and until she was 11 she had not spent a full year at school. In the absence of stable education, it was books – including Louisa May Alcott’s Little Women – that helped and guided her. “I was rescued by librarians,” she would explain later.View image in fullscreenGloria Steinem in her New York City flat, November 1990.Photograph: Barbara Alper/Getty ImagesI was struck by the courage she had shown in exposing the reality of the shiny world of Playboy bunny clubs, and the magazine she co-founded, Ms, never shied from covering difficult issues, such as sex trafficking and sexual harassment. But it was her books that stayed with me: Moving Beyond Words, Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, Marilyn: Norma Jean …Steinem believed that any meaningful change had to grow like a tree. From the bottom up. She not only founded women’s organisations and became a leading voice in second-wave feminism, she also saw the women’s movement as her chosen family. She said she had learned feminism from Black women. For her, race and gender were inextricably connected: “It is not possible to be a feminist without being anti-racist.” She was equally cognisant of class barriers. She passionately wanted to connect local, national and global feminisms.When people asked her how she managed to remain optimistic, she said it was because she did not stay in one place. Just like in her childhood, she kept travelling. “Perhaps the most revolutionary act for a women will be a self-willed journey – and to be welcomed when she comes home.”She was not perfect and not always right, and we also need to be able to talk about that – in a calm and nuanced way. Her contribution to generations of civil rights and women’s rights has been immense and genuine.Gloria Steinemwould have made a fascinating character in a novel – with her resilience, her courage, her determination, her trailblazing and her contradictions.She would not give up the fight for women’s liberation, and nor must weRhiannon Lucy CosslettBritish Guardian columnistI first encountered Gloria Steinem in much the same way as I met her feminist contemporaries – on my mother’s bookshelves, which I ransacked. Although as a teenage girl in the late 1990s I had very much swallowed the post-feminist narrative (much to my mother’s disappointment) that the women’s movement had accomplished all it needed to, I still read every book for adult women that I could get my hands on. I credit Steinem’sundercover Playboy Bunny piece– which was extracted in one of the books – with the fact that I started to question the raunch culture that was all around me (and never bought a Playboy T-shirt). That is the power of good journalism – it echoes through the decades.I found Steinem again at university, in the aftermath of a violent attack that galvanised me, as it can so many women, and have been a great admirer ever since. When I was in my 20s, setting up my own feminist magazine – the Vagenda – her work was a big influence. Her vocal and inclusive activism, her willingness to reflect on her missteps, her sense of humour and her refusal to give up the fight even when times were very dark indeed have all been an inspiration.Her book dedication to the British doctor who granted her an abortion at the age of 22 despite it not then being legal – in which she writes “I’ve done the best that I could with my life”, as she had promised him he would – struck a chord with so many for a reason: it’s a profoundly moving testament to the freedom that access to abortion grants a woman, even more so in the aftermath of the repeal of Roe v Wade. I find it so very sad that Steinem leaves a world where reproductive rights remain under severe threat. She devoted her life to this and other crucial questions of women’s liberation. She would not give up the fight, and nor must we. Onwards, in her honour.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I co-founded an orchestra 18 years ago. Since then, I’ve seen doors close for working-class musicians | Robert Ames | The Guardian
description: I have lost patience with the sector’s talk of diversity when it refuses to acknowledge those people who can’t afford to keep playing, says conductor and composer Robert Ames
Author: Robert Ames
Headline: I have lost patience with the sector’s talk of diversity when it refuses to acknowledge those people who can’t afford to keep playing, says conductor and composer Robert Ames
Content: Sigur Rós performing with the London Contemporary Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall, London, 30 September 2025.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSigur Rós performing with the London Contemporary Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall, London, 30 September 2025.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesOpinionClassical musicI co-founded an orchestra 18 years ago. Since then, I’ve seen doors close for working-class musiciansRobert AmesI have lost patience with the sector’s talk of diversity when it refuses to acknowledge those people who can’t afford to keep playingWed 9 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTShareI’ve spent most of my adult life working in classical music – for the past 18 years as the co-founder and conductor of the London Contemporary Orchestra (LCO), an organisation I’m stepping down from today. During that time, I have found myself increasingly angry athow much harderit has become for someone without money behind them to build a life in the sector.There used to be a route in. As a child from a working-class background, I could pick up an instrument at a state school, get cheap lessons through the local, council-backed music service and play in youth orchestras (borrowing a viola because my family couldn’t afford one).The route was never easy or fair. As a teenager, I spent summers doing everything from being a binman to working on a farm to pay for music courses. During those weeks, of course, I wasn’t practising – people from more privileged backgrounds could spend the summer getting better while I scraped together the money to access some of the same opportunities.Still, the route existed. Now we are dismantling it while talking endlessly about “access”. Today, working-class musicians arebeing priced outby countless unavoidable costs: lessons, instruments, train fares, courses, high rents (especially in London), unpaid preparation, cancelled dates.I’ve worked with enough musicians to know that talent turns up everywhere. Opportunity doesn’t. After my undergraduate degree, I was determined not to leave London. It was the strongest freelance market in the country and leaving felt like walking away from my best chance of building a career. I couldn’t afford the rent, so I sofa-surfed for months at a time. Occasionally, I slept rough. I wanted to be a musician and assumed this was simply what I had to do.When I co-founded the LCO, I went years without making any meaningful money from it. I remember early business meetings in posh restaurants when I didn’t have enough money for a Tesco meal deal. I’d turn up starving, pretending I wasn’t hungry while everyone else ate. It was humiliating.Now imagine another young musician trying to build an orchestra – but they have family money behind them and help with housing costs. Both musicians put in the same amount of work and spend years without properly paying themselves; but, while on paper they are taking the same risk, in reality, the consequences are not remotely the same.That, to me, is class in a nutshell: two people can work equally hard and take the same gamble but one has a much bigger margin for error. The ability to work for little or nothing is itself another form of capital.More than 70% of musicians working in the UK today are self-employed or freelance. Under the current Musicians’ Union/Association of British Orchestrascategory 1 agreement, the minimum fee for a section musician for a rehearsal and concert day of up to six hours is £163.18. But behind that can sit 15 years of training, an expensive instrument and hours of unpaid preparation. The six hours on the call sheet, though, is the only bit you’re paid for.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on the arts in schools: classrooms need more creativity | EditorialRead moreThis is why I lose patience with some of classical music’s language around diversity. There are brilliant schemes and brilliant people doing the work, but eventually you hit the economics. You cannot outreach-programme your way out of London rent, and you can’t diversify a workforce while refusing to talk about who can afford to stay in it. I have watched so many excellent musicians give up early in their careers. People who were absolutely good enough, but simply couldn’t afford to keep doing it. It is easy to say they lacked commitment or didn’t want it enough. Maybe they just ran out of money.If the people who make it through the industry’s elite training programmes increasingly come from similar economic backgrounds, classical music doesn’t just look narrower; it thinks narrower. It hires, programmes and talks to that small group of people, then acts surprised when people call it elitist.Some will say I’m encouraging the lowering of standards. In fact, I want higher standards. If we care about excellence, why would we only search for it among people whose families can afford the training and to subsidise the years of professional uncertainty that follow?I made it through and now have a conducting career I adore. But if I only just managed it in the relative comfort of the Blair years, with incredibly supportive parents behind me, what on earth are working-class kids with musical aspirations going through now?Or, more worrying, are they looking at the whole thing and deciding it’s not even worth trying?Robert Ames is a conductor and composerExplore more on these topicsClassical musicOpinionYoung peopleWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Blanche d’Alpuget wasn’t just Bob Hawke’s wife. She was a fierce intellect who only saw the good in people | Craig Emerson | The Guardian
description: Blanche was an enthusiast for Bob’s reconciliation with Paul Keating – and delighted in the restoration of their friendship
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Blanche was an enthusiast for Bob’s reconciliation with Paul Keating – and delighted in the restoration of their friendship
Content: Former Australian Prime Minister Bob Hawke and his wife Blanche D'Alpuget in 2006.Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFormer Australian Prime Minister Bob Hawke and his wife Blanche D'Alpuget in 2006.Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty ImagesOpinionLabor partyBlanche d’Alpuget wasn’t just Bob Hawke’s wife. She was a fierce intellect who only saw the good in peopleCraig EmersonBlanche was an enthusiast for Bob’s reconciliation with Paul Keating – and delighted in the restoration of their friendshipFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 9 Sep 2026 01.49 EDTFirst published on Wed 9 Sep 2026 01.30 EDTShareBlanche d’Alpuget laughed a lot. She dwelled on the good in people, rarely complaining about the bad or commenting on what she might have considered their weaknesses.To remember Blanche as Bob Hawke’s wife, while accurate, also diminishes her. She was a prolific author who had deep insights into people she knew and many whom she didn’t.Blanche d’Alpuget, writer and wife of Bob Hawke, dies aged 82Read moreBlanche was not entirely happy if she didn’t have a new book on the go. She would immerse herself in research for the next one, taking no break from the one just published.We had many discussions about the Middle East, the historical origins of the conflict and the personalities involved. It was, she concluded, a diabolical problem with no obvious solution.Thirty-six years ago, Bob asked me if he could be the godfather of our first child. And so it came to pass, Blanche always joining Bob in welcoming him into their home at Sydney’s Northbridge.Blanche was an enormous source of advice and comfort to Bob. On many occasions in his declining years, she invited my partner and me to their home for dinner where, at Bob’s urging, we talked of spirituality – including life after death.Blanche was convinced there was one, which she fully expected to enjoy and assured Bob he would too.View image in fullscreenBob Hawke and Blanche d'Alpuget on their wedding day in Sydney in 1995.Photograph: Patrick Riviere/Getty ImagesThe form of the afterlife that Blanche believed in was not entirely clear to me. Mostly it resembled the spiritualism of one of the eastern religions, although she did ask me to arrange for a Catholic bishop to visit Bob.Upon our many happy visits to the Northbridge house we would, however, be out of favour if we failed to bring Bob a caramel milkshake. So, we never failed the test.For a bit of respite, we would go to the movies together, leaving Bob with a carer.View image in fullscreenBlanche d'Alpuget and Bob Hawke's granddaughter Sophie Taylor Price address the memorial service for the former prime minister at the Sydney Opera House in July 2019.Photograph: Mike Bowers/The GuardianBlanche was an enthusiast for Bob’s reconciliation with Paul Keating, spending a lot of time with him discussing the good old days when Bob and Paul worked together and enjoyed each other’s companionship. She was delighted with the restoration of their friendship.Blanche loved her son, Louis, deeply. So much so that for an extended period Louis set up residence in the boathouse at end of their garden, enabling him to provide a constant source of companionship and love for Bob and Blanche.On 10 May 2019, I stayed with Bob for what was to be his last weekend, the night before the wedding of Louis and his fiancee, Brianna, in the Blue Mountains. Blanche was delighted that Bob made the trip to witness her beloved son’s marriage.View image in fullscreenCraig Emerson with Bob Hawke and Blanche d'Alpuget in Emerson's office in February 2008Without Bob’s company Blanche would get quite lonely, living alone in a fabulous apartment overlooking Hyde Park in Sydney.But now, somewhere in the universe, she would fully expect to be reunited with Bob and resume their decades-long romance.Craig Emerson worked as a member of Bob Hawke’s staff and visited Bob and Blanche often during Bob’s declining yearsExplore more on these topicsLabor partyOpinionAustralian politicsBob HawkecommentShareReuse this content

title: Russia is raining death on Ukraine’s women and children. Our hands shake, but we keep going for love | Alina Sarnatska | The Guardian
description: Our skin has thickened into armour, but I do not want survival to take away my tenderness towards others – or myself, says author and playwright Alina Sarnatska
Author: Alina Sarnatska
Headline: Our skin has thickened into armour, but I do not want survival to take away my tenderness towards others – or myself, says author and playwright Alina Sarnatska
Content: Aftermath of a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Yan Dobronosov/ReutersView image in fullscreenAftermath of a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, 8 September 2026.Photograph: Yan Dobronosov/ReutersOpinionUkraineRussia is raining death on Ukraine’s women and children. Our hands shake, but we keep going for loveAlina SarnatskaOur skin has thickened into armour, but I do not want survival to take away my tenderness towards others – or myselfWed 9 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.17 EDTShareMy grandma was as hard as nails. She had just turned 17 when the Nazis entered her village in the Kyiv region, near what is now the city of Bucha. She hid in the attic to avoid being taken for forced labour. They didn’t find her that time, but a few weeks later she was caught working in the fields. They put her in a cattle wagon and took her to Germany. She escaped and walked a couple of hundred kilometres back to her village. Grandma said that life was hard for everybody during the war, but she was lucky.In the past month, two of my friends here in Kyiv happened to tell me that their hands have started shaking during Russian airstrikes. Everybody who knows that my hands shake during airstrikes tells me their stories. One day, during an airstrike in the Donetsk region, I had a meltdown and have never recovered. Today you could say I am an ambassador for people whose hands shake during airstrikes.Those two friends said the same exact thing: their hands never used to shake before and now they do. Each one wrote: “I don’t understand what’s just happened to me.”For nearly five years, the Russians have been targeting these women and their children with drones, rockets, jet-powered drones and missiles. They havethreatenedus with nuclear weapons. They have used anOreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missilein combat; carried outa siege; again threatened a nuclear strike; tried to freeze us by destroying Ukraine’s heat and power systems in the middle of winter;blown up a dam, flooding two city districts; used more drones and fired yet other types of long-range missiles at Ukrainian cities; organisedterror attacks; and, once again, threatened to wipe us out with nuclear weapons.In the early hours of 19 July, the general staff of the armed forces of Ukraine reported amassive combined Russian attack: 41 missiles and 125 drones, with Kyiv as the main target. Next morning, I got a message from my friend Valya. “Everything was fine, and then all of a sudden something happened,” she wrote. “Everyone but me is at home asleep. I’m the only one who’s so anxious.”After every airstrike, the women I know “pull themselves together”, take their children to preschool, and go to work. Because children need to be fed – and if the state-run preschool doesn’t have a bomb shelter, the private one that does costs money. The women I know sleep beside their children in the corridors of their apartment buildings, in underground parking garages, in the metro or in pedestrian tunnels. “Everything’s fine,” say these women. After Russia fires dozens of missiles at Kyiv overnight, they say: “It was loud, but everything’s fine.” And they wonder why their hands shake and they even blame themselves for being weak.View image in fullscreenRussian missile strike in Kyiv, 8 September 2026.Photograph: ReutersMy grandma’s name was Dina and she was as hard as nails. She would get very angry when I snuggled up to our relatives. Once, my grandma’s sister was over and I climbed on to her lap and wrapped my arms around her. Grandma Dina yelled at me: “Get down, what a disgrace, you’re a big girl now!” I was seven. My grandma was afraid I would be spoiled. Whenever I cried, she would say to my mother: “Look how you’ve spoiled her, how will she cope with life?”Grandma Dina liked to feed stray cats. Grandpa protested, but she did it anyway. When she went out to feed them, for a few minutes she became a completely different person. First, she scolded them for being a nuisance, wearing her usual face. Then, as they ate, she would start to smile a bit and stroke their thin, fluffy backs. With one hand on her thigh, she would lean over and pet each cat once or twice, smiling. Then she would pick up the bowl, straighten up, and her expression would return to normal.One morning, I found a large grey cat dead under a bush; a cat that my grandma had been feeding for 10 years, as long as I had been alive. He had probably died of old age or sickness. I burst into tears and ran to my grandma. She rolled up a towel and gave me a whack on the ribs. “Now stop that crying, you’re a big girl now!” When my mother came home from work in the evening, I said: “I think Grandma’s a robot.” To which mum replied: “Nonsense, now go finish your soup.”There was nothing soft about Grandma Dina. If she were still alive today, she would be well prepared. She didn’t know much about getting along with people, but she did know how to pull herself together.Now I understand that she could not cut herself any slack or allow herself any feelings of self-kindness and that’s why she also felt no compassion for others. Compassion was too risky for her.And it’s true, we cannot let ourselves be as emotional or compassionate as we were before the war. We cannot live, let alone work, as we did before. On top of that, war reveals the sharp contrast between our reality and the cult of the self displayed on social media. Viral posts about “success, energy and choosing yourself” are irrelevant to anyone caring for a sick child when it is 5C inside your apartment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEnduring daily death and the violence of Russia’s attacks has changed us irreversibly. The skin of Ukrainian women has thickened into armour. These women take part in combat, live under constant airstrikes, and keep working and caring for their families through it all.But if it were up to me, I would keep my belly soft. I still want to hug people, hold them close, and feel the warmth of their hands. So what if Grandma Dina would say I’m not ready for life? I think that love is worth the risk.We stay calm because our children are watching us, because they need to be taken to preschool in the morning, because there is still work to do. But when resilience becomes an obligation, every trembling hand starts to feel like a personal failure. I do not want survival to take away my tenderness towards other people, or towards myself.Translated from Ukrainian by Larissa BabijAlina Sarnatska is a Ukrainian writer, playwright and war veteran. She is the author of two books and nine plays, and her work has been staged and presented internationallyDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
