title: The Orwellian machinery critics are desperate to protect is the algorithms, not laws that seek to reduce harm | Ed Coper | The Guardian
description: Critics of Australia’s digital duty of care bill stand in defence of the right of platforms to promote harm over health, rage over reason, and fake over fact
Author: Ed Coper
Headline: Critics of Australia’s digital duty of care bill stand in defence of the right of platforms to promote harm over health, rage over reason, and fake over fact
Content: ‘Calling something “Orwellian censorship” is just one of the many sure-fire ways to get noticed by social media algorithms,’ Ed Coper writes on Australia’s digital duty of care bill.Photograph: Posed by model; MementoJpeg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Calling something “Orwellian censorship” is just one of the many sure-fire ways to get noticed by social media algorithms,’ Ed Coper writes on Australia’s digital duty of care bill.Photograph: Posed by model; MementoJpeg/Getty ImagesOpinionSocial mediaThe Orwellian machinery critics are desperate to protect is the algorithms, not laws that seek to reduce harmEd CoperCritics of Australia’s digital duty of care bill stand in defence of the right of platforms to promote harm over health, rage over reason, and fake over factTue 8 Sep 2026 21.04 EDTLast modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.18 EDTShareThe algorithms have been kind to Pauline Hanson, which must be why she was so quick to jump to their defence when the Albanese government moved to rein them in this week.“Labor is copying the Chinese Communist Party’s censorship playbook,” she posted on Facebook, of all places – you know, the platform that is alleged to havecompliantly adoptedthe Chinese Communist party’s censorship playbook, in order to operate in China.Last week,Hanson called the reforms “Orwellian machinery”. She joins a chorus of those crying censorship fromSarah Henderson to Matt Canavan. The“deeply sceptical”Angus Taylor will surely soon follow.An algorithm off switch isn’t enough. Big tech needs a duty of care over addictive designs | Zoe DanielRead moreThere is machinery at play, for sure, and it is Orwellian: keeping us under constant surveillance; bombarding us with misinformation, and suppressing any corrective dissent. But that machinery is the algorithms those critics are so desperate to protect, not the laws that seek to reduce the harm they cause.Calling something “Orwellian censorship” is just one of the many sure-fire ways to get noticed by social media algorithms. They love a reductive argument stripped of reality, and lashed with emotive exaggeration.They love hysteria, outrage and conflict. There are rewards aplenty for those who peddle in them, even if it breaks society in the process. In the online attention economy, extremism sells. So every grievance grifter and grandstanding grafter rushes out to game the algorithm and send digital effluent cascading down our feeds in the form of “angertainment”.It’s what leads teenage boys to the manosphere, where the number of young men who think “a woman’s place is in the home” hasgrown by 400% in the last five years in some countries. Or teenage girls to an eating disorder, withone poll of 730 Australian frontline eating disorder workersfindingevery single respondentblamed social media.These are the ideals critics of the government’s push stand in defence of: the right of the platforms to promote harm over health, rage over reason, fake over fact. They stand for the rights of Silicon Valley to censor Australia, by giving big tech bros control over what we are allowed to see and read.What does the federal government’s proposed legislation do? It allows Australians to choose whether they want their feeds to be censored or not.An “opt out” pop up will ask users who they want in charge of their feed, the platform and its personalised recommendations (read: mining your attention with harmful clickbait) or the user who can instead see posts from accounts they choose to follow (read: social media circa 2014). The only censorship to be suffered will be by big tech, who all of a sudden lose control of your information diet.The second change the legislation will bring is akin to making sure that diet doesn’t kill you, in the same way the government “censors” food companies by telling them they aren’t allowed to sell yoghurt pouches laced with arsenic.This is the “duty of care” the laws will impose on digital platforms to make products that are safe for human consumption – in the same way any other industry must already do.This is not radical. Manufacturers have no “free speech” to make products that injure consumers. “Big Brother” tells theatres where to put fire exits. Theme park operators are “censored” from building rollercoasters that crash and burn.Social media platforms should likewise have a legal duty of care to build digital rollercoasters that don’t crash, and provide fire escapes from the toxic bin fire of their content.As AI madness encroaches, we need human connection more than ever. But we’ll have to fight for it | Van BadhamRead moreIn fact, a duty of care is the best way to rein in the harms social media algorithms cause preciselybecauseit is not censorship. Post-pandemic efforts that proscribed content to be removed (like anti-vaccination conspiracies) failed because it made the conversation about free speech. It wedged support for a healthy town square based on what you say in it.Shifting to put the responsibility on to the platforms to make their design safe, shifts the government’s role to one of enforcer not censor. Leave the outrage merchants free to shout into the ether but remove the rewards that amplify them when they do so.Duties of care impose a legal responsibility to proactively avoid foreseeable harm. The harms of these platform design choices are foreseeable. We see them every day. Hanson and other’s bad faith grifting is merely one of them we saw in recent days, tomorrow it will be something else – so long as we continue to allow the algorithms to censor our feeds.Ed Coper is a political commentator and the author of Angertainment: How Social Media Outrage Ruined Everything. He is the chief executive of communications agency PopularesExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionDigital mediaFreedom of speechAustralian politicsSocial media bancommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought a devil was about to appear from the smoke’: Jerry Hsu’s best photograph | Photography | The Guardian
description: ‘The black cloud emerged from a grate in the street. I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic – just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city’
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: ‘The black cloud emerged from a grate in the street. I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic – just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city’
Content: ‘There is a noir that is pervasive here’ … an image from the photobook How About Never.Photograph: © Jerry Hsu. Courtesy of the artist and MACKView image in fullscreen‘There is a noir that is pervasive here’ … an image from the photobook How About Never.Photograph: © Jerry Hsu. Courtesy of the artist and MACKMy best shotPhotography‘I thought a devil was about to appear from the smoke’: Jerry Hsu’s best photograph‘The black cloud emerged from a grate in the street. I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic – just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city’Interview byCharlotte JansenWed 9 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis image was taken in 2011 or 2012, just after I had moved toLos Angeles. I was downtown, an area I don’t go to that much, walking around with my camera. Some black smoke started to emerge from a grate in the street – I guess something underground was on fire. It was hilariously cinematic, as if some sort of devil was going to appear. It was really just one of those eerie, spontaneous things that happen in a city. There is a very powerful feeling of surrender when I am photographing. I have to submit to the authority of ignorance when I’m out there.I grew up in San Jose, which is a sprawling American suburb – there’s no city about it. I came to LA because I was depressed where I lived, and I had just met my future wife, who didn’t want to live in San Jose either. LA is not really a city, it’s hundreds of places. You can drive 15 minutes and be in a completely different environment – the beach, the mountains. There’s a weird sentience to the city, if you let it take you. I get an inexplicable desire to just get in the car and go.Despite the fact it’s sunny every day, there is a noir that is pervasive here. I really like the dark part of the city. There’s a transgressive pulse, and if you search hard enough, there’s a lot of intimacy too. In my book How About Never, there are photographs of big things – fires, hard-hitting events – but at the same time, the smaller things. Cities are cruel and I wanted to capture that, but I also found compassion.double quotation markAs a skateboarder, I’m hardwired to react quicklyAfter I had done the edit for the book, I looked at it and realised that it was also about my relationship with my wife. The photographs span from the time we met to when our marriage ended earlier this year. My wife is a prominent character in it, although you don’t see her face until the end. It’s a very vulnerable photograph of her in a hospital bed. I have a lot of beautiful photographs of her, but I didn’t choose those. I think that in all relationships, vulnerability is the key to how we truly connect, and that was difficult for us. The book is a fantasy of what I was searching for, a dream about what I wanted it to look like and what it couldn’t be – all of the opposing forces, all the fire, water, destruction – and at the same time, hope and beauty. These are the contradictions you find in a relationship.I started skateboarding at 12, and at 16 I turned pro. I was a professional for 25 years. I guess the most obvious connection between that and photography is that skateboarders are constantly seeing the environment in a way other people don’t. We see a park bench, a handrail or an embankment and we think about how we can manipulate it for our purposes. There’s a constant searching and endless curiosity, thinking about how to make an environment our own. As a skateboarder, you’re also hardwired to react quickly – you have to reach a flow state and not hesitate to do something that might be life-threatening. It takes a lot of focus to process information quickly – it’s a type of premonition about what’s about to happen.Skateboardingtaught me from an early age that I have permission to view reality how I want; to take from it what I want. It gave me the permission I needed to make my own choices, which helped a lot with photography, and in my life generally.I am interested in dreams, and in my book I treated the city as if it were my subconscious. I wander through it as if I am in a dream. A dream shows you images and is trying to tell you something about yourself. LA was doing that to me, it was showing me all these things I was attracted to, and I was capturing and collecting them without knowing what I was going to do with them.I have always been painfully shy and interacting with the world is not easy, but this connects me with it and it’s how I can speak about it.Photographyis a solitary practice and making work can be so isolating - I was scared to show my work, scared of being rejected or misunderstood, but I wanted to tell this story. People look at this book and think it’s bleak – and sure, it is, but there’s also a lot of hope in it. The last image of a cat, moving out of the frame to the right, is about moving forward and going on living, despite all of this.How About Neveris published by MACK.View image in fullscreenJerry Hsu’s CVBorn:San Jose, California 1981High point:My new book, How About Never.Top tip:Always research. Copy artists you are drawn to and your voice will eventually emerge.Explore more on these topicsPhotographyMy best shotLos AngelesSkateboardingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It detonated right outside our house’: the explosion that started an incredible podcast series | Podcasts | The Guardian
description: Josh Baker is the journalist behind the BBC’s smash hit I’m Not a Monster. He’s back with his most extraordinary investigation yet – to solve the mystery of Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria 14 years ago
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Josh Baker is the journalist behind the BBC’s smash hit I’m Not a Monster. He’s back with his most extraordinary investigation yet – to solve the mystery of Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria 14 years ago
Content: ‘A car bomb broke my back’ … Josh Baker in Raqqa, Syria.Photograph: Mauricio GrisView image in fullscreen‘A car bomb broke my back’ … Josh Baker in Raqqa, Syria.Photograph: Mauricio GrisPodcasts‘It detonated right outside our house’: the explosion that started an incredible podcast seriesJosh Baker is the journalist behind the BBC’s smash hit I’m Not a Monster. He’s back with his most extraordinary investigation yet – to solve the mystery of Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria 14 years agoZoe WilliamsWed 9 Sep 2026 07.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2012, the US marine turned freelance foreign correspondent Austin Tice disappeared inSyria. If he’s still alive, he’ll be the second-longest detained journalist in the world. That, says Josh Baker (speaking to me from Wales), was the podcast he thought he was making: “We thought we were looking for a missing person, and what we fell into was almost like a Bourne novel, utterly extraordinary. A world of espionage, spies, dictatorship.”It’s also a story of American exceptionalism – the way the US saw itself in relation to the rest of the world. Moreover, “I don’t mean this in a crass way,” Baker says, “but through Austin’s story, we also learn a lot about the last 14 years of the civil war in Syria. We really go inside the regime’s industrial complex of disappearance and torture. As episode two begins, Assad is gone, and we enter into these facilities.”Ultimately, the hunt for the people who know the truth about Tice, and the hunt for those responsible for these atrocities, are one and the same. “A lot of my work for the last decade has involved intelligence and espionage and dealing with intelligence agencies, and I have never received so many leaks from so many different places as I have with Austin Tice – from every direction imaginable. It is absolutely extraordinary.”This is Baker’s third series of I’m Not a Monster for the BBC. The first two – one about an American woman, Sam, who disappears into theIslamic Statecaliphate with her young children when her husband becomes a sniper, and the other one about Shamima Begum – are extraordinary pieces of journalism. But just as extraordinary is the backstory of how they came about.View image in fullscreen‘We fell into a world of espionage, spies, dictatorship’ … I’m Not a Monster host Josh Baker.Photograph: Jamie Simonds/BBCNow 37, Baker started as a night editor on the foreign desk of the Times, and did “a little bit of reporting on the Serbian refugee crisis, and from the Middle East”. By the mid-10s, he was directing Battle for Iraq (a Guardian/PBS co-production), embedded with Iraqi special forces. “The story of the day was that the coalition forces were defeating Isis, were kicking their ass basically. And the reality was quite different.” He got caught in the centre of Mosul and by nightfall had been offered a place to stay by a family, explosions and fighting happening all around. A radio operator woke the team with a warning, “and I could hear shooting”, he remembers, “but without wanting to sound like a war bro, it was all going one way and it was all American weaponry. The sound is different when it’s Isis.”What he didn’t hear until too late was a massive articulated lorry, trying to manoeuvre its way down the street to deliver a car bomb. “I know this bit because Isis, the bastards, were filming from a drone. It detonated right outside our house and I was buried in the collapsing building, and broke my back.”As he was recovering in England after his evacuation, a source of his heard he’d been injured and got in touch. “He’s now almost like a friend, but a source like that always has an agenda,” Baker says. “He showed me a home video from inside Raqqa, which was then the Isis capital, of a young American boy called Matthew being forced to assemble a suicide bomb. This wasn’t a propaganda video, it was a home video.”Matthew was Sam’s oldest son. “I was obviously in a mental state, having just walked out of something by the skin of my teeth. But I thought: ‘I’m gonna find this kid,’ which sounds incredibly idealistic, but seven months later, I did.”View image in fullscreenAn undated photo of Shamima Begum.Photograph: PA/PA WireThe Begum season also came out of that suicide bombing – a Dutch IS bride had been in Mosul at the same time, and some years later privately messaged Baker on Twitter, saying she was in the same refugee camp as Shamima Begum and her children (all three of whom have now died). Baker was more than familiar with Begum’s story – he’d been working as assistant producer onWelcome to the Mosqueand had been inside her east London mosque the day she and her school friends disappeared in 2015. But his new source was the start of an incredibly rich picture of what life was like for these girls and young women when they reached Syria – the deprivation, the violence, the forced marriage, the jeopardy.Baker was also, after a long research trip to Turkey, able to piece together the role of Canadian intelligence in getting Begum across the border, an act which in itself (in my view) was cynical enough that it should solidify Begum’s case that she is more victim than terrorist. He plays down the credit for that exclusive – had it been an action of British intelligence, he says, he’d never have been able to prove it, “because of the tradecraft. Whereas if you look at some of the American or Canadian, or even some European agencies, the tradecraft doesn’t seem to be there in the same way.”The Dutch woman was repatriated to the Netherlands, where she served some of her prison sentence, before it was overturned on the basis that she had been groomed and abused by her husband. “Tens of thousands of people from potentially as many as 100 nations were convinced to go to Isis,” Baker says. “They had a highly effective campaign. Which isn’t to say that someone who’s been with Isis isn’t a threat, but you will struggle to find a security expert who’ll say that our current strategy” – stripping people like Begum of statehood – “is making us safer.”Baker and his colleagues received a large number of death threats after that documentary. It touched on everything: terrorism and foreign policy, who gets to be British and whose Britishness will always be conditional, how much transparency one can ever expect from one’s government. “By the end of that programme, it wasn’t really about Shamima any more.”“In Britain, when people say they have an intelligence source, they often mean they’ve spoken to a press officer,” Baker says. “In America, and particularly in Washington, that world is much more accessible. You can meet intelligence officers or senior law enforcement at dinner parties or even in bars. And still, a great deal of what I’m told I either can’t stand up or I’m told I can’t use. I will say, though, that under the Trump administration, people have become much less inclined to speak.”View image in fullscreenThe second-longest detained journalist in the world? … Marc and Debra Tice, the parents of Austin (seen in the portrait to the left), speak at a press conference in Beirut, 2020.Photograph: Joseph Eid/AFP/Getty ImagesThat access really shows in the Austin Tice podcast, which feels extremely close to the source, and urgent in a way that you wouldn’t think possible for a case that, 14 years on, one would expect to be cold. “Genuinely, our first mission was to try to get answers to Austin’s mum. But also, I really want people to care about what happened in Syria, because it’s obscene. Conservatively, 100,000 people have been disappeared. One of the reasons I left news is I got very tired of having to explain complex things in a matter-of-fact way. The privilege of doing this kind of narrative investigative journalism is that I can slow down and make you care about the people.”I wonder whether Baker chose Tice’s story because he identified with him: a young guy in a war zone, playing stark odds and never knowing which, among myriad dangers, might be decisive. “No, what I identified with was his mother. I remember seeing her do a press conference, nine or 10 years into his disappearance, and thinking about my own mum. I’m from a single-parent household – we’re very close. I just thought, ‘Jesus Christ, what an awful existence to have.’”He thinks he has emerged from this investigation with “a pretty decent idea about what may have happened to Austin. Whether or not we could ever be definitive about it is a different thing.”In the UK, the first episode of season three of I Am Not a Monster is availableon BBC Sounds nowExplore more on these topicsPodcastsSyriaShamima BegumIslamic StatefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Forget vinyl v digital debates, this kind of musical ‘authenticity’ brings real rewards | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Period instruments are miles away from retro affectation, and as two Proms this week will show, can actually bring historical music up to the moment
Author: Tom Service
Headline: Period instruments are miles away from retro affectation, and as two Proms this week will show, can actually bring historical music up to the moment
Content: Timely … Mary Bevin (Euridice) reaches up for Gyula Orendt (Orfeo), in the final act of Orfeo, a collaboration between the Roundhouse and the Royal Opera featuring the Early Opera Company’s period instrument orchestra.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTimely … Mary Bevin (Euridice) reaches up for Gyula Orendt (Orfeo), in the final act of Orfeo, a collaboration between the Roundhouse and the Royal Opera featuring the Early Opera Company’s period instrument orchestra.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianTom Service on musicClassical musicForget vinyl v digital debates, this kind of musical ‘authenticity’ brings real rewardsTom ServicePeriod instruments are miles away from retro affectation, and as two Proms this week will show, can actually bring historical music up to the momentWed 9 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.26 EDTShareNostalgia. What a kick. And what a commercial boon for the music industry. Love the sound of 60s pop and 70s disco? You need the original synths if you’re a composer or producer. You listen to music on digital streams? Loser! Join the retro-future of vinyl enthusiasm, and feel the grooves under your fingers like your parents or grandparents used to. Or you can even make music physical again through the horrible medium of cassettes: all that plastic, all those tiny liner notes, all that high-speed dubbing.Retro-futurists cherish what they claim is the extra warmth and sonic richness of vinyl, but there is no acoustic reason why vinyl is better. It is in fact objectively worse as a carrier of sonic information than any high-resolution stream of the same track, song or symphony. For cassette nostalgists, if it’s got that old-fashioned tape hiss, it sounds more “real”. We’re now looking for things to sound less clean. Because we distrust today’s technological utopia, we want signs that our music is less polished, less perfect, and thus more human.But what the recording industry is doing now with its return to vinyl, classical music has been doing for decades. Musicians and musicologists have long been obsessed with learning about the origins of the music they study and play, to experience what the technology of instruments and performing cultures of earlier centuries actually sounded like, whether the 12th-century Germany of Hildegard of Bingen or the 19th-century Vienna of Beethoven and Schubert.View image in fullscreenJan Steen’s A Young Woman playing a Harpsichord to a Young Man (probably 1659) in the National Gallery, LondonPhotograph: The National Gallery Photographic Department./The National Gallery, LondonDavid Munrowbrought medieval and Renaissance music to the mainstream across TV, radio and recordings in the 1970s and showing what instruments such as shawms and crumhorns could do;Roger Norringtonand John Eliot Gardiner set up choirs and ensembles to do the same for 17th and 18th-century music, and Nikolaus Harnoncourt led the charge through the music of later centuries, putting the ethos of early music research into the lifeblood of chamber groups and large-scale symphony orchestras in music from Schubert to Bruckner.But where the claims for vinyl or cassettes’ “authenticity” are bogus when it comes to actual sonic fidelity, it’s different when comparing older instruments in classical cultures and their modern counterparts. Earlier instruments have different qualities of sound and expression. The sound and feel of a harpsichord that Bach was writing for in the 18th century is vastly different to a grand piano made today: the plucked strings of the harpsichord mean that the sound of each note disappears quickly, where a Steinway can create halos and continuities of sound. French horns that can play in any key are taken for granted today, where previous generations had to literally pull their brass instruments apart to play one set of notes or another. It’s a similar story for strings and woodwinds, as earlier generations of musicians had to play with the temperamental realities of gut strings that don’t stay in tune, and reeds that couldn’t be relied on.But the sounds that earlier orchestral instruments make aren’t “worse” in the way that cassettes or vinyl are. Instead, their differences invite other ways of playing for the musicians, and they open up new dimensions of feeling for us. The difference between Bach’s music when it’s played on modern instruments in what is now – ironically – an old-school approach, using vibrato in the strings, lush lyricism in the rest of the orchestra, and full-scale choral forces, compared with the leaner sounds that smaller period instrument ensembles make, isn’t only a difference of soundworld, it’s a gulf of meaning and feeling.Listen to these two performances of the opening chorus of Bach’s Matthew Passion:Karl Richter conducting his massed Munich forces in 1979, andPaul McCreesh leading the Gabrieli Consort in 2003.They’re playing the same piece, but these are radically different experiences. Richter’s reading of the work is about making a vast immovable musical monument, while McCreesh’s – played nearly twice as fast, using just one voice to each part – is an invitation to us as individuals to empathise, to bear witness, to be part of the drama.View image in fullscreenJean Rondeau plays Bach’s Goldberg Variations at Milton Court on the harpsichord for a 2018 Barbican concert (read our review)Photograph: Alecsandra Raluca Drăgoi/The GuardianThat’s the key: these are new, contemporary feelings that period instrument performances open up. As the pianistVikingur Ólafsson said, the idea that if you play on old instruments you’re making the exact sounds that Bach, or Beethoven or Mahler would have heard is neither truly possible, and nor is it the point. Our ears, our bodies, and our whole listening culture is different. (Which reminds me ofJaneane Garofalo’s immortal cameo as the “serving wench” Melindain the medieval-themed restaurant in The Cable Guy: “There were no utensils in medieval times, hence there are no utensils at Medieval Times. Would you like a refill on that Pepsi?”)In the final few Proms concerts of the season you can hear the latest developments of classical’s retro-future explorers, all playing “period instruments”. On Thursday, the musicians of Arcangelo performBach’s B Minor Masson original instruments, and the next night, there’sMahler’s Ninth symphonyfrom the Mahler Academy Orchestra playing instruments that fit the specifications of the ones that Mahler himself ordered for the Vienna opera in the early 1900s. Period instruments have more grain, more colour, more guttural directness and more lyrical intensity than their modern counterparts and so to my mind are better equipped to reveal the emotional imperfections, ambiguities, and expressive complexities of the music they’re playing.That makes me sound like a cassette-fetishising nerd. Oh dear ... In fact, I’ll go further and say that performances such as the Mass in B Minor and Mahler’s 9th at the Proms will have an authenticity that no recording format, analogue or digital, can reproduce. These are one-off performances that will be made and witnessed by those human beings, true to themselves in every moment. All these historical instruments aren’t really about getting closer to past times but to the power of the present tense.This week Tom has been listening to:On repeat, the Berlin Philharmonic’s Proms with Kirill Petrenko. I know, I’m a broken record on this, but theirElgar and Tchaikovskywas inspired and inspiring: they found new depths of feeling and resonance in every moment. Magic.View image in fullscreenInspired and inspiring: Kiril Petrenko conducts the Berlin Philharmonic at 2026’s BBC PromsPhotograph: BBC/Chris ChristodoulouExplore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicProms 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Streaming from the cloud was meant to change games forever – what happened? | Games | The Guardian
description: Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordable
Content: Fans playing the cloud-based game Doom at the 2019  Gamescom in Cologne, Germany.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFans playing the cloud-based game Doom at the 2019  Gamescom in Cologne, Germany.Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty ImagesPushing Buttons newsletterGamesStreaming from the cloud was meant to change games forever – what happened?Once hailed as the future, even the likes of Google, Sony and Microsoft have struggled to make streaming games fun, fast or affordableDon’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKeza MacDonaldWed 9 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 10.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn August 2009, at the very first Gamescom expo, I sat in a small meeting room in Germany and played Mario Kart and World of Warcraft on a laptop, via technology that was then completely new: cloud gaming. It was a demonstration for a yet-to-be-launched service called Gaikai that promised to let you play any game in a browser window, without a console. (Here is anancient videoof that demonstration, featuring a very young Keza.) With a single click I could launch into any game, hosted on servers hundreds of miles away. It really did look like the future.Since then, plenty of companies havetried to be the firstto truly crack game streaming, vying to be the Netflix of games. Sony ended up buying Gaikai for $380m (£242m) in 2012; its technology now powers the streamable classic games library on PlayStation, and the PS5’s advanced game streaming. OnLive, Gaikai’s first competitor, launched in 2011 but shut down after less than a year, leaving Sony to acquire all its patents. Google’s Stadia cloud gaming service also imploded, launching in 2019 and shutting down three years later.Despite the fact that people simply don’t seem to want game streaming services – or at least not enough to pay a stand-alone monthly subscription for them – Sony and Microsoft have remained steadfastly committed to the idea, bundling game streaming into their PlayStation Plus and Xbox Game Pass services. I use both quite regularly when I want to check out a game quickly, mostly because modern download sizes are ridiculous (Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, say, takes up nearly 150GB of my PS5 space, almost a quarter of its usable storage). Who wants to do 30 minutes of hard drive management every time they want to play something new?Last week, however, Microsoft announced that it wasintroducing time limitsfor game streaming: you’re now allowed 5-15 hours a month, depending on your subscription tier. And yes, you’re right:that is not enough time to play through even one single average-sized game. This brings Microsoft’s previously unwavering commitment to cloud gaming into question – and when even Microsoft with its infinite resources can’t seem to make it work, is the writing on the wall for game streaming as a whole?View image in fullscreenData-hungry ... streaming games such as Mario Kart World requires a whole load of data.Photograph: NintendoIn the early days, the biggest problem with streaming was input lag: the time it took for the game to respond to your button-pressing. Normally, when you’re playing a game this lag is imperceptible. Via streaming, it would often be horribly obvious, your character taking maybe a full second to jump after you’d pressed the A button. Not all games rely heavily on timing and finesse, but a lot of them do, and playing games on a minor time-delay felt nauseating.This is much less of an issue now, but another problem has only gotten worse: game streaming requires the instantaneous transmission of alotof data, making it taxing on your internet connection and expensive for the service provider. Here’s a comparison: watching an hour of Netflix uses about 1GB of data. An hour of game streaming via Xbox requires about 4GB. Microsoft’s servers have to stream you the video of your live gameplay, and continually receive and interpret your controller inputs. No wonder Microsoft suddenly wants to limit your hours.The cloud gaming model has always been based on the idea that data infrastructure would become faster and cheaper in the future. Its selling point is outsourcing computing power so that you can play whatever you want without upgrading your console or PC, or even without having one at all. Unfortunately, thanks to AI companies and their chatbots’ bottomless demand for computing power and energy, the opposite has happened. Data and computing power are nowmoreexpensive. Ironically, this change has been driven by Microsoft itself as much as anything else: a huge chunk of the company’s spendingwent on data centres and AI infrastructurein the last fiscal year. This suggests that Microsoft is choosing to prioritise data provision for users of Azure and Copilot over its gaming customers.Will this affect you? Probably not. Only 4% of all Game Pass subscribers use it for more than 15 hours a month, Microsoft said in ablog postannouncing the changes. Which brings us right back to the question: if cloud gaming really is the future, why is nobody using it? It’s been a long time since that 2009 demo, and this technology has still yet to meaningfully break through. Is it time to give up on it?Alongside Sony and Microsoft, there is one other player left in this death match: the US-based tech firm Nvidia, whose GeForce Now game-streaming service (launched in 2013 and revamped many times since) might just be the world’s most successful. Nvidia has beenriding highon the AI boom, becoming the most valuable company in the world. Its computing hardware powers all the datacentres that the rest of the tech industry has been building, to satisfy imagined future AI demand. Perhaps, when all of this shakes out, it will be the only company left that can afford to provide game streaming services at all.What to playView image in fullscreenUnashamedly laborious … Kingdom Come Deliverance II.Photograph: Warhorse StudiosI have been variably unwell for most of the summer, and in need of something absorbing, so I dived intoKingdom Come Deliverance II– think Skyrim, but 15th-century historical fiction.I was impressed immediately by the outstanding script, story and performances, all of which are much more humorous and entertaining than I was expecting from a hardcore medieval RPG. And I also love how unashamedly laborious this game is: you must control each swipe of a drawn-out sword fight; you have to manually grind and mix herbs for health-restoring concoctions; and if you want anyone to speak to you, you must regularly wash your face (and grubby tunic) so you don’t stink. Last night, I spent 20 minutes hammering out horseshoes in the forge. The opening hours have you hauling sacks of flour around while a tavern landlady swears at you.I can’t help but respect this naturalist commitment to grime and busywork; knight-life isn’t all horseplay, you know. I have spent many, many hours with this game and I am still basically a stinking peasant. I may well never finish it, but I am resolved to atleastget to the point where I have my own steed and a pair of decent boots.Available on:Xbox, PlayStation 5, PCEstimated playtime:55+ hoursskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to readView image in fullscreenLooking beautiful … The remastered Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.Photograph: NintendoA Nintendo broadcast on Tuesday spilled a bunch of new details about the upcomingZelda: Ocarina of Timeremake, which I’m relieved to say is looking beautiful. Link looks doll-like in the updated style, and Hyrule Castle Town looks a bit like a living Playmobil village overlaid with a watercolour-ish filter that makes the whole game look like something half remembered. (I am somewhat less enthused by the addition of voice acting to the cutscenes; Navi was already annoying enough.) Check out thedemo here.For the Ringer, frequent Guardian games contributor Lewis Gordon has writtenthis excellent long-readon Japanese publisherCapcom’s current streak of brilliance, talking to a host of executives and developers about exactly how the company has bucked the trend while the rest of the games industry is on fire.Patrick Miller– better known as pattheflip – has published athought-provoking reflectionon how and why some players become overinvested – even dependent – on video games. “I say this as someone who has loved video games his whole life; if games serve a load-bearing function in someone’s life, it’s the life that needs fixing, not the games.”At the end of last week, theWhite Housereleased this horrible littlepropaganda arcade, featuring nasty riffs on popular games, such as a version of Tetris where you have to build a wall on the Mexican border to stave off “the coming horde”. That particular gamewas later removedafter The Tetris Company expressed its opposition.What to clickGrand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?Thieves target mail order sales as Pokémon card prices soar‘Ruin and decay bring a chance of rebirth’: Hidetaka Miyazaki on uniting players in a damaged worldQuestion BlockView image in fullscreenNo combat required … Eastshade, where you take on the role of a painter rather than a fighter.Photograph: Eastshade StudiosReaderPierosent in this question (along with some super-nice feedback on the newsletter – thank you, Piero!):“I enjoy the occasional foray into story-driven RPGs, such asKingdom Come Deliverance,Skyrimandthe Baldur’s Gateseries, but as I get older I’m finding the continual combat sections overwhelming and dull. Could you recommend me some good RPGs that don’t rely on combat as the main game mechanic?”You’re not alone, Piero – for a surprising proportion of players, combat is just something you have to do in order to get to the bits of a game that you find more interesting. Most RPGs these days have a “story mode” option that at least makes all the fighting trivially easy, if you’re not interested in engaging with it. There is of courseDisco Elysium, a complex role-playing game with no combat at all; likeCitizen Sleeper,it is mostly text-based. I have heard good things aboutEastshade, an open-world game where you’re a painter rather than a fighter. I’d also suggestPentiment, though it’s a very different style from Skyrim. AndYonder: The Cloud Catcher Chroniclesis worth a look if you don’t mind cutesy.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: You’re So Special review – painfully funny tragedy of a stardom seeker | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A dance teacher for toddlers dreams of bigger things in Julia Grogan’s frantic one-woman show
Author: Anya Ryan
Headline: A dance teacher for toddlers dreams of bigger things in Julia Grogan’s frantic one-woman show
Content: You daren’t look away … Julia Grogan in You're So Special at Soho theatre.Photograph: Alex BrennerView image in fullscreenYou daren’t look away … Julia Grogan in You're So Special at Soho theatre.Photograph: Alex BrennerTheatreReviewYou’re So Special review – painfully funny tragedy of a stardom seekerSoho theatre, LondonA dance teacher for toddlers dreams of bigger things in Julia Grogan’s frantic one-woman showAnya RyanWed 9 Sep 2026 07.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe mind of a performer, hungry for her big break, is cracked open in Julia Grogan’s one-woman follow-up to her dramaPlayfight.At first, her dream is in motion: Miss June (played by Grogan) is on a chat show, giving breezy answers about her Oscar nominations and being recognised by monks in Holland & Barrett. And then, with one question from the audience – “Any advice for people who want to be something?” – the stage warps back to reality. Actually, Miss June is a baby ballet teacher, with a class of toddlers ready to be taught turnouts and pliés.But all her lusting after Daisy Edgar-Jones’s life may have paid off. Miss June has been offered a spot on a TV show, and you can bet she’s told everyone in the town she grew up in – where she still lives – about her good fortune.Directed by Rachel Lemon, this is a story of success and stardom in reverse which is played out like a horror show. Soon it turns out the producers don’t actually need her, so it’s back to the village hall, jointly used by Twinkly Stars ballet school and an All Addictions group, to beg for her job back and prepare for the end-of-term sharing.View image in fullscreenOnly a second away from a screaming outburst … Grogan.Photograph: Alex BrennerFramed as an epic tragedy and told in acts, You’re So Special shows fame as a manic obsession. Miss June has bulging, twitching eyes and is always one second away from a screaming outburst. She speaks to the three-year-olds with a desperate, Dance Mom-esque quality: “You might feel pressure to lose weight – do it,” she commands. When she learns that one child’s parents are TV producers, she sets her sights on grabbing herself some time in the spotlight. And the whole time she is spurred on by the memory of her own dance teacher telling her she was “special” as a child.Despite being alone on stage, Grogan conjures a vivid whole world. The personalities of the mind-drifting kids are unmistakable through her expert miming, and never once do we doubt her frantic, deep need to reach for higher things. Grogan is a wonderfully watchable actor – you don’t dare look away for fear of missing another flash of a breakdown. She is also painfully funny. Miss June’s career may have stagnated but Grogan is doing brilliant things.AtSoho theatre, London, until 26 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreComedy (Stage)Soho theatreComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Inglourious baristas: why is Brad Pitt making coffee for 16 abusive dogs? | Brad Pitt | The Guardian
description: In new film The Heart of the Beast, the A-lister’s bond with his loyal mutt proves crucial. In Spike Jonze’s new advert, Pitt is rather more subservient
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: In new film The Heart of the Beast, the A-lister’s bond with his loyal mutt proves crucial. In Spike Jonze’s new advert, Pitt is rather more subservient
Content: Well groomed … Brad Pitt in the advert.Photograph: De'LonghiView image in fullscreenWell groomed … Brad Pitt in the advert.Photograph: De'LonghiBrad PittInglourious baristas: why is Brad Pitt making coffee for 16 abusive dogs?In new film The Heart of the Beast, the A-lister’s bond with his loyal mutt proves crucial. In Spike Jonze’s new advert, Pitt is rather more subservientStuart HeritageWed 9 Sep 2026 06.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrad Pitt has a new movie out this month, The Heart of the Beast, about an emotionally damaged man who forms a life-saving bond with a dog. If that sounds familiar, maybe it is because you have seen The Call of the Wild. Or maybe it is because you have seen A Dog’s Way Home. Or maybe it is because you have seen Dog. Or, look, you get the idea.But perhaps Brad Pitt knows that getting people to see something as unimaginative as The Heart of the Beast is an uphill struggle, because that would explain why he has just made an advert that looks and feels much more like the Brad Pitt dog movie that deserves to be made. In short, it is an advert where Brad Pitt gets loudly disparaged by a number of dogs for an extended period of time.As reported by Variety, the commercial is for the De’Longhi Magnifica Duo, an all-singing, all-dancing coffee machine that retails in the UK for about £700. But really the product is beside the point. The main point is that the advert, running to almost two minutes, sees Brad Pitt stumble around cluelessly while a small army of real dogs – all of whom have names, some of whom are dressed in human clothes – shout insults at him.As he wanders into his living room, some of the dogs (in subtitle) tell him that he woke up too late. They tell him to make a hot coffee and, even though he has started to make a cold one, he drops his head and sullenly obliges. Then another dog says that he can’t have any coffee at all until his attitude improves. “OK,” he mumbles in return, like a put-upon sitcom dad. The dogs berate him for his slovenliness and his stupidity and, when he finally snaps and tells them to go and fetch a stick, they make him fetch a stick for them instead.It’s a weird advert. It is slightly reminiscent of that bizarre Chinese commercial for Chinese vitamins from a few years back, whenTom Hiddleston cooks you breakfastbefore looking straight into your eyes and promising that he’s going to have sex with you. The difference is that, while you could tell that Hiddleston desperately hoped that nobody would see his ad, Pitt’s has been made for an American market. He wants you to see this.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: De’LonghiOf course, it helps that the weirdness is deliberate. The commercial was directed by Spike Jonze, the visionary director of no films at all for the last 13 years. The world has been crying out for a new film by Jonze, and if the closest we’re going to get is a film where Brad Pitt gets insulted by a dog named Kyle, then that will have to do.In fact, the more you consider it, the better a move this advert seems for Pitt. Compared with the derivative grit-jawed Americana of The Heart of the Beast, it demonstrates that he’s much better when he’s allowed to be funny. And if it underlines a connection between Pitt and dogs along the way, creating an implied synergy with his movie, then that’s OK too.It’s also a big step up from Pitt’s previous De’Longhi commercials, the majority of which just required him tostand still and smoulder for a while. Those commercials could have starred anyone. You could have put a carrot on human growth hormones and it would have adequately done the job. At least this one has a bit of personality.Only the De’Longhi sales team will know if this has been a successful gambit or not, but speaking personally I think it works perfectly. With any luck it will bring Spike Jonze out of retirement, and Brad Pitt Gets Shit-Talked by SomeDogswill be a motion picture by next Christmas.Explore more on these topicsBrad PittAdvertisingDogsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Even better than the Real Thing? The overlooked Black music scene of 1970s Liverpool | Music | The Guardian
description: Despite the city’s backdrop of deprivation and racism, vibrant nightclubs and daring artists thrived – but after No 1 success for the Real Thing, why was the scene ignored?
Author: Claudia Efemini
Headline: Despite the city’s backdrop of deprivation and racism, vibrant nightclubs and daring artists thrived – but after No 1 success for the Real Thing, why was the scene ignored?
Content: The Real Thing, at the time of their No 1 hit You to Me Are Everything.Photograph: Screenbound International Pictures LtdView image in fullscreenThe Real Thing, at the time of their No 1 hit You to Me Are Everything.Photograph: Screenbound International Pictures LtdMusicEven better than the Real Thing? The overlooked Black music scene of 1970s LiverpoolDespite the city’s backdrop of deprivation and racism, vibrant nightclubs and daring artists thrived – but after No 1 success for the Real Thing, why was the scene ignored?Claudia EfeminiWed 9 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMonths before the Real Thing’s You to Me Are Everything became a UK No 1 hit in 1976, lead singer Chris Amoo took the unreleased song to the Timepiece, a nightclub devoted to Black music tucked in between bars on Liverpool’s Fleet Street. His DJ friend Les Spaine stuck it on, and the empty dancefloor “just filled up, and nobody, not one person in that place, had heard the song before”, Amoo says with pride on a call from his home on the outskirts ofLiverpool. “That’s when me and Les looked at each other and thought: you’ve got something there, brother.”The track’s symphonic majesty and romantic vocals captured the hearts of millions, and it peaked in the charts during 1976’s summer heatwave. Fifty years later, Amoo is on tour with his fellow bandmate Dave Smith in celebration of its anniversary. But the Real Thing were just the most high-profile group from an underground funk and R&B scene which emerged in 1970s Liverpool, upheld by a generation, predominately from the Toxteth area south of the city centre, that embraced Black American culture.They were not inspired by the city’s household names like the Beatles, Amoo says; instead, it was from seeing groups like the Jackson 5 and the Temptations on television that he thought: “They look like us – we can do that!” Likewise Spaine, now considered a godfather of the UK’s funk scene, grew up in a household with a deep love for Black American music: “Nat King Cole, the Drifters, the Ink Spots, Five Blind Boys of Alabama, all them sorts of things that my old man used to play.”Black US soldiers residing in Burtonwood, a nearby airbase, brought the latest records to Toxteth on weekends, leaving them with friends or at clubs, as well as “clothes, those really fantastic baseball boots and the apple hats that they used to wear. We’d learn all the new dances and songs,” Amoo says.View image in fullscreenLes Spaine, photographed at home in Hampshire in 2022.Photograph: David Levene/the GuardianSpaine started DJing with the imported records he amassed, Amoo formed the Real Thing, and as each made a name for themselves in the music business, they became mostly immune to the colour ban that Black people faced. “I could get into many clubs, Chris could, but the majority of people from Toxteth couldn’t,” Spaine says. “We weren’t morbid about it; there was a saying back then, ‘that’s the way it is’. You could have signs saying no this, no that. This was before laws came in prohibiting that.”Located in town among nightclubs that enforced a colour ban, the Timepiece became the club for Toxteth’s Black community to let loose. “We had big screens and I’d go and visit all the record companies to get these 16mm films,” Spaine remembers. “Then we’d have a back projector and all of a sudden these people could see Michael Jackson, Rufus and Chaka Khan.” As for the dress code, “we were soul boys, so you had to be immaculate; we had mohair suits and Ben Sherman shirts”.People of all races would travel from across the country for their all-nighters. “Everybody who loved Black music went,” says Barbara Phillips, former member of Distinction, a vocal harmony band formed in Liverpool in 1976. “It was the only place where you kind of felt safe.”View image in fullscreenThe Real Thing pictured in Toxteth in 1977.Photograph: Goddard Archive/AlamyLiverpool had been home to Black communities since the 18th century. During the transatlantic slave trade, enslaved Africans were brought to work as servants or sold at auctions in the dock area. Following the abolition of slavery, sailors from across the world, many from West Africa, worked on trade ships and contributed to the war effort during the world wars. Many settled in Toxteth. “The Windrush is a wonderful thing that we should all be proud of, but Black people have been contributing and in this country, especially in Liverpool, for hundreds of years and there’s a narrative to make it sound as if we all came in 1948,” says Spaine, whose Sierra Leonean father was a merchant seaman in Liverpool.Both Spaine and Amoo speak fondly of their experiences growing up in Toxteth in the 1950s and 60s, “this melting pot of poor white people, Chinese people and Black people and we all just got on really well,” Spaine says.“If you were getting up to a little bit of mischief, you’d have older women shouting ‘I can see you Christopher, I’m going to tell your mother and father’,” Amoo laughs. “They shouldn’t be shouting at us because we were 16 at that point, but there you go.”The warmth in the community was offset by deprivation. “There was no money coming into Toxteth, no businesses that could thrive,” Amoo says. Those hardships, along with racial profiling by police, were a driving force for 1981’s Toxteth riots, which lasted nine days and resulted in widespread damage, hundreds of injured officers and the death of a man who was rammed by a police vehicle.View image in fullscreenDistinction. Left to right: Donna Alleyne, Mandy Smith, Barbara Phillips and Sue PhillipsBut when the Real Thing topped the charts in 1976, their entire community was jubilant. A Black band from Liverpool had got to No 1 – the first Black British band to do so. “The whole city was behind them,” says Phillips, and her group Distinction soon had a first of their own: never before had a Black British female group been signed to a major record label.Distinction formed in the basement of their local community centre where they had vocal lessons from Vic Christian, whose brother Garry had success with the multi-racial Liverpool band the Christians; Phillips’s father was calypso musician Lord Woodbine, who mentored the Beatles. “We liked to think that we were funky, also harmonies were our big thing,” Phillips says. “We used to copy the Three Degrees because that was the nearest to what we saw ourselves as. But I think we were too young to be like anybody, because everybody we looked up to they were proper women, and we were just girls.”The band members – Phillips and her sister Sue, plus Donna Alleyne and Mandy Smith – were still just teenagers when they got a deal with EMI, but, Phillips says, the label “would sign an artist but just sit on them for a year. You wouldn’t get to release anything, and that kind of happened with us.” They got picked up in Germany by the Hansa label who released their single That’s the Way I Like It in 1982, “the nearest we got to making it”. They spent a month in Germany touring cities and US air force bases, but their career soon fizzled out.Spaine describes Distinction as “wonderful: they could harmonise, they could move”, and highlights other Black Liverpudlian acts such as the Chants and Colin Areety, “but most of them just kept local. I think in them days we always had this idea that everything American was best; the Real Thing were holding their own but there were lots of acts here which weren’t given the push given to American acts. You just did not have that interest from London.”The UK recording industry and music fans “absolutely weren’t ready,” says Phillips. “They didn’t mind blue-eyed soul – white singers who covered Black music – but they didn’t really want to buy into Black UK artists. I can remember a poster of us and it had on it ‘four coloured girl singers’. That sounds like 200 years ago!” Instead, Phillips found success elsewhere, writing for stage, TV and radio and setting up a talent development agency.Making an album in the 1970s was incredibly costly compared to now, Amoo says, which stripped some artists of opportunities. “First, record companies would have to find you a writer if you didn’t write yourself. Then they’d have to bring you down to London because there was nowhere up here to do it. Then you’re paying God knows how much an hour for studio time. For a vocal group like Distinction, you’d have to bring in a musician to make the track. For acts like them it was difficult, and they were good: a nice female vocal group, basically like our younger sisters.”‘We had no future. So we made a future for ourselves’: the untold history of Welsh reggae sound systemsRead moreEven the Real Thing, Les argues, do not get the credit they deserve as a band. Their song Children of the Ghetto released in 1977 has been remade by several artists from Earth, Wind & Fire’s Philip Bailey to Mary J Blige. “Chris and Eddie wrote Children of the Ghetto, and Americans pay it more credit than the UK lot do.” But the Real Thing eventually had their story told in Everything, an acclaimed 2019 documentary, and Amoo remains grateful for his career. “We have been airbrushed out quite a lot,” he says, “but there’s a hell of a lot of experiences that the Real Thing have had that most other bands in the country can only dream of.”And for all the difficulties the scene faced, Spaine’s memories of Liverpool’s Black music scene in the 70s still remain equally strong and rosy. “You didn’t make a great amount of money but you worked for the weekend – you literally lived for the weekend. Those nights, you forgot all your troubles.”The Real Thing play We Love the 70s at Butlins, Bognor Regis, 12 September;then touringinto 2027Explore more on these topicsMusicR&BPop and rockLiverpoolRaceBlack British cultureSoulfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why we’re giving £100,000 apiece to a horse box gallery, high-street drop-in and Midlands museum | Art | The Guardian
description: Culture is part of how we rebuild communities – these awards by the Freelands foundation recognise organisations promoting creativity and opportunity at grassroots level
Author: Henry Ward
Headline: Culture is part of how we rebuild communities – these awards by the Freelands foundation recognise organisations promoting creativity and opportunity at grassroots level
Content: Art movement … the Burton at Bideford’s Art Box.Photograph: Olga VynnykView image in fullscreenArt movement … the Burton at Bideford’s Art Box.Photograph: Olga VynnykArtWhy we’re giving £100,000 apiece to a horse box gallery, high-street drop-in and Midlands museumHenry WardCulture is part of how we rebuild communities – these awards by the Freelands foundation recognise organisations promoting creativity and opportunity at grassroots levelWed 9 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTShareIf politicians are serious about rebuilding our communities, they need to recognise that art and creativity are not the finishing touches. They are part of the foundations.Andy Burnham recently said that culture is too often dismissed as a distraction, a “nice to have”. Yet, as he put it, “it’s about making sense of your own reality”.Culture is not something we add once the work of rebuilding communities has been done. Culture is part of how we rebuild them. It creates places where people meet, gives them agency, opens doors into careers they might otherwise never have imagined, brings life back to empty buildings and struggling high streets, and gives communities the opportunity to tell their stories.But we have been steadily stripping away the infrastructure of arts education that makes this possible.View image in fullscreenNew horizons … an Artist Lab walk and talk organised by Signal.Photograph: Courtesy of SignalIn schools, provision for arts subjects has declined. TheCultural Learning Alliancereports a 42% fall in arts GCSE entries since 2010. At universities, art education has faced an increasing battle to justify its existence in relation to future economic validity. And in museums, learning teams are often the first to face cuts when funding is stretched.The government’s curriculum review and renewed commitments to museum funding suggest an appetite to think differently. But if we are serious about changing the direction of travel, we should look beyond policies to the organisations already doing the work.The newFreelands awardsare one way of doing that, committing £1.5m over five years to recognising progressive visual art education across museums, galleries and arts organisations. It’s central to Freelands Foundation’s mission to champion art education.Our first three winners, each of whom receive £100,000, demonstrate what is possible.In Barrow-in-Furness,Signalhas become an essential part of a community dominated by the shipyard and now building nuclear submarines, that is remote and culturally underserved. Their artist development programme gives local people the agency to respond to their surroundings and create opportunities for others. After years of occupying temporary spaces, Signal has transformed a vacant building in the town centre into a place with real community purpose.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMore than one route into cultural life … Wolverhampton Art Gallery.Photograph: Tyler Whiting. Courtesy of Wolverhampton Art Gallery.Burnham has ambitions to revitalise high streets and give communities back the spaces they value. Signal shows what that looks like. An empty building becomes a cultural space, which becomes a community asset, and this becomes part of the renewal of a town.The programmes for young people atWolverhampton Art Gallerydemonstrate another essential principle: that there is more than one route into cultural life and creative employment. They’re giving opportunities to develop projects, build confidence and explore careers outside conventional academic pathways. If we are serious about widening access to the creative industries, we need programmes like these.In rural North Devon,the Burton at Bidefordhas responded to a very practical problem. Teachers told the gallery that their schools could no longer afford trips. Their answer was theBurton Art Box: a converted horse box that takes art directly into primary schools. It is wonderfully simple. And it tells us something important: access to culture is not just about whether an institution exists. It is about whether people can get to it.These organisations are working in places where opportunities to engage with art, develop creative skills or enter the cultural sector can be severely limited. They are not waiting for perfect conditions. They are finding imaginative ways around the barriers in front of them. We should be paying attention.We need to rebuild the infrastructure of art education. That means schools, colleges, universities, museums, galleries, libraries, studios and community organisations. It means ensuring that the people of Barrow,Wolverhampton, North Devon and every other location across the UK have the opportunity to encounter and make art. We need an education that equips us not only to know things, but to imagine, question, collaborate, make and contribute. And we should put the organisations already embedded in our communities at the centre of that ambition.Because if art really is about making sense of our own reality, then access to it cannot be a luxury reserved for those who happen to live in the right place, attend the right school or can afford to pay.Culture is not what we can afford once everything else is fixed. It’s one of the things that will help us fix it.Henry Ward is artistic director of the Freelands FoundationExplore more on these topicsArtArts and humanitiesArts policyWolverhamptonDevoncommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is not sustainable’: London’s Gate theatre to close after nearly 50 years | Stage | The Guardian
description: Formerly based above a Notting Hill pub, the theatre earned a reputation for radical plays with new talent yet had a 100% loss of Arts Council England funding in 2022
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Formerly based above a Notting Hill pub, the theatre earned a reputation for radical plays with new talent yet had a 100% loss of Arts Council England funding in 2022
Content: Maryam Grace, Isabella Nefar, Emily Renée, Juliette Motamed and Afsaneh Dehrouyeh in Wish You Were Here by the Gate theatre, 2024.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreenMaryam Grace, Isabella Nefar, Emily Renée, Juliette Motamed and Afsaneh Dehrouyeh in Wish You Were Here by the Gate theatre, 2024.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianStage‘This is not sustainable’: London’s Gate theatre to close after nearly 50 yearsFormerly based above a Notting Hill pub, the theatre earned a reputation for radical plays with new talent yet had a 100% loss of Arts Council England funding in 2022Chris WiegandStage editorWed 9 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Gate theatre in London, which has punched above its weight ever since it was founded above a Notting Hill pub in 1979, is to close permanently next month.The announcement comes four years after the theatre had what it described as a “devastating” 100% cut to its Arts Council England funding of just over £300,000, losing its status as a National Portfolio Organisation (NPO). The Gate had relocated a few months earlier to a new, more accessible home at Theatro Technis in north London. In 2024 it announced it was no longer viable to be based year-round in one building and began to work peripatetically with partner venues.The Gate theatre’s creative daring gave a tiny stage international scope | Michael BillingtonRead moreIn a statement released on Wednesday, the theatre cited the lack of regular subsidy, as well as rising production costs and increased competition for funds from trusts and foundations, as creating a precarious situation. Thanks to key supporters, the Gate had still been able “to deliver extraordinary work under incredible pressure” it said, but “it has become apparent that this is not sustainable in the long-term”.Atri Banerjee, artistic lead at the Gate, said “it has been the hugest honour to help lead the artistic mission of the organisation through trying times”. The Gate, added Banerjee, “has always been a place that has understood that looking outward is the best way to look more closely at oneself; where artists could arrive with different languages, different traditions, different perspectives, and be met with curiosity, encouragement and support. The Gate is closing, but the international, experimental and generous spirit it has championed will continue in the artists and audiences who have been changed by it.”View image in fullscreenThe Gate theatre, when it was housed in Notting Hill.Photograph: Martin Argles/the GuardianThe Gate was founded by Lou Stein above Notting Hill’s Prince Albert pub in 1979. Stein directed its inaugural production, At Swim-Two-Birds by Flann O’ Brien, and served as artistic director until 1985. Over that time, Stein directed productions of The Emperor Jones by Eugene O’Neill and an adaptation of Hunter S Thompson’s Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, and the Gate opened a second home, at the Latchmere pub in Battersea (now home to Theatre503).Stephen Daldry, Katie Mitchell and Sarah Kane all directed productions at the Gate. Actors including Sophie Okonedo, Jude Law, Kathy Burke and Paterson Joseph appeared there and its stage was used to showcase a rich variety of international talent. Its artistic directors have included Daldry, David Farr, Erica Whyman, Thea Sharrock, Christopher Haydon and Ellen McDougall. From 2007 to 2012, Natalie Abrahami and Carrie Cracknell ran the space together.The theatre always retained a reputation for presenting radical and political plays while also ushering in new talent. Its notable successes included Danai Gurira’s Eclipsed, George Brant’s Grounded and Lucy Kirkwood’s Hedda. The recent productionsWish You Were Hereby Sanaz Toossi andBootycandyby Robert O’Hara were highly praised by the Guardian.View image in fullscreenElectrifying performers … Bimpé Pacheco and DK Fashola in Bootycandy by Robert O’Hara at Gate theatre.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianChair of the board, Rahul Streatfeild-Sinha, said: “For generations of artists, the Gate has represented a place where international perspectives could be placed at the centre of British theatre; where experimentation has been welcomed; and where audiences could encounter stories, artists and ideas from beyond their immediate experience. It is with an extremely heavy heart that the Board has come to the decision to close.”Interim executive director, Alice Linnane, hailed the tenacity of the staff and creatives who had worked with the Gate. “Its closure is an acute loss for our industry and for artists. Like so many arts organisations across the UK, we have been operating in an incredibly difficult climate. Funding that reduces in real terms year-on-year, rising costs, and a fiercely competitive fundraising environment have left many of us living hand-to-mouth, and this has unfortunately become impossible to sustain.”The theatre company Stockroom, which also lost its NPO status in 2022, closed at the end of last year.Explore more on these topicsStageArts fundingTheatrenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tame Impala frontman announces he will no longer sign autographs due to ‘aggressive’ collectors | Tame Impala | The Guardian
description: Australian musician Kevin Parker will also no longer take photos with fans at hotels and airports, claiming ‘autograph hounds’ using children to gain access
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Australian musician Kevin Parker will also no longer take photos with fans at hotels and airports, claiming ‘autograph hounds’ using children to gain access
Content: Tame Impala’s Kevin Parker said as well as no longer signing autographs he would not meet with fans in the parking lot after shows ‘for the time being’ after being warned of ‘the obvious security risk’.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenTame Impala’s Kevin Parker said as well as no longer signing autographs he would not meet with fans in the parking lot after shows ‘for the time being’ after being warned of ‘the obvious security risk’.Photograph: Publicity imageTame ImpalaTame Impala frontman announces he will no longer sign autographs due to ‘aggressive’ collectorsAustralian musician Kevin Parker will also no longer take photos with fans at hotels and airports, claiming ‘autograph hounds’ using children to gain accessSian CainWed 9 Sep 2026 02.13 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTame Impala frontman Kevin Parker has announced he will no longer sign autographs, citing “aggressive” professional collectors who he claimed had used children in order to get his signature.The 40-year-old Australian musician, who is currently on tour in North America, shared a series of Instagram Stories on Monday to explain the decision.“Hey guys quick PSA to say due to the rise of aggressive autograph hounds I won’t be signing anything or doing photos out the front of hotels or at airports at all anymore, so if you happen to catch me please don’t be offended if I say no,” he wrote.“I wasn’t that passionate about it before but they’ve started using kids which I think is all kinds of wrong. Love you guys.”Parker also said he would no longer meet with fans in the parking lot after shows “for the time being” after being warned of “the obvious security risk”.He said that while he had previously met with fans in Europe after his shows, “the numbers were getting out of control and we don’t have the security to manage it … so my team has asked me not to. So please have the best time at the shows and get home safe!”Oasis recordings up for auction despite band’s objectionsRead moreParker is not the only celebrity to institute a rule against signing autographs. Beatles drummer Ringo Starr announced in 2008 that he would no longer accept fan mail or sign any items, citing his frustration at seeing the items ending up for sale online.Singer Billie Eilish similarly stopped signing autographs in 2019 after she “realized all anyone did was sell everything that I signed, so I stopped doing that”. She said fans would get angry: “They wait outside for you and then immediately they don’t get what they want and they boo you, and fucking curse at you. I’m like, ‘Bro, I’m 17’.”Comedian and actor Steve Martin has long handed out a business card that reads: “This certifies that you have had a personal encounter with me and you found me warm, polite, intelligent, and funny.”Star Trek actor William Shatnerwill not sign an autograph or take a picture in public and reserves signatures for convention appearances and charitable organisations,writing on social media in 2018: “I sign autographs constantly for charities and other organizations. I’m just not going to take autograph or photo requests in public because one leads to 50 which leads to hundreds which I don’t have time for.”And Breaking Bad actor Bryan Cranston no longer signs autographs outside organised events. “After 18 years of signing everything for fans, I’m retiring,” hesaidin 2018, but left the door open for selfies.Explore more on these topicsTame ImpalaAustralian musicnewsShareReuse this content
