title: Last Seen review – this gripping Apple TV thriller is one of the standout shows of the year | TV crime drama | The Guardian
description: Patrick Brammall and Maxine Peake star in this superbly acted and absolutely riveting drama about a father who thinks his missing daughter may still be alive after a mysterious phone call
Author: Luke Buckmaster
Headline: Patrick Brammall and Maxine Peake star in this superbly acted and absolutely riveting drama about a father who thinks his missing daughter may still be alive after a mysterious phone call
Content: In Last Seen, Patrick Brammall does a great job of portraying an ordinary person who has been profoundly changed by extraordinary circumstances.Photograph: Ben King/Apple TVView image in fullscreenIn Last Seen, Patrick Brammall does a great job of portraying an ordinary person who has been profoundly changed by extraordinary circumstances.Photograph: Ben King/Apple TVTV crime dramaReviewLast Seen review – this gripping Apple TV thriller is one of the standout shows of the yearPatrick Brammall and Maxine Peake star in this superbly acted and absolutely riveting drama about a father who thinks his missing daughter may still be alive after a mysterious phone callLuke BuckmasterTue 8 Sep 2026 21.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 04.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast Seen is a classic, twisty thriller with a killer premise: a grieving father, whose young daughter went missing years ago and is now presumed dead, one day receives a phone call that he is convinced is from her. Hats off to director Christian Schwochow for delivering such a muscular, propulsive experience: I felt deeply invested from the start and by the third episode I was totally hooked. Getting between me and the screen would have been like trying to take a steak away from a dog.Ian (Patrick Brammall, fresh from the very differentColin from Accounts) is a former cop who now works for Australia’s 000 emergency phone service (the equivalent of the US’s 911 or the UK’s 999). His daughter Maggie disappeared 11 years ago. Ian is now six months sober and separated from his ex-wife (Jessica Wren). He eats alone, at home, with an unopened vodka bottle on the table in front of him, as if to say to himself: “I could, but I won’t.” He blames himself for the past and cannot move on.Colin from Accounts season 3 review – TV’s most charming romcom comes to a funny, emotional endRead moreThe aforementioned telephone conversation features prominently in the show’s trailer, though it actually takes place at the end of the second episode. Which sounds like a long time to wait, though the series has a lot of groundwork to establish and wastes no time doing so. As for the person on the other end of the line: I’ll take a very cautious approach to spoilers and won’t say anything more.The real MacGuffin – the event that truly sends the story barrelling forward – actually arrives before that important phone call, when the remains of a small child are found in Victorian bushland, near where Ian lives. The obvious conclusion is that these are Maggie’s remains. Ian rushes to the crime scene, starts sniffing around, and injects himself into the investigation. Things, of course, are not exactly what they seem. The plot thickens.Writer Kris Mrksa has adapted Ryan David Jahn’s novel The Dispatcher into a script that, for me, brought to mindan interview with Breaking Bad and Pluribus creator Vince Gilligan, in which he revealed the two fundamental questions that his writing rooms revolve around: “Where’s a character’s head at?” and “What happens next?” These questions are clearly driving Last Seen too.Brammall does a great job portraying an average person who has been profoundly changed by extraordinary circumstances; Ian is embittered, emboldened, aggrieved and enraged. We like and care for him, even when he’s unhinged and desperate. It’s also good to hear Brammall perfectly deliver quintessentially Australian lines (such as “my life’s still in the shitter”) in a naturalistic way we don’t always hear on television.Another key player emerges in a local, Henry (Brendan Cowell), who is the brother of Ian’s friend Donald (Daniel Henshall). Henry and his wife, Jenna (Maxine Peake), have some, shall we say, unconventional ideological views, that are best left for the series to unpack.View image in fullscreenTerrific: Maxine Peake and Brendan Cowell in Last Seen.Photograph: Ben King/Apple TVCowell is darkly magnetic, imbuing Henry with a heavy-hearted stoop and the measured cadence of someone who might be hiding something. Maybe many things. It’s a superb performance, eclipsing my previous favourite Cowell role – as a tinnitus-suffering police officer in the Australian cop movieNoise. Peake is also terrific as Jenna, carving out an enigmatic and deeply conflicted space, and bringing great weight to simple lines. This is a superbly acted show, buttressed by top-notch writing: all the characters are so interesting and richly layered.As the first Apple TV series made entirely in Australia – it was filmed in Victoria, where it is set – Last Seen has the aesthetic polish we’ve come to expect from the streaming platform: a high-end, prestige drama gloss. This kind of sheen can sometimes leave their shows feeling a little homogenised, but here it works a treat, thanks to the sharp eye of Bonnie Elliott, who is one of Australia’s most accomplished cinematographers (my favourite work of hers includesSpear,These Final Hours, andUndertow).But as good as it looks, it’s the people and plots in Last Seen that will stick in your head. It doesn’t just pile on the twists; it makes the twists really matter, because we always understand, with painful clarity, the emotional consequences for the people experiencing them. This is riveting television, and one of the standout shows of the year.Last Seenis onApple TVnowExplore more on these topicsTV crime dramaApple TVTelevisionDramaAustralian televisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Who do you really believe?’: the true crime fans who became a part of the story | Documentary | The Guardian
description: In HBO’s gripping new docuseries A Killer Story, a crusading couple become convinced that woman accused of murder is innocent
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: In HBO’s gripping new docuseries A Killer Story, a crusading couple become convinced that woman accused of murder is innocent
Content: A Killer Story is a three-part HBO documentary series about the 2002 double homicide of a Topeka, Kansas, couple and the grueling two-decade legal battle that followed.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenA Killer Story is a three-part HBO documentary series about the 2002 double homicide of a Topeka, Kansas, couple and the grueling two-decade legal battle that followed.Photograph: HBODocumentary‘Who do you really believe?’: the true crime fans who became a part of the storyIn HBO’s gripping new docuseries A Killer Story, a crusading couple become convinced that woman accused of murder is innocentAndrew LawrenceWed 9 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAman and a woman are murdered in cold blood inside their Topeka,Kansas, bedroom under cover of darkness in 2002. Suspicion quickly falls on the man’s ex-wife, Dana Chandler, with family and forensic evidence painting her as the jealous type. But the county prosecutor at the time declines to pursue charges in large part because nothing places Chandler at the scene of the crime. It’s only after a politically motivated prosecutor is appointed and CBS’s 48 Hours airs a 2009 report rehashing the case that Chandler is arrested on two counts of premeditated first-degree murder in 2011 and condemned to consecutive life sentences the following year.How the mob took Hollywood: the story of organized crime and the moviesRead moreNo doubt: the story is hot copy. And more than likely, Chandler’s conviction marks the conclusion if a husband-and-wife team of true crime enthusiasts hadn’t become convinced that the real killer was still walking free. “There’s a lot of questions that remain,” says film-maker Matthew Galkin. “But when you start to unpack the crime itself, there’s a lot of hoops to jump through and a very high bar to clear in order for her to have pulled this off.”A Killer Story, HBO’s latest true crime deep dive, takes Galkin and producing partner Josh Levine on a six-year steeplechase to answer the burning question of who murdered Mike Sisco and Karen Harkness. It’s a three-part journey driven not just by their collective skepticism of its three bombshell legal outcomes, but led by one of the country’’s foremost cynics.Joe Sexton doesn’t just look the part of a hardscrabble newsman, with his resplendent gray mane and goatee for doubtful stroking. “We would talk about noir films, a Sam Spade-type character,” Levine says. “But he also had this [flavor] of Capote in In Cold Blood.” Sexton makes himself unmistakable to the ear with his Brooklyn pottymouth and easy enough to spot in his bright North Face windbreaker vests. “At the end of the second trial, we interviewed the foreman in the jury, and one of the things he told us was that they had given nicknames to different people,” Sexton recalls. “The bald 6ft 8in prosecutor with the big beard was the Son of Anarchy. The older defense lawyer with glasses was Mr Magoo. The nickname they gave me, which I’ve kind of leaned into, was Tracksuit Jesus.”A Pulitzer prize-winning veteran of the New York Times and ProPublica, Sexton has a deep wariness of the juicy lead. In the first episode, Sexton still radiates with contempt as he recalls the 3,000 unsolicited emails he received from Eileen Umbehr, a self-described pyjamas housewife who couldn’t let Chandler’s conviction stand. It wasn’t until Umbehr wrote Sexton to tell him that the Kansas supreme court would hear an appeal of Chandler’s sentence in 2016 that Sexton conceded there was no more avoiding a trip to Topeka, site of the landmark school-segregation case that reached the US supreme court.It’s at that point the lens widens on Umbehr, who proves to be more than just a concerned citizen. Her husband, Keen, is a lifelong good troublemaker who went from toiling as a garbageman to uncovering local government corruption for the town newspaper with scoops collected along his garbage route. When the county moved to cancel his garbage contract in retaliation for his muckraking, Keen filed a first amendment lawsuit that went all the way to the US supreme court and won a 7-2 decision in 1996. It was all the motivation Keen needed to go to law school and open his own practice. (Fun fact: he also ran for governor as a libertarian, losing in 2014 to Republican former US senator Sam Brownback.) Years later, Keen and Eileen helped assemble the materials and arguments that prompted the Kansas supreme court to review Dana Chandler’s conviction – and overturn it.That final revelation, of these plucky underdogs winning yet another challenge to the legal system against all discernible odds, marked the first time I pumped my fist watching a documentary. Gaskin and Levine really make viewers fall hard for the Umbehrs – who offload 200 acres of inherited family property to fund the legal defense for Chandler, who goes from crusade cause to actual client. And the doubts they raise about Chandler’s guilt aren’t trivial.There’s a reason why she wasn’t prosecuted initially, after all. The Sisco-Harkness murder bore the classic hallmarks of a hit job, with the assailant breaking into their home undetected, spraying them at close-range with machine gun fire without hitting anything else even once, and leaving without a trace. Chandler, meanwhile, lived more than 500 miles away in Denver. But because she had recently sent a series of exasperated messages about Sisco, with whom she had a tumultuous marriage and shares two children, and bought two spare fuel canisters at an auto parts store – with her credit card – then, naturally, she had to be the one and only suspect.Astonishingly, the idea of a frail midwest divorcee hypermiling her Mitsubishi econobox across state lines to go full Tony Montana with a subsonic machine gun that was once reserved for the Israeli military wasn’t enough to stoke reasonable doubt, let alone seed it. “Over the three prosecutions, the basic gameplan was, ‘Let’s make her as ugly and unpleasant as we can,’” Sexton says. “I used to think there were limitations about what could be entered into evidence as prior bad acts. But that’s all it was: ‘Well, she showed up and cursed out her husband at a soccer game …’”View image in fullscreenDana Chandler in A Killer Story.Photograph: HBO/APThe alternate-killer theory the Umbehrs present, casting suspicion on Harkness’s son-in-law Jeff Sutton, falls apart – ultimately revealing a legal beef between Keen and Sutton dating to the latter’s days as a county attorney and leaving the garrulous Eileen at a notable loss for words. After that second trial in 2022 ends in a hung jury, Chandler is tried a third time, shocks everyone by representing herself and goes down in flames – despite the prosecution manufacturing a witness. (The witness even admits as much on camera!)“It’s the same evidence in each trial, actually even less because they start throwing things out,” Levine says. “You go from the second trial where there’s a six-day deliberation and they can’t come to a decision in an hour and a half in the third trial. I think it dovetails nicely with our interest in all these people telling their stories for all these years. So it’s like, who do you really believe?”Once again, you can’t help feeling most for the Umbehrs, who literally bet the farm on Chandler’s exoneration, view her legal Hail Mary as the height of betrayal and cut off all communication and support. That leaves Sexton, Galkin and Levine without a tidy ending for their documentary, but with plenty of observations to offer on the complexities of the criminal justice system, the persuasive effects of true crime mills like 48 Hours and the dangers of confirmation bias – especially when it compounds. “Honestly, I believe she would’ve been free had she not fired her lawyers and represented herself in a massively self-destructive move that almost never turns out well for anyone who chooses it,” Galkin says. “Joe says it well in the series: knowing your case really well and arguing it effectively are two different things.”In her defense, though, one could also see how failing to win freedom after more than a decade behind bars might make someone with the best counsel act rashly. It’s also difficult to overlook the role a more robust press might have played in, at the very least, underscoring the undeniable reasonable doubt in Chandler’s case. “Certainly local coverage in Topeka at the time of her arrest was in the pocket of prosecutors,” Sexton says. “They’re in bed with 48 Hours, tipped local reporters off to her arrest. Topeka, like many towns its size in America, has had its local press eviscerated. But CBS 48 Hours comes in and does a show and has a bunch of crying family members saying, ‘This woman did it.’ Well, that’s all you need.”A Killer Story starts on HBO on 10 September and will be available on HBO MaxExplore more on these topicsDocumentaryHBOFactual TVTV crime dramaTelevisionUS televisionUS crimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Dispatches asks Tommy Robinson awkward finance questions  | Television | The Guardian
description: Matt Shea investigates the far-right activist. Plus: grooming gang victims tell their stories in an important documentary. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Matt Shea investigates the far-right activist. Plus: grooming gang victims tell their stories in an important documentary. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: A year’s investigation … Matt Shea reports in Dispatches: Tommy Robinson – Where’s the Money Gone?Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenA year’s investigation … Matt Shea reports in Dispatches: Tommy Robinson – Where’s the Money Gone?Photograph: Channel 4TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Dispatches asks Tommy Robinson awkward finance questionsMatt Shea investigates the far-right activist. Plus: grooming gang victims tell their stories in an important documentary. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Priya Elan,Hollie RichardsonandAli CatterallWed 9 Sep 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDispatches: Tommy Robinson – Where’s the Money Gone?10pm, Channel 4Does his mum still call him Stephen? One of many awkward questions that could be asked about the football hooligan turned far-right rabble-rouser Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson. And reporter Matt Shea is asking a few of them in this investigation, after spending a year analysing public records and documents connected to Yaxley-Lennon’s prolific yet somewhat shadowy fundraising.Phil HarrisonKirstie and Phil’s Love It Or List It8pm, Channel 4Is it better to be open-plan or walled up, ask our hosts as we revisit two couples from 2023. Aneri and Nihar were divided on their Hertfordshire house: was it isolated or did it have the perfect, ahem, location location location? Meanwhile, Chester’s Carl and Katy wanted to upgrade to a more modern family abode.Priya ElanBookish8pm, U&AlibiView image in fullscreenProof reader … Mark Gatiss as Book.Photograph: UKTV/PAMiranda Richardson guest stars as former Nazi and notorious book thief Duchess Alberta in the post-second world war detective drama this week. Book (Mark Gatiss) travels across Germany to the curious medieval town of Würl to catch her – when a body is found in the creepy Schloss Von Bode castle.Hollie RichardsonBritain’s Forgotten Girls9pm, BBC TwoThe issue of grooming gangs has become a cynically exploited political football. This horrifying documentary allows many of the girls involved to tell their stories. It’s clear that there is no cultural specificity to either victims or perpetrators – it’s a problem related to other forms of criminality, and to a poisonous version of masculinity.PHProfessor T9pm, ITV1An actor’s nightmare plays out live on stage, when a prop knife is switched for a real one during a performance. A tragic accident or something more sinister? DCI Maiya, DS Dan and Professor T investigate a theatre company riven with rivalries and grudges. Meanwhile, Zelda Radclyffe’s tarot cards hint at a “highly significant” romance in Jasper’s future.Ali CatterallSpencer Banks Remembers: Penda’s Fen10pm, BBC FourDavid Rudkin and Alan Clarke’s 1974 Play for Today, Penda’s Fen, is an astonishing piece of work – a coming-out and coming-of-age story but couched inDeep Englandmythology and folk horror tropes. title: All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling review – a joyous love letter to Diana Rigg  | Biography books | The Guardian
description: Beautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated women
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: Beautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated women
Content: Diana Rigg in 1967.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library/AllstarView image in fullscreenDiana Rigg in 1967.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library/AllstarBiography booksReviewAll About My Mother by Rachael Stirling review – a joyous love letter to Diana RiggBeautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated womenFiona SturgesWed 9 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe late actorDiana Riggdeclined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage was “all rather pagan, don’t you think? … A lot of women see it as security. Well, I’m not a woman who yearns for security.”Taking over from Honor Blackman as the high-kicking Emma Peel in the 1960s spy series The Avengers, Rigg refused to play subordinate sidekick to Patrick Macnee’s Steed, turning her character into a beacon of female empowerment. When Rigg learned that not only was Macnee paid significantly more than she was, but the camera operator was too, she demanded a raise. She got it, but that didn’t stop the press from labelling her as a grasping diva. Fifty years later, she told Newsnight: “Equal pay. That’s what feminism means to me, only that.”On the stage and screen, Rigg specialised in fierce, complicated women: Medea, Phèdre, Mother Courage, the wimple-clad Olenna Tyrell in Game of Thrones. Yet in life she refused to take herself or her job seriously. Her fear of appearing earnest led her to decline offers of a biography. Now, six years after her death from cancer, her daughter, the actor Rachael Stirling, has taken on the task of documenting Rigg’s life. All About My Mother is a funny, intimate, often joyous and beautifully written eulogy to a woman who didn’t suffer fools yet remained blithely self-mocking and down to earth. Asked what it meant to be made a dame, she replied: “I think it means I’m not supposed to say ‘fuck’ anymore.”Blending memoir and biography, Stirling builds a portrait based on her own recollections, plus research into Rigg’s performances, writings, recorded interviews and press cuttings collected and stashed in a trunk by her late grandmother Beryl. The book, Stirling says, “is not a detached narrative … This is what I know, what she said, what I’ve learned, what I want to write, what she wrote and what I think she wouldn’t mind my telling you.”Wild anecdotes of stars behaving badly include the time Rigg was lured to Benny Hill’s house with the promise of a party, only to find she was the sole guest. When he appeared in the garden proffering a drink and a semi-erect penis, Rigg turned away, shouted “LOOK! PARSLEY!” and scarpered. George Lazenby’s claim – false apparently – that Rigg deliberately ate garlic before their love scene in On Her Majesty’s Secret Service led to a scathing war of words between the two actors via a series of open letters.As a youngster cutting her teeth on the stage, Rigg was a livewire: funny, rebellious, ambitious, given to corpsing from her own onstage pranks. Landing the role of Peel at 27, she found herself with a throng of male fans who wrote in their droves. Rigg put her mother in charge of letters, some of which took Beryl by surprise. She went to the police about a man who regularly sent clippings of his pubic hair in the post. “It turned out he had been bombarding loads of other women with the fruits of his bush,” notes Stirling. “How he managed to maintain his steady, seemingly luxuriant supply we will never know.”As a mother, Rigg was doting and intense. She would weep dropping Stirling off at boarding school and in the holidays they were inseparable. “I suppose we became what you could call co-dependent, though I didn’t know the word for it then,” Stirling reflects. In a hilariously stomach-churning chapter called “Squeezums”, Stirling describes their ritual of zapping each other’s pimples using tweezers, a piece of loo paper and perfume as antiseptic.Stirling followed her mother into acting, and Rigg could be fiercely critical of her daughter. On the rare occasions they performed together, Rigg would treat her less like a co-star than a personal assistant, though Stirling nearly always saw the funny side. Her book doesn’t shrink from her mother’s flaws and contradictions, but it remains, above all, a feel-good tale and a love letter. Now, before the first night of a new play, Stirling eats a grain of her mother’s ashes in order that “I am cloaked in her, shielded and shrouded by her. I am her. My mother is my superpower. She always was.”All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling is published by John Murray (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroom  | Technology books | The Guardian
description: A refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from them
Author: Simon Usborne
Headline: A refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from them
Content: A teacher guiding a group of kids in a coding class.Photograph: Hispanolistic/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA teacher guiding a group of kids in a coding class.Photograph: Hispanolistic/Getty ImagesBook of the dayTechnology booksReviewWhat Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroomA refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from themSimon UsborneWed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation that was suddenly becoming available to the average consumer: the calculator.Many parents and teachers feared that the gadget would undermine a basic skill and a pillar of education – one of the sacred three Rs – producing generations of dumbed-down drones who could reach for a device in their pockets to avoid the hard graft of arithmetic.But Cockcroft didn’t see it that way. Instead, he proposed embracing rather than fearing the calculator. Students should be taught with and without one – and tested accordingly.“Cockcroft is unwilling to pretend that the oncoming wave of technological progress can be dodged,” economist Daniel Susskind writes in his urgent new book.A former Downing Street policy wonk who is now also a researcher at the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford University, Susskind casts himself as the Cockroft of the 2020s. In an era of confusion and hand-wringing (if not outright panic) about the implications of AI, he makes the technologist’s case for breathing, learning and grasping the opportunities it presents.double quotation markHe warns against the folly of ‘future proofing’ when the horizon is so foggyThe maths comparison only goes so far, of course; even accounting for the hubris of the AI industry, its achievements have already wrought changes that now make the calculator seem about as consequential as the corkscrew. But while the scale of the disruption is new, the historical context is, to some extent, reassuring.The book’s title neatly taps into the techno-angst of the modern parent about a future of extreme uncertainty. If traditionally we passed down wisdom with an open-minded but fairly clear sense of how it might apply to a new generation, “today, it feels like that sense of continuity has broken. In truth, we cannot be sure the advice we gave our children last year still works for the next.”Susskind, a father of young children himself, tries to anticipate a future of artificial general intelligence (AGI) – when AI will outperform us at every economically useful task. (We now have access, via ChatGPT, Claude and the like, to what’s known as artificial narrow intelligence: systems that are good at performing specific tasks.)In an AGI world – one that it’s easy to imagine is round the corner after reading Susskind’s book –whole careers but also the very meaning of work will change. Susskind urges politicians, parents and teachers to start paddling into that wave now.He warns against the folly of “future proofing” when the horizon is so foggy. He recalls the David Cameron government’s rush to teach kids how to code, just a few years before it emerged as one of the things that AI does best. Instead, schools should teach children to learn with and without AI, while also doubling down on the basic skills that we should never lose sight of.He envisages a future of personalised learning, in which AI-trained teachers will deploy the technology as assistant tutors rather than attempting to cater to 30 children as a blob. Graduates entering white-collar industries that stand to be most disrupted should harness AI to free them from the drudgery of, say, reviewing legal documents in a basement and instead hone their craft earlier in AI-simulated trials. Middle-aged careerists should not “retreat to inherited practices” or kid themselves that they occupy “safe” professions; we must remember the underlying problem our professions seek to solve and reimagine how to do so in an AI-assisted age.Susskind neatly weaves the conceptual and the practical. And while there was apparently no time in this slim work to consider the more immediate ethical implications of AI (its reliance on stolen creative work, its environmental toll) and the questionable personal qualities of so many AI bosses), as a call to action in the face of an unstoppable tide, his book is at once challenging, compelling and refreshingly optimistic.What Should My Children Do? How to Flourish in the Age of AI by Daniel Susskind is published by Allen Lane (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
