title: ‘Would they fight or hug?’ The Oasis comeback film’s makers on shooting fans, vicars, police – and the Gallaghers | Music documentary | The Guardian
description: The crowds wept and prayed, police used their song lyrics for briefings and a vicar gave a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. The directors of Don’t Look Back in Anger relive their wildest ride ever
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: The crowds wept and prayed, police used their song lyrics for briefings and a vicar gave a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. The directors of Don’t Look Back in Anger relive their wildest ride ever
Content: ‘You could see them getting closer every night’ … Liam and Noel on stage in Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Harriet TK BolsView image in fullscreen‘You could see them getting closer every night’ … Liam and Noel on stage in Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Harriet TK BolsMusic documentary‘Would they fight or hug?’ The Oasis comeback film’s makers on shooting fans, vicars, police – and the GallaghersThe crowds wept and prayed, police used their song lyrics for briefings and a vicar gave a sermon about brotherly forgiveness. The directors of Don’t Look Back in Anger relive their wildest ride everDave SimpsonWed 9 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger review – mammoth tour movie brings the joy and poignancy of reunionRead moreOn 4 July last year,Oasiswere all set to start the first gig of their hugely anticipated comeback, 16 years since the band imploded after Liam Gallagher swung a guitar in the direction of brother Noel’s head backstage in Paris. However, just 20 minutes before showtime, there was no sign of the singer. Some 74,500 fans in Cardiff’s Principality Stadium were going crazy, while Noel was left impatiently pacing around the venue’s loading bay, presumably wondering if everything was about to fall apart again.“Then the monitor I was watching all this on suddenly cut out,” says Will Lovelace, the director who was filming the comeback. “When it came back to life, suddenly Liam and Noel were there chatting. Then they walked out to this eruption.” Later, Noel is filmed expressing incredulity that his long-estranged younger sibling could “skip the final rehearsal, then just rock up, grab my hand, and I’m like, ‘What the fuck?’ And off he goes, sounding like he’s 30 years younger. And I’m like, ‘You absolute mad cunt.’”double quotation markThey hadn’t been in a room together for 16 years. Then Liam walks in, drops his bag and goes: ‘Are we ready then?’The Cardiff entrance is one of the more dramatic scenes in Lovelace and co-director Dylan Southern’s film Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger, which briefly dwells on how the fractious working-class Manchester tearaways became the biggest rock band in the world in the 1990s before concentrating on how, 30 years later, they did it all again.The Oasis Live 25 tour consisted of 41 concerts across 14 countries and five continents, playing to more than two million people. Don’t Look Back In Anger captures the supersized raw power of those gigs but also packs an unexpectedly emotional wallop, showing how a bitter, long-fractured relationship between two feuding brothers was healed by the power of their own music – not just over themselves but over those millions of fans.View image in fullscreen‘It seemed bigger than Oasis, something a lot of people needed’ … rapturous fans at one gig.Photograph: Courtesy of Oasis: Don’t Look Back in AngerThe cameras capture Noel’s stunned admission that he “wasn’t prepared for the intense outpouring, a sense of what it meant to people”. Lovelace insists it was the same for the directors. “We arrived in Cardiff unprepared for this tidal wave of emotion. It seemed bigger than Oasis, something a lot of people needed. I don’t think we understood the magnitude of it. I was overwhelmed.”Southern and Lovelace’s previous music films include the New York indie scene rockumentaryMeet Me in the Bathroom(2022) and LCD Soundsystem’s live farewell,Shut Up and Play the Hits(2012). Southern says it “never came up” that the pair also madeNo Distance Left to Run, the 2010 documentary about Oasis’s avowed rivals, Blur.The directors have their own history with the Manchester band – as fans. Lovelace remembers, as a teenager growing up in the Fens, East Anglia, listening to Definitely Maybe on a Walkman and thinking: “This is the first music that feels like my own.” Southern saw them in 1994 at the 200-capacity Hull Adelphi, when the working-class northerners “felt like our band”. When tickets went on sale for Oasis Live 25, Lovelace was “in a car on my phone failing to get a ticket” while Southern “eventually gave up”.double quotation markA guy sits cross-legged on the floor and prays while singing along to Slide AwayThey were later approached about “a big project”, but weren’t told what it was and were sworn to secrecy. Then they were put together with Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight, as scriptwriter, and the project got under way. “Filming rehearsals in London took a lot of negotiating because they’ve never allowed that,” says Lovelace. “It was never going to work if we just went in there with our cameras,” adds Southern. “We had to come up with a way to be invisible.”So they hid cameras in all the sound kit. “We had a grotty Portakabin outside in a heatwave so we could monitor everything,” says Southern. “It was completely unglamorous,” grins Lovelace. “But for six weeks, Oasis didn’t see us or our crew.”The band reacquainted themselves with songs they hadn’t played for years, at this point with Noel singing, while the directors trained a camera on the door to catch Liam’s grand arrival. They waited and waited.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to be in there among the crowd’ … Dylan Southern, right, with Will Lovelace and at the UK premiere.Photograph: Jeff Spicer/Getty Images for The Walt Disney Company Limited“Nobody knew exactly when he was coming,” says Southern. “There was a palpable tension. We knew we had these historically volatile characters, so you ask yourself, ‘Are they going to fight – or hug each other? And of course they do neither. They have a job to do. Apart from a very brief photoshoot, they hadn’t been in a room together for 16 years. Then Liam walks in, drops his bag and goes, ‘Are we ready then?’ Two hours later, while they’re playing the outro to Champagne Supernova, he picks up his bag and leaves. He did that every single day. And then suddenly they were playing the gigs – and the tension started melting. You could see Noel and Liam getting closer every night.”Thirteen gigs were filmed, but the directors wanted more than a concert film so they recruited people with what Southern calls “a unique eye. We employed cinematographers to hold every camera, rather than someone who filmed Stereophonics last week.”This meant the likes of Haris Zambarloukos (Belfast, Beetlejuice, Beetlejuice), Lol Crawley (who won an Oscar for The Brutalist) and Moonlight Oscar-nominee James Laxton. Southern had observed that classic rockumentary films such as Monterey Pop and Gimme Shelter were made by “the greats of the period”. He even held a camera himself. “I wanted to be in there among the crowd,” he explains.View image in fullscreen‘I’d forgotten how funny Liam was’ … the brothers backstage in Don’t Look Back in Anger.Photograph: Simon EmmettThe film includes unusually personal footage of fans of all ages. A South Korean free diver explains how the band’s lyrics helped her through depression; a teenager in floods of tears is comforted by a stranger; a guy sitting cross-legged on the floor prays while singing along to Slide Away; a young woman who survived the 2017 Manchester Arena bomb but was left with “survivor’s guilt” realises the meaning of it all is “to not look back in anger”. Southern sums it up: “The effect the music has on people is like magic. In the film, Liam says, ‘It’s like it comes from somewhere else.’”The narrative was further helped by a series of “unexpected gifts”, as Southern calls them. “Before we filmed, we went to Burnage [where the Gallaghers grew up] and took everything in. We went in St Bernard’s Church, opposite their old primary school, and asked Father Luke if we could film. We had no idea that, on the only day we could shoot, he would read the passage from the Bible where St Peter asks Jesus, ‘How many times must I forgive my brother who sinned against me?’ And he is told, ‘Not seven times but 77 times.’ Then he built his whole sermon that morning around Noel and Liam.”Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger: what we learned from the year’s biggest rockumentaryRead moreAnother gift was unearthing archive footage of Noel revealing he has a “character flaw that means I can never forgive … anyone, ever”. This is then gradually demolished over the film. There’s also a comical police sergeant at one gig whose team briefing is formed from Oasis song titles. “We’re just going to have to Roll With It,” he says. “It’s The Masterplan.”A sadder moment arrives in Sao Paulo, as the band hear that Stone Roses bassistGary “Mani” Mounfieldhas died aged 63. We see the musicians in shock, Liam dedicating Live Forever to “our dear friend, our hero”, and a visibly shaken Noel playing the guitar solo while staring up at Mounfield’s face on a screen above the stage. “There are probably versions of Live Forever that were technically better,” says Southern, “but that had to be in.”With as many as 20 cameras on the go at once, the directors ended up with “hundreds and hundreds of hours” of footage. Among the more painful editing decisions was having to omit a three-minute close-up of a teenage girl in tears to Talk Tonight, because it just didn’t fit anywhere. And, while the film is low on gossip and revelations, there is power in what remains unsaid.View image in fullscreen‘Caught beneath the landslide’ …Noel on stage.Photograph: Courtesy of Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger“The reconciliation didn’t happen in rehearsals,” says Southern. “It started happening on stage and continued happening.” Lovelace adds: “They’re healing this enormous chasm not in private, but in public. And things were forgiven without saying a word. Maybe that’s part of what people are responding to.” Mostly, the Gallaghers are interviewed separately, but by the end they’re giving their first joint interview for two decades – as reflective older men, praising each other’s contributions, laughing at each other’s humour and the “madhouse” of Oasis.“We are in contact way more than we ever were before,” says Noel. “I’d forgotten how funny Liam was. All the little things that used to annoy us about each other have gone away.”Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger is in Imax and cinemas on 9 September in the UK, 10 September in Australia and 11 September in the USExplore more on these topicsMusic documentaryOasisPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: DAU review – Ilya Krzhanovsky’s crazed Soviet inferno reaches its central character | Movies | The Guardian
description: The director’s bleak epic project about the scientist Lev Landau finally focuses on the genius maudit who inspired the series
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: The director’s bleak epic project about the scientist Lev Landau finally focuses on the genius maudit who inspired the series
Content: Spectacularly pessimistic … DAU.Photograph: Phenomen BerlinView image in fullscreenSpectacularly pessimistic … DAU.Photograph: Phenomen BerlinMoviesReviewDAU review – Ilya Krzhanovsky’s crazed Soviet inferno reaches its central characterVenice film festival:The director’s bleak epic project about the scientist Lev Landau finally focuses on the genius maudit who inspired the seriesPeter BradshawWed 9 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow would it be if Christopher Nolan got sidetracked while making Oppenheimer, and decided to spend 20 years and millions of dollars of other people’s money reconstructing the Los Alamos HQ in all its minute detail, which would be the site of a gigantic immersive multimedia project, releasing epic and sexually explicit sidebar movies about … someone who worked in the commissary … or a scary incidental guy from the CIA … before finally getting round to the fundamental main-event movie with Cillian Murphy as the A-bomb’s father?Perhaps it would be something like Ilya Krzhanovsky’s authentically mad, obsessively sexual, and spectacularly pessimistic epic project about the Soviet scientist and Nobel laureate Lev Landau, or “Dau”, whose work spanned the 1920s to the postwar and cold war eras, and whose notional endorsement of free love the DAU movies escalate into a dissolute sex addiction. Khrzhanovsky gives this a kind of classical Hellenic distinction by fictionalising a Greek background for our mysterious horny hero, whose indulgences coexist with his self-questioning obsession with his own genius and loneliness. It would be vulgar and irrelevant to wonder if Khrzhanovsky, like any artist, is in fact working on a self-portrait. But you surely can’t work on a (still unfinished) project like this without a strong personal connection.Here, at all events, is the latest Dau iteration, a more conventionally conceived biopic about Lev Landau (although we don’t see him getting the Nobel – perhaps that’s a separate film). Apparently this is the feature that Khrzhanovsky originally envisioned before the creative Big Bang that created the Dau multimedia universe. His first offshoot pictureDAU. Natasha(2020) was about two women who work in the canteen of Dau’s research institute, a place drenched in sexual tension and political paranoia and violence. The next film to come was the grisly epicDAU. Degeneration(2020), set in the late 60s with Dau himself – still here a peripheral character – on his deathbed.Now we have a more straightforward story, albeit one streaked with Boschian visions, and stroboscopic visual breakdowns. Dau, played by Greek-Russian musician and actor Teodor Currentzis, is a garrulous, brilliant, melancholy theoretical physicist touched with genius which the audience has to take on trust (none of the various setpiece speeches about quantum mechanics are assigned to him). He cheats on his wife Nora (Radmila Shchogolieva), humiliating her with his flagrant extramarital indulgences; he is interested in human nature, human behaviour and human ethics and the way in which these correlate with the coming revolution in physics.Dau is also part of a consensus among scientists that their work should not be used for warlike purposes. This lands him in big trouble with the military authorities, particularly the terrifying bullet-headed KGB man Vladimir (Vladimir Azhippo), a chilling character from DAU.Degeneration. He is saved from prison by his friend Kruptisa (Anatoly Vasilyev), a fictional variant of the real Soviet scientist Pyotr Kapitsa – on condition that he swallows his pride and his principles and agrees to work on the bomb. Dau rewards Krupitsa by letting him down, vacillating and betraying him.It is a mad, daunting, haunting film which somehow persuades you that Landau is at the sulphurous centre of Soviet tyranny. How is it that this figure has spawned, is spawning, this massive, proliferating, multiplatform, multimedia phenomenon, so bizarre, so detached from what we think of as the accepted commercial rules for any artwork, that it is still difficult to believe it exists at all? What an enigma it is – and what an adventure.DAU screened at theVenice film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsVenice film festivalRussiaEuropeFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Call My Agent! The Movie review – the gang get back together and c’est formidable | Movies | The Guardian
description: The screwball French comedy is back as a film that actually works, thanks to putting Andréa and Noémie at the heart of chaotic events and bringing all the old faces back
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: The screwball French comedy is back as a film that actually works, thanks to putting Andréa and Noémie at the heart of chaotic events and bringing all the old faces back
Content: Hitting her stride ... Camille Cottin as Andréa in Call My Agent! The Movie.Photograph: Christophe Brachet/NetflixView image in fullscreenHitting her stride ... Camille Cottin as Andréa in Call My Agent! The Movie.Photograph: Christophe Brachet/NetflixMoviesReviewCall My Agent! The Movie review – the gang get back together and c’est formidableThe screwball French comedy is back as a film that actually works, thanks to putting Andréa and Noémie at the heart of chaotic events and bringing all the old faces backLeslie FelperinWed 9 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt last: a beloved-TV-show-to-film-spinoff that doesn’t suck! The original French series is a screwball-speed office comedy about a boutique Parisian talent agency, and was a ratings and critical success in its homeland when it started back in 2015. Its acquisition by Netflix grew the audience internationally and spawned a stable full of remakes across Europe and Asia. In the meantime, several members of the original French cast have become proper stars in their own right, especially Camille Cottin and Laure Calamy, and this sequel, set five years on, is smart to put these two at the heart of the latest instalment. And of course, there are the obligatory turns from properly famous actors playing themselves, including Laetitia Casta, Vincent Macaigne, Laurent Lafitte and some guy namedGeorge Clooney, best known these days for appearances on vaporettos in the Venice lagoon.Like many great sitcoms, this one always understood that failure, rather than success, keeps the wider narrative arc more interesting and relatable. So the last episode of the series left the gang at talent agency ASK (which stood for Agence Samuel Kerr, after the founder, who died in the first episode), dispersed to new gigs and careers; the band, in effect, broke up. Five years on, the stars have aligned to bring them all back together to work on Andréa (Cottin) and Noémie’s (Calamy) new film project, so the title Call My Agent! The Movie works on more than one level.So now, silver fox smoothie Mathias (Thibault de Montalembert) is running a small agency with his daughter Camille (Fanny Sidney) while Mathias and his secretary-lover Noémie are finally officially together. Noémie, always a natural organiser, has become a producer with her own hit TV show that looks suspiciously just like Call My Agent! Thanks to complicated (and mostly backfiring) machinations on Mathias’s part, Noémie ends up producing their former colleague Andréa’s first feature as a writer-director.Enter Casta and Macaigne as the leads of the film within the film, the latter represented by ASK alumnus Gabriel (Grégory Montel), who went off to be the token nice guy for a hateful all-business rival agency. Andréa has in the interim split up with her girlfriend and co-parent Colette (Ophélia Kolb), although that means we get a custody battle to add a bit of drama. Thankfully, everyone’s favourite comic reliefs, old salt Arlette (Liliane Rovère) and assistant turned actor Hervé (Nicolas Maury) are still in the ensemble – even if Arlette is somewhat underused until the last act.Writers Fanny Herrero, Lison Daniel and Violaine Bellet, along with director Émilie Noblet, skilfully open the tap and let the stream of industry-insider jokes flow at an even pace but make sure that the final product never feels smug, sentimental or self-congratulatory. The energy flags a tad in the midsection, but by the time Andréa’s film starts shooting and a cascade of bad luck descends on the set to wreak havoc, the comedy hits its stride again. Formidable.Call My Agent! The Movie is on Netflix from 10 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsFranceComedyGeorge ClooneyFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Blue Film review – polarising sex worker drama is well-acted and deeply disturbing | Movies | The Guardian
description: A camboy meets up with a convicted paedophile who turns out to be his old English teacher in Elliot Tuttle’s uncomfortable drama
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: A camboy meets up with a convicted paedophile who turns out to be his old English teacher in Elliot Tuttle’s uncomfortable drama
Content: Early on a sense of skin-crawling unease sets in … Kieron Moore as Aaron Eagle in Blue Film.Photograph: Peccadillo Pictures/PAView image in fullscreenEarly on a sense of skin-crawling unease sets in … Kieron Moore as Aaron Eagle in Blue Film.Photograph: Peccadillo Pictures/PAMoviesReviewBlue Film review – polarising sex worker drama is well-acted and deeply disturbingA camboy meets up with a convicted paedophile who turns out to be his old English teacher in Elliot Tuttle’s uncomfortable dramaCath ClarkeWed 9 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere havereportedly been audience walk-outsat screenings of this indie drama from young American film-maker Elliot Tuttle, a two-hander about a sex worker hired for the night by his former English teacher, a convicted paedophile. In interviews Tuttle has said his film was rejected by several major festivals. What makes it so uncomfortable is not the sex; mostly what we see on screen is two men talking. But early on a mood of skin-crawling unease seeps in, and it remains for every second of the film’s 82-minute run time.Kieron Moore plays Aaron Eagle (not his real name), a Los Angeles sex worker and camboy. In the video content he livestreams, Aaron is a dom; gym-perfected and tattooed, he hurls homophobic insults at his fans. One night, he arranges to meet a client who offers to pay $50,000 for one night. The retirement-age man who answers the door of the Airbnb turns out to be Aaron’s former English teacher Mr Grant (Reed Birney), who was sacked after attempting to rape a 12-year-old pupil. Aaron was not the victim, but the teacher says he has always been in love with Aaron – though he is no longer sexually attracted to him.It’s a film about the stories we tell about ourselves, re-remembering narratives to fit who think we are. Grant does have flickers of self-awareness. But he’s also monstrously self-justifying, pompously telling Aaron that his paedophilia would have been accepted in ancient Rome. The script’s attempts to empathise with his character felt a little simplistic to me, but Birney’s performance is horribly convincing, and Moore is also very good as Aaron, vulnerable under the swagger. It’s a difficult watch: at times feeling like the emotional equivalent of watching these people getting their skin peeled off, layer by layer.Blue Film is in UK and Irish cinemas from 11 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsSex workreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Gate theatre’s creative daring gave a tiny stage international scope | Theatre | The Guardian
description: For five decades, this enterprising venue – which is now shutting up shop – broadened the horizons of British theatre
Author: Michael Billington
Headline: For five decades, this enterprising venue – which is now shutting up shop – broadened the horizons of British theatre
Content: Shattering … Paterson Joseph in The Emperor Jones at the Gate theatre in 2005.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenShattering … Paterson Joseph in The Emperor Jones at the Gate theatre in 2005.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreThe Gate theatre’s creative daring gave a tiny stage international scopeMichael BillingtonFor five decades, this enterprising venue – which is now shutting up shop – broadened the horizons of British theatreWed 9 Sep 2026 08.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 08.41 EDTShareLondon’s Gate theatre, not to be confused with its Dublin namesake,is no more. A combination of factors, including rising costs, declining funding and its move in 2022 from its original home in Notting Hill Gate, means that it will cease trading next month. But it is worth celebrating its achievement over five decades. It has been an astonishing nursery of talent and has always stood for a defiant internationalism. “I sometimes think,” I once wrote, “that one learns more about world drama at the Gate than at any other London theatre.”That was the dream of its founder, Lou Stein, who in 1979 took a tiny room over the Prince Albert pub and turned it into a 56-seat theatre that kicked off with Flann O’Brien’s At Swim-Two-Birds. You climbed the pub’s well-worn stairs and found yourself in a space that embraced the world. Not only that. In 1982 Stein launched an offshoot above another pub, the Latchmere in Battersea, where I still recall Susannah York as the Amazonian protagonist of Kleist’s Penthesilea.Where Stein led others followed. His successor was Giles Croft, who ran the Gate from 1985 to 1989 and, taking a snapshot of his final year, I find the following list of shows: two Russian plays in Denis Fonvizin’s The Infant and Bulgakov’s Adam and Eve, a Marivaux double bill of The Colony and Island of Slaves, Heiner Müller’s The Task and a neglected English classic in Susannah Centlivre’s The Wonder. Nowhere else in the UK could you find a programme of such rich eclecticism.View image in fullscreenUnrivalled eclecticism … Pioneers in Ingolstadt by MarieLuise Fleisser at the Gate theatre in 1991.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianStephen Daldry took over in 1989 and I remember this young man in specs and scuffed sneakers standing at the top of the stairs welcoming people to the theatre as if they were guests in his home. Daldry not only introduced thematic programming – one of his seasons was called Women in World Theatre – he also showed that anything is possible in a small space. One of his discoveries was of a Bavarian dramatist, Marieluise Fleisser whose Pioneers in Ingoldstadt from the 1920s involved, in Ian MacNeil’s breathtaking design, a cast of 30 crossing a bridge. I recall Daldry telling me that such ventures were only possible because the Gate was unsubsidised: plug into public funding and it would not only be artistically accountable but would also have to pay Equity rates.Daldry was clearly a brilliant director. He also encouraged others. It was at the Gate that I first became aware of Katie Mitchell through her productions of Euripides’ Women of Troy and Gorky’s Vassa Zheleznova in which Paola Dionisotti in the title role memorably demonstrated the private cost of capitalist success. Daldry stimulated another young director and his eventual successor, Laurence Boswell, to pursue his obsession with Spanish drama. It was thanks to Boswell that we got to know such classics as Tirso de Molina’s Don Gil of the Green Breeches, Lope de Vega’s The Gentleman from Olmedo and The Great Pretenders in which Louis Hilyer was an actor-manager who so identified with a Christian martyr he was playing that he ended up being spectacularly crucified.View image in fullscreenGenuine domestic tragedy … Paul Ready and Kelly Hunter  in Cuckoos at the Gate theatre in 2000.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianIf I dwell on those early years it was because the Gate, particularly during the mean and insular Thatcherite 80s, was proving that there was a world elsewhere and that it was possible to create infinite riches in a little room. But all the directors who followed put their own individual stamp on the Gate. During David Farr’s tenure we saw Sarah Kane’s incest-dominated Phaedra’s Love. Mick Gordon’s reign gave us Peter Hall’s staging in 2000 of Giuseppe Manfridi’sCuckoos, which showed two lovers permanently stuck in an act of anal intercourse: for all its sensational surface a genuine domestic tragedy.‘This is not sustainable’: London’s Gate theatre to close after nearly 50 yearsRead moreA succession of female directors went on to reconfigure the space while extending the repertory. Erica Whyman staged a season of adapted Greek myths. Thea Sharrock gave us a shattering production of O’Neill’sThe Emperor Jones, later seen at the Olivier, with Paterson Joseph as the fugitive hero. The joint tenure of Carrie Cracknell and Natalie Abrahami saw Lucy Kirkwood’s post-IbseniteHeddaand Christopher Haydon and Ellen McDougall each valiantly kept the show on the road while reinforcing the Gate’s capacity to take one by surprise. But when it left its Notting Hill Gate premises and moved to Camden Town it inevitably sacrificed some of its identity. Other London theatres, such as the Almeida, the Finborough and the Arcola, were increasingly venturing into the territory it had once owned. The public funding which Daldry had once eschewed also proved unreliable. But, while dwelling on the Gate’s demise, we should glory in its success in enhancing so many careers and in showing that the one sure way for a small theatre to make its mark is by taking gigantic risks.Explore more on these topicsTheatreSarah KaneStephen DaldryPaterson JosephCarrie CracknellLondoncommentShareReuse this content

title: Jane Eyre: A Musical review – more Disney romance than Victorian gothic | Theatre | The Guardian
description: This production has a talented cast and looks the part, but the characterisation is thin and the songs are often cloying
Author: Holly O'Mahony
Headline: This production has a talented cast and looks the part, but the characterisation is thin and the songs are often cloying
Content: Fairytale echoes … Charlie Burn and Ashley Gilmour in Jane Eyre: A Musical.Photograph: Victoria DaviesView image in fullscreenFairytale echoes … Charlie Burn and Ashley Gilmour in Jane Eyre: A Musical.Photograph: Victoria DaviesTheatreReviewJane Eyre: A Musical review – more Disney romance than Victorian gothicSouthwark Playhouse Elephant, LondonThis production has a talented cast and looks the part, but the characterisation is thin and the songs are often cloyingHolly O'MahonyWed 9 Sep 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMuch like Emerald Fennell’s film ofWuthering Heights, this musical version of another Brontë sister’s literary masterpiece is lovely to look at. Designer Morgan Large’s monochrome palette fashions the women in black corseted dresses with attractive ruffles and delicate mesh detailing. Behind them on a screen, a mist appears to roll over sketches of moorland, graves and barren trees. It’s winningly atmospheric. But also like Fennell’s film, there’s too little beneath the frills in an adaptation (music and lyrics by Paul Gordon, book and additional lyrics by John Caird) that struggles to tap into the substance of Charlotte Brontë’s 1847 novel.Though smart-mouthed and bolshie as a child (played commendably on press night by Emily-Rose Samuel), there’s scant sense of a strong-willed, independent thinker in Charlie Burn’s adult Jane, who under Caird and Megan McGinnis’s direction is as pure and polite as a fairytale princess. Nor is there anything dark or dangerous about Ashley Gilmour’s courteous, too-charming Rochester.View image in fullscreen‘Flimsy material’ … the cast of Jane Eyre: A Musical.Photograph: Victoria DaviesThere are echoes of Cinderella and Beauty and the Beast in Jane’s journey here, the Gateshead Hall and Lowood school chapters of which are rushed through in order to bring her into Rochester’s orbit at Thornfield Hall.The songs dilute the story’s grit and hardship with syrupy sentiment. The overuse of twinkly wind chimes and pop-style scoop notes become musical tics, shifting the dial closer to Disney romance than Victorian gothic. Early numbers The Governess and Forgiveness are particularly cloying. But the better songs – including Jane’s Sweet Liberty and Rochester’s As Good As You – contain hints of Schönberg and Boublil’s Les Misérables (the original UK production of which Caird co-directed). And if the material itself is broadly one-note, this is still a fine-tuned production that runs like clockwork.The cast of 11 – about half the size of the musical’s original Broadway run in 2000 – is packed with West End talent for this long-awaited London premiere. It’s just a shame they’re working with such flimsy material.AtSouthwark Playhouse Elephant, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMusicalsSouthwark PlayhouseCharlotte BrontëreviewsShareReuse this content

title: East Is East review – the classic cross-cultural comedy is as sharp as ever | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Thirty years on, Ayub Khan Din’s play about dual-heritage life in the 70s is revived for a tour with an exceptional cast
Author: Nick Ahad
Headline: Thirty years on, Ayub Khan Din’s play about dual-heritage life in the 70s is revived for a tour with an exceptional cast
Content: Tyrannical patriarch … Bhasker Patel  as George (front) in East Is East at the Bolton Octagon, with Zaki Ali as Tariq, Matthew Khan as Saleem and Maya Dhokia as Meenah.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenTyrannical patriarch … Bhasker Patel  as George (front) in East Is East at the Bolton Octagon, with Zaki Ali as Tariq, Matthew Khan as Saleem and Maya Dhokia as Meenah.Photograph: Pamela RaithTheatreReviewEast Is East review – the classic cross-cultural comedy is as sharp as everBolton OctagonThirty years on, Ayub Khan Din’s play about dual-heritage life in the 70s is revived for a tour with an exceptional castNick AhadWed 9 Sep 2026 09.02 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThirty years ago a play opened at Birmingham Rep that might have been expected to have limited appeal. East Is East, the story of a mixed-race family from the north of England surviving 1970s Britain as the father tries to marry off two of his sons, was then turned into a film. It crossed cultures and became a Bafta-winning box-office hit, following the success of Ayub Khan Din’s play.View image in fullscreenBetween cultures … Samantha Power as Ella, Maya Dhokia as Meenah and Victoria Brazier as Auntie Annie.Photograph: Pamela RaithBolton Octagon, 10 miles down the road from the story’s setting of Salford, celebrates the anniversary with a new production directed by Kash Arshad. In Arshad’s hands the script’s comedy is mined and brought to life by an exceptional cast, with Samantha Power as Ella, the matriarch of the Khan family, giving an award-worthy performance.East Is East is an important piece of work for people such as myself, Arshad and much of the cast playing Khan’s children. The language of the play describes us as “half-caste”; I tend to use mixed-race and some of the cast prefer dual heritage. Whatever the preferred term, the play captures the nuance of growing up between cultures.Eating bacon while throwing around curry powder to cover the smell, laughing at racist jokes where people who look like your family are the punchline – these are moments recognisable to mixed-race families. Khan Din’s cleverness was to capture the subtleties of having a white mum and a brown dad and, in that specificity, find universal appeal.The tyrannical patriarch of the family, George, is played by Bhasker Patel. He lacks the gravitas and intimidating physique of Om Puri, who took the role in the film, and the production is better for it. Here is someone who feels ignored and, with his smaller frame, when he explodes it is the lashing out of a man who cannot bend the world to his will. He has a softness with his children, who all create distinct personalities, Maya Dhokia particularly good as the family’s sole daughter.When the children discuss whether or not they are English, the echoes of balaclava-wearing men in Dover might be heard by some in the auditorium. A surprisingly funny and relevant piece of work, three decades on.AtBolton Octagonuntil 3 October. Then atCitizens theatre, Glasgow, 7-17 October;Derby theatre, 20-24 October;Salisbury Playhouse, 3-14 November.Explore more on these topicsTheatreBoltonreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Evanescence review – devastating power and range from one of rock’s great vocal talents | Music | The Guardian
description: The titanic choruses and stormy metal riffs of latest album Sanctuary are the perfect foundation for Amy Lee’s astonishing, skyscraping vocal range
Author: Christopher Lord
Headline: The titanic choruses and stormy metal riffs of latest album Sanctuary are the perfect foundation for Amy Lee’s astonishing, skyscraping vocal range
Content: Moving through the registers … Amy Lee of Evanescence on stage at the First Direct Arena.Photograph: Seanen MiddletonView image in fullscreenMoving through the registers … Amy Lee of Evanescence on stage at the First Direct Arena.Photograph: Seanen MiddletonMusicReviewEvanescence review – devastating power and range from one of rock’s great vocal talentsFirst Direct Arena, LeedsThe titanic choruses and stormy metal riffs of latest album Sanctuary are the perfect foundation for Amy Lee’s astonishing, skyscraping vocal rangeChristopher LordWed 9 Sep 2026 08.27 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 08.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo watch Evanescence in concert is to be spellbound by founder Amy Lee’s astonishing voice. The Arkansas band’s gifted mezzo-soprano lends their music vocals that range from skyscraping and spectacular to haunting and devastating. She soon moves through the registers on the opener Sanctuary, setting the stage for a show during which her vocals seem to scale ever greater peaks, even when you are convinced that there are no octaves left to conquer. And she makes it look effortless, striding around the stage, headbanging and fist-pumping the air.It’s standard promotional protocol for a band to lean on their new album on tour, but it still shows impressive faith in their audience that tonight Evanescence perform all but one song from Sanctuary, which is also the title of their sixth LP. Jordan Fish, formerly of Bring Me the Horizon, produced most of it and his metallic influence is clear: pummelling drums, titanic choruses and walls of stormy riffs make the band’s new material noticeably heavier than the gothic hard rock of their earlier years.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAmy Lee of Evanescence: ‘I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers’Read moreGoing Under is one of those brooding, decades-old staples. Caustic chugging guitar clears the way for towering choruses to explode into life, sparking enormous singalongs with Lee at the helm. Afterlife is anthemic, anguished pop metal while Calm Down is a groovy, synth-heavy number that creeps towards the most colossal breakdown of the night. It’s also the point when the band first utilise every inch of the stage, activating rising platforms and synchronised tongues of flame – drummer Will Hunt bolts upright from his stool to give the floor toms an almighty whack.Perched at the keyboard for the penultimate song, My Immortal, Lee thanks the band’s crew, her fellow musicians, and the fans who have brought them “across the ocean over and over again, growing up together” for more than 20 years. Lee, 44,recently told this paperthat she can see herself performing into her 60s, which is good news. In music generally – not just rock – a singular talent like hers is not so easily replaced.Explore more on these topicsMusicMetalPop and rockreviewsShareReuse this content

title: I co-founded an orchestra 18 years ago. Since then, I’ve seen doors close for working-class musicians | Robert Ames | The Guardian
description: I have lost patience with the sector’s talk of diversity when it refuses to acknowledge those people who can’t afford to keep playing, says conductor and composer Robert Ames
Author: Robert Ames
Headline: I have lost patience with the sector’s talk of diversity when it refuses to acknowledge those people who can’t afford to keep playing, says conductor and composer Robert Ames
Content: Sigur Rós performing with the London Contemporary Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall, London, 30 September 2025.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSigur Rós performing with the London Contemporary Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall, London, 30 September 2025.Photograph: Jim Dyson/Getty ImagesOpinionClassical musicI co-founded an orchestra 18 years ago. Since then, I’ve seen doors close for working-class musiciansRobert AmesI have lost patience with the sector’s talk of diversity when it refuses to acknowledge those people who can’t afford to keep playingWed 9 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTShareI’ve spent most of my adult life working in classical music – for the past 18 years as the co-founder and conductor of the London Contemporary Orchestra (LCO), an organisation I’m stepping down from today. During that time, I have found myself increasingly angry athow much harderit has become for someone without money behind them to build a life in the sector.There used to be a route in. As a child from a working-class background, I could pick up an instrument at a state school, get cheap lessons through the local, council-backed music service and play in youth orchestras (borrowing a viola because my family couldn’t afford one).The route was never easy or fair. As a teenager, I spent summers doing everything from being a binman to working on a farm to pay for music courses. During those weeks, of course, I wasn’t practising – people from more privileged backgrounds could spend the summer getting better while I scraped together the money to access some of the same opportunities.Still, the route existed. Now we are dismantling it while talking endlessly about “access”. Today, working-class musicians arebeing priced outby countless unavoidable costs: lessons, instruments, train fares, courses, high rents (especially in London), unpaid preparation, cancelled dates.I’ve worked with enough musicians to know that talent turns up everywhere. Opportunity doesn’t. After my undergraduate degree, I was determined not to leave London. It was the strongest freelance market in the country and leaving felt like walking away from my best chance of building a career. I couldn’t afford the rent, so I sofa-surfed for months at a time. Occasionally, I slept rough. I wanted to be a musician and assumed this was simply what I had to do.When I co-founded the LCO, I went years without making any meaningful money from it. I remember early business meetings in posh restaurants when I didn’t have enough money for a Tesco meal deal. I’d turn up starving, pretending I wasn’t hungry while everyone else ate. It was humiliating.Now imagine another young musician trying to build an orchestra – but they have family money behind them and help with housing costs. Both musicians put in the same amount of work and spend years without properly paying themselves; but, while on paper they are taking the same risk, in reality, the consequences are not remotely the same.That, to me, is class in a nutshell: two people can work equally hard and take the same gamble but one has a much bigger margin for error. The ability to work for little or nothing is itself another form of capital.More than 70% of musicians working in the UK today are self-employed or freelance. Under the current Musicians’ Union/Association of British Orchestrascategory 1 agreement, the minimum fee for a section musician for a rehearsal and concert day of up to six hours is £163.18. But behind that can sit 15 years of training, an expensive instrument and hours of unpaid preparation. The six hours on the call sheet, though, is the only bit you’re paid for.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on the arts in schools: classrooms need more creativity | EditorialRead moreThis is why I lose patience with some of classical music’s language around diversity. There are brilliant schemes and brilliant people doing the work, but eventually you hit the economics. You cannot outreach-programme your way out of London rent, and you can’t diversify a workforce while refusing to talk about who can afford to stay in it. I have watched so many excellent musicians give up early in their careers. People who were absolutely good enough, but simply couldn’t afford to keep doing it. It is easy to say they lacked commitment or didn’t want it enough. Maybe they just ran out of money.If the people who make it through the industry’s elite training programmes increasingly come from similar economic backgrounds, classical music doesn’t just look narrower; it thinks narrower. It hires, programmes and talks to that small group of people, then acts surprised when people call it elitist.Some will say I’m encouraging the lowering of standards. In fact, I want higher standards. If we care about excellence, why would we only search for it among people whose families can afford the training and to subsidise the years of professional uncertainty that follow?I made it through and now have a conducting career I adore. But if I only just managed it in the relative comfort of the Blair years, with incredibly supportive parents behind me, what on earth are working-class kids with musical aspirations going through now?Or, more worrying, are they looking at the whole thing and deciding it’s not even worth trying?Robert Ames is a conductor and composerExplore more on these topicsClassical musicOpinionYoung peopleWork & careerscommentShareReuse this content

title: Grand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner? | Grand Theft Auto VI | The Guardian
description: Historically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romance
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Historically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romance
Content: Couple who slay together … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesView image in fullscreenCouple who slay together … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesGrand Theft Auto VIGrand Theft Auto VI: can playing a video game count as cheating on your partner?Emma FlintHistorically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romanceWed 9 Sep 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 05.33 EDTShareThere was never any doubt that Grand Theft Auto VI’s extended look would elicit a viral reaction from the internet. Having won the Game Awards’ Most Anticipated award twice consecutively, Rockstar’s forthcoming crime opus is one of the most frothed-over games in recent memory, or indeed ever. It’s nothing short ofa cultural phenomenon.One aspect of the game has provoked an unexpectedly vehement response on social media: not violence, but romance. Protagonists Lucia and Jason are in love, you see, and as a player, part of your job is keeping their spark alive and their relationship strong, so that their criminal escapades are underpinned by a strong connection to one another. Holding hands, enjoying a date at the beach, spontaneously texting one another when apart – all of these interactions will strengthen their bond. You’ll be putting in a lot of work to ensure this couple thrives, which is why some people have come to believe that playing GTA VI counts as micro-cheating.View image in fullscreenCheating at games … Lucia and Jason in Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesTakes on this are all over social media. Multiple users have shared posts claiming that if you romance characters in video games such as GTA VI you’ve been unfaithful to your partner;TikTok account El Michelle remarkedthat simply playing the game is cheating. “In absolutely no human way is my fiance playing GTA VI,”posted Shelby Haas, another TikTok user. “You literally have to maintain a relationship with a girl […] you have to take her on dates, and you can have sex with her. […] Don’t let your boyfriend or fiance or husband play GTA 6.”Over on TikTok,a post by Landrystates that GTA VI “is basically the same as cheating”, continuing: “I guarantee you, if your man is playing GTA VI and keeping his little girlfriend alive on that video game, he’s most definitely the type that’s following models.”GTA VI is by no means the inventor of in-game dating – hello,Baldur’s Gate 3, in which you can romance and have sex with any (or several) of your eight companions, including a druid who transforms into a bear. And surely we all remember trying to persuade our Sims to get off with each other. For at least 20 years dating and romance have been a significant element of all sorts of different titles; there is an entire (immensely popular) genre of dating games devoted to playfully living out virtual relationships.Even so, due to its unrivalled online presence, GTA VI will be many people’s first exposure to the idea. Video game newcomers on TikTok seem especially exercised about the lengths their partners will go to to maintain a happy in-game relationship with Lucia, though it’s worth pointing out that it goes both ways: playing as Lucia, you’ll have to put just as much effort into maintaining a strong relationship with Jason. (The notion of maxing out the romance with Jason hasn’t provoked nearly as intense a response.)It’s easy for people to revert to off-the-shelf misogynistic accusations about “jealous” and “overreactive” spouses in a situation like this, and indeed, many counter-commentators have done just that. “‘GTA VI is literally cheating’ is something I would say if I was a jealous, insecure hag […]”declares one TikToker.In the comments on one Instagramvideo, someone opined that GTA VI “promotes lust”, resulting in a massive pile-on.But what if this isn’t knee-jerk jealousy? Behind these rather laughable concerns about virtual girlfriends, there are valid insecurities here over the idea of one’s real-life partner being more invested in a fictional character than a real-life relationship. Especially for young people, we’re in an age of loneliness and disconnection, fuelled by being chronically online. It’s one of the greatest paradoxes of modern society: despite being able to instantly engage with anyone or anything, these interactions are superficial and fleeting.View image in fullscreenLovers’ arms … Grand Theft Auto VI.Photograph: Rockstar GamesThe dating scene right now is bleak. Dating columnist-cum-novelistAnnie Lord believesthe way we treat each other is part of the problem: “People treat each other as disposable because they’ve got the mindset of an app.” Factor in the growing influence of the manosphere, which many say has“ruined dating”, and it’s not hard to comprehend why experts say we’re experiencing a global dating crisis. Since 2014, the number of young people without close friendships/relationshipshas “risen fivefold”. Joke all you want about oversensitive gen Zs, but they are experiencing life in a social vacuum.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIf you’re dealing in real life with men who don’t even text you back, let alone take you on a date, it’s easy to see why it would sting to watch them engage enthusiastically in a video-game relationship with a virtual woman whom they shower with expensive gifts, bouquets, and thoughtful messages. AsTikToker RawTJR’s postjoked: this is “how mfs gonna be treating Lucia in GTA 6 while treating their irl gf like shi”.“I will NOT stand for people calling these partners ‘jealous’ or ‘overreacting’ when they clearly are trying to voice real concerns about their relationships,” wrote trans activist and sex educator Dee Whitnell in anInstagram post. “If someone feels underappreciated in their relationship but sees their partner fulfilling these needs for someone else (even if it is a game character), it’s totally understandable why they would feel a bit frustrated.”As someone who exploreseveryromance option in all games that allow it, I personally think it’s absurd to class in-game romances as a form of cheating – though I appreciate that individual boundaries can differ. People might more reasonably channel their concerns into conversations around AI companionship sites, such as Candy AI and DreamGF, that offer virtual sexbots. As far back as 2023 we were asking if anAI chatbot could be classed as cheating– and the technology has vastly improved since then.More than anything else, this unexpected controversy around GTA VI highlights how dissatisfied and lonely many people are within their relationships. And a video game isn’t going to change that one way or another.Explore more on these topicsGrand Theft Auto VIGamesGrand Theft AutocommentShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route: a trek through the mountains of north-west Sweden | Sweden holidays | The Guardian
description: A remote 18th-century chapel deep in Sami lands is the goal of the Präststigen, a 37-mile trail that traverses some of the country’s most spectacular scenery
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A remote 18th-century chapel deep in Sami lands is the goal of the Präststigen, a 37-mile trail that traverses some of the country’s most spectacular scenery
Content: The Präststigen or Priests’ trail in northern Sweden.Photograph: Arctic SwedenView image in fullscreenThe Präststigen or Priests’ trail in northern Sweden.Photograph: Arctic SwedenSweden holidaysEurope’s wildest pilgrimage route: a trek through the mountains of north-west SwedenA remote 18th-century chapel deep in Sami lands is the goal of the Präststigen, a 37-mile trail that traverses some of the country’s most spectacular sceneryHugh CollinsWed 9 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 14.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIwasn’t exactly in “Sunday best”, but I had madesomeeffort. Well, I’d changed my underwear for the first time in a couple of days and given myself a baby-wipe bath. Still, as we filed into the chapel at Alkavare, I felt more a member of an expedition than a congregation. We sat on the low wooden benches, waterproof jackets rustling and leather walking boots stamping on the flagstone floor to keep warm. Fortunately, the priest, Mogens Amstrup Jacobsen, appeared to be a “man of the Gore-Tex”, as well as a man of the cloth, as he unzipped his own black rain jacket to reveal his dog collar. As the service began, the Arctic wind whipped through cracks in the dry stone walls, insulated only with reindeer hair, and candles flickered in their brass sconces.My slow Swedish summer on the tranquil islands of ÖstergötlandRead moreI had hiked to Alkavare following thePräststigen, or “Priests’ trail”, a 37-mile (60km) route from Kvikkjokk that could stake a claim as Europe’s wildest pilgrimage route, and certainly one of its most beautiful. The Präststigen follows the path that priests would once have taken to the chapel, built in 1788, to perform a service each summer, and today, on the last weekend in July, intrepid hikers and perseverant pilgrims can attend that same service.Alkavare sits on the western border of Sweden’s Sarek national park, home to many of the country’s highest mountains and steepest valleys, yet with no campsites or tourist huts and only scant sections of the more famous Kungsleden trail. There are no other marked paths and to hike here means wild camping, a heavy backpack and a sense of adventure. It was described by famed Swedish diplomat Dag Hammarskjöld in 1926 asvår sista stora vildmark– “our last great wilderness”.View image in fullscreenWild camping en route.Photograph: Arctic Sweden“I hate it when people use the term ‘wilderness’,” Christian Heimrot from Laponia Adventures, a local guiding operator, told me, as I joined him on the research exhibition for a new Präststigen group trip launching next year. “This is a living landscape, people have lived, worked and shaped this land for thousands of years.” Indeed,Sarek national park, (as part of the wider Laponia region), was recognised as a Unsesco World Heritage Site in 1996 for both its cultural and natural value.double quotation markThere are no other marked paths, and to hike here means wild camping, a heavy backpack and a sense of adventureThe Sami, Europe’s last Indigenous population, have braided themselves into these landscapes as tightly and beautifully as the thread of pewter in their traditionalhandicrafts. The Sami word for the Laponia area isSápmi, the same word they use to refer to themselves, highlighting the indelible link between people and their environment. Sarek sits on the Sami’s traditional reindeer herding grounds. While they might now use motorcycles and snowmobiles to follow and herd the reindeer, their knowledge of and kinship with this landscape remains undimmed.So, not wilderness, then, but certainly wild. To even reach the start of the Präststigen, I had crossed the Arctic Circle on the road north from Luleå, met with Christian at his warehouse in Jokkmokk (home to the famous Sami winter markets each February) to load up our rucksacks for the six-night trip, and journeyed an hour farther west to the town of Kvikkjokk. From there the trailhead was a short boat ride across Sakkat lake.The first section of the trail climbed steeply, switchbacks tightly coiled in birch woodland; wild blueberries and cloudberries littered the path. Eventually we left the woodland and reached the ridge for our first proper view of Sarek. Away to the north was the cloud-covered summit of Bårddetjåhkkå, where in 1911 Swedish geologist Axel Hamberg built an observatory to conduct meteorological and glacial studies.View image in fullscreenThe trail involves walking through icy rivers, as there are no bridges.Photograph: Arctic SwedenWe slept soundly, as we eased into the rhythms of wild camping – water collected from a gin-clear lake, a hearty supper of reindeer stew, and an eye mask to keep out the midnight sun. The next day we hiked deeper into Sarek via the Vállevágge, the skies the blue of the Swedish flag, the silence only disrupted by the occasional breath of wind.We were following the guidebook Priest’s Path by Hans Fowelin (currently only published in Swedish), and while there was no marked trail, Fowelin had plotted a path of cairns we were supposedly to follow. While some were solidly built square towers, most were little more than one rock propped up against another, mere whispers of waymarkers in a landscape of scree and moraine.Alongside the familiar buttercups and heather there were bright blue blossoms of mountain gentian, red ptarmigan berries and otherworldly looking wild angelica, a source of vitamin C for the Sami. Sarek was visited by botanist Carl Linnaeus during his epic expedition through northern Sweden in 1732, and the first part of the Priest’s trail is sometimes referred to as Linnaeus’s trail.On our fourth day of hiking Alkavare chapel appeared on a bluff above the glacial blue waters of Alggajavvrelake, surrounded by high peaks and valleys. It was utterly beautiful. I had a grin on my wind-burnt face for most of the day, one that even wading across rivers (a common feature of hiking in Sarek), shin-high in glacial meltwater, failed to dim.After rowing across the Miellätno river, using one of the rowing boats left on each bank by the park rangers, we climbed up to the chapel late on Saturday evening where Jacobsen greeted us with a beaming smile.View image in fullscreenPriest Mogens Amstrup Jacobsen was flown in by helicopter to lead the service.Over tea, he told us he had been dropped off by helicopter at Alkavare with his family on Friday morning and this was his first time leading the service here. Others in the diocese no longer volunteered. “It is physical, hard work and the days are long,” he said, before heading off to re-tar the chapel’s roof and fix one of the rowing boats that had come loose and floated away down the river – returned, later, swinging beneath a helicopter.double quotation markThe chapel had been originally built not as an act of benevolence, but as part of the forced Christianisation of the SamiSunday mass began promptly at 11am the following morning for our small band of pilgrims (we numbered 11 in total, including the priest). The altar had a simple wooden cross and cloths on loan from the church in Jokkmokk. They were in the poster paint palate of traditional Sami clothing and a reminder that it was for the Sami that the chapel had been originally built – not an act of benevolence, but as part of the forced Christianisation and eradication of their shamanistic beliefs in the 18th century.View image in fullscreenAlkavare chapel.Photograph: Hugh CollinsAfter the service we sat outside for coffee and pastries, before beginning our hike home. Christian was keen that we hiked via Sweden’s point of inaccessibility orotillgänglighetspunkten, just over the border from Sarek in the Padjelanta national park. This is the country’s point furthest from any road or town, about 31 miles (50km) in fact, and is often cited as western Europe’s remotest too. Marked with no cairn or monument, just a circle of quartz stones and a trio of reindeer antlers, it felt no more or less remote than most of the previous week’s hiking. And I was struck that what made Sarek and the Präststigen special wasn’t just the scenery, as beautiful as it was, it was the people – the Sami, Hamberg and Linneaus, and the motley congregation we’d briefly joined, and it was a route firmly deserving of more visitors. “I told you,” Christian said, grinning, “It isn’t a wilderness.”The trip was provided byLaponia Adventures, which willlead a guided, small-group trip along the Priest’s Path to Alkavare in July 2027, and offers equipment rental and advice for independent hikers. For more information on Sarek national park and northern Sweden, visitarcticsweden.comExplore more on these topicsSweden holidaysScandinavia holidaysWalking holidaysEurope holidaysWalkingAdventure travelfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Don’t bin those spent corn cobs! Turn them into a delicious chowder instead – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: A simple, stripped-back soup that lets the freshest, sweetest corn and fluffy, floury potatoes do all the work
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: A simple, stripped-back soup that lets the freshest, sweetest corn and fluffy, floury potatoes do all the work
Content: Tom Hunt’s corn cob chowder.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian.View image in fullscreenTom Hunt’s corn cob chowder.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The Guardian.Waste notFoodDon’t bin those spent corn cobs! Turn them into a delicious chowder instead – recipeA simple, stripped-back soup that lets the freshest, sweetest corn and fluffy, floury potatoes do all the workTom HuntWed 9 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleToday’s super-simple corn chowder is inspired byone I came across on NewEngland.comthat relies on an old zero-waste trick; namely, scraping the spent cobs to release the pulp and sweetcorn “milk” still left on the cob. Like asparagus, corn is best eaten as fresh as can be, so look for whole ears with bright green husks. Keep in the fridge and, for the most flavourful soup, aim to cook them the same day.Corn cob chowder“Keep it simple” is my new motto. My favourite way to cook at home is as simple as possible: steamed vegetables, ferments and one-pot dishes such as pilafs, risottos, soups and stews. This means an easier life, with less time grafting in the kitchen, so I can cook from scratch for the whole family almost every day without burning out.Sticking to that motto, I wanted to create a very simple, stripped-back chowder that can be made with just fresh corn and a few pantry staples. There’s no cream, stock, garlic, flour or chives, not least so I can honour this incredible ingredient during its short season when it is at its absolute best. Fluffy, floury potatoes and fresh, sweet corn cobs do the heavy lifting, delivering intense flavour and a creamy texture without the need for stock or cream.Serves22corn cobs40g butter1 onion, peeled and finely diced200g floury potato(about 1-2; maris piper, king edward, estima, say), finely dicedFinely grated zest and juice of¼ unwaxed organic lemon, or lime500ml whole milk1 bay leaf(optional)Chopped parsley, to finish (optional)Remove the husks and silk from two ears of corn. Stand each cob on its end in a wide bowl, hold on firmly and use a sharp knife to cut off the kernels in strips. Hold each cob over a second bowl and use the back of the knife or tablespoon to scrape off all the mushy pulp and milk from the cob.Melt 40g butter in a heavy-based saucepan on a medium heat. Add the diced onion and saute gently for five minutes, until soft and translucent but without browning. Add the corn kernels, diced potato and lemon zest, then cook, stirring, for a few minutes.Add the milk and optional bay leaf, then simmer gently for 15 minutes, until the potato is tender.Ladle a third of the chowder into a bowl, leave it to cool a little, then blend with an immersion blender (or mash with a masher). Stir this back into the pot and bring back to a gentle simmer. To finish, stir in the reserved corn milk and the lemon or lime juice, season generously and serve with extra pepper and optional chopped parsley.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteVegetablesSoupAmerican food and drinkSummer food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: In praise of the bitter: Alexina Anatole’s recipes for tahini panzanella and curried corn farinata | Food | The Guardian
description: In Ayurvedic cooking, bitter ingredients are celebrated for their ability to refresh and rebalance. Here, the elegance of tahini and the cleanliness of grapefruit do the heavy lifting
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: In Ayurvedic cooking, bitter ingredients are celebrated for their ability to refresh and rebalance. Here, the elegance of tahini and the cleanliness of grapefruit do the heavy lifting
Content: Alexina Anatole’s tahini panzanella.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenAlexina Anatole’s tahini panzanella.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodIn praise of the bitter: Alexina Anatole’s recipes for tahini panzanella and curried corn farinataIn Ayurvedic cooking, bitter ingredients are celebrated for their ability to refresh and rebalance. Here, the elegance of tahini and the cleanliness of grapefruit do the heavy liftingAlexina AnatoleWed 9 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 01.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBitterness has long had an image problem: is it delicious or disgusting? Here’s another contradiction: though bitterness seems as if it should sit alongside hot, pungent flavours such as mustard and horseradish, in reality it cools more than it builds. In Ayurvedic cooking, for instance, bitter ingredients are valued for their ability to refresh and rebalance, and those are qualities that run through both of today’s dishes, from the elegant bitterness of tahini in the panzanella to the clean bite of grapefruit in the dipping sauce for the farinata.Tahini panzanella (pictured top)Prep10 minCook25 min, plus restingServes2-4500g largetomatoes, eg, beef, oxheart or monterosa1 tsp flaky sea salt½ small garlic clove1 tbsp sherry vinegar, or red-wine vinegar1 tbsp pomegranate molasses1 small red onion, peeled and very thinly sliced½ tbsp capers, finely chopped, or nonpareilles, which are already petite enough½ tbsp sesame seeds, lightly toastedBasil leaves, to garnishFor the croutons125g sourdough, crusts on,torn into rough pieces2 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil½ tsp flaky sea saltFor the tahini dressing2 tbsp tahini1 tbsplemon juice1 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil¼ tsp fine sea saltHeat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. Chop the tomatoes into haphazard, chunky pieces and put them in a colander set over a bowl. Toss with the flaky salt and leave to drain for 10–15 minutes.Meanwhile, spread the bread pieces on a baking tray, toss with the olive oil and salt, then bake for 10 minutes, until golden. In a bowl, grate the garlic into the tablespoon of sherry vinegar, to help take the edge off.Make the tahini dressing by whisking the tahini, lemon juice, olive oil and salt, then gradually add about two tablespoons of ice-cold water until the mix is the consistency of double cream (the amount of water will depend on the thickness of the tahini).Transfer the drained tomatoes to a serving bowl and stir in the pomegranate molasses, sliced red onion and capers. Add the sherry vinegar and garlic mix, and the croutons, and toss thoroughly. Stir through the tahini dressing, then leave for five to 10 minutes, so the croutons soften a little. Serve garnished with the toasted sesame seeds and basil leaves.Curried corn farinata with grapefruit dipping sauceView image in fullscreenAlexina Anatole’s curried corn farinata with grapefruit dipping sauce.Prep10 minRest15 minCook40 minServes3-4 as a light lunchFor the farinata100g chickpea flour½ tsp ground turmeric½ tsp garlic powder/granules½ tsp fine sea salt1 tsp cumin seeds, toasted1 tsp coriander seeds,toasted4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil75g tinned sweetcorn, drained, or frozen and defrosted3 spring onions, finely slicedMint leaves, to serveFor the grapefruit dipping sauce4 tbsp fresh red grapefruit juice(from about 1 grapefruit)1 tbsp rice vinegar1 tsp caster sugar1 red chilli,finely chopped (seeds and all, if you like things spicy)In a large jug, combine the chickpea flour, turmeric, garlic powder or granules and salt. Gradually whisk in 230ml cold water, ensuring there are no lumps, then leave to rest for 15 minutes.Heat the oven to 230C (210C fan)/450F/gas 8. Roughly crush the cumin and coriander seeds, until broken up but not fully ground.Make the dipping sauce by mixing all the ingredients in a small bowl.Place a 20cm nonstick, ovenproof frying pan on a medium-high heat. Once hot, add three tablespoons of olive oil and leave to heat for a minute. Meanwhile, whisk the last tablespoon of oil into the batter.Add the crushed spices to the pan, let them sizzle lightly in the oil for 30 seconds, then pour the batter into the centre – it should sizzle. Sprinkle over the corn and spring onions, then bake for 25 minutes, until golden and crisp around the edges. Remove, leave to sit for a minute, then turn out on to a board. Cut into wedges and serve at once with the dipping sauce and mint leaves.Alexina Anatole is the author of theSmall Wins Substackand Sweet: the Secret to the Best Desserts, published by Square Peg at £27. To order a copy for £24.30, go toguardianbookshop.com.Explore more on these topicsFoodSaladTomatoesFruitVegetablesBreadHerbs and spicesrecipesShareReuse this content
